I have only played Chapter 1 at this point. The only reason I didn't pick up the season pass is because I am waiting for the rest of the episodes to come out as I want to binge play this.
Anyways, this game is a real gem so far. Everything about this game is carefully crafted and entertaining. It follows a "Chapter" format, there being 5 planned chapters and an epilouge. Each chapter is its own story.
Graphics: I love the overall visual design and style of the new King's Quest. Character models look like a combination of beautiful cell shaded animations and elegantly painted caricatures. They really come to life and i enjoy how they really help animate the emotional journey being conveyed in the story. Backgrounds are just as stunning, hand painted, and remind me of live wallpaper for your desktop, except way better. Overall the aesthic nature of this game is top notch.
Gameplay: The gameplay of King's Quest is similar to other adventure titles. You get to run around in a world, obtain quirky items and try to solve puzzles and things of that sort to progress the story. I can also say that puzzles are intuitive and make sense, and controls are very fluid and easy to interpret. The end puzzle in chapter 1 can be fairly difficult, but other than that I cannot say I really got stuck on anything for very long, however I contantly felt a nice challenge.
My first playthrough took me 7.2 hours. It may take you a bit more or less depending on how things click for you. I missed a bunch of achievements which are like hidden details in the game to find. These achievements offer some reply value if you missed any your first time around.
Story: If the title doesn't already give it away, your the king and your telling your grandaughter  a story. These are cutscenes and gameplay is done in the flashback segments, which is most of the game. I loved all the characters in this story, they all really had a place and a purpose. Each character felt unique and brought something genuine to the table in order to help carry the story along. Theres not too much more to say on the subject as that will spoil the best part of the game, however, Christopher Llyod from films such as One Flew Over The CooCoos Nest and BTTF Trilogy ect voices the king as an old man. Its amazing. The rest of the voice acting is done by other notable, recognizable voices you can look up on google ;).
Audio: Besides the voice acting being great the music is really well done and keeps you in the moment and helps build the up environment.
Final thoughts, great chapter and I cannot wait for all of them to come out. If you don't care about waiting, grab the season pass and you can play chapters 1 & 2!!

King's Quest starts off easy, presenting you with obstacles that barely qualify as puzzles, but as you progress through the first chapter, the puzzles slowly grow more sophisticated. Puzzles are the meat and potatoes of the game, and to progress anywhere you'll need to solve them. And there's generally a large variety of them.
The first chapter is easily the best. It has the most content by far and is the most interesting. You're allowed to explore the humorous kingdom of Daventry as you go about your quest to become another of the realm's silly knights.
As you move on to the other chapters, you are likely to feel disappointed at their individually small scope. In general, the other chapters confine you to small areas, re-use much of the existing assets and locations, and are generally very short in comparison to chapter 1. I think it would be fair to say they often feel more like interactive stories than an adventure game.
On the plus side, what content there is in chapters 2-5 is enjoyable enough for what they are. I liked all of the puzzles, and never came across one I felt was unfair. Even in chapter 3, where most of them are just variations on the same type of puzzle.
The final chapter was probably the chapter that felt the laziest. because it relied pretty much entirely on locations you'd already been to previously. But again, the puzzles, especially by the end, were great.
Throughout the game, you'll meet fun and endearing characters that are hard not to grow fond of. There's also a good amount of emotional moments when things, good or bad, happens to some of your favourites.
Overall, I recommend King's Quest. But a part of me is frustrated to know just how great this game could have been, had the developers put the same effort into chapters 2-5 as they had in chapter 1.

I bought it thinking that there would be a few new, cool additions, improved graphics, and a bunch of really cool new things in general. How wrong I was... The new suits that give you abilities are glitchy, and sometimes fail to even work properly. Combat isn't 'intense', or 'improved'. In fact, it's actually worse than the original CoD games. Battles end up being left completely to luck, knowledge of a map is nearly useless due to the fact that someone can boost-jump around the map and end up on your head before you even realize that the games started. Graphics? Don't even get me started on graphics! Now, my computer isn't a GOD that's true. But I feel as though a computer that can handle 180+ mods on Skyrim (most of which are mesh, and 4k texture overhauls), should be able to handle at bare minimum the 'normal' texture quality on a CoD game. Not for Advanced Warfare apparently. Even set on the lowest possible quality, the game constantly lags, and crashes. Making the game very VERY hard to play. Not only that, but at the highest possible quality, the textures on everything look shoddy, with little effort thrown into them. That being said, don't just assume I'm a 'halo fan-boy'. I've loved CoD since MW1, and still play Black Ops 2. But this game has to be the absolute worst game I've EVER played. -10/10 I'll stick with the real CoD games.

After you play through whatever level you loaded, the next level loads *instantly*. So does the one after that and so on. That said, don't let such reviews detract from what follows.
I played this game when it was first released and loved it. A couple of decades later I am no less impressed. I don't game enough to give a TL;DR about the mechanics and all that trash. This game is just unapologetic violent fun, pure and simple. There is no plot to it to distract from the fun factor: just "go postal", shoot everything that moves, and have FUN.
It's been a while since I've had a game make me laugh out loud or "whoa", but this is that game. The time I accidentally detonated a Molotov cocktail too close, setting myself alight in the process, and then running into a crowd of innocent people, arms aflail all the while, is the kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥you excitedly tell friends and/or coworkers about as soon as you get the chance.

Strictly an upgrade of the original Postal : 6 extra levels, improved character sprites and controls and a few new gamemodes. The gameplay is more similar to a twin-stick shooter now but you should still use the same tactics in higher difficulties, namely trying to blast multiple opponents together or kiting them at the edge of your screen. Even though it has a title that implies lots of maniac shooting and carelessness, Postal really makes you work for your kills.
It's a 10/10 for me. I would recommend it to all fans of isometric/top-down shooters and to those that like the Postal series in general. It does not dissapoint.

TL;DR at bottom, because who has time to read about the game they're considering paying good money for?
I guess a lot of people have had issues running the game, but it's worked perfectly fine for me, start to finish.  The one exception is that occasionally, after completing a challenge, the screen would go black.  But if I just pressed spacebar, the black screen would go away, so no real downside there.  No real way to tell if it'll work for you other than to just try it.  I know that's rough, but there's nothing to be done about it except wait for patches.
As for the game itself, oh my word, I have never had this much fun since I was a little kid at a theme park.
Yes, the open-worldliness is somewhat linear, but who cares?!  You're armed with a flippin' wingsuit, a boss parachute, one incredible piece of impossible grapple technology, and you have an RPG strapped to your back!  (I never even used the RPG, that's how many options you have for utterly obliterating the countryside)
The story?  Kind of forgettable, but perfectly entertaining for the duration of the game.  One phenomenal thing, though. No spoilers, but in the final story mission, you have to press a button to make a decision, and that moment hit me hard, and made me question my entire experience until that point.  I was not expecting that kind of depth from the game that lets you nuke entire cities in order to "liberate" them.
This is not a realistic game in any sense of the word.  You're basically playing your own superhero origin story, as you learn to master the skies by failing repeatedly, and watching your limp body go careening across the ground for a few hundred meters, before standing right back up like you just tripped over your garden hose.  Once you get the hang of flying, though, you will never do anything else.  I spent a good 10 hours sightseeing, just wingsuiting around the country, feeling the virtual air beneath my virtual feet, and enjoying life to the fullest in my not-so-tiny sandbox.
Game duration and/or size.  I went for 100% completion (the only game which has ever enticed me enough to do so) which means I more than doubled my playtime trying to complete all of the (otherwise optional) challenges.  Still, as massive as the game is, it's never as overwhelming as some openworld games are (for example, every Bethesda game ever).  Plenty to do, but not too much.
Controls for driving are...  Difficult at best.  For the main game, you don't even need to drive, because it's faster (and a lot more fun) to just wingsuit in a straight line, rather than drive along curvy dirt roads and go way out of your way to get to the same destination.
Story missions can be a bit of a drag, especially in escort/defend missions, but I only had to restart a few of them, and only one of those was because of a stupid NPC and not my own mistakes.
TL;DR Imagine if Michael Bay made video games, but they didn't suck.  9/10

This is an absolutely fantastic game, even better than the first (which I replayed just before this was released). Each level in Dishonored 2 is extremely rich with lore, NPC dialogue, side quests, puzzles, secrets, stories, and plenty of rewards should you choose to seek them out. Fans of the original game will remember the heart which still points to runes, but there are many things to be discovered in areas where the runes are not located. You’ll find it very satisfying to explore in almost any direction… it really feels like you are placed right in the middle of people’s lives, with the option to partake in their struggles or glory as you choose.
My favorite aspect of the game is its replay value. I have often felt many games are sorely lacking in this quality, so when I discovered there are two different characters to play with drastically different abilities I was pleasantly surprised. Also, during a play through it is not possible to max out every ability with the available ‘experience points,’ so you will have to pick and choose which skills apply best to your playstyle. The playstyle itself has four major categories, all of which can result in different end-games. You can play as stealthy or loud, and also choose to play as a killer, or non-killer (knockouts). Dishonored 1 did not provide an easy way for players to knock out a guard once you had been spotted, but this mechanism has been introduced in Dishonored 2, which opens up a really interesting and fun playstyle option.

Full disclosure, I'm not very far into the game.  Without dropping any spoilers, I've just started Chapter 4.
I haven't had this much fun playing a survivor horror game in a long time.  The clunky combat of the 1st Evil Within is fixed.  Combat and movement feel smooth and fluid.  This is a good thing, because I find myself relying on stealth to progress.
Stealth feels very satisfying and fair.  Yes, sometimes the AI gets crazy and spins around for no reason to catch you, but every mob has a pattern.  As long as you follow the pattern and you're mindful of the sightlines, you'll be ok.
I like that you can break LoS and hide and mobs will leave you alone.  They won't follow you forever, and you actually have a chance to get away.  That's a good thing, because ammo is scarce.
If I had any complaint, it would be that the game isn't really optimized that well.  What else do we expect from Bethesda, I guess, but my GTX 1080 has problems staying above 60 fps at times on high settings, 1440p--particularly the very opening scene.
All around though, I'm having a lot of fun with this game and would recommend it to any fan of survival horror or 3rd person action.  The story is a little bit off the rails, but you should expect that going in.  Just roll with it and enjoy it for what it is.

The Evil Within 2, a stellar sequel to a great survival horror game. The town of Union is much more open ended this time around, compared to the first game more linear progression.
+Exploration is a risk vs reward system in many cases if you aren't prepared with enough ammunition and health packs. Many of these hidden caches are well guarded.
+New graphics system looks great, although some might miss the slightly more rustic style from the first game with the barb wire and such.
+Amazing set pieces and environments overall, and a good mixture of atmosphere regarding horror and more action packed moments.
+Bosses and enemy diversity this time around was fantastic, really neat effects too.
-Not sure  i liked the constant ammo respawn on bosses.
-Hit detection may be an issue at some points. Enemies hit with a direct shot took no damage but the second shot hit.
Specs:
I7 950 3.4ghz RX480 4gb 6gb RAM. Game ran super crisp for me at constant 50 to 60 fps on ultra settings at 1080p. No stutter or any fps dips. Only complaint was a 5 random crashes but checkpoint system softened the blow so it wasn't too bad.
In closing:
If you enjoyed the first game, It's back in all its glory, Although different voice actors and slightly new aesthetic from the town of union. With an open world exploration, great looking bosses, tons of references to different horror films and games. With a nice mix of action and horror and even collectibles, The Evil Within 2 gives a great experience.

This game has had serious problems ever since its release. It was nearly unplayable for many, and it had a lot of features that people missed. I really didn't like this game after release. The AI was non-existant, the campaign was soulless, and I never bothered trying the multiplayer. However, I believe the game is worthing getting now.
The game has seen a year of continuous patching, and additional content has been added. The game was not worth buying at release, but now it is much better. The modding community for this game is phenomenal as well, and anyone who plays this game without trying out different mods is really missing out.
The AI has been signifigantly improved and is as good as Total War AI is probably going to get. From what I've seen the multiplayer glitches and bugs have been resolved. My only issue with the game still is the design choices regarding the Campaign. I still do not like the way provinces work, and I never get to fight battles on open land. The majority of the battles take place in wall-less city battles, and those can get boring fast. I still don't like the politics system either. Because of the time period, major families should have been an important part of the game. The generals in the game are still random people and you won't care about their survival. They die? You'll replace them instantly. They get blackmailed? Doesn't matter, you can regain gravitas over a few turns anyway. The political system drains the fun out of the campaign for me, and I don't really see that changing.
The DLC is a hit and a miss for me. I wouldn't have minded if they had one country of the cultures they introduced put in the game for free, and then you can buy culture packs to unlock others that you want to play as. I don't like that you have to buy culture packs to play as a faction that should have been represented anyway. The major campaign expansions weren't that great for me either. I preferred the expansions on the scale of Barbarian Invasion, that create entirely new factions and a campaign scale that was the same as the original. The DLC campaigns feel so limited, I just didn't enjoy playing them. I would say ignore the unit packs, unless you really like what they offered (I did get the female pack dlc).
Overall, I believe that people should give this game a try now. It has seen another year of development at this point, and if the game was released in this state, I believe the backlash would have been less severe. I love this series. However, I still do think that this was the worst Total War released so far. And yes. That includes Empire.

TLDR First episode´s good enough that I bought the whole season right after finishing it. At the very least I would absolutely recommend anyone and everyone to try out the first EP, it is easily meaty enough to be worth it alone.
Firstly the game itself. It is absolutely gorgeous, very funny(and generally well written) and flows beautifully. The main puzzle area is expansive; there is plenty to do but it is managed and handed out to the player correctly. The puzzles, items, locations and characters all are plenty crazy enough while still making sense in their own context and I didn´t come across any ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t moments old adventure games seem to be famous for. I cannot stress enough how effortless going through the game felt while there still was a whole actual adventure game there. The voice acting is great.
Now what really stuck with me from ep1 is how bright, positive and lighthearted it is on the whole. It takes itself seriously and has its serious moments, but it has a truly childrens story-like quality/atmosphere to it that not many games strive for let alone hit as well as King´s Quest does. It doesn´t take the easy way out to please the largely adult audience by having a bunch of snarky dialogue/sarcasm/whatever but goes all in on a true fairytale style and comes out unscathed and better for it.
Finally I have no particular nostalgia towards adventure games. I´ve only played and love certain modern ones (J.U.L.I.A, Morningstar) and naturally the Telltale games(WD S1, Wolf and Tales). And King´s Quest absolutely blew me away in how much prefer it to any of these. As far as I´m concerned King´s Quest looks miles better, is more engaging(thanks to the gameplay), has better characters and straight up has more content presuming future episodes keep it up.

BLUF:
This is game making done right in the sense that it was not created out of greed and delivers on a fun, casual playthrough for hours.  All in all, I would have paid for this and still been very happy.  Given that it is free, you're a dodo if you don't try it.  That's right.  I said it.  DODO.
FULL:
A great Free-to-Play that seems to knock most paid applications of RPG Maker out of the running.  The story is solid, the levels are well defined and logical, and the combat is casual.  This is genuinely a game created out of passion for creating something fun and enjoyable.  It also offers certain challenges for those wishing for something more 'intense' via hard modes for bosses.  There is a skill upgrade factor that is very simple (akin to a mobile game), and  an equipment crafting system that relies on farming for a limited time to get items.  The 'side-quests' offer additional bonuses, but you do not have to deviate from the main game for hours on end to complete them. There are multiple endings and, now don't cry, you must - I repeat - you MUST get all three endings to truly appreciate the story, the arc, the character development.  However, It is a simple save before and during the final boss battle to go back and experience everything. There is even a mini-game built into an after game bonus room.  The Dev grants access to a bonus room after completing a short after-game survey, and in the room you are able to peer into all the character models and understand why the dev chose to do the things he did.

This is the perfect Halloween game.  That thought hit me as I exited my safehouse and was greeted by the scene of dozens of zombies shambling around and feasting on flesh under a foggy night sky in a creepy-@ss, delapidated neighborhood.  This game is awesome.  I'm 5 hours in now and don't want to stop.
- Great PC version: Looks stellar and has plenty of options to play around with. I disabled motion blur but kept everything else cranked up.  Runs at around 70-90FPS on my GTX 1080 & i7 7700k, which seems a little low, all things considered.  Not sure how it'll run on mid-range rigs, but I don't really have any complaints. Volumetric fog combine with dynamic lighting & shadows to pump up the creep factor.
- Thoughtful design: A mostly-linear story meshes perfectly with open-ended design that allows you to embark upon sidequests in the neighborhood that are usually worth doing. The challenge on Nightmare (the highest difficulty) is just about perfect.  I feel powerful enough now to take on the standard zombies pretty confidently, which is saying something since just one of them used to terrify me.  But...I just exited an encounter where I shot an explosive crossbow bolt right at some ugly-@ss multi-headed puking monstrosity... and it only made it angry at me!
- Rewarding progression: You've got three progression paths in the game: crafting, weapon upgrades, and character upgrades. These are all handled brilliantly.  As you play through the game, you're given just enough to feel adequate but never enough to feel overpowered.  In the open-ended encounters, you are encouraged to approach combat creatively.  Spec into a stealth build and you can play your own version of Metal Gear Solid, except against putrid monsters with glowing eyes and green blood.  Spec into a melee or gun oriented build, and you can pop out of cover long enough to give a zombie a threatening "Come at me bro!" stare so that he'll charge at you, straight into a tornado of knife swipes.
- An interesting story: I'm normally not one for long-winded exposition and games that try to be movies. But if a game can pepper just enough story to give me incentive to keep playing - and this one does - I'm down.  The writing is great, as is the voice-acting.  The story itself involves some metaphysical themes and toys with your sense of reality as the player.
I definitely recommend grabbing this game, especially in the leadup to Halloween as the Evil Within 2 sets a perfect spooky tone for the holiday.
My rating: 9.0/10

[Gameplay] — pretty fun, especially on harder difficulties or without powers. Not much changes there, except for an opportunity to play as Emily with all new powers and such.
[Story and dialogue] — it's a poopooface. With Dishonored 1 already being pretty straightforward and having obvious plot twists, second installment somehow managed to make it even worse. Characters are dull and not interesting, dialogues are a bore, hub area is blank, no serious plot twists throughout nine missions and final fight + "concequences" sequence are just a joke.
[Optimization] — well some people whine about it being glitchy and all, but i barely noticed that. Having a dated PC i was amazed that sometimes this game performed extremely good (i have Radeon 9700 HD and about 8 gb RAM i think). Sure there were plenty moments when FPS counter dropped to 30~50 but i didn't mind, because it's still very much bearable. From what i've read patch 1.3 fixed lots of stuff, but i'd expect them to implement some new updates focusing on that issue. Besides there are several optimization tweaks developed by Community so you only have to google it.
[Overall thoughts] — it's fun, level design is great, locations are okay but the biggest issue is that i, personally, didn't get any satisfaction from the closure. It's kind of abrupt and weak, but that just might be me. Arkane Studios also added some neat gameplay things, like time travelling in some levels (not a spoiler, was mentioned in trailers before) and ability to play the game without powers. Also Chaos system is not so strict as it used to be, so you can still get a "good" ending while killing some enemies. Oh and i found the game to be short (full exploration, all side quests).
I'd say wait for the sale and grab it when it's on 50%.

I bought this game while on sale, didn't even know it existed until it popped up in my queue. I wasn't expecting all that much from it, but what I got was a grand adventure in the best sense. From the little things like being bitten when you stick your hand in a bush to even feeling for characters you only spend a short time with everything in it was been thoughtfully planned.
I'm only 3 hours in to the first episode (chapter 1) but I'm amazed it's actually lasted that long considering it's episodic.
*Gameplay*
Overall it's very simple, you move around the screen select a few things and do a few puzzles, using your items is a bit weird at first, since you need to go to your menu and select the item instead of having a pop up that says you can use it here (I don't play many puzzle/quest games so I'll assume this is the norm) While not complex, it is very satisifying to play.
*Voice acting*
Some of the best voice acting I've heard in a game in a long time, with some very famous talent thrown in. The biggest one being that Wallace Shawn (Vicinni, Princess Bride) is in this and just put a huge smile on my face when I noticed it. It also has Christopher Lloyd (Back to the Future), And to my surprise Zelda Williams.
*Story*
Not going to give anything away, but it keeps you on the edge of your seat, which shocked me as I haven't wanted to hear more or see more of a story in a game in a while. If you like silly humor, bad puns and some underhanded jokes you'll enjoy this a lot.
Overall even if I did not get it on sale I would still highly rate this game.

POSTAL Redux, released in 2016, is a remaster of the original POSTAL 1, released in 1997. Again, you play as the Postal Dude as he kills everyone in his way leading up to the Air Force Base.
There's really not much to say. If you want more information, read up on my POSTAL 1 review. However, there are a couple new features and levels that make it so much better than the original. Mouse aiming, reticle that indicates enemy health, and Super POSTAL levels and Super Diverly made it in, including Osaka, Tokyo, Earthquake, Shanty Town, and a couple others.
Overall, POSTAL Redux makes the original POSTAL experience a lot better and it's still a great dark isometric shooter. I'd give this version of POSTAL a 8/10.

This game BEGGED to be a twin-stick shooter.
I tried to play the original Postal many times over the years, but just couldn't get over the janky keyboard controls. With this Redux, using a gamepad feels a lot more natural and the game is a hell of a lot more fun to play.
It's violent, dumb and shallow, but it's a blast. Not for the feint hearted.

4.2.1
Redux comes with multiplayer deathmatch/co-op, the classic campaign along with their expansion levels, and the new single player mode, Rampage, where an actual scoring system comes to play.
The controls in Redux are far more superior to the classic tank controls, but the game's nice enough to add tank controls anyway if you so wish to play it that way. You can now run and shoot with better precision and it plays more like an actual twin stick shooter with full controller compatibility. The game is much lower in difficulty compared to the classic thanks to the ability to properly run & gun.
Practically every action is rebind-able for both controller and KB+M; even the controller settings have a small array of specific settings for it, though I'm afraid I don't understand what half of those mean. It's only a little more optimal to use KB+M since you can switch weapons faster there and aiming with a mouse makes targeting easier.
Music is non-existent throughout the campaign so you're kind of encouraged to play your own (in)appropriate songs whilst going postal.
Just like the classic, the only objective is to simply run around the current level and kill enough hostiles to pogress to the next level. In Redux, you only need to reach a certain high percentage of dead hostiles to progress to the next level; anyone else remaining becomes optional.
There are no checkpoints throughout the entire game and the only one that exists is the auto save file in the regular campaign right as a level starts so you're forced to restart the entire level if you die.
The regular campaign is just a basic "kill this many hostiles to progress" deal. The lower the difficulty you select, the more mindless the game becomes since enemies won't hit hard, there are less of them on the map, and etc. etc. You can breeze through all the levels in under an hour on Easy mode without much worry on dying. On higher difficulties you're forced to be more cautious and efficient with your weapons. Fancy enough, ammo is always in abundance if you know how & when to use the right weapons, regardless of the difficulty setting.
For whatever reason, there's no level select option in the regular campaign and there aren't enough save slots for all the levels if you decide to save a level per slot. You can start the campaign from the very beginning with or without the expansion, or just begin the expansion by itself. True level selecting is only available through the multiplayer stuff and Rampage.
Rampage is designed to be a  new game mode using the same base maps where you're strongly encouraged to get a high rank based on your score. There are enough weapons & ammo in each level to get you the highest rank per map. You can get through all the levels to get the Rampage ending without worrying about the rank at all but then the point would be missed. Rampage is much faster paced compared to the other game modes due to the various ways you're scored, such as switching up what you kill with and how fast you can kill everyone. The rocking, fast-paced music that comes along with it accentuates the entire mood of Rampage.
Depending on the map, scoring is either very strict, very forgiving, or somewhere in between due to how the levels were originally designed so it won't necessarily get harder the further you progress in Rampage. There's no difficulty setting for this mode either anyway. Getting the highest rank means having to replay levels over & over again (usually) if you're not lucky enough to get an A+ on the first try.
Multiplayer mode is now a feature in this remake but there aren't usually anyone playing so it's pretty unreliable to find someone to play with in-game. I haven't tried the deathmatch but the co-op, which is just the regular campaign plus the expansion levels on a high difficulty, can be pretty fun with others. Unfortunately, there are no breaks between level transitioning; you move on immediately without wait when a level's done, no one respawns until everyone dies or beats the level, and all weapons & ammo acquired are always reset when you exit the current play session. You can play the co-op mode alone or with clown bots to get the co-op ending if you have no one to play with.
Hard to say if there's even a story in this game, but if there is any, it's interesting to say the least although it's not very big and they're told through the loading screens as small diary/journal entries. If that's all the case, then the regular campaign, Rampage, and the co-op mode actually have their own story being told through their respective loading screens & endings.
The graphics in-game are a bit too cartoon-y for my taste and that's probably a result of the "high definition" thing cleaning the graphics up. The art for the loading screens and endings though are still pretty metal.
As earlier mentioned, the game may have been too faithful to the original, bringing in the good as well as the bad.
All the maps are once again just pre-rendered images and the only things 3D are the character models. Maps end up having very confusing playable layouts.
It's still hard to tell what you can and can't walk on or shoot through half the time in way too many areas, and some things collide with your gunfire where they shouldn't. Some walls are apparently not walls at all and seemingly thin objects are wider than they appear. I've had a few instances where enemies shot through certain walls to hit me.
Unless you're in a clearly open area, it can become extremely dangerous for you to throw a molly or fire a rocket because they have too high a chance of colliding with what they shouldn't in a "realistic" environment. Even shooting at enemies sometimes doesn't get their hitboxes due to the different kinds of isometric perspectives in each map, even despite the crosshair being targeted directly at them. This especially goes with fire-based weapons regardless of them clearly being in the middle of the fire.
None, if not most, of these issues would likely exist had the entire environment at least be in 3D with a 2D feel or somewhere along the lines.
The developers seem to have a lot of respect for Hatred. Through a small cheat, you can unlock Hatred's own Antagonist as a character skin. He's fully voiced and is somehow more detailed than the Postal Dude in a manner of speaking. You can even make the game's color scheme look like Hatred's through the video options.
The game's supposed to be very dark in theme but the cartoon-y in-game graphics and a lot of the silly voice acting from the NPCs throughout the game make it lighter than it looks, with the expansion levels being the lightest.
Redux has its share of bugs and issues but it sets out to do what it does successfully, be a simple game about going postal. The price for it drops very low occasionally, too.

This game is awful - and for a horror survival game, this is a good thing.
It will leave you cowering in fear from inside numerous lockers, from under beds, or behind whatever shelter you hope will be enough to conceal your presence, with your eyes glued to your motion tracker, waiting for that damn blip to disappear.
You'll hold your breath in suspense, when the xenomorph nears your location, knowing you're done for if you're spotted.
You'll be all ears - sounds are everywhere, and each and every one of them could be the xenomorph....or not....you just never know.....and you're never safe.
Sure, you'll have access to a few weapons, if you can find them.....
Nothing in this game comes easy, and for the most part your own mind - your own fear, is your number one enemy.
You don't play this game.....it plays you. It plays you psyche and it plays your senses, and does it wonderfully.
The athmosphere in this game is highly because of the amazing work done with the sound....all the way down to your panicked gasping for air after having to run for it
The environment graphics are pretty simple, and the film grain effect adds to the simplicity, plunging you right in the middle of the 1979 sci-fi horror that started the Alien franchise.
The detail of the xenomorph however, is extraordinary, and this combination just adds to the feel.
You'll be afraid, you'll be desoriented, you'll be running, and you'll be hiding.
You'll be panicking to reroute power or opening locked doors, while being hunted.
And you'll be dying......a lot!
No horror game has had me jumping like this, since Amnesia.
Highly recommended if you're into this kind of game.
However, if you're hoping to do a speedrun with guns blazing, this probably isn't the game for you.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.

First of all I am neither qualified nor worthy to write a decent Review on this Masterpiece in the making. Second of all bear with my poor English for me not being a native speaker. I must say due to the first point I have never written a Review on Steam and I will refrain from doing so in the Future but since I was a little Kid I was fascinated by ants and this game seems like it was just created for me.
But for now lets cut to the chase. Everyone who has a Heart for Ants wont be dissapointed by this game.
As the Mods and Developers already stated many times Empires of the Undergrowth is an early Access with more content coming soon. As for now this game contains 4 challenging Missions in "Formicarium Mode" plus Two even more challenging Formicarium challenges which you need to pass to further advance in "Formicrium mode". And without spoiling the best about the Formicarium challenges lets just say they come with a very amusing "twist".
Atmosphere 10/10: The narration during the levels reminds of a documentary- very good Voice Acting. As for the Music: very fitting, dramatic or calm or simply catching the scenery perfectly. To be honest Ive spent quite alot of Time just Listening to the Soundtrack.
Setting (10/10 or less depending on your wish for a realistic Setting):
Let me further explain this strange rating. You manage a colony of gene stealing ants in "Formicarium mode". These Ants do hopefully not exist outside of this game for they are capable of raising other specimen as their own.
These other Specimen in Empire of the Undergrowth so far are Formica Rufa and Formica Fusca which are real Antspecies. You play your first two Missions as Formica Fusca then you must finish the First Formicarium challenge as your Gene stealing Ant colony. After that you finish the next two Missions as Formica Rufa before you can try your Luck at the Second Formicarium challenge. So you have both some really cool "Fantasy Ants"(you can determine their coloring also) and beautifully modelled realistic Ants with the promise of more of them still coming.
Game Mechanics 10/10 (early acces):
- Moving Ants through Pheromone Markers which is a great more realistic concept than just controlling them as in most
other RTS Games.
- By completing the Formicarium Missions you get Ressources to Upgrade your Gene Stealing Ants
- Building Tunnels and Chambers to help your Colony to survive
- Variety on Mechanics like: a rising Tide or Ladybugs trying to diminish your Food Ressources
- Underground and " Above Ground" Missions
- Wide Variation of Enemys to your colony with still more coming soon
Community and Developers 10/10:
- Really dedicated Mods in the Forums answering every Question in a polite and efficent Way.
- Livestreams in which you can witness the Development and even make Suggestions
- Passionate Community of Ant Lovers who try their best to make this game even better
- Frequent Bug Fixes (I didnt encountered any so far).
But for now it seems like I have dropped my Beetles so this Review ends here :D.

I enjoyed this game so much I played it through twice, back-to-back, and I very seldom do that. It's everything the first Dishonored was, but with a better story, more gameplay polish and slightly prettier graphics.
Expect a playthrough to take anything from 8 to 16 hours, depending on how you play. As you'll see from my playtime, I reeeaaaaallly took my time on both playthroughs.
Dishonored 2's challenge is two-pronged: combat can be very hard on the most difficult setting and requires the use of your powers and the upgrade of your weapons and items to succeed, and sneaking successfully through a level requires patience and careful observation as enemies are much more aware than on lower difficulties. There are advantages and disadvantages to both, but no matter your approach I'm sure you'll have fun.
Once you know your way around, though, the sneaking challlenge diminishes somewhat - I found finishing the game a second time with Corvo in Sneak Mode to be surprisingly easy as difficulty ramps up enemy combat effectiveness more than anything else. Since I didn't fight anyone 'cos I was sneaking, the difficulty spike meant nothing to me.
The Powers, however, seem better-suited to players who want to kill everything. I finished my second playthrough with Corvo without killing anyone, and the only powers I upgraded to the max were his Time Stop and Blink abilities as they were all I actually needed. I think I had something like 16 runes in my inventory when the credits rolled.
While the core mechanics of the game are excellent, it's actually the level design that steals the show. There are so many ways through each level (if you're ever stuck, look up), and the levels themselves are just spectacular. The Clockwork Mansion is just so clever, and the time-travelling seventh mission is one I won't be forgetting anytime soon. It's clear a considerable amount of thought by some very clever people went into the level design.
And then there's subtle ways the environments and story change depending on whether you're stab-happy or if you favour a less lethal approach. You simply must play this game through to the end with both Corvo and Emily and both play styles to truly appreciate just how much work went into it.
Apparently there's also a New Game+ mode coming in a December patch, so maybe I'll re-play the game and focus entirely on combat (my Emily playthrough saw me switch from stabby to sneaky about half-way through). The mere fact that I am considering doing that should tell you all you need to know about how good the game is.
If you like sneaky games, get it. If you like first-person fighty games, get it. Even though I got Dishonored 2 for free, I'd have been only too happy to have spent my own money on it.

I never truly had a desire or any sort of determination to play any game where you have to waste a lot of time to play a casul game and plain farming, but Borderlands 2 changed my perspective on that.
I want to tell you how I felt the first time touching this game. I got BL2 from my friend and he told me that "it's pretty goood". So I delightfully thanked to him for being kind and he didn't bother to play with me also teaching me how the game mechanics works along the way. Bottom line, it was just simply fun and unforgetable. At first glance, I thought it's just gonna be some FPS story based game, but there's just that magic where it's not just a simple as that. I always had a thought what is that magic, either how amazing the story is written, how smooth the gameplay works or just the fact that this game was meant to play and mess around with your friends.
The story is about the vault hunters, the protagonists of the BL series where they dedicated their life on searching some weapon n whatever in a world called Pandora. However, the vault hunters' plan was choked by the hyperion leader, Handsome Jack where his plans to eradicate them and the people who lived in Pandora as well. Want to know more? buy it or spoil urself with utube. The story is just simply outstanding, though there are some plot holes which I think it might spoil the fun.
The gameplay is also outstanding. I played the first borderlands on the xbox and it was kinda fun, but I felt it was also kinda slow paced. BL2 fixed that and everything works at just about an equal pace. When it comes to shooting, the default sensitivity is a bit high but thankfully you can change it [I put it to 15 FYI].
Of course, the borderlands series is rather known for its farming system and BL2 is no exception. Even though this game only have hundreds of weapons, the variants and the different parts of those weapons will take you a decade to count them all [unless you have a gibbed editor and can solve it in less than 10 minutes or so]. By the time you got your favorite weapon with the perfect variant, you will proud of yourself and you will feel this big accomplishment the fact that you just beat the living hell of the person/creature your farming for hours and finally got what you want... kinda sounds wrong tbh
But In my opinion, the reason why BL2 is still being played till this day is the fact that you can experience all the things I mentioned earlier with your friends. The game becomes 100x times more fun when you gather your *expert farmer* type of friend, *the loot ninja* type of friend, & *the no idea what's going on* type of friend. It was rage inducing, yet strange, but also the best moments I ever had. Borderlands 2 is pretty much one of, if not the best casual game you can afford and still going strong till this day

TL;DR
If you're a fan of Silent Hill 1-3, Resident Evil 0-4, and Alan Wake, get it.
TEW was really, really good. Great story, great atmosphere, kickass monster designs, amazing and comfy environments, and even though the PC port felt clunkier (at first) than when I originally played it on console, it blew me away.
TEW2 expands on everything good the first one did. Nightmare difficulty feels just right and it is honestly the way this game should be played (blind for your first playthrough). The atmosphere of the game just feels right. There are very few scripted jump scares and this is really a game where you have to map out your plan of attack (if you intend on attacking) otherwise you'll be left bloody and out of ammo.
Overall I'm very happy with this game so far. Far less linear than the first and even though I was very uncomfortable about it at first, it really opens up how you play the game and customizes the experience for your own.
Sincerely thankful that Bethesda and TG let Shinji Mikami and his team do another. Hopefully they continue to expand on the series or give him the opportunity to start another IP.

Improves on the first game in literally every single way possible. Possibly my GoTY so far, its that good. I had no idea it was an open game like this, I thought it was totally linear like the first was. Honestly kind of reminds me of deadspace, just constant sense of dread, no real idea whats going on, but you cant put it down. Perfect mix of horror, gore, and just pure shock but doesnt overdo any of them. Not many games engage me enough to where I want to play several hours per sitting, but this is one of them. Great job Tango/Bethesda, yall got yourselves a winner.

*SPOILER FREE*
I'm completely rewriting my review now that the full game is out.
You have to understand when you read this review that I grew up with the classic King's Quest games. I loved them and played them over and over. As kids, we didn't have as many games at our disposal as kids (and adults) do today. So I really cherished those games and my imagination probably even made them better than they *really* were.
So when it was announced that King's Quest was returning, I was extremely excited and nervous.
Now, having played the whole thing, I am so happy I bought it. Is it perfect? No. But it doesn't have to be. The original games weren't. We all had things we loved and things we despised about the old games. That's normal.
But this game is worth your time if you really loved King's Quest.
The team that made this clearly cared about King's Quest as much as we (the players) did. It shows in every decision they put into it.
The puzzles are fun and mostly fair (something I haven't been able to say about a game in quite a while). But the story is really what sold me on it.
So, if you're up for one more adventure with King Graham, put on your adventurer's cap and try out this game. The adventure continues if we keep it going!

Don't be fooled by my hours played. This game is incomplete. Bethesda is one of the greatest gaming companies out there and have come out with some serious hits. Furthermore, The Elder Scrolls is one of my favorite franchises of all time. That's why I had to give this game a fair chance. Since this is a negative review, I'll start with the positive. The lore is fantastic. Every quest you do is unique and fun, and it doesn't ever really start to feel grindy. The game's story is fully immersive, and lives up to the expectations that players would have of the title. I credit a large part of this to the five-star voice acting. Next, the action combat system is above average. It's fun enough that a mere four classes is more than enough to have lots of different specs and fulfill any role in the typical rpg trinity (tank, healer, dps). Rolling around like a ninja on your nightblade, or standing in the fray and blasting your enemies with fire as a Dragonknight, the game exceeds in entertaining the typical nerd's thirst for role play. And lastly, the pvp of the game is wonderful. Despite the quests being so good, pvp is where the real fun began. Building siege weapons and tearing down castles with hundreds of other players truly gave me the full sensation of a raid.
Now here's where the game fails miserably: it is full, and I really do mean full, of bugs. Whoever they hired to do the programming must have gone to DeVry or something, because every little step you take in the game has a bug. Whether the game lags terribly, crashes suddenly, or leaves you in the dreaded perpetual loading screen, it happens all too frequently. Now, even the very best games have programming errors. But when it's this noticeable, you have to ask yourself whether the people who made the game even cared, or whether they just half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥it in order to rake in our cash. Either way, it makes the game incredibly frustrating, and nearly unplayable. For a $50 game that is supposed to be the end of an era of arguably the best videogame series EVER, this is just unacceptable. And for that reason, I cannot in all good conscious recommend it.

Without them the game can become frustrating as the alien AI is merciless in tracking you down. Once you understand the unwritten rules surrounding the alien behavior, however, is when the game really hits its stride and you can begin exploring the beautiful Sevastipol station (which the developers spared no expense in detailing).
This game really belongs in everyone's game collection but for those who are fans of the franchise, Sci-Fi fans or horror fans in general it is an absolute must own.

Are you the kind of gamer who almost exclusively enjoys super-fast first-person games in which you race about at lightning speed, effortlessly shooting hundreds and thousands of enemies with the aid of a seemingly inexhaustible supply of ammo loaded into a vast array of super-duper-mega-weapons which never jam and are capable of obliterating almost an entire herd of beasties in a single mouse-click? Then you may well enjoy the Serious Sam games...and should probably give THIS one a wide ♥♥♥♥in' berth.
System Shock 2 is one HARD sonofa♥♥♥♥♥ of a game. At first I thought it might just be me - as it so often is - but a quick chat to a Steam friend who's much more of a "natural" at games than yours truly confirmed that not only had he found it challenging, he had in fact found it SO frigging difficult that he just threw in the towel altogether, before the match had even officially begun.
This game is NOT from the user-friendly era we're used to nowadays, in which kind-hearted games essentially hold your hand for the entirety of the journey, like an oh-so-generous "self-help" coach who won't let you give up, no matter how hard times might get. This game is more akin to a brutish boot-camp commandant, who just can't wait to push your worthless face down into the mud one more time, just in case you weren't suitably humiliated the first ninety-nine times.
In short, this game DOES NOT PLAY NICE. But for the most part, it does at least play FAIR...unlike, say, the recent Slender: The Arrival, a game whose difficulty can be mostly attributed to rather dubious design and execution. Whereas System Shock 2, for all its frustration-inducing mean-spiritedness, is in fact an EXCEPTIONALLY well-designed and executed piece of work. But a game for the weak-hearted or impatient it most certainly is not.
Weapons jam and need to be repaired, frequently. There's♥♥♥♥♥♥all healing, certainly in the earlier stages. And the maps, one of my few genuine "complaints" about the game, almost require a degree in Interstellar Architecture to follow. To make matters trickier, there aren't any arrows helpfully pointing you in the "right" direction at all times, and it's basically up to you (or the always-generous Google) to work out just what the hell all those items you keep picking up actually do (and which ones you should bother to keep, when your limited Inventory space inevitably fills up almost every time you search a new area...hell, it took me a while to realise that all the pot plants I'd collected were basically extraneous)!
And what about all those different skills you can choose to spend your all-too-precious "cybermodules" on? "What the heck do I need a 'Research' skill for, you crazy, crazy game?", I hear you cry. Well, the simplest answer to that question is, "That all depends on HOW you want to play the game."
Basically: don't expect to explore all the possibilities System Shock 2 has to offer on the first playthrough. I personally didn't even TOUCH any of the "Psi" attributes, and only barely scratched the surface of all that the "Tech" stream of abilities has to offer. (For all the dumb♥♥♥♥♥people out there, like me, maybe just stick to being a half-decent fighter to begin with...doesn't take a genius to work out what a gun is for, while the worthiness of the "Hack" skill, for example, may be a tad more obscure at the outset.)
So okay, I get it, it's hard and it's complicated, but is it actually any GOOD? Well, one need only look at its LEGACY to see how important and influential this game has been.
Unfortunately for System Shock 2, it appears to have been released at much the same time as a certain tiny slice of gaming history called Half-Life, and it would appear that that game and its subsequent franchise stole much of SS2's thunder. But have you also heard of a series called the Bioshock games?  Well, this is the "spiritual predecessor", designed by much the same people. You can also spot the influence this game has had on, say, the Dead Space and F.E.A.R. franchises from several small galaxies away. The more "RPG"-ish aspects of Borderlands, et al, would also appear to owe something of a debt herein, what with the space-age vending machines you can use to purchase ammo and healing and so forth from.
A true trail-blazer of a game indeed. But how do the graphics and sound stack up against modern games, then? Well...okay, the graphics have dated a little. But they're more than made up for by some of the most imaginative and downright disturbing sound design in VIDEO GAME HISTORY. It's nothing less than a work of art, ya'll. And the story, while suffering from the limitations which are unavoidable when you're talking about a lengthy game where you basically traverse large distances while killing lots and lots of "baddies", is about as good as you can reasonably ask such things to be.
Look, it's not a completely "perfect" game. As well as the aforementioned maps, there's other frustrations to be overcome and/or tolerated, such as the incredibly irritating tendency for a completely random "wandering" enemy to waltz into the room in which you thought you might finally have sufficient breathing space to listen to that "PDA" you've been carrying for the past several minutes. You're gonna have to learn to do things like bring up the Inventory screen and heal yourself WHILST RUNNING down a corridor avoiding enemy fire. And most of all, you're gonna learn to Save just about every time you pick up a new item or defeat a fresh enemy.
But with a little patience and just a teeny tiny bit of skill - Lord knows, I have precious little of the latter - you might actually manage to defeat the completely insane HAL - whoops, make that SHODAN - and emerge triumphant in a world ruled over by rampant technology. Sounds like a nice change from your normal day-to-day existence, don't it?
Highly recommended to anyone who enjoys a not-entirely-mindless "shooter", and an absolute must-play for anyone with an interest in the history of such games. Doom, Quake, Half-Life, THIS...that's just about the list, I believe. I guess I should probably play System Shock 1 some time, too. Dang, no rest for the wicked...
Verdict: 9.5/10.

I enjoyed this game so much I played it through twice, back-to-back, and I very seldom do that. It's everything the first Dishonored was, but with a better story, more gameplay polish and slightly prettier graphics.
Expect a playthrough to take anything from 8 to 16 hours, depending on how you play. As you'll see from my playtime, I reeeaaaaallly took my time on both playthroughs.
Dishonored 2's challenge is two-pronged: combat can be very hard on the most difficult setting and requires the use of your powers and the upgrade of your weapons and items to succeed, and sneaking successfully through a level requires patience and careful observation as enemies are much more aware than on lower difficulties. There are advantages and disadvantages to both, but no matter your approach I'm sure you'll have fun.
Once you know your way around, though, the sneaking challlenge diminishes somewhat - I found finishing the game a second time with Corvo in Sneak Mode to be surprisingly easy as difficulty ramps up enemy combat effectiveness more than anything else. Since I didn't fight anyone 'cos I was sneaking, the difficulty spike meant nothing to me.
The Powers, however, seem better-suited to players who want to kill everything. I finished my second playthrough with Corvo without killing anyone, and the only powers I upgraded to the max were his Time Stop and Blink abilities as they were all I actually needed. I think I had something like 16 runes in my inventory when the credits rolled.
While the core mechanics of the game are excellent, it's actually the level design that steals the show. There are so many ways through each level (if you're ever stuck, look up), and the levels themselves are just spectacular. The Clockwork Mansion is just so clever, and the time-travelling seventh mission is one I won't be forgetting anytime soon. It's clear a considerable amount of thought by some very clever people went into the level design.
And then there's subtle ways the environments and story change depending on whether you're stab-happy or if you favour a less lethal approach. You simply must play this game through to the end with both Corvo and Emily and both play styles to truly appreciate just how much work went into it.
Apparently there's also a New Game+ mode coming in a December patch, so maybe I'll re-play the game and focus entirely on combat (my Emily playthrough saw me switch from stabby to sneaky about half-way through). The mere fact that I am considering doing that should tell you all you need to know about how good the game is.
If you like sneaky games, get it. If you like first-person fighty games, get it. Even though I got Dishonored 2 for free, I'd have been only too happy to have spent my own money on it.

As a fan of the original, I was looking forward to playing Dishonored 2. In the original, I really enjoyed the stealth aspect, and the ability to get creative with the different abilities. Dishonored 2 brings more of the same in abundance. This is both good and bad. Here's my (spoiler free) breakdown, but the TL:DR version - I give it a 5/10;
Graphics: There's a bit of polish on the game engine when compared to the original Dishonored. Unfortunately hovering over some items can be hit-or-miss in terms of whether or not the interaction prompt becomes visible. This, I found frustrating - especially when you are taking out a guard during a tight window, and trying to throw said guard over your shoulder to go hide the body.
The Story: The story is good, and works well with the narrative backdrop of books and newspapers. It is engaging, pulling the player along into a mystery that is fairly complex, though at times a little confusing unless you understand some core concepts behind the game's world, such as what the void is, and how it works. I also enjoyed the few easter eggs dropped in referring back to various NPC's and side quests in Dishonored.
The Game Mechanics & Gameplay: This, I feel, is where the game mostly fails. A vast majority of the game plays exactly like the old game, with some small variation. Instead of rats, you have bloodflies. They have additional security features and guard types, but aside from that, it is variation on a theme. I felt like they had the opportunity to really shake things up with game mechanics, but really...they didn't.
That's not to say they didn't introduce some very interesting gameplay - they did, and the "new" stuff I really enjoyed. For starters, you can choose to play Emily, who also has her own unique abilities. Additionally, they introduce a really cool mechanic towards the latter half of the game. Unfortunately, I do not believe they capitalized on the mechanics introduced, making it more of a gimmick to play with only sparingly rather than an integral part of the gameplay loop for the late game.
Last, but not least, after several "missions" the game starts feeling old and repetitive, in spite of some attempts to introduce new, late-game mechanics to keep things interesting. This, quite frankly, outweighed my enjoyment of the story, and eventually found it a struggle to continue playing.
Conclusion: While there's been some noticeable upgrades, and provides the player with another great story in the Dishonored universe, it suffers and ultimately fails on its failure to evolve its gameplay. Iteration is not evolution.

I waited many weeks since this game's launch and that wait is worth it. Dishonored 2 is a wonderful game, not a masterpiece, but it comes pretty close. Runs fluidly well on my GTX 980 (not the Ti), i7 4790K, 16GB, Win 7 64Bit PC, Very High preset @ 1080p 60fps without any issues. No frame loss, no stuttering, no crashes whatsoever. Beautiful game in terms of visuals, nothing new in terms of gameplay; if you played the first Dishonored, you will feel right at home. Although, providing the player the option to choose between Corvo, and Emily is a welcome change. I recommend playing and experiencing the story as Emily first for obvious reasons. But it will be fun to go back and replay the adventure as Corvo, with a different take on the world around that character, not to mention the different endings depending on your choice of character, and the actions you committed all along, including critical decisions in vital points of the campaign.
I will admit. I bought this game first for my Xbox One but I didn't beat it. While the game looked decent visually and played okay at 30fps, the PC gamer in me wanted the best experience. So I waited until Arkane Games / Bethesda patched the game up until the latest beta patch. Then I jumped in. Bought the game while it was on sale briefly following Black Friday at 33% off. I am glad I did. Loving it so far as you can tell from my 43+ hours of game time. The PC version blows the Xbone One version out of the park in terms of visual fidelity and frame rate. It's a known thing but I never experienced anything like those unfortunate folks for whom the game is not performing the way it should. I hope they too can enjoy this lovely game.
All in all, I recommend this game to any fan of first person action or stealth genre. If you have a good enough PC, please get this game. Or, you might want to wait for a slight price drop if you are anxious about performance issues. But don't ignore this wonderful IP.

I am a diehard  fan of the original King's Quest series, having grown up learning how to type & spell by playing these games (back before the point & click style). While there's a bit of a departure in style with this latest King's Quest, there's still a very strong link to the old series. It's worth mentioning that many of the King's Quest games were departures from the established predecessors (and I'm not referring to King's Quest VIII, which is essentially only a King's Quest game in name). The characters are well fleshed-out with a sense of humor, all with their own personality. The puzzles avoid the "Sierra moon-logic" of the past, while also being clever enough to be fun to figure out. The only downside that I've found is that I personally prefer the more realistic art style of King's Quest VI, although these graphics are still quite beautiful. I also prefer being able to manually save when ever I'd like instead of having the game decide automatically when to save, with only one save per slot. Regardless, as an old fan, King's Quest has been very enjoyable.

Well, shoot, how does someone start a review for a game that is as controversial today as when it came out? Bad distasteful puns aside, I’m sure one of my friends has questioned my morals or thinks of me an edge-lord by simply playing the game.
What was simple curiosity about playing POSTAL in 2017 led me into an introspection at the usage of violence in games, the importance of context, and the utter hypocrisy inherent in games that showed me that you shouldn’t play PR because it’s a game but more so because what you’re playing is a work of art.
At the risk of sounding callous, I felt no remorse from this game. There are various reasons as to why in gameplay terms, but I think I should debunk a few concerns.
No, there is no correlation between violence in games and real-life. There are numerous studies to show that if there is any correlation, which is direct correlation fallacy, it is the exact opposite; games purge violence thoughts through exaggerated violence. This is not a sign of being desensitized but recognizing the utter absurdity in the violence, which is why as a squeamish person I did not feel bad. POSTAL also has zero sense of immersion or premeditation like in Hitman or Manhunt, so the violence is more a form of Catharism in the moment.
In gameplay terms, there are various aspects that remove empathy you may have when playing. The first of which are enemies that do fire back, which include cops, military personnel, miners with explosives, and turrets. Compared to Hatred, your enemies are more comical and “video-gamey” that helps with the campy nature rather than emphasize how serious it is. Second, the AI is stupid, especially for the civilians, so the utter lemming-like attitude takes away any remorse. Lastly, the mundane nature  of killing 90% of HOSTILES (not civilians) emphasizes you to be more creative in your kills to find any semblance of entertainment.
Ultimately, however, whatever interest you may find in setting fire to a marching band or at an elderly home becomes hollow and death becomes meaningless, which goes to show the difference between mindless violence and violence with a purpose.
The fundamental issue, a topic not a fault, is that The Postal Dude is epitomizes the death of context. Context is the circumstances surrounding the event that emphasizes its relevance. This is why when you start off by massacring a neighborhood it sounds horrible; whereas when you are playing it for yourself you might as well be shooting at aliens or zombies.
Everything about TPD is a rejection of context. For starters, his name itself is someone who has had enough and goes on a rampage. However, in many games that play with as much violence, there is usually a reason behind the motive as an excuse. While there is a backstory to give little, if any, context to TPD, the only thing you experience when you play is a needless rampage killing in Campaign-Mode. The only reason you kill is because the objective marker tells you to kill 90% of enemies, and there are achievements to not kill any civilian or to kill everyone. Only in the newly featured Rampage Mode is there a score-modifier, which goes to show how utterly devoid of meaning is in the base game itself. The ending is the only time the game seeks to find retribution for its existence by classifying TPD as the byproduct of modernity.
The problem with PR as a game is that many games have features that accomplish the same thing or there are games that explore violence with more purpose. Spec Ops: The Line and Undertale—two games I never thought to share the same sentence—explore the consequences of choice in gameplay and story. In terms of raw gameplay, Hitman and Manhunt explore the same dubious nature of violence, and any recent Grand Theft Auto game lets you play with friends to accomplish the same goal of mindless violence. The reason why these games are more effective at dealing with these issues is the first victim in POSTAL’s slaughter, context.
POSTAL is the only game I can think of where the death of context was the point of the game, and the purpose of eliminating all context was to showcase the hypocrisy in games.
Back when POSTAL originally came out, almost every character in video games was some form of a heroic characters with redeemable qualities. Upon its release, POSTAL solidified the existence of antiheroes in games. Even to this day, I couldn’t find someone more deplorable than TPD without the purpose to be comically evil (Overlord) or to make evil a topic to explore for the sake of storytelling (Tyranny).
What makes TPD redeemable as a character is solely because his existence points to a hypocrisy in games that showcases how violence is used and justified. The fact that you could replace the violence with any other character or replace the enemies into other conventional excuses would be mere interpretation if it wasn’t for the original POSTAL ending. After massacring thousands of people, the Postal Dude arrives at an elementary school. When you try to play the game, you will find that none of your weapons work and the Postal Dude cannot kill any kids before he gives into insanity. Why? It’s because it’s a video-game and M-rated games cannot let you kill them.
This taboo in games is still prevalent, and more strongly barred, in games like Skyrim where children are immortal or in the case of Metal Gear Solid 5 they put a fail-state on their deaths. The fact that the original ended this way to poke fun at the trope emphasizes how TPD was meant to be commentary of how games use violence without equity.
However, I’ve talked only about the original; the Redux changed it and offered three replacements. As you can imagine a lot has changed between 1997 and 2017, and I cannot fault the developers for feeling that the original ending would have been more distasteful today as they explained why they changed it. Unfortunately, none of them reach the meta-commentary heights of the original and only offer fan-service for TPD, and the result is that even PR is an addition to the commentary of how hypocritical games are today from how they once were before.
As painful or distasteful as the idea may be, I think taking out that ending was not for the better. This situation reminds me of something Holden Caulfield once said, “Certain things, they should stay the way they are. You ought to be able to stick them in one of those big glass cases and just leave them alone.”
You might be wondering why I have only glossed over the gameplay and features. It’s because if you want to play the game itself there are vastly better alternatives that do everything POSTAL sets out to do better, and even the sequels, as shoddy as they are as games, offer more to gain from the gameplay itself.
The reason why I deliberately opened this up into an artsy-fartsy critique is because I think the people that enjoy Chinese Room games would appreciate POSTAL more so than edgelords or people who enjoy dark-humor. (As underhanded as that comparison was to Chinese Room, at least POSTAL offers more of a game.)
All I need to say about the actual gameplay itself is it does what it is meant to do. The extra levels add some needed comedic value to the game and the additional modes such as Coop and Rampage add some longevity or purpose. Some may decry the censorship as a reason to not buy the Redux; however, the original is still available, and this verison offers something more playable to modern gamers.
Perhaps you may think that this critique was from buyer’s remorse or a pointless endeavor to justify this game’s existence as historical shock value. All I have to say in response is you can mail your complaints to the nearest post office and pass along the message,
*Puts sunglasses on*

The controversy spins around the fact that in the game you play the role of a mad man, known only as “postal dude”, who basically goes into a rampage, killing everyone around him based only on his own delirious ideas of “purifying the Earth” or something. Another controversy is that the game hints a few references to some macabre school shootings that happend by the time of the game’s release in the 90ies.
The game is an isometric shooter, where you move your character around the evironment while trying to aim and shoot everyone on sight. Scattered around the corners you will find new weapons, ammo and a few power ups that will help you in your journey of insane murder. You will be running around towns, parks and a other populated areas, all filled with random “innocent” people and also hostile ones, like cops, rangers, soldiers and other agents of the law trying to stop you. Kill 90% of the hostiles and you can move to the next level.
This version has a LOT of improvements to add, starting with the controls, which are much, much better now. The combination mouse+keyboard has now a very fluid gameplay, with resposive controls, unlike the 90ies version, where controls were clunky AF. Also, all the DLCs were added and a few more singleplayer modes were add too, making the game much larger and potentially replayable. There are also a few easter eggs, like some references and modes related to other games, such as Hatred and Such.

I've been playing SMITE since closed beta and I would recommend this game to anyone who is interested in MOBA's but just can't quite get into the isometric MOBA's like DOTA 2 or League. However, SMITE does have plenty of issues that are easily fixed or balanced, which Hirez does nothing about.
Here's some pros and cons:
-Smite is good for new moba players
-The community is GENERALLY less toxic than other moba games
-The Gods (Heros, Champs) are generally very well done and-
-3rd person makes you feel more connected to your God
-I don't consider SMITE to be a FTP game. Unlike DOTA, you have to grind to unlock every God with favor you earn. However you can purchase the Ultimate God Pack (for about 30$ last I checked?), which gives you all current and future Gods forever. This is the best FTP deal you will probably ever see.
-The community gets more toxic the higher your level gets. Still not as bad as other moba's, but still toxic nontheless.
-Poorly balanced Gods. And still poorly balanced after public testing.
-Hirez nerfs and buffs Gods only because of the SPL (Pro League). Leaving ranked and casual less important and broken.
-Hirez constantly ignores broken Gods and underperforming Gods (That aren't always played in the SPL). Even after multiple community threads, comments, and even surveys.
-SMITE is free, however ... in the recent year they've been adding more and more cosmetic skins that you can ONLY get in a chest roll that will give you a 1 and ___ chance of getting the item you want to buy, regardless of the money you spend. I want to spend my money on what I WANT, not what Hirez wants.
, even though it is still the baby in the genre. I would recommend SMITE. but be warned about the cons of this game. Hirez, like most companies, started out great but is generally getting more and more greedy by the day. And they do tend to ignore their community even more nowadays.
I would give SMITE an 8.5/10.
