This was one of the first games I played on my first PC build back in early 2013, long before this showed up on Steam. At the time, I didn't have Windows so I played it to completion on Ubuntu through WINE because I was a huge Half Life fan and the original game was the very first FPS I played on PC (at the time, it was a 2009 Mac Mini running a WIndows XP virtual machine). It was amazing to see an old game from 1998 brought back to life with the Source engine despite the problems of running a modern game through WINE. What makes this a great, fan built game? The level design is amazing and every detail shows the amount of work that went into each one. It's especially good work for an amateur development team. I would recommend this game solely based on the levels and environments. The gameplay is also solid with great FPS action that the original did so well. It's always entertaining to place a trip mine in a doorway and watch a HECU Marine get gibbed to bits as he haplessly rushes through. The soundtrack to this game is another plus. An original composition, it really adds to the atmosphere of the levels and the gameplay. The only criticism I have of this game is the voice acting. It tends to be amatuerish and sometimes falls flat especially the voice acting for the marines but this is understandable given that this game was first developed by amateur volunteers who were just fans of the original game.  They more than make up for this defect with their passion and dediciation. I look forward to the upcoming Xen levels and seeing how Crowbar Collective will bring the strange world of Xen to life.
I cannot thank the creators enough for revamping my favorite game of all time. They bring back the half-life I grew up with and have made me play the game over and over again.

I just finished playing this on hard difficulty and this is one of the best games I have ever played. Terrifying, suspensful , stressful, yes... but wildly entertaining as well. I highly recommend playing this in a dark room with headphones on for full effect. In fact, headphones are an absolute must for this game as the environmental audio is pivotal to survival. Without them the game can become frustrating as the alien AI is merciless in tracking you down. Once you understand the unwritten rules surrounding the alien behavior, however, is when the game really hits its stride and you can begin exploring the beautiful Sevastipol station (which the developers spared no expense in detailing).
This game really belongs in everyone's game collection but for those who are fans of the franchise, Sci-Fi fans or horror fans in general it is an absolute must own.

I waited until after some of the patching to buy this game and it works fairly well for me performance wise other than some amusing glitches.  That being said, I'm rating off of gameplay and storyline as opposed to the questionable release given I didn't suffer those problems.
The good:
I think it's smoother than the first Dishonored (at least playing as Emily as I haven't yet played as Corvo).  There are a lot of options as to how to go about solving problems and you can be murder heavy or not and still go through the game altering your chaos level.  The game feels like a really fun version of the older thief games with a steampunk bent - all good things in my opinion.  I thought the story was a bit questionable at first but explained better over time.  I'm avoiding specifics to avoid spoilers.  I really liked some of the detailing given to previous characters and the way that Emily's character seems to grow up more as the game goes on.  It is a lot of fun to play in my opinion and I'd recommend it to other players.  I'm already hoping they'll do some dlc levels and extras since my largest complaint would be it only being 9 chapters.
The bad:
It felt short to me, though I think it was probably around the same length as the first Dishonored chapter wise.  I feel like they could do a lot more with the world and that they only brush the surface.  The chaos system is a bit strange, and while I don't know for certain how it works - it felt as though mass murder didn't mean much as long as you made specific choices in the game involving the npcs and how they were dealt with.  That sort of made putting effort into being sneaky a little meh.  The endings felt fairly limited for a game with so many great options.  Otherwise, I can't really complain, as I said above I'm already hoping for some dlc for the game when they're done working on the patching issues.  I can't complain about performance problems since I haven't really had many.
Overall I'd say the game is a great one, and a stellar one for fans of the all too rare stealth genre of games.  I would say it was well worth buying and I am really glad I did.  I look forward to playing through again on corvo to see the differences in play, but at least on Emily the game was just a pleasure.

I was a big fan of the "old" Telltale Games, before their ever increasing focus on narrative made them forsake gameplay to the point that it's debatable whether their more recent titles can be called games at all. I've played adventure games from a number of other developers since then but I can safely say King's Quest is the first game to really grip me with the same kind of charm.
The graphics are greatly designed and decent if not exactly envelope-pushing, music is pretty good, and voice acting is quite good as well. The gameplay is delightfully classic, perhaps a bit on the easy side but not as much as you might fear. There are occasional action-like sequences and death lurks around some corners in the old Sierra spirit, but the action is easy enough to handle even for a reflex-impaired guy like me and death can be rewound instantly (and is always accompanied by groaner puns).
The episodes also have a branching pathways element which compared to modern choice games is more honest about the relative unimportance of your decisions, but somehow also manages to make some of them feel more important. The length per episode seems fair enough, especially with the replay value from different decisions. (If you make a couple of mistakes in the second episodes you'll very likely want to redo it, even if the game seems to counsel against that.)
Most importantly, the game has a nice sense of humor, good (though not especially deep) writing and a special charm that ties everything together and makes you willing to forgive a lot. The most important flaw to forgive being that newer episodes seem to reuse old characters heavily, not unlike old Telltale used to do. If you loved old Telltale or generally liked oldschool point-and-clicks, pick this up and keep an eye on the developer.

After a year of patching, the game now truly stands where it was supposed to be in its original launch date. Many fixes have been applied including stability fixes, gameplay improvements such as political overlook, and a bran new building chain.
The Grand Campaign features a number of factions from different "races" to play as including the Ancient Powers of Rome, Carthage or Macedon. There are also completely optional DLC's to choose from including faction packs (Nomadic factions, Greek states or Barbarians), or, if you prefer new campaigns to show your power and subjugate your foes, you can choose between Caesar in Gaul (featuring Caesar's conquest of Gaul), Hannibal at the Gates (featuring the Second Punic War between Rome and Carthage) or the brand new campaign which comes with the Emperor Edition; Imperator Augustus (which focuses on the Second Triumvirate and the Roman Civil War that changed Rome into an Empire).
If somehow, you get bored of all this additions, you can always try the hundreds of mods available for the game. The game has alot to offer, for all types of people. All in all, the game is good now, it's just the player to decide what to do. Will you follow the course of history, or change it?

It's a short game(5.4 hours for me, including the 10-ish minutes I spent in the bonus room) that has active combat (bumping into enemies to hit them), diverse bosses, and a neat little story(with 3 different endings) that borders on sisterly love without being over-the-top. Its english isn't the best but the developer clearly isn't skilled in speaking/writing English so fair enough and it's also free. Oh, did I mention that? A 5 hour game that is great at killing a few hours and it is *free*. Now, it's not so simple as "It's free so it's good". The specifics that you need to know are the usual ones. I'll list them in seperate paragraphs to make it at least a little organized.
The story is, well, it's pretty linear and straight forward but it definitely opens for being expanded. Since I don't want to spoil anything, all I'll say is it has a plot-device that is basically "magical essense that can possess and control others", which personally is something that bugs me because I hate mind-changing/controller/possession themes. Since this is the internet, I'll ignore the fact that it's R34 bait for seduction-porn because, yeah, that's a thing. It's not thoroughly explained in the game but it seems like it's only relevant to the tower you enter. Overall, not a bad story but not amazing. As I said, no spoilers, so you'll have to experience the story for yourself.
The combat gets repetitive sometimes, with skills to let you spice it up but the skills are really only useful against mini-bosses(optional bosses, to be technical) and bosses but only because you can kill normal enemies pretty easily with your basic attack. I've been told the combat is similar to Ys, in that you bump into enemies to fight them, so that's what you can relate it to. There's are four skills, each with their own uses(in combat and actually progressing through the game). Other than that, there's not much to discuss. It's pretty simple but somehow fun, until it gets repetitive.
The actual maps themselves are a bit plain. The "journey" is pretty linear but then again you are going up a tower so expecting diverse locations and intricately designed rooms is a bit odd, even if it is, assumedly, a magic tower. There are occasional side paths that lead to special mini-bosses(which tie into upgrading your equipment) and chests that give you helpful bonuses. There are also 3 grinding/arena type of areas that tie into upgrading your equipment as well. In fact, it seemed like these areas were designed entirely for getting more materials(I will explain that in the next paragraph) and that's it. Now, the maps are diverse in terms of your *location* but there aren't a lot of them. There's about 4 different locations you go throughout the game within 5 hours. You can't back-track when you go from one section to the next, so there's that.
This game has a crafting system, so there's your warning. It's a simple crafting system but it's still there. You craft by using materials you get from enemies (generic names e.g. fairy cloth, fairy crystal) but you can also upgrade your equipment by using the previously crafted equipment and crafting it together with what we'll call an "upgrade gem" and some more materials(which increases with each "tier"). There are only 4 tiers and 3 sets(one from each section of the tower) of equipment for 5 slots on your character, as per every RPGMaker game. Honestly, it's just a distraction to keep you doing something different once in a while. Your only issue will be when you need to upgrade your equipment for bosses but that might take about 10-ish minutes if you have no materials.
The music was actually pretty good for a free game. Nothing that stands out, other than one of the songs that had something that sounded like the dubstep-bumping/drumming sound. That was just odd in a game that has otherwise instrumental-esque music. Everything is good here, unless you don't like that type of music. It fits the game very well.
All-in-all, it's a pretty neat game for being free. It's not too short but it's not too long, the combat is pretty simple yet amusing, the music was very good, the crafting system wasn't a hindrance, the story was interesting for what it delivered but it was pretty linear. What would be my verdict? 7/10 simply because it was a pretty good game for a free game. There wasn't a lot of expectations as a free game, so you probably should heed my words and do not have high expectations. Just like any movie with as high expectations as Star Wars EP 7.

Fun and engaging, but fairly shallow for the price.
I was hoping for an experience that spawns from a queen and a few workers, into a sprawling colony that extends its territory all over the garden and scales that experience well enough to be fun in the early and late game, and hopefully offer some creativity in where the strategy fits into it.
You get the queen and some workers, but beyond that initial colony growth the game falls short of my dreams. The game gets choppy when you get a few dozen ants. You can get steamrolled on easy mode, while a match in one of the gamemodes I tried was lasting so long that I ended up quitting and going to bed.
The hive management feels simple and constrained, with the strategy being a basic numbers meta where you need to balance the workers/soldiers/food in a specific way to beat each level. My favorite RTS games are ones that feel like a creative outlet where plenty of playstyles can achieve victory, but Empires of the Undergrowth is not one of them.
I don't think it was worth the pricetag at £15.99, but with so few ants games around I can't hate a dev team for trying. I had some fun with it, and there's some cool mechanics that kept me engaged. While it's not the ant-covered garden I dream of, having a mad scientist accidentally drop a beetle into my ant tank felt like as good of a fight as any action game I've played.

This game has a huge potential to become an amazing game.
It's obviously early access and still has a long way to go (especially in terms of content) but it has been fairly stable for me so far. There's a few bugs/glitches here and there but for an early access game the quality is pretty good (played far worse and only very few that were on par or better).
Currently there's only 3 ant species in the game, one that you use for your formicarium (a persistent sort of home base you can expand and return to after playing a scenario) and the two others you play in the scenarios. More are planed and more will come though.
The levels are fun to play and although the real AI hasn't made it into the first release it shows that the developers have a good understanding of level design and that you don't need advanced AI to make good scenarios (the proper AI is on it's way and acutally fairly far developed, it just wasn't required for the early access levels for which scripting was fully sufficient so it's development was delayed in favor of other things that actually were required for the early access release, like mostly fixing bugs that sprung up during the closed beta test to get a most stable and bugfree release client).
I applaud the developers for NOT going with the general "just smash everything that isn't you color" theme RTS games seem to favor these days but instead giving us four VERY different scenarios with interesting objectives and different gameplay (clearing an underground map, fending off invading slave-maker ants that steal your brood, surviving against the environment and variosu critters for three days on a beach with rising and falling tide, surviving an Onslaught of two ant colonies trying to take over your nest before their own nests on the lower levels get flooded).
I'm looking forward to the next scenarios (potentially with leafcutter ants) which will undeoubtatedly be quite different again.
Another thing I really love about this game is the way units move. This is NOT StarCraft where you can micromanage every single to the point of playing a tabletop game, this game is about MACRO.
Each of your unit groups (ants from connected nesting tiles are automatically put into one squad and you can put multiple of these squads into a group) can be called to a position by placing a pheromone marker. About half of the ants will react isntantly to the marker, more will follow it over time. This may seem annoying at first but once you've understood how this system works when fog of war gets implemented you'll appreciate it as it basically gives you full line of sight over the entire range of your "ant trail" resulting in a huge amount of map control (barely anyone can sneak past a large ant trail and if the trail is attacked at one point the battle will quickly escalate due more and more ants quickly accumulating at the conflict site).
As to be expected in every early access game the units themselves have some balancing issues (upgrading brood tiles just isn't worth it as more ants are always better and the Formica rufa shooters are ridiculously overpowered) but none of these actually detract from the gameplay or the fun, so they don't matter in the end.
Right now the game has 2 formicarium challenges (with your genetically modified Formica ereptor ant), 4 missions (2 with Formica fusca and 2 with Formica rufa) and the 4 old demo levels (with a Formica ereptor/fusca hybrid colony). If you play them all (including the old demo levels) that should keep you busy for about 10-20 hours (depending on how well you do).
It seems a fair price to me, especially when considering that the final product will be much more and have features like a freeplay mode, more missions and more ant species (obviously) and a campaign.
The developers have been working on this game for years so it is unlikely that this project will be abandoned. The team is small though (3 programmers and a community manager), but they're working really hard and development speed should increase once all major bugs (especially those related the unit navigation aka units getting stuck which still sometimes happens around the entrance areas and cliffs) are squashed - the game has made amazing progression in that regard during the closed beta test so I'm confident this soon will be an issue of the past.
TL'DR:
This game is lots of fun and has a vast potential to become an AMAZING game. It is not your average RTS game and that's good. Obviously it is still in early access and doesn't have tons of content but the content it has is good and makes you want more. I can wholeheartedly recommend it but if you think it's not worth buying yet just put it on your "followed games" list and keep an eye out for future updates.
(p.s. I got the game for free but I am not affiliated with the developers in any way. In fact I was gifted it due to my feedback posts on the game's official forums so I could take part in the closed beta test and give further feedback as I wasn't able to back/buy the game at that time due to technical issues.)

I was tempted to write a full review of Emperor Edition as a new release of Rome 2, the game we should have had 1 year ago, but decided you didn't deserve to be subjected to acres of my rambling, though this is still pretty bad. So I'm just looking at what were the main troublespots within the game as I saw them.
Basically, it is now fixed. Bugs are very few and far between, crashes almost non-existant and it now processes AI turns at a decent rate.  This is the state it should have shipped in, but given it took them 1 year to get here, Sega would clearly not have been prepared to pay for this much development time without a return when they could just get their loyal dupes (that's us) to pay for it and playtest it for them.
Graphics are improved, look at all the screenshots they are eager to show you. Though it is still not really up to the standard of the pre-release footage they gave us glimpses of way back, insisting it was all in engine unfinished work that would get even better. that claim was quietly ditched and never referred to again.
The AI is still lacking, though it is clearly much improved on launch. It no longer sends units running in pointless circles or gets irriversibly stuck on terrain.  However some individual units are still broken due to terrible AI, for example cataphracts, some of the heaviest and most expensive cavalry in the game, can still be easily broken and destroyed by 2-3 units of slingers, some of the cheapest units in the game (It should be possible for slingers to break cataphracts, but it is the ease with which they can do it that is the problem). It is also still very much a case of quantity beats quality for the AI. Stacks and stacks of the cheapest troops for you to mow down, used with only the most rudimentary glimpses of strategy.
Agent spam is still as much of a problem as it always has been, you have to find your own fix for that (thanks modders). Technically this was not a bug, so I suppose CA would say it is working as intended, though it is incredibly frustrating, and about as far form realistic as you could get.
The political system. Well, at least there finally is one, after a fashion.  The previous system was an incredibly lazy turn counter towards an inevitable civil war with a few half hearted attempts to disguise it, clearly done by an intern during his lunch break. Now you have a turn counter that you can modify and influence to an extent.  It is still barely worthy of being called a political system and has none of the attachments we grew to love from previous Total War games, like family trees, nominated successors etc.
The other factions in your government are a shadow of a cardboard cutout. They occasionally take random political actions against you, though never in pursuit of a greater goal, and they have had so little attention paid to them that there is nothing that you can pursue in revenge. It in no way feels like you are struggling to hold your empire together against different factions.  I am sad to say that this is the biggest failure in my eyes mostly because it barely feels as though they even tried. Take a glance at Crusader Kings 2 for an example of how to make a political system with internal faction politics on a fraction of CA's budget.
In summary, I would recommend Rome 2, because it is now a slickly presented game that is largely bug free, and plays well and will hold your interest, as long as you don't look too closely at the mechanics, and I also think this is probably the best we are going to get. However the weak political system is indicative of the general lack of depth to the game. It finally deserves a score around the 80-85% mark that the 'professional' fanboys gave it on release.
This is the standard that it should have been at at launch and it is important to remember the shocking state it was launched in, and remind CA and Sega that we remember, or they will try exactly the same thing with their next game.

It's unfortunate that this game has been rated so poorly on Steam purely on the basis of a choppy start. I certainly understand peoples frustration, however having waited a few weeks for the patches I've now put in a fair bit of time and I can confidently say this game is exceptionally good - even better than the first title in my opinion.
The ingenuity behind the level design is astonishing. I haven't encountered a game offering so many routes to objectives with such intricacy. Exploration is very rewarding - although the storyline is linear, the scale and detail of the maps makes the game at times feel like a sandbox title. The graphics, although arguably technically not the best to date, are absolutely beautiful, with particular attention paid to clever lighting, shading and use of colours. If you enjoyed the first game or you enjoy challenging stealth titles, Dishonored 2 is a must buy.
The performance issues appear to have been resolved with one exception. I would strongly recommend to Nvidia users disabling HBAO+ in advanced options - as with a lot of other titles (GTA V, Far Cry 4 etc.) it really does kill the frame rate. With the GTX 1070 I can play the game at 2560x1440 at a mix of Ultra/Very High, TXAA and adaptive resolution disabled and the performance is flawless. HBA0+ was enabled by default however and I found the game very choppy before disabling it. The graphical difference without it is marginal, you won't miss it.
Edit: Having now completed the game I can reiterate that it was truly excellent, definitely game of the year for me. I have had no performance issues whatsoever since disabling HBAO+. After completing it I immediately decided to replay it on hard with a different playstile - with a huge backlog of games I've yet to play I can think of no higher praise than this.

after i'm done with the wonderful postal 2 package of the rws i finally got my hands on the postal redux. as a person who actually played the original postal back in the day, i cannot say i had the best of time playing it, it was an average endeavour with an "original" premise, playing a mass shooting maniac was both controversial and refreshing and for a person who is not offended by every other thing that's been thrown on his way, it was a nice idea, but the game itself was not great, especially the controls were a big part of the problem plus for me the lack of a comprehensive story was a huge red flag. but on the other hand the hand drawn graphics and some insanely clever ideas here and there ( "the marching band" is a wonderful example) and the dark, mysterious core material turned this into a welcoming experience for me.
and now with the redux we have the definitive remastered edition of this hiccup of a game, do i recommend it? well... i'm sort of not sure. don't get me wrong the game is great if you're the fan of the series. with added content (even the famous super postal episodes are here) improved graphics and most importantly "much better controls" this game is and should be a "must". and i can't wrong the game in any of those areas but, since the controls are better now, the game is very, i mean VERY easy. and you can beat it in 2 hours if you just try to speedrun it ( even less than 2 hours if you're better than me at playing games - and you are-). the game offers multiplayer, co-op and rampage modes, which are huge additions but i cannot find anyone online for two of these modes and the rampage mode is not my cup of tea since i'm a linear campaign person. the rampage mode only did the trick for me for an hour or so. afterwards the only choice for me was to uninstall the game.
all in all, this is an improvement over postal original on every ♥♥♥♥ing level and the definitive version of the game. if you're going to buy a postal game, start with this game, if you want a twin stick shooter with a darker edge buy this game, if you see this game on the sale ( but only on the sale) buy this game. i can recommend postal 2 and the wonderful add on even if they're not on sale, but this one, imho is an exclusively "sale" material because it will keep you occupied only for couple of hours but let's be honest you will enjoy the hell out of those "couple of hours".
note: and yes, i know rws is still improving the loading times, but i think they still need some improvement.

I first saw EotU at a convention a year or two ago and instantly knew it was a game I never knew I'd always wanted. Maybe that doesn't make sense, but it's the only way I can think to describe it - a seemingly very niche appeal yet the whole group of friends I was with were intrigued by this new, innovative entry to the minion-management/base-builder RTS genre. Is there a succinct name for it? MMBBRTS is a bit of a mouthful...
Flash forward to now and I'm delighted with this game. It's great fun, it's challenging and it has a unique charm. I feel like I'm doing Slug Disco's creativity a disservice by comparing EotU to the Dungeon Keeper games but both EotU and DK stand out as groundbreaking games in the MMBBRTS genre. SimAnt is possibly another entry worth mentioning here but, as I never played it (BOO SHAME SHAME), I can't really give any meaningful commentary.
The gameplay, as I said before, is quite challenging. The initial tutorial seems overwhelming at first but once you start messing about you'll soon get a hang of how things work. Be prepared to restart your Formicarium due to poor strategy - I got my head kicked in by the first challenge mission for the Formicarium because I'd built a colony entirely of worker ants. I didn't realise I had to unlock the soldiers in the tech tree! Derp. Ended up having to restart my campaign to fix the formicarium.
The graphics are way beyond what I expected. They certainly don't
to be realistic for this type of game and yet I'm so glad they are. I find my skin crawling whenever I tunnel into a spider's lair or accidentally unleash a horde of devil's coach horse bugs. UGHHHH!
My only gripe with the game is, as mentioned earlier, if you build your Formicarium poorly to begin with you'll have to restart your campaign if you want to reset it. Not the end of the world but a bit annoying, especially as my impatience made me restart the first level several times after my base got wiped out by the big boys.
In an era of ♥♥♥♥♥♥, broken early-access games, Empires of the Undergrowth stands out as a shining gem, crafted by a company with a genuine love for their game coupled with the talent to make it work. I can't wait to see what the future will bring, both for this game specifically and for Slug Disco as a company.
Pros:
Great concept
Great gameplay (so far)
V Good graphics
Interesting campaign - the mixture of the longplay Formicarium with the standalone missions works nicely so far.
Cons:
Very few, mostly things that I feel will get ironed out in future releases.
Tutorial is a bit confusing and initially feels overwhelming
No subtitles
Can't reset Formicarium without starting new campaign

I was a big fan of the "old" Telltale Games, before their ever increasing focus on narrative made them forsake gameplay to the point that it's debatable whether their more recent titles can be called games at all. I've played adventure games from a number of other developers since then but I can safely say King's Quest is the first game to really grip me with the same kind of charm.
The graphics are greatly designed and decent if not exactly envelope-pushing, music is pretty good, and voice acting is quite good as well. The gameplay is delightfully classic, perhaps a bit on the easy side but not as much as you might fear. There are occasional action-like sequences and death lurks around some corners in the old Sierra spirit, but the action is easy enough to handle even for a reflex-impaired guy like me and death can be rewound instantly (and is always accompanied by groaner puns).
The episodes also have a branching pathways element which compared to modern choice games is more honest about the relative unimportance of your decisions, but somehow also manages to make some of them feel more important. The length per episode seems fair enough, especially with the replay value from different decisions. (If you make a couple of mistakes in the second episodes you'll very likely want to redo it, even if the game seems to counsel against that.)
Most importantly, the game has a nice sense of humor, good (though not especially deep) writing and a special charm that ties everything together and makes you willing to forgive a lot. The most important flaw to forgive being that newer episodes seem to reuse old characters heavily, not unlike old Telltale used to do. If you loved old Telltale or generally liked oldschool point-and-clicks, pick this up and keep an eye on the developer.

So far i am very optimistic that this will be a good game that is better than it's predecessor, it runs well and certainly does not have the issues the Original suffered at launch, the graphics are good, but not great and the performance is solid with only a few drops here and there.
The gameplay is very similar to the first one but one of the most distinct differences is that the game world, so far, is far more open allowing you to take different routes to either the current main objective or one of the side ones.
The controls are also notably better, i personally didn't have much of an issue with the originals after fine tuning them using the very good sensitivity adjusters the game had, but i think that people who take more of an issue with this than me will be far happier with how Sebastian controls in this one.
Other differences and improvements over its predecessor include a crafting ability to upgrade weapons and create items such as ammunition and healing items. there is also a Stealth skill ability branch that you can spend GG on.
There is also a good selection of difficulty modes available from the outset so Veterans of this game and/or genre should be able to enjoy an instant challenge if they want it.
I would also like to assure you that so far it is still Survival Horror, it hasn't been turned into an action game and Stealth, which has been improved on in this one, is essential to survival.
If you liked the first game and/or the Last of Us then i think that you will enjoy this too.
If you have any questions then please ask away and i intend to update this review as i play through it.

*Sigh*...This was one hell of a hype. The continuation to the conveluted and horrifying game that was The Evil Within. The presentation was terrific, the trailers promising and the reviews assuring. Yet what I saw was just not what I, and maybe some more people, did not expect. It's disapointing.
Let's start with the good things: The game looks good. The facial animations, lighting and sound are well made and fit. The overall visuals do look fine as well. An additional plus is the removal of the cinematic bars, which allows the player to utilize their 30 inch monitors to the fullest. The shooting felt a bit too easy and the guns all lacked any sort of punch they had in the previous game.
There is not much to say about the gameplay. The game holds your hand most of the time, always making sure you see enemies coming in, making sure to show you what they can do and all of that is happening in a locked camera mode. Only after numerous cinematics, displays and alike, you get your controlls back. I played this game on Survival and it was not the Survival I was prepared for since the last game.
And now for the main course: The story. Now, I am not sure what went wrong here, but in comparison to the previous installment, this game threw all mysteries, enigmas, questions and subtlety out the window. The enemies were just dudes that scream a lot, dudes that burn, dudes use flamethrowers...Where are all the monstrosities ? Where are the enemies that overpower you with their sheer size ? Where are the enemies, that you have to analyze yourself and find their weakness (speaking of the Amalgam from the previous game) ? There is no threat in this game; no real danger that makes you carefully examine your surroundings to deal with them (speaking of the fight with Laura in the previous game). This game just puts you into a horror movie for 12 year olds. It features some gore; tries to fit in some spooky stuff like jumpscares and alike. But it all gets ruined by the orchestra that begins to play if you get spotted or have to fight a boss.
I have been waiting for this game almost as bad as for Fallout 4, but this game was dumbed down and ruined by too many bells and whistles. And by bells and whistles I mean church bells and 20 dog whistles happening at any moment of confrontation in-game. Now, I am not sure if I am the only who has noticed the more than obvious Resident Evil 6 vibe at the end (Kidman was turned into Ada Wong, for example), but it sure did not help save the story.
It truly confuses me when I hear known cirtics saying that the game has been improved since it's last game but -honestly- I do not see any sort of true improvement. It was all made easy; everythign made not as challenging as the previous installment was. And that is truly a shame.
Some may say that I am comparing the game too much to the predecessor. And those are right, becasue I expected the mystery to continue, the challenges to remain or get improved and the grotesqueness to be more...grotesque. But int he end it all led to a non-scary, cliché-filled wannabe horror that does not deserve anything higher than a 6/10.
I only recomend this game for those who truly want to find out the stroy and maybe, just MAYBE, you won't be as disapointed as I got to be. Tread with caution, fellow fans. This is just another case of a bad sequel like Condemned 2 or Resident Evil 6.

Elder Scrolls Online: Tamriel Unlimited [Review Thus Far]
I have to say, this is by far one of the most beautiful, immersive and overall,one of the most fun MMOs I've ever played.
MMORPGs and just RPGs in general have been my go-to games for the past 8 years, and I think I've just about played all of them, but this one takes the cake.
Gameplay: A lot of questing, but questing isn't all that matters.  I honestly don't mind the mass amounts of questing you have to do, as all of the quests have voice acting which makes that much more immersive.  Aside from the quests, the other things you can do, such as the boss-camps, delves and just exploring in general, makes this game just that much more exciting to play.  And if that's not enough, there can always be surprise random events that can happen while in the open world.  I've been playing this game with my brother for the first 14 levels so far, and if playing the game isn't fun enough, playing with another person makes it all the better.
Graphics: Oh my God, this game is beautiful.  If you can play this game on Ultra settings, you may need to put your eyes in a wheel chair.  As I said before, this is by far, the most beautiful game I've ever played.  Every province is something special, and the regions and zones inside of that province are a sight to see.  I've played mostly on the Pact, but I have given AD and DC a try, and all three factions are graphically promising and are all beautiful in one way or another.  The makers of this game did an amazingly stunning job with the graphics.  I've played maybe 20-25 hours so far (again, ignore what Steam says I've played), and I can't help but appreciate all the places I've gone through.
Combat/Battle Mechanics: Very well done.  The use of dodging and actually having to move around while fighting makes this game a very good seller.  The mechanics for combat can make some very intense battles when fighting the bosses in Group Instances.
Classes/Roles: One thing that's to be specified.  YOUR CLASS DOESN'T DETERMINE YOUR ROLE.  And that's perfectly fine with me.  You don't have to be a Dragon Knight to be Tank, or a Templar to be a Healer.  You can be a Sorcerer Tank or Nightblade Healer if you want.  You can use any weapon and any armor in this game!  Yep, Dragon Knights can use Destruction or Restoration Staves if they want to.  There is many many variations in this game.  You can be Nord Werewolf Templar with a Bow in Light Armor if you honestly want to do that.  Hey!  You can really be any class and not fight, and all you do is just make food and/or craft items!  It's all up to you!
Miscellaneous: Crafting system is complex, but fair and makes sense after a while.  Cooking and Alchemy are a thing and are important to the gameplay.  There is a Justice System where you could become a fugitive (pick-pocket, murder, assault).  There is a lot of things I've covered but probably forgotten.  Don't stand in the fire!
At this point in time I haven't tried out the PvP yet, but I can only imagine it's fun as Hell.
Overall Pros:
Buy-to-Play: $60-80 Price Tag ($23.99 for the Christmas Sale!!, however there is an in game store for buying mounts and such.)
Graphically Stunning
Extremely Immersive
Fun to play with friends
Good Combat System
Graphically Stunning
Main Storyline is compelling and very interesting
A very rewarding game
Crafting System is good
Justice System makes the game very diverse and fun.
Roleplayer friendly
Dialogue and voice acting are great!
Did I forget to mention the graphics?
Extremely large game
Nothing in this game really pisses me off
Overall Cons:
It's definitely not your typical Elder Scrolls Game
Overall Overalls:
Again, not your typical Elder Scrolls Game, but that doesn't bother me at all.  Definitely not bragging, but being a player of this series for 5 years now, TES games definitely leave a mark in the RPG world and are definitely unique to other games.  Although Bethesda and Zenimax had to take ESOTU a slightly different direction, this game is still fun as Hell.  I definitely see myself playing this for a long time, and maybe making another review.  And if it really matters, I've never made a review for any game before (Please ignore the amount of games I have too, I was sharing a Steam account for the longest time before branching out to games like ESO), but I have to say, with the 20-25 hours I've spent so far, I really just had to get this review out there.
Lastly, I highly recommend this game to everyone.  I believe that TES players will enjoy this alot, and MMO players will enjoy it as well.  Get it before the sale ends!
Thanks for reading!

Short, sweet and sure as hell is there a reason why the reviews for this game are overwhelmingly positive.
You might be skeptical about all the RPG Maker created games popping up on Steam constantly, some free, some not. Well, this one is free, and it absolutely surpasses every single one of those.
Don't let the generally short playtime of most reviewers deceive you. It's admittedly a short game, but it's worth the time. Every minute of it was enjoyable; the game's design is ingenious. Everything is accomplished in real time, as the developer has promised, you don't have to use an attack button in this game. Just walk into your enemies and you will attack them automatically. Needless to say, there are skills you can unlock which
require pressing keys to use, but each and every one of them are unique in their own way. Likewise, all of Eternal Senia's bosses have stark differences between one another.
For a free game created with literally zero budget, I must say that both the art and soundtrack of Eternal Senia are superb. The emotions of the characters (mostly the protagonist Senia) are vividly expressed in all the frequent interactions that occur. The developer did use assets from Ragnarok Online to create this game, so it's obvious that the sprites and environments do have some level of quality at least.
The main thing I had a problem with was the rather shabby translations. It should be known that the developer's native language is Chinese Mandarin and that Eternal Senia wasn't meant to be published in English in the first place. I'm not complaining too much about it as the story was still easy enough to understand and the mistakes were minor, but a better job could've been done in that area.
Then there's the story. Well, Eternal Senia is free. It won't take you more than a few hours to clear it. Go ahead, download it... and shed some tears.

----------- REAL REVIEW BELOW---SPOILERS, KIND OF
Edit:
Over playing this game religiously, my view of it has drastically changed.
On a serious note, this game relies way to heavily on it's predecessor, which is an undoubtly better game for story and world design. Dark Souls II is clunky, unrefined and the team who made it showed such little effort to actually make a convincing world.
The addition of the DLC upset many people, one of which I was NOT. I was hoping for some redeeming PvE content in this game, but in the end it turned out the first DLC was good (except the trio), and the other two were absolutely trash  with rehashed bosses and TONS of plays on Dark Souls 1 references that really just make you cringe at how minimal the effort is to actually make these DLC's.
The NPC AI in the DLC has gotten better, but with the inclusion of gestures and other small things, they become more like scumbag players who have mild autism. There are just too many throwbacks and not enough original content that was introduced in the DLC.
The amount of bosses actually went DOWN in the final DLC, which should have been the one that gave closure or atleast a good finish to what should have been something that drew the same allure as Dark Souls 1 and Demon's Souls.
PvE stands no chance to Dark Souls 1 or Demon's Souls, which shows how much a director can influence the production of a GOOD, quality game. The disconnectivity in this game world can be explained as a lore point, but it boils down to being bad game design regardless.
Watching a place be under water and walking two feet and getting to it fully refurbished isn't something that is neat and thought provoking, it is immersion breaking. This game is put together like an abstractionists wet dream painting, there is no order or logical progression like the previous games.
I know I keep referring to the previous games, but that is what you do in a series. This game doesn't hold up to this pre-decessor and it's acknowledges this by crutching itself on material from the past by throwing in tweaks to them and thinking they are witty in the process.
On an actual gameplay PvE standpoint, there is also alot of controversy to their devotion to "difficulty". Dark Souls 1 and Demon Souls were difficult because of mechanics that made enemies and bosses intricate, most of the time. (Looking at you, Flamelurker, Dragon God, Bed of Chaos).
In Dark Souls II, the difficulty is ramped up indefinitely, but only if you find that being consistently 2-3v1ed in boss fights is actual difficulty and not just cheap artificial difficulty through micromanaging. Micromanaging does not take skill, it simply makes you have to pray that the RNG Gods don't make all three bosses sync their moves up to be .25ms after each attack where it is impossible to dodge out of.
There is a blatant difficulty throw in this game by just mashing you into a small area with multiple hard-hitting enemies.
Bottom of the Line:
PvP in this game is better mechanically, except for the millions of hackers because FROM SOFT DkS2 team is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and removed VAC.
PvE: Don't expect anything like the previous games out of this game if you're looking for an engaging world and story like its two previous. If you haven't played either two, you'll probably enjoy this game because the Souls games are a relatively unique experience, as generic as this one is.

This engine is killing this line of games. By wanting to expand their fanbase, they have alienated the original players.
The foundations of this game are still flawed. Wonky diplomacy, dismal AI, limiting construction system, formation commands on the battlemap disrupt the formation, focus on micro-animations in a macroscopic game (kill moves make cavalry charges only effective on the morale level, not the amount of fighting men), tech trees are barebone and have no requirements for upgrades (best (lategame) units available in early game), dismal loading times, buggy multiplayer, no speed bonus for naval transport, useless army stances (with current AI and diplomacy, raid and fortify have little use), random map gen (so ambushes can start with v unfav terrain), lack of family tree, etc etc.
This game is barely playable with a ton of mods, but never a challenge (if it is, then solely due to the number of enemy troops).
This Emperor Edition is the first playable version, which should have been available in nov '13, yet we live a year after launch.
Never mind the DLC-pushing and empty expansions while the state of the game is still shoddy.
This game needs a MASSIVE overhaul to become enjoyable. Either EA listens and works together with the community, or this series of games is in danger.

The sirens wailed in my ears as I gripped the pulse rifle tighter. All around me were the corpses of enemies who had been killed by the deadly xenomorphs. I stepped through a passageway and was mortally wounded by acid spit. As I laid there, slipping away into the unknown as enemies flanked me on all sides, John Rambro appeared over me and whispered, "I've got this, bro..."
Broforce is a game I've been playing on-and-off for more than a year, and it still manages to entertain and surprise me with its cheesy 80s bravado, constantly-evolving gameplay and a robust custom level community.
Ushering players in with an eagle's cry and a gruff military commander with a rockin' mustache barking orders, the game tasks players with infiltrating various Vietnam outposts and cleaning out the enemy resistance, using one of many different heroes who can be unlocked via rescues. These run the gamut from standard 90s action heroes (like Rambo or the Terminator) to female heroines (Ripley, Cherry Darling) to cult favorites like the Boondock Saints or the Rocketeer.
There really is no plot to speak of, but you won't care anyway because you'll be too busy spamming burning hot American justice into the hearts of faceless goons to care. Every level features a variety of enemies, traps and challenges to keep players on their toes, and the later stages (as of this writing) pit you against massive alien enemies and hordes of rocket-spamming foes.
One of the most interesting parts of the game is how fluidly every hero controls, and how many different gameplay mechanics are at work here. Whether it's John Mc-sorry, Bro McClane and Rambro's standard assault rifle spam, Cherry Broling's hover-by-way-of-Princess-Toadstool ability, the Brocketeer's double-jump or the Boondock Bros' AI helper/respawn ability, there's a wealth of ways to complete each level.
The game is definitely inspired by Contra, and can definitely be punishing in later stages, especially given that while you may have superior firepower, you're about as fragile as tissue paper. Each bro dies in one hit, forcing players to be mindful at times about how many additional lives they have.
The custom campaign mode is where the game really shines, and what gives it such exceptional replay value. There are a lot of custom maps, ranging from fully-fledged stories to brutally-difficult challenge maps.
The game is also hilarious when played in co-op or multiplayer mode. I've had the privilege to play this with friends multiple times, and the "rescue a bro, get another player in to help" mechanic works very well. Sometimes it's fun to screw over your friends by blowing out the floor underneath them and letting them fall to their deaths.
Broforce will definitely appeal to anyone who grew up in the 80s or 90s and can laugh at the various references and shout-outs to past franchises. Even for an Early Access title, it's very well-made (barring a few bugs every now and again), and is one of the best retro action platformers available on Steam right now.
If you don't buy it for yourself, do it for America.

They managed to do everything right, and seem to have cut out many less desirable aspects of the
series.
This time around you actually get to control your character directly (controller support is great - Steam controller too). They added in some really awesome action sequences in between the classic point-and-click puzzle solving. Its all very interactive. The artwork and graphics are superb. The voice acting is some of the best I have seen (they even have some A-list actors). The narration reminds me mildly of
in the sense that you are actively living a story/fairy tale. Its all very well done.
+They manage to keep the same
as the classics; details such as a nonlinear fairy-tale world and creative solutions to puzzles.
+Graphics are beautiful. Very much attention to detail (ie. the lighting and the cape, the forests feel alive)
+Cinematography is top-notch. It feels like you are playing a
or
movie. The characters are well developed.
+The story telling is really fun, and sucks you in. My wife and I couldn't stop playing. It is a joy.
+Controller support is smooth.
+Voice acting is absolutely great (and I will also mention the volume mixing levels are perfect - they focus on hearing the voice front-and-foremost, which for some reason tends to be problematic in these types of games).
+There certainly seems to be several paths one can take - hinting at tons of replayability.
+One major welcome difference from some of the old titles is that the puzzle solving is not as random or silly. Things tend to be fairly logical (or as logical as they can be in a fairy tale world).
-Very minor, but it would be nice to have a button or a way to skip certain animations while puzzle solving. Some can get redundant, but it is minor because of how short the animations/sequences tend to be.
Totally worth full price, IMO.

If you like Dungeon Keeper and RTS games, this game will be right up your alley. It's a little light on content, but it shows promise and has a nice polish to it. It doesn't do an amazing job of explaining the controls and mechanics, but you pick it up pretty easily if you're familiar with how an RTS plays. I'm excited for more of this game. Empires of the Undergrowth is a RTS/Tower Defense-esque game with hints of Dungeon Keeper. I honestly had a hard time finding something I didn't like about this game. It doesn't have the most intuitive UI or controls but they're fairly easy to pick up. The game doesn't really have a proper tutorial. It kind of throws you into your first level alongside a barrage of tooltips and hints that tell you how to play the game. Nevertheless, once you learn to play, it's really not any harder to pick up any other RTS. However, Empires of the Undergrowth has two mechanics that help it stand out.
First of all, are the two 'layers' of gameplay. You have your nest, where the level must be carved out like a Dungeon Keeper style game, and then the surface which plays more like your typical RTS. This gives the game a very interesting mechanic as later maps reveal a day and night cycle which brings out strong creeps at night giving the opportunity for adventurous players to explore or protect their own assets (such as aphid fields) or lets cautious ones retreat to the safety of their nest.
The Formicarium is another unique mechanic. It gives the player a sort of 'home base' so to speak. I thought at first it was some kind of hub world but the Formicarium is more like your home base. You can do levels where you act out scenarios as other ant colonies. By doing these, you unlock food, upgrade points, and expansion points for your base. The Formicarium also has challenges, which function as a kind of wave survival. You can also upgrade your ants at your base and unlock new units. After completing the early access content, you are given control of the wave spawner, allowing you to swarm yourself with enemies. This were fun but it seemed that you were able to survive extremely large amounts of enemies by just retreating to your nest, using its entrance as a chokepoint.
The game is also fairly polished and it runs well. It probably won't win any beauty competitions but it certainly isn't the ugliest thing. The music also stood out to me. It seemed very fitting and was really well done. The voice acting, while not phenomenal, is more than adequate. There are 3 VAs in the game, a male scientist, a female scientist, and a narrator. The narrator and female scientist are very subdued and appropriate sounding for the game, while the male scientist has kind of this 'anime villian' kind of voice. It isn't bad, but it could probably be dialed back a bit.
Either way, Empires of the Undergrowth stuck out to me. It's an early access game so there isn't a lot of content, but the content it does show has a LOT of potential. I was pleasantly surprised when I picked this up. This game shows promise and I can't fault it for being a little slim on content as an early access game. The content that IS there shows a hell of a lot of promise and I think it does a great job at providing a varied experience of the game.

Alien: Isolation is easily the most ambitions, bold and uncompromising mainstream game of 2014. And that lead to the mixed reviews it initially received: the game plays with you.
The game doesn't take you by the hand. Where other sneaky action games like Dishonored are power fantasies and present the players stealth abilities as a strength to overpower your enemies, hiding is your only option to survive. Alien: Isolation is extremely slow, it's repetitive (depending on how much you die) and it's unfair - and that's why I'm absolutely in love with it.

That game manages to be both good and an homage to the first Alien movie (which you need to have seen before playing this).
Alien:Isolation fits pretty well in this new generation of horror games where you mostly hide and run from a more powerful enemy. Forget about running and shooting a gun, this is a stealth game before anything. If you enjoy such game, like Amnesia or Outlast you should be pretty satisfied with this one. It gives the player more option than these two to deal with enemies. You still get a few weapons that can be used against humans/robots to kill them or against the Alien to scare it. You will also get a few items to heal, hide or distract enemies. But even with these weapons you'll spend most of your time avoiding combat and hiding/sneaking (especially when the Alien is around).
The game visuals do not use the most high tech visuals but the artstyle used in this game is perfect. It's a retro-scifi art (think space vessels with old green text computers) that is in perfect harmony with the 1979 movie Alien. You'll feel right at home and the different rooms feel organic. Lips synchronisation (during cutscenes) and character movement are not the best I have seen.
One of the possible issue someone may have is that the environment gets kind of repetitive. While it is a necessity due to the scenario (being on a single spacestation) it can feel a little monotonous after a while and you start to quickly no longer really look for details around you. If you played the Dead Space series this is kind of the same phenomena.
Sound and music are perfects, music will oppress you when appropriate and the sound is of really quality to make you believe all this retro-scifi tech with its many bips and scratching video/audio. Definetely a A+ in this department.
Scenario is decent. Nothing too surprising but it's entertaining enough to keep the player interested and looking for more. I did not find the game too difficult (on Hard, recommended difficulty) and felt both challenged at times while still progressing without frustration. Once Hard is finished, you will Unlock Nightmare difficulty. My first playthrough took me 21-22 hours with a good amount of exploration. This is pretty long for that kind of game that usually go for the 8 to 12hours range. So this is definetely a good point.
Game mechanics are usually standard for that kind of game, you hide from sight, crouch to make less noise, run only when necessary and hide in closets. You will also have your dose of crawling through vents and hiding in corners. Being an alien movie they give you a radar which is very useful against the alien that can move very fast or through vents. This radar requires a key to be pressed to show which add to the immersion. There are electronic devices scattered through the game that allow you to change some effect in rooms (unlock doors, disable lights, etc) but their usefulness felt somewhat lacking most of the time, it could have been somewhat more interesting or allowing more options or more rooms to be affected. The game allows you to go everywhere in the station as long as you have the "keys" to do so, somewhat like the first metal gear solid.
If you are an alien fan and enjoy stealth games, you just cannot miss that one.

The Evil Within 2 is great, cannot reccomend it enough. It has some optimization issues with high end nvidia cards for some reason, but that doesn't seem to apply to everyone with those cards anyways. Unfortunately with stuff like this, the only people who post about it are the people having issues, obivously no one is making threads like "hey, just checking in to say that TEW2 works great on my card".
Anyways, it is both a return to form and an upgrade on the genre. I grew up playing Silent Hill and the original Resident Evil on the PS1.  Not only did these games really get me into gaming, but they also solidified what my favorite genre would be throughout my whole life. As time went on, these games started to get more linear and linear in the gameplay, obviously the story was almost always linear because of the genre itself but the gameplay turned into being thrown into a hallway, or being thrown into a small map and going from area to area, starting in a forest, going to a big facility, going underground maybe, idk. But it didn't start that way, going back to the original Silent Hill games and the first Resident Evil, you were thrown into one pretty large map (although bigger in SH than RE) and you had to explore it. Some parts would take puzzles to explore, some others would just take equipment you didn't have yet and that's how they worked - instead of limiting where you could go by only giving you one direction to go in, they gave you a whole map to explore.
That is what this game is, they give you a town like in Silent Hill and you explore it; unlike Silent Hill though, the other things than the main story to do in those towns aren't just a few secrets, but a whole load of side quests with story and lore in themself. They've taken the open world formula from the original (and best) survival horror games and just improved upon it. The scares are in there, the atmosphere is amazing and the gameplay is just reminiscient of everything I love about the genre. They have brought life into this genre, and I thank them. The first Evil Within was more like an homage to the survival horror games like RE4, and this one is more like an homage to the survival horror games that are like Silent Hill 1 and 2. But it isn't just a bad recreation, it is the perfection of the art. They went the extra mile, just using inspiration to get them there.
This game will not be for everyone, but if you liked Alan Wake, Resident Evil, Silent Hill or the first game then you have to play this because you will love it!

The Evil Within 2's story takes place after the events of the first game, and we play as the same main character from the previous game, Sebastian. However, unlike the first game, The Evil Within 2's story seems much more streamlined, understandable and easy to pick up on. In addition, there are plenty of notes/files and side-missions across the game to help better understand the story (and learn more about it). In my opinion, the game improves over its' predecessor in nearly every aspect, from gameplay, which is now much smoother, enemies, level design and more.
The "hub world" in this game is extremely well designed, nearly every house is enterable, and enemies and items have been carefully placed around the world. You can see the interior of each house, regardless of whether it's relevant to the main mission or not, has been carefully crafted. The graphics in this game are also beautiful, they aren't the best, but they definitely are decent, and playing on near-max settings, the environments look extremely detailed.
Moreover, the game is well optimized, and the black bars from the previous game have finally been removed, however, you can turn them on if you'd like to. Sebastian also now has multiple unlockable outfits, there is a shooting range with a bunch of minigames to hone your aiming, a wide variety of new enemy types which are faster than ever, a new pistol and a lot more. Not only that, but the length of the story has drastically been increased as well. I'm only 9-ish hours or so in at the time of writing this review, and I'm only at Chapter 6 (there are 17 chapters in total), bearing in mind I didn't do all the side-missions, and am playing on casual (the medium difficulty, Survival, was already a huge challenge, so the difficulty of this game will no doubt prove challenging to most people).
Overall, I highly recommend anyone who was a fan of the first game, or the survival horror genre to pick this game up, you will love it. To me, The Evil Within 2 is the best third-person survival horror game of 2017, in conjunction with Resident Evil 7 being the best first-person survival horror game of 2017. Pick it up whenever you can, you won't regret it.

I have to give Dishonored 2 a lukewarm thumbs up. I am a big fan of Dishonored and came into the sequel full of high expectations. While it is a solid game with some nice new twists it actually feels less of a game than the original.
The original Dishonored began development as an action game and the stealth features were largely tacked on as the game design evolved (per the devs). Dishonored 2 was promised to have better stealth development as it was built into the game from the outset. Unfortunately the physical stealth mechanics (ignoring powers for a moment) are actually pretty simple... croutch and get high. Darkness doesn't help much and getting under tables doesn't help much. But croutch in a transom and you are well nigh invisible. The stealth mechanics in the original were simple more fun than in the sequel.
The tweaking of Corvo's powers a nice but as I was going for a shealth build not really ground breaking. The ability to switch control from animal to corpse to human was welcome but I found myself not using the power as much as I did in the original game. The reason is that rats are much more squeamish in 2 so are harder to get ahold of to control. Add in the relative lack of rat tunnels to navigate and the stealh usefullness of the power diminishes.
The Princess's powers are a VERY nice addition. I went with a more lethal/high-chaos build for her and linking NPCs together for kills is great fun and the shadow form made for really creepy kills. In fact her powers were the high light of the game for me.
One thing I was really looking forward to was the difference in the environment when playing low chaos vs high chaos. The original game did this well. I didn't really see any environmental changes at all between the 2 states. The ending chanbged but that was to be expected.
Dishonored 2 is a solid game and is totally enjoyable by Dishonored veterans as well as players new to the franchise but the developers got lost along the way and missed too many opportunities.

I'm conflicted about this game.  I will rate it for what it is and not for what it was.  With the correct mods, the game holds value.  Without the mods, the game is noteworthy.  Still, it feels like a game where they had a vision for a system further then just combat, but could not execute it.  I'll just give a rating on a 1-10 scale on what I feel without mods compared to the previous title, Shogun 2.  I will not compare it to Rome 1.
Graphics - 7 : There is nothing super about this area, and in fact does not feel far from Shogun 2.  Not much to say about it.
Combat - 8 : In depth strategy and control make the combat feel important, and if you don't mind micro managing units, this game hits the correct flavor bone.  It really is a treat, and you are rewarded with less troop losses from spending the time fighting battles, instead of just auto derping.  Archery, cavalry, infantry, and more each with unique rock paper scissor type of bonuses against eachother.  Siege warfare is a bit lack luster (especailly compared with once again its previous title) due to poor AI, but against other players it is a great deal more interesting.
Story - 4 : Story is not the goal of the game, and I'm proud to say it has never taken away from the Total War series, but if you are looking for a good story just read about these wars instead of playing a video game, or look for an RPG.
Hero Units - 3 : They really went down in this.  They did so well with little scenes in Shogun 2 (ninja failures successes), and with unique abilities that made each have strengths the others couldn't possibly give you.  In Rome, you are essentially getting the same exact person with different skins and different names for almost the same moves.  One of the biggest failures in the game in my opinion, but I'm sure there are others that would disagree.
AI combat - 6 : You have to make a leap in difficulty if you really want it to be a 6, since the basic AI is mostly garbage.  You will find diplomacy with the AI is very simple.  Combat with them is sometimes a laugh, I had one group of AI attack my town, but instead of attacking the town they stayed outside of it, watching it intently.  It was as if they wanted me to leave the town to attack them, so I had to wait 30 minutes for the battle to end.  It was a staring contest, and I won.  You won't always encounter these issues, but you will see them at least once in a campaign, and that is being generous (unless you auto derp a whole bunch, and even then you probably will see something that will make you giggle.
Gameplay - 7 : I was going to give this a lower number, but the start of the game is pretty good now that they spend an entire year fixing it.  Yay?  I won't go into too much detail on it, but there will be a point in a play through where you realize you are literally just going around taking stuff over one by one by one, waiting on a civil war to happen.  Until that civil war happens, the game feels like a grind.  I absolutely hate grinding, but if you don't mind building stuff in over 20 cities while just going from city to city to city doing the same thing over and over again, then this game is perfect for you.  The major difference is shogun 2 wasn't as big, and realm divide happened pretty quick, and when everyone unites against you the game chances into a whole new pace that creates a welcome change at almost a perfect time, keeping you from a real grind.
So, overall I will recommend this game, but with caution.  If you are looking for the past glory of total war games, I say just replay those, but if you are tired of the past games and have a few hundred hours to kill, feel free to try Total War Rome.  (Just a heads up, there is a great deal I did not mention in this.  The game is massive, and there are many things I just don't have time to cover like glitches/bugs, historical accuracy, units, map, ect ect.  I love the total war series, and I apologize in advance to anyone I offend.)

The original series had a profound impact on my childhood, and even a lasting effect on my life since. This game is a worthy successor to the original series. A funny and engaging story, and brilliant graphics updated for the modern day which still maintain that fairy-tale aspect of the original. I can't wait for the next episodes!

The first chapter is fun, though I really feel that they have missed out on one of my favorite aspects of the King's Quest stories...the fairy tale aspect.  Seems like they could have easily exchanged Graham for Guybrush Threepwood and it would have worked just as well.
Chapter two is out now, and it has definitely filled in on the fairy tale aspect.  But it is considerably shorter than the first chapter.  I also dislike that they force you to replay the chapter if you want to get all of the achievements.  I appreciated that in the first chapter it was a possibility, if you were thorough.  Still an enjoyable game but I am concerned as to where it will go from here.  So far each chapter seems to have taken place prior to an older title.  Chapter 1 occurs prior to the original, and chapter 2 prior to KQ2.
Will update as more chapters come out.

The original Postal while famous for it's controversial themes and gameplay had aged extremely poorly. Postal Redux, the new and improved remake of the first game is a much welcome suprise from Running with Scissors. The controls are far simpler and make the game playable in this modern era. Two new levels have been added along with all of the past bonus content added to the original.
Other than this very little has changed. Everything is as you remember the original game to be, only with new, improved artwork and unfortunately a lot of the same issues. Level design is still a bit awkward and despite attempts to make the camera and traversing buildings work smoothly. It still becomes very hard to see what is in front of you and where your character is located in the urban levels.
Some people may want to avoid the high impact themes but mainly these devolve into teenage style angsty violence rather than something actually offensive. If you were interested in the original and found it too hard to play, or was already a fan, this is something you will enjoy.

Though I was very late playing the original Half-Life, this fan remake struck a nostalgic chord for me. And though I hold to the belief that no game can or will ever be perfect, this game serves to highlight what can be accomplished by a dedicated team. It seems that this game started as a labor of love, and that really shows through in the gameplay. It's that attention to detail, that capturing of essence that makes this game feel like the original hl. Going into it, I kind of expected it to be just annother attempt to capitalize on the popularity of half-life. It was after all virtually identical save for the graphics update and a few minor tweaks. But in my opinion it did half-life justice, bringing an older game into a new life to be enjoyed for many a year to come. So I really just wanna say thanks to the devs, for making a game that really shines, while not overshadowing it's inspiration.

There are multiple means to your objectives depending on your skills, although only some playthroughs can get to certain areas or make use of certain items.
Save your AP ammo!

System Shock 2, 1990s gaming's swansong, can boast the honor of having written the book on complex hybrid FPS gameplay, open-ended skill progression, conceptual horror, sound design and environmental storytelling. Now that I think of it, that means it's pretty much written the book on everything in modern-day gaming.
Games still emulate it, either directly or indirectly, to this day; and more recently in the 2010s, there's now a strange sort of niche genre around it, which I nickname "Shocklike" games (for instance, when Bethesda rebooted Prey 2, they demanded up front that the game be designed as if it were "System Shock 3"). Even incompetent and ethically bankrupt publishers swear by it; that's got to mean something!
Oh, and you ought to play it. Not only does it still hold up remarkably well, but the experience it offers remains unparalleled in its quality, unique in its atmosphere and overall, really freaking great.
