Other than Lesuire Suit Larry & a handful of Police Quest titles, I was more on the LucasArts side of the fence in respect to 90's point & click adventure gaming & as such came into this without any reverence or knowledge for the past King's Quest series.
As far as fantasy setting adventure games go, other than Simon The Sorcerer & to a lesser extent the Discworld spin-off games, this series is regarded as kind of the defacto knights and wizards avenue for storytelling in the genre. To it's credit, in a category of gaming that went up it's own backside with trying to out surreal it's competition when it ran out of unique story settings, it knows what it's going for.
King's Quest is (and has always been) very twee & full of non offensive attempts at humour, especially puns. More then often this comedy misses more than it hits and ends up coming across like a low-budget, imitiation, straight to broadcast Disney cartoon. 30 years ago, this was passable in a video-game where intelligent script writing wasn't something expected out of a bedroom sized husband and wife programming team. Nowadays however, especially with three decades of bonafide classics that have come since, the bar is astronomically high to aim to try and create a 'funny' game.
Attached to a somewhat shakey story premise which borrows perhaps a little too heavily from the film 'The Princess Bride', both the art direction and voice acting are really rather good with plenty of recognisable talent taking on character roles. The background art in particular is stunning & while perhaps small in scope being released as an episodic game rather than a fully realized project, the work that's been done by The Odd Gentlemen so far is impressive.
The actual puzzles are certainly not on the abstract side of the spectrum which is usually the death knell of any point & click regardless of how good its story is. However, In going for accessibility, other than basic movement there is really only a singular interact button which seems somewhat limited with no method for combining objects or other verbs that you'd see in a SCUMM-era game. This could make the challenge of progression seem trivial for more seasoned players.
There is also a liberal scattering of QTE's & FPS targeting action sequences, which while not as offensive as some would make out don't really add much to the experience. It's very unlikely that players new to point & click games are going to start off with this franchise with more recognisable brands like Walking Dead or Game Of Thrones also on offer, therefore making the game 'accessible' just seems a sure fire way of alienating the already limited audience.
Episode 1 of a what is set to be a 5 episode series will take you roughly 4 hours to complete. Very much in keeping with the Telltale games model who's recent success it seems the brought back to life Sierra brand is trying desperately to imitate.
How much you're going to enjoy this title seems dependant on how much nostalgia you have for Kings Quest of days gone by. Despite clear effort going into this product, it just doesn't feel like it has an interesting story to tell or anything new to bring. If there was a middle ground between a yes and no recommendation I would definitely have selected that one.
While I wouldn't suggest buying the season pass until it can be judged if they can keep the quality consistent, Episode 1 might be worth a try if you're already well versed in the classic adventure game genre. If this isn't the case, instead I'd recommend one of the more popular Telltale offerings or the recent deluxe remasters of some of the 90's classics such as Grim Fandango, Gabriel Knight or BrokenSword.

I am surprised at all the postive reviews; this is not a bad game, but it isn't the best thing to ever grace the Alien franchise either. Without the Alien brand name, you never would have heard of this game as anything but another console oriented FPS lacking innovation, plagued with gigabytes of mediocre cutscenes and marginal voice acting.
Pros: ... I am thinking... Hmmm doesn't crash; very stable. PC controls are fairly well executed, rare for a console targeted title. It has a space theme. Better lit than the Doom3. There mom, I said something nice...
Cons:
Typical linear, overly scripted, written for console hardware, FPS title intertwined with a low budget, barely B grade horror movie. Has a lot of gravity for a space themed game.
I've only ever been scared by the games Doom, Clive Barker's "Undying", and F.E.A.R 1/2 (honorable mention: STALKER series). The only thing scary in this game is how frighteningly algorhythmic and dumb the A/I is. I am not exagerating slightly: the clunky artificial feel of the Alien and NPC behaviors breaks any immersion the game might of had, making "fright" an impossibility.
The net effect A/I behavior has on gameplay is to make basic movement aggravatingly slow, cheaply turning ten hours of normal gameplay into thirty hours of painstakingly slow boring hide/creep/wait cycles; you can't do anything but creepy crawl most everwhere without the Alien using you like a catnip filled plushie toy.
You might be startled once or twice (I wouldn't call it "scared"), and only when the devs resort to cheap scripted sound events. Scary once, dumb twice, maddening thrice.
I won't say avoid this game, but wait for the "Gold" Collectors edition to sell under $19.99 with all DLC before buying if you are really interested.

I understand, that there is not much to do for your PC but even though, I have maxed out settings on a 5 years old PC, the graphics are incredible, the atmosphere is dense. The locations are straight out of the movie, and the sound... my cylon god... the sound!
People say, that in order for a movie to be less scary, instead of covering your eyes, you should cover your ears.
The sound carries the game immensely and it comes all from the movies. Sometimes you sit and hide, and although you have some vision in the tight spots, what you really need is to listen if the Xenomorph is still near you. It also adds to the creature itself, as you hear with every step just how big and menacing this thing really is.
I have never been this scared in a game, but be advised, that this game takes its darn time to get going.
The gloves came of some time near the 4th hour of the game and from there on be sure you are not to jumpy or have a heart condition.
I thought, that once I have been killed by Xeno a few times, I would get accustomed to the death animations, but as of now it really depends on the situation, but believe me this is still no sight I like in the middle of the night.
Adding to the whole thing is the brave but old school save system. You cannot just hit F5 and hope for the best... You need to spend a lot of time on your knees, hiding in closets, vents and under beds in order to crawl to the relative safety of the safe point... and saving is not instant... you can get killed while saving.
I also very much like the hacking mini games which coupled with the fact, that you are VERY vulnerable during them, make them really tense.
The game is long, which adds to the survival simulation aspect, after several attempt to finish the hunt, you REALLY are tired and long for a sendoff for Ripley for civilisation and possibly on a new horrific adventure.
I am totally blown away by this game. It might not be a game of the year, but as this is a very different game from your typical AAA title it might be the UNDERDOG of the year.
The game you should play, but most probably have not! Best use of a lisence since... Arkham... (and I do know Shadow of Mordor exists... I have it :D )
on the game difficulty: People (like the IGN review) claim the Alien AI is unfair, and the game gets frustrating... well I had no such expierience, although VERY tough, the ALien seemed to "play fair"... when it was let loose it was mostly my fault when I screwed up, and there were sections were you very safe from it for entire sections... but you NEED to be a patient person. Do you like to feel fear and anxiety?  Do you like to forget your life and feel completely immersed in your game?  If you said, "Yes Sir, thank you Sir." then this game is for you.  I am recommending this game because it is perfect for what it is.  It is a sci-fi survival horror game set in the Alien universe.  The environment is beautiful and it matches the technology of the original Alien movie perfectly (even down to the clunky buttons, the old computer screens, and the sounds).  When you start the game you literally feel like you are in a ship from the first Alien movie.  The graphics are beautiful, and the AI is amazing!  The AI doesn't feel like its run on an algorithm.  It is completely unpredictable.  There is no exploiting the AI in this game.  You can't control it no matter how hard you try.  This is very good, because none of us play games just to cheat our way through them...  right?  So with that said.... I recommend this game.
However.... this game is for the gamer who wants to feel the fear that Ripley felt in the original Alien movie.  Helpless, alone, and scared.  I learned a lot about myself while playing this game.  I learned that I do not like being hunted without being able to turn the situation around and be the hunter.  In this game, you are not the hunter, and I don't think you will ever be the hunter... you are the hunted.  You are completely helpless in this game.  You will find yourself hiding under desks almost♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants.  I learned that in these types of "be the hunted or the hunter" situations I tend to try and get the upper hand and kill off threats.   In this game you can't do that, and it definitely  raises the anxiety level.  Don't get me wrong, its not frustrating in any way... its doing exactly what its supposed to do. This game is meant to instill fear, and it does that perfectly.  If something is chasing youm it doesn't mean its game over.  If something grabs you, you can still get away (sometimes).  There are tactics to avoid and divert enemy encounters, but you are not going to "clean the map of all threats".  So with that said, you must now ask yourself something... do you like fear?  Do you like thrills?  Jump on board the station and see if you can survive.

Broforce is a fun, arcade side scrolling game developed by Free Lives. It was highly sucessful after it's release in 2014. The game is a throwback to action movies from the 1980s, through it's over-the-top action and intense gameplay. The game seems simple in design at first, but after playing for a while, you pick up on the attention to detail that makes this game such a gem.
The controls are simple as well, making it easy to pick up and play. The game runs smoothly and you really feel like a movie hero, slicing and dicing through hoards of no name grunts. As the game goes on, both the game itself and the player made maps (which I'll cover in a moment) add a level of challenge, keeping the game fresh.
As well as the pre-made maps the game comes with, it also has a built in map editor where players can create their own maps to share on the Steam workshop. By being able to share maps, the game maintains a level of mystery. Some maps are made to be played with a somewhat stealthy playstyle by using tunnels and multiple routes and ways to complete maps, whereas others encourage you to go all out, guns blazing, and blow as much stuff up as you can!
In my opinion, the game is best played in co-op. As much fun as it is to run around as MacGyver or Chuck Norris on your own, having a buddy along for the ride just adds to the hilarity that ensues when you play a map or two... or three... five...

The only downside I find to the game was that I just burned myself out. I was having so much fun planting explosives and hip firing that I would just play... and play. The game loses it's appeal after a while. This is not a game you'll sit down and play for hours to level up your character, or build that new house, or go on that raid. This game is purely for the fun aspect. Apart from that there's a total lack of story, but eh. EXPLOSIONS!!!!
Final Ratings:
Graphis: As a throw back to the retro, the graphics breathe life into the old style of game design. They're not next gen, but they're sure as hell prettier :P. Also runs better than next gen.
Gameplay: Broforce is fast paced and over the top. It doesn't have deep game mechanics, but I think we all love a bit of shoot-em-up.
Story: What story?
End result: I give Broforce a solid 7.5 outta teyyan.

When i finally got around to playing the first Evil Within about a year ago i was very impressed by that game, especially considering all the problems it had at launch, and when i completed it i couldn't wait for a sequel. I didn't find out about this game until two days before release while i was replaying the first one and was very surprised.
My first thought was that surely they are going to ruin the sequel, remove everything that was good from the first, fill it with microtransaction and the pc release would be made with the least amount of effort possible to make it "run", but i decided to give it a chance and look and behold: A pc friendly game without any microtransactions.
Just because you enjoyed the first game that's no guarantee you will like this, it's not just more of the same. Rather than a linear game with levels designed to be played in order you have a fairly open world. As soon as you complete the tutorial part of the game you are free to go anywhere you want in the first area, whether you want to just get on with the main mission or if you want to go scavenge some ammunition.
Progression with the main missions is required to unlock further areas so it's not truly open world.
The story is nothing special and is quite boring and predictable and will make no sense if you haven't played the first game but it ties up most of the loose strings from the first game.
The general enemy design is mostly the same, general zombie like enemies with the occasional deliciously macabre enemy or boss.
Most of the gameplay is largely unchanged. The basic enemies are nearly identical to those from the first game and there's a boss fight trown in here and there. You have much of the same weapons including the agony crossbow wich is now named warden crossbow for some reason. You can still sneak up behind enemies and kill them with a sneak attack or you can just shoot them until they're dead. You can also still throw bottles into the enmies head to stun them and allow you to stealth kill them, although it's more difficult to do now.
Green gel is now mostly found from killed enemies rather than found lying around and is used to unlock and upgrade various abilites such as increasing max health, reducing weapon sway or letting you move faster when crouched.
Weapon parts, wich can be found lying around, is now used to upgrade weapons and bolts at workbenches and ammo pouches can be found in various places to allow you to carry more ammo of a certain type.
There is also a crafting system where you can find things such as plants to make medicine or gunpowder to make ammo.
Crafting anything but medicine costs more resources if done in the field rather than at a workbench making you consider if you should use that gunpowder now to make some bullets or save it to make more later.
Ammo management is still a very important thing, especially at the beginning of the game where you really feel the pain of each miss or even just getting a bodyshot instead of a headshot.
On a more pc specific note i have to say that this is a good port. There's settings for turning on/off motion blur, depth of field and bloom for those who hate that (i do). You can select a fov from 45 to 90. There's a generous mouse speed setting meaning you probably won't think it's too fast at the lowest setting (or the other way around) and no mouse acceleration or other mouse issues apart from a slighly floaty mouse in the menus.
There's settings for sprinting and taking cover to be hold or toggle, a lot of hud options, and there's also a setting to enable the letterboxing from the first game (the horror!) with a joke in the description showing they realise it was a big mistake to make it forced in the first game and that they also have some humour (there's another joke about it when you beat the game and unlock it).
A surprisingly well made pc port wich i have only a few gripes with: no console (yet) and it could have had more graphics options. In fact there's not really any real graphics options like textures, effects, particles etc.. so if you don't have a good computer you're out of luck.
One thing i found very annoying was what i can only call a graphical glitch wich i guess stems from the rendering method they use. It's the same one that alien isolation had where there is a lot of odd aliasing and shimmering where there really shouldn't be any and the in game anti aliasing (fxaa, taa or both) barely has any effect on it while making everything blurry.
I finished the game on survival(normal) in about 15 hours but i'm already looking forward to replaying it on nightmare(hard). There's also classic mode when you've beaten the game once: No autosaves, limited manual saves and no upgrades (neither weapons nor abilites).
I encountered only a single bug where i went into a room, acivated an event, some things happened(no spoilers) and when it was over i couldn't open a container inside. But there was an autosave from about 2 minutes before that i reloaded.
This time i opened the container before triggering the event and everything worked as it sould.
All in all a good game, but lacking the feeling of the first. More a twisted lovechild of several other games and franchises including Resident Evil(there's several clear homages to RE4), Silent Hill, Zombiu, the latest Tomb Raiders and a few others.

The game has enough save points though. Only once I was annoyed that I lost one hour playtime in a open world map because I died, maybe try to save more often in those levels.
The horror atmosphere was good most of the time. It sadly got a bit lost in those open world levels. Generally I don't think the horror is as good as in the first game. It has been a bit mainstreamed I guess. Also the first game had a more rusty feeling to it. It still had plenty of scares to keep you on edge, especially in the main story levels.
Graphics are just marvelous. They really improved over the first game. It was amazing to see the detail that went into the characters. The game also runs fluid and has MANY options including a FOV slider! Some people complain about performance issues. I didn't had any. Solid 50+ FPS on ultra settings 1080p with a GTX 970 and i7 6700K. There might be more optimisations later with patches and driver updates. I also ran into a graphic bug which displays textures with weird squares. Forcing anisotropic filtering in the driver fixed it. Probably gets fixed later.
The sound is really good! Especially the score is top notch. Some of those orchestral tracks sounded really amazing! Wouldn't mind a physical limited release of it (like on vinyl).
Despite those small hiccups, the game really plays and runs good. Bet it will be even better later. Definitely worth the money for me! I absolutely enjoyed every minute of it. Might actually be GOTY for me! Is the first better? Phew, that is really difficult to answer and a personal taste question. I guess for me they are on par. TEW2 has better gameplay while TEW1 has better horror. Decide for yourself. Generally they improved pretty much all aspects in TEW2 (except horror).
Rating 9/10

The Elder Scrolls Online is part of the ever popular Elder Scrolls franchise; this is the first multiplayer instalment however. The game was released on PC in April 2014. The game got rid of the subscription to play in March of 2015; however a full purchase of the game is still required for account activation.
The game is set in Tamriel, much like the other games, but you are able to traverse many more different locations compared to the previous game's one location model. The game play in this game is quite similar to the other games in the series, in that you can play in either first person or third person camera, and everything is largely nonlinear. The game throws in a good mixture of quests, events and of course, exploration.  You are able to play as a number of difference racers, some of which I have not seen before in the Elder Scrolls series, so it’s nice to see more variety here. Along with four different classes to select, Templar, Dragonknight, Sourcer, and Nightblade.  The combat in TESO is similar to that of World of Warcraft, you have a set number of action bars available, and you mash the button you want to use, there is of course an optimum rotation your character should be using rather than just rolling your face across the keyboard though. I much preferred this combat system to what of Oblivion even though it may come across as simplified.
Whilst the game is an MMO, I have to say I only really played it as a single player experience. You will occasionally run into the odd other real player when you are out in the world, but there is no real need to interact with them. Each time you level up in game, you are given points to spend in three main stats, health, magicka and stamina – along with a skill point. These skill points can be spent on new abilities for your class, a different weapon set, your race and even any guilds that you are a part of. This allows you to mould your character to exactly how you want it to be. I went with a rogue type character that snuck in and killed enemies before they had a chance to realise I was even in the room, but there are plenty of other play styles.
Since this is an online game, the graphics are going to be a little watered down, but the game still looks really good, comparing it to an unmodded Skyrim, it is actually on par with its style if you ask me. I was playing with everything maxed out and on 4k resolution, but even so, it looked gorgeous. Some of the environments you are in look so flush and vibrant with wild life. If you are playing on a less powerful computer though, you will find a huge amount of graphical options that will allow you to lower the settings to get the game to run – this does make the game look very poor though, it isn’t a very well optimized game sadly.
The story in Elder Scrolls Online is something which really hooked me straight away. I learnt more about the lore of Elder Scrolls in this game than all of the others combined. The plot is indirectly linked to the other games, and takes place a thousand years before the events of Skyrim, and 800 years before Morrowind and Oblivion.  There is a huge amount of lore to be found in the game, whether it be a quest, or a book, or a random event, there is plenty to learn about if you are interested in the lore of Elder Scrolls.
This game has some fantastic voice acting in. Every single NPC that you need to talk to for a quest is fully voice acted and is done to an extremely high quality level. I was expecting having to read a lot from my past experience with MMO games, but I was pleasantly surprised that I could sit back and enjoy the dialog between the NPCs. This may have been why I took so much more information in than previous games in the series.
The locations and zones that you will find in Elder Scrolls Online are ginormous. One of the very first zones you visit is one of the biggest I have seen in a game. It takes you a good 15 minutes of just walking to go from one side to the other. A lot of it does tend to be emptiness with the odd random enemy sadly though. The towns seem to be a hive of activity from either other players or NPCs so it gives you a sense of not being alone in the huge world.  There is one main quest which you will follow throughout the course of the game, but in good RPG style, the meat and bones comes from the side quests. Each line of quests has its own backstory, a problem you have to solve, and then a resolution which will sometimes result in you having to make a decision and then you will be given a reward, and in most cases this will be equipment. Whilst most of the quests in the game can be considered repetitive, I didn’t really feel as if I was completing the same one over and over again – because I was so immersed in the story, I wasn’t just going to kill X amount of bandits, I was aiding the nearby village from future attacks, so on and so on.  Some of the quests can be hard to locate the quest giver, but as you get close to an NPC that will offer you a quest, you will get a marker on your map.
I have been playing The Elder Scrolls Online for almost twenty hours, and I am only level 15 with my character. The max level for any character is 50, meaning there is a boat load of content in this game and I am by no means getting bored at all. I can see there being a large amount of replay ability too. Creating a different character with a different play style will no doubt give you another 200 hours of content after you finish your first. You also have the end game content as well, such as veteran dungeons, crafting, and of course, PVP.
Technically, The Elder Scrolls Online is technically sound. I had no issues with bugs, crashing or glitches. Everything is working as intended with no problems. Obviously you are going to need a stable internet connection to be able to play properly; but with the large amount of settings to configure, you should be able to get the game to run on almost anything. I would like to have seen a field of view option, but maybe I am asking too much there. The game also has capabilities of using add-ons, I didn’t find a need to use any, but should you require some, you can use the Curse client to manage and install them all for you without any issues.
In summary, if you play this game as a single player experience, or maybe even hook up with a friend to play through, you will get a huge amount of enjoyment out of it. If you go in expecting it to be a bustling MMORPG game, you will be servery disappointed.  I am having an awesome time playing and I am thoroughly enjoying every moment of my experience in The Elder Scrolls Online.

Just Cause 3 is definitely one of the best feeling open world games that has come out in recent years, and I really think thats saying something.
About five or so years ago when Just Cause 2 released it got less than stellar reviews, but the general consensus was that it was a great summer blockbuster fill in game to hold you off until the fall season of games come out. Back then that was all Just Cause was to people, and the past few years have been good to Avalanche Studios.
They've released Mad Max as a standalone game, with a likely franchise to come in the future which leaves their cash cow (Just Cause) to experiment and change up.
On that note, there's virtually nothing that changes about how terrible the vehicular handling has been. As it was in previous games, I wish to god they didn't focus at all on driving. You would think after four years driving would be improved, even tweaked a bit, especially with Mad Max under their belt. Here it feels like it was deliberately scrapped and something else slightly worse was replaced with it. Same thing can be said for flying and riding bikes. The upshot? You can pull unrealistic maneauvers and nitrous boosts in virtually any vehicle, which makes up for the terrible mobility.
Its like they knew it was terrible but didn't change it because they either didn't have time or didnt have money to bother with revamping the driving mechanics. I feel like all of the focus in Just Cause 3 was focused on ironing out the wing suit.  More on that in a bit.
Vehicles suck. They handle worse than poorly and I advise staying away if you really wanna enjoy the game.
Combat is far more improved in Just Cause 2. Not at all varied, but the reaction times of NPCs is much smoother and character animations adds for more immersive kills and takedowns. You'll be spending most of your time in the air though so I wouldn't worry about how they look. When the♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan enemies don't stop spawning until the base is captured, which keeps the pace up. While they aren't too complicated to beat I wish that the enemies had a bit more acrobatic ability than what they have.  Harnesses and rope darts would be great additions to make them worth♥♥♥♥♥♥against me.
They never are, and I feel like every time I go up against another barrage of choppers or a herd of tanks my suspension to disbelief in the fight is shrinking. I kick♥♥♥♥♥ The trick is to do it flawlessly.
The weapons aren't as varied as you would hope but there are plenty and trust in me they got plenty of stopping power.
The greatest addition to Just Cause 3 is without a doubt the wing suit. In previous games Rico has amassed a reputation as a daredevil with lots of useful gadgets, but we could never hold him in the same light as Batman or the Green Arrow. If he isn't a super hero in your eyes now, then your blind. Indeed the Scorpion's grapple hook/wing suit combo give him the ability to fly indefinitely and with some impressive maneuvers. I don't even touch vehicles anymore because of how easier and quicker it is to fly there. The controls of flying are a bit difficult but super addicting once you get the hang of it.
I would spend $44.99 again just for the wing suit.
A bittersweet design choice is locking upgrades and perks behind obnoxious challenges and game activities. Some of these are fun, tasking you with flying and blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up. Above all th epoint is to get you to really pay attention to the detail of the game before you get cool upgrades, I'm okay with this, but it shows how terrible certain mechanics are IE: Driving, etc.
They got us to play the game to get the perks we wanted, but is a frustrated customer what they really wanted?
The game runs like butter for me and I'm rocking a gtx970 with an i7-3770 ivy bridge. I know that performance was stunted in the earlier days of release because of how the online leaderboards kept signing people out.  There has been some debate and contraversy about the online mechanics in the game having you sign in (LOL its a single player game). It seems silly at first but considering how many players there are per day playing the game and how quickly and often they are trying to break each others record, the leaderboards are an awesome awesome addition. Basically, everytime you get in game other players have beaten your record or set new ones. It adds an arcade atmosphere to the game because I'm reminded that on top of the tethers and obsenely large explosions and high octane action, its just an unrealistic and insanely engaging game that asks you to come back and bask in your own shenanigans, if not the records of shenanigans of others.
The map is huge, as one can imagine. I'm not sure that the terrains are improved because I haven't seen the entire map but it blew me away when I saw it.
If you found Just Cause 2 fun, you will find this addictive. If you found Just Cause 2 boring, you will find this slightly appealing because of the wing suit. Don't ♥♥♥♥♥ about it not being realistic, don't kill yourself if its not keeping your attention after five hours (I can't stop playing for some reason), and don't make speeches about how stupid it is.

All in all Dishonored 2 is as great a sequel as you can hope for. Once most of the technical stuff was fixed the game ran pretty well, looked great and felt awesome. I wouldn't say the story was a dissappointment, but it felt a bit lackluster compared to the original.

Smite starts off as the best moba ever but, turns into a very repetative experience that stops you from playing it as much as you might want to, lets dig in.
It's easy to pick up but, hard to master. The controls are simple (for a moba) and the familiar camera angle makes you feel more in control. The game's well optimized and looks fantastic. There's usually minimal ability clutter with a few exceptions. The strategy is more straight forward than most mobas and even a little on the generic side which can make the game less stressful but, almost boring after 500+ hours.
There are several game modes to play. Each are detailed and geometricaly balanced. They have their own meta but, the traditional 3 lane (conquest) typically lasts a good 10-35 minutes or more depending on how the game is going. Victory can be achieved very early due to smites steeper comeback curve. If this does happen any team can vote to surrender after 10 min. Unfortunately many of the games are over before 10 min is even reached but, you'll never have to sit through a 40 min stomp session.
They all have their combos and counters for eachother but, don't do so as hard as other mobas. To simplify things further, Smite gives each god a recommend role: Hunter (adc), Mage (mid), Warrior (solo), Gaurdian (supp) and Assassain (jung) which are interchangeable between gods. In unranked you can have two of the same gods out at once just not on the same team. Hi-rez isn't the best at balancing them, there always seem to be a handful that completely eclipse the others.The gods might come from ancient mythology but, their voice overs tend to be on the 2010 derpy side. Imo they are coming out with too many new gods too fast, it's killing the meta.
Builds are fun and easy to make, you'll find that many gods use similar builds with small changes to augment them or adapt to different circumstances. The items themselves are way less impactful compared to your god's level but, will make all the difference in your performance. Again, when it comes to balancing hi-rez falls a little short, some items are stupid good for any mode on any god and some are almost useless.
There's a lot in smite to collect and with enough playtime almost everything can be bought using in game currency (gems). You'll start out with a handful of gods and by the time you get the hang of them you'll be able to unlock more. You can also buy gods outright if you want, there's a lot of freedom. People ♥♥♥♥♥ a lot about having to unlock the gods but, buying the god pack for $20 is like buying the game.
It blows, don't get me wrong its great in terms of moba communities but, I still found it tiring to shrug off players giving me♥♥♥♥♥♥for trying to learn and adapt to each update. Even in unranked players expect you to know every god, every item and every strat. If you go ask for help you might as well go ♥♥♥♥ yourself instead, it doesn't matter how hard you try or how well you play, it only matters if you're better than the other team. Play with your friends.
Smite's offical forums are♥♥♥♥♥♥ to stay up to date
is great, you can also voice your feedback and vote for things like balance changes.
If you're looking for a more casual moba that you might be able to take very far, smite could shine down some favor upon you. It IS a moba tho, it still requires a lot of time, perseverance and above all patience.

I have been playing this game for awhile now. I played it before it went on steam mind you. This is my review of the game and the moba genre in general.
Why should you play smite?
Well first off the game is amazing. It is a fresh take on the moba genre. The difference about SMITE is it is 3rd person, not top down. That changes EVERYTHING. Seriously, EVERYTHING. The way you ward, gank, aim, fight, lane, EVERYTHING. The other big difference is that the Champions or heros are insted Gods. They are from all sorts of mytholgys. Hi Rez takes pride in making them just like their lore .
I play LoL, DOTA, HOTS etc. Why should i like this game?
The game is again new and fresh. It also a little easier to learn how to buy and move. However, Aiming is much harder in this. Autos or Basics are skillshots not lock-ons. That means you need to aim where they land and how to control where they go. Also most skill are skillshots no lock-ons.
What can i do in SMITE?
There are many different gamemodes, Such as Arena. Arena is like TDM. You have 500 tickets to start off with. The goal is to kill Gods, minions, and help your minions reach the portal. If a god is killed its -5 points to the enemy team. If a minion is killed by a god -1 or if they reach the portal -1. The winner is who gets the other team to 0. This is just one of the many gamemodes made. Conqest is the traditional moba gamemode. 3 lanes, Left, Mid, Right, And a jungle. The goal is to reach the enemys Titan and kill it. But first you must destroy the enemy towers and phenoixs.
Whats the community like?
Meh. It kinda is getting worse and worse but it can get better.
It used to be AMAZING. Everyone was nice and toxic behavior was little to none because of the V button. The V button as i like to call it can say somthing in chat witha voice. For example-
Press VG2
It says GANK MIDDLE LANE.
Simple right?
It has it for everything you need. Telling when to gank to if you are out of mana.
Overall this is one of the best mobas out there. I HIGHLY reccamend this game. Sorry for bad spelling if there is any.

What can be said about postal that hasn't been already said before, i was curious to see how a 1997 game could be remade for today's gaming atmosphere , I loved the original postal game and played it back then on a Pentium 2 pc , So after playing Postal Redux i can honestly say its worth the money, for new players of the series, But for the older players it's a sticky deal only purchase affair. I think a lot could be focused on making the in game experience better than just the graphics.
Note : i will not be covering the co-op / online/ rampage  modes , never a fan of those modes. I dont think this classic needs those modes either. When the game name already says postal.
Here are my Pros and cons on the game.
- New levels, the  Excess Postage campaign of 23 levels is amazing  playing those 23 levels alone in one go is enough to make you go postal and understand why this series is a hit with many fans.
- The graphics are updated and its much more easier on the eyes now. Good visuals and effects.
- Co-op mode , should be fun although i stayed away from it due to the bad pings i get<regional issue not the game>
- They have added neat retro stuff like filters you can try em out to ruin your eyesight.
- Retains the tank controls , love it.
- No improvements to the guns , i think the guns are much worse here in accuracy and range here than the original game, the flamethrower is practically useless since it gets blocked out by the objects, frequently, the machine gun replacement is way worse than the original gun. shotgun, pistol , rocket launcher are your only accurate options specially for non civilian kills.
- Heavy system requirements , i think this will be a major turn off for the older fans who ran the original game on way older systems that this game demands minimum of 8gb ram.
The devs have explained the requirement here do be wary of it
-Long initial loading time this has been major turn off because in game like postal you tend run through the levels quickly and death is frequent visitor . I have never seen such a complex loading system in a game before to break it down.
- There is one loading screen when you select single player mode.
- There is one more longer loading screen ( it might take upto 5 minutes depending on your config)
- Between the levels there instant loading sometimes and a bit of loading later.
- If you die , expect another long loading screen to reload.
- Not sure how to put it but the new engine is not that smooth, although it ran great for me most of the times , there was a lot of slowdowns and freezes in various parts. i hate to imagine how this would be in the multiplayer/co-op modes.
-
, i guess its the PG era we live in now.
It was a sting of nostalgia playing postal again in the modern redux, But i would jump into the original game any day , it just shows how complex gaming has become today just grab the original and play it and see the difference. It is just so much easier and fun to get in and play.
Knowing how good RWS are with the fans and supporting their game releases , i expect them to smooth out the game even more and fix the issues. Smooth gameplay should be the focus of the game over other things, that fast and easy gameplay is what made the original a classic.
Hoping for a good sequel to postal 2 , the other one must not be mentioned.
The game is easily a 6.5/10 , would have been my favorite postal game  if the game was easy on the hardware requirements, which would have allowed many of the casual gamers with entry level hardware to play it.

This is a bit of a funny review to write, since the Steam's rating system of good or bad once again shows it's thorough uselessness. I would like an Average or Just OK rating. :/ In the end I recommended it anyway (mostly because it is free).
First of all, for the TL;DR fans - the game is OK and, since you don't have to pay anything, it probably won't hurt you to play it. However the game has some problems, mostly rooted in the sticky movement, that can make the game a bit of a hassle to play for the wast majority of the experinece and a downright infuriating mess at the final true bossfight. The narrative is OK, but nothing too amazing. It's all just OK.
GAMEPLAY
For the most part it is a rather simplistic run into mobs until they explode and retreat if you need to recover HP ordeal. Since HP recovery is fast and crafting can quickly make you very powerful, the was majority of the gameplay is very easy (mobs die in 1-2 hits and take 1 damage for the most part, if you craft [and why wouldn't you?]).
Crafting materials are dropped plentifully and if you are like me and have to explore until you find all the chests (which is optional obviously) you will quickly find yourself too powerful and bored with, unfortunately, the majority of the game.
The game picks up only during the dungeon end bossfights, for which you can choose the difficulty (why couldn't there be a difficulty setting for the whole game?). Most of these fights are far tougher than the rest of the game, but still not very difficult and relatively simple, apart from the last boss.
At first I was happy that finally there was a tough encounter, but this joy of mine quickly faded. You see, the game has a very sticky control scheme and, when the bossfight is highly reliant on quick and precise movement and hitting anything can stop you for a long time, the gameplay goes from a fun challange to an immense round of maddening shouts.
I can't even say that the developer really screwed up with the control scheme, because it isn't his/her fault, it is the fault of the RPG Maker engine. Since the usecase of the engine doesn't really include necessity for fast movement in more than 4 directions on a less strictly defined square grid, the game suffers a lot for it. As it is, the one potentially engaging encounter seems to be more of an omen to the game then a boon. (Died 5 or 6 times on the damn thing and mostly because I got stuck on the spawning mobs. Also those lasers starting out as small lines and then growind 3 squares wide didn't help for immediate reaction.) :/
STORY
As previously mentioned, it's ok. Kind of a shame really, since I found the game would have benefitted from a less direct storyline. It's really just a straightforward adventure with a really rather predictable end boss. So much so, that I thought this was all gonna be a set up for a bigger twist that never came. However as simple as it is, it doesn't offend and it makes sense for the most part. Alternatively it could have used some kind of a mystery subplot or mystery in the core story that players had piece together themselves. Overall it's just OK. (I could be more specific, but that would require spoilers.) :/
OVERALL
If I had to rate it, the game would be 6/10. However I can easily see that if you are a less picky person or find the story interesting, this game would be far more interesting for you and would score higher.
(Scores are subjectived and don't mean anything anyway, but why not toss in a random number if you can, makes everybody seem very scholarly without ever needing to base the notions on anything).
Sorry if I misspelled anything, but I have to honest about the fact that I just don't care enough to proof read this. :/

If I could describe this game it would be like Hydlide. Except less of a grind and like 1000 times better with more music, better enemies, a better (and touching) story, and a great way to grow the character (physically and story wise.) Getting your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you? Try upgrading your gear like the tutorial says to do. There was lots of heart and soul poured into this masterpiece and to top it off it's free. Though on the shorter side I give it 9/10. (I don't believe in a 10/10 as no game is perfect.) It's not about grinding to get the best loot in order to take down that one boss, but in fact is more like Binding of Issac where you have to memorize the pattern of attacks for the boss, though there is a warning area to give one time to evade. There is only 4 gear sets to help you along the way. (Three really, but that last two sets of gear has been since the beginning with no way of repairing it.) On top of it there are books in each section, some found and crafted and others by sidequesting, that up your stats. Like I said earlier this is a shorter RPG game as most are that come out of RPG Maker, but the time spend in game is actually based on story rather than grinding or slaying monsters. A story that in which may leave you in tears or at the least a bit heartbroken as the outcomes do not look towards a happy ending that we, as a society, want to see. Most of the RPGs made through the program used here rarely disappoint and this is not exception to that statement. With nothing left to say I will give a vauge hint to the new players of this title. The pendant is more important that you may think it is.

Let me be brief. This game has a long lineage to live up to. And sadly, it falls short. It appears to have the look and charm of the old Kings Quest, but lacks the heart.
The story is just fine. The artwork is fantastic. But it's been reduced to a simple (and very short) one-click adventure. Gone are the days when you could click on everything and get a humorous response. Gone are the brain baffleing quanderies and mysteries. It's got one cursor that does it all, and quick-time events are the action of the day.
Kings Quest was about puzzles. About combining items in creative ways. About turning over every rock, sticking your hand in every hole, picking up everything that wasn't nailed down, and poking every sleeping bear (or dragon). But it was about humor and dialog. Much of which is missing from this game.
If you're looking for Kings Quest.... this isn't it. Tis' but a shadow of it's formor glory.

If you grew up enjoying Sierra quest games like I did then King's Quest will be a massive treat.  With it's modern animation style graphics, excellent characters and a fun story it feels more like a Pixar movie than a video game.  The characters have amazing voice acting including quite a few little pop-culture references often with the characters from the original material that is being referenced (such as competing in a battle of wits against Wallace Shawn from The Princess Bride).  This is not just a quest game though and it includes some arcade style action sequences, a hilariously awesome horse race and the aformentioned battle of wits, which plays out like a chess game.  The backgrounds are stunning to look at and, even with a slightly less than powerful laptop like I'm running, the levels of texture is astonishing.  The court and countryside of Daventry are amazingly rendered and, in many cases, are actually laid out in a similar way as in the original series.
Very Highly Recommended!!!!

Let's break this game down into two catagories: Gameplay and Game Performance
Gameplay:
The game is a "blast" to play and is filled with tons of things to do that will keep you busy for hours of fun. But...
Game Performance:
The game is so poorly optimised for PCs that I cannot overlook the total and utter lack of polish missing from this title.  From the release day, JC3 has been riddled with crashes, frame rate drops and texture issues.  So much so that it completely DESTROYS the gameplay and makes this a "play it on the console only" game.
While I have your attention let me point out that "Game Performance problems" is not a new thing in the PC market as of late.  Clearly titles like JC3, Tomb Raider and now infamous Batman: Arkham Knight are examples of developers either outsourcing their PC port developement or not dedicating enough resources to QA before release.  In other words, PC is a small/dying market and therefore distributors will not dedicate resources, aka money, to such a small piece of the overall pie and will tolerate a certain threshold of sloppiness.  Sorry us, this has been an issue since the dawn of console and sadly, will never change.
But... there is abosolutely no excuse for not patching or optimising game breaking bugs as soon as possible.  Which in this case, Avalanche simply has not done to my satisfaction.  So shame on Firaxis and Square Enix for allowing such a poorly ported game to hit the market.
Final Verdict:
DO NOT BUY

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is an amazing simulation with lots of features. The game starts off slow with you borrowing trucks from other companies and doing local deliveries, but later in the game you will soon get your own truck and be hauling cargo across the whole of Europe. When you accumulate enough money or get a loan, you will also be able to buy a garage and hire drivers to carry cargo for you. You can use your hard earned money to upgrade your truck with new transmissions, engines, wheels, tires, paints, and more. And if you ever get tired with the base game, which would take a long time, lots of mods are available on the Workshop and there are many new DLCs available. This game is constantly updated by the developers as well. It's a great, fun game with lasting appeal.

tldr: A bargain bin quality game even when it came out in 1997 that only gained cult status because of its extreme and controversial subject matter but was very fairly and accurately harshly judged by critics. Its even worse sequel and an unmentionably bad 3rd game don't help its case either. One of the worst game series I have ever seen and also one of the most undeserving of any praise or any attention period.
The devs fixed the startup load time which was insane, around 3-5 minutes, but the load times between levels is still way longer than it should be for such a small game. Even when you do get to play, it is just as bad as the original game. Take a look at the metacritic score of 53/100 and just know that even that low of a score is being very generous. Updating a bad game with WASD+mouse movement does not make it any better and this game is living proof of that. The only reason the original Postal got just enough fans to reach cult status and have a sequel was because of its over the top subject matter, that you are simply a dude who goes psychotic and starts killing everyone around him. It got mostly bad critic scores for a good reason, as critics were objective enough to see this game's numerous and egregious flaws. Its fans are too dumb to be objective enough to gauge this game for what it actually is: pure garbage. It just goes to show how bad a game can get away with being as long as it has enough shock value. It was never a good game and neither is this redux, and Postal 2 is even worse. Not to mention Postal 3 is widely regarded as one of the worst games of all time with some of the lowest scores I've ever seen critics give a game, and I know how bad it is because I've unfortunately tried it too.
Just a few of its big dumb flaws include:
One hit from a rocket turret didn't kill me, it took 3, but the problem is the first hit knocked me down and allowed for a second then 3rd hit before I could regain control. Enemies can hit you from off-screen too just before they become visible on the edge of the screen. Your guy takes too much damage making you always have to tip-toe around and be ultra careful. If you get caught on fire from a molotov, the game steals control from you and you always run screaming out in the open where the most gunfire is and get smashed from all directions. This version is just as gut wrenchingly ugly as it was back in 1997 and just as bargain bin quality bad.
You know what I could go on but who cares? The developers who made this game series sure didn't and the entire postal series is proof of that. 4/10 sucks in every area, still better than Postal 2, but most games are anyway without much effort.

[NOTE: This review won't take into account the confirmed technical issues that have been reported on the PC port of Dishonored 2, for the simple reason that this reviewer didn't experience them thanks to his hardware and the application of post-release patches, so he can't write about something he didn't witness. Therefore, you'd better refer to other users' reviews as far as these issues are concerned]
Dishonored 2 is the first sequel to the original game by Arkane Studios. Taking place fifteen years after Dishonored, the tenure of Emily Kaldwin as Empress is twarted by a coup orchestrated by Delilah Copperspoon, miracously returned from her exile in the Void, and her Serkonian allies. The player's goal, which can be accomplished by taking control of either Corvo Attano or Emily, is to travel to the Southern country of Karnaca and target Delilah's supporters there before attemping to reclaim the throne in Dunwall.
As far as gameplay goes, Dishonored 2 can be considered a straight and meaty update to the original Dishonored's formula: the levels are now larger, more complex in design and offer the player more ways to reach their objectives; players looking for a non-lethal playthrough can now choke enemies during combat, incapacitate people while falling on them and vent their frustration at more mechanical/"no consequences" enemies; the player's arsenal has been expanded new bullets and bolts with different new effects to better suit your weapons to your own playing style; picking up either Emily or Corvo as the player's character allow to experience an entirely new batch of different powers; the characters handle themselves much better and their movements and animations feel more fluid and precise. Suffice to say, if you liked the freedom the original Dishonored gave you, you'll also find it here, and severely enhanced.
When it comes to the added lore and the overall plot, Dishonored is basically a double-edged sword. For one, Karnaca as a setting is both leagues different from first game's Dunwall, with its own culture and esthetics, and yet feels right at home in the series. Also, the sequel expands on several plot points from the original, providing some new and juicy revelations and explanations. The story itself, however, isn't that much different from the sequel, to the point of being redundant (the legitimate Empress gets dealt with and you must work through the main antagonist's inner circle till you can get the right heir back on the highest seat), and at times both Emily and Corvo (who is provided a voice starting from this game) give away a somehow shallow performance (to the point you are not sure if they care at all about everyone and everything in the world).
Aside from some very minor nitpicks, Dishonored 2 keeps up the good name of the original game and provides players with a fun, highly interactive gameplay experience and a gorgeous setting that really leave high hopes for the future of the whole series

For eveyone that is not aware, System Shock 1&2 were the forerunners of Bioshock. One other thing that System Shock had was a complete sense of anxiety, stress, and adrenaline pumping action. If you play this game you will find that you have to effectivley manage your resources, including what what skill trees you pusure as it will mean life or death at all difficulty levels. Yes the graphics will seem dated, that is being worked on by modders, heck there may already be an updated graphics mod already completed.
That being said, from one gaming enthusiast to another, get this game. This is a piece of video gaming history that ranks with Deus Ex, Thief, Half Life, and a few others.

This re-imagining of king's Graham early adventure is a definite departure from the early text adventures or the later point & click titles. Those familiar with Telltale Game's adventure titles will probably feel comfortable right away as the control scheme is somewhat similar. The only time you will be using your mouse (unless you're playing with a controller) is to select items in your inventory or to aim with your bow.
There is a number of action sequences that will require you to dodge obstacles or respond to quick time events. Fortunately they're sparse enough that they don't distract too much from the adventure.
You play the role of young Graham, acting out his past adventures as the old king narrates the story along with your progress or failures, as he's telling the tales of his youth to his granddaughter. If you get yourself killed, the king will mention that's what would have happened if he had pursued that course of action, then you're brought back moments earlier and can pick back up.
The game look pretty good and the graphics have a certain charm to them. The voice acting is top notch and really bring some depth to the characters. There's a lot of humor and some charming puns along the way.
The first episode gave me about 6 hours of game play to completion. Most puzzles are logical but a tad on the easy side. Don't expect to be scratching your head much at what to do next. Most puzzles can be solved in more than one way and there's no way to put yourself in a situation where you can't complete the game.
The story is somewhat linear and achievement hunters might have to go through it more than once as there's a lot of hidden achievements and many of them are easily missable with no way to get back to them once you've moved past the part of the storyline where you can get them. You can still expect a bit of back tracking as you search for items or for clues about what to do next.
So far, the game stands pretty well on it's own and is a decent addition to the King's Quest franchise. Die-hard King's Quest fans may be disappointed to see the game strayed a bit from it's roots and that it's not nearly as challenging as the olden titles.
The reason why I can't give a positive review for the game at this time, is because unless you bought The Complete Collection, there is no way to get the game's last part. Sierra has confirmed on
that the epilogue is exclusive to The Complete Edition and they have no intention to release it separately.
Furthermore, from the moment you have Episode 1 in your library, you can no longer purchase The Complete Edition as you're considered to be owning it already. And adding the Season Pass will not provide you with the full content. Unless you bought the whole thing right away, you get cheated out of the last part of the game.
If you're a fan of modern adventure games, this one is definitely worth it. However, if you care about getting the whole content, wait until you can afford to buy The Complete Collection.

The Emperor Edition has solved the vast majority of problems that were in the original release a year ago, but I feel there are still issues with the general design of the game which hold it back from greatness.  Performance-wise, it seems a hell of a lot better.  I have a laptop with an i5 3210m, 8GB RAM and an HD 7670m (not a top gaming rig by any standards) and I can run it with an acceptable FPS at Very High settings.  When I first bought this game I struggled to run it at Medium.  This goes for the campaign map and the battle map.
The weird movie-tinge to the graphics in battles is gone, which improves the visuals to no end from my perspective.  The colours all seem a lot more vivid and realistic which add to the immersion.  I haven't seen any weird gurning faces yet either which helps.
The main problem with this game, which hasn't been changed at all, is the 'streamlined' campaign map, which gives you no idea what you're doing half the time.  Shogun 2's (in my opinion the best of all the Total Wars) was easy to manage and gave you a clear picture of what was happening everywhere at once.  I find Rome 2's clunky and unintuitive by comparison.
The AI has been massively improved in a year.  I haven't once seen a ship cruise through the town square or a besieger hold back his five siege towers while sending his entire army up one ladder.  Battles now last about 20 mins on average in comparison with about 6 minutes in the original release, because the enemy uses his forces in a smart way.  This also goes for the campaign map, where AI decisions actually make sense now.  It's easy to get trade agreements with factions it should be easy to, and other states hate you or love you for realistic reasons.
If you've been holding off buying this till it's fixed, now's the time.  I doubt it'll get much better than this.  To be honest, this is what the original release should have been.  Maybe we can see this free upgrade as a belated apology from Creative Assembly for nearly destroying one of the best game series of all time.  I accept, for now.

I'm going to be incredibly critical of this game, I love this game and it is fun, but it lacks. You NEED mods to play this game. (Some mods can/may fix some of these issues)
How this game lacks/requires to fix:
>Working testudo - one that doesn't die when under missile fire (the whole point of a testudo). Ironically, this was done perfectly in Rome 1, so why the backwards step?
>Working hoplite phalanx - a phalanx is supposed to be a tank when attacking from the front, but in the current game it's average against swordsmen & will die easy against good sword men - it's only supposed to be weak when flanked. Rome 1 wasn't a perfect display of a hoplite phalanx, but it displayed the phalanx traits well.
>Working Pike Phalanx - The whole idea of a pike phalanx was to pin, whilst other troops - such as cav or melee inf - flank & kill. In Rome 2, pre-emperor patch, the pike phalanx was impenetrable and did big damage, now post-patch, it is easily penetrable and does low damage. It is simply supposed to be impenetrable and do low damage (with rising damage according to troop quality). Rome 1 mods mastered this very basic mechanic well, so why does a professional company like CA (the actual creators) fail repeatedly?
>Garrisons in settlements SHOULD be RECRUITABLE. In the game, you build a building and may get, say a unit of slingers added to the garrison. If it's a high-risk of invasion settlement, then you may need to park an army inside the settlement, perhaps permanently. BUT, you only have a limited number of armies, so you may get into a situation where you cannot simply move, or that the majority of your armies cannot move, EVEN if you can afford more armies, purely due to the illogical and arbitrary "max number of armies" imposition. This is why you should be able to recruit into a garrison, as well as an army. Say, if you recruit into a garrison, then that garrison army cannot be used offensively. Fair enough. That means that you only get a max number of OFFENSIVE armies according to the size of your imperium, which would be more logical than simply a max number of armies. (People have suggested simply being able to peel of individual units from an army and have the ability to place them in a settlement)
>Edicts - they should have NO max number. The bonuses you get from edicts are so very meagre, sometimes negligible. Having a max of only a few negligible bonuses is ridiculous. Tax harvesting was only 5%, which was nothing. Now it's 15%. but that's still hardly any. If my province is making 1000 per turn, that's only an extra 150 gold. Which is not enough to buy anything. It is a nothing amount. Even late game when a really good, expanded settlement is developed, and is worth 3000 for the whole province, then thats only an extra 450. 450 gold late game is also negligible because in late game everything is expensive. POINTLESS. If you were guaranteed 1 edict per completely-owned province, then those  negligible amounts could at least add up.
>Roman legions - they don't use legionary tactics and do not steam roller the barbarians, like how they should. IT WOULD make the game imbalanced in favour of Rome, but that's the whole point, and THAT would additionally offer a real challenge to anyone playing as another faction - to fight the mighty rome and actually win. Due to the ridiculous "kill animations" required to complete a kill, you will never be able to have the 3 soldiers on 1, kind of scenerio, which is what that era of warefare was all about. Rome 1 was on a basic engine, but it displayed this warefare PERFECTLY. If some legionaries were fighting a barbarian unit, then they could gang up on the last guy.
>Arrows and missiles: in M2TW if you were on a hill and fired atop it, then you got a range bonus, depending on the height you were firing from: the higher you were (in comparison to the enemy unit) the greater the range bonus. This could translate into a few archers actually throwing back a larger force, that could not otherwise win, if it wasnt for the hill - a kind of agincourt-esque scenerio. Of course, when you were firing up-hill, then the opposite would be true - your arrows' range would be reduced depending on the steepness of the hill. On Rome 2, it's ALWAYS the same. Also the missile units can only fire in front of them. (because their "target zone" is a partial section of a circle shape. In old tw games, they had a 360 degree angle of attack. So if an enemy got behind your lines, then they could PIVOT on the spot and shoot behind them. Now they physically have to move and rearrange their formation/positioning, which messes up lines and often leaves them exposed. It is just madness. Also, make the range of their shots on flat ground larger - because they get hardly any kills in before the gap is shut. Or make the units move much slower, if you want the range to be the same.
>Make the size of armies larger (more individual units per army) and/or no limits of number of armies. Yes, I know that that you can have combined allied army battles where you can control up to 40 units at a time, but i mean singular armies. They should have at least 25 - 30 (if not more) max number of units per singular army. THIS would greatly justify having to be forced to have a max number of armies, per imperium size, rather than how much you can afford. (Though tbh, as the seleucids, I maxed out the number of armies and navies mid-end game and just had piles of money sitting there doing nothing. I maxed out buildings and upgrades, as well. So I had well over a million gold in my treasury sat doing NOTHING at the end of every turn. It is logical, that if you can afford more armies, then that should be the ONLY thing holding you back from doing so.
>Diplomatic options for trading provinces/regions (like in old games). I remember playing NTW, and a losing enemy wanted peace. They had nothing to offer, no money, no anything EXCEPT a region. If they didn't offer a region, then I could destroy them. The treaties for peace from war, throughout ALL history has been the trade of land between factions in order to secure that peace. So it should be added. Also TECHNOLOGY SHOULD BE tradable, like in empire/napoleon. (I havent played shogun 2 - the area and period do not interest me, so I cannot compare) This meant that if a nation was far ahead in terms of social tech and you were ahead in terms of military tech, that you could TRADE tech, or even concede tech for a PEACE settlement.
>The current UI & faction colours are also awful - they rid the game of the old ones and replaced them with light colours that (at least for me) hurt my eyes after a while, it's just too bright.
>Minor discrepancies such as the seleucid generals screaming "FOR ROME" as they are attacking an enemy on the campaign map, which is just ridiculous. Also, the ships can still sail through land sometimes (at least the AI's does sometimes) which breaks immersion. Also if you or the enemy attacks by sea with a large force, then you will run out of room to land all your men (as there are "X" amount of spaces for units to land on, which may mean that you will have to speed up the battle-speed to x3 and wait for like 10 minutes for the clock to run out, or end up losing the battle.
>New Politics system: I don't like it. Personally, I'd like a three-family (or more) kind of system (almost separate factions of the same faction), like in Rome 1, where you all fall under the same banner - Rome - and you all conquer territory for Rome, til one of you becomes popular, then you can seize power in civil war. You could add the politcal actions to this, so you could hinder pleb support for a good rival general or adopt someone to your family, which would affect support and relations with the others. A lot of critics say that slow walker zombies are easy to deal with. I can't entirely say they're wrong; they're slow, they're dumb, and you could simply
them. With a gun, you could just line up the sights to their rotten foreheads and pull the trigger. Even without a gun, something as basic as an axe, or baseball bat, or crowbar could finish off a zombie with tea time to spare.
The problem this game presents is that zombies never travel alone.
Some of my personal thoughts:
-Teamwork in this is extremely vital; if you can keep your smarter buddies alive, they'll be sure to return the favor. While not impossible to complete the game on any mode alone, it becomes improbable as you have to singlehandedly bob, weave and kill through tens, or hundreds if on survival, of zombies, on top of your teammates reviving as runners and coming after your flesh.
-Firearms aren't wonder weapons. The .22 rimfire weapons are as weak as they sound, but ammo is notably more plentiful, making it a more practical choice. The powerful revolver can multi-shot through two or three zombies' heads without slowing, but ammo is about as common as a unicorn more often than not. Make EVERY shot count...unless you're on a survival map, with a flare gun and a lot of flares. Then it becomes somewhat of a joke.
-Don't forget to bring a flashlight (since you can dual-wield a flashlight with pistols and one-hand melees!); dark areas are
dark. More than once I have nearly sh@t myself or emptied a magazine spraying wildly at the lone zombie that suddenly loomed out of the darkness at me, nearly grabbing my sorry hide.
-Melee combat is as dangerous as it is practical. Two-hand melee weapons are generally the most powerful weapons in the game, within in the right hands, but you can't carry the flashlight and exhausts you quickly. All one-hand melee weapons require at least two hits to the zombies' heads or necks to kill, on top of their already measely range. This is why the machete is such a sought-after melee weapon amongst the experienced, as before the official Steam release it had the killing power of an axe in one hand. It has been nerfed a bit, but it is still the most powerful one-hand melee in the game.
TL;DR
Be smart, be tactical, and make friends. If you don't know something, find out at your earliest convenience. You're less likely to become a zombie yourself that way.
My one and only complaint about the game itself is the lack of long-term progression that many other games have. But that is a very small price to pay considering the quality of this (free!) game.
Oh, and if you've read Max Brook's Zombie Survival Guide, you can pretty much carry over that knowledge. NMRiH is clearly inspired and built around Max Brook's ZSG and WWZ, as many of the more subtle references will suggest.

Let's break this game down into two catagories: Gameplay and Game Performance
Gameplay:
The game is a "blast" to play and is filled with tons of things to do that will keep you busy for hours of fun. But...
Game Performance:
The game is so poorly optimised for PCs that I cannot overlook the total and utter lack of polish missing from this title.  From the release day, JC3 has been riddled with crashes, frame rate drops and texture issues.  So much so that it completely DESTROYS the gameplay and makes this a "play it on the console only" game.
While I have your attention let me point out that "Game Performance problems" is not a new thing in the PC market as of late.  Clearly titles like JC3, Tomb Raider and now infamous Batman: Arkham Knight are examples of developers either outsourcing their PC port developement or not dedicating enough resources to QA before release.  In other words, PC is a small/dying market and therefore distributors will not dedicate resources, aka money, to such a small piece of the overall pie and will tolerate a certain threshold of sloppiness.  Sorry us, this has been an issue since the dawn of console and sadly, will never change.
But... there is abosolutely no excuse for not patching or optimising game breaking bugs as soon as possible.  Which in this case, Avalanche simply has not done to my satisfaction.  So shame on Firaxis and Square Enix for allowing such a poorly ported game to hit the market.
Final Verdict:
DO NOT BUY

This is already a very fun game, and with further upgrades it could be awesome. It captures the 'feel' of being an ant queen, with some interesting strategic concepts unique to this game. It lacks the strategic depth of something like Starcraft, but given the subject material that's not surprising.
One significant innovation is that the construction of buildings requires a rather high cost and support only a single ant each--but replacing an ant is automatic and cheap (but not free). This means that constructing a large army is hard, but if a large army is lost it can be replaced quickly. This leads to an interesting debate, about whether it's better to keep a 'reserve' of resources in case you suffer casualties, or spend it on increasing your army size.
Now for the complaints:
1) There's no real pop cap in the side missions, only limited by the number of buildings you currently have. But there is a pop cap in the 'home base'. This seems unnecessary, and limits your options when you need to defend it.
2) There's a big difference in difficultly between the side missions and the 'challenge' (i.e. home base) missions--the latter are much tougher. The idea is you can play the side missions multiple times, to build up your forces at your home base. The problem is that this forces you to play the same missions over and over, no variety, which gets annoying after a while.
3) The game right now is really just tower defence--defend against waves of enemies. It would be much better to include multiple ant colonies, each one attacking and defending. How cool would it be to send in an ant commando force to assassinate another queen?
I recommend supporting this game now, because it's already worth the money. And it could be incredible in the future.

Very entertaining. While the game is/was in early access during this review, my feeling is it's already good and it will get even better for the full release, so I recommend it. The visuals, music and voiced narration gives the game a BBC documentary feel to it. The main campaign is set in a laboratory where scientists are testing your capabilities as a colony, additional "side quest" scenarios will let you grind up some resources for your brood to prepare for the tests.
You control the ants using pheromone markers, they can be grouped and each group controlled separately. You control the flow of ants for a macro strategic advantage rather than squad based tactics or micro managing single units. It's all about getting into that swarm mentality, all or nothing battles where overwhelming the enemy is the only option. Single ants are useless, but the swarm can clear the entire area of all living things in minutes.
As such, timing the resource spending and marker positions is crucial for success. Overspend or misplace a marker at the wrong time and your colony might not be able to recover.
While the game is a bit short on content at this time, it is very much playable, stable and fun. All the core mechanics and controls are solid and given time more content will be added. More game modes will also be added in the future, I'm guessing there will be something like sandbox, capture and hold, etc. If they add multiplayer this would be my new favourite strategy game.
While the Linux port had some issues early on, the devs have already patched that and with my 15 hours of gameplay in Linux I have not run into any technical issues.

I would like to talk about this game from graphic setting aspect as it is the one thing I was most concerned about, for an obvious reason; the first game's graphic issues. Fortunately, Tango Gameworks has done it right this time;
Next is resolution. As for this particular one, as someone who plays PC game on a not so capable laptop, I always appreciate developers who provide those low resolution, namely 640x480 and 800x600 for the sake of being able to play more smoothly. The thing is resolutions with 4:3 aspect ratio don't usually work properly in many games(when played in 16:9 widescreen). The game got squeezed or stretched in the wrong direction or in some games, they ended up with small screen instead. This game maintains aspect ratio while also scale it to full screen
TL;DR You can play this game with any resolution in full view without the game being distorted.
If you are one of those who is still reluctant to get this game because of the first one's graphic issues, I can assure you that there is no problems like that anymore.
Note: Some options like Volumetric light, SSAO, SSR can be disabled but give very little fps raise (just 1-2; between disable and medium). Resolution makes most of the difference in fps rise or drop.
For your information, here are my specs:
Laptop: Asus K501UX
CPU: Intel Core i5-6200U
GPU: Nvidia Geforce GTX950M  Vram 2GB
RAM: 12GB
OS: Windows 10 Home 64bit
I play at 1280x600, on medium (motion blur disabled, it's not my thing), and I got 28-33fps most of the time
