[NOTE: This review won't take into account the confirmed technical issues that have been reported on the PC port of Dishonored 2, for the simple reason that this reviewer didn't experience them thanks to his hardware and the application of post-release patches, so he can't write about something he didn't witness. Therefore, you'd better refer to other users' reviews as far as these issues are concerned]
Dishonored 2 is the first sequel to the original game by Arkane Studios. Taking place fifteen years after Dishonored, the tenure of Emily Kaldwin as Empress is twarted by a coup orchestrated by Delilah Copperspoon, miracously returned from her exile in the Void, and her Serkonian allies. The player's goal, which can be accomplished by taking control of either Corvo Attano or Emily, is to travel to the Southern country of Karnaca and target Delilah's supporters there before attemping to reclaim the throne in Dunwall.
As far as gameplay goes, Dishonored 2 can be considered a straight and meaty update to the original Dishonored's formula: the levels are now larger, more complex in design and offer the player more ways to reach their objectives; players looking for a non-lethal playthrough can now choke enemies during combat, incapacitate people while falling on them and vent their frustration at more mechanical/"no consequences" enemies; the player's arsenal has been expanded new bullets and bolts with different new effects to better suit your weapons to your own playing style; picking up either Emily or Corvo as the player's character allow to experience an entirely new batch of different powers; the characters handle themselves much better and their movements and animations feel more fluid and precise. Suffice to say, if you liked the freedom the original Dishonored gave you, you'll also find it here, and severely enhanced.
When it comes to the added lore and the overall plot, Dishonored is basically a double-edged sword. For one, Karnaca as a setting is both leagues different from first game's Dunwall, with its own culture and esthetics, and yet feels right at home in the series. Also, the sequel expands on several plot points from the original, providing some new and juicy revelations and explanations. The story itself, however, isn't that much different from the sequel, to the point of being redundant (the legitimate Empress gets dealt with and you must work through the main antagonist's inner circle till you can get the right heir back on the highest seat), and at times both Emily and Corvo (who is provided a voice starting from this game) give away a somehow shallow performance (to the point you are not sure if they care at all about everyone and everything in the world).
Aside from some very minor nitpicks, Dishonored 2 keeps up the good name of the original game and provides players with a fun, highly interactive gameplay experience and a gorgeous setting that really leave high hopes for the future of the whole series

I had a lot of fun with this game. That being said, in hindsight, I have a lot of issues with it.
The game essentially consists of capturing slimes, raising them, selling the "plorts" which they release after being fed, and exploring/unlocking new areas for new slimes, resources, and additional farm space. Additionally, there is a storyline tied in with the previous owner of the ranch who leaves you notes scattered across the map, and your love interest writes you letters as you progress in the story.
I can say I went through the entire adventure mode without fully reading any of the notes or letters relevant to the story. They all come in big blocks of text that I just don't find interesting. It could have gone a long way to have other ranchers on the map with you, NPCs who you could talk to or accept side quests from. Instead, it is just you alone with an enormous map and thousands of slimes. While I liked finally unlocking new areas, ultimately the adventure mode didn't really feel like an adventure. But hey, I also didn't read about the point of the adventure to begin with.
I liked the different biomes, though so much of the game was spent walking back and forth, running until your stamina replenishes and then waiting for it to fill back up, and making resource runs that take entire in-game days. With only four inventory slots for the entire game, the constant running has given me literal eye strains.
If you're fast, you could probably discover everything in the game in about 25 hours or less. For a game centered around exploration, farming, crafting, and an entire storyline, it doesn't feel like a lot of content. Once you finish the adventure mode, continuing the ranch seems pointless. I spent several hours post-game redesigning my ranch, getting extra resources and late-game upgrades, though I'm at a point where there is not much else I feel like continuing. This game has minimal customization features that are fun, but do not give any replay-value long term. I cannot really imagine starting a second save file unless I happen to open this game years later.
I understand this was an early access game, which I'm surprised by simply from the fact that it feels incomplete. I was pleased with the first post-release update, but should you really be releasing a "map" update AFTER you release the game? Little pieces of content like this missing left me confused.
At the end of the day though, it's a fun game. I didn't even get it because it seemed cute, I thought the first-person perspective in this genre looked fun, and the reviews are so good! Just would've loved to see it after some more time in development.
Simply because I had more cons than pros, I won't be recommending this game, but it has a lot of potential. Would buy again if on sale. Still interested to see future updates.

TL;DR: The mechanics work, but they're clunky and force the player to waste time. Exploration means running back and forth because the player's inventory is extremely limited, and it's not like there's much to see— the game isn't graphically impressive, and the zones don't have much in the way of unique assets. The difficulty level is nonexistent, and it feels like there's nothing to do but busywork after visiting every zone.
Slime Rancher is a solid enough game, mechanically (in that it generally isn't buggy and things basically work, but it ends up falling short of comparable games— Harvest Moon-style farming games and pure sandboxes, like Minecraft). The art style seems more gimped than stylized— everything looks smooth and bland, though this may have been a necessity in order for the gameplay to remain reliably smooth with so many objects and entities moving around. I have played through what content was available once during the beta (just before the Ancient Ruins area was released) and again just after release (main story completed, entire farm bought and covered in fully-upgraded buildings, plenty of research and cosmetic upgrades purchased).
The most basic mechanics of the game, moving and using the Vacpack, are remarkably flawed. Walking and jumping work just fine, but the Vacpack spins objects before sucking them up into an inventory slot, which can cause some to fly past the player. It gets tedious waiting on items to reach the player. Then, it gets even more tedious when you have to eject a large quantity of anything, such as when you sell items or retrieve items from a storage building. There is no "eject all" function for an item slot, and
. There is one extra pseudo-slot that only holds water, but the limited number of total slots, low total quantity limit per slot (even after multiple upgrades!), and inability to carry multiple stacks of items (any individual item can only be carried in one slot at a time, up to that slot's quantity limit) make item management
throughout the game. Sprinting cuts down on travel time, but it uses energy, which is slow to refill and also necessary for the jetpack. The jetpack has almost no lift, and it sometimes activates when the player is just trying to jump. Most areas that the jetpack allows the player to reach are devoid of anything.
My post-release playthrough took about 15 hours, which seems low for a sandbox-ish game with a seemingly-large amount of customization to do. The Ranch is fairly limited, with about 2 dozen plots on which to keep slimes, raise chickens, and grow crops (along with a couple of other utility buildings). It's definitely possible for someone who truly desires efficiency to brainstorm various layouts for the Ranch, but the limited number of plots are extremely constrictive when compared to a more free-form sandbox. The same logic applies to gadget and decoration placement, which is performed on numerous, but unmoveable, locations around the game world.
Exploration is somewhat interesting due to there being several different game regions with different plants and slimes available, but these things you find are like not enough cheap, bland butter spread over too much bread. Almost all slimes and plants function identically, and the few unique mechanics ultimately don't matter. The geography of new zones might have different colors and a few unique assets, but it still mostly looks like shaded mud. Inventory management becomes even more problematic when exploring a new region— you can only carry four different things, but you have multiple new commodities to bring back to your ranch. Late game exploration involves placing different plorts (produced by slimes after they eat; can be used to get money, build gadgets, or fulfill trade offers from NPCs) in slots that look like the slime that made that plort. This means backtracking across zones just to carry new things back, then coming back with the correct plorts, and doing so again if more new things are found/different plorts are needed.
I didn't complete the main story for the sake of seeing it all— the entire narrative is comprised of very short, uninteresting tidbits of text. The content of said narrative can be boiled down to two very hokey love stories. One is written through notes left by the previous Slime Ranch owner, Hobson Twilgers, throughout the explorable areas of the world, and the other is written by the player character's best friend/love interest/whatever (Casey) in letters sent to the player as they spend more time in-game and explore more regions.
These love stories fall apart because the game effectively has no meaningful characters— Hobson's love interest, another Rancher (Thora West), only exists as a single "welcome" message and a few mundane quotes viewed with her trade offers. Beatrix only receives character development through Casey's emails; the only thing the player really learns about her is that she's outdoorsy. Beatrix is the only character with a visible model, which is seen in the player's home and the main menu, though a picture of Casey seen from behind is visible during the credits. They come across as a couple dreamt up by a stereotypical Tumblr user— Beatrix is a person of color with mint-green hair, and Casey is a musician with multiple ear piercings, punk-style bright pink hair, and
.
Character customization (other than the Vacpack color schemes) would be wasted due to the game's first-person perspective, but there might as well be no Beatrix LeBeau or Casey.
After finishing the story and reaching the end of the final area, the player receives... Nothing in particular. A few secret "vaults" are unlocked. They're full of valuable plorts, which is pretty meaningless by the time the player gains access. You could just stop playing the main mode and play the 5-day challenge mode, or you could spend some time retooling your farm with different slimes, but it all feels meaningless. The devs added a money sink that provides paint jobs for your home, ranch, and Vacpack (what little you see of the player model while playing), but making money just means running back and forth between slimes, slime food, and the market. Making money also means sitting still, holding down the left or right mouse button, waiting for large amounts of whatever to enter or exit your inventory, and remember: only four item slots. There are some gadgets you can place around the farm to slightly reduce how much running back and forth you do, but you'll still spend inordinate amounts of time waiting on the Vacpack to suck and spew. There are some collectibles in the form of treasure pods, but these are more frustrating than fun. If they provide items, they use up valuable inventory space on stuff you didn't expect to have to carry, or they provide location-related cosmetic junk. Treasure pods require a special, expensive upgrade that seems to only be unlocked after a certain number of days have passed, which means the player will likely be forced to ignore countless pods for a long period of time (in my case, the main story was over and I didn't care to continue with my already-full Ranch before I could open the top tier of pods) before they can be interacted with.

Latest update (9/15/17) Broke the game. Crashes on launch every time. Deleting and moving on.
What starts as a highly addictive farm-style game will eventually leave you craving much more than what is available at launch. The devs have laid the groundwork for what could be an incredible game, but as it is right now, it just feels empty. In the end there's no point to all the collecting and upgrading. Once you get the labratory it turns into a waiting game, pitting you against the odds while wasting time trying to build the only worthwhile machine- teleporters. The time investment required negates any advantage a teleporter would have given you. The market system makes little sense, except for the fact that the more YOU sell, the less you will make in future days as it gets saturated. The devs were kind enough to add a map in the first update- why they hadn't had that in since Alpha I have no idea, and there still is no minimap functionality, even as an upgrade.
All in all it's a fun little game, but feels completely unfinished. I feel like it could be awesome in a year or so, if the devs care about the game and the community. I wish I could recommend this, but I'd wait until it's on sale for now. There just isn't enough content here, even though me and my whole family played it non-stop for over a week. A 7/10 would be generous, but I do have faith that the devs will continue to add content and systems to make this game fun for more than a few days.

SMITE is a good idea and a fun game. At times. At other times it makes me want to never play computer games ever again. And its not just a case of: "I'm bad at the game and I'm just being salty", or "I can't take a loss", because I can. What I can't take is having periods where I can't get a single win for a week because every single game is determined beforehand by the matchmaking. This also serves to diminish the sense of accomplishment from any wins you do get, as they weren't you playing well, they were the matchmaking. This isn't to say that there are no good games, there are, but rather that they are few and far between. This, in addition to horrifically overpowered playable gods and almost chronic power creep, make me very much warn against playing this game.

It's the good old world of Dishonred, with its unque setting, stunning visual design, lots of crawlspaces and highly corrupt but silly guards. I love it. And the soundtrack is pretty good.
However, the plot and writing aren't particularly impressive. I've dropped the game for a week mid-playthrough and now I don't even remember what was happening there or why I should care. I kinda hoped D2 would be an improvement over D1 in this regard. Oh well. Some of the NPCs' lines and Emily's high-chaos random comments are truly ridiculous and cheesy. The whole morality/"chaos" thing still feels artificial and disturbing at times given the choices you have to make and their consequences. Anyway, I weren't looking to play D2 for the story or the acting (but hearing guards declaring their urgent need to pee over and over again can get annoying).
Regarding the performance and visual quality, things didn't go well after the release. There are still rampant technical issues. Looks like the latest patch has sacrificed texture and shadow detail, now the shadows are all glitchy, triangular and flickering, and textures pop in visibly when you move closer. Antialiasing produces noticeable artifacts, like banding and flashing pixels. I've noticed numerous holes between meshes, ffs. I still enjoy the game, but these problems do ruin the immersion at times.
I'll recommend against buying D2. If you liked D1, you're still going to buy this game anyway (although waiting for a sale is a reasonable option), and if you didn't, the game isn't going to offer much more for you.
P.S. Shooting guards with sleep darts causes them to launch into walls or into air with great force for some reason, killing them instantly.

This is one of those few games you're better off buying for a console.

The biggest reason for this? Hackers.

It doesn't appear as if the people responsible for moderating the online community devote much energy to preventing people from hacking this game. You'll be hard pressed to find a lobby that doesn't have at least one hacker. Note: I'm not talking about people who use hacks for things like getting inifinite kill streak bonuses--though you will eventually come across those people. I'm talking about more subtle hackers who employ tricks that enable them to see enemies through walls without any in-game items being used. Things like that. These people can be found in the majority of CoD:AW online lobbies.

Beyond that, you'll be lucky to find any lobbies with people playing objective based gametypes. If you want to play something other than Deathmatch, you'll be waiting a while.

All in all, this game can be fun to play... it's just usually not.

This is an excellent game that should not be missed.  It is the best game I have played in a long time.  When I was younger (high school/college days) while playing a great video game, it was pretty normal for me to stay up way too late playing it and then I would drag myself out of bed to go to school.   Then, at school, I would sit there and think about the game.  I would think about some awesome part that I had completed or contemplate what was to come.  Then I would go home and start back playing the game as soon as I could.  Now that I am older, have a real job, and have different priorities, I am not usually willing to sacrifice sleep to play a video game.  Every now and then I might try to stay up a little bit later and crank out some play time on a game, but I'll almost always get tired quickly and end up going to bed earlier than I wanted to.  Alien is the first game in the past several years that had me staying up playing all hours of the night and then consumed my thoughts the next day when I was not playing.  Its atsmosphere captured my attention and did not let go until I had beaten it.  It took me back to a gaming bliss that I haven't experienced in a very long time.
With the limited amount of time that I have to play video games these days, I have to rely on reviews to narrow my list of games that I want to play down to the games that I will actually have time to play.  The review outlet I use most is IGN.  Over the past, I have disagreed with some of their reviews but, in general, I feel they are pretty accurate.  That was not the case on this game.  IGN gave this game an abyssmal score of 5.9.  This is probably the most inaccurate review I have ever seen from them.  I am writing this review for people like me, who rely on those scores to decide on what games to play.  If I had just seen that score and stopped there, I would have missed out on playing this incredible game.  Luckily, after reading the comments section of that review, I saw that I lot of people disagreed.  The more I looked into it, the more I saw that most people disagreed.
The IGN reviewer commented that the game was too long and that he spent most of his time hiding in a locker.  If you spend most of your time hiding in a locker, you are playing the game wrong.  One of things I love about this game is that it doesn't hold your hand in order to cater to the generation of spoiled modern FPS players that we have now.  One of the funnest parts of the games from my childhood was actually having to figure what I needed to do and figuring out how to do it isntead of having everything explained to me.  This game harkens back to that glorious time in gaming.  The game doesn't coddle the player, but it will teach the player as long as the player has the patience to learn from their mistakes.  I am not going to go into detail explaining how to play this game, as that makes up a good portion of the fun, but I will tell you this, don't spend all your time hiding in lockers.  Keep moving and when you get killed learn from your mistake and try something else next time.
The reviewer I mentioned earlier did not seem to learn from his mistakes.  He stubbornly tried to keep hiding in lockers even though he was getting killed time and time again.  This led to the game taking him longer to complete than it probably should have.  The reviewer obviously didn't get it.  It would be like if the reviewer of a demon/dark souls game had decreased the score because it was too hard when in fact those games were praised for their difficulty and for requiring the player to learn from their mistakes and adjust accordingly.  Yeah the difficulty might turn some away, but if you have the patience it will lead to a very rewarding experience.
Anyway, if you've read through this long winded review and the game still sounds interesting to you, do yourself a favor and go buy it right now.  Do NOT go steal it somewhere.  Go buy it so that this excellent game can earn enough money to get a sequel.

First time playing the game, and got to say in my opinion it is the first old game I've played that has survived the test of time. The grandpappy of Bioshock is still lively.
The story is meh, no real surprises but enough lore and logs to help flesh out what happened. I havne't played system shock 1, but in my opinion I didn't need to in order to enjoy this game.
The weapons.....oh boy. I have heard jokes about how fast the weapons degrade and start jamming but WOW I still was naive about it. You'd think this would be a downside, but it actually leads to some of your most exciting moments. Fighting a tough robot or something and your weapon jams, scrambling to take cover and quickly repair really gets you stressed out haha.
Last thing I'll mention is the difficulty. I play normal setting in all my games and this one felt like it got a difficulty curve on the 3rd floor. Enemies and turrets start being able to kill you VERY quickly. Like in Bioshock or Borderlands, you have special respawn machines; but unlike those games you have to go find them and turn them on before you can respawn. Otherwise your saving and loading A LOT. The difficulty never wavers after that point, but you do. You start to figure out weakness, enemy tactics, and what gun to have ready just from the sounds. This made me feel like a beast, enemies that once killed me in an instant if I was careless I started to tear though.
I'll end it here. The control is amazing, too many skills to discuss, and if your even thinking about playing this then you already accept the dated graphics as ok. There is no reason to pass this classic up ESPECIALLY if get it on sale like I did.

I was really excited to hear about this "new" King's Quest. I was a huge fan of all the Sierra Games, particularly the King's Quest series. I feel this new version is true to the spirit of the old King's Quest and is a joy to play. It is not a remake, but rather a new game told from the perspective of an aging King Graham. He shares his adventures with his Grandaugher through wonderful stories, which is the 'game" you play. It is more adventure game then a "choice" game, like the Tell Tale Games (which I also thoroughly enjoy). It is presented in "chapters" and I felt the first chapter was generously long. I have played many "episodic" games, and I really felt like I got my money's worth for Chapter 1. I'm really looking forward to the next Chapters. The quests/puzzles aren't necessarily hard, but you will have to think about a few of them. I went back to my old school adventure roots and "mapped" out the areas, so I could keep track of places I still had things to do and where items where. If you enjoyed the old King's Quest games, then this is a no brainer as a delightful walk down memory lane.

I played the first chapter of the game and I loved it. I thought it was beautiful, charming and witty. It's not a difficult game  by any means, the puzzles are quite logical and the story is quite engaging, so far. Zero complains about the game itself, if you like graphic adventures, do yourself a favor and buy this game.
However, and this is the reason for my negative review, there is one important aspect to consider when buying it. If, like me, you want to try the game and you only buy the first chapter thinking that you can get the rest as they come, think again. If you do that, you won't be able to access the epilogue of the game, an extra chapter reserved only for those who pay for the whole thing upfront. I understand that this is Sierra's way to incentivize customers to pay the $39.99 and locjk the sale but, what about those of us who tried and actually liked it? Can we not get the epilogue? Well, unless you pay $39.99 to buy the game again on top of the $9.99 you paid for the first chapter, you can't.  I would really like to be able to access the whole experience without having to pay $49, but I guess I won't be able to.

Once upon a time there where only text based adventure games.
No pointing, no clicking, just the clickety-clack of the keyboard as you typed commands like "Go East" and "Get Shovel" in response to colourful statements such as:
"You are standing at fork in the road, there is a shovel."
In addition to the lack of any sort of graphical interface the interaction itself could be hugely frustrating as you struggled to find the command the game required to carry out the simplest of actions.
"Use Shovel"
"Equip Shovel"
"Dig with shovel"
etc. could (at least in the early days) result in the constant response of
"I don't understand that. please enter command >:"
Typing things like
"Just dig a bloody hole"
didn't work either, it was an unforgiving system which required as much patience as it did imagination.
These text based games were the humble beginnings which blazed a trail towards to classic Lucas Arts adventures most of us think of as defining the pointy-clicky genre in the 90's.
Whilst Lucas Arts might be the first name that springs to mind when thinking of "old school" point and click adventures, there is another... "Sierra".
Lucas Arts might have wowed the gaming crowd with Islands of Monkeys and Days of Tentacles, but Sierra was there first, they're credited with releasing the first computer adventure game to feature graphics (well monochrome line drawings accompanying the text) but it was an achievement and laid the way to several great Sierra games including two of the greatest gaming franchises from the "days of yore" Space Quest and Kings Quest.
Whilst Space Quest is sadly still waiting for a reboot (I miss you Roger Wilco),
I'm happy to report that Kings Quest is back... and this time it's episodic!
This "Re-imagining" of Kings Quest is available in five episodes and delivered as a story told by old King Graham about his youth, his adventures and his eventful past.
Have you ever seen the movie "The Princess Bride"? (If not you should, it's a classic!)
Anyway, the format of Kings Quest is very similar to that movie, just replace Columbo with Doc Brown from "Back to the Future" and you're there.
That's right, Kings Quest is narrated by the wonderful Christopher Lloyd, his engaging voice giving life to Old King Graham as he recounts his adventures to his granddaughter Gwendolyn.
This re-telling of Kings Quest also moves away (just a little) from its point and click roots. It's still an adventure game, you'll explore the Kingdom, hunt for items and solve puzzles, but this time you have direct control of Graham as he quests around and interacts with the people of Daventry. (I played the game with an Xbox controller and it worked great!)
Death in Kings Quest comes along now and then but it isn't an obstacle, instead it adds an extra layer of humour to an already amusing game whilst playing on the story telling narrative.
Should you manage to get yourself gobbled up by a beastie or crisped to a cinder by a dragon you'll be treated to a witty narration saying something along the lines of "and that's what would have happened if I'd done that..." before the game jumps back to the moments before your death so you can make a different choice.
It makes you smile and keeps the game flowing pretty smoothly.
Episode One takes us back to Daventry as we follow Graham as teenage wannabe knight arriving in the Kingdom for the first time.
A knights tournament is about to take place, all Graham needs is an entry ticket and a way to get to the Tournament Theatre (Daventry is having "bridge issues" so that isn't as easy as you might think) but this is just the beginning of Grahams problems.
There's a chivalry test to pass and an initiation quest to complete before he can even compete in the three main trails of strength, speed and Wits to become a real knight of Daventry.
The game plays out in true adventure style as you hunt for items to help you overcome the various challenges the tournament presents.
You'll be talking to the locals, competing against (and joining forces with) other knight hopefuls and combining inventory objects just like the good old point and click games of yester-year.
There are different solutions to many of the puzzles too, the branching conversations are witty and well written and the puns are so bad they go beyond terrible and come out the other side, the side which makes you smile at their awfulness.
As Gwendolyn states herself during the narrative with "Old Graham" the puns start to grow on you.
Whilst the bulk of the story takes place in the retelling of events from Grahams past, we are treated to the odd cut scene set in the "present" revolving around old King Graham and the lives of his grandchildren. These intriguing snippets do a great job of weaving a separate storyline into the narrative and breaking up the knightly shenanigans of the past.
Graphically it's perfectly pretty with colourful and well animated cartoon style visuals.
Grahams cloak fluttering around behind him as he moves is a very nice touch.
The hand drawn art style makes each scene look special, It often feels like playing through a quality Disney movie and for an animated title I can't think of higher praise than that.
I've already mentioned the great work Christopher Lloyd does as the voice of the old king but credit should also be given to the other vocal talents in the game.
The standard of voice acting across the board is very high, there's no weak link here, all the characters in Daventry feel.... well... full of character.
With a Royal Lineage dating back to the early 80's, The Kings Quest franchise has been around for a long, long time.
This episodic return of the game is not only welcome but surprisingly good.
You don't need to be familiar with the previous titles either, everything you need to know is encapsulated within the game.​
As an episodic title it's longer than you'd expect too, the first episode clocks in at over 6 hours which is way better than the 2 hours of content I've come to expect from other episodic titles.
Kings Quest: A Knight to Remember is an entertaining tale with interesting puzzles, great voice work and beautifully hand drawn visuals.
The reboot of Kings Quest is off to a flying start.
Family friendly gaming at its best!

So, I brought this game tonight, and without even realising it I have already invested 4 hours into this masterpiece.
I thought I wouldn't like it at first as I am not usually a fan of the horror-game genre and thought it might all just be sneaking around enemies and avoiding combat. However, I was pleasantly surprised and taken aback by the immersion this game gives you, the options you can take to approach enemies and the amount of detail and love that has been put into the game!
Shinji Mikami has just created one of the best games this year, probably the best horror game in the last 3-4 years too. There were moments where I was actually generally fearing for my characters life, which is what a horror game should be all about!
I will be playing this through from start to finish for sure, hell I might even have to play it twice if it keeps getting better and better (which currently it is) and I haven't even left the starting town yet (if there is even more after this town, I'm assuming there is another part to it which i can hopefully explore!) as I have been doing the side quests and collectibles before moving on, trying to make sure I don't miss anything. However it's up to you which way you take the game, you can go to the story zones, or do the side quests and collectibles first then go and do them. Character freedom is quite broad in this game!
The only cons I really have are the fact that the combat system, in terms of swapping weapons and inventory managment, can be a little bit finnicky on the PC at times, also I am not soooo sure about the open-world setting, don't get me wrong it's great at times, and I love stumbling into random houses I haven't seen on the map yet, however I would have probably preffered something a little more linear (which I rarely say) as it can get a little confusing planning a route sometimes and knowing what buildings you have explored. But that's just a matter of personal opinion and I'm sure many other fully enjoy it and would actually hate it more linear. All in all this game is amazing however, so far I rate it:
7.8/10
However as I play more this rating might go up!
If you want to see some screenshots of the gameplay/cutscenes too, make sure to check out my profile screenshots. However, be warned there might be some spoliers that I haven't tagged as they don't seem like major spoliers in my eyes, but could be in some other's eyes!
Well worth the £40 I payed for it!
Edit #1 - So I've completed the game now, and holy hell was it an awesome ride. Althought I haven't played many survival-horror games in the past as it isn't really my genre, this game was the best survival-horror game I have played to date! It has amazing world detail (I kept finding myself stopping and taking screenshots/staring at the craziness around me!) as well as a nice level of difficulty which can be fine tuned to how you want it! The surivival difficulty for a casual player like me was nice, as it's progressivley gets harder at a nice rate, not making it an easy ride especially near the end were I found myself out of bullets and having to frantically scramble about for the resources I needed, while avoiding the numerous crazy mobs and mutant-like creatures that move about union!
All-in-all, while trying to explore most of the buildings (bar about 4-ish) the game can take around 14-16 hours, which for me is a nice amount of time especially if you are binging the game and completing it in two to three days like I did (Although I actually advise you spread it out more for obvious health and enjoyment reasons). I really hope they do actually add some DLC missions later on, as I would love to see more of this world! I can also see myself re-completing the game once I have got through the rest of my game collection as I really enjoyed the experience, reminds me of the first time I played through Bioshock for some reason!
Highly reccommend, one of my personal GOTY for me!

I have finished the "story" mode and I felt obligated to leave a review.  Slime Rancher is a simple game, it's not very deep, however it's entertaining.  You are on a planet inhabited by slimes and chickens.  You travel around sucking up slimes, produce, and chickens with a vac gun, then deposit them into corals.  In the case of the produce, you can either feed the slimes directly or plant them.  As you progress, you can purchase upgrades to your equipment such as more vac space, auto-feeders for the slimes, and more health.  The game is easy, I only died because I fell off a few ledges.  You actually don't "die", you get knocked out and wake up the next morning outside your home.  You can't furnish your home, the actual  customization is rather sparse, however I still had a good time.
Great game if you enjoyed the first one!

Dark Souls II Review
Fun, yet frustrating
I’m fighting against a skeleton wielding a large greatsword. I roll out of its way to dodge its first attack and immediately parry a second one with my shield. With my enemy off balance, I quickly get in a couple of slashes with my broadsword and get his health down significantly. At this point, I’m feeling confident that the fight is almost over as I roll out of the way of the skeleton’s next attack. But, to my horror, I anticlimactically fall off a cliff and die which forces me to lose all the souls I've collected.
Mouse flies in one direction, the keyboard flies in the other, and somehow there is a fist-sized hole in the monitor.
It seems to us that frustration is the currency that From Software likes to deal in when it comes to the Dark Souls franchise and Dark Souls 2 is no exception. There were many times we became frustrated as we played the game. But perhaps not for the reasons many who have played, or will play, the game will expect. But we’ll address that soon enough.

Charming Game. My dad and I used to play the original game together, and the game nicely updates the story telling, graphics, and interface for the 2015.  Certainly a fun challenge, and there are multiple (MULTIPLE) ways to approach puzzles, often in nonlinear ways that affect your options for solving future puzzles without you even knowing it.
Storytelling reminds me of the new 'Bastion' game, and (no spoilers) the dynamic between player and storyteller likely sets up some important plot development in later chapters.  The game also is not afraid to make fun of itself or the archaic adventure text genre, which makes for some good laughs.
If you're good at puzzle adventure games, you can complete Chapter 1 in under 10 hours but there's plenty of replay value as there are MULTIPLE ways to solve the story, but not in the 'you know you're about to make a plot choice that will affect the world one way or the other' that is common today.  For example, my Dad was asking me for a hint because he was stuck after fighting (no spoilers), and I didn't even know (no spoilers) was in the game on my playthrough.  Your choices can be that subtle, but that game-changing.
My only concern is whether the other Chapters will actually be released in a timely manner.  I'm not sure I agree with this 'but the set, but only get the tea cups to start' approach to video games... Oh well, here's hoping!

I have only played the first episode (as of right now), but there are a few things to consider, if you would like to purchase this game:
- Do you like puns?
- Do you like walking?
- Do you like fairy tales and quirky characters?
- Do you not mind the occasional quick time event?
- Are you okay with not having to give the cookie to the dog for it to share its bone with you that you can use as a flute to wake up the princess who will give one of her golden locks away for you to help making a violin that plays the song of time if you ask it nicely (and similar, rather tangled puzzles)?
Then you're in for a treat. The storytelling with its two layers (past and present) and the gorgeous surroundings and colors make the first episode a really nice entrance to the new world of Daventry.
The characters all have their own quirks and attitudes, but this does not mean they are flat so far. There are no overly complicated plot-twists though.
There are fail-states, mind you, but the auto-save feature will put you back right before it. It is a pity that you cannot save manually in order to play through all the story options, and that you cannot skip cut scenes.
Please be sure to put your savegame on a USB or something, if you need to change PCs, because Steam Cloud is not supported.
But this would be as far as my criticism goes.

System Shock 2 is a "cult" game the way the film Silent Running is cult, many people have heard of it (in Sci-Fi anyway) few experienced it.  Plus System Shock 2 sold pretty badly back in the day and physical copies were hard to find.  But now you can remedy this gap in your gaming knowledge!
Made by Looking Glass Studios (the first two Thief games) with music by Eric Brosius (ditto) System Shock 2 is the forerunner that influenced (among others) Deus Ex, Bioshock, Portal and Dead Space.  If you enjoyed any of these games I say give SS2 a shot.

Just Cause 3 is, with no doubt, my favourite game. Just Cause 2 was my favourite game before this was released, and JC3 fixed all the mistakes JC2 had made, most of which I wasn't even aware of until JC3 fixed them. The game is, similarly to it's sequels, based around blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up. Unlike it's sequels, however, JC3's descruction is all dynamic, so that no two explosions are the same. The map is huge, about 1000 square kilometres. The story has improved, and I actually enjoyed it, unlike the previous two games, where the story was all about the insanity of the missions. At the end of the game, you are given the option to re-opress any base you feel like, which is something that was missing from JC2 and is a great way to keep you playing, as there are so many ways to blow something up, whether it be shooting it, using the grappling hook to tear it apart, blowing it up with a tank, or just flying a jet into it. The game runs fine for me, and i don't have a very powerful pc at all, but i have heard that some people have had issues who are running it on more powerful rigs, so look into that if you decide to buy this game. The wingsuit is great fun, and the grappling hook and parachute have been improved since JC2 as well.
This game is basically JC2, but staggeringly improved, and with so many new features that it is definitely worth the price tag. This game ddoes depend on your interests, so it might not be for some people, but if you just want to have fun, this game is where you should look.

Awsome game and really well polished for an early access title. This is most definately a faithful remake of Half-Life compared to Half-Life: Source. The voice acting is good but not great (certainly an improvement over the original Half-Life). The music is kick♥♥♥♥♥with an intense soundtrack playing when first reaching the surface while soldiers are firing at you and bombs going off around you. Please be aware that this game is not without its bugs like the NPCs going back in forth when they don't have anymore targets to attack or if I fire my weapon at a scientist he would just stand there not reacting. The multiplayer is solid and plays more like the original Half-Life. Everything is there but with limited character customization and some bugs like the text being scrambled up for some odd reason or the player's animation getting glitchy while standing around sometimes. This game seems more like a solid title rather than early access and even back in 2012 this was an early access game worth of its title. This game is a must play for the fans of Half-Life and worth checking out if you are new to the series.

Overall, I really enjoyed this game (finally managed to finish it now :) ).
It drags on a bit in the second half, creating a few moments of "Come oooon", but it also manages to change pace frequently enough in that half to avoid the issues horror games face as their main horror gimmick starts to wear thin.
I would however advice anyone - even if you're terrible at video games - to play on Hard. The added danger and the added speed of the alien do a lot to make the game more scary, and really help in those situations where you feel like there's no possible way you can get past this (hint: it's nearly always "Use more items!"), which fits in well with being just a human against the alien.
Graphics are well done, sound is *amazing*, gameplay fits well with being overly clunky at times creating pressure from not being able to do things fast enough, voice work is well done and the game has enough surprising moments to keep you tense all the way through.
Really liked this. I can understand why it's not for everyone (it's a similar style of creepy horror game as Amnesia TDD or Outlast), but if you enjoy this type of game, do give it a try. :)

I held off on buying this one until it was 50% off ($24.99). I do not regret the purchase.
Pros:
Excellent atmosphere
Excellent stealth-based horror
Excellent music
They recruited some of the original movie cast for audio logs including Sigourney Weaver, Yaphet Kotto, and Mac McDonald.
Cons:
After seeing enough dark corridors with blinky lights, they all look somewhat same-ish. Learning to rely on the map became instinct. This is my own personal gripe, I like being able to memorize the layout of hallways and corridors for some fast-footed-fleeing.
Trekking back and forth across a map just to trip a switch while dodging the alien was fun for the first 20-30 hours. Seems like the alien got 10X smarter in the last few levels and I didn't realize until halfway through the game that everything nearby can hear your movement detector beep if you use it.
Facehuggers scurrying along the floor seemed difficult to hit accurately with anything but the flamethrower.
If I had to be forthright about my personal experience with this game, it would be that I was secretly pretending I was playing System Shock 3 at times sans Shodan & Xerxes. It had hacking, droids, bodies and light gore. I'm thinking if the team who created the Dead Space series worked with the team who created this game & the team who created Outlast to make System Shock 3 - the entire world would rejoice.
Fear factor - Somewhere in between any of the Dead Space games and Outlast. I love these kinds of games.  My only regret is that you never find any weapon capable of blasting an alien to bits and painting the corridors acid-green with it but I guess that requires more animations and textures. Scary scary game!  I'm a huge Alien Universe fan, and I felt this game is probably the best one made for that universe. That said, the visuals are amazing, the alien is random and incredibly deadly, the game offers a solid challenge (hard mode), and it's the closest I think any of us will get to being in the alien universe.  The controls are solid, the sounds are amazing and terrifying, and the music engine plays all the right pieces at all the right times - adding significantly to the dark, isolated atmosphere.  The weapons add just the right balance of play without making you feel unstoppable.  The minute-to-minute decisions you choose yield consequences that matter for survival.  A great amount of detail went into the alien, as well.  Though some design and sound decisions for the alien I felt were'nt quite right, the creature as a whole is daunting and terrifying. It also has hidden Oculus Rift DK2 support that can be enabled from the configuration file which adds even more immersion to the universe if you have a Rift.
This is probably the strongest game in the sci-fi survival horror genre, and it's worth picking up if you are into that kind of thing (which I am!).  I've never been so happy to be hunted by the scariest creature in the universe!

Follow-up to my personal "favorite game of all time (any platform)", part 2 (or 3 if counting Demon Souls...which I didn't play due to its exclusive release) is just as brilliant and rewarding - if a bit different - than its predecessor. Overall, this version is a bit more accessible and user friendly - which, being a "Souls" game, some will argue makes this the weaker game.
I disagree...there is still plenty of room to fail (and fall :)) and make mistakes over and over again, and enough surprises (especially when revisited in NG+) that will make you sneer at their cruelty. Yes, underneath the new UI polish, the friendly travel and hub system, and the brighter environments, it's still a Souls game that will have you swinging the controller in wide overhead arcs towards the nearest wall...but you won't be able to let go, because the game will keep sucking you back for one more try until you achieve victory. And then it's on to the next challenging locale or boss.
Environments are highly varied and huge with tons of loot rewards to those who fully explore all the deep recesses. Co-op summoning is streamlined and prevalent, especially to fight the boss battles (a number of which feature multi-bosses). Yes, the bosses can be soloed for more of a challenge, but the co-op fights are just as rewarding for their chaos and rewards (low risk if you offer yourself to be summoned, and if you win, you regain your humanity and all the benefits of sitting at a bonfire, plus you get a portion of the boss souls! Woot! Rinse/repeat for huge soul gains!).
Some of the early concerns - the scarcity of human effigies in game, the diminishing health bar after every hollowed death, the limit of mob respawns resulting in a limit of soul farming - all turned out to be eventually moot (see co-op summons above :) ). Basically, the system changes provide a wider "play it your way" spectrum...harder if you never rely on summoning (or being summoned), or bring in some help when you want it to get over a hurdle.
At the end of the day, is Dark Souls 1 or 2 better / harder? Don't care...I find it best to look at them as part of a HUGE continuous saga that I hope will have many more chapters.
NG - ended level 142, 90hrs
NG+ - ended level 206, 50hrs
Favorite boss: Chariot Executioner
PC port much improved over DK1 port last time.

I bought this game back when it was first released a year ago.  There were definite problems with the game at that time and the game seemed to be released way to early.  However, the developers at CA stuck with it and fixed most of the glaring issues and have polished this game into a finished product.  The game right now, as of the release of the Emperor Edition, is what the game should have been when they released it.  I can say that any doubt you may have due to initial reviews of this game should be erased, because almost every problem that was brought up at the time of release has been fixed.  They have given us a free campaign, a few free DLC packs, and have developed   other DLC that is worth the small price as well.  Is the game perfect?  No.
I wish AI could be better, but we have to accept that the AI will never be able to act in a Human sense.  Does that mean they are a pushover? Not at all!  The AI provides a challenging game.  I started a campaign recently as Rome on Very Hard (not even Legendary) and felt the AI pushing me back into Italy as I tried to expand out.  They keep you on your toes.
The additional campaigns provide a fresh map and playthrough experience, as well as offering new factions to choose for the Grand Campaign.  There are so many factions to choose from at this point, that I have trouble making up my mind which to play.  I probably have 20 saved campaigns, and I have only really touched maybe a third of the playable factions.
The unit selection does leave a little to be desired, but some of the DLC's add some depth here and there, enough to where its not an issue for most factions.
Multiplayer Campaign:  I think this is one of the better selling points of the game.  I like to play with others to try to conquer each other or to conquer the AI.  Unfortunately, you can only choose to be always allied or always at war.  I didn't like this decision, but it doesn't limit the game too much.  You and your partner can choose any 2 playable factions for the multiplayer campaign.  This means you can be as close to each other or as far from each other as you desire.  This provides for some interesting opportunities.  The downside is that they do take a while to play, as you can spend 5-10 minutes on a turn easily without even fighting a battle in there.  Game options allow you to make a time limit on turns and battles, though, to make game play faster.
The bottom line is this:  If you are a Total War fan, you should be looking to buy this game.  Ignore the original reviews, as they are no longer relevant.  Possibly wait for it to go on sale, but this should be a definite buy at this point for anyone who enjoyed the original Rome Total War or any of the Total War series.

Now it's something like 15 years after its original release, and for the third time, i'm playing it being fascinated with the game.  (Got it off Ebay ages ago, to get an uncensored and english game, because back then every even remotely violent game got censored in germany - imagine green blood, no gore and shenanigans like that)
Sure the graphics are video game stone age material. But does it bother me? Not at all.
Because here we have one of those games, that went down in the annals of history, pretty much overall met with praise. And rightfully so.
You see, back then... developers had trust in you. Trust in your cognitive abilities, to find your way without visual markers hitting you in the face. Trust in you to manage your characters stats, health, equipment, weapons the way you see fit (Deus Ex *cough*). Trust in you to be involved enough and try again and again, should you die a lot or have to figure out how to approach certain things.
All this in a creepy Sci-Fi-Horror environment, that lets you fight for survival. Even if you're out of AP Ammo to shoot that motherly cyborg midwife, you grab your wrench and hit her in the face, because this game does something to you many games, and in fact most games nowadays, fail to accomplish - you care about it, it's world, its mechanics. You're involved and immersed.
Now, this game is fairly linear, although you'll backtrack often and are soon free to go where you please on the ship. You're on a leash, but it won't feel like it. Because the developers didn't shove it down your throat, and you're too busy surviving, thinking about how to spend your nanites and cyber modules, remembering in which chemical storage the Gallium was, or cowering in fear while something wants you to become one with the many, adding to the bliss and glory of the biomass.
For me, this is one of those rare games that are actually challenging, without feeling tedious, boring, overly repetetive or have you farm and grind your way to virtual goodies that are a complete waste of time. (I`m not a big fan of the usual MMO, obviously) And on a sidenote, UI and interaction don't feel too dated to me. It all works just fine, even before everything was about streamlining, casualizing and big flashing hints on the screen so you don't feel inconvenienced for even a second, because you couldn't be bothered to actually think about what you're doing.
Yes, it is 2014 now and you can count the polygons on your screen. But the atmosphere is killer. Don't be a swine, acknowledge the pearl before you. You can improve the visuals with mods, but if that is all you care about, you're missing out on a freakin' masterpiece. People don't get nostalgic and speak about it in an ominous voice or flat out hype this game over a decade later for nothing. Not all was good back then, and not all sucks now, bot some oldschool quality is sorely missed for sure.
Worth every buck and all your attention. Even if you're just checking out what all the fuss is about with this gem of a game.

I have just recently added Smite to Steam even though I played this game for over 1k hours in the last year or so. As far as MOBAS go, I believe only Dota 2 comes ahead of Smite. Smite is certainly simpler and easier to get into. It is quite fun and engaging right off the bat. And, yes, it takes some skill to get good and be an efficient team player. The last hit rewards gold to all makes it so it needs less micromanaging but, at the end of the day, someone in the team will be building stacks and will be keen to last hitting, which is pretty easy anyway. The god (hero) pool is quite large and varied, and mastery of any god in Smite takes only a few games. The quality of the graphics and character detail are excellent. The games are often shorter than other MOBAs, maybe with the exception of HoTS, as there are many casual games modes, all different from each other. The main mode (the league conquest) is still the most enjoyable, in my opinion. Getting to play ranked games is much faster than in Dota 2. As far as the community goes, well, there are plenty of kids playing the game, as it is logical, and there is no real banning system from Hi Rez (I have never seen anyone banned from a report). So, imagine. Kids will do what kids do (you know the drill - rage quit, place the blame on others, take no reponsibility, no patience, gratutitous insults, bullying). Thankfully you can mute people, similarly to Dota 2. However, the games being a bit more action packed early that in Dota 2, the raging usually starts right away. There is less of that getting comfortable on your hero during early stages of the game than in Dota 2.
All and all, Smite is a great game, truly free to play, which rewards good individual and team play. You can progress in this game spending no money (or very little if you want to support Hi Rez) and acquire all sorts of gear.
The pro community is small but watching their games is engaging. There are plenty of pro players with a healthy streaming schedule. The casters do a good job most of the time, even though they should start droppìng the "education" component from their casting, as the viewing community is well versed in the game by now.
In conclusion, play the game and check the community out. Start with a few gods, master these and see what role you like. The rest will work itself out.

I have only played the first episode (as of right now), but there are a few things to consider, if you would like to purchase this game:
- Do you like puns?
- Do you like walking?
- Do you like fairy tales and quirky characters?
- Do you not mind the occasional quick time event?
- Are you okay with not having to give the cookie to the dog for it to share its bone with you that you can use as a flute to wake up the princess who will give one of her golden locks away for you to help making a violin that plays the song of time if you ask it nicely (and similar, rather tangled puzzles)?
Then you're in for a treat. The storytelling with its two layers (past and present) and the gorgeous surroundings and colors make the first episode a really nice entrance to the new world of Daventry.
The characters all have their own quirks and attitudes, but this does not mean they are flat so far. There are no overly complicated plot-twists though.
There are fail-states, mind you, but the auto-save feature will put you back right before it. It is a pity that you cannot save manually in order to play through all the story options, and that you cannot skip cut scenes.
Please be sure to put your savegame on a USB or something, if you need to change PCs, because Steam Cloud is not supported.
But this would be as far as my criticism goes.

I'm more of a solo player, however, after being completely disappointed by almost everything Early Access, Hurtworld was a nice break. I chose to go the route of a solo server to experience the general standing of content the game had to offer, and wasn't that disappointed. There are however a few flaws.
1.) Yes, the game is about survival. However, there are folks that would like to team up and throught past experiences w/ almost any game, that's not going to happen. 99% of the time it is highly suggested that you should run away if you even catch someone in your sights. They will find you... And they will kill you.
2.) The vehicles need to be fixed badly. I'm not talking about vehicles in general. When you get one, it's great. However, as it stands... You can no longer modify parts. You used to be able to remove certain parts from vehicles. Not anymore. Now you have to pray you find four wheels, an engine, and etc. It's THAT hard.
3.) Players have gotten really smart in their ability to abuse the game. Right off the bat it was glitching through walls. Now it's building their settlements COMPLETELY around "towns" where important items can be found.
All in all, there are several things I do not like. Some of that is through no fault of the developers, but the other side is just in the players. First, everyone is cocky. Sure, some may help, but it is rare. Unless you dedicate yourself to finding a group via the forums or etc, any attempt is going to suck. Secondly, while I understand it's a hardcore survival game, logging out perfectly fine and then logging in freezing to death, in the middle of the desert, w/ full cold gear is no fun. That's not a challenge. That's just pure suckage. It's unfortunately happened more than once and no one has been able to explain to me what causes it.
I'd suggest buying it, but like all Early Access games, on sale. I do believe there should be a limited on Early Access titles and Steam has really gone to crap because of them. (I'm looking at you DayZ SA, Landmark, H1Z1, and others.)

I bought this game back when it was first released a year ago.  There were definite problems with the game at that time and the game seemed to be released way to early.  However, the developers at CA stuck with it and fixed most of the glaring issues and have polished this game into a finished product.  The game right now, as of the release of the Emperor Edition, is what the game should have been when they released it.  I can say that any doubt you may have due to initial reviews of this game should be erased, because almost every problem that was brought up at the time of release has been fixed.  They have given us a free campaign, a few free DLC packs, and have developed   other DLC that is worth the small price as well.  Is the game perfect?  No.
I wish AI could be better, but we have to accept that the AI will never be able to act in a Human sense.  Does that mean they are a pushover? Not at all!  The AI provides a challenging game.  I started a campaign recently as Rome on Very Hard (not even Legendary) and felt the AI pushing me back into Italy as I tried to expand out.  They keep you on your toes.
The additional campaigns provide a fresh map and playthrough experience, as well as offering new factions to choose for the Grand Campaign.  There are so many factions to choose from at this point, that I have trouble making up my mind which to play.  I probably have 20 saved campaigns, and I have only really touched maybe a third of the playable factions.
The unit selection does leave a little to be desired, but some of the DLC's add some depth here and there, enough to where its not an issue for most factions.
Multiplayer Campaign:  I think this is one of the better selling points of the game.  I like to play with others to try to conquer each other or to conquer the AI.  Unfortunately, you can only choose to be always allied or always at war.  I didn't like this decision, but it doesn't limit the game too much.  You and your partner can choose any 2 playable factions for the multiplayer campaign.  This means you can be as close to each other or as far from each other as you desire.  This provides for some interesting opportunities.  The downside is that they do take a while to play, as you can spend 5-10 minutes on a turn easily without even fighting a battle in there.  Game options allow you to make a time limit on turns and battles, though, to make game play faster.
The bottom line is this:  If you are a Total War fan, you should be looking to buy this game.  Ignore the original reviews, as they are no longer relevant.  Possibly wait for it to go on sale, but this should be a definite buy at this point for anyone who enjoyed the original Rome Total War or any of the Total War series.

Like its namesake, Postal Redux features all of the original Postal levels and gameplay but on a new engine with loads of improvements.
Gameplay-wise not a whole lot has changed. Rather than pressing the “next level” button you now run to the exit area for a stage after killing the requisite number of baddies. Controls are also improved significantly for gamepad and the overall “flow” of the game feels much smoother than the original. There are a few new weapons but I found the shotgun, missile, and flame weapons to be pretty much all you need to complete the game on nightmare difficulty.
The graphical overhaul has made for a much more enjoyable experience and little details like being able to tell different kinds of police and soldiers apart as well as what weapons they’re holding is a nice touch. Animations for all characters are also very fluid, contributing much to the improved flow mentioned earlier. The soundtrack that accompanies all of this is likewise also improved and things sound better than before.
The original Postal was a decent game with a few flaws here and there. Redux manages to pave over those flaws and present itself almost as if it were its own unique game. In fact it’s so much better and comprehensive than the original that you might as well just play this one instead, especially since the story is more or less the same.

I have just recently added Smite to Steam even though I played this game for over 1k hours in the last year or so. As far as MOBAS go, I believe only Dota 2 comes ahead of Smite. Smite is certainly simpler and easier to get into. It is quite fun and engaging right off the bat. And, yes, it takes some skill to get good and be an efficient team player. The last hit rewards gold to all makes it so it needs less micromanaging but, at the end of the day, someone in the team will be building stacks and will be keen to last hitting, which is pretty easy anyway. The god (hero) pool is quite large and varied, and mastery of any god in Smite takes only a few games. The quality of the graphics and character detail are excellent. The games are often shorter than other MOBAs, maybe with the exception of HoTS, as there are many casual games modes, all different from each other. The main mode (the league conquest) is still the most enjoyable, in my opinion. Getting to play ranked games is much faster than in Dota 2. As far as the community goes, well, there are plenty of kids playing the game, as it is logical, and there is no real banning system from Hi Rez (I have never seen anyone banned from a report). So, imagine. Kids will do what kids do (you know the drill - rage quit, place the blame on others, take no reponsibility, no patience, gratutitous insults, bullying). Thankfully you can mute people, similarly to Dota 2. However, the games being a bit more action packed early that in Dota 2, the raging usually starts right away. There is less of that getting comfortable on your hero during early stages of the game than in Dota 2.
All and all, Smite is a great game, truly free to play, which rewards good individual and team play. You can progress in this game spending no money (or very little if you want to support Hi Rez) and acquire all sorts of gear.
The pro community is small but watching their games is engaging. There are plenty of pro players with a healthy streaming schedule. The casters do a good job most of the time, even though they should start droppìng the "education" component from their casting, as the viewing community is well versed in the game by now.
In conclusion, play the game and check the community out. Start with a few gods, master these and see what role you like. The rest will work itself out.

My brief review:
As an adult, and a fan of adventure games both classic and modern, King's Quest feels frustratingly linear and patronizing.  There's potential, but it misses the mark in a few small and big ways and I can't recommend it for most people.  However, it's definitely worth a look if you have children or younger family members.
Slightly longer:
The 2015 King's Quest is a mixed bag, but not one that I can recommend for most players.  Graphically, the game feels very last-generation (except, bizarrely, for the cape animation) with few options to choose from.  Just the ability to enable some higher anti-aliasing would have been nice as the game is pretty jaggy.  It's obvious that the developer is trying to ape the Telltale style, but there's a level of charm in the animations and writing which don't hit their goal... which is unfortunate because King's Quest is desperately -- gaspingly -- trying to be charming.  They overdo it.
The gameplay is incredibly linear and patronizing (a bit simple even by Telltale standards), the tone is forcefully schmaltzy, and I can only begin to express how BRUTAL it is that the game lacks a dialogue/animation skip.  Seriously, the fact that you can't skip anything just puts a huge spotlight on all the flaws.  The dialogue, which is inherently (mind-numbingly) repetitive, grates after just the second time.
I'll say this: the lack of outright failure does NOT bother me and the way that's handled with the narrative device is genuinely inspired.  I hated in old adventure games when I could die or completely screw myself over because I didn't do a small thing earlier in the game.  I'll never miss that, and I don't think that King's Quest is missing anything by being "easy."
I also got the sense that the publisher is eying an eventual mobile release.  There's just something about the structure of the world, and its controls, and its options, and it's graphics that tells me a mobile release is in the future.
It's not all bad.  It's not even mostly bad.  If you're looking for a game that can be played by your children, this probably hits that sweet spot.  While it's difficult to call this game an “homage” to the Princess Bride, since through sheer quantity of lifted elements it can only be called a ripoff, nonetheless the core story beats and voice acting are a cut above.  I expected Christopher Lloyd to come off as depressingly old, but his performance is actually perfect for his character.  The only character that annoyed me was the granddaughter, Gwendolyn.  She's such a well-worn trope, a cliche, that it had me rolling my eyes whenever she chimed in or we got a glimpse of her B-plot.
There's a potential to this new King's Quest that goes unrealized, but it's there.  It's enough that I haven't completely written off future acts, but I'm not counting the days.  A Steam sale and a dialogue skip might be enough to sway me.  Until then, I can't recommend this game to most people... but if you have children, give it an honest look.

This game is an excellent continuation of the story from the original + DLC.
Having played through the original + DLC and games like Thief; I have to say, that it has been fairly easy to do a Clean Hands & Shadow acheivement playthrough first-time on normal difficulty.
In terms of Dishonored 2, I put this down to some things I noticed.
Firstly, there are obviously far less rats etc due to the plague having been ended. However I feel that, even for low chaos, there could and should have been scripted events regarding Bloodflies attacking civillians or guard patrols getting too close to buildings marked as infected.
Secondly, I noticed some scripted kill events involving characters. One in particular comes to mind; Overseers executing civillians for heresy but it does not count against you in the stats menu. The only one I recall which does need intervention is the second level stopping a civillian being fried by a wall of light.
Thirdly, The witches were quite disappointing for the simple reason they were not setup to blink around(unless alerted). From the original, part of the challenge was when the Assassins and Brigmore witches blinked around catching the player unaware. They should have been blinking all over the place.
I am glad that my suspicions were confirmed regarding the character Billie Lurk during the later parts of the game. It will be interesting to see what directions DLC will focus on.
The notes, audiographs and journals collected leave me craving for more content.
I wish the achievements for taking the non-lethal approach were included as they add a bit of flavour(for example the alternative approach to Byrne & Paulo in Dust District)
I recommed this game overall. Took me longer to complete than the first entry, but that is a good thing(especially when priced at £40)!

Dishonored 2 follows almost the exact formula that made the original great. Clever level design with difficult enough gameplay make for an overall enjoyable experience. My only real complaint is that the story is a little too short. I personally would've liked to see a few more missions. This is made up for in the replay value of this game which, like it's predecessor, is very high. I will certainly be giving this another few playthroughs in the future.

The game is pretty passable, so whatever gamebreaking bugs people were finding didn't make it into my version of the game. That aside, I played a nonlethal powerless run and I can say without a doubt that the powerless option is the most pointless, dissapointing, infuriating, bad, terrible option they put in the game. It's a complete waste of time. There's no acknowledgement from the ending, which renders my decision to not use powers meaningless. I chose it expecting that doing so would save Emily from being corrupted or manipulated by the outsider, but it was actually meaningless which infuriates me to no end since I really cared about giving Emily the best ending possible.
As for nonlethal options, most of the game is pretty good with giving nonlethal/low chaos options for the targets, with the notable exception of the ending level. Not only did I get no indication there was a nonlethal option by the game, but when I was forced to look up the method on the internet, I encountered a bug which prevented me from completing the game without replaying half the level.
Similar to the first Dishonored, the ending cinematic feels short and incomplete, more like a reminder of the decisions you made rather than an actual ending. I was left feeling cheated of the ending I though the game deserved. I suppose I was naive in thinking that I could get a fulfilling story from a game that obviously prioritizes gameplay, but that would have brought Dishonored 2 from a passable game to a great game. Too bad.
I'd recommend this game to a person wanting to kill or choke their way to power since the gameplay is generally as good if not better than the first game, just don't expect much from the story.

Postal Redux is a damn fine game.
It may not have as interesting of a story as Postal 2, but it's gameplay is the true selling point. This game is fun, really fun. I honestly think I enjoy the gameplay here more than Postal 2, which is saying A LOT. It just feels so good to mow down enemies however you want, but in more of an old school arcade style than Postal 2.
This game is a perfect remake in terms of feeling like the original, but BETTER in gameplay. The art in this game is also phenomenal. Not a modern art masterpiece or anything, but it is very appealing, with the 3D models on point, looking very nice. The backgrounds and art between levels is also very visually impressive. The best way to play this game is with a keyboard and mouse, so if you have no controller, it's more than fine. The sound is also very interesting, as you can hear both screams, and Rick Hunter himself. Rick Hunter does a good job as the Postal Dude once again, and delivers good lines.
The best thing about Postal Redux is that you can tell the developers care A LOT about the player. Not only is this game cheap, but its sheer fun makes it worth a lot more than most, if not all modern generic shooters. This game is pretty cheap, and for it's price, it's well worth it. And rather than adding new levels in some cheap DLC, they put them in a free update. Running with Scissors has had DLC before, but it felt very justified, with Paradise Lost being basically Postal 3.
I haven't tried multiplayer for Postal Redux yet, but I'm sure it's fun. One issue hardcore fans of Postal 2 may find is that you HAVE to kill people. In the original Postal 2, killing was pretty much optional. While it is incredibly fun here, it may rub certain fans the wrong way.
OVERALL: Postal Redux is a fun game that is simple, but still incredibly enjoyable. It's worth every penny it costs and then some. It delivers the definitive version of the severely overlooked Postal 1. If you haven't already, buy this game, and Postal 2 with the DLC. You won't regret it, these games are fun, and buying them gives Running with Scissors the funding TO MAKE A REAL POSTAL 3. Postal Redux is simply a blast. BUY IT NOW, IT'S ONLY 9 BUCKS!

So this game is an improvement in almost every way to the first one. There's only two things that have bugged me so far and that's the ability to essentially pause the game and craft in fights which pretty much eliminates the tense moments and the GPU usage issues which I hope are addressed soon. I just completed the chapter of King's Quest. It took me about six hours to complete the story and then another two hours to come back in and get all the achievements that I missed.
This game is a big nostalgia trip for a lot of people, but I've got no previous experience with the series and only middling experience with adventure games in general. However, I thoroughly enjoyed this game.
It is an absolutely stunningly gorgeous game. I heard on Game Grumps that apparently a lot of the scenery was handpainted for the game? If so that's incredible.
The voice acting is much better than what I expected. Including some more well known actors like Christopher Lloyd and Wallace Shawn.
Overall though, the game is very simple. There were only two parts of the whole thing where I felt challenged, and they were both "boss fights" and neither one was particularly difficult in itself, just hard for me to understand what I was supposed to be doing.
It's been said before, but this a game that grows on you. At first you might be put off by some of the cutesy nature of things, or the rather simple plot, but it's definitely a game that appreciates subtlety and details like *SPOILER*when in the prologue you complete puzzles with a bow left by a dead adventurer and then later you travel through the cave with that very adventurer, giving more meaning and weight to a part of the game that you've already completed. *END SPOILER* The simple writing and use of puns and wordplay as jokes grew on me over the course of it, and I left feeling fairly satisfied at the end of the Chapter. On that note, because this is an episodic game, I'll likely try to write more of this review for each chapter.
This is also notable for being one of the few adventure games I've seen which has multiple solutions to puzzles available, so if you prefer more off-the-wall adventure game mechanics, there's likely a solution like that, and if you think in more of a straightforward fashion, there's that as well.
