I have just recently added Smite to Steam even though I played this game for over 1k hours in the last year or so. As far as MOBAS go, I believe only Dota 2 comes ahead of Smite. Smite is certainly simpler and easier to get into. It is quite fun and engaging right off the bat. And, yes, it takes some skill to get good and be an efficient team player. The last hit rewards gold to all makes it so it needs less micromanaging but, at the end of the day, someone in the team will be building stacks and will be keen to last hitting, which is pretty easy anyway. The god (hero) pool is quite large and varied, and mastery of any god in Smite takes only a few games. The quality of the graphics and character detail are excellent. The games are often shorter than other MOBAs, maybe with the exception of HoTS, as there are many casual games modes, all different from each other. The main mode (the league conquest) is still the most enjoyable, in my opinion. Getting to play ranked games is much faster than in Dota 2. As far as the community goes, well, there are plenty of kids playing the game, as it is logical, and there is no real banning system from Hi Rez (I have never seen anyone banned from a report). So, imagine. Kids will do what kids do (you know the drill - rage quit, place the blame on others, take no reponsibility, no patience, gratutitous insults, bullying). Thankfully you can mute people, similarly to Dota 2. However, the games being a bit more action packed early that in Dota 2, the raging usually starts right away. There is less of that getting comfortable on your hero during early stages of the game than in Dota 2.
All and all, Smite is a great game, truly free to play, which rewards good individual and team play. You can progress in this game spending no money (or very little if you want to support Hi Rez) and acquire all sorts of gear.
The pro community is small but watching their games is engaging. There are plenty of pro players with a healthy streaming schedule. The casters do a good job most of the time, even though they should start droppìng the "education" component from their casting, as the viewing community is well versed in the game by now.
In conclusion, play the game and check the community out. Start with a few gods, master these and see what role you like. The rest will work itself out.

Slime Rancher is one of the most surprising games I've played. I picked it up while it was still in early access after seeing a youtube video that piqued my interest, and played through the content that was there at the time. It was fun, but there wasn't too much to do. I made a note to come back and check it out again after it came out.
And boy, they did not disappoint. Monomi Park are a shining example of how early Access can- and should- be. Every single gameplay concept was explored deeply. Gameplay loops were complicated and intertwined. And there was a huge amount of content- and it even felt paced just right, making sure I was always interested and plannign ahead for how I'd get past that locked door, or what paths I still had to explore. The map feature, which was not present when I first played, have also done a fantastic job of helping you navigate some of the rather complex, branching paths.
After nearly 40 hours of gameplay, I can only think of one complaint- the requirements for extractions for treasure crackers is ridiculously too high. But that's such a minor complain that it barely even registers. Slime Rancher is one of the most pure, innocent, and entertaining experiences I've had in gaming, period. This game helped soothe me when I felt stressed.
Another huge plus- without giving too much away, there's a bit of a romance story in this game, and it's queer as hell, and it's wonderful. I truly appreciate the work of the writers in crafting this story.
All in all, I would not hesitate to give Slime Rancher my endorsement. It's worth it at any price.

I like challenging games, and I don't mind having to try several times to complete parts of a game. When I heard about DS2 and how 'difficult' it was, I was looking forward to it.
What I didn't take into consideration was the truly awful porting of controls from console to PC. The actual difficulty in this game is getting your controls to work properly. So, after 1.5 hours of arsing around trying to get my char to ♥♥♥♥ing jump by pressing space (which you can't do, by the way, so don't try), I moved on to trying to play. The next problem you come to, after the awful controls, is the terrible interface. Buttons which don't work when you click your mouse on them, random objects with no apparent purpose, inability to use items, lack of information about, well, anything...
Regardless, off into the world I went, with my huge, [/i]slow[/i] sword (which I couldn't change to two smaller weapons due to the aforementioned terrible interface), I rolled around a bit and 'jumped' (which you have to do while pressing three different buttons, no less) and collected shiny things which float over bodies, and spoke to some cat. He wasn't even a nice cat. All was going swimmingly, until I met two giant trolls. My fantastically laborious sword was barely unsheathed before I was clubbed to death upside the head.
. Not one to give in easily, I practiced my backstepping and rolling about like a prat, and returned to the trolls several more times. No chance.
thought I. Unfortunately, all the other ways had some kind of death-ensuring circumstances to take me right back to that first campfire in Majula. The sword of clumsiness merely hindered my frantic attempts at circling the opponent, the lack of ability to move smoothly due to the ♥♥♥♥ed up keyboard controls probably didn't help, and the silly interface ensured that I was unable to do much of anything, really.

Review for Emperor Edition:
All the updates leading up to and including the free Emperor Edition update have turned Rome II into a great game. They have added upgrades to the culture system, seasons and seasonal effects (both visual and in applying bonuses or penalties), campaign and battle balancing, more playable factions and units, building chain revamps (more variety of buildings and chains), and various performance improvements.
The latest update, which upgrades the game to Emperor Edition for free, has modified politics and civil war in ways that are very impactful to your campaign. You have reason to constantly track your family or partys influence, having to assasinate your own generals for fear of sparking a civil war or engage in political actions to improve your influence. Failure to do so results in harsh public order and tax penalties that will really cause you problems if you dont handle your politics correctly.
The update also adds improvements to the user interface (color coding various things and reworking the politics screen), although overall the ui is not as visually appealing as in previous games. It also adds the Imperator Augustus campaign, which adds the playable Armenia faction to the Grand Campaign as well. It uses the Grand Campaigns map while adding various roman factions and changes to other factions to fit the setting.
Overall the game is as it should have been when it launched last september. However, the user interface still a downgrade from the beautiful Shogun 2 scrolls. You also dont get as attached to your generals as in previous games (partly due to the lack of a family tree and the minimal importance given to aquired character traits). I would have also liked to have seen the return of the system where some settlement buildings were spread out across their territories (e.g. the farms or gold mines of Shogun 2 being represented on the campaign map as potential targets). It got removed in favor of the province system and of armies using the raiding stance in enemy territory, even though both systems could have worked in tandem to greater effect. It would have also made strategic raids of provinces more interesting since you had an additional, strategic target to attack or defend besides settlements, ports or other armies.
In short, the game has substantially improved since launch and the Emperor Edition is a testament to that. I give the game in its current form a solid 9/10.

I was super excited about this game. So excited I asked my boyfriend to purchase a copy so we could play together. I really really tried with this game, especially since I spent about $80 on it including the $14.99 monthly subscription.
Why you should skip this game, even if you're an Elder Scrolls enthusiast;
1. The quests, for the most part, are repetitive and boring.
2. Unless you're in a guild, PUGS are pretty much non-existent. Maybe I was on the wrong server or didn't get "far enough" into the game. While the world itself isn't empty, as someone used to the bustling presence of PCs in Stormwind, it was  a bit jarring to receive radio silence when I typed LFG in the chatbox.
3.I really don't care about the main story line. Oblivion and Skyrim (especially Skyrim) hooked me into the story automatically, sending me to various parts of the realm to meet even more interesting NPCs who, if I did something for them, would become allies during the game. Complete a quest for someone in ESO? You get your gold prize and then nothing else.
4. Every barrel or box in a city cannot be looted. What is this flickery?
5. The crafting is pretty good for the skills I chose; alchemy and cooking; but having to find recipes was kind of obnoxious. In Skyrim you have a list of recipes and are able to cook them based on whether or not you have the ingredients on hand. The "Find the recipe" game just seems like a way to add a level of complexity to the game that is completely unnecessary.
Many people I've read have said "Stop comparing ESO to Skyrim." I think this is unrealistic. Most of the people who bought this game did so because they enjoyed Skyrim or any other titles from Bethesda. Yes, I know this is Zenimax, Bethesda still had SOME input.
Overall the game is BORING. Maybe I'll give it another go some time in the future, but at this rate I'm forcing myself to play it because I invested money, not because it's fun.

I love adventure games. Loved them since the days of the likes of Day of the Tentacle, Sam and Max, Monkey Island, Discworld, Simon the Sorceror (thought I should mention at least a couple off non-Lucas ones just to show that other companies were actually capable of making good ones).
What I'd suggest to the makers of this game is, can you please go back and play some of the above mentioned titles? Then make a game that actually fits in that genre?
The problems with this title are numerous but first I'll tell you what things it at least does
than the recent Telltale fare which it is trying so desperately hard to copy. I think it's only fair to review it in this way since they chose to design it this way.
1. Animation. Whilst I think the graphics themselves, if you take a still screenshot, are pretty much identical to the quality of recent Telltale works, the animation is a huge improvement. Telltale's animations are janky and horrible, they are trying to be cartoonish and stylised but it never works and comes down with a serious case of Uncanny Valley. King's Quest, on the other hand, seems to have taken some lessons from proper cartoon animation and the characters move around in a really nice way, usually with exaggerated movement and humour. This is perfect for the art style they have gone with and is a solid part of the production.
2. Voices (and dialogue). Well, it would be hard for them to go wrong with some of the big names they got behind this, although Christopher Lloyd is doing a bit too much of the kindly old grandpa for my tastes, rather than delivering his lines with any wit or agency. Still this is so much better than Telltale whose voice direction generally makes me cringe. The actual writing of the lines is far far better, still leaving something to be desired, but a lot of Telltale's dialogue is just plain unforgivably bad, especially when dealing with a property like Game of Thrones which, y'know, is quite well known for having awesome writing on the TV.
And unfortunately that's it. They've managed to actually make gameplay even worse than TTG. Yes there are the familiar elements that I love to hate in the modern crop of adventure games, such as QTEs and WASD controls, action segments, entirely linear plot and exploration (no matter how much they claim to have a branching storyline), puzzles that can't really be classed as puzzles when it's basically "press A to continue". But they've somehow managed (and this is really truly impressive when I think about it) to bring all these elements together in an even worse, less consistent, and more linear, redundant and patronising way than even TTG manage.

For those unfamiliar with Postal 1, it is far different in tone and gameplay of the more known Postal 2. Postal 1 was a rudimentary isometric shooter in which you are placed in the shoes of a homicidal madman. You progress through levels by only really having to kill hostiles, though there is no penalty or reward for killing innocents as well. In-between loading screens you are given a brief vague description of the main characters current thoughts/views with hellish imagery and sounds. The game is mostly un-nerving with an occasional mix of dark humour. While the game originally was very basic, it's execution stuck with me as it's an interesting portrayal of a decent into madness. I really wanted to see where it all lead rather than experience the actual gameplay.
Seeing Postal Redux on sale for $2.50 got me excited to experience this game in a new way and I'm happy to say it doesn't dissapoint for the most part. The games levels retain the same amount of detail with a bit of polish and the models are now more modern besting the original polyginal characters. All the loading screens have been updated as well coming as close to the originals as possible with updates such as animations and screen effects, the screens also retain the creepy musical loops from the original. A big improvement to the gameplay is the overall control feels far more natrual in this adaptation, with feeling of fighting with the controls as in the original. All of the key levels from the original here are present plus some new ones.
However, the games ending level is changed from the original games.
In the original:

In the Redux:
This isn't a deal breaker in my opinion but I think it would be beneficial to view the original ending on YouTube as I feel it matches the games tone more. The ending screens and text though, are pretty much the same otherwise.
In short: Aside from a slightly altered ending Postal Redux is a great way to play as a mass shooter who believes he's saving the world from...something. It is also a far more funner to play and a bit more polished than the 1997 original.

Review for Emperor Edition:
All the updates leading up to and including the free Emperor Edition update have turned Rome II into a great game. They have added upgrades to the culture system, seasons and seasonal effects (both visual and in applying bonuses or penalties), campaign and battle balancing, more playable factions and units, building chain revamps (more variety of buildings and chains), and various performance improvements.
The latest update, which upgrades the game to Emperor Edition for free, has modified politics and civil war in ways that are very impactful to your campaign. You have reason to constantly track your family or partys influence, having to assasinate your own generals for fear of sparking a civil war or engage in political actions to improve your influence. Failure to do so results in harsh public order and tax penalties that will really cause you problems if you dont handle your politics correctly.
The update also adds improvements to the user interface (color coding various things and reworking the politics screen), although overall the ui is not as visually appealing as in previous games. It also adds the Imperator Augustus campaign, which adds the playable Armenia faction to the Grand Campaign as well. It uses the Grand Campaigns map while adding various roman factions and changes to other factions to fit the setting.
Overall the game is as it should have been when it launched last september. However, the user interface still a downgrade from the beautiful Shogun 2 scrolls. You also dont get as attached to your generals as in previous games (partly due to the lack of a family tree and the minimal importance given to aquired character traits). I would have also liked to have seen the return of the system where some settlement buildings were spread out across their territories (e.g. the farms or gold mines of Shogun 2 being represented on the campaign map as potential targets). It got removed in favor of the province system and of armies using the raiding stance in enemy territory, even though both systems could have worked in tandem to greater effect. It would have also made strategic raids of provinces more interesting since you had an additional, strategic target to attack or defend besides settlements, ports or other armies.
In short, the game has substantially improved since launch and the Emperor Edition is a testament to that. I give the game in its current form a solid 9/10.

One of the biggest problems with this game is the fact that Creative Assembly not only played favorites with with playable factions in but also made some insanely stupid choices when it came to the battle mechanics.
The Romans, Seleucids, and Egypt are by far the worst examples of CA playing favorites with factions. And what makes the Seleucids and Egypt so overpowered is the fact that they have everything in their army roster, while the Romans  just have some of the most overpowered infantry in the game. I know that Roman infantry should be good, but not invincible.
And this leads to the problems in a number of the battle mechanics and or abilities that were brought to Rome 2.
While Rome 2 did bring some really great battle mechanics like the Line of Sight or visual or whatever you want to call it system. The one that lets you be able to hide your troops with terrain and such. I don't fully know what to call it.
First. The broken Formation Attack ability.
This stupid ability was broken because it allowed any unit with it to hold their formation pretty much no matter what. Pikes get attacked from the side of rear? No problem, they'll just turn and fight like it was nothing.  A unit of elite Roman melee infantry gets attacked from 3 sides at once? It's all good, they'll just fight and hold off the enemy like nothing.
Second, and worst of all, was what CA did to siege battles. CA did one of the most absolutely stupidest things that they could've ever done.
They allowed the defenders to see the attackers during the deployment phase.
Stop and think about what that means, and read it again slowly.
This is wasn't just a campaign only featue, it was in custom and multiplayer battles as well.
It took out almost all tactical and strategic options that you could've previously tried in a siege battle, pretty much killing easily 90% of all possible strategy in siege battles.
It's like giving one team of paintballers night vision goggles while forcing the other team to go out into the dark with nothing of the sort. his down right ruined sieges, and this is coming from someone who was truly loving the assaulting cities. I was truly loving becoming a master of siegecraft.
And if anyone thinks I'm wrong, I dare anyone who owns Rome 2 to try to play a 1v1 siege battle with almost any faction and see if you can win as the attacker.
It's pretty fun, in my opinion.~

SMITE is a 3rd person moba. Simple? Simple. Well, your 3rd person viewpoint in this game is a lot different. Unlike HoTS, League of Legends, or Dota 2, SMITE does not use its same camera angle, and instead is directed behind the god you are controlling. SMITE has characters from different cultures such as Greek gods like Apollo and Artemis, or Chinese gods like Ne Zha and Huo Yi. Gameplay is very different from other mobas because you are viewing from a different angle, making skillshots feel very different than before if you have played from the LoL/Dota 2/HoTS viewpoint. Also, autoattacks are aimed too, making last hitting for gold or pushing more satisfying. Now, onto my opinion.
Personally, I really enjoy this game and very surprised I didn't try this game out earlier. This game has very satisfying and refreshing gameplay, and the gods have very fun kits to play around with. Finally, an Alien game that isn't just a texture pack for an also-ran first-person shooter.  In fact, it isn't an also-ran for ANY shooter-- you shoot something in this game, you die.  Pretty much every time.  You get sneaky or you wind up dead.  They've finally done it right.
If you buy this for no reason other than to walk around and gawk at the ship and station, you'll probably still be happy.  The artwork isn't just gorgeous and authentic, it descends from the only plausible way to justify, and therefore keep, Alien's 1979-era future look in 2014: everything in space gets beat to crap on a daily basis, and only simple stuff keeps working.  Therefore, everything is simple, crude, and tough.  CRT monitors (fixable) are everywhere, flat-panels (fragile) aren't.  It's astonishingly faithful to the films without feeling dated.
But it's faithful in a more important way-- in a way that later Alien films weren't: you, as a human, are trivial for the alien to kill, and far, far too easy for it to find.  It, meanwhile, is a nightmare god lusting to send you to hell as rapidly and painfully as possible.  The idea of fighting it rapidly looks horrifically under-informed, especially after you notice some less-enlightened folks try it.
The music, likewise, is an excellent companion to the original score, and if you're a fan of the series, that's half your immersion right there.  Sound effects with pretty good positional imaging add to the claustrophobia and paranoia very well, and if you play this in the dark, your cat is probably going to give you a heart attack a some point.
Pick it up, make some popcorn, turn out the lights, throw on good headphones and get spoooooooky into it.  You'll have a great time.

After playing through this game, I've been left to wonder. Why is it that such an old title, with outdated graphics and such simple AI, is by far more stress inducing and more terrifying than most current horror games? Seriously, this game had me terrified as I ran around trying to determine whether or not it was safe for me to try opening up my inventory to repair my weapons. The enemies are a constant threat, as most of them will respawn indefinately, so there is always some voice screaming in your ear, and you'll have no way to gauge where it's coming from. Weapons have a degredation system, and slowly break down with use, so you'll find yourself either throwing weapons away constantly, sticking to the few weapons that don't degrade, or scanning the area frantically for maintenance tools and working on your repair skill. SHODAN and the Many as the two primary antagonists are absolutely fantastic, and will fascinate, terrify, and aggrivate you throughout the game.
If there was anything that I had any real problem with, it would be the AI, as enemy patterns are incredibly easy to figure out, and there are some real simple tricks in certain areas to prevent them from attacking at all, (although I won't say what they are), but the need to explore should get you past that issue, and quite frankly, the AI, despite being now quite old, is still leagues better than some other fps and horror games I've played.
I seriously recommend this one, as it is by far a true gaming masterpiece and classic. Play it! PLAY i-it Noooowww Meat.

Slime Rancher is one of the most surprising games I've played. I picked it up while it was still in early access after seeing a youtube video that piqued my interest, and played through the content that was there at the time. It was fun, but there wasn't too much to do. I made a note to come back and check it out again after it came out.
And boy, they did not disappoint. Monomi Park are a shining example of how early Access can- and should- be. Every single gameplay concept was explored deeply. Gameplay loops were complicated and intertwined. And there was a huge amount of content- and it even felt paced just right, making sure I was always interested and plannign ahead for how I'd get past that locked door, or what paths I still had to explore. The map feature, which was not present when I first played, have also done a fantastic job of helping you navigate some of the rather complex, branching paths.
After nearly 40 hours of gameplay, I can only think of one complaint- the requirements for extractions for treasure crackers is ridiculously too high. But that's such a minor complain that it barely even registers. Slime Rancher is one of the most pure, innocent, and entertaining experiences I've had in gaming, period. This game helped soothe me when I felt stressed.
Another huge plus- without giving too much away, there's a bit of a romance story in this game, and it's queer as hell, and it's wonderful. I truly appreciate the work of the writers in crafting this story.
All in all, I would not hesitate to give Slime Rancher my endorsement. It's worth it at any price.

As a big fan of the halflife series, I can tell you, the amazing story, along with fun and exiting action, makes this in my opinion, the best remake ever. I give Black Mesa a 10/10 and HIGHLY recommend this to anybody, fps player or not.

TL;DR - If you like Half-Life or are scared of 1990's graphics, this is something you want to check out.
Long Version:
First things first, a little history. This was a mod that took a long long time to develop. They released it in 2012 for free (and you can still download it for free). Valve saw their work and gave them their blessing to continue working on the project through Steam and release a full game and be paid for their efforts. Obviously, a small independent studio that doesn't have Triple-A funding and actually cares about the product they release is going to need some time to perfect their craft. Keep in mind Valve themselves completely scrapped Half-Life 2 when they didnt like it and started from scratch. This is why Xen (The last part of the game) is taking so long. Not to quote Halo, but they want to send their tribute to Half-Life out with a bang.
But that's not to say there has been radio silence from the developers. Quite the opposite. Periodically, the developers will release fine tuning updates to help improve what they have already done, including porting the entire game to an updated engine. While every Alpha game on Steam is a gamble; what you're getting for the price is a fantastic game regardless if you're a hardcore fan of Half-Life. Gameplay is phenominal, storytelling fits right into the same style of the original. You aren't spoonfed the plot through cutscenes or NPCS spewing exposition faster than they could vomit. You get to figure stuff out on your own. Mild spoilers, but basically on a normal day of being a theoretical physicist who shoots lasers at alien rocks, everything goes wrong and you have to figure out why you're being shot at by both aliens and US marines (who are subsequently being shot at by US Black Ops) and how to stop it.
However, nothing is without its flaws, including Black Mesa (despite how much I glorify it). My biggest gripes are really nitpicky things that really only bother diehard fans who are perfectionists, like myself.
The music is amazing in most places, but randomly will fall out of sync with both the Half-Life style and the other soundtracks. For example, the opening music for the Black Mesa transit system is perfectly done and matches the style of Half-Life exactly. The theme that plays during the HEV startup is honestly better than the original soundtrack. For the most part the soundtrack is really great, but like I said, sometimes it detours. Personally I wouldn't have pianos used so often. Half-Life usually uses sythesizes, even during dramatic moments (like the end of Episode 2) since the ambient sci-fi and "spacey" electronic synth feel is typically associated with Half-Life. That being said, Half-Life 2 does use pianos occassionally, like in Triage at Dawn, but even that is accompanied by heavy synths. For the most part it is a techno/electronic soundtrack. Also, the ending credits sound like they're plucked with a shamasin or ukulele something. I don't get it.  Obviously the soundtrack is nitpicking and it shouldn't make or break your decision for getting this game. It's just that for someone who is such a big fan of the original, not hearing "Something Secret Steers Us" while I fly into a giant pit on an exploding, derailed train is a little disappointing. When Xen does come out, the Devs are going to need to get more music, and I hope they change a few of their songs in the first parts of the game.
Also, the cringey KSP loading messages like "Loading Proton Packs" or whatever shouldn't be there. Sorry, but it really doesn't fit in a Half-Life game...

+ three current unit castes (with sub-specializations): worker, melee, ranged. More are coming!
+ fun 'Dungeon-keeper'-esque base-building macro
+ streamlined resource management (no upkeep costs/starvation, though if you're out of food during a battle, you've probably already lost)
+ clever, squad-based micro system
+/- current number of levels and reward quantities implies you'll be replaying levels, though you can do harder difficulty levels to keep things interesting
- animations are still clunky
- unit models and/or UI icons need more distinctions between them. That's tricky, because you still want the colony to look biologically like one species, but I really can't tell what castes I'm looking at when playing as Wood Ants or Black Ants
Cant wait to see more stuff added to the game.

This will be a review for people who have never played the game.
Should you care about this game and why? It's over a decade old and you've got these people yammering on about how good it is, and now you might be wondering if you should bother with it or not.
This is the first time I've played this game and I have to say that there is some excellence to be found here and some annoyances, just like in any good game.
This is an FPS with RPG elements, with heavy emphasis on RPG. You'll want to research a bit about character creation before you start, or you could just have a go at it, if you don't mind maybe having to restart half way through.
The sound design in this game is what really makes it for me. I turned the music off as soon as I started. The atmospheric sounds really hit the spot. I played with 2.1 speakers (that's two speakers and a sub) and it really worked that sub. The character logs in the game are fully voiced. You can also replay the logs and you will probably have to because sometimes you'll be walking along, listening to a log and a scripted log will come up, playing the two simultaneously, which was kind of annoying.
You'll want to reconfigure the controls for a more modern set up. WSAD and all that good stuff. The game feels pretty natural after you get set up.
The gameplay, coupled with the forboding machinery and sound effects, is really tense. I found myself making extensive use of the leaning keys (Q and E) in order to peek around corners to see if I could get the drop on an enemy before they got one over on me.
The story, while not a direct sequel, does borrow heavily from System Shock 1. Having never played the first in the series, the story still works for me because they fill you in on the basics in the intro.
The level design is, for the most part, pretty good. I didn't have to wonder or wander too much in order to figure out where I was supposed to be and exploration was rewarding. Things start getting a little weird near the end and I have to say that, while at first, I felt the game was stretching out a bit for time, it ended up making me feel like the last two or three hours were a necessary trial. BTW, there's no waypoint markers, in case you were wondering, but then what's the point of exploring if you've always got an arrrow telling you where to go??
So, if you can deal with reconfiguring controls, dated graphics (there's a few texture resizing mods that are good), some old fashioned exploration without waypoints, and the last few hours feeling a little like a hail mary denouement, it is pretty good.
I don't have the rose-tinted glasses to tell you that it's a cornerstone of PC gaming or that everyone who has business calling themselves a gamer should have played it, but I would say that I might actually play it again someday and that's not something I say often.

This game.
While on a glance the graphics might seem dated by today's standards, this is one of those games that shows that a lot of love and attention was given to all the little details to ensure the end product will be as enjoyable as possible. As a survival horror game, part of the experience comes from careful resource management, from ammo, to health, and even your "experience points". Because your ability upgrades are restricted this way, a player can't simply "grind away the difficulty", like most other RPGs (both eastern and western) allow you to do. But at the same time, the mechanics are balanced enough such that even if a player isn't "optimal" about point distribution, they can't necessarily cut themselves off from playing further. The game is reasonably challenging to a newcomer from beginning to end. It also strikes a decent balance between progression and exploration, so it doesn't feel too linear to some, or too overwhelming to others.
This game is shaping up to be one of my favorite games. I only wish I had found it sooner.

For fans of the old Kings Quest series by Sierra games will indeed love the first chapter of this reinvigorated franchise.
This first chapter is littered with lovely situational puzzles, a fantastic episodic story, wonderful voice acting, mezmerizing art direction, and astounding music that create a nostalgia so think it will have old fans brushing it from their faces.
For new players this game will still be fun and satisfying to play, especially for younger gamers. If you enjoy good puzzles and a well written story then do yourself a service and at least try the first chapter.
Although the quick-time events were a little TOO liberaly sprinkled througout the game, I tried not to let it weigh down the entire experience for me. However, if your feeling toward quick-time events are more strict than mine, it may be more annoying for you.
Despite the quick-time events I felt the game was an overall fantastic experience with player's choices having a real impact to plot progression. For the price I'd suggest anyone at least give the first chapter a shot. As for me I cannot wait for the second chapter as I predict that the game will only get better as the chapters progress in the hands of the Odd Gentleman.

Probably the best horror survival game I have ever played. It stays true to the atmospheric terror of the first Alien movie. It's as rich in storytelling as it is in depth. And combined with a beautifully crafted environment delivering vast attention to detail, and featuring the original 80s Sci-fi tech you recognize from the first Alien film, this game gives you an experience as beautiful and thrilling as it is horrorfying.
If you enjoy rich storytelling and the utter helpless terror of a great horror survival game, then this is something for you! If you're more a of a shooter gamer who likes difficult enemies which you blow apart with powerful weaponry, then I urge you to look elsewhere. This is an open world experience where ammo will be scarce, violence your last option, and hiding your best chance for survival.
Even though this is one of the best games I've ever played, and I really have no complaints what so ever, there are a few things I picked up on which I believe everyone will not be as quick to forgive.
First of, the game does an amazing job of slowly leading you into a terrifying atmosphere, a sense of being slowly sunk into a dark pit before everything starts to hit the fan. As you started encountering the various threats throughout the game, they were all terrifying and creepy at first, but eventually become tedious and predictable.
Another thing was the pacing. They did a really great job in mixing up the experiences, and mixing stressful and horrific moments, with slower sections where you could take a breather. Sections dedicated to exploration and storytelling. However, these intervals eventually become predictable as well, and followed a sort of pattern. I really didn't mind, but it might be something others would pick up on.
The game had a lot of elements to it which existed to give you a sort of second chance, as well as deliver a sort of diversity in the gameplay. Things like; hacking a wall terminal to turn off the lights, or building gadgets to create traps and make a strategy. In the beginning these were all a welcoming touch in addition to the stealth-run gameplay. But eventually this too became predictable and something you did without thinking.
These are all the things I can think of really which you might not approve of, but in light of the general game's awesomeness, I really didn't care, and I doubt you will either! Coming back to praising the game however, there is one last point I like to give it.
Beside the fantastic story and the lovely way it tells the story, it has a lot of content which is mixed up and makes it all feel balanced and fun, even if you're scared. It is not a game where you will be constantly chased down a hall by an Alien, and filled with gameplay all just focusing on getting away from a monster. Not at all. The Alien is the absolute best part of the game. It is big, horrofying, relentless and fierce. It's scary, with other words. But what made it so, was the fact that you weren't alway chased by it. Sometimes you might have taken a wrong turn, and ended up in a room full of desperate survivors. A challenge you could handle with violence, should you choose to, and it added a welcoming diversity in experience.
When you heard the Alien coming for you, it was run, hide or die.

Now, you might already know that Postal is not a "nice" game. Unlike Postal 2 it's not even a sarcastic dark humorous game. It's disturbing, yet stress-relieving. It shows age despite the fantastic update, but there was still nothing as surprisingly good. Something that doesn't turn into a cringe-fest or something that is outright unpleasant to play.
If you haven't played the original, this is a top-down action game about a Dude who went Postal and started a murder spree in a small town. There's no real story, no real reason. Just a lot of disturbing level intros, clearly unhinged main character, unnerving industrial noises for soundtrack and many weapons to kill all "hostiles" (armed opposition, mostly police) with an option to kill everyone else too. What's surprising is that, while what happens is not "nice", game never becomes disgusting to play. Oddly satisfying, in fact, if you're frustrated especially. Additional levels are more in tone with sarcastic Postal 2, but the original is all darkness, without being depressive.
If you have played the original, this is a fantastic update that keeps the tone of the old game but subtly updates and improves it in every possibly way. With mouse and gamepad support, nice level intro animations, new 3D models and redrawned 2D backgrounds. There's bunch of new stuff too and no more "press F1 to end level" not obviousness -_-. As someone who could never finish the original due to outdated and clunky controls, I was happy to finally play the game to the end. The only thing that could be viewed by some as a "downgrade" is the fact that the final mission is "toned down". To be fair, though, the current version feels like it makes more tonal sense and fits the mood much better.

Eight years (and counting) in development, this love-child of the Half-Life fan community, the god of remakes, outmatched all our expectations of how would Half-Life look in Source Engine. The jury is really still out on this.  What's there is very stable, as good of graphics as you'd expect from a finished game, but there's still quite a bit of work to be done on the content side.  There's some interesting scenarios that show you what the game can offer... rushing to grab snacks off a beach before the tide rolls in and night comes, bringing lair raiding wolf spiders... but there's really only four scenarios like this for now.
For now you basically have tank units, and ranged units, or different variations of the two.  The workers ants are there just to help collect food and nest maintenance.  These are ants, of course, so there probably will never be a unit that melts your enemies face and clones his body.  This isn't Total Annihalation...
The graphics are great though, and you really get the feeling that you're on the business end of running this colony.  I hope they figure out a way to add some more depth to the strategy side of the game, without making face melting ants.
Job well done so far.  Is it worth $20 USD?  Perhaps not in its current state, but if it continues along these lines and given enough time, I'd say probably.  It's not Rimworld with ants.  Not yet.

Hurtworld, while being in Alpha, runs phenomenally well. Gameplay is smooth with minor kinks being worked out every couple weeks. The devs are very responsive to community feedback while not bending to the whims of upset tweens who seem to believe their opinions are weighted more heavily than others, and battlemu1e (a member of the dev team) has hopped into Official servers recently asking for player feedback and help addressing current latency issues in isolated zones. Each week, expect a dev blog where the developers outline what they've been busy with during the workweek and plan to implement soon.
Great dev team, great game, and a mostly friendly community. I can see my free time dwindling away for months and months to come. 10/10. Join the fun!
Edit as of April 6, 2016:
Where do we start? It seems /r/Hurtworld is the best place. The developers abandoned their subreddit roughly a month ago after a number of upset teens posted mean things to them. It seems they've also mostly abandoned the Steam forums, not to mention their Facebook and Twitter. The developers' interaction with the community has come to a screeching halt, Official servers rarely see more than 10 people online at any given moment, there hasn't been a content update in over two months, and, just a few days ago, when the Official EU West server went down, it took them two full days to reboot it.
I had a huge amount of trust in the developers at first, but that's mostly all out the window. Not to say Hurtworld doesn't run smoothly and play well (it does), but I'd strongly recommend holding on to your cash before eagerly  handing it to Bankroll. Give it a few months and check back. Perhaps an update will show up before too long, but this EA game is developing too slowly even for the most patient of us. And trust me, we've been patient.

I had big expectations for this game since the E3 trailer, and until now I'm not being disappointed at all.
This game has a bigger impact compared to The Evil Within 1 from the first moment and feels much better than the previous one under almost any aspect for now.
(These are opinions from the first 2/3 hours of gameplay).
First of all, seems like the developers have learned from their previous mistakes, and many annoying and deeply wrong things are not present in The Evil Within 2, like the black bars at the top and the bottom of the screen, and the lock at 30 fps. The animations feel much better done, more fluid and more realistic (I personally hated the running in the first game). Ambientations are awesome: chapter 1 gave me already the good old third person survival horror feelings, and even if there was no shooting and not much action, I still enjoyed it more than chapter 2, which is still very good.
Is good even to see some semi-open world space for The Evil Within 2, with secondary quests that make the game longer and more various, and probably help you understand deeper the most hidden details of the story.
Another very important thing are the dialogs: finally the dialogs in this game make sense! Cause in the first game I had the feeling that dialogs were completely random.
The story and the characters (enemies and bosses included) seem much more interesting and much more detailed compared to the previous game. Even the voice actors played very good for me, unlikely other people's opinion.
The only not impressive things I found out are the AI, a bit clunky and not very clever at times, and some facial animations, like the Kidman ones, which are not very well done like Sebastian's in my opinion.
Looks like we have a good survival horror game guys.

To be honest, I am not a big fan of the first title, it really has a lot of issues.

If you liked the predessessor, you should definitely play this game, or you have already bought it;
If you didn't like the predessessor, I still suggest you give it a try. If you don't like it, you can ask for a refund. But I believe the first 2 hours of the gameplay will make the game grow on you.

Remember when AAA titles could pull off being scary? Well, those times are back with possibly the most criminally under celebrated game this year. "Alien: Isolation" demonstrates a huge risk taken by Creative Assembly, as it's a game that's unwilling to comprimise its core experience to grab a larger audience. Sure, CA recenently patched in an easier difficulty mode, but it wasn't at the cost of anything... in fact, they accompanied it with a new harder difficulty as well. Hell, the game even recomends you play on hard mode. Enough about this games values tough, you're probably want to hear about gameplay... right?
First off and foremost Alien Isolation is about survival. You can't kill the Alien, you can only temporarily scare it off or distract it at best. The threats you can kill, like the looters and malfunctioning androids found on Sevastopol Station, are often better left alone because any of the sounds accompanying conflict can draw the almost ever-present Alien out of hiding to ruin your day. As a result, stealth is a huge part of the game. There's a robust peeking system that allows you to look arround cover with ease while staying concealed, places to hide (like lockers), and gadgets you can craft out of the scraps you find laying arround. Although you have a good array of tools, you should never get too confident... as the Alien can easily get to any place you hide and supplies are finite. It's also worth mentioning that saving is done through save points, which adds a geat deal of tension yet bestows an amazing feeling of accomplishment when you get passed hard sequences and make it to a treasured save point.
More importantly, the Alien AI is brilliant. It's unpredictable outside of scripted events and it actually feels like a real life predator hunting you. It's great at luring you into a false sense of security and then snatching you into a vent when you least expect it, and even adapts to your actions on the harder difficulties. Although you have a motion tracker, it too can draw you into false feelings of security because the Alien moves damn fast and at times it isn't afraid to dash through it's patrol paterns (which is terrifying!)
Overall the game nails Alien perfectly... the aesthetics, the execution, the atmosphere. Alien: Isolation raises the bar so high for the Alien franchise that's it's not just a good Alien game, it's a damn good survival horror game and is easily the best Alien game ever made by a large margin. It's the game Alien fans have been dreaming of for years. The only potential downfall is that it's about a fifteen hour experience depending on your pace of play, which might be a little content light for some people.

For those of you who never played the original Postal, I'll let you know that it wasn't a wacky and silly game like Postal 2 is. This game tried its hardest to be as offensive as possible. It was an isometric shooter that had only one goal in mind: kill as many cops/swat/soldiers/ect as you could while innocent civilians run around in the crossfire, until the game allows you to move on to the next level. Postal 1 caused quite a stir during 1997 in both the media and in politics, but combined with mindlessly fun gameplay and dark attempts at humor, the game became the definition of a cult classic.
For those of you who have played the original Postal, this redux version polished a lot of the old things while adding in a bunch of new things. The graphics look far better, there's new levels to play on, there's a brand new "rampage" game mode that adds more playability, it supports 4 player coop, and there's a new revolver to shoot people with. But probably the best thing about this Postal Redux is that the dreadful controls from the original have been fixed. Gone are the tanky and sluggish feeling the old game had for controls, they've been replaced with full mouse support. Things like moving around, aiming, and shooting feels natural and is a breeze to do now.
My only real complaint is that it feels like there's much less dark humor in this redux than there was in the original. However, if you're a fan of the postal series, or just like playing games with wanton and senseless amounts of violence, Postal Redux is well worth the $8.99 to buy it. 4.0/5.0

I didn't have the framerate issue that others are describing, but as a fan of the first, I was sorely disappointed with this game.
I know there is a great debate about strengths and weaknesses of a silent protagonist. I know that it will depend on the medium or type of game the character is in, but generally I lean more towards preferring silent protagonists. I mention this because I want to be honest with my bias and preferences, but I find playing as Corvo absolutely unbareable. He will simply not shut up.
You can argue he had no personality in the first game. That's fine, and I'd give you that to some extent (even though the choices you made and how others reflected on whether you were low or highly chaotic helped establish your character). Dishonored 2 went the entire other path in that Corvo will monologue and reflect on just about everything, usually offering absolutely nothing  that you, as the player, weren't already thinking or literally nothing of value whatsoever. There were multiple times where I'd be given the option to "inspect" something, like a painting, only to have Corvo just say the name of the painting. No thoughts. Nothing substantial. This happens a lot. Then, when he does begin to say something actually worthwhile, he waits until you've turned on an audiolog or you're trying to listen in on someone's conversation. Now, you can go back and look at the logs later in the menu, but it's just poor design to have Corvo talk over these logs by having him speak up at the worst times. Emily does this too, but seemingly less frequently.
Emily is rather fun to play. I'm far more tolerant of her exposition just because we only got a couple of glimmers of her personality from the first game.
Another issue I had is just trying to care about story and the people. I'm an old school role-playing gamer, and I have always been the type who would spend the time to read as much fluff as possible. Books, newspapers, flyers. I played many first-person games making sure to get close looks at all the small details at a person's desk or room, making sure I take in everything to get an understanding of who they are. You know, the show don't tell approach. The first Deus Ex and Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a master of this. Dishonored 2's fluff and material is uninspired, dry, and frankly I just couldn't bring myself to care. I would go around Karnaca with the heart that has Empress Jessamine imprisoned within it, and while I'm aware it is random for the non-critical NPCs, after doing it enough times I found myself not wanting to help any of them. It's one thing to be a person of poor morale character, but so many in Karnaca are just horrible human beings. At least in Dishonored 1, doing the same thing around Dunwall, there was some deep tragedies in their lives that made you care somewhat, inspiring you to want to do what you could to better their lives.
Had there been an option to give the Duke your full support, by the time I made it to his palace, I would have happily done so.
Much like in the first Dishonored, while the designers encourage you to play with low chaos, sparing people, they don't give you a lot of tools to go about it. Nearly all the bone charms were useless to a non-lethal/stealth playthrough, and I had well over 15+ outsider runes unused because the powers offered are catered only to a lethal player. Non-lethal means to handling enemies, the sleeping darts, are exceptionally rare whereas you can find pistol bullets and regular darts nearly everywhere (there is a bone charm that gives you a chance for additional darts upon pick up, one of the few absolutely necessary for a non-lethal run).
Finally, there were some weird glitches with NPCs and some relatively poor pathfinding with AI combatants. I just didn't enjoy my time, but as a completionist I did put in enough time to beat it with Corvo and (relatively soon) Emily.
The only saving grace for me was what the potential future DLC character/story will be because I'm assuming it's going to be

I rate this game 7/10 for some specific reasons that keep it from being perfect.
SMITE is one of the most updated MOBA's out there today, with new gods, expansions, etc., the game never truly gets old. SMITE features various amounts of game modes to play such as "Joust'
(3v3), 'Siege' (4v4), and the classic MOBA game mode, 'Conquest' (5v5). There is also a feature called 'Game Of The Day' where a unique game mode with a set of rules is picked everyday. If you win atleast once in every game mode, you get 'First win of the day' bonuses for 'favor points'
The micro-transactions in this game are completely optional. You can have never spent any money on the game and still be as good as people of have spent 100$+. As an even better feature, Hi-Rez gives many ways to earn 'favor points' and 'gems'. The only problem with the MT's in SMITE, is the awkward prices. For instance, 400 gems costs 7.99. I dont know if I'm the only one bugged by it but its just my opinion. I think it should be changed to like 5.00$ or 10.00$ ; an even price.
Characters/Gods in the game definetly need some work and is the main reason SMITE isn't the most popular MOBA out there today. Most of the time when Hi-Rez releases a new god or godess, they are either brokenly OP, or completely useless. They have a PTS (public test server) where people can give feedback on the latest updates but I dont think its very effective, considering new gods like Susano coming out right now that is currently broken (not op, broken.)
I think that Hi-Rez definetly needs to test their updates more before releasing them to the full game. It can become very frustrating when an update comes out and every player spams the new broken/OP god. For example, when Chiron first came out, he was insanely OP. He was one of the most used ADC (Attack Damage Carry/Hunter) in the game. Hi-Rez did the right think and decided to try to make him not as broken. Instead, they completely ruined Chiron and now, you will never find him in the SPL, or in Competetive games. This happens to often with updates. Hi-Rez needs to find a solid ground with the roles and gods before releasing them.
This is the reason I am not giving SMITE a 10/10:
-Broken/OP Gods
-Useless Gods
-Feedback is basically useless.
-Awkward MT prices
Other than those reasons, SMITE is an amazing MOBA, and I definetely recommend you try it out!

System Shock 2 is an amazing game.  Chances are some of your favorite games have been heavily influenced by this masterpiece.  Games such as Bioshock, Deus Ex, and Dead Space come to mind.  As this game is an FPS/RPG hybrid, it showcases a wide array of weapons as well as a plethora of options available to customize your character (SOLDIER G65434-2).  The beginning of the game can be both hard and overwhelming to new players due to the combat and inventory systems, as well as the vague objectives.  After a few hours, a sense of the gameplay and the game's pacing can be developed.  However, this game will not hold your hand.  Much of my time spent in this game pertained to retracing hydroponics a handful of times while seeking environmental regulators, searching for keypad codes, deciphering my vague objectives, and finding locations such as engineering and command control.
Many "luxuries" found in modern games are nonexistent, adding to the difficulty and suspense.  The rapid rate of weapon degradation and attempts at navigating your inventory while running away from the Many really are unnerving.   These features rarely allow you a sense of security with your current inventory or upgrades.
Due to its age, this game has some annoyances.  The respawn system paired with the lack of autosaving can be a real hassle.  When entering a new area, you must activate a machine and supply DNA in order for you to be recreated, or respawn.  This system requires you to save extremely often until you find this machine, or restart all progress in the area.  When forgetting to save in new areas, I would sometimes miss things on my second try because I had already gotten them (though it hadn't saved).  Your grid-like inventory will not automatically rearrange itself to fit new items.  For example, if you have a 2x2 open space in your inventory and attempt to pick up a 1x3 weapon, the weapon will be dropped.  You must rearrange the 2x2 opening in your inventory to accommodate the 1x3 gun.  Some of the more dated features are actually rather enjoyable though, like the peeking mechanics.  You are able to angle your character some degrees to the right or left in order to peek around corners or out of "cover."
System Shock 2 did nearly everything right, and most of the game holds up to its age.  However, many of the scares felt by those who have played in the past won't easily shock modern players.

Genre: Survival Horror, RPG, FPS
-Background-
This, hands down, goes in my Favorites bookmark in my Steam Library and is easily in my favorite games of all time. At first, I was very skeptical as to why there are alot of good reviews on this game because it is almost, if not, 15 years old. So, I watched/read more reviews about it, and it peaked my interest. I bought it on the humble bundle store for a mere $2 and I would now buy it at full price if I didn't already have it. I'm about 10 hrs into the game already and close to being finished.
-Story- (SMALL SPOILER)
The story seems generic at first; some unidentified threat aboard a human aircraft in space. The sight of the hybrids didn't help either; however when you start piecing together all the logs/emails you start to notice that it is something more than just alien-like creatures in space. In addition, since I did not play the first System Shock, I was very surprised when I was introduced to the main threat in the game. As I stated earlier, most of the story is threaded by the emails and logs that you collect; some of the story is also given to the player to interpret by the atmosphere and the environment (text written in blood on walls, bullets scattered around the floor next to a human holding a gun, walls torn out showing electrical wiring, etc). Like I said, I'm not finished with the game yet, so the story might completely change towards the end, but I still believe the story is one of the good elements of this game. The only con that I had with story, (SMALL SPOILER) was the absence of living NPCs. The game might have intended for you to feel isolated and alone, but I wanted to hear someone's opinion about the whole disaster without just listening to audio logs.
-Gameplay-
The gameplay to me is reminiscent of the old survival horror games such as Resident Evil, Silent Hill, Dino Crisis in terms of resource management. The layout of the RPG elements remind me much of Deus Ex Human Revolution and Dark Souls 1(you have to carefully attune your skillpoints, if you don't you will die lol). Like all the games mentioned above, the player can choose to go a stealth route or a gun-toting maniac, this allows the player more freedom to choose what type of playstyle he/she wants to do and this is good in a pretty much linear game (although you will need to backtrack at some areas). Also, the tutorial is pretty decent, but in your first hour, if you are like me, you will be confused as a rock as to what exact skills to upgrade and invest in. The only con I would give this game in terms of gameplay is how in the beginning, you are sluggish in terms of movement, which is bad imho because it makes the game feel slow and lengthy.
-Sound Design-
The background music and the soundtrack is pretty amazing. The background music is ominous and mechanical. All you head most of the time is the clang and moving gears of machinery and the sound of broken wires. The soundtrack is pretty fitting too; its sounds futuristic and somewhat scary. System Shock 2 is the progenitor of the Bioshock series.  It's also better in almost every way.  I liked Bioshock, for a play through.  Great graphics, beautiful scenery, lots of atmosphere, nice story, decent gameplay.  You know what it lacked?  Depth.  And System Shock 2 has it in spades.  It is easily one of the most immersive games you will ever find.  If System Shock 2 had never existed, the Bioshock series would never have been made.  Bioshock was sold to the gaming industry and public as a "spiritual successor" to System Shock 2.  The critical acclaim and cult status of SS2 is the street cred Ken Levine used to get Bioshock made.
In System Shock 2 you begin the game as a man entering into UNN military service.  This prologue of sorts is both a tutorial and how you choose your initial specialization.  Oh, I guess I forgot to mention that System Shock 2 is, essentially, an FPS/RPG hybrid.  Bioshock was fun, you get plasmids and weapons to help you kill the splicers, but at the end of the day - that was it.  Just weaponry of sorts (ok, the pipe/water hacking was kind of cool).  In System Shock 2 you can choose to be a Psionics user who telepathicallly affects the world, a computer/engineer sort who can hack and fix things, or a combat-loving, bullet-stopping Marine.  Three wildly different play styles.  Are you the "mage" type who uses Psionic powers to grab items from a distance?  Send blasts that break enemies in twain?  Maybe you are a "thief" type who hacks into vending machines and is able to fix broken weaponry; who survives by hiding in shadows?  Or maybe you're a barrel-chested "warrior" who can weild every weapon and is ready to put some proverbial foot up some♥♥♥♥♥  The game lets you have at it.  And you're not tied down into those three simple classes.  You can be a Psionics user who hacks into stuff.  Or you can be a Marine who uses psionic skills.  Sure, why not?  How you spend your cyber modules to learn and improve skills is entirely up to you.
After you spend a few years in the service you end up on the historic maiden voyage of the intergalactic spaceship Von Braun which has a new-tech faster-than-light drive.  It's piggy-backing the Rickenbaucher, a military vessel.  While on mission they respond to a distress signal from Tau Ceti V, which they investigate, and everything unravels from there.  You awake from a cryo-tube to find your body augmented, your memory gone, and the ship in crisis.  Did I mention this FPS/RPG hybrid has elements of horror?  Oops, my bad.
You receive communications from an enigmatic person (sound familiar Bioshock players?), and you make your way into the ship little by little.  You pick up audio logs and emails that unravel the mystery in tiny increments.  You have to scavenge, because you don't have anything... and who knows where they are... they pop up everywhere...  The Many.  And you have little to fight with.
Survival is the name of the game.  Exploration is necessary.  You come across items and you have no idea what it is.  You can research it, if you have the hardware, software and the skill.  You better figure out what it is.  Research it and you learn something new.  This helps you better fight this mysterious enemy.  Oh great...  I need a chemical to continue researching this object.  In which closet, on which deck, is the chemical stored?  Let me check the various chemical manifests I've found...  hmmm... gotta go back to deck 2.
System Shock 2 is largely non-linear.  Yes, you have to "unlock" areas before you can explore them, but the game requires alot of traversing through familiar territory to gain access to rooms or items that you didn't have before and the gameplay changes as the game progresses.  The enemy, "the many", wander the ship.  You will never "clear" an area.  They will keep coming.  There is no safe zone.  You have to conserve your ammo while exploring the ship and figuring out how it is you can put a stop to what has happened, or at least survive.
The graphics are a bit dated, but there has been a modding community hard at work for years to rectify this.  They are currently working to make a unified patch, but until then you can find the available graphic and other mods here:
Final word: There is a reason why this game is such a reknown cult classic.  This is the best FPS/RPG sci-fi horror game ever made.

Everyone who wants the sensation of being inside a different world, overcoming great challenges and experiencing an incredible multiplayer should play this one.

A thrilling story, great voice acting, awesome and appropriate music, superb visuals and excellent gameplay make Alien: Isolation one of the very best horror games I have ever played.
You play as Amanda Ripley, the daughter of Ellen Ripley (Sigourney Weaver's character and the protagonist of the Alien franchise movies), who is looking out for clues about her mother's whereabout after she disappeared years ago during the events of the first Alien movie. Her search leads her to the Sevastopol, a station that upon RIpley's arrival is experiencing rampant chaos at the hands of its inhabitants - who are waging a civil war between factions - , rogue androids and the
.
The Alien is, needless to say, the highlight of the game. Not only is it the antagonist, but also the whole game and its mechanics are centered around it. Never do you feel truly safe and secure, for there is no door, no barricade, no hole in all of the station that can provide you with enough shelter. For starters, it uses the vents to navigate the sation, so if you shut yourself inside a room, even overriding its door and locking yourself shut, the Alien will come crawling out of some hole. You can hide inside a locker, but even there you must be on guard, for if the Alien hears the beeping of your motion detector it will seek you out, and you must lean backwards and hold your breath and hope for it to go away. Its usage of vents means that you must watch out for dripping saliva, the only sign that gives away the Alien when it stalks the halls of the station looking out for prey from above, and avoid those vents as much as you can, for walking below them means insta-death. It is worth noting that while the Alien is not always there when you enter an area, it may very well enter it if it hears loud noises, such as gunshots. Also, when the Alien is in the area but content with wandering through the vents - that is, a great portion of the game, make sure to crouch your way through the level. At first it may feel like a chore, but it beats standing up and walking some steps only to have the Alien appear out of nowhere and kill you outright. Finally, as you would expect, the Alien is impossible to kill. At best, you can scare it away with a flamethrower or a molotov - or a pipe bomb, for that matter - but it will sooner or later come back for you.
Apart from the Alien, as stated, there are some scattered human survivors in the Sevastopol and the androids. These are so creepy that sometimes they would scare me even more than the Alien did - but the facehuggers did the most of it, quite frankly. To deal with all of these enemies, there are tons of weapons lying about the space station, and you can even craft some makeshift weapons yourself, such as the aforementioned Molotovs and Pipe bombs, as well as EMP mines and even some gadgets to help you sneak past those pesky enemies, such as the noisemaker - an artifact that emits a beeping sound for a few seconds when thrown - and the smoke bomb. Finally, you also get to craft medkits and heal yourself. How cool is that?
On a side note: whenever you are reading computer logs, hearing audio logs, doing minigames (such as cutting a metal lid open or decoding/hacking your way through a system) and whatnot time goes by, even when you are saving the game! Thus, you can get killed while doing any of these, and therefore it would be advisable to make sure you are somewhat safe before attempting any of these. Just so you know: you can access the logs afterwards, using the Tab key, but it gets tedious after a while and you will probably keep on playing after skimming through them while looking for something specific on a terminal.
Speaking of
, I would like to mention that the game's weakest point by far is its absolutely ludicrous "save point" system, by which you have save stations scattered throughout the levels and you have to pull down a lever there to save progress. Now, most of these are properly placed, located at regular intervals, but some of them are so far away that whenever you die - and you shall die a lot while playing this game - you are forced to play some instances all over again, until quitting out of sheer frustration. While I understand the logic behind this system - that is, to make the player actually care for not getting killed - it should have been a togglable option, ala Bioshock and its vita-chambers.
On the technical department, the game is almost flawless: I experienced little to no bugs when playing - at least none that I remember - and it runs really smooth, despite having awesome graphics and being quite the looker. Its sound effects are amazing- truly, the sound of the Alien going through the vents and the facehuggers chilling screams will get on your nerves before long - and the voice acting is great, with the main character being the most believable of them all. The music is always there to set the mood for the game,  either relaxing you, making you uneasy or outright stalked and hunted.
There are a couple of DLCs released for this game, but I have yet to try them out. There is also a challenge mode to be played, but after finishing the main story if just felt lacklustre.
Finally, I would like to state that even as I was finishing the game today, a patch came out adding two new difficulties: Novice and Nightmare. Since I played the game on Hard, which until today used to be the hardest setting, I am not really aware of the changes introduced with these new modes, but I hear that Nightmare has some twists, such as less HUD information - which I was hoping for ever since I started playing the game, to feel more immersed - and a faulty detector - not quite my cup of tea, but anyway, worth checking out I suppose.
Despite the annoying save point flaw - or perhaps, to some extent, thanks to it -, the game is a masterpiece, being the finest game in the Alien franchise ever as well as the ultimate Alien experience and a true homage to the original Alien movie. I would go as far as stating that it is one of the very best horror games I have ever played. If you are a fan of the Alien franchise and/or horror games, then you should get this game right away.

As per users,  the game runs like crap in most system,  thus the low user ratings. As an owner of quite powerful system, the game ran quite fine for me even before the patches. 50-ish fps on ultra on outside open areas and 70-90ish in indoor area. Enough of performance talk, let's talk about the game. By the time I'm writing the review, the game has already gotten action/adventure  game of the year award of 2016, so you already know the potentiality of this game already, or maybe you don't cause of huge negative impact on steam reviews due to the technical issues it had.
I'm no reviewer so my point of view could be wrong.
One thing I wanna say straight ahead:
Arkane Studio surely knows their game. They follows the "if it's not broken, dont try to fix it" approach and that is clearly apparent in their 2nd installment of the famous stealthy first person game. They perfected everything that was there in Dishonored 1. Every game mechanics is more polished and fun to play with. You can have multiple approaches for overcoming problems. And you can build your character like that. Either you can go stealthy merciful soul or you can go full vengeful assassin. Heck, you can beat the entire game without killing anyone, just like first game.
All playstyles have their moment of fun and rewards. And this time it's double the fun, because now you have 2 playable characters who's powers are completely different. So the game will play abit differently for both of them. My first playthrough was with Emily and I must say I just love her character. She is well developed, quite powerful and very enjoyable to play with. Surely I wanna play with her one more time after Arkane gonna release New Game+ later on.
Corvo I haven't played with yet, so can't say his playstyle from personal experience, but I heard he has his own Dishonored 1-ish charm. The game is worthy to play with Emily and Corvo both. It's not linear at all despite of being not open world, cause you can adept different playstyle and the final conclusion will depend upon it. So I'm completely leaving it to the players for playing the game in high or low chaos, the system for what D1 was so famous for. Basically, if you go killing everyone, you will have high chaos, thus dark ending. Or if you like to knock out the baddies rather than killing, you can have low chaos, thus optimistic ending. You are the maker of the story and it'e ending.
Speaking of story, I was a huge fan of the first Dishonored and was kindda unsure how the 2nd game will turn out. But to my surprise, it held up to the first game and more. The story doesn't necessarily require you to play the DLC's of the first game to understand. But you would get more details if you do, the story will open up more and will make sense.
The gameplay, omg...is pure pleasure for fans of old Dishonored. Dishonored 2 polished what they had on the first game and now it's a pure bliss. The high chaos assassin or killer approach is hell lot of fun. Full gun blazing and Slashing enemies with sword while doing combos with powers looks waaaay cool and are very very satisfactory.
And you can even play the entire game without your special void power. There is a 'no power' mode in the game itself. But the game will be tough in this mode.
I find the game little bit easy even on medium, so if you are looking for more challenge then I must suggest to play it on hard.
Not to mention the replayablity it has.
Graphics and art is subjective, and to me, the game is very pretty. Sure, it's not that pretty game in it's time. But the detailed levels and it's art style stood out eventhough the game used old IDTECH 5's heavily modified version (VOID). And the steampunk world they presented is very believable. And as I'm a sucker for artstyle, the game is very much eyecandy for me. loved it!
There are some problem regarding the positional audio that I've found, but it's very negligible and can be overlooked as the game have really cool voice acting, musical scores and audio effects.
Just get the game and play it if you are a stealth game lover, or get it if you are into this genre. The current steam ratings are not doing justice for this game and I must say this game deserves a full 9 out 10 ratings, despite of all the technical flaws it has.

This is a very difficult game to review.
On one hand, it's what I think anyone who has played Just Cause 2 could have possibly wanted; physics-based destruction of nearly every object in the game (except for terrain and most buildings, as is with most games that have destructible environments). It adds a host of exciting vehicles and weapons to demolish everything in your way with. It evolves on Just Cause 2's fundamental mechanics that made it so fun. It also adds a wingsuit, which I will forever hold as the most fun way to travel in a videogame, ever. This is basically Michael Bay: The Videogame, and I absolutely love everything about it. As someone who enjoyed Just Cause 2 very much, this is the greatest sequel I could have possibly dreamed of.
However, what makes it hard to recommend is the bevy of performance issues people have been having with the game. It's incredibly fun when it works, but this is a very intensive game that is probably not on the good side of the optimisation fence. The game barely runs for some, and for those that it runs for a fair few have performance issues and graphical issues, some which render this game unplayable.
Personally, I haven't been affected by these problems too much, but if you go to the game's subreddit or Steam discussions, you will almost always find complaints about how well, or badly, the game runs.
For reference, my specs are as follows:
i5-4440
Gigabyte GTX 970 G1 Gaming (overclocked to 1505 Mhz on the core - 7800Mhz on the memory)
8GB RAM
