So, Sledgehammer Games has come under the rule of Activision and a 3-year cycle has been established. Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare is Sledgehammer's first installation of CoD that they have control over (They helped with map design on Modern Warfare 3, but that was under Infinity Ward).
Pros:
- FREAKING EXO-SUITS. Before you point fingers that they ripped off Titanfall, this isn't a jump-pack that helps you parkour, it's a frickin' suit that turns you into something of a Superman! You can double-jump, dash-jump, side-dash, dash-dash, and loads of cool sh!t. REALLY nice change of pace from a slower, more camp-central game like Black Ops 2.
- Future of Today. Weird pro, right? Yeah, but it's true. This does seem like a highly possible future of today and it's pretty awesome.
- A Slice of Quake. Yep, you read it right. Since this has massive mobility and it's a lot of running around having tons of fun shooting that one guy that side-stepped you and punched you from the side. Fast-paced, short matches, and quite arcade-y.
- Kevin Spacey. Even though I'm not really a fan of movies, this guy was top-notch as the head honcho of Atlas.
Cons:
- Murky Graphics. Graphics can be nice, but aren't really modern. The CoD engine just can't keep up.
- Lack of Weapon Variety. *Sigh* Yep, I was afraid of this too. The weapon variety is still fairly lacking, despite the addition of some gimmicky weapon passives, akimbo miniguns, and lazors. I'm just disappointed that they didn't go further.
- LACK OF DEDICATED SERVERS. ONE OF THE MOST GLARING ISSUES OF THE PC VERSION IS THAT THERE'S NO FRICKIN' DEDICATED SERVERS. Don't give me the excuse that they went down the Black Ops 2 route of "Servers, but still Matchmaking" because they DIDN'T. Hosts can be clearly seen with the best pings.
- LACK OF ANTI-CHEAT. THIS IS THE SECOND GLARING ISSUE AND PROBABLY THE WORST. There's a distinct lack of ANY FORM OF ANTI-CHEAT. The patch notes may say there's "Increased Security", but that's a complete load of bull. There's no anti-cheat to speak of and this game will die because of it.
Overall: Don't buy this game until anti-cheat and servers are openly added into the game and CONFIRMED. It's fun, but that's QUICKLY destroyed by the huge population of cheaters and lack of dedicated servers. If you're desperate for a fast-paced shooter, I've heard Toxikk fits that bill.

System Shock 2 is the progenitor of the Bioshock series.  It's also better in almost every way.  I liked Bioshock, for a play through.  Great graphics, beautiful scenery, lots of atmosphere, nice story, decent gameplay.  You know what it lacked?  Depth.  And System Shock 2 has it in spades.  It is easily one of the most immersive games you will ever find.  If System Shock 2 had never existed, the Bioshock series would never have been made.  Bioshock was sold to the gaming industry and public as a "spiritual successor" to System Shock 2.  The critical acclaim and cult status of SS2 is the street cred Ken Levine used to get Bioshock made.
In System Shock 2 you begin the game as a man entering into UNN military service.  This prologue of sorts is both a tutorial and how you choose your initial specialization.  Oh, I guess I forgot to mention that System Shock 2 is, essentially, an FPS/RPG hybrid.  Bioshock was fun, you get plasmids and weapons to help you kill the splicers, but at the end of the day - that was it.  Just weaponry of sorts (ok, the pipe/water hacking was kind of cool).  In System Shock 2 you can choose to be a Psionics user who telepathicallly affects the world, a computer/engineer sort who can hack and fix things, or a combat-loving, bullet-stopping Marine.  Three wildly different play styles.  Are you the "mage" type who uses Psionic powers to grab items from a distance?  Send blasts that break enemies in twain?  Maybe you are a "thief" type who hacks into vending machines and is able to fix broken weaponry; who survives by hiding in shadows?  Or maybe you're a barrel-chested "warrior" who can weild every weapon and is ready to put some proverbial foot up some♥♥♥♥♥  The game lets you have at it.  And you're not tied down into those three simple classes.  You can be a Psionics user who hacks into stuff.  Or you can be a Marine who uses psionic skills.  Sure, why not?  How you spend your cyber modules to learn and improve skills is entirely up to you.
After you spend a few years in the service you end up on the historic maiden voyage of the intergalactic spaceship Von Braun which has a new-tech faster-than-light drive.  It's piggy-backing the Rickenbaucher, a military vessel.  While on mission they respond to a distress signal from Tau Ceti V, which they investigate, and everything unravels from there.  You awake from a cryo-tube to find your body augmented, your memory gone, and the ship in crisis.  Did I mention this FPS/RPG hybrid has elements of horror?  Oops, my bad.
You receive communications from an enigmatic person (sound familiar Bioshock players?), and you make your way into the ship little by little.  You pick up audio logs and emails that unravel the mystery in tiny increments.  You have to scavenge, because you don't have anything... and who knows where they are... they pop up everywhere...  The Many.  And you have little to fight with.
Survival is the name of the game.  Exploration is necessary.  You come across items and you have no idea what it is.  You can research it, if you have the hardware, software and the skill.  You better figure out what it is.  Research it and you learn something new.  This helps you better fight this mysterious enemy.  Oh great...  I need a chemical to continue researching this object.  In which closet, on which deck, is the chemical stored?  Let me check the various chemical manifests I've found...  hmmm... gotta go back to deck 2.
System Shock 2 is largely non-linear.  Yes, you have to "unlock" areas before you can explore them, but the game requires alot of traversing through familiar territory to gain access to rooms or items that you didn't have before and the gameplay changes as the game progresses.  The enemy, "the many", wander the ship.  You will never "clear" an area.  They will keep coming.  There is no safe zone.  You have to conserve your ammo while exploring the ship and figuring out how it is you can put a stop to what has happened, or at least survive.
The graphics are a bit dated, but there has been a modding community hard at work for years to rectify this.  They are currently working to make a unified patch, but until then you can find the available graphic and other mods here:
Final word: There is a reason why this game is such a reknown cult classic.  This is the best FPS/RPG sci-fi horror game ever made.

Update: After completing the game multiple times, I have to go back on what I said. This game is not only bad for a Souls game, its a bad game overall for multiple reasons.
Most notably the combat- its much worse. The satisfying feeling of weight behind each attack in DS1 is nowhere to be found here. Poise and faith have been nerfed to oblivion, allegedly for PVP reasons(which begs the question why sorcery and hexes are still so OP). ADP is probably the worse design choice in any Souls game ever made.
The game is broken on a fundamental level, including its controls. Unless you use AutoHotke, this game is unplayable with Mouse+KB. Some people may not find this as a problem, but such a lax approach to console ports is damaging.
I could go on but there's hardly any point. There is no single huge issue with the game that makes it bad. Its the thousands upon thousands of little things that you notice the devs messed up that build up and make you hate this.
If you want to play a Souls game, don't play this one, you have much better alternatives in DS1,DS3 and BB. Hell,even Demon Souls has a better grasp on what makes the Souls series great than this game.

This game is truly wonderful, there's a lot of hard practice within the game and you can't just always rely on one tactic to win. Every enemy has been balanced along with the weapons and armour to always give that feeling of struggle, no matter how high in strength you are. PVP however is where this game is let down, mainly because the players who play this game like to make use of the cheapest tactics they can manage in order to win. Here's just a list of what to expect if you try doing Dark Souls 2 PVP:
Channeler's trident with any magic buff and poison infusion while spamming heavy attack to drill hit you and just stack poison? Check.
Infinite HP hacks? Check. (I've encountered at least 46 different players doing this so far)
Poison/Bleed estoc to bypass shields? Check.
Infinite stagger caestus build? Check.
Prebuffing and then using poison fog/toxic mist/dark fog/acid surge as you are summoning in so you get poisoned/have your armour and rings broken before you can even act? Check. (watch out would be dragons, this happens to you a LOT)
Prebuffing and then trying to backstab you as you are summoning in? Check (Dragons again...)
Waiting right by where you appear and spamming fire tempest or other AoE spells so you have no time to act when you summon in? Check. (dragons especially)
Abusing rolls to ensure no form of magic will ever hit them? Check. (Oh yeah, if you roll? You can't get hit by most magic unless it's a flat out hit. Not a fun thing if you get forced into PVP and you're a caster of any form).
That's just a short list of the cheap tactics I've seen being put to use while I have played Dark Souls 2. Players will not try to play fair and as a result, it ruins the experience for the people who are trying to play the game fairly. Most even take PRIDE in this factor and you can find tons of builds to accompany these tactics so as to 'pwn maximum number of noobs' as one person put it.
I will complement Dark Souls 2 however as it has made co-operative play (especially with friends) much, MUCH better than Dark Souls 1. You get a name engraved ring you can buy that allows you to connect to players using the same 'god' that you choose using the ring. There's a large selection of gods and goddesses so you have little risk of being summoned by someone who you don't want to be summoned by. There's also two forms of aid you can do: Shades (which last a certain time and vanish when they've either killed so many enemies or have been there long enough, you can tell if a shade's about to vanish because they start turning black) and phantoms (Just like Dark Souls 1, they vanish when you beat a boss usually). A nice thing they've made sure to note is while there are areas where phantoms can't be summoned, shades can still be summoned in some of them, allowing for you to still recieve aid from your friends if you need it (and some areas you really DO need it.
For those travelling alone, From Software hasn't forgotten about you. Almost every single boss has a NPC phantom or two somewhere nearby that can aid you if you are unfortunate enough to have the dark souls 2 server lose connection or if you lose connection to steam. What's more, some of them have storylines that grant you their equipment if you accomplish them.
Overall, there's plenty of nice things in Dark Souls 2 that I would really want to praise. There's a vast array of weapons, armours and items to help you on your journey and it's possible to make all kinds of playthroughs (I've even seen someone playing a run as a character named after and tooled up exactly like Simon Belmont from castlevania. That was funny to play along with!).
If anything, it's Dark Souls 2's PVP that lets it down in the long run and a lot of the covenants make use of PVP to rank up so you are kind of forced to face it at some point if you want the most out of covenants... though thankfully you can switch covenants freely in Dark Souls 2, which is a god send.
There was one other thing that disappointed me though (and this is more a personal nitpick than anything else)... the weapons while vast and arrayed... well, it doesn't exactly have the same kind of fantastic variety that Dark Souls 1 had. I thought it was neat when I could get a sword made out of crystal or the dark sword from the darkwraiths (I was pleased the armour was back but COME ON FROM SOFT, why no sword to go with!?) which all had really unique designs and stood out. Granted, there are a few nice and unique weapons but I just feel it's lacking there. Who knows? Maybe the DLC coming out will provide us with some more really neat tools of destruction? I sure hope so!
Would I recommend Dark Souls 2? Yes, VERY MUCH YES I would recommend this game. But there are things that you need to be aware of when you pick this game up and I hope this review will help those who are considering this game for various reasons to consider before picking it up. From Software is making constant balance checks with this game so maybe they might see some of the problems and deal with them but in the meantime, thank you for reading my review and I hope it gave you all information about Dark Souls 2 that will help you decide to buy the game.
Good luck, and hope you're prepared to die all over again. You'll be doing it a lot.

Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

There are two sections to the gameplay, the first being in the form of missions, in which you build and advance forward, whilst upgrading your ant nest spreading out across an enclosed map until you complete each given mission objective which normally is domination.
The second aspect is in the formicarium (test lab) in which you build your nest, working your way through a sorta of basic tech tree using the rewards from the above missions. battles in this mode are conducted by the scientist unleashing a X-amount of enemy bugs into your cage.
The overall game is quite hard, on anything but the more easier levels, and experience is the key with this game. So start of with easy is my personal suggestion. it can be rather too boring on easy, but not half as frustrating as the higher levels.

This game is brilliant fun, and has vast amounts of potential.
The game is split into two elements, firstly the formicarium (ant farm) is where you expand your colony and improve, to the sound of the voice acted dialogue of a pair of scientists who are studying you, one of which is apparently extremely perverse and loves to see you suffer. In this mode you are able to improve the genetics of your ants by spending "royal jelly" and so choose their strengths and weaknesses and when you're powerful enough you can participate in formicarium challenges, the completion of which will result in some extra food, territory points (needed for digging within the formicarium) and some royal jelly. The issue is that food is fairly sparse in the formicarium and so in order to make reasonable progress, you need to play the missions.
Different missions are available depending on the level of your formicarium, at first two missions are available. After improving the formicarium to level 2 by completing the challenge, you will be able to participate in the next two levels. At the moment only 4 missions are available, but with 4 difficulty settings as well as an added "challenge mode" (which adds a twist to the level you are playing) there should be enough to keep you busy for now. Each of these missions is narrated beautifully in a way which wouldn't be out of place in a nature documentary.
In addition to this, there are an additional 4 "Alpha game modes" accessed from the extra modes section of the main menu, and there will be a custom and freeplay mode in the main game,
Due to the excellent narration I actually found this game very educational and I came away from playing it knowing a lot more about ants and their preditors than when I went in bare in mind however that some artistic license has been taken with some species in order to provide better gameplay.
Finally, the in game music is brilliant, a brass orchestral track really sets the tone and the music changes somewhat dynamically with the in game action.
I bought this game knowing that it's still under development, I was aware that the amount of content was somewhat limited but this game archs back to a time when RTS games where innovative. This is the first truly innovative RTS game I've played in years and I really can't wait for the future of this game.

The first 6-8 hours are GREAT! but...
I really liked it early on, with the game being very relaxing, but later becomes increasingly tedious and samey to a point of not being relaxing anymore. I just wish there was some kind of "Ranch Robot" I could get for the ranch that would mitigate even %50 of the upkeep I do everytime I run back.
I think I've played for about 8-9 hours at this point, and I don't like how the late game is turning out.
It feels like it's missing something mechanically speaking from the slimes. Slimes just feel in the way a lot of time, and don't interact enough to be fun.
Imagine a game where you had a very limited inventory, and a chest you can run back to in order to store items. Now imagine that you had to do increasingly frequent maintenance on the chest to keep it from breaking under the weight of the items you put in it. If you imagine the chest is a ranch, and some of the items as living things, you'd pretty much have Slime Rancher.
It starts out really nice, building the ranch up feels good, but then you unlock other sections that extend your ranch and that's when the game starts getting too tedious for me, because you have to travel between different sections with increasing frequency as you get more and more kinds of slimes to manage and different food you have to grow for your slimes to eat. So, you're running back and forth trying to grab food, feed slimes, get the selling product called "plorts" that the slimes pump out as a result, and put the "plorts" into the selling machine. That process gets longer and longer everytime you add a new type of slime to your ranch. I wanted something like a robot or helper to help mitigate the tedium, but it never came.
Besides the increasing amount of tedium, I couldn't help but feel like the game was missing something mechanically or in the way the slime A.I. interacted with eachother. Like for example, at one point I thought I was stuck without the jetpack upgrade, but then I grabbed a largo and bunnyhopped off it to get enough height to get up on the path that led to the exit. It's always (1) suck up the things, (2) put 'em in your inventory, and (3) take 'em home or wherever the things need to go. The only real obstacles for the most part is the amount of time it takes to get somewhere, and whether or not you can jump and jetpack somewhere. (WHY DOES THE ENERGY TAKE SO LONG TO RECHARGE?! The most the frustrating part of the game was not being able to jump somewhere until the "jump & sprint" energy bar recharged, so you just stand there, kind of annoyed until it did.) I wish I felt like there was more to this game than me wondering how to minimize the amount trips home and running around I'd have to make in order to get enough items, to get a key, to do it all over again.
Is it worth a try? YES!
Is it worth trying to 100% complete? Probably not.

A thrilling story, great voice acting, awesome and appropriate music, superb visuals and excellent gameplay make Alien: Isolation one of the very best horror games I have ever played.
You play as Amanda Ripley, the daughter of Ellen Ripley (Sigourney Weaver's character and the protagonist of the Alien franchise movies), who is looking out for clues about her mother's whereabout after she disappeared years ago during the events of the first Alien movie. Her search leads her to the Sevastopol, a station that upon RIpley's arrival is experiencing rampant chaos at the hands of its inhabitants - who are waging a civil war between factions - , rogue androids and the
.
The Alien is, needless to say, the highlight of the game. Not only is it the antagonist, but also the whole game and its mechanics are centered around it. Never do you feel truly safe and secure, for there is no door, no barricade, no hole in all of the station that can provide you with enough shelter. For starters, it uses the vents to navigate the sation, so if you shut yourself inside a room, even overriding its door and locking yourself shut, the Alien will come crawling out of some hole. You can hide inside a locker, but even there you must be on guard, for if the Alien hears the beeping of your motion detector it will seek you out, and you must lean backwards and hold your breath and hope for it to go away. Its usage of vents means that you must watch out for dripping saliva, the only sign that gives away the Alien when it stalks the halls of the station looking out for prey from above, and avoid those vents as much as you can, for walking below them means insta-death. It is worth noting that while the Alien is not always there when you enter an area, it may very well enter it if it hears loud noises, such as gunshots. Also, when the Alien is in the area but content with wandering through the vents - that is, a great portion of the game, make sure to crouch your way through the level. At first it may feel like a chore, but it beats standing up and walking some steps only to have the Alien appear out of nowhere and kill you outright. Finally, as you would expect, the Alien is impossible to kill. At best, you can scare it away with a flamethrower or a molotov - or a pipe bomb, for that matter - but it will sooner or later come back for you.
Apart from the Alien, as stated, there are some scattered human survivors in the Sevastopol and the androids. These are so creepy that sometimes they would scare me even more than the Alien did - but the facehuggers did the most of it, quite frankly. To deal with all of these enemies, there are tons of weapons lying about the space station, and you can even craft some makeshift weapons yourself, such as the aforementioned Molotovs and Pipe bombs, as well as EMP mines and even some gadgets to help you sneak past those pesky enemies, such as the noisemaker - an artifact that emits a beeping sound for a few seconds when thrown - and the smoke bomb. Finally, you also get to craft medkits and heal yourself. How cool is that?
On a side note: whenever you are reading computer logs, hearing audio logs, doing minigames (such as cutting a metal lid open or decoding/hacking your way through a system) and whatnot time goes by, even when you are saving the game! Thus, you can get killed while doing any of these, and therefore it would be advisable to make sure you are somewhat safe before attempting any of these. Just so you know: you can access the logs afterwards, using the Tab key, but it gets tedious after a while and you will probably keep on playing after skimming through them while looking for something specific on a terminal.
Speaking of
, I would like to mention that the game's weakest point by far is its absolutely ludicrous "save point" system, by which you have save stations scattered throughout the levels and you have to pull down a lever there to save progress. Now, most of these are properly placed, located at regular intervals, but some of them are so far away that whenever you die - and you shall die a lot while playing this game - you are forced to play some instances all over again, until quitting out of sheer frustration. While I understand the logic behind this system - that is, to make the player actually care for not getting killed - it should have been a togglable option, ala Bioshock and its vita-chambers.
On the technical department, the game is almost flawless: I experienced little to no bugs when playing - at least none that I remember - and it runs really smooth, despite having awesome graphics and being quite the looker. Its sound effects are amazing- truly, the sound of the Alien going through the vents and the facehuggers chilling screams will get on your nerves before long - and the voice acting is great, with the main character being the most believable of them all. The music is always there to set the mood for the game,  either relaxing you, making you uneasy or outright stalked and hunted.
There are a couple of DLCs released for this game, but I have yet to try them out. There is also a challenge mode to be played, but after finishing the main story if just felt lacklustre.
Finally, I would like to state that even as I was finishing the game today, a patch came out adding two new difficulties: Novice and Nightmare. Since I played the game on Hard, which until today used to be the hardest setting, I am not really aware of the changes introduced with these new modes, but I hear that Nightmare has some twists, such as less HUD information - which I was hoping for ever since I started playing the game, to feel more immersed - and a faulty detector - not quite my cup of tea, but anyway, worth checking out I suppose.
Despite the annoying save point flaw - or perhaps, to some extent, thanks to it -, the game is a masterpiece, being the finest game in the Alien franchise ever as well as the ultimate Alien experience and a true homage to the original Alien movie. I would go as far as stating that it is one of the very best horror games I have ever played. If you are a fan of the Alien franchise and/or horror games, then you should get this game right away.

No More Room In Hell Review
Sometimes I hate my job and the industry that surrounds it. I made 14 spins of my "Wheel of Review" over the last 2 weeks and came up with 5 zombie games(Survivalist, this,H1Z1,Dying Light and Zombies Ate my Neighbors) to review. Of those 2 companies PR departments ignored my emails entirely, 1 actually responded (Survivalist) and the other 2 are a retro game and a free game on steam.
I look at the next 2 months of releases and find yet MORE zombie games(and a couple dlc's). I guess this complaint merits it's own article entirely. It won't color my judgement of this game in anyway, but even my tolerence of the genre is starting to wear thin.
NMRIH is a source engine game developed  by a independent group of people for no monetary gain. So basically, it's a stand alone half life 2 mod. That actually put up a red flag for me, many source engine mods are actually really really bad. Also quite a few of them that go on sale are also pretty bad, so needless to say my expectations were really low going into this.
Then I actually played the game. I was actually shocked, it was really good  for a small mod team game.
The first thing that hits me is the sound quality, more specifically the music. Huanting, deep and very atmosphere building. Each track soudns like a orchestra did it yet, I know that it was some underpaid guy in a small recording room somehwere doing all this himself. Someone needs to give that guy a job, he did stellar work on this games music.
I can't exactly say the same for the sound assets. Most of the melee weapons make the sounds you would expect them to make when you swing or hit someone with them(say that aluminum bat makes a proper *tink* sound on impact). The guns I can't say the same for. The shotgun and handgun(9 mm) both sound nothing like the real thing but the mac 9 and revolver are beefy and have a nice kick to them. They are more than passable however.
Graphically speaking the game is a source game. Source engine has never really been all that impressive to look at. Thankfully the developers of this game managed to dodge a bullet by stealing a trick right out of Steven Spielbergs book; using the cover of night properly.
See, in good light the human eye is exceptional at spotting the uncanny valley non-sense most games shove out. The trick around this is make everything low light and hard to see. The persons imagination will attempt to fill in the blanks. A good example of this is the T-rex from Jurassic Park. His CG was actually really ugly(it was 1998 afterall) but to clever use of lighting, puppets and sound made them very believable.
NMRIH does something of the same thing, most of the enviroments are low light and it makes the gritty low resolutions of the zombies that much more better looking for it. You will still notice the low textures of walls and builkdings and the like, but the idea that they are rundown and broken makes you expect them to look kinda ugly. It's actually almost clever.
Gameplay wise there are 2 modes, get out of town and wave mode(at least that's what all the servers seem to be running) one if heavily movement and objective based and the other is campy. Both modes require the teams to actually know what theya re doing. Leaving a  single person with limited equipment to defend themselves results in a very dead teamate, which also results in a  very fast zombie spawning which ironically punishes your teamates for being greedy ♥♥♥♥♥, which I like.
I also noticed that freshly dead teamates also have  higher chance of infecting others, so losing 1 person can seriously hurt a team. There's also the downside that folks can troll teams this way as well, though it doesn't sem to happen often(most trolls just take all the weapons they can carry rather than spawn themselves as undead.)
Splitting up weapons is very key to everyone making it out alive. Personally I'm a  fan of  big melee weapons like the sledge hammer of that massive wrench. Probably the best way to devide up weapons is folks with big 1 shot melee weapons get just that at the start while those with smaller melee weapons get guns to compensate, then move from there.
Ammunition and medical supplies are also scarce, as they should be. Having them be abundant would remove all the tension from the hordes shambling at you (no one is afriad of zombies when you're packing enough ammo to gun down Robocop).
There are some minor issues I have with the game. Firstly, multiplayter can be a nightmare, you will occasionally get a 9 year old yelling about how many times he ♥♥♥♥ed your mother last night (jokes on him, mines dead. hope he's into necrophelia) or have no concept of what "sharing" is (Seriously, do kids NOT watch Sesame Street anymore?)
My other major grump with the game is the fact that in groups of zombies, one can clip backhand you through other zombies. I'm not sure if this is intentional or not. Maybe it's a way to make sure the player doesn't go all Batman and wipe out entire hordes of the restless dead with a soup ladel; a way to remind the player that his character in game was probably a music teacher before this and not a walking tank of death and destruction. (Except that guy that looks like that one guy from the Big Lebowski).
It does have the side effect of making multi-hit kill melee weapons much weaker than they need to be. It's maybe a minor nitpick since 2 handers are sort of abundant, but it's entirely valid one.
The other Bugbear in the room is the lack modes. The game however, is entirely free so this is kinda almost negated by that alone (Also, no ♥♥♥♥ing micro transaction ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t).
In conclusion NMRIG is a work of love, not profit (well they sell the sound track, but dear god is that sound track really good). The problems that game has are easily outshined by the good. The clipping issues seems intentioanlly left in and the lack of mode selection ; whole a problem, doesn't subtract from the rest of the game enough to matter.
If you're looking for a good time , NMRIH does just that.

POSTAL Redux is a revamped version of the original controversial game of the same name; POSTAL, developed and published by Running With Scissors (RWS for short). The original game, when it was released, was a controversial game due to its amount of violence towards the police and towards the innocent. Thankfully, RWS hasn't given up on their POSTAL series (except POSTAL 3, we will pretend that never happened) and has continued to develop and improve their games
POSTAL Redux has an improved engine, if I am not mistaken this game was developed with the Unreal 4 Engine, better graphics, better sound and better music. Everything better. It also includes a Co-Op option which the original game did not have
So what is the best way to describe POSTAL and POSTAL Redux?
If you heard of the not so recent game, also controversial, called Hatred. Which was a game about a person going rampage and shooting police and many innocent people. POSTAL and POSTAL Redux are like Hatred, only better and more enjoyable
You play a simple guy called The Postal Dude and the main objective of the game is to shoot as many hostiles as possible (after 90%, you are free to go to the next level) which includes shooting police and many, many innocent people and also causing havok which is what made POSTAL Redux fun and enjoyable
Now, I am not the type of person who is easily offended. I've played both POSTAL Redux and Hatred and wasn't offended, I watch the South Park series and played the South Park games and whenever I see things that other people get offended by, I don't. So I understand why the POSTAL series caused so much controversy but at the same time, I don't care
The game is much more dark than its sequel, and this was a shock to me as I watched so many videos of POSTAL 2 (and now I own the game) where you hit people and urinate on them whereas in POSTAL and POSTAL Redux, it seems like Satan has taken over your soul and you just want to murder people. A huge shift in tone between the two games
The gameplay is that of any type of shooter. Shoot as many people as possible without dying. The camera is that of an isometric perspective, meaning that the camera is of a top down perspective. The graphics (which POSTAL suffered quite a lot and were quite ugly) have greatly improved in the Redux version. The music is sick and twisted which I surprisingly liked and the voice acting by both the Postal dude and the innocent victims is good
To play POSTAL and POSTAL Redux, you will need an open mind or someone like me who isn't easily offended and the game is certainly not playable for people who are easily offended. I would only recommend POSTAL and POSTAL Redux to people who don't mind the subject matter or people who are not easily offended, otherwise, steer clear away from POSTAL, POSTAL Redux or POSTAL 2
If you are interested in POSTAL, I would highly recommend purchasing the Redux version of it!

Enough of performance talk, let's talk about the game. By the time I'm writing the review, the game has already gotten action/adventure  game of the year award of 2016, so you already know the potentiality of this game already, or maybe you don't cause of huge negative impact on steam reviews due to the technical issues it had.
I'm no reviewer so my point of view could be wrong.
One thing I wanna say straight ahead:
Arkane Studio surely knows their game. They follows the "if it's not broken, dont try to fix it" approach and that is clearly apparent in their 2nd installment of the famous stealthy first person game. They perfected everything that was there in Dishonored 1. Every game mechanics is more polished and fun to play with. You can have multiple approaches for overcoming problems. And you can build your character like that. Either you can go stealthy merciful soul or you can go full vengeful assassin. Heck, you can beat the entire game without killing anyone, just like first game.
All playstyles have their moment of fun and rewards. And this time it's double the fun, because now you have 2 playable characters who's powers are completely different. So the game will play abit differently for both of them. My first playthrough was with Emily and I must say I just love her character. She is well developed, quite powerful and very enjoyable to play with. Surely I wanna play with her one more time after Arkane gonna release New Game+ later on.
Corvo I haven't played with yet, so can't say his playstyle from personal experience, but I heard he has his own Dishonored 1-ish charm. The game is worthy to play with Emily and Corvo both. It's not linear at all despite of being not open world, cause you can adept different playstyle and the final conclusion will depend upon it. So I'm completely leaving it to the players for playing the game in high or low chaos, the system for what D1 was so famous for. Basically, if you go killing everyone, you will have high chaos, thus dark ending. Or if you like to knock out the baddies rather than killing, you can have low chaos, thus optimistic ending. You are the maker of the story and it'e ending.
Speaking of story, I was a huge fan of the first Dishonored and was kindda unsure how the 2nd game will turn out. But to my surprise, it held up to the first game and more. The story doesn't necessarily require you to play the DLC's of the first game to understand. But you would get more details if you do, the story will open up more and will make sense.
The gameplay, omg...is pure pleasure for fans of old Dishonored. Dishonored 2 polished what they had on the first game and now it's a pure bliss. The high chaos assassin or killer approach is hell lot of fun. Full gun blazing and Slashing enemies with sword while doing combos with powers looks waaaay cool and are very very satisfactory.
And you can even play the entire game without your special void power. There is a 'no power' mode in the game itself. But the game will be tough in this mode.
I find the game little bit easy even on medium, so if you are looking for more challenge then I must suggest to play it on hard.
Not to mention the replayablity it has.
Graphics and art is subjective, and to me, the game is very pretty. Sure, it's not that pretty game in it's time. But the detailed levels and it's art style stood out eventhough the game used old IDTECH 5's heavily modified version (VOID). And the steampunk world they presented is very believable. And as I'm a sucker for artstyle, the game is very much eyecandy for me. loved it!
There are some problem regarding the positional audio that I've found, but it's very negligible and can be overlooked as the game have really cool voice acting, musical scores and audio effects.
Just get the game and play it if you are a stealth game lover, or get it if you are into this genre. The current steam ratings are not doing justice for this game and I must say this game deserves a full 9 out 10 ratings, despite of all the technical flaws it has.

The plot of Postal is deliberately kept vague as to not distract from the gameplay. From what can be gathered through the original website, manual, and the game itself, an average man known only as the Postal Dude discovers that a mind altering substance has been released on the town of Paradise, infecting the populace with insanity and blood-lust. Capped off by his sudden eviction from his home, the Postal Dude believes himself to be the only sane man left and sets out to put an end to the madness in his town, which he believes originates from the local Air-Force Base. Now to the gameplay of POSTAL. This game is one of my favorites maybe my favorite game i've played, the gameplay is fun and action packed and scary and the game never gets dull to me no matter how many times I have played it through (3 times on The Original POSTAL and 3 times again on POSTAL: Redux). One thing great the redux does is fix the controls, as when I play the original it took a bit to get used to the controls but for the redux I caught on immediatly. Another reason why you should buy redux is the fact that it is a faithful recreation of the original (they did add one new map though being The Carnival and they added a new weapon, witch both I absolutely love) and don't forget CO-OP, one of the biggest reasons to buy the redux is for the co-op.
POSTAL: Redux CO-OP: I aboslutely love that they added CO-OP with this game, it is really fun to go play this game with friends, as me and my friend had a blast going around paradise blasting our way through "The evil" ;P (One thing is that if you plan on getting for co-op get a copy to a friend as their is no servers open most of the time sadly :c)
TL;DR: BUY THE GAME ALREADY, oh yeah and don't play on easy, play on hard; the more difficult this game is the more fun it is.

As someone who didn't enjoy any Postal game I gotta admit the Redux is quite an improvement over the 1997 version.
First of all, the control schemes are now much more fluid and intuitive. Instead of rotating "A" and "D" moves the character to the left and to the right of the screen. This modification might sounds like a tiny one but it greatly improves on the gameplay as it is easier (and more fair) to dodge missiles coming at you and running for cover. Of course, the enhanced visuals are greatly appreciated not to the mention the additional survival mode.
Despite all of these improvements the game is not without flaw since the level of violence feels the same as the original. I may sound like a desensitized person but I was hoping for a more gory game, like some dismemberments and gibs. Also, the arsenal is a bit lackluster. The rocket launcher, napalm launcher and flamethrower are more or less useful since they are high risk high reward. This is why I ended up using the submachinegun, the shotgun and the magnum most of the time.
Overall Postal Redux is definitively worth a buy although being only a decent game.

This is a very difficult game to review.
On one hand, it's what I think anyone who has played Just Cause 2 could have possibly wanted; physics-based destruction of nearly every object in the game (except for terrain and most buildings, as is with most games that have destructible environments). It adds a host of exciting vehicles and weapons to demolish everything in your way with. It evolves on Just Cause 2's fundamental mechanics that made it so fun. It also adds a wingsuit, which I will forever hold as the most fun way to travel in a videogame, ever. This is basically Michael Bay: The Videogame, and I absolutely love everything about it. As someone who enjoyed Just Cause 2 very much, this is the greatest sequel I could have possibly dreamed of.
However, what makes it hard to recommend is the bevy of performance issues people have been having with the game. It's incredibly fun when it works, but this is a very intensive game that is probably not on the good side of the optimisation fence. The game barely runs for some, and for those that it runs for a fair few have performance issues and graphical issues, some which render this game unplayable.
Personally, I haven't been affected by these problems too much, but if you go to the game's subreddit or Steam discussions, you will almost always find complaints about how well, or badly, the game runs.
For reference, my specs are as follows:
i5-4440
Gigabyte GTX 970 G1 Gaming (overclocked to 1505 Mhz on the core - 7800Mhz on the memory)
8GB RAM
1TB WD HDD (Windows installation and game both on it)
Additionally, this game doesn't take as well to overclocking as some other games, as I can normally run a higher overclock without issue on other games, but Just Cause 3 crashes within 30-60 minutes with that same overclock.
What I hope you can get from this review is that this is a great game, but what stops me from recommending this 100% is the performance issues, so my suggestion is that you buy this game and try it out, see if it works on your system, but know that you might end up abandoning it in your library or simply refunding it if it doesn't work well on your system.

It was fun, but I think overall JC2 was better. In 2 the controls were easy to use, but the game wasn't overly simple. I spent weeks exploring and conquering that map and had fun just wasting time connecting enemies to various things.
I've already finished conquering the map for JC3 after a couple days, but there was more frustration on the part of trying to move around. It seems like I couldn't ever quite get the hang of when to hit 'E' or spacebar. Also, rudder control on planes, Z & C, are hard to get to when you also have to steer with WASD and throttle up/down with 'SHIFT'/'CTRL' (also, why is there rudder control on planes, but no rotation on helicopters!?).
Further, grappling enemies to objects in JC3 just didn't feel as natural and streamlined as it did in JC2. In 2 I hooked enemies to speeding cars, planes taking off, windmill blades, etc. In 3 it's like the opportunity rarely presented itself and when it did I couldn't quite get it to work. I'd either end up accidentally killing the enemy or having to give up to avoid being killed. There was always an enemy BEHIND me calling for backup, so there was little chance that I'd have a moment to relax and just focus on the task at hand - hooking a guy to something in a hilarious way.
To sum up: JC2=790 hours of laughing, JC3=149 hours of swearing.
Don't get me wrong, it was still fun and it's worth playing. The world looks amazing and, while I've already conquered the map, I still have all of the challenges to do, hidden objects to find, and worst case there is an option to return an area to the enemy so you can conquer it again.

The enemies so far are very much the same to those in the first game, theyre decent enough to make it challenging on harder difficulties especially with the limited ammo. I recommend if you play this game play it through on Nightmare, anything lower and the game is probably too easy. The story is interesting so far, they do a great job setting up the environments just like in the first game. The new main boss in the game is cool as well, you get to see some sneak peeks of him almost right off the bat and already his abilities are unique and interesting. I would recommend the game if you liked the first one, if you're considering buying this but havent played the first one I would say buy that instead to see if you like this kind of game. I don't generally write reviews, but this game is an acception. I really think that the dev of this game deserves some love, because it's rather obvious that there was a lot of time and effort put into the game.
Pros
- Free (Seriously, why wouldn't you get a free game? It's not like you're losing anything if you get it. Heck, if you don't like it, you can just uninstall it...)
- Interesting gameplay.
- Sweet-ish Story
- Bosses are challenging, but not impossible. Which I think is pretty important for a game.
- The way you upgrade skills is not the way I've seen most RPGs handle it. Instead of just usage, you actually put points into it and level it up. Similar to Okami.
- Hidden collectables that are actually useful.
- Rewards for collecting said hidden collectables that actually helps you in the long run.
- A good sense of progression with each level.
- The visuals are cute. (Not really sure if this is something most people care about, but hey, I liked it...)
Cons
- If you plan to power level, you won't have as great of a time as you would've if you were to just play the game normally.
- Once you leave an area, there is no way to go back. It's kind of understandable, but I still found it kind of odd.
- If you want to get the best armor, you'll have to grind a bit. Same with the best weapon.
Overall, if you are even slightly interested, I would suggest giving it a look over. Even if you don't like it, you should at least give the creator constructive criticism. Heck, from what I know, this is the creator's first jab at a game.

2014 GOTY
The work and the dedication that went into making this insanely immersive game continued to amaze me until the very end.....Oh and that ending.... taken right from the book of Christopher Nolan's Inception. Play it to see it.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I will get the negatives out of the way.
There are several climactic moments in the game when you think the game is about to end, yet it doesn't. That doesn't mean I wanted the game to end necessarily, it's just that the amount of these climaxes diminished their effect gradually. Nonetheless, I have enjoyed them all.
It DID get tedious in the last 3-4 hours having to flip the switches and having to start the power there and there, having to look for key cards and having to constantly check the map to plot the route and then subsequently plan the escape route. It was just too much work, but you DO play as engineer in the game for a reason, for many reasons, actually.
I played on hard yet I barely had to use the crafted items for the most part. I was able to save most of them until my weapons were temporarily taken away.
The first 4-5 hours were kind of frustrating, insofar as hiding from the alien goes, but as soon as you figure out the amount of seconds you get on average when the radar blip moves away and as soon as you learn to differentiate when the alien is above you in the vent or on the other side of the door and as soon as you learn that sneaking constantly with the radar up is not really necessary and then you start getting a handle on this cat and mouse fight. Things get a LOT easier once you get the flamethrower about 6 hours in. Even on hard mode I never once came close to running out of flamethrower fluid. It does not kill the alien but small bursts of it do scare him away long enough for you to either find a way out, flip a switch, use a blow torch or what have you.
Clunky combat does get in the way at first but I have learned to deal with it. After a while it really was not a big deal.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
As for the positives - too many too name, I am sure I will keep editing this review when more of them come to mind.
Well, for starters, this is by far the best game by movie adaptation that I can think of. After I beat the game I have popped my blu ray version of the first Alien and could not believe just how accurate the game design is to that of the movie.
I loved the graphics. They were pristine, crisp, shiny, realistic, polished. The smoke, the view of the cosmos, the creepy android design, the level design were all great. Lighting could use some work though.
The foes are tough to kill. Almost each one required a planned and careful approach.
The flashback scene to the distress beacon almost brought tears to my eyes. It was beautiful. It was nerve-racking. I have immediately started googling away for Prometheus 2.
The exploration requires thought and planning. Backtracking makes sense. The crafting will make encounters easier and the upgrades may yield access to new areas but that means that you may deal with the alien or other foes for a longer time instead of proceeding to the main objective.
I liked playing as the protagonist. I really did like Ripley Jr.. She has her own inner thoughts, she has a body with legs (although I never saw her cast a shadow, nor did I see anyone else cast any shadows), she takes a while to run, to hide, to climb, she can hold her breath, she does get scared and startled, she does express her feelings constantly - that really doesn't happen in most games that are driven by silent protagonists. Creative Assembly learned plenty from Outlast (insofar as the realistic first person "human" control goes). She does not really grow as a character though. In the end we still know very little about her.
The game is long, like very long. If you play this game from start to finish by fully immersing yourself at night without playing any other game in the meantime then you are guaranteed to have a blast.
We really don't get nearly enough of amazing titles like this.

This game is truly wonderful, there's a lot of hard practice within the game and you can't just always rely on one tactic to win. Every enemy has been balanced along with the weapons and armour to always give that feeling of struggle, no matter how high in strength you are. PVP however is where this game is let down, mainly because the players who play this game like to make use of the cheapest tactics they can manage in order to win. Here's just a list of what to expect if you try doing Dark Souls 2 PVP:
Channeler's trident with any magic buff and poison infusion while spamming heavy attack to drill hit you and just stack poison? Check.
Infinite HP hacks? Check. (I've encountered at least 46 different players doing this so far)
Poison/Bleed estoc to bypass shields? Check.
Infinite stagger caestus build? Check.
Prebuffing and then using poison fog/toxic mist/dark fog/acid surge as you are summoning in so you get poisoned/have your armour and rings broken before you can even act? Check. (watch out would be dragons, this happens to you a LOT)
Prebuffing and then trying to backstab you as you are summoning in? Check (Dragons again...)
Waiting right by where you appear and spamming fire tempest or other AoE spells so you have no time to act when you summon in? Check. (dragons especially)
Abusing rolls to ensure no form of magic will ever hit them? Check. (Oh yeah, if you roll? You can't get hit by most magic unless it's a flat out hit. Not a fun thing if you get forced into PVP and you're a caster of any form).
That's just a short list of the cheap tactics I've seen being put to use while I have played Dark Souls 2. Players will not try to play fair and as a result, it ruins the experience for the people who are trying to play the game fairly. Most even take PRIDE in this factor and you can find tons of builds to accompany these tactics so as to 'pwn maximum number of noobs' as one person put it.
I will complement Dark Souls 2 however as it has made co-operative play (especially with friends) much, MUCH better than Dark Souls 1. You get a name engraved ring you can buy that allows you to connect to players using the same 'god' that you choose using the ring. There's a large selection of gods and goddesses so you have little risk of being summoned by someone who you don't want to be summoned by. There's also two forms of aid you can do: Shades (which last a certain time and vanish when they've either killed so many enemies or have been there long enough, you can tell if a shade's about to vanish because they start turning black) and phantoms (Just like Dark Souls 1, they vanish when you beat a boss usually). A nice thing they've made sure to note is while there are areas where phantoms can't be summoned, shades can still be summoned in some of them, allowing for you to still recieve aid from your friends if you need it (and some areas you really DO need it.
For those travelling alone, From Software hasn't forgotten about you. Almost every single boss has a NPC phantom or two somewhere nearby that can aid you if you are unfortunate enough to have the dark souls 2 server lose connection or if you lose connection to steam. What's more, some of them have storylines that grant you their equipment if you accomplish them.
Overall, there's plenty of nice things in Dark Souls 2 that I would really want to praise. There's a vast array of weapons, armours and items to help you on your journey and it's possible to make all kinds of playthroughs (I've even seen someone playing a run as a character named after and tooled up exactly like Simon Belmont from castlevania. That was funny to play along with!).
If anything, it's Dark Souls 2's PVP that lets it down in the long run and a lot of the covenants make use of PVP to rank up so you are kind of forced to face it at some point if you want the most out of covenants... though thankfully you can switch covenants freely in Dark Souls 2, which is a god send.
There was one other thing that disappointed me though (and this is more a personal nitpick than anything else)... the weapons while vast and arrayed... well, it doesn't exactly have the same kind of fantastic variety that Dark Souls 1 had. I thought it was neat when I could get a sword made out of crystal or the dark sword from the darkwraiths (I was pleased the armour was back but COME ON FROM SOFT, why no sword to go with!?) which all had really unique designs and stood out. Granted, there are a few nice and unique weapons but I just feel it's lacking there. Who knows? Maybe the DLC coming out will provide us with some more really neat tools of destruction? I sure hope so!
Would I recommend Dark Souls 2? Yes, VERY MUCH YES I would recommend this game. But there are things that you need to be aware of when you pick this game up and I hope this review will help those who are considering this game for various reasons to consider before picking it up. From Software is making constant balance checks with this game so maybe they might see some of the problems and deal with them but in the meantime, thank you for reading my review and I hope it gave you all information about Dark Souls 2 that will help you decide to buy the game.
Good luck, and hope you're prepared to die all over again. You'll be doing it a lot.

This game takes the features commonly seen in RPGs and cuts away at it down to the skeleton. Which is not a bad thing. I spent around five hours with this game, debating whether I'm impressed or sad.
The visuals are very simple but there's a lot of care and attention into making every screen make sense. The characters can look a little out of place sometimes, as there are a few sprites here and there which were probably used from the default models from RPGMaker and they don't really go well with the handmade models. The two main characters are also extremely obviously based off of a female Swordsman and a female High Priest, both from the Ragnarok Online MMORPG. I wish the creator would have put a little more work into making them look more unique, because it truly is very obvious. That said, the hand-drawn portraits and models look nice.
Every level is carefully designed with its share of unique challenges, from exploding enemies to platforming. It's genuinely impressive how much love was put into each and every segment of the game world -- even being a linear game, there's a lot of incentive to truly explore and gather materials, as well as tackle the secret levels for special rewards.
The combat system is very reminiscent of the Ys series; this game wears its inspirations on its sleeve but I believe that's a good thing. It's relaxing but, at the same time, it can be quite challenging to overcome certain bosses even though there's not even an attack button. The skill system isn't as fleshed out as it could be and using SP to increase the skills is very simplistic -- most of the time, you'll just want to dump the points in all skills equally but only a couple are really ever truly useful (at least up until where I am). Even still, each skill has its very own application and they stand out from each other.
The story is extremely generic but it keeps itself mysterious enough that it doesn't need to shove itself down your throat. I believe this was the right decision. The narrative wouldn't be interesting enough to flesh out every 30 minutes with exposition so the choice to keep it to a sheer minimum and focus instead on Senia's confusion was appropriate. It's a little weird that all bosses (up until where I am) are basically variations of a succubus but that's not a real complaint or anything. Just something that annoyed me a little bit. I'd also like to point out that the game's text sometimes suffers from a severe lack of proof-reading by a fluent English speaker. There are a LOT of grammar mistakes and even some conveyance problems, particularly in dialogue. It's too bad because it harms the already very vanilla storyline. It's an issue that's easily fixed. It may add to the charm for some players but, in my case, it's a little cringy at times.
I noted at the start that I didn't know whether to be impressed or sad. This is because, on one hand, I'm impressed at the amount of sheer love the creator put into making this game. Most complaints I noted above could be justified by the fact that the game was made on absolutely no budget and it's being distributed for free. I'm sad, however, because this is one of those games which will find it very hard to get publicized due to its nonexistent marketing campaign and minimalistic approach.
As an indie game, this is clearly a step behind a lot of videogames as far as technology goes. As a labour of love, being distributed at absolutely no cost, with no DLC or any strings attached, this deserves my utmost respect and admiration.
This is free. Download it. Play it proudly. Now.

Alien: Isolation is an odd game. The team at The Creative Assembly built what is probably the most-immersive atmosphere I've seen in a game. It captures, perfectly, the retro 1970s futurism in the original film. CRTs, clunky mechanical keyboards, and plastic greeble abound. And in this world you've got posters, scrawlings, decals, terminals, audio logs, and all manner of things to catch your eye and draw your attention. The lighting, sound design, and level construction are masterfully done and, for about 98% of the game, they remain consistently good and interesting - the entire station rarely loses its sense of menacing claustrophobia and inescapability.
All of that, however, is ruined by the game's single weakest element: the Xenomorph. The alien is, functionally, a mobile Game Over trigger. You have no means of defeating it and, at your best, are only capable of warding it off; even then only for three to ten seconds. So what happens when the alien shows up? You hide. You hide and you wait. Then, once he gets bored and buggers off back into the vents, you can resume the game. This is novel for the first half-dozen times you encounter it, but the gimmick overstays its welcome in short order. This reaches its zenith of irritation and absurdity when you get to segments wherein the alien is set to patrol an area as if it was a security guard. It's ridiculous and slows the game to a crawl. But the alien isn't the only threat on the station, which leads me to the best part of the game:
The (horrifying) synthetics! Combined with the retro-futurism, the synthetics really make the game feel like you got an advance copy of Routine. They're scary from the moment you see them and the fear factor only ramps up as the game goes on. They make the game enjoyable. They're a threat you can usually ignore, but it's immensely satisfying to overwhelm them once you get some firepower. They also have wonderful dialog.
The story is generally ok, but the lengths to which they force Ripley to go get sillier as the game goes on. (Especially at the end.) The voice acting is also acceptable.
In short, if you download a mod to disable the alien, the game's quality will improve significantly. Otherwise, play it on easy just so you don't have to put up with its irritating nonsense.
Completion time will be north of 15 hours, which makes it a fair purchase at $40 or so.

Tl;dr: same story as everyone else. Optimization was and to an extent is (for some) still terrible. Release state was abysmal. Wait for more patches and a sale.
My rig:
i5 4690k OC 4.4GHz
GTX970 SSC
16GB ram (8x8 in single channel due to faulty mob)
Runs Titanfall 2 and BF1 maxed out smoothly despite single channel ram so take what you will from that.
As of patch 1.3 (almost one month since release) there are still some weird graphical issues going on but it seems mostly smoothed out if you fiddle with the settings enough. I managed to get stable framerates at 1080p by locking the FPS to 45 and turning most things up to very high. That being said, the game shouldn't have been released on PC as it was. A delay would have been preferable. Arkane and Bethesda messed up.
As most reviewers have said, I'd probably give the game a thumbs up if not for the state of the optimization. It's got a well built world to play around in and the NPC's are less rigid than most other games. They seem to be a living part of the world rather than just set pieces. The dialogue can be a bit cringe at points, but it's rare enough to be forgivable. I had a few frustrations with the control scheme at first but it's definitely workable. Overall it's an enjoyable experience if you're a fan of the stealth genre or the world of Dishonored.
As for the graphics, it's a pretty game. It really is. Is it the prettiest game of 2016? No. Battlefield 1 is by far better looking and Titanfall 2 (made in heavily modified Source, btw) is as well imo. Opinions over art style will differ, but in plain graphical fidelity it's pretty handily beaten by other holiday releases. The issues people have had since release are not because this is a new AAA game with the fanciest graphics to date that require a beasty GPU with 6-8gb of vram to run, it's because Arkane chose to cannibalize the ID Tech engine and turn it into the Void engine. I assume because it was at hand and saved on licensing fees. Wrong move on their part.
If you really wanna give the game a shot I HIGHLY recommend waiting for a sale or picking it up on console. Definitely don't give Bethesda/Arkane your $60 for this either way. They knew the state of the game when they released it and took advantage of Bethesda's new day 1 review policy to push it out the door anyway. I regret buying at release and being too stubborn to return it while I had the chance. By this time next year it'll hit less than half price in Steam sales and (hopefully) be properly optimized. This will definitely be my last day 1 purchase from Bethesda for a long time to come.

In
, you play as Mike Jansen, a man who has just woken up in a daze in his own living room apparently unaware of what just happened to him. When he comes to he is confronted by... Mike Jansen. Same voice, same face, same person. There are two Mike Jansens in the same room and it is up to you figure out what is going on and answer the question: Who is Mike?
This game is a short visual novel and is almost entirely story-based. You, as the player, make choices along the way in answers to questions the other characters ask or different actions to take. The choices to these decisions dictate the course of the story and which ending you achieve. In total, there are nine different endings in this game.
The game itself is a light psychological horror game and on the shorter side. It should take only around an hour to achieve all of the endings. For a short game, I thought it was pretty good overall. The art itself was rather good and served its purpose well. The use of music to help enhance the mood of the game at various points was skilled. The main point of a visual novel is the story which was good. You start out the game with very little information on the situation so there is a bit of a mystery aspect involved. Without going into spoilers, I would also say it is definitely worth going through all of the endings to see how the story plays out differently.
If you like visual novels, this short and free game is worth a play.

I played this game before it was released on Steam.
As like the other Fervent game, Cupid, this one is really good for a short, free visual novel.
The story gets complex and like Cupid, depending on your choices, your ending and role in the game changes. You could be the real Mike as well as the fake. The choices are small and subtle but impact your story greatly. The art is great. The writing is good and overall for a free visual novel, it's really good.

Now before we get to the spoilers, I am going to say that this is by far one of the best psychological horror game I have played but I don't play many horror games so take it as you will. This is still a decent visual novel never the less.
The scare factor comes from how helplessly uncertain and vulnerable the game makes you feel due to the lack of information you are given, the tone of the music and the atmosphere. It messes with your head and even the idea of saving your game does not help you. For what you assume is the truth can change. The characters around you are constantly playing their own agenda and the player is generally oblivious to what is happening.
These ideas are toyed with from the start and are a constant theme placed throughout this short visual novel.  I can’t recommend this game enough because trying to figure out who mike is and what happened to him is very satisfying and will hurt you when you get to one bad ending after another.
Warning this section contains major spoilers and is not recommended to read if you have not played the game.

I decided to write this review a bit early for those on the fence here on the day of release, but I plan to write a more proper review later once I've finished the game. So I've played this game for 9 & a half hours at this point, and barely just finished Chapter 4 (of 15+ chapters). First hour and a half was taking it slow and exploring around in the first two chapters, the next six & a half hours was Chapter 3 and doing EVERYTHING you could in the open world level, 30-45 minutes was committed to me doing the special shooting gallery minigames added to the Save Area once you reach Chapter 4 and getting all the rewards, and then the last 45-60 minutes was going through Chapter 4.
I should mention I'm playing on Nightmare difficulty, and playing with almost all my HUD off. Only things I kept on were my reticle, item pick-up info, and some stuff for later like partner health gauge. The game started off REALLY challenging on Nightmare, I was getting my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me during all of Chapter 2 and the start of Chapter 3, but I really got a handle of it. I managed to kill every single enemy in Chapter 3, mostly with stealth. Learned a few techniques. I explored every inch of Chapter 3, there is a LOT hidden in it. The side-quests are the obvious ones, but they've literally littered the town with so many interesting things off the beaten path. I'll get back to this.
There is so much I want to say, but I don't really know where to start. Firstly, as a horror enthusiast, this is a REALLY neat horror game. On paper and at first it seems pretty basic, but it slowly reveals it has a lot more up its sleeve. I want to say so much, but I also feel I shouldn't to keep most of it a surprise for others who decide to dig into it. All I'll say is if you don't explore Chapter 3 you're doing yourself a huge disservice, there's literally so many fun, interesting, and unique scenarios to find, and not even just in the side-quests. There's also 5 hidden levels of sorts which are worth finding and experiencing in my opinion among everything, and some do some neat things and touches in the game, like there's this ghost woman who if you do her side-quest will begin to haunt you through the whole game, but will not haunt you if you don't do the side-quest..
To be honest I wasn't really sure what to think of it all at first. Chapter 1 & 2 for a example while I was playing I wasn't quite sure what I thought of it, though in retrospective there was a lot of really cool moments, one of my favorites being when you look down a dark corridor with your flashlight and a giant strange black and white fuzzy eye is staring back at you, then blinks and disappears. The game has so many creative touches if you look around and interact with things. And I began to love it more and more as I played Chapter 3, at the start still uncertain but as I began to get into the groove of it I began to love it.
You can tell the team behind this are very passionate for horror and horror games and had a lot of fun making this, it's full of so many small touches everywhere, it's got so much love for other horror stuff. Chapter 2 is in many ways almost like some pseudo walking sim horror game like Layers of Fear is what it reminded me most of, then Chapter 3 experiments with all sorts of things all over the map, and Chapter 4 has some fun with a unique take on defenseless first-person horror, but with reasoning that makes more sense than usual. But things are paced well to not only keep you on your toes but keep things interesting, and feed well into each other so far.
Chapter 3 I think some people will have a gut reaction to dislike the open world chapter it is on principle and initial impressions, and to be honest I wasn't sure what to think at first myself, but it is incredibly unique and begins to become very immersive, interesting, and fun to explore as you go through it. It's NOT an empty open world by any means, literally every area is intentionally designed with no randomized features, and it's better for it. It's basically a giant horror amusement part with surprises tucked away into every corner, if you'll look for them, and a lot of twists and turns as you dig deeper into the overworld and a lot of interesting, fun, and tense scenarios packs into every area of the map almost.
Despite the fact I've played this game for nearly 10 hours now, I'm still fairly early in. There's a lot more I want to say but kind of also just want to discuss, and then plan to play a lot more tomorrow. I'm finding now that I'm done playing for now I can't stop thinking about this game. I feel like this game is a very different beast than the first game, I'm not sure everyone who loved the first game will love this one even and some people who didn't really like the first game may end up loving this (it still is tellable it's The Evil Within and made by the same team, but they have made some very bold decisions and tried some very different things design wise which kind of makes The Evil Within all at once reminds of several things, and yet feel rather unique on its own, kind of like the original game but in a completely different way).I can already tell this game is going to go on at the very least to become a cult classic with some sectors of horror fans, it's surprisingly unique in many ways and if you let it, it can really begin growing on you.
