The year 2017 will mark the second decade since the landmark, cult-classic game POSTAL was released into the world. Controversy sparked from every corner of the dark title, especially due to its gruesome ending and remorseless killing. It took Running With Scissors a few years, but they finally latched on to the success of the series and eventually birthed POSTAL 2 and 3 into the world; those are reviews for another time, however.
POSTAL Redux is not just a simple graphical overhaul of the original title, instead it's a complete revamp of the game done in Unreal Engine 4. The makeover definitely shows, not only in the aesthetic presentation of the game, but also the fluid, up-to-date controls that make the Redux so much easier to play over its predecessor. There are many notable differences between POSTAL Redux and the first POSTAL, which will be taken a look at within this review.
For those who have played the first POSTAL, feel free to skip this paragraph. Those of you questioning what the game is all about, stick around. In POSTAL, you play as an antagonist who's simply known as The Postal Dude; some say he's schizophrenic, some say he's a madman, some like to believe he's a pretty nice guy. Either way, The Postal Dude has a theory that his hometown of Paradise, Arizona is being flooded with mind-altering substances; he starts believing that he is the only individual who is unaffected. Once he gets evicted from his home, he starts a murderous rampage of blood-lust, and doesn't stop until he reaches the Military Air Base; where he believes the source of the noxious gas is stemming from.
For long-time fans of the series, you may be upset to know that Running With Scissors have changed the iconic ending in the Redux. There's no longer
. The interpretation of this is up to the individual, but the same end cutscene is still present after the last "level" plays out. In my experience, the new Redux ending is much less impacting than the original, and the game loses some of its overall morbidity due to it.
The original POSTAL had 21 levels, plus four extra levels from the Special Delivery expansion pack, the Redux only has 17 levels in total with one of them being the newly created Carnival map; so it's safe to say that Running With Scissors trimmed the fat a little bit. As well, the difficulty of this title is nowhere near that of the original, and seasoned players will find even the hard difficulty severely lacking in comparison to POSTAL's "11" difficulty setting. However, this could be something that is fixed in the future, as the Redux has been receiving regular updates since its release in May, 2016.
The developer claims that the visuals are a "faithful" recreation of the original, and quite honestly I haven't seen a difference in them other than the fact that they're of higher resolution and thus much more clear. This is a good thing, as it genuinely looks as though the original hand-painted backgrounds have been re-scanned in a superior format; if someone redid all of the backgrounds, kudos to them as they look like the real deal. As for the character models, they're noticably upgraded from the Playstation 1-era models from the original game, and you can even change The Postal Dude's trench coat color.
It's safe to say that the Redux functions like any other modern top-down shooter now. In the original, it was difficult to control The Postal Dude with both the keyboard and mouse, due to the games age and engine limitations. The Redux sees to it that the mouse control is extremely fluid, as is the aiming/targeting system and ability to switch between weapons with the scroll wheel. Not to mention, the Redux can also be played with a console controller, for those who are not fond of keyboard and mouse controls.
Other than the upgraded visuals and lack of levels, POSTAL Redux has some other notable changes. One of the biggest additions is the new executions. In the original game, no matter what gun you were using The Postal Dude would switch back to his AR-16 for the execution of downed enemies, now each gun has its own unique animation. Another fantastic feature is when playing on Hard mode, the journal entries that show up between levels read as they appeared in the original manual of POSTAL; on Easy and Medium they simply stay the same as what is shown in the first game. There's a new revolver weapon, the machine gun (or SMG in this version) has a higher rate of fire and range, the shotgun and spray cannons do not share the same ammo any longer, the journal entry dates all read 2017 as opposed to 1997, and the newly introduced Rampage mode is a bit like the Gauntlet Challenge from the original game.
Sadly, POSTAL Redux does have a major downfall; the game likes to crash... a lot. The amount of crashing that still occurs despite the numerous updates to the title is unacceptable. Running With Scissors just released an update that implemented 4 player co-op, yet they cannot find the time to rectify crashes that skew the players experience with the game? That's just hard for me to believe. The game will crash during level transitions, during start up, but most of all during the Rampage mode.
With that being said, if you can live with the amount of crashing that this game likes to do, then POSTAL Redux will be a great addition to your collection of violent, twisted, dark humored games. The complete engine overhaul has really brought the classic POSTAL title up to speed in the modern world, although it would be nice if Running With Scissors left all of the levels intact instead of picking which ones to keep in and leave out; it would've also been nice to have the original ending. The audio is also completely remastered, so The Postal Dude's witty and sarcastic comments  can be heard crystal clear now. As well, I'm sure the newly introduced 4 player online co-op will appeal to a large range of gamers. If you've never played POSTAL before, this is an excellent starting point. If you're a long-time fan of the series, you won't be disappointed.

Or as I like to call it, “screw you Political Correctness”.
This is a game mostly about getting to be the best ‘Bros’ in movie and television history, and getting to run around as them. It pays a bit of homage, partially out of necessity to available “bros”, to all the biggest, best (and worst) action bros. Imagine if you could run around as the Terminator, Conan, and that one marine played by Arnold in the first Predator movie. Would that not be awesome (and CG heavy)?
But again, as I said, bit of limitations. So far in playing (4 hours) I’ve unlocked only two non white dudes, BA and Blade specifically, and as odd as this is to say about a game about bros, only one girl, Ripley from the Alien movies. *Correction, I just unlocked Machete.
Story: Like any good action movie, this is mostly about the great white hope showing up and dispensing freedom (IE: laying waste) to some generic terrorist looking dudes in... wait, Vietnam? Yeah, Vietnam. Along the way, you’ll also be saving fellow Bros, the more you save, the more Bros you get to play as.
Gameplay: It’s mostly about going from area to area in successively more difficult levels and blowing the absolute hell out of everything in your path. Get ready to dispense freedom using shotguns, missiles, rockets, and yes, CHAINSAW HANDS. Also, get ready to die, A LOT.
No seriously, I can’t stress that part enough. You are going to die darn nearly constantly. I was playing the Alpha Build, early access version on Steam and dear god did I burn through a lot of lives.
The Good, The Bad, The Ugly: It is so awesome getting to play as one of your favorite heroes, and kinda disheartening how sucky some of them turn on in comparison to others. Seriously, Indiana Jones is less effective than Agent K. The Terminator is pretty much unplayable unless you got your back against a wall, which is pretty much the opposite of the point of being the Terminator.
The Glitches: Ok, this is an Early Access, and an Alpha Build, so grain of salt with any complaints here. There was several times I died and there was absolutely nothing on screen. I was just sliding down a wall and died. The game also would experience slow downs (and the one guys power, or when a boss character showed up, just randomly the game would seriously slow down, sometimes all but freezing. The only pattern I really noticed was typically Walker, Texas Ranger and missiles were on the screen at the same time, but it did occasionally happen with other guys too.
Final Verdict: Worth the money. Play it.

Tl;dr: same story as everyone else. Optimization was and to an extent is (for some) still terrible. Release state was abysmal. Wait for more patches and a sale.
My rig:
i5 4690k OC 4.4GHz
GTX970 SSC
16GB ram (8x8 in single channel due to faulty mob)
Runs Titanfall 2 and BF1 maxed out smoothly despite single channel ram so take what you will from that.
As of patch 1.3 (almost one month since release) there are still some weird graphical issues going on but it seems mostly smoothed out if you fiddle with the settings enough. I managed to get stable framerates at 1080p by locking the FPS to 45 and turning most things up to very high. That being said, the game shouldn't have been released on PC as it was. A delay would have been preferable. Arkane and Bethesda messed up.
As most reviewers have said, I'd probably give the game a thumbs up if not for the state of the optimization. It's got a well built world to play around in and the NPC's are less rigid than most other games. They seem to be a living part of the world rather than just set pieces. The dialogue can be a bit cringe at points, but it's rare enough to be forgivable. I had a few frustrations with the control scheme at first but it's definitely workable. Overall it's an enjoyable experience if you're a fan of the stealth genre or the world of Dishonored.
As for the graphics, it's a pretty game. It really is. Is it the prettiest game of 2016? No. Battlefield 1 is by far better looking and Titanfall 2 (made in heavily modified Source, btw) is as well imo. Opinions over art style will differ, but in plain graphical fidelity it's pretty handily beaten by other holiday releases. The issues people have had since release are not because this is a new AAA game with the fanciest graphics to date that require a beasty GPU with 6-8gb of vram to run, it's because Arkane chose to cannibalize the ID Tech engine and turn it into the Void engine. I assume because it was at hand and saved on licensing fees. Wrong move on their part.
If you really wanna give the game a shot I HIGHLY recommend waiting for a sale or picking it up on console. Definitely don't give Bethesda/Arkane your $60 for this either way. They knew the state of the game when they released it and took advantage of Bethesda's new day 1 review policy to push it out the door anyway. I regret buying at release and being too stubborn to return it while I had the chance. By this time next year it'll hit less than half price in Steam sales and (hopefully) be properly optimized. This will definitely be my last day 1 purchase from Bethesda for a long time to come.

Maybe not genre defining but holy crap this game is fun.  I love Dead Space games and RE4 and for me Evil Within 1 was just ok.  Just a bit above average.  But this sequel is something else altogether.  We got a semi-open world now w/ safe houses, optional side missions, plenty of incentive to explore and scavenge for weapons, ammo, crafting components and herbs for healing items.  The gel upgrade system is back and it's basically the same (which was my favorite part of the 1st game anyway) which isn't a bad thing at all because there's plenty of options for upgrades.  Sebastian isn't really unique but he's way more likable in this game because they actually gave him a back story and a personality this time around.
I didn't realize how starved I was for a good 3rd person action survival horror game until now.  This game delivered big time for me and blew my expectations away.  The first Evil Within for me was like a 6/10.  This one is easily an 8 or 9/10 for me (I'm not finished yet these are just my initial impressions).  I binged this game all day like an addict.  The only thing that's gonna get me off Evil Within 2 anytime soon is a 12 step program.
Can't pull myself out of this...

The questions remains. Is it better than The Evil Within? Well, yes, it is, but not entirely as there are some things I disliked about the second entry. For starters the basic enemies are rather average in design and the AI isn't as good as it was in the first entry. Bosses aren't as fun anymore though they still look amazing. And that's it, the only negatives I see in this entry. I'ts a much better Survival-Horror with a better implemented story, environments and replayability is guaranteed if you are up for a challenge of 7 saves only.

I'm gonna actually bother writing a review for once in my life (which goes to show how much I care about this game).
Where to start... The Evil Within 2 is a great leap from the first EW. This however is something positive. Now, while it seems that TEW 1 fans hate this game, and people that like TEW2 hate the first one I'd like to say that they are both great games. The Evil Within 2 however feels like more of a complete package to me than The Evil Within 1. It adds light RPG elements, focuses heavily on a masterfuly crafted story, adds amazIng new enemies and very memorable bosses and gives you the feeling of accomplishment while still making the experience interesting and challenging. Add the very nice updated graphics, the all-new open world, exploration-heavy locations, the remodeled shooting mechanics (that add a very satisfactory punch to every weapon) and the nicely thought out upgrade system and you have yourself (what in my opinion even deserved to be GOTY) an amazing experience.
TLDR: TEW 1 but much better (especially the story!).

Postal Redux is an isometric shooter with a very dark and unnerving spin since instead of killing demented demons or aliens, your job is to slaughter civillians and those who would come to their aid. Postal is a very unique game since in many other games you might play as the noble knight who vanquishes demons or maybe an elite special ops soldier who stops terrorists but Postal poses a very unique question, what happens when the demon is you? Postal is essentially a game that takes the traditional good guys beat bad guys mindset and turns it on its head and puts you in the role of making sure that the bad guys win. This is a very unique game since even in the other Postal games they're more comical and here in the original instead of laughing while peeing on people you're setting towns aflame and fighting with the demons in your mind.
Postals game mechanics are very simple and very sweet, if a bit repetitive at times. Postal gives you a variety of weapons you can use ranging from basics like a revolver or a shotgun to a flamethrower and a rocket launcher. The problem is that you're given so many weapons but you only end up using one or two of them since you can use those same weapons for just about every situation in the game. I wish there was more variation with the enemies as well since they're all the exact same thing with the only difference being their models, weapons, and the amount of bullets they soak up. The levels however, are varied and interesting as you fight at carnivals, in a military base, or even in a mine at one point. The levels are generally very straightforward with the exception of a couple secret areas off to the sides where you can grab some extra armor or ammunition. When you make a game with the main mechanic being shooting people you have to make sure that the guns feel very responsive, unique, and fun to use and that's something Postal definitely doesn't do. The first gun you get is an MP5 submachine gun and it feels incredibly responsive but also extremely weak at the same time and this is how just about all the games weapons feel which is a shame since shooting people is ninety nine percent of what you're doing in Postal.
Postal is a game that set the standard for what was considered to be crossing the line and although some may find the game disturbing there is something to be said about a company like RWS who was willing to cross that line and push the boundaries or what is considered okay. While the media called the game deplorable and claimed it glorified violence Postal is actually quite an interesting look into a fascinating story of a man gone mad by the stresses of modern life and really makes you think as to whether you're a murdering psychopath who butchers people and laughs or maybea broken man who was locked up for reasons he couldn't understand.
Postal Redux is a psychotic look into what happens when instead of butchering demons, the demon is you.
Great redux. Get if you enjoy the Postal series ( especially the original ).

Postal Redux is a solid HD remake/revision of the original controversial title from 1997. With better aiming, graphics, sound, and the new "Rampage" mode, this is a must for any Postal fan. If you want to see what the original title was all about, but don't feel like fussing with older software; "Redux" is for you. Another solid HD port of a older, and indie PC title.

What's the defining factor for a medium of entertainment to be worthy to be called a "classic"? It varies, it greatly varies. The most common ones, the ones that everyone can agree with are those which receive a "universally acclaimed" status, the innovative, genre-defining games, or the highly stylistic ones, though it usually lack on substance. And then there are the arguable "so bad it's good", "niche", "bold", "guilty pleasure" one. And that, everyone, is what embodies the original 1997 Postal.  A game that echoes controversy since it's release, panned by critics, yet loved by many. It's bold, it's a niche, sub par quality all across the board, it's certainly a guilty plleasure. It's the ultimate slasher B-movie of video games. Edgy, disturbing, tasteless, and pretty much senseless. But why? Why a game with such "quality" receieved a classic status? It's simply because Postal is self aware, it capitalize it's strength perfectly, it has one solid and clear purpose, that is GOING ♥♥♥♥ING POSTAL.
Simplicity and straightforward-ness is the key, Postal is a "twin stick isometric mass murdering and maniacally laugh your♥♥♥♥♥off while you do so" game, and that's it. Compared to the more well known, evenly infamous, satire-laden successor, Postal 2. Postal 1 has a darker, more serious tone.  Adapting an arcade style level where you have to kill a certain percentage of total hostile in order to continue (would be a good way to teach kids some math). It's a game that knows it's audience (read: Edgy teens that constanly has a bad day but well aware that burning down their entire neighborhood is illegal). And that's why it holds a special place on the rank of classic video games.
Twenty years and "Mass murdering and laugh your♥♥♥♥♥off while doing so" games are getting more accepted, more open, mainstream, and "inventive". Games like Postal is considered comical violence this time around, so when the news arise that this little diamond is getting a remake, I can't help but wondering, is it really the right move? Yes, it is!
Postal Redux, to put it simply is basically the entirety of Postal has a major conversion to Unreal Engine 4. It's 1997 Postal as you know it, with much improved graphic and effects, reworked sound design, and having a modern control scheme. Aside minor gameplay tweaks, a new weapon, and the Rampage Mode, Postal, at it's core remain unchanged. Gameplay is more faster paced and more fluid, since the transition from 2D sprites to 3D model and much better aiming are the most welcomed changes. There is also a Rampage mode that turns Postal to a fully arcade game, with high score and kill multiplier that adds some replay value and challenge. I'm glad that RWS know exactly what they are doing, working on what really matters on modern video games, it's the pace and fluidity.
Though, with these overhaul a little bit of things has to be "sacrificed", with the much cleaner, more professionally handled sound design and softer, more HD looks of the game, the creepy and disturbing tone of the original Postal is noticeably toned down, the overall roughness and budget-tier production of the original is the defining characteristic, which is unfortunate.
While I think Postal Redux is one of the most successful remake for me, the game itself didn't age well. As I said earlier, people are no stranger to violent video games as of now, in fact they are getting more open, complex, and inventive. Simplicity is both the strength and weakness of Postal Redux, I won't go to the strengths because I've allready cover that, let's focus on the weakness. Simplicity brings repetitiveness, most of the time. There is simply not enough replay value on Postal Redux, finished the campaign 2 times, get all achievements, and the rest on Rampage mode everytime you have a bad day. "Is it the whole point of Postal?", you ask. Well yes, it is, but with "only" that, I think the price is bit too high. Yes, I know RWS will keep it updated just like they did with Postal 2 (which is awesome), but I still think it's kinda lacking. Opening the gate for mods, at the very least a level editor will be a welcome addition, and MP seems cool.
In conclusion, Postal Redux is a remake, done right. RWS knows what makes Postal good, and don't tinker with it, instead they worked with something that really matters in order to "modernize" a game. Postal Redux is a glorious reminder of the infamouse 1997 classic, brought back to life with all of it's mindless fun-madness. It's a throwback of the simplicity of 90's games, a proof that you just need a clear purpose and capitalize on it to make a fun game, though it did bring lack of replay value, with the absent of mods, for today's standard.

The game took me roughly 24 hours to beat the campaign, and it is one of the most unique games I have ever played.  In a world taken over by military shooters and dragon slayers, this game felt like a breath of fresh air. This is a true horror survival game, and I highly recommend it.

BROFORCE!
Or as I like to call it, “screw you Political Correctness”.
This is a game mostly about getting to be the best ‘Bros’ in movie and television history, and getting to run around as them. It pays a bit of homage, partially out of necessity to available “bros”, to all the biggest, best (and worst) action bros. Imagine if you could run around as the Terminator, Conan, and that one marine played by Arnold in the first Predator movie. Would that not be awesome (and CG heavy)?
But again, as I said, bit of limitations. So far in playing (4 hours) I’ve unlocked only two non white dudes, BA and Blade specifically, and as odd as this is to say about a game about bros, only one girl, Ripley from the Alien movies. *Correction, I just unlocked Machete.
Story: Like any good action movie, this is mostly about the great white hope showing up and dispensing freedom (IE: laying waste) to some generic terrorist looking dudes in... wait, Vietnam? Yeah, Vietnam. Along the way, you’ll also be saving fellow Bros, the more you save, the more Bros you get to play as.
Gameplay: It’s mostly about going from area to area in successively more difficult levels and blowing the absolute hell out of everything in your path. Get ready to dispense freedom using shotguns, missiles, rockets, and yes, CHAINSAW HANDS. Also, get ready to die, A LOT.
No seriously, I can’t stress that part enough. You are going to die darn nearly constantly. I was playing the Alpha Build, early access version on Steam and dear god did I burn through a lot of lives.
The Good, The Bad, The Ugly: It is so awesome getting to play as one of your favorite heroes, and kinda disheartening how sucky some of them turn on in comparison to others. Seriously, Indiana Jones is less effective than Agent K. The Terminator is pretty much unplayable unless you got your back against a wall, which is pretty much the opposite of the point of being the Terminator.
The Glitches: Ok, this is an Early Access, and an Alpha Build, so grain of salt with any complaints here. There was several times I died and there was absolutely nothing on screen. I was just sliding down a wall and died. The game also would experience slow downs (and the one guys power, or when a boss character showed up, just randomly the game would seriously slow down, sometimes all but freezing. The only pattern I really noticed was typically Walker, Texas Ranger and missiles were on the screen at the same time, but it did occasionally happen with other guys too.
Final Verdict: Worth the money. Play it.

First review for me personally. The reason being the mixed overall reviews. TL;DR, if you were into dishonered 1, just buy the game.
First of all; I have yet to encounter performance issues aside from a very occasional screen artifact, despite running 1440p with 980ti sli (Had to update nvidia drivers however, which I'm not a fan of).
Secondly; please name me one other title that lets you make your own decisions, and is not actively steering you towards a playing style. Of course you do influence the game ending, but the charactal development from the start is all up to you. Hell, you can even choose to play as Corvo OR Emily. Both with different powers to choose from. Also, it is possible to play the game without powers(!). On top of that, play however you like, 100% level exploring/stealth, or just go full berserk. It's all rewarding IMO. That's some serious level-planning right there.
However, I have not yet finished my 1st playthrough yet, may I encounter any issues performance/story-telling wise, I will concede.

I absolutely love this game. I loved the first Dishonored, and the world of Dishonored 2 feels so much more fleshed out. Karnaca feels bigger, full of apartments and people and markets and things. Seriously love the increased upward mobility too, as a stealth player. There is a little lag on higher graphics settings, but the graphics themselves are gorgeous. The Royal Conservatory level alone is worth the lag. The outsider shrines are varied and beautifully designed. Each level feels like it's own little slice of the world. I will say there are a couple things I missed from the first game, like the extended epilogue, and more of the Outsider's commentary in general (it feels more plot device and less commentary on player behaviour). The plot, while enjoyable, didn't quite have the personal stake that the first game had, and it felt overall that the difference in chaos was reflected more by the state of Karnaca's government than difference in companion behaviour and reaction (something I loved about the first game).
That said, I've played it twice thus far and am on a third playthrough. Gorgeous. I'm hoping we get a Billie Lurk DLC, because that would just be the cherry on top of an already amazing cake.

The game did well in many areas in my opinion. I liked the improvements they did with the upgrades for both the powers and the weapons, I liked the level designs and overall how they played out, and I also loved the story. The upgrades were more vast in this game, giving much more options to attune a play through to however you wanted it to be. The level designs were great, they felt more like
where the levels were bigger and more open. Also the story was great, I loved how it touched upon things from the first game and even the DLCs. There is
more good things I have to say about this game then bad things.
Now, to touch upon some negatives. The biggest of which would of course be the FPS issue since day one and there's also the fact the game doesn't have a mission select like the first game did. The FPS discussion could be it's own thread for days, so to keep it simple and civil we'll leave out specs. I've personally seen FPS issues across all platforms (PC, Xbox One, PS4), no game is perfect and they're even working on fixing it. However, it's still there and something anybody new should know before buying this game. The only in game thing I didn't like about Dishonored 2 is the fact the game did not have a mission select like the first game did. Meaning if you miss something in a level and don't have a save file, then you're replaying the game
. It's a
game, but nobody wants to reply the game just because they missed something. Also no mission select effects other aspects of playing the game, such as speed runs, finding bugs, glitches, routes, making guides and such else. With all in all said, it's finally come down to would I recommend it.
So, would I recommend a great stealth game that has a great story and level design. The answer is, yes. I
recommend anyone to get this game that loves the first Dishonored. I also recommend it to anyone who loves stealth games, this game does some good justice to the genre. I can sit and rant on for hours about what I love about this game but honestly can't think of more then two points about what I don't like. The game is simply put, great. 62 hours, 7 play throughs and I'd still play it more!

Thankfully, I didn't experience any major technical issues (aside from a few framerate drops, but nothing too serious), so I could enjoy the experience without any hiccups. And enjoy I did because Dishonored 2 is a worthy successor to the highly acclaimed Dishonored. The plot is still not very satisfying, but you just don't pay too much attention to it anyway, busy roaming the interesting setting and using, for good or evil, all your cool powers (or not, you can just rely on your own muscles). I beat the game as Corvo on low chaos and now I'm looking forward to trying it out as Emily - the murderous maniac, slaying anything that breathes.
Good fun, would play again. And again.
A DLC where you play as the Outsider or have some Outsider/Void-oriented missions would be rad, just saying.

I saw this game while flipping through the visual novel tag and was intrigued by the idea of how a clone situation would be handled so I decided to give it a try.
I am quite grateful that I did.
The game is short, and can probably get all the content of it out in about a few hours, however shortness in this case I would not describe so much as fault, but that it's length makes it shine in efficiency in that in an event that transpires within probably an hour of one night in the game, the author manages to flesh out some believable characters in a short span of time.
The premise is that you are Mike, and awake to find that there is another Mike in your house. The events that follow are attempts in sorting out the confusion of figuring out what is going on and attempts of deducing who is really who by means of Mike's girlfriend Sarah. How you the player answer and respond determine how things eventually pan out, and with 9 different endings ranging from Good bad and the in-betweens, you will be digging to the bottom to find all the outcomes this game offers. I know I did.
Without going into spoilers, I wanted to note that the scenario of two of the same person in the room is a great two for one combo of a mystery that simultaniously provides oppurtunity to show the quirks and flaws of the two Mike's and his girlfriend. Halfway of trying to figure out who is who the characters become quite likable in a short amount of time, and depending on which endings you get will lead to some chilling and strong feelings on how the clone issue is resolved. Bonus points in that in obtaining more and more endings show darker and more sympathetic sides to the characters in obtaining them.
As an aside I also quite enjoyed some of the questions and food for thought that arises from the game being a bit of a philosophy dork myself.
Read/play this novel. It is not a long grandoise journey through kingdoms and mountains, but what Who is Mike does is offer you a short walk through an extremely interesting park, that ultimately makes you want to go through it again several times when you come back to start. It's chills, feels, some laughs and a potent dose of bittersweet all delivered in one sitting and a few reloads.
9/10, would highly recomend to just about any general person that's fond of reading.

I was very critical of the first Evil Within(in fact it's my most popular steam review) and ended up not recommending it. I liked the game, but I thought that a lot of the ideas and executions it had fell flat. I'm happy to say that The Evil Within 2 is everything a sequel should be and VASTLY improves upon the original.
The Evil Within 2 plays like RE4(one of my favorite games of all time) with some Silent Hill influences. It's a really fun blend of action, survival horror, and 3rd person gameplay where everything feels fluid. A big criticism I had for the oringial game was that stealth element felt tacked on where here it actually feels viable. Another thing I'm enjoying is the open area they give you to explore this time. Union is much more interesting setting than the last game(which I felt was really all over the place) and the 'small town where something has gone terribly wrong' thing it has about it only makes me want to explore it more.
As for performance, I'm running this with a 1080 and 32gb of ram and performance is pretty good despite some drops when you enter some new areas or fire is on the screen. The majority time I'm getting around 60-70FPS so I'd say it runs pretty well.
Will play more but for now I'd say if you want a good survival horror game(or even a good 3rd person shooter/action game) The Evil Within 2 is worth it.

Let me just start by saying that this is a very good game. I can't remember any other game ever having given me the chills as much as Alien: Isolation. Jump scares, yes, but not such a feeling of dread.
Now, I said that it is a very good game, but it is not flawless, so let's just get the niggles out of the way.
- The UI and interface. This is a console port, so the user interface is clunky on the PC. Now, because of this being a survival/horror game, the UI isn't extremely important, but it does show that it isn't designed for the PC, especially in menus and the journal where you can't use mouse wheel to scroll of mouse to choose an item. Not a big deal for a game such as this, but noticeable nevertheless; I can't help but the feeling of "Meh, close enough" on the interface design.
- Animations. All in all, the animations are well done, but there are some exceptions, some of which actually affects gameplay. For instance, when you are done hacking a terminal, or even when cancelling a hack, the entire animation for closing the security hacker plays, often leading to just giving up instead of cancelling something, because you're dead before Amanda manages to put away the tool. Same with doors. If the door is closing, it's closing, and you have to wait until it is fully closed before the cycle to open it again can start. Makes me wonder what H&S would say, especially if someone was under a door while it closed... Also, I have climbed a few ladders in my life, but I've never tossed my head from side to side like Amanda does. What's that about? Last, but not least, it is slightly amusing how Amanda wrenches open lockers to hide in, especially when she's been sneaking up to it and try to be quiet. A slightly less enthusiastic way of opening lockers could have been good. :)
- Level design. There is some very obvious railroading at times, with liberal use of invisible walls. When you see that someone has laid planks across a gap and the game stops you from crossing because you have to go around, it does break immersion somewhat. To be fair, this happens only a very few times.
Those are some of the bad things, and for a game released in 2014 they are very few. Now over to the good stuff, and holy carp, there's so much good stuff!
Let's start with the atmosphere and the setting design. The station and ship designs looks like they're taken straight from Alien. You get the feeling that these are locations that are used and lived in, that the inhabitants could be just around the corner (If not... You know. Alien.). The designers have held true to the technology as envisioned in Alien, resisting the urge to replace CRT with LCD, keyboards with touch screens etc., and I think that the game as a whole is better for it. The lighting is also brilliant when you play with recommended gamma level. It is dark enough that you need the torch from time to time, but not so dark that you walk blind most of the time. When seeing that the torch needed batteries, I was very dubious at the beginning, but the designers has planted enough batteries that, with a little bit of thought, you shouldn't run out. I do prefer a chargeable torch, as in Metro: 2033, but in A:I the torch design is well done.
Moving on with atmosphere: Sound. The sound design in A:I is brilliant. I don't know what more to say. The scary music bits are played to great effect, sometimes raising my pulse past 120. At least. The sounds of the xenomorph are also very well done, giving you not only clues to where it is, but also what it's doing. You will become especially familiar with the sound of it seeing you...
As the xenomorph was mentioned: AI. The artificial intelligence is also brilliant. The xenomorph will learn from your actions; if you use lots of audio distractions, it will start ignoring them; if you hide in lockers a lot, it will start taking a closer look at lockers. Whoever designed this AI is evil. And brilliant. But also evil. But brilliant.
Despite my mention of some obvious railroading at the start, the level design in A:I is very good. Yes, you are being led from location to location a lot, but there is also the option to go back and look over levels again, there are often optional routes, and not least, the blind terror of having a xenomorph hunting you often makes you forget that you are being guided into yet another trap. ;)
All in all, despite some minor flaws, Alien: Isolation is a very, very good game. I will go so far as to say that it is one of my top ten games ever, and without a doubt the best game of 2014.
Addendum:
Having played the game some more, there is one more thing that has to be mentioned: Manual save stations. This feature is atrocious. It is the single worst feature of the game, by a large margin, and I can't think of a single more immersion breaking thing to add to a game. Whoever decided to add this feature to A:I should be ashamed of themselves. Not only is a game mechanic being pushed to the front of your list of priorities, but the way it is implemented is that Amanda actually saves the game in character! Talk about breaking the fourth wall, game developers! This is just rubbish. It's pure bad. Luckily, the rest of the game is so good that this isn't a game-breaking feature, so my recommendation still stands, but this could have been a much better game with a quick-, menu-, or autosave system.

Sevastopol Station is one of the most finely designed game environments in years. There's tiny details of the daily life of the station hidden in every nook and cranny, all of which is faithful to the design philosophy of emulating the 1979 Alien film. The EVA sequences are all uniquely breathtaking as well, though also disturbingly claustrophobic thanks to the brilliant sound and visual of being inside the spacesuits' roomy helmets.
Exploring the world CA has built is worth the price of admission, but the gameplay also has quite an alure. The titular alien is as menacing as ever as it stalks you mercilessly through the game's 18 chapters, while the station's creepy caretaker 'droids are considerably more disturbing (and frustrating). The people you meet along the way rather curiously have the least personality of all the NPC's, though their deaths at the hands of the alien will still elicit a sympathetic twinge after you've been stabhugged more than once yourself.
The overall tone of the game goes through numerous peaks and valleys of tension: a frighteningly tense cat-and-mouse game with the alien might be followed by a series of simple fetchquests interlaced with quicktime events where the creature makes no unscripted appearances at all, but the best parts are spread fairly evenly throughout the somewhat predictable plot.
Be warned, there are some game-breaking bugs that can pop up if you're running the game on a lower-end machine, but nothing that can't be overcome by backing up one or two saves. The worst I hit required me to briefly run the game in an 800x600 window until I'd passed the point I was stuck at, but admittedly I did not have my PC properly set up to play the more graphically demanding second half of the game.
Overall, the exquisitely tense stealth/action survival gameplay combined with a perfectly realized sci-fi setting make this an experience you shouldn't miss, but if you don't have the best PC you'll probably have a better experience playing it on a console.

Successul hide-and-seek simulator! Im not even a huge survival horror fan and I am enjoying this game immensely. Instead of writing a thesis paper I'll keep this as brief as possible.
1.) Creepy, they did a great job making that creature as scary as it is on the big screen. Actually more so, becuase here you get to witness the dammage the Alien can inflict firsthand. The music is also a perfect companion to the lanky xeno trolling around the space station. Overall environment and creature effects 10/10 easy day
2.) Its challenging. You'll die...alot...but every time you need to devise a different plan to overcome the situation. I will say, that some of the deaths felt cheap, but those were few and far between. The AI in general is good. it gets more realistic the higher you increase the difficulty.
3.) Time consuming. You'll spent alot of the game crouched, under a bed, desk, or in a closet, waiting for the xeno to get tired of looking for you. You will also spend hours passing through the same places in the station again and again making it seemingly redundant. It didn't bother me much. Its a space station, there are only so many places you can go, plus I loved wandering around looking at the scenery. Even the waiting never got old because you can hear the creature outside.
Like I said, Im not a huge survival horror fan and it's got me hooked. Give it a shot, its definetly worth it.

Because it has stellar atmosphere, excellent graphics, and I'm sure that if I just suffer through this gameplay for long enough I'll be able to cram the Alien out an airlock and just wander the station, read the logs and fight the robots without just being instantly murdered by a godmode murder monster.
Scary and immersive, this game makes you want to rip the Oculus off your head, but keeps you coming back for more.

Performance issues marred the launch of what would have otherwise been a perfect game. At this time, the game is relatively stable, and I have had a grand time playing it. It's a worthy successor to the first game, and better in many respects. The combat feels even more fluid and challenging, and while Corvo's powers largely remain the same, Emily boasts a wide range of new and interesting ones. Admitedly the story feels like a bit of a rehash (you're framed for a crime you didn't commit and now you need to hunt down and eliminate those who framed you), but I think this is excused by the fact that Karnaca and its inhabitants feel like a living, breathing world, full of wonders and mysteries to explore. Each character has depth, and their interactions with you change depending on how you play the game. Like the original Dishonored, there is a Chaos system, which tracks the amount of people you kill and what sort of decisions you make. Choosing to play non-lethally will result in a more positive outcome, and vice versa. The stealth gameplay is delightfully difficult; there are a large variety of ways to approach each and every situation, and careful planning is rewarded. The AI are also noticeably smarter, and more observant. All in all, Dishonored 2 is a well-crafted, intriguing game that is a joy to play.

Pretty much exactly like Postal 1, but works perfectly on modern systems. (The original one requires some tinkering on most machines, and some machines just can't run it at all due to game breaking bugs.) The controls are more intuitive (mouse + keyboard instead of tank style), the graphics are updated to look a bit nicer, and there's more sound effects. It seems they mostly just took Postal 2 sounds and reused them here.
I beat it in I think about 3 hours, so that might be too short for some people considering it's $15, but I think it's a great game. If you're a Postal fan it's worth buying this one.

Since the vanilla game is still available for purchase, I'm going to focus only on the differences between that and the Redux version.
+++ All the levels have been reworked and now have HD graphics. This means better looking, higher resolution maps with added effects such as sirens for the police cars, falling leaves for trees and animated water on the bridge level.
+++ The most noticeable of all are the 3D characters - no more pixelated Dude and NPCs; everybody looks very detailed.
+++ Fast-paced combat: The game is now much faster, thus more enjoyable.
+++ Better aiming system: It helps to see the crosshair appearing on enemies that can be shot from a certain distance already. Bullet spread is also visible. Overall better weapon handling - if you're a sharpshooter you're going to love the new revolver which is a great addition to the already existing weapon selection.
+++ Beside the campaign we now have a Rampage gameplay mode which makes the game a little more arcade-ish with the added score system. Multipliers keep increasing with each kill but only for a short period of time. This is a great mode for hardcore fans and for those looking for an extra challenge.
--- Several missing levels. I understand the absence of the high school (with the ongoing school shootings this is perfectly understandable), but other levels such as the holiday resort or the city devastated by earthquake are also missing. A new carnival level has been added with machine gun wielding clowns but it does not make up for the missing ones.
UPDATE (October, 2016). The game now has coop and the missing levels such as earthquake and mall are back. There's also shanty town and two Japanese maps. They are hilarious and heaps of fun to play.
This is how you do a remastered edition! This is a great version and is a must for Postal fans.

Everyone reaches a point in their lives when you just want to throw your hat into the air... punch the wall...  kick a few doors open, pull out a rocket launcher and blow stuff up... Ok.. well normal people never really have these things, sure we get angry but normally it passes.  Postal is what happens when a man gets pushed to the edge.  Tired of living by the rules society deems right, he throws caution to the wind and goes full on rampage mode ala Rambo  in the original first blood movie.  The major difference is Rambo had loads of Snarling, and Stallone...  Postal has... The Postal Dude and Loads of killing..  the whole point of Postal is to kill everyone, whether they be police officers, swat team, the army, innocent people enjoying a parade.. It doesn't matter.  Postal was pretty much a gigantic middle finger salute from the gaming industry trying to censor what we all love.
Nearly 20 years has passed since the original Postal released back in 1997.... Back in 1997 times were simple a blue dress was just a blue dress, and Cigars were made for smoking not... well anyway.. As time moved forward the original mass murdering simulator remained untouched, a relic of gaming past, adored by those who played it, feared by those who think technology is evil.  Relatively unknown to those who think a game needs cutting edge graphics to be good..  Fast Forward to 20016 and Postal has finally gotten the treatment it deserves, brought in line with modern technology, updated, improved and a reminder that no matter how screwed up life has gotten, kicking back, killing untold number of pixel shaped people can be a fun and exciting prospect.   Improved graphics, sounds and controller support.
The story remains the same, the Postal dude has had enough, he's been pushed, kicked, and abused for long enough, he's ready to take action, kick butts and chew some bubble gum (I think he's chewing bubble gum.. maybe that's Duke Nukem)  Starting from his home, you emerge and begin your visceral rampage on the people he thinks have wronged him....
The game is an isometric third person shooter.  The game features numerous weapons "The Dude" can use in his mission to end his oppression.  Assault Rifles, shotguns, pistols, rocket launchers, etc etc etc.  The goal of each level is having the Dude, kill a certain % of the population before heading to the exit.  The game features 17 levels, including a new Carnival stage. Enough Murder, madness and mayhem to make Charlie Manson smile...  Also newly included to the Redux version of the game is Rampage mode, which allows the gamer to go after the high score..

Good game, bad company.
The game has an arcadey third-person shooter feel that is not bogged down by cover systems or waiting for your character model to face where your camera is pointing, lending to responsive* movement (excluding the server-sided driving) and shooting, when the server is not lagging and when your computer isn't stuttering from the game needing way better computer specs than it should need -- which ends up being a barrier of entry that shuts the game off for a lot of people once they experience how bad the game runs on their computers, and one that limits the play performance of the ones that stick around. You can make some pretty cool player-created content with APB's level of customization if you put the time and effort to doing so: characters, car designs, clothing designs, images, and music.
The good game is marred by various problems stemming from the lack of players and the resulting unbalanced matchmaking. The more experienced players are put up against newer players, a disparity made even worse when involving veterans -- who may have over several hundred or thousands more hours of experience over the newer players. Newer players get absolutely destroyed by the veterans, who are more likely to possess premium items, and start perceiving the premium items as pay-to-win, despite the cash shop guns not even being the major contributing factor. Misconceptions of in-game mechanics, perceptions of unfairness, and the toxic players in the game contribute to this player-unfriendly environment that fails to retain players.
The company has been slowly losing staff and good PR for years. The departure of various known player-facing devs (and their associated dramas). The merging of G1 and the Reloaded Productions (the developers of APB). The "Engine Update" that was supposed to uplift the game to a better technical foundation never arrived in Q2 2014. Sparse communications with the players (aside from cash shop announcements). The burst of communication after every change in Community Manager (Jericho, Jobs, and now Tiggs) and then a return to the normal, sparse level. Their contract with Deep Silver to develop and release the engine update for APB for consoles (!?), and the role of their contract's non-disclosure agreement in the non-communication with the players. Not making anymore promises (and statements) so as to avoid backfire (i.e. Q2 2014, Soon™, and So Close™) when they don't happen. The closure of the UK office. The backburner content and general neglect of the players and the main PC platform as a result of them focusing on the supposed engine update (before and after the release of the console APBs). The debacle with 3rd-parties selling KTTW packs and the chargebacks leading to G1 practically holding the affected players' accounts hostage for ransom. These all contribute to the doomsday-esque atmosphere on the forums and (to some degree) in-game, and a general feeling of no-confidence.
Regardless of whether or not the game dies or if the engine update actually comes out, I won't be there to see it. Thanks to the people spamming accounts to exploit the free Labor Day codes, my account somehow got flagged as part of these exploiters even though I rarely played anymore, and despite the fact I didn't touch any of the Labor Day codes on any of my accounts (I only have one). There is no recourse for this either, all they (Grub, Puck, and Tiggs) tell me is that my account was observed exploiting these codes despite me imporing them to investigate my case. So I made my obligatory posts on the APB forums (actually a friend of mine did because my forum account got silenced after I sent in the first support ticket) and Steam game hub about it, which were subsequently deleted. I know no one cares, especially G1, but I care. Nothing short of delivering a Request for Arbitration to their Huntington Beach, CA office may make them care.

Honestly, I can see why people enjoy this game. It can be pretty fun to manage a trucking business. I really have a hard time enjoying the life of a trucker if I'm trapped in the cab all the time. It gets reeeally boring. The only way I can see this game as being really redeemable is if you have a good FFB wheel with an H shifter. If you play with a more basic wheel with limited steering rotation and no shifter like me (Logitech MOMO), it's terribly unfun. God forbid a controller or even a keyboard *shuddering intensifies*. This game is at its best when you can totally immerse yourself as the man behind the wheel in full control of everything in the cab.
I don't think I can recommend this after playing games like My Summer Car. In that game, you were much more in control of your environment. Now obviously getting drunk as ♥♥♥♥ and delivering explosives may not fit in this type of game (or would it?) This game would be much better and more immersive if it allowed you to exit your truck and walk around the world as you can in MSC. Maybe let you go into an occasional diner or motel. Collect different items that you can take on your travels. If these two games were mixed to a reasonable degree, it would be fantastic. Bottom line though, I would rather live the life of a trucker, not the truck.
The upgrades you can give the truck feel completely unimpactful unless you remove the governer setting in some .ini file. Even when not considering top speed, I could still barely climb an on ramp with a trailer with some considerable upgrades. It felt no different from stock. Maybe way down the line of upgrades and trucks you could feel the difference but I'm not willing to spend that much time for such a small increase in performance.
In the end, if all you care about is the driving aspect of trucking and you can enjoy driving with whatever setup you have, go for it. I personally was left fairly unsatisfied after 30+ hours of trucking.

Just like its predecessor, Dark Souls 2 draws you in with an interesting visual art style, then beats you down until you learn.  All "Souls" games are firm but fair, and this one is no exception.  If you put time and effort into it, the feeling of victory after putting down that enemy that had you beat so many times, or feeling like you can finally catch your breath once you find the next bonfire, is extremely rewarding.
If you've played Dark Souls, there are changes for the better and changes for the worse, but in the end I feel it balances itself back again to deliver a fun, engaging game.  For those story-seekers, there's a very deep story there, if you're willing to find it.  Unlike traditional role-playing games, where the story centers on the PC, you make your own story via your actions, and you unearth (sometimes literally) the lore of the world you inhabit through artifacts that you find or wield.  On the description of the rarer or more unconventional weapons and items, you get a glimpse of the past.  You must find more to get a clearer picture.
In all, a very rewarding gameplay, story, and visual experience.  Highly recommended.  Praise the Sun!

Dishonored 2 would make a stellar painting or series of screenshots. It makes a pretty poor game, however. Story and storytelling are poor, gameplay is meaningless, sound/music design is poor, but the visual aesthetic is beautiful.
It's almost exactly the first game's story. Nothing new to see, nothing new about which to think or ponder.  You're screwed by a surprise sister of the first game's Empress who says "you always get to be the princess when we play castle. Now, I wanna play princess." A coup ensues, and now it's your job to get her and her cronies back. How vengeful do you feel?
You get to pick which character you play--Corvo or Emily. For some reason, the bad lady freezes the one you don't pick in stone. Why is the one you didn't pick the one who gets frozen? Why didn't the one you picked get frozen? They're both standing right next to each other when it happens, and the bad lady can turn people into stone with just about zero effort.
There's also a massive inconsistency at the end. Freeing the character who was frozen in the beginning means simply touching their frozen face. But, you can only do this after you've won the final encounter with big bad. Why? What just happened? I couldn't touch the statue and then take the other character with me to fight the big bad?
And then once the story ends, you tell the character you just unfroze to stick around--you'll tell them the story of what happened. Then fade out and you get one of those narrated still image sequences to just barely touch on how things go after the story ended.
Characters narrate their feelings out loud as if reading the writer's notes, verbatim. They do the same with plot points. You'll walk into a room while two witches are talking about how to take the boss out non-lethally. That room and those NPCs exist in just about every stage. Additionally, the protagonist you choose will narrate solutions to puzzles in front of you as well, although desperately trying to be coy about it. "Hmmmm...a broken thing...I wonder if it's still broken in the other timeline????" Then Blue barks happily and licks the time travel button. They do the same as a means of telling the player how they need to accomplish the next objective.
Pointless lore dumps and flavor spills also distract from the main quest constantly. Page after page you'll find of song lyrics, backgrounds on the whale trade, the history of Karnaca, and on and on until you ask yourself "Wait, what's this game about, again?" None of that lore does even a single thing for this game's main story. Rather than play it savvy and use the story to add little bits of lore each game, they created the same story as last time and then contrived ways to dump all the lore on us at once.
Voice direction makes this a story that's impossible to take seriously. When someone's bad, they speak as though every line is going to end with "MUAH HA HA HAAAAAA!" When a character is angry (especially Emily), they lower their voice to cartoonish pitches and mumble something grim to their self through vocal fry. Even goofy stories should at least give the consumer something to think about when it's over. These characters don't even reflect a sliver of reality due in part to their voice direction.
You will never have any idea where a person is in this game. The only times I was right when I played was when I just happened to guess correctly. Someone will sound like they're right behind you, but turn around and nothing. Then, you find out they were on the other side of a wall. In one instance, a man and woman were singing some kind of song in a courtyard. Passing through a nearby doorframe completely silenced them. Passing back through it made them clear as day, once again. This was a doorframe that was facing the courtyard in which they were singing.
Music is also designed poorly. There's not much of it at all. However, the final confrontation just randomly has some quasi-orchestral piece playing in the background. This piece is mixed in so loudly that you won't hear what the last boss is saying when you finally confront her. Not good.
You have supernatural powers, of course, but they don't make the gameplay insteresting at all. They boil down to different ways to "press left trigger to win this encounter." Mesmerize distracts people nearby so you can just walk up to them an execute them or just walk by them. Possessing rats lets you find vents that let you bypass lock puzzles or enemies. Doppelganger basically does the same thing as Mesmerize, except it can be upgraded to fight bad guys instead of just look at them stupidly and run away. In all cases, you just look at the thing you want to bypass, you press left trigger, and then you've bypassed it. No brainpower necessary.
Sword fighting is okay, but it's really just wait for their attack animation, then block, then attack for an insta-kill. But that's all it is.
You can Google screenshots to know exactly how the aesthetic works in this game, so I'll just say it had a significant impact on me as I explored.
Don't buy this game unless you're just looking to pass 20 hours of time to relax or something. Instead, just Google the screenshots to enjoy the pretty scenery.

This is a fantastic sequal to a great game. If you've played the first Dishonored then you'll be able to pick this game up very easily. The story was great, though at time of writing i've only played through with Corvo. This game is most definitely my game of the year. With everyone saying they had issues tech wise I have a GeForce GTX 960 and played on medium settings since launch had no issues with frame drops or performance issues of any kind.

Dishonored 2 throws you 15 years after the events of Dishonored, where you get to choose to play as either Emily Kaldwin, or her father, Corvo Attano, in a fight to reclaim the throne from usurper Delilah Kaldwin, long long sister to previous Empress, Jessamine Kaldwin.
The gameplay has been improved upon immensely from the previous game, with a new bonecrafting system and spell upgrades, this game will always keep you actively wanting to find materials and runes to improve them. The combat is very fluid and has improved slightly since the previous game. There's a lot more interesting animations for killing people now.
They also improved upon the cover system, which is awesome.
The story is short, maybe around 2 hrs per mission, but with a lot of content and side quests blooming within these missions, you will always be questioning if you should be looking for side quests or jumping into the action.
Now even though the story is short, it isn't entirely bad. It plays out almost exactly as you think it would but the world of Dishonored has all these different choices and outcomes that it's not dull.
Playing as Emily Kaldwin.
My first play through with Emily Kaldwin was so much fun, all her different abilities really made the game feel different when compared to my Corvo play through, who isn't given any new abilities. Emily's far reach is probably the best spell in the game, it has so much potential. You can  use it like blink to get to places you can't normally get, you can pull items from above for stealth play through, and also you can pull enemies to either incapacitate or kill. I enjoyed my Emily playthrough immensely and can't wait to jump back on her for another one.
Now I know a lot of people have had performance issues with this game, I fortunately didn't really have any. I tinkered my settings a lot to find the best combination (Pre beta patches). The only time I had an issue was the timetravel map, but I assume a lot of people would of.
Anyways, I was fortunate enough to play it without issues.
I highly recommend this game, it's an amazing sequel to an amazing original game.

I Have played League of Legends for 7 years and I have soon quit beause of how the community and the company turned into.League of Legends lacks new content (Game modes) for how popular the game is and when they release a new game mode it's only for a week, this lack of content and repetitivness of the same game modes and maps has bored me and I promised myself I will never like a MOBA again. I tried Smite and it absouletly surprised me of how much better this game was then League of Legends.
These are the things that I have found that made this game amazing compared to League of Legends.
-100% Skill Based, League of Legends also takes skill but they had masteries and runes people had to purchase and level up in the game in order to use which gave an unfair advantage to newer players or people who doesn't have the money to purchase runes.Which was a big hassle to deal with when you just want to get into a game.In Smite everyone starts the game w/o the runes and masteries B.S which gives every player an even chance on winning.
-The Balancing is ridiculously Amazing! In League of Legends when someone snowballs very hard it is very hard to comback from it and usually ends up in a loss. In Smite I've had so many games where my team made a comback against very early fed players because of one mistake their team made.The Balancing is designed that one mistake can end it for the team in league of legends the fed team can make multiple mistakes before actually impacting them.
-You get Free Gems!! this is compared to Riot Points in league in where you can use it to purchase skins and can even use normail ingame currency to buy skins making this game 100% F2P in my mind.
-Fast Pace Action ,this is what really sold me, Action. In league you would have to farm a lane for like 10 boring mins to actually get anywhere.In Smite action starts as soon as you reach the jungle and the battles are intense.
-The community is not bad mainly because there are no restrictions to what needs to be in a lane because of how great the balancing is in the game you can play w.e you want in which ever lane you want,compared to league in where you get snaped at if you don't play adc support bot, there are less restrictions in this game which is what gives it a unique game style and I reccomend  everyone to play it if they quit league.
-The champion loading screen takes at the very least 20 seconds to start! Compared to those long 5 min timers in league where you have to wait for that toaster to finish loading up.
The only bad thing I've found in this game is the Game launching bugs in where your friends are kicked out of the champion loading screen and when they relog they are in the game lobby while they are really in the game disconnected and with no way of going back in it because they will just get kicked back into the lobby again,this is my only complaint with the game really.I don't want to get reported for afking when it was a game error.

System Shock 2 is an excellent and original game. Then Bioshock came along and spoiled ev- just kidding. If you have ever played the original bioshock or any of the thief games (Excluding the garbage that was released in 2014) you'll love this game. It is an exploration game that is one you will kind of just wander around through and slowly but surely make progress in. It's kind of cool to see how much bioshock was inspired by this game considering its many similarities. System Shock 2 is at best, a cruel game. Any firearms break down quickly and have limited ammo, so it's impractical to use them. In truth you are better off using the wrench for all your killing needs. If you miss one hit, you could find yourself getting battered to death by a ton of angry polygonal beef jerky monsters that used to be people but now carry lead pipes and shotguns all the while begging you for death. In all honesty, your best course of action may be to give them what they want. 9/10

In thirty years of gaming, since 1984 I have NEVER been enthralled with a game such as the case with System Shock 2. Play this masterpiece for two-hours and I swear you'll be hooked. It is one of the finest games ever developed and in my time I've just about played them all. The game is creepy, frightening, and intelligently written - enough to make veteran gamers shutter - and that's saying a lot. It's no wonder System Shock 2 has earned a place within the Gaming Hall of Fame. Once in your lifetime you must experience this game. I have only one regret. I wish the developement team that made this masterpiece could be reassembled to give the game a proper make-over with today's moderen graphics. I would tremble like a school-girl at the possiblities.  SS2 holds its rightful place within my top-ten games of All-Time. Its Number One. Any surprise?

This is one amazing game. It's atmosphere drew me in immediately, it's gameplay challenged me from the start while feeling intuitive and fluid. System Shock 2 is easily one of irrational games' finest works of all time. I love how it let me make the character my own from the first moments.  Yes, the graphics are a little behind the times, but it only adds to the charm.
Pacing is perfect, deliberate and flowing (if you've spec'ed your character properly.) The one bit of advice i would offer a new player is this: Do not be afraid to restart. Experimenting with each of the three specializations at the beginning of the actual campaign may be helpful in getting a sense of what really suits you versus what you initially thought would suit you and/or solidifying your choice. Ultimately it all depends on personality, when you find the difflculty and the set of skills that compliment your playstyle, it's a phenomenal game.

Having played this game for a reasonable number of hours over 7 months now and growing, I feel like it's time for a review. This game offers one of the most in-depth and realistic zombie apocalypse experiences around. The worlds you will quickly familiarise yourself with are dark, seedy, deadly and scream doom at you. You are not a god like individual like in Left 4 Dead who can withstand the onslaught of 100 screaming zombies, you are mortal in this game. If a zombie grabs you, and bites you, there is a very real risk that you can bleed to death or become infected, thus slowly watching yourself succumb and face the inevitable unless your fellow survivors aid you, or kill you to spare the trouble of the rest of the group facing another zombie.
You have to have good resource management in this game, as everything, including ammo, uses up precious space in your already limited inventory. Is the map as dark as the bowels of a mine? You have to use a flashlight, but cannot use a double handed weapon while carrying one, use a pistol instead, provided you have one. All of these factors require you to think outside the box of regular zombie apocalypse video gaming. Resources in this game are scarce and scattered like needles in a haystack that you must salvage for yourself. There are no conviences in this game, it is brutal, gory and outright fantastic, which also relies upon the element of teamwork if you want to survive.
The downside to this game, is that it is a sharp learning curve for newcomers, but once the weapons and survival system has been learned, the game is very hard to put to rest. Indeed, when there is no more room in hell, there's plenty of room in your gaming inventory, and this game should be one of them.

No More Room in Hell is a Source Engine mod. The beta was released on Halloween 2011, after nearly seven years in development. In October 2013, No More Room in Hell was released on Steam as a stand-alone game.
Gameplay:
This is a Co-operative play with up to eight players, where you fight against zombies. There is 30+ weapons that you can use it to fight against zombies.
There is 2 game mods:
Objective: In mission/objective mode, players must follow the instructions given by the game. They must find the rescue vehicle. It could either be: a train/metro, a helicopter or a tank. These vehicle differs in each map.
Survival: In Survival, players must survive a series of waves of zombies. The amount of zombies increase as the waves continue, making each wave harder. After to 8th-10th wave the game will bring in the rescue vehicle and the players must get to it in time. After every 2-3 rounds a supply helicopter comes around the players and drops a supply box where the players can unbox and use the items.

Dishonored 2 would make a stellar painting or series of screenshots. It makes a pretty poor game, however. Story and storytelling are poor, gameplay is meaningless, sound/music design is poor, but the visual aesthetic is beautiful.
It's almost exactly the first game's story. Nothing new to see, nothing new about which to think or ponder.  You're screwed by a surprise sister of the first game's Empress who says "you always get to be the princess when we play castle. Now, I wanna play princess." A coup ensues, and now it's your job to get her and her cronies back. How vengeful do you feel?
You get to pick which character you play--Corvo or Emily. For some reason, the bad lady freezes the one you don't pick in stone. Why is the one you didn't pick the one who gets frozen? Why didn't the one you picked get frozen? They're both standing right next to each other when it happens, and the bad lady can turn people into stone with just about zero effort.
There's also a massive inconsistency at the end. Freeing the character who was frozen in the beginning means simply touching their frozen face. But, you can only do this after you've won the final encounter with big bad. Why? What just happened? I couldn't touch the statue and then take the other character with me to fight the big bad?
And then once the story ends, you tell the character you just unfroze to stick around--you'll tell them the story of what happened. Then fade out and you get one of those narrated still image sequences to just barely touch on how things go after the story ended.
Characters narrate their feelings out loud as if reading the writer's notes, verbatim. They do the same with plot points. You'll walk into a room while two witches are talking about how to take the boss out non-lethally. That room and those NPCs exist in just about every stage. Additionally, the protagonist you choose will narrate solutions to puzzles in front of you as well, although desperately trying to be coy about it. "Hmmmm...a broken thing...I wonder if it's still broken in the other timeline????" Then Blue barks happily and licks the time travel button. They do the same as a means of telling the player how they need to accomplish the next objective.
Pointless lore dumps and flavor spills also distract from the main quest constantly. Page after page you'll find of song lyrics, backgrounds on the whale trade, the history of Karnaca, and on and on until you ask yourself "Wait, what's this game about, again?" None of that lore does even a single thing for this game's main story. Rather than play it savvy and use the story to add little bits of lore each game, they created the same story as last time and then contrived ways to dump all the lore on us at once.
Voice direction makes this a story that's impossible to take seriously. When someone's bad, they speak as though every line is going to end with "MUAH HA HA HAAAAAA!" When a character is angry (especially Emily), they lower their voice to cartoonish pitches and mumble something grim to their self through vocal fry. Even goofy stories should at least give the consumer something to think about when it's over. These characters don't even reflect a sliver of reality due in part to their voice direction.
You will never have any idea where a person is in this game. The only times I was right when I played was when I just happened to guess correctly. Someone will sound like they're right behind you, but turn around and nothing. Then, you find out they were on the other side of a wall. In one instance, a man and woman were singing some kind of song in a courtyard. Passing through a nearby doorframe completely silenced them. Passing back through it made them clear as day, once again. This was a doorframe that was facing the courtyard in which they were singing.
Music is also designed poorly. There's not much of it at all. However, the final confrontation just randomly has some quasi-orchestral piece playing in the background. This piece is mixed in so loudly that you won't hear what the last boss is saying when you finally confront her. Not good.
You have supernatural powers, of course, but they don't make the gameplay insteresting at all. They boil down to different ways to "press left trigger to win this encounter." Mesmerize distracts people nearby so you can just walk up to them an execute them or just walk by them. Possessing rats lets you find vents that let you bypass lock puzzles or enemies. Doppelganger basically does the same thing as Mesmerize, except it can be upgraded to fight bad guys instead of just look at them stupidly and run away. In all cases, you just look at the thing you want to bypass, you press left trigger, and then you've bypassed it. No brainpower necessary.
Sword fighting is okay, but it's really just wait for their attack animation, then block, then attack for an insta-kill. But that's all it is.
You can Google screenshots to know exactly how the aesthetic works in this game, so I'll just say it had a significant impact on me as I explored.
Don't buy this game unless you're just looking to pass 20 hours of time to relax or something. Instead, just Google the screenshots to enjoy the pretty scenery.
