My visual settings are in the medium range with some settings bumped to high. The game runs well, if you face issues, there's no problem dropping the settings down a touch, it still looks stunning.

This is a fantastic sequal to a great game. If you've played the first Dishonored then you'll be able to pick this game up very easily. The story was great, though at time of writing i've only played through with Corvo. This game is most definitely my game of the year. With everyone saying they had issues tech wise I have a GeForce GTX 960 and played on medium settings since launch had no issues with frame drops or performance issues of any kind.

Dishonored 2 throws you 15 years after the events of Dishonored, where you get to choose to play as either Emily Kaldwin, or her father, Corvo Attano, in a fight to reclaim the throne from usurper Delilah Kaldwin, long long sister to previous Empress, Jessamine Kaldwin.
The gameplay has been improved upon immensely from the previous game, with a new bonecrafting system and spell upgrades, this game will always keep you actively wanting to find materials and runes to improve them. The combat is very fluid and has improved slightly since the previous game. There's a lot more interesting animations for killing people now.
They also improved upon the cover system, which is awesome.
The story is short, maybe around 2 hrs per mission, but with a lot of content and side quests blooming within these missions, you will always be questioning if you should be looking for side quests or jumping into the action.
Now even though the story is short, it isn't entirely bad. It plays out almost exactly as you think it would but the world of Dishonored has all these different choices and outcomes that it's not dull.
Playing as Emily Kaldwin.
My first play through with Emily Kaldwin was so much fun, all her different abilities really made the game feel different when compared to my Corvo play through, who isn't given any new abilities. Emily's far reach is probably the best spell in the game, it has so much potential. You can  use it like blink to get to places you can't normally get, you can pull items from above for stealth play through, and also you can pull enemies to either incapacitate or kill. I enjoyed my Emily playthrough immensely and can't wait to jump back on her for another one.
Now I know a lot of people have had performance issues with this game, I fortunately didn't really have any. I tinkered my settings a lot to find the best combination (Pre beta patches). The only time I had an issue was the timetravel map, but I assume a lot of people would of.
Anyways, I was fortunate enough to play it without issues.
I highly recommend this game, it's an amazing sequel to an amazing original game.

There's not enough psychological visual novels in this world. It's my favourite type of game and it's always a shame when I start to run cold on new titles. I found this one for free and the premise instantly hooked me and I'm glad i played this one.
The description explains everything you need to know about the plot, minus spoilers, so I will not discuss it.
First, the presentation is great, especially for a free title. I love the design of both characters and they are well-drawn. They also have several poses and some scene-specific drawings.
Second, the dialogue is fantastic. The dialogue made me feel like I got to know both characters in such a small length of time and no dialogue felt out-of-character or unrealistic for the situation.
Thirdly, the game has nine endings that all got me interested and asking questions. I'll admit I had to look up a guide to find endings 6-8.
Fourth, I would have paid money for this honestly. I know it's short (it took me an hour to get all the endings), but I felt my time was well-spent and I would come back just to re-experience it and to show a friend.
So yes, get it. It is free and more than worth your time if you are into psychological visual novels.

When the game first launched it was depressingly dissapointing. All around mind you, not due to one thing or major point, but just all around depressing. Battles lasted five minutes top, the political and family intigue was rather hollow and siege battles were laughable. Multiplayer was a series of connections timed out or flat out unplayable due to a the computer player taking more time then necessary to complete a turn.

Alot has changed, battles all around last longer, my units(or the enemies) don't just rout now at the slightest bit of poking. AI armies now consist of balanced rosters( they used to comprise of all slingers/ range). The AI in siege battles now actually use their siege weapons and do not just enmass at the gates waiting for some torches to burn it to the ground! Pitch battles now last around 10 to 15 minutes.
The political and family intrigue still needs work, however those updates were not included in the beta patch. There are promises and I have seen screens of a complete overhaul in this area, including how civil wars within your empire work. Quality patching have brought back my immersion into this great series. Im excited to see what the future holds for one of my favorite time periods in history and with that I have to say:
HIGHLY RECOMMEND PICKING UP THIS GAME.

Despite a shaky release, the much-needed patches have turned this game into something that resembles the glory of strategy gaming that was the first Rome: Total War.
Firstly, the campaign mode is horrendous amounts of fun which will start to vacuum up all of your spare time as you progress further. The trusted recipe of a turn-based campaign with Real-Time battles has again proved that it is just as effective at immersing you in the world as the first time we saw it hit the RTS Stage.
The historical accuracy of the game as a whole is also to be commended as it teaches you as much about Classical civilizations as any texbook.
The real time battles are beautifully designed with expansive maps and game options that will mean you can never truly say "I've played absolutely everything there is to play in Rome 2." Intense close-quarters combat will keep you entertained as you listen to the death screeches of your enemy.
If and when you get tired of the campaign and skirmishing with bots, there is always a strong multiplayer mode which will pit you against your friends, or perhaps you'd prefer to fight with them online. Well, I leave that to your discretion

Postal Redux is a remastering of the original postal game with updated graphics and controls. One thing I will mention is that the controls are much better than they were in the original postal. (Seriously they were♥♥♥♥♥♥in the original)
Pros+
-Much better controls (even better shooting than the recent game Hatred)
-Decent variety of weapons
-We got good ol Rick Hunter reprising his role as the Postal Dude. (we even have Corey Burton who did the dude in Postal III narrating the ending.)
-Really messed up and awesome looking illustrations. (my Favorite is the one in the credits and in the main menu)
-a good handful of levels with more coming in a free update
Mixed opinions+/-
-while the shooting is very spot on it also means the enemies can't really miss shooting you unless they're throwing grenades, shooting rockets, or firing napalm launchers. It can make it hard not to die.
-Ignore this if you have been a fan of the Postal Series since the first Postal...but the tone here is much different than Postal 2. It seems to be focused on a much more gritty and twisted theme than offensive, low brow humor. (although I really don't have a issue with it. I enjoy dark stuff, but it can be a little surprising.)
-the graphics aren't the best, but I didn't have a issue with it. I know others might though, but it's freaking Postal so who cares XD.
Cons -
-Those god damn rocket turrents! They keep firing rockets non stop when your in their view which means they can keep blasting you and you keep getting knocked down. I can count at least 6 times I died thanks to this, and I know you can duck, but I didn't even have enough time to do that while the Postal Dude was getting up....plus ducking isn't helpful when your forced up against a god damn wall.
-The Air Force Base level. This level was complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to me since there were so many god damn swat officers and so many buildings where they come out of. Plus I had times where I forgot a guy south of me had a ♥♥♥♥ing napalm launcher which resulted in a cheap death because you have barely any control over the Dude when he's on fire! The only pro I have for this is that after this you get to the final level....and see a lot of messed up♥♥♥♥♥♥ So at least the payoff was worth it.
-The AI is dumb as rocks. Innocent civilians run around like idiots so it makes it hard to do a pacifist route when the civilians are too dumb to run away from the dude than running in circles.
-There are no subtitles.... I know there's not that much talking in Postal, but it's almost impossible to hear Corey Burton in the Ending due to the other sounds being much louder than him.
Verdict:
Postal Redux is a very good remastered version of the original Postal video game and for $15 dollars you can't go wrong. So if you wanted to get into the first game or you just want a decent amount of fun shooting pick this up. It's worth the money.

This is about as good as gaming gets. It's a celebration of everything that made Ridley Scott's 1979 scifi/horror film both terrifying and fantastic, with such attention to detail that you're instantly immersed.
It's apparent from the get-go that this game was lovingly crafted --the music is the first thing to set the mood, with the same wispy orchestral notes as the opening frames of the movie. The original film's 1970s retrofuturism is replicated faithfully here as well. Instead of the touch screens and air displays that dominate visual hardware in modern science fiction, the gear in Alien: Isolation is old school, with the same tactile terminals and monochrome monitors used in the film. This is 1979's version of the future of human interstellar exploration, and it's corporate, bleak, and lonely.
The game's developers should also be praised for creating a worthy female protagonist. The designers clearly worked hard to make Amanda Ripley look just enough like her mother, and the character is the antithesis of the hyper-sexualized female avatars seen in a lot of games. Amanda Ripley doesn't tote an impossibly big gun or wear boob armor, she's just an ordinary engineer clad in Companywear, searching for any clue about her missing mother's fate.
There's so much to praise about the visuals, sound and attention to detail, but it's the gameplay that ties it all together and makes Alien: Isolation memorable. I can't think of another game that succeeds so well at creating an oppressive, uncertain atmosphere where the player really *feels* their characters' fear.
There are genuinely tense and terrifying moments -- one second you're inching down a darkened hallway, the next you're diving into a storage locker just in time to watch through the slits as the Alien stalks by. Other times you're forced to crawl for cover under a desk or a gurney, with the Alien so close you can hear it breathing and hissing. But it's not just rooms and hallways. You'll find yourself looking over your shoulder in vents, and watching the ceiling for the slow-dripping slime that indicates the Alien is lurking in an open shaft above. In some sections of the Sevastapol space station the danger is compounded by hostile androids and frightened survivors who'll shoot anything that moves.
The game is relentless and never lets you feel comfortable. The moment you get sloppy -- not using the motion tracker, jumping out of cover, etc -- you'll get snatched up or impaled by a tail.
While Alien: Isolation almost does its job too well, there are a few chances to sit back and enjoy the scenery as well, including one sequence that brings one of the film's most memorable scenes to life. I cannot recommend this game highly enough.

This game was a bit like the Star Wars prequels for me. I went to the midnight screenings of all 3 movies, hyped to the hilt with Star Wars fever, ready to love it as much as I loved the original trilogy when I first discovered that as a child back in the early 90s.
Coming out of the theatre my initial impression was always a positive one. But on the drive home, away from the jedi cosplayers, away from the thunderous cheering when "A long time ago etc" first came onto the screen and the opening score kicked in, when I finally had time to myself to gather my thoughts, I started seeing flaws. At first a few minor things that annoyed me. Then a few more. Within about half an hour I was already starting to realise that it wasn't a good movie at all, that I'd just been caught up in nostalgia, no matter how much fun I had at the time. It made me a little sad the first time I realised just how badly those movies actually sucked (yes, even the third but if you like it that's cool :D ) though by the time the third one came around I had a healthy dose of skepticism to go with my hype so it wasn't as surprising. It even happened a bit with the new one. Hindsight can sometimes ruin what was a great initial experience.
Anyway so Just Cause 3 is sort of like that.
I LOVED JC2 when I got it. Loved loved loved it. It's one of my top 10 favourite games of all time. So you can imagine my hype coming into this one. I even got a new video card just to play this (and it's run smoothly the whole time thankfully so I can't comment on the performance issue stuff).
It had fantastic gameplay combined with that B-movie/not taking itself seriously at all storyline that just made it entertaining as hell. I couldn't put it down and I still hop on from time to time to liberate a few more bases or towns.
Really all JC3 needed to do to succeed in my eye was more of the same basically. And in some ways that's exactly what I got but in others it dropped the ball pretty badly. I guess I should just list the pros and cons for ease.
PROS
CONS
That's all I can think of off the top of my head. Don't get me wrong, I had a blast and I still recommend it and am looking forward to the upcoming DLC but every time I take a step back and think about my time playing it, I seem to only see mostly negatives.
So yeah if you loved JC2 then you should still like this, just don't expect to have your mind blown this time around. If you never played JC2 and you like the sound of basically being a superhero blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up then you should like this as well. Just try not to think about it too much :)

I was super pumped for this game. The previous entry in the series, Just Cause 2, was exactly the right kind of high-octane open-world shooter I live for. When I finally got into it the experience was like nothing before. And I think part of that novelty is what made the game seem so good. That, and some meticulous level design combined with weapon balancing and a reasonable default difficulty level.
Just Cause 3, on the other hand, doesn't seem nearly as revolutionary an experience. It's a good game, but it doesn't feel
good. The elements are all still there, but the ratio in the mix wrong just enough to throw it off.
First, let's talk about the positives. The wingsuit. OMG. The wingsuit. It's probably the closest I've felt to nirvana in a video game. When the (admittedly repetitive) music hits the melody at that exact second when you pull off a harrowing inches-from-the-ground turn it's like nothing else. The sense of wonder and excitement something like that can generate made me feel like a little kid again. It was in those fleeting moments when the game shined and I was transported to another realm where all my daily worries and cares didn't exist. I was flying.
But sadly there's little else that even comes close to how the wingsuit made me feel. The problems begin with the fact that there's only a single difficulty, and only a single save slot. Why these features that existed in 2 were dropped from 3 boggles my mind, as I see both as necessities for a game like this. Although my leading theory is that it was an attempt to make Just Cause more GTA like. Which is obviously a mistake. The reason 2 was so successful is precisely because it had sufficiently differentiated itself from that behemoth of the third person shooter free roam genre.
The difficulty falls apart in both directions. Combat by itself is usually too easy to be interesting in Just Cause simply because Rico is such a bullet sponge compared to his enemies. But when things are hard they are frustratingly so.
Part of what made 2 so incredibly fun was how overpowered the helicopters were. Flying around and destroying base after base was such an addictive waste of time that I lost many hours to it. But in 3 the SAM sites being vastly improved combined with way less manueverable helos means that you can either try to snipe from an extreme distance (which isn't always possible given lines of sight) or risk only getting a few shots off before you're grounded. This ultimately results in having to assault bases on land, which when examining the game design as a whole seems to be exactly what the developers were pushing towards. Why is baffling. Perhaps they were trying to extend the life of the game by making destroying a base take longer. If they were consciously trying to increase the difficulty of air assaults then they entirely missed what made 2 so good: that sense of power and invincibility.
Some of the challenges - particularly with the wingsuit - did get me to the point of rage quitting a few times. But that's where the game should be difficult: the optional challenges. Alas, the number and difficulty of both the car and plane races were disappointingly low when compared to the many wingsuit courses.
The world as a whole was also too sparse. It's one thing to have a huge, massive island nation to explore, but when the distance between anything important is so extreme that traveling becomes a chore, something is wrong. In 2 I never felt like I was waiting for very long to get somewhere new and exciting. But here in 3 I could sometimes drink an entire coffee while holding down the throttle and still be nowhere near my objective. This is one area where the developers should take a lesson from Fallout 4: density matters more than actual size. It's all relative to how far away in time the fun things to do are.
Finally, 3 has not improved upon the story, writing, or voice acting in any meaningful way. This is a more serious Just Cause, accompanied by a more serious cast. And that's generally worse, as it takes away from the silly antics and tone of what's happening outside the cutscenes. De-emphasizing Sheldon and instead including a couple diverse, joyless mercenaries only hurt things further. Going back to Rico's home - where he has more to lose and should care about the outcomes more - was a bold move, but it fell flat.
Just Cause 3 still has a ton to do. And it's mostly fun. There's explosions galore. Just the right amount of collectibles. Some zany stunts and a few challenging challenges. It doesn't quite live up to what came before, but if you've already experienced 2 and liked it then you could do worse than continuing the adventure here.

Empires of the Undergrowth is currently an alpa game where you control an ant nest. At the moment the game is limited with 4 possible missions, and two challenges. The two challenges. You basically get a formicarium where you control a small nest that is limited in how much you can change it, and the food available (it even comes with a tech tree).
You unlock more food, upgrades as well as how much of the nest can be dugout by completing the missions you get two missions that basically teach the basic game mechanics. After completing a mission you'll return to the formicarium with some royal jelly (used to unlock two types of ants and improved ant abilities). When you're feeling confident in your ant abilities you're able to launch your first challenge which will put your formicarium through several trials. If you manage to complete the challenge you'll unlock two more missions and a second challenge.
Control of the ants is not entirely direct. Instead you can assign groups of ants (1 to 5) which are then directed to patrol from your queen to a pheromone marker. That can present some issues in that there may be occasions when your ants might walk in to a fight one by ones but as long as you're aware of what is happening this is generally easy to manage.
While I recommend the game as I personally enjoyed the challenge and narrative of the game, it should be noted the game is short as it currently is with not a lot of replayability. I am personally looking forward to seeing the game more fleshed out!

The Evil Within 2 is held back by a forgettable story and annoying AI issues that would probably put a serious damper on your gameplay experience if you were playing on Nightmare difficulty. And yet, it also does exactly what a horror game should do, and it does it well. Despite its flaws, The Evil Within 2 is a thoughtfully constructed horror rollercoaster ride that strikes a delicate balance between giving the player the power to fight back, and also making them realize that sometimes, all those guns and gear won’t save you from the terrors you can’t understand.
Pros
+The semi-open world environments are a nice addition that reward exploration, and don’t ruin the pacing.
+Side objectives are few, but meaningful and feel like part of the story.
+The crafting system has been greatly improved and adds to the tension of resource management.
+Brilliant use of lighting and horrific imagery that really messes with the player.
Cons
-The story is unmemorable.
-The AI is both hilarious and frustrating at the same time.
Overall rating: 9/10

For some reason, Steam is showing the six hours it's taken me to finish the single player (during which it crashed or locked my computer up approximately twice for every one of the game's 15 levels) rather than the ~50 hours I have in the multiplayer.
Four months from launch, Activision still haven't added the promised dedicated servers, so the netcode is terrible console P2P networking with aggressively bad lag compensation up the wazoo. The game's population has dwindled to the point where the game will struggle to find you a TDM or Dom lobby, and you can completely forget about playing any other game mode. If you leave a match because it contains a blatant aimbotter (which is the case maybe 1/3 of the time) and requeue, you'll be dumped straight back into the same lobby you just left. The weapon balance is terrible, and the devs went out of their way to buff the guns that were already the most overpowered, meaning 80% of the people you will encounter use one of two guns.
This isn't worth your time or money at £45. It's not even worth your time or money if you can get it for half or less of that price. Avoid like the plague, which is a shame because the exo movement system is really fun.

In short this game is spectacular, be patient, and you will be rewarded. The combat, the environments, and even the frequent deaths all serve to build an immersive atmosphere that will draw in all but the harshest of critics.
It's worth whatever you pay for it, and Dark Souls II will offer hours of high value gameplay.
I highly recommend.

I rarely feel the need to write a review for a game. Today however, I break that streak once again.
Now, before buying this game, I made sure to play Dishonored 1 first (which i highly reccomend you do); dishonored 2 meets the expectations brought in the first one - infact it beats it.
Getting the obious out of the way - this game is gorgeous, and the creators took so much time and effort making the world come together, including even the finest moving parts, truly living up to and improving upon the steampunk world the first game tried to create.
If you look at my library, you will see I have a lot of games, atleast for my standards - about eight tenths of my library did not wow me as much as this game did with their creativity.
The game has eight missions, and atleast five of them astonished me like no other game has, with the things you could do in them, especially in mission four - ill let you find out what mission 4 is on your own. Now, I dont want to spoil too much, but you will do things in this game I have never seen tried, its like an illusion of realisim and I love it... as hard as that is to explain. Dishonored 2 is a brilliant show of extraordinary gameplay, somthing I don't expect from and action game. Infact, dishonored is a better assasination simulator than hitman, and riding very close to assasins creed (imo).
I play very little story driven action games, and refunded bioshock because it was too out-there for me; dishonored however is just right. If you arent one for steampunk games, or are trying it out, I highly reccomend this game be your first, as it is the perfect combination of realism and fantasy.
As I tried to describe this games intricacy, I could only describe this game's level of intuitive design to that of the portal series, as odd as that may sound - you see, only portal had as much moving parts and care put into the game maps as dishonored 2 does. Both games create an illusion of realism. Everything lookes as though it could be created in real life, showing every detail in its mechanism as it moved, making the doors, hidden walls, hinges and clockwork actually look like they belong, with little clipping to be seen. Everything in this game, with some exceptions, look like they have a place in the world, and dont just clip into eachother.
I am really hoping the titanfall campaign is as beautiful as this, since this game has set the standard for moving parts and carefull design... a games beauty isnt just in its textures.
Now, I know I've talked a lot about how the game LOOKS, not how it plays - it plays better than dishonored one. If you liked the gameplay in dishonored one, you will like two. I also don't want to praise the gameplay because I have very little experience with other, similar action games (other than hitman and assasnins creed), so I have very little to base my perspective on.
Final notes,
I understand people have been having severe problems with this game, but I have not - I am among the lucky few, I suppose. It's a risk, but it's one I would suggest, I use a gtx970 and an intel i5 4430... I can run the game perfectly on ultra (if that helps anyone). Honestly, you wont know if it works until you own it, and I'm sure you can figure out if your game works before the two hour threshold.
One last, very important thing to mention - BUY DISHONORED 1 FIRST! Seriously, buy it. Not just the game, but the dlc too! Dishonored two makes many referances to the old game. If you dont get dishonored 1, you will still understand the story arc, but may be less sensative to certain events or referances - you may even miss cool expository which only someone whose played dishonored 1 would understand
- QUICK EDIT
I got 30 hours from dishonored, with dlc, and 22 or so hours on dishonored two, so I can only imagine what their DLC will be like (HYPE). That being said, dishonored two provides as much gametime as the old one, not losing gametime for graphics.

Like every other gamer in the world, I'm getting a little bit sick of the Zombie fetish the industry has acquired. Sure, it gives you a chance to have enemies without having to set up a huge plot, and it's a gorefest, and who doesn't love wave games, but the theme is running dry.
No More Room In Hell (or "NMRH" as it will be referred to from here on) is another addition to stack onto the piles of zombie games currently being developed. It's your standard team-based, zombie-wave-killing title, with a few interesting twists and tricks that, while refreshing, feel recycled and outdated.
The game itself is nothing new. You buy a gun, or pick one up, and you mow down as many zombies as you can before you die. There are various character models (one of them Patrick Bateman from American Psycho, and other pop-culture references) and, actually, a pretty good selection of guns. The games mostly take place in indoor arenas, with very maticulously detailed rooms, and enclosed spaces. You meet up with your teammates, and (hopefully) stick together in order to kill a lot of zombies. One thing I liked is that the stages have some areas where, even with your gamma adjusted, it is pitch black. It's actually a little daunting, and sparks a small amount of fear, to step into one of these pitch black areas when you know it could be filled with a bunch of zambambos ready to sample your flesh.
And that bring about another interesting mechanic that I don't remember seeing before: Your teammates resurrect as slightly more powerful zombies if bitten. This was marginally terrifying the first time it happened. Your character has an unbelievably small amount of health, and medpacks are scarce at best, so you don't feel overpowered. Your ammo is incredibly scarce, and each time you reload, your character calls out how much ammunition they actually have left, which makes you think heavily about your ammo conservation. Lastly, there is NO auto-reload, so if you're pinned down by a whole host of zombies, there's a legitimate panic as you decide. "Should I press the reload button, or try to change to melee?"
The bad news is that if you ever come to that decision, you're already dead. There is currently a 120 second respawn timer, which stays alive so long as there's one teammate left in the map. The waves themselves are fairly simple, at least at first, but there is an EXTREMELY sharp difficulty curve come wave 2. So far, I haven't made it past wave 2, so I can't tell you if there are any MORE zombie types, but so far it's apparent that some are much faster than others.
The standard enemy you come across is the standard cookie-cutter "slow" zombie. They lumber around, and can only be killed with shots to the head (which is a big plus). The next type starts around wave 2, and in the 6 or 7 rounds I played, nobody made it past wave 2. This wave introduces the runner, which it may not surprise you to learn, are very very fast. Couple this in with the realistic mag size (depending on the gun) and the manual reload, and they are nearly impossible in large numbers. It would seem that the best way to counter this is with the entire team stacked up in a corner somewhere, but the final mechanic makes this less likely.
The mode I played had the stipulation of a military rescue team heading to our location. The map was a small abandoned house with a basement, and several points of entry. There were three 'zones' (a, b, and c respectively) that had to be protected, and so our team would rush to the nearest zone to clean up the infestation. Lose all your zones, the military won't come to help. The only problem is that multiple zones can be attacked at any time, forcing you to split up your team, which will then be picked off by the aforementioned runners.
The UI for the game is poorly constructed. There is a default radial selection for your guns (which can be remapped) which just comes across as clunky with keyboard/mouse, although mouse wheel selecting is still functional. The ADS (aim-down-sights) seems accurate enough, but often seems misleading. Unless you're carrying a pistol, you're also always switching between your gun and your flashlight, which, due to the radial selection, is impossible to do when it matters the most.
This is a very difficult game, as it currently is. Rounds are very short (due to the runners), and headshots aren't as easy as they sound. The maps are a little bland, and the UI itself is a little messy (ie. having to type '!guns' into the chat just to access the shop), but the game is, without a doubt, the most realistic zombie wave game I've played to date.
To wrap up, it's worth a download, especially while it remains FTP. I hope future patches correct the difficulty curve itself, as having the runners all come on wave 2 is particularly daunting, and makes the game a little less fun and a little more frustrating. Fans of Killing Floor, Left 4 Dead, and other wave-based FPS games will appreciate the design, but will be left wanting something better.

Another AAA game released in an unfinished state.  But it's arguably playable now with beta update 1.3.  If you don't know already, Dishonored 2 is a first-person stealth/action game designed to be equally proficient as a stealth game and an action game.  You can finish the game without ever getting detected and without ever engaging in combat, or you can do the opposite.  Levels are sprawling and non-linear but overall story progression is linear.  It features two selectable protagonists, each with unique powers (which are like spells).
Finishing Dishonored and its two story expansions (The Knife of Dunwall and Brigmore Witches) is an absolute necessity, since most of the character exposition and development for Dishonored 2's characters actually relies on those.  Which is a knock against Dishonored 2 by the way.  Plus, Dishonored is an incredible game, better than this one all around and still gorgeous, so don't even think about starting this franchise with the sequel.
The most annoying issues are the graphics glitches; shadows popping/flickering, ambient occlusion glow, some texture flickering.  Performance has improved a lot with this update but it isn't where it should be, especially with the frame pacing issues that persist.
At 2560 x 1440 on an overclocked GTX 1080, i7 6700k @ 4.6 GHz, and 16GB DDR4 3000 MHz RAM I average 75-100 FPS outdoors now (but some places in Karnaca go below that) and oddly enough 65-90 FPS indoors.  Frame pacing issues exist at all frame rates, but less consistently at 120 FPS on the dot.
Audio has some glitches like voices outputting to non-existent surround channels on stereo/2.1 systems, or voices disappearing when turning away from them even on surround setups (5.1 surround here).  AI has navigation issues.  Some clipping issues remain.  Level design is incomplete since in some places you can see in between the tiles.
Technicalities aside, I am happy to report that Dishonored 2 retains the amazing art style from the first.  Levels are bigger and more open than ever before with so many ways to advance and approach objectives.  Although it may have fewer unique environments than the first, and decals like graffiti and propaganda are far more repetitive.  On that note, readable texts around the world are more repetitive as well; it seems this game has less of them than the first.
Gameplay mechanics are almost perfect.  Very similar to the first, improved melee combat responsiveness and a few new features like countering after perfectly timed blocks.  In direct combat you can now grab a hold of someone and use them as a shield, choking them out in the process but you can throw them in front of you which is useful against groups of enemies.  For some reason leaning is toggle only.  Crouching is toggle only and is oddly laggy.
AI is improved and has better detection than virtually every other stealth game at least on hard mode or harder.  Creatures actually see out of their eyes, they react more quickly to detections, and there's no "If I see you then everyone else sees you" garbage.  Due to the non-linear level design, the ability to climb any and all ledges (no contextual crap like 2014's Thief atrocity), environmental interaction (which could be better), the fact that light/shadows affect concealment, and the powers if you choose to accept them, Dishonored 2 like the first game are on a different level than every other modern stealth game of its kind.  Only the classic Thief games can compete.
Corvo's powers are the same as the first but with more upgrades, so they're all awesome.  Emily also has incredible powers, more geared toward stealth though.
The story is complete mediocrity compared to the first.  It hardly has any characters, and all characters, factions/groups, and plot events and devices do not have nearly enough exposition.  Dialogue is generic and utterly unremarkable.  The story was clearly rushed.
So Dishonored 2 is far from a perfect sequel.  Technically it is still a mess, the story is very disappointing, but the art design is remarkable and the gameplay fluidity/smoothness and fun factor are to die for.  Wait for it to be complete, all patched up, and then buy it.  But remember, you MUST finish Dishonored, Dishonored: The Knife of Dunwall, and Dishonored: Brigmore Witches before playing this one.  Especially with Dishonored 2's lack of character development and exposition, seemingly relying on playing the first game and expansions to the first game.

I was very nearly going to give this game a positive reveiw as an inoffensive, functional free indie piece with a simplistic but heart-tugging story. Right up until the final boss.
When you open your pitch for a game with "I believe that gaming should not be anything complicated or diffcult,
but a relaxing and pleasure experience", one thing you should maybe consider not doing is making the final boss the equivalent of the elevator fight scene in Winter Soldier, only with lasers. While the game DOES build up to that speed with increasingly elaborate bosses throughout the game in strong contrast to the essentially zero-effort main combat, the final boss is a sharp increase in that mostly by way of severely limiting your arena and only shrinking it further as the fight progresses, all while area of effect attacks go off incessantly. There's a market for Bullet Hell games, but it's generally not the "casual RPG" crowd.
The game's both free and relatively short - only three main areas discounting the 'tutorial,' all of which follow roughly the same formula - so there's not much else to discuss or complain about, but the final boss's sheer density killed whatever lukewarm goodwill I had built up over the adventure. Legend of Grimrock also had a bafflingly terrble final boss, but at least that game builds up an expectation of sadistic difficulty before turning into a twenty-car pileup of frustration. This is more like if an album full of soothing mood music suddenly launched into an ear-busting guitar solo on its final track apropos of nothing.
From what I hear the endings were all kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥anyway, so I don't feel I'm missing much.

With simple controls, an endearing storyline, glorious music, and the best boomerang fairy in existence, Eternal Senia is a great play for all four hours.
Combat is simple, walk into an enemy to attack them, and they attack simultaneously. Eventually Senia learns some skills, which can be used with a simple button press. But just because it's simple, doesn't mean it's boring. A variety of enemies from evil plants to fallen angels are ready to take Senia on with lasers, lightning, and some really sharp leaves. Boss combat gets even more interesting, and while a few principles stay the same for each of them, they are far from being identical.
The music Is wonderfully crafted to evoke just the right emotions, everything from the tranquillity of a rainy summer night, to the dark feeling of a demonic cave. It loops very well, keeping the ears entertained. The rest of the sound effects beautifully represent the actions taking place as well. None of the effects draw you out of the experience, as RPG maker games often do.
The art is well designed, flowing between the game field pixel art, dialogue portraits, and the occasional full art piece flawlessly.
The story is beautiful, and while some may be unsatisfied with the endings, I feel they were done tremendously well. Yes, I did say  ending
. Three of them, to be exact. Don't worry about your actions suddenly having unintended consequences, you'll be warned when it's coming, and are provided with plenty of times to back up your save. Which also means that you don't have to replay the entire game to see all of them.

I Have a lot of experience with this game which makes me more than qualified to make a review.
I Have played League of Legends for 7 years and I have soon quit beause of how the community and the company turned into.League of Legends lacks new content (Game modes) for how popular the game is and when they release a new game mode it's only for a week, this lack of content and repetitivness of the same game modes and maps has bored me and I promised myself I will never like a MOBA again. I tried Smite and it absouletly surprised me of how much better this game was then League of Legends.
These are the things that I have found that made this game amazing compared to League of Legends.
-100% Skill Based, League of Legends also takes skill but they had masteries and runes people had to purchase and level up in the game in order to use which gave an unfair advantage to newer players or people who doesn't have the money to purchase runes.Which was a big hassle to deal with when you just want to get into a game.In Smite everyone starts the game w/o the runes and masteries B.S which gives every player an even chance on winning.
-The Balancing is ridiculously Amazing! In League of Legends when someone snowballs very hard it is very hard to comback from it and usually ends up in a loss. In Smite I've had so many games where my team made a comback against very early fed players because of one mistake their team made.The Balancing is designed that one mistake can end it for the team in league of legends the fed team can make multiple mistakes before actually impacting them.
-You get Free Gems!! this is compared to Riot Points in league in where you can use it to purchase skins and can even use normail ingame currency to buy skins making this game 100% F2P in my mind.
-Fast Pace Action ,this is what really sold me, Action. In league you would have to farm a lane for like 10 boring mins to actually get anywhere.In Smite action starts as soon as you reach the jungle and the battles are intense.
-The community is not bad mainly because there are no restrictions to what needs to be in a lane because of how great the balancing is in the game you can play w.e you want in which ever lane you want,compared to league in where you get snaped at if you don't play adc support bot, there are less restrictions in this game which is what gives it a unique game style and I reccomend  everyone to play it if they quit league.
-The champion loading screen takes at the very least 20 seconds to start! Compared to those long 5 min timers in league where you have to wait for that toaster to finish loading up.
The only bad thing I've found in this game is the Game launching bugs in where your friends are kicked out of the champion loading screen and when they relog they are in the game lobby while they are really in the game disconnected and with no way of going back in it because they will just get kicked back into the lobby again,this is my only complaint with the game really.I don't want to get reported for afking when it was a game error.

So, where to start? I was a bit skeptical at first, despite knowing that these devs won’t ever change, i was still a bit scared that any other Postal game after the first and the second ones will be less fun  and won’t be the same, because, to be honest, in the recent years the gaming community started getting very sensitive to certain aspects of violence. And i don’t like to say this, but we need to face the fact that violence is part of the human nature, of course, that doesn’t necessarily mean something good, and it surely doesn’t mean you should replace this kind of behavior in the real life.
And i strongly believe it’s a good thing if developers (generally speaking) are adding such senseless violence, racism, and various other kinds of hatred. And please, don’t get me wrong, I am not racist, nor homophobic, i don’t believe in any of these intolerant groups, but these are things you see them in your daily life, they are everywhere, and i think we need to accept the fact that for the moment they are still a big thing, and i believe that trying to ignore them in movies and games doesn’t do anything good, on the contrary, we are running away from the ugly truth.
This is life, good and bad aspects, good and bad people.
Now, about Postal Redux, I was glad that i was proven wrong, nothing changed at the very core of Postal.
The game is polished, and it was improved alot graphically speaking, the VFX in this game are also eye-pleasing.
You have a good variety of weapons and explosives to create mass chaos with, and each of them are very fun to use.
The difficulty option does its job pretty well, i tried the game in both the easiest difficulty and the hardest one, for example in the hardest difficulty, you might die once or twice every level until you figure out the best pathway to start your killing spree, and the difficulty option adds extra hostiles, changes some enemy types, and also changes how often you find health/guns/ammo.
Isometric games tend to be confusing at times, even the original Postal was a bit confusing. In this one it was slightly weird only when you were walking and having to shoot enemies from multiple directions at the same time, but i think this is not something unusual.
Also.. SECRETS! I personally loved when games had secret areas hidden throughout them, and i am glad this one has some aswell, they might not feel so rewarding as the ones in Duke Nukem 3D, let’s say, but it’s nice when you find them (not very hard).
I think this is everything that could’ve been written at this section of the review, if you are familiar with Postal, you know it is a simplistic game with not a rich background story, but a rich and fun Shoot’Em Up experience.
What some people might not be very fond of, the actual playtime, for me it was around 1.6 hours, but as far as i know, the first one was also the same.
On the bright side, you will probably love to replay this quite often.
Also, a new mode was added, Rampage, in which you you mantain killstreaks and try to get high scores, i still have yet to play it properly, but i am happy overall that they've added some new content to this great cocktail of insanity.
Not sure if this soundtrack fits Postal Redux as it should, but it is amazing.
It made me feel energic, it made me feel like i was going literally insane. I loved it! Unique, very dark and mysterious but also with a strong psychopathic vibe to it.

DISCLAIMER: I received this product for no cost for the purpose of reviewing. However, this does not affect my views and opinions of the game.
If you've played the original postal, then there might not be a whole lot for you in this review aside from the changes made
the original. This is the first time I've played a Postal game despite owning "POSTAL" & "POSTAL 2" on Steam. This means I'll also be looking at the game from a mechanics point of view as well as it's play-ability.
As many people already know, the Postal series has you as some dude, (appropriately named; "Postal Dude") shooting up civilians and any hostile enemies trying to end his rampage. The game is a 2D top downish-isometicish twin-stick shooter. The story is almost non-existent from what I can tell, but the blatant unprovoked violence was once something of controversy when the original game first came out.
--------
I have looked at the graphics quality of the original game and have compared it to the redux version. I can say that there definitely was an improvement, which is to be expected. It's sharper and more polished than the original. It also accents more of the detail there is in the game. Without the comparison, and taking into account that it is an indie title, the visuals are still pretty decent. They aren't amazing, and really aren't on par with a lot of the other games coming out, though you could also say that making a redux version could not tamper with the actual visuals too much, as it's more of a "restoration" of the title. All in all, I do think it's fine, and the retroish style will also appeal to others. The game is not that demanding and seems to be optimized fine. It can run on almost any lower tier graphics card and CPU.
--------
I'm not entirely sure if the sound assets were changed or if there was a quality improvement to the original, though the game's soundtrack, gun noises, and one liners are decent. The sound assets are all a tad muffled, though I think it adds to the experience of the game, and somehow it fits. Although I'm not much into the metally rockish grunge kind of music that the soundtrack consists of, I can see how some people would enjoy it, and it does really compliment the game's theme.
--------
The game mechanics were not changed from the original game at all from what I can tell. You run around killing people. It's a very simple system. You have a certain amount people you have to kill before moving on to the next stage. You can pick up a variety of weapons that each need ammo (aside from the starting gun). You can pick up ammo and health in some stages. Knowing when to use which guns with certain enemies is also key, as some guns do more damage than others. The enemies also have they're own arsenal, so you have to be careful not to take too much damage from them, as well as avoid environmental obstacles like fires and barrels, although you can also use these to your advantage. Although simple, the mechanics are solid and get the job done.
--------
As someone who never played the original, the game is decent. It has a few difficulty settings depending on how good you think you are at the game. It's not the kind of game I'm personally into, and I wasn't around when there was all the controversy surrounding the original. This means I probably don't appreciate the title to it's fullest, however I know there are people that do, and because the game is somewhat of a classic, I know there are people that would enjoy having a much more up to date version of this game.
Thanks to the devs for giving me the opportunity to review the game, as well as anyone who took this review into consideration, I hope it helped.

I was super pumped for this game. The previous entry in the series, Just Cause 2, was exactly the right kind of high-octane open-world shooter I live for. When I finally got into it the experience was like nothing before. And I think part of that novelty is what made the game seem so good. That, and some meticulous level design combined with weapon balancing and a reasonable default difficulty level.
Just Cause 3, on the other hand, doesn't seem nearly as revolutionary an experience. It's a good game, but it doesn't feel
good. The elements are all still there, but the ratio in the mix wrong just enough to throw it off.
First, let's talk about the positives. The wingsuit. OMG. The wingsuit. It's probably the closest I've felt to nirvana in a video game. When the (admittedly repetitive) music hits the melody at that exact second when you pull off a harrowing inches-from-the-ground turn it's like nothing else. The sense of wonder and excitement something like that can generate made me feel like a little kid again. It was in those fleeting moments when the game shined and I was transported to another realm where all my daily worries and cares didn't exist. I was flying.
But sadly there's little else that even comes close to how the wingsuit made me feel. The problems begin with the fact that there's only a single difficulty, and only a single save slot. Why these features that existed in 2 were dropped from 3 boggles my mind, as I see both as necessities for a game like this. Although my leading theory is that it was an attempt to make Just Cause more GTA like. Which is obviously a mistake. The reason 2 was so successful is precisely because it had sufficiently differentiated itself from that behemoth of the third person shooter free roam genre.
The difficulty falls apart in both directions. Combat by itself is usually too easy to be interesting in Just Cause simply because Rico is such a bullet sponge compared to his enemies. But when things are hard they are frustratingly so.
Part of what made 2 so incredibly fun was how overpowered the helicopters were. Flying around and destroying base after base was such an addictive waste of time that I lost many hours to it. But in 3 the SAM sites being vastly improved combined with way less manueverable helos means that you can either try to snipe from an extreme distance (which isn't always possible given lines of sight) or risk only getting a few shots off before you're grounded. This ultimately results in having to assault bases on land, which when examining the game design as a whole seems to be exactly what the developers were pushing towards. Why is baffling. Perhaps they were trying to extend the life of the game by making destroying a base take longer. If they were consciously trying to increase the difficulty of air assaults then they entirely missed what made 2 so good: that sense of power and invincibility.
Some of the challenges - particularly with the wingsuit - did get me to the point of rage quitting a few times. But that's where the game should be difficult: the optional challenges. Alas, the number and difficulty of both the car and plane races were disappointingly low when compared to the many wingsuit courses.
The world as a whole was also too sparse. It's one thing to have a huge, massive island nation to explore, but when the distance between anything important is so extreme that traveling becomes a chore, something is wrong. In 2 I never felt like I was waiting for very long to get somewhere new and exciting. But here in 3 I could sometimes drink an entire coffee while holding down the throttle and still be nowhere near my objective. This is one area where the developers should take a lesson from Fallout 4: density matters more than actual size. It's all relative to how far away in time the fun things to do are.
Finally, 3 has not improved upon the story, writing, or voice acting in any meaningful way. This is a more serious Just Cause, accompanied by a more serious cast. And that's generally worse, as it takes away from the silly antics and tone of what's happening outside the cutscenes. De-emphasizing Sheldon and instead including a couple diverse, joyless mercenaries only hurt things further. Going back to Rico's home - where he has more to lose and should care about the outcomes more - was a bold move, but it fell flat.
Just Cause 3 still has a ton to do. And it's mostly fun. There's explosions galore. Just the right amount of collectibles. Some zany stunts and a few challenging challenges. It doesn't quite live up to what came before, but if you've already experienced 2 and liked it then you could do worse than continuing the adventure here.

This blew my mind.
As a hardcore Alien and sci-fi fan, I've been waiting for a game like this for a while now. The gameplay was good enough (terrifying), but what really caught my attention was the enviroment design and the lore. The ship interiors are like something straight from Ridley Scott himself and the lighting makes all those corridors, 70's style sci-fi rooms, vintage terminals, and chunky monitors look incredible, not to mention very realistic. I liked the slow pace of the game, just like Alien, it adds to the dreadful atmosphere of when you hear the alien all around you with that 3D sound or when you see it searching for you in the dark distance.
I have a strong hatred for those Working Joes, they way they say they are trying to help while strangling you or how they have an obsession for killing people with magazines just creeps me out.
It was cool to use Amanda Ripley (Ellen Ripley's daughter) as the protagonist, and the Nostromo references were a great way to link the story up. I liked the other characters too, especially Ricardo and Samuels (Marlow was a real prick), they were good additions to the plot.
This is game is definitely a favourite of mine and I look forward to more games from Creative Assembly (hopefully more sci-fi stuff).

Mike is an ordinary guy who one day finds himself talking to a doppelganger - a being who looks, talks & walks like him... or at least, almost :).
I say almost, because Mike's got a girlfriend (Sarah) who happens to have a very keen eye (she is a cop after all), and is capable of sniffing out the slightest of lies, spun by her potentially soon-to-be husband.
The story starts with one version of Mike, bumping into & answering to what looks like another version of himself (in what appears to be a living room).
From this point onwards, the player is given the choice to either proceed truthfully (or deceivingly) while being subjected to a series of personal questions by none other than the fierce & feisty girlfriend Sarah.
There's a total of 9 endings (where you end up being the real mike or an impostor, who gets to stay, leave, live or even die!), depending on the answers given.

Playing through this game i immediately began to wonder whether it would live up to any sort of rebirth of the franchise or even the idea and aspirations the original games gave, that sense of wonder and intrigue the world offered, no matter how big or small. Even with the original creators blessing i was skeptical, but to my surprise Odd Gentleman not only hit the mark but really pinned down what King's Quest did for me back in the 90's: atmosphere and story. Yes a lot of people may say they lacked this back in the day due to graphical and storytelling limits for computers then, but it was the world and environment and fantasy that helped it tell the story it needed to, and the reboot here does that perfectly. Aside from a few minor gameplay glitches i experienced as well as being somewhat simpler in difficulty, this was greatly superseded by the music, characters, and overall atmosphere and artwork that really accomplished far more than i expected. Voice work, backgrounds, the world itself has been given a lot of love and it really shows as you play. If you came for the difficult, open-ended world of the original KQ games this might not quite do it for you, but if you are looking for a game that delivers a calm and serene world and be taken into bite-sized tales woven by King Graham himself in his older years, this game delivers and more on what it has promised in the first game alone in this reviewer's experience. Play it, and may Daventry be all you dreamt it would be!

I loved this game!  The first episode lasted a long time - longer than I have come to expect from games with episodic releases.  The graphics were beautiful!  It was fun and funny.  I also thought the interactions between King Graham and his granddaughter Gwendolyn were heartwarming.  There are different ways to solve each of the puzzles: being kind, being tricky and smart, or being strong (possibly violent).  My first time through I went with the kindness route.
If you are a casual gamer or loved the first King's Quest games, you will love this game!  I've noticed that most of the negative reviews seem to come from hard-core gamers that compare the game to first-person shooters or other games like that.  This game is not meant to be that.  It's fun and I think it is a great introduction to casual adventure gaming.  Also, totally family friendly so your (older) kids should be able to play it as well.  There are a couple parts that require a little coordination that I had to try a couple of times, like shooting the arrows at the ropes while floating down the river.  But it wasn't too hard that it took more than a few tries.
Recommendations for the developers: make it possible to skip the cutscenes or the commentary, at least after the first time.  I also thought that he did walk around decently fast the first time, but having two speeds to his walking (or having walking and running) could be nice.
Some other reviews mentioned that you have to steal a "wheel" from one of the stores.  Actually, you can pay for it.  Even though all the shopkeepers are gone, there is a tin available in each of the shops where you can put your money.  Don't worry, you still have enough money left to finish the game.

okay, first off, i am a Katawa Shoujo fan, so before i start talking... Hanako and Lilly, Flashbacks and Feels.
i didn't know what to expect, to be honest i thought that it would be yet another free game that you'll play to pass time or some form of grinder to play for a while to actually be able to do any damage.
boy was i wrong.
it is a rather stable balance between easily won and "oh for the love of god!", sometimes you'd feel able to win easily, sometimes you'd just feel like you're in for some trouble, and a tush handing session.
the sprites are so clean and cute, the images are amazing, though some of the effect sprites like the lasers and such do sometimes glitch and you'd see the borders of the sprite, but it's generally fogrettable.
the combat reminds me of YS: ark of napishtim, easy to play and easy to follow, i love it.
the difficulty remains generally the same, level up, get better gear, get higher damage, beat enemies from 2-hits to a one hit finish, the enemies are ranging from a cannonfodder to a son of a protestant ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, the tactics go from one to one, to one over many, easy enough to do.
the map ranges from a wide and open fields to alleys tighter than a nun's butt, and each sector gives you a range of enemies to kill, either you completely bash them till they die one by one, or use your specials to hit with higher power or chain kills.
SPOILERS AHEAD, STORY REVIEW:
okay, it seems like a Cliche type of game at first, but it fits this game like a glove, the idea behind it is heartwarming and heartbreaking, your character is extremely determined and very resilient, the objective is great, but an old and overused cliche, though it is used correctly, but it still makes it feel a bit overused by the abundance of games that used the "i will save Onee/Onii-chan even if it kills me".
the Onee-chan is beautiful, sweet, kind, she'd do anything to help you, even if it kills her, what a surprise there~!
though she is doing a noble thing, she has the skills, but she's not in the emotional status to partake in such journey, a place that will take your mind takes a great will, going there without preparing for external forces taking your mind over is suicide.
so, the game is free, the gameplay is spot on, the creator is not forcing you paying anything or doing so crazy crap to actually win the game, he tried his best to make a good game, and he did what's better, he created a great game.
also... Senia is Hanako, Magaleta is Lilly, Malphiq is Rin, the succubus is Shizune, the fairy is Misha~!
Perfect execution on every level. Just play it if you like ARPG and feels. And if you don't, still play it.

System Shock 2 is a must buy for ANYONE who likes Action RPGs, First Person Horror, or story-driven games. This game was the inspiration for BioShock and was made by most of the same team. Irrational Games with some help from the gods of the First-Person RPG, the now-defunct Looking Glass Studios, crafted an amazing first person atmospheric RPG experience that has some of the best writing and deepest mechanics of any game ever. The visual style has aged pretty well aside from the character models but mods can fix it or you can just ignore the visuals entirely because the sound design is where the game shines. The haunting moans of the hybrids, the slow beeps of security cameras, the announcements from an AI totally oblivious to what has happened, and of course, the taunting of one of gaming's greatest female characters, SHODAN. If you like BioShock, System Shock 2 is BioShock but better.

No more room in hell is an amazing mod that feels like a standalone game, the combat style and rarity of guns really counteracts the typical "ammo everywhere" style of zombie apocolypses this generation of gamers are currently akin to, unlike most games in the genre of zombie survival games, no more room in hell offers an experience that cannot be found anywhere else, its tense, scary and at times, funny, nothing is as funny as hitting a zombie with a sledgehammer and watching his corpse ragdoll down the stairs, killing several more zombies in the process.
No more room in hell offers a rather dark look at the zombie apocolypse, no humour, no funny characters, the players are left in a sick, twisted, dying world and are forced to fight for survival against zombies, fast zombies and even children zombies, there aren't many zombie games that end with you cowering in a corner with a gun in your mouth as your vision is taken over by the infection, leaving you to decide to pull the trigger or let yourself turn as your group fight on, hoping against hope they can win, unaware of your current state. 10/10 (must play)

Once you get past the "wow, I'm controlling ants!" part (which a lot of people fail to do, it seems), it's pretty easy to see why I'm leaving a thumbs down and getting a refund.
Game tries so hard not to be like other RTSs that it gets rid of things that actually make RTSs fun, balanced, and exciting, and ends up just being a clunky mess.
To expand upon this as people have been asking, basically instead of being able to command your units effectively, you just give them a general area to go to, some will go there and some will not. The ones that DO go there will often wander around the nest after a few seconds, then make their way back. The enemy units are, however, extremely coordinated and will go directly to your queen with no hesitation. This means any real fight is just you desperately trying to get your units to behave as the enemy steamrolls throughout your nest. The developers have claimed this is "realistic" ant behavior, but anyone who has observed ants in the wild knows that ant colonies will swarm around predators very effectively once the threat is identified and marked.
And let me just say one of my favorite games of all time is Dwarf Fortress. I am fine with not having complete and direct control over every single one of my units. I just think there should be a "mark predator" command or something that makes your soldier ants stop wandering around and get to fighting.
Also, as you can see from the comments on this review, the community for this game is trash and likes to respond to legitimate criticism with "YOU MAD?". Christ man, it's 2017.

Oh yes, it has been 17 years since the last game in the series, and now it is time again to go on an epic adventure with King Graham once again. But this time we relive the memories of King Graham as he tells about his epic adventures to his young granddaughter Gwendalyn. And with that said let's begin the review.
[The Story]
King Graham is becoming very old, but the tales are a long way from over. Graham is now on his older day, telling the stories of how he came to be where is now this very day, to his granddaugther Gwendalyn (Which is the daugther of Prince Alexander and Cassima from the prequal “Heir today, Gone tomorrow”). The stories goes gradually in chapters from how Graham became a knight, how he later on became king and afterwards what happened on his travels when he had become the ruler of Daventry.
Already in the 1. Chapter there has been fantastical creatures, colorful NPCs, epic enviroments, wonderful humor, and a delectable variety of puns, as we all that has played the prequals came to love the series for.
[Gameplay]
The gameplay of this game is very traditional for almost any point and click games out there. But this time the developers thought of the players which prefer to play with a controller and made the game so a controller port was the most natural in the world.
But as said before it is very traditional to the Point and Click genre and there are items to be picked up and puzzles to be solved all over the place. The puzzles are very clever and sometimes one needs to sit for a minute and think about what on earth could be the solution.
As it has become very popular to implement a multiple-choice mechanic into games as of late, to create some variation to the gameplay and test the players, so of course did the developers “The Odd Gentlemen” the same thing with this game. Not so much that it alters/changes the main story too much, but enough to create some originality to the individual players game and produce a sense of choice.
The deaths are as goofy as they were in the prequals, and to keep the tradition there will be sass after death happen. The only difference this time, is that it is Grahams granddaughter Gwendalyn that calls you out for being silly dying that way.
[Graphics]
The graphics are very pretty and special because the textures of everything in the game was handdrawn. It gives the game an epic and beautiful feeling while venturing forth in this fantastical world.
It's a 3d game but the handdrawn textures makes it look like something straight out of a storybook. Colorful and Beautiful.
[Sounds/Music]
The sounds in this game are very good and realistic to the real thing. Birds, wolves and even wind sounds like the real deal and with the graphics, creates a good enviroment for the players to immerge themselves in.
The music is mostly orcestral and has a nice epic feeling to it while you walk around in the enviroment.
The voiceacting are also very good and contains voiceactors that has a very successful career.
Voiceactor cast:
Chistopher Lloyd (The voiceactor of Emmett “Doc” Brown from Back to the Future, Uncle Fester from The Addams Family and Judge Doom from Who Framed Roger Rabbit)
Tom Kenny (The voiceactor of Spongebob SquarePants, Ice King from Adventure Time, Heffer Wolfe from Rocko's Modern Life, The Mayor and Narrator from The Powerpuff Girls, Carl from Johnny Bravo, Dog from CatDog, Eduardo from Foster's Home for Imaginary Friends, Rabbit from Winnie the Pooh and Spyro from the Spyro the Dragon franchise.)
Micheal Benyaer (That was a voiceactor in Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen)
Loretta Devine (That was a voiceactor in Crash)
Gideon Emery (Voiceactor from Teen Wolf)
Jean Gilpin (Voiceactor from Frozen)
Michael Gough (Voiceactor from Batman: Arkham Origins)
Andy Pessoa (Voiceactor from Transformers: Prime)
Kevin Michael Richardson (Voiceactor from The Cleveland Show)
Kath Soucie (Voiceactor from Rugrats)
Fred Tatasciore (Voiceactor from Marvel's Avengers Assemble)
Richard White (The voice of Gaston from Disney's Beauty and the Beast)
Micheal-Leon Wooley (Voice of Louis the Alligator from Disney's The Princess and the Frog)
[The Conclusion]
All in all I am fully in love with this game, and think of it as a great comeback to the series after 17 years since the last release. I find the world beautiful and interresting, the NPCs funny and well written, the story epic and worth immerging into and the Puzzles clever and challenging. I would fully recommend this game to anyone that like the Point and Click genre, or just likes to have a nice adventure infront of the screen. Or preferably both!

Do you like Resident Evil?
Do you like Silent Hill?
Do you like Alan Wake?
Do you overall like 3rd person atmospheric survival horror?
Did you play and enjoy the first game?
If your answer to any of the aforementioned questions is 'yes', then stop what you're doing right now and buy this game! Let the horror and weirdness galore begin!
FULL REVIEW SUMMARY:
Now, that I'm almost 80 hours into the game (and still not entirely done yet), I want to share my final thoughts on this incredible experience. Obviously, it's one of the best games I've played this year and there were a lot of good games. Now, I'm not good at categorizing reviews, so I'm going to summarize my thoughts as best as I can.
First of all, it's inevitable to compare it to the first game and I personally have mixed feelings here. There were a lot of great things in the first game that are absent in the second, but the second added some needed spice, especially for NG+, which immensely improved the replayability, which was very weird in TEW with the chapter selection nonsense. Right now, I'm attempting the classic mode and it's a total adrenaline rush! I know people loved the AKUMU mode in TEW, but it was a bit too much for me to handle, while classic mode is much more manageable.
I feel like if you're a diehard fan of the first TEW and RE4, you might be slightly disappointed, since the game ends up feeling way more mature and closer to RE7, minus the 1st person aspect, which to me was a huge plus. As a side note, I liked RE7, but kept asking myself "why is it in 1st person?", I really hope they'll be back to the classic 3rd person view in the future. Otherwise, the gameplay felt great! You got your green gel, but in addition, there's now a crafting system, which really added the much needed variety that the first game lacked. Both gun play and stealth feel great, mostly letting you decide how you want to approach certain situations.
At first, I wasn't on board with the open world sections of the game, but I eventually warmed up to them and now can't even imagine the game without them! The non open world areas are on a whole different level though, as they are stunning, confusing, horrifying and yet brilliant, as expected from the ingeniously twisted Shinji Mikami!
The enemies and especially the villains were great, not as iconic as the first, but still fascinating on their own. The story is great, while not being a direct continuation per se, but instead expends on a substory from the prequel. I've seen people debate on whether they should play the prequel and I say absolutely! While not being as great, at least in my opinion, there are too many references during the sequel, especially some throwbacks to the incredible DLC, that it might get a bit confusing as to what really happened in Beacon. Again, I highly suggest playing both, if you want the complete story experience, preferably playing both back to back.
To wrap it up, I cannot recommend this game enough, as it will sadly be overshadowed by many other great games coming out this Broketober. If you love 3rd person psychological survival horror, it's a must buy!

The game is tense, and does its best to make sure that you never feel safe, which is certainly a very different (and more exciting) brand of horror than the jump scares that are the norm of today. It's not even very dark most of the time, most of the horror is psychological and is driven by you doing your best to survive.
I feel that from a gameplay perspective, this vastly outshines Bioshock, or at least Bioshock Infitite. Well worth a try if you enjoyed the Bioshock series and are disappointed by the continual dumbing-down of its gameplay, or if you enjoyed Deus Ex, as it is very similar in terms of being a hybrid of tetris-inventory RPG and FPS gameplay.
The graphics are definitely where the game has not stood up the test of time, as even when it came out in 1999 it didn't look very good. However, there are mods such as SHTUP and Rebirth that improve the model and texture quality, the models being the most lacking back in the day.
In short: worth a try. It is perfectly compatible with modern systems, thanks to the recent NewDark patch, and is definitely worth it to see how much Bioshock Infinite has thrown away the series formula. And if you thought GLaDOS was the universe's scariest evil AI, you're in for a surprise.

System Shock 2 is, without a doubt, one of the most challenging and *literally* physically straining games that I have ever played. Any fans of Sci-fi, horror, or games like Dead Space and Bioshock should definitely give it a try. My own terrifying playthrough was 13 hours of hell. Instead of relying on jump scares, System Shock 2 prefers to latch on to your sanity and slowly pry. While the enemies aren't the most terrifying or challenging, your scenario is. Being completely alone an a vessel floating in the far reaches of space doesn't help put the mind at ease. The DETERIORATION of your weapons, to the point where they jam and are rendered useless, not to mention the scarcity of ammunition provides a healthy amount of fear. Health is also scarce, and it takes time to build skills for more efficient playing. Transversing the sheer magnitude of the Von Braun, entirely on foot, while avoiding enemies as much as possible made me tense enough to require regular chiropractic visits for the rest of my life. Not really, but it feels like it. Lastly, SHODAN's voice always haunts you, taunts you, breaks you. She never stops and she's always one step ahead. This game is a truly horrifying experience.

Great game. Who ever played a part of the Total War series knows the concept: you build up your own empire in a turn-based strategy part at a world map. Whenever one of your armies or fleets enters combat, you take command in classical real-time strategy manner. And most important: Rome II offers you to do this in 2-players coop.
Imho the concept is great. In the strategy part you manage your provinces, build buildings, recruit your army and do diplomatic stuff with other nations. You need to make sure that your forces don’t have to fight at too many fronts at the same time, take care of your finances and decide where to reinforce your armed forces with which kind of unit.
In tactical combat you command exactly the units that you brought to this battle. No wild reinforcement spamming or tower rushing like in other real-time strategy games. No artificial balancing. You have to fight out whatever situation your strategic decisions have lead to.
Basic combat principle is rock-paper-scissors: cavalry beats melee infantry -> melee infantry beats spear infantry -> spear infantry beats cavalry. Of course there are different version of each unit type (light, medium, heavy), ranged units (javelin men, archers), artillery, siege weapons, ships and even special units like wardogs and elephants (really bad♥♥♥♥♥..). And combat is influenced by a variety of other factors, e.g.:
- attacks in the flank or rear of a unit are quite effective
- units have a morale, and if it drops too low (e.g. due to effective enemy attacks, or other friendly units already fleeing) the unit might not follow your orders anymore and flee
- units fight better in formation
- weather (e.g. during rain you can’t use flammable arrows/javelins, during fog you can hardly see what’s going on at the battle field)
