I picked up Redux two days ago since I own the original Postal, Postal 2, Postal 3, and Paradise Lost. Aside from P3, the series is awesome. This remake did capture the original gameplay fairly well and the new rampage mode is fun, though difficult to score high on. That's probably due to my lack of skill with isometric shooters since Postal was probably the last one I played!
The graphics are goregeous, gameplay is smooth, and aside from the final level being completely different (ending too), the game was great. Being able to customize the controls is awesome, as I seem to recall installing the original Postal on Windows 7 had issues with controlling the dude. In fact, if you tried the original via GOG and were displeased, you REALLY should try this remake. It will leave you satisfied.
Now, the downside. While I love the game, there are two issues I have with it. The first is that Windows randomly pops up a message about low memory while playing, and the second is that the sound doesn't always work. It shouldn't be my system as I exceed the minimum requirements and at idle have less than 20% of my memory used. In fact, I have a 2.8GHz dual-core i3, SB X-Fi Gamer with 64MB SRAM, and 4GB of system memory. The minimum is 4GB, but I would expect minimum to work, especially as I exceed everything else. The worst part was that when the ending video sequence took place all I heard was clicking or popping. It wasn't the original ending so I am not sure what I was seeing. Hopefully these issues will be fixed in future patches.
Overall, I would reccomend the game to anybody. It was a blast playing it and the price is fair.
*UPDATE*
The game uses the Unreal Engine 4. 4GB is the minimum as this is a 64bit game engine. Placing this onto an i5-2500 with 16GB of RAM fixed everything. I even tried this on an older system of mine, a Pentium D 960 with 4GB of RAM and the game ran well enough to beat. To those complaining about long load times, get a system that was built in the last five years and you're golden. I did experience long load times on the Pentium D (Dell XPS400) system, but it has PCI-E 1.0 and the original SATA specification! SATA2 or 3 and the game loads in about fifteen seconds. Throw RAID0/5/10 under it and it would probably be better.

POSTAL Redux
Isometric Shooter
Running With Scissors
Running With Scissors
is a remastered version of the 1997 isometric shooter developed and published by Running With Scissors. I played the original game multiple times (even with its outdated controls) and I love the FPS sequel. I can safely say that this is a remaster done right.
Honestly, there is basically no story. You play as the Postal Dude, a guy who is fed up of the world and goes postal (which is, go on a killing spree). Compared to its sequels, this is much more bleak and depressing and neither funny nor satirical. However, it also isn't offensive and controversial just for the sake of it (
).
The game adopts the original isometric camera angle, and updates the look of the original art style, bringing back some good ol' nostalgia. Each level feels different from the other, ranging from city ghettos and mines, to carnivals and small towns with marching bands. The only thing that kinda looks outdated are the character models, and the environments do lack color variety, but it fits the grim tone that the game is going for like a glove.
What I would really like to see in a future update is a little bit more gore: right now there are only head exploding if you execute people with the shotgun and burned bodies if they got hit by fire. I would love to see gibs when you use the rocket launchers, or limb removals when a grenade goes off.
The game is a twin-stick shooter with a simple goal: to kill every hostile in the level. You start off with a machine gun, and you slowly start acquiring an arsenal of death featuring shotguns, flamethrowers, rocket launchers, and even an all-new revolver. There are also civilians (and sometimes even animals) that can be killed, earning this game the title of
.
The controls are very smooth, especially compared to the original version: simply being able to aim and shoot using the mouse changes the entire game. There is also a new game mode called Rampage, which is a Score Attack mode with lots more civilians and enemies in the levels, encouraging the players to use different weapons and playstyles to get higher scores.
The enemy AI is decent, and usually plays more on the defensive staying behind walls and covers instead of rushing towards the player. (On the higher difficulty levels especially), they deal a lot of damage, so keeping check of the location of every single health pack in the levels is paramount.
The updated soundtrack and sound effects are great: the hard-rock music pumping through the levels keeps the adrenaline up to 11, and the screams of agonising civilians who are about to get their head blown off by a shotgun blast are oh so satisfying.
The game features the original 17 levels (with the ones from the expansion pack to be released later for free) and the new Rampage mode. Also, knowing the developers, the game will be constantly updated for years to come, and I wouldn't be surprised if they manage to add even more levels, Workshop support, multiplayer modes and even new DLC just like they did for the now 13-year-old POSTAL 2.
Overall, this is a very fun and satisfying twin-stick shooter with good replayability and with multiple updates to come. Highly recommended to fans of the genre and of the original game. And it definitely is better than Hatred.

I had high hopes for Just Cause 3. and
of them were met. I personally neither really liked nor really disliked Just Cause 3, but I wouldn't recommend it in its current state, unless you really liked JC2.
For the people that really liked Just Cause 2 and want improvement on that, you'll get what you want...mostly. Some things are changed in odd ways, like the races now essentially being mandatory for progression. And anyone who played JC2 knows that the races are one of the worst parts. It feels like a way that they're padding the experience, but that's OK, because spending time in the world of JC3 is very fun. It feels like an actual world, and I love that.
The destruction in JC3 is an improvement, but it also gets really boring after a while. The actual engine for destruction is good...but they're using it on the same bases and cities, and it feels very copy/pasted all over the map. Explosions are definitely an improvement for taking bases rather than those collectible boxes from JC2.
The race and collectible upgrade system have been combined. You get "Gear Mods" depending on what race and how well you did. Those let you upgrade your cars, grappling hook, nitro boost, and others. No matter what it is, though, it realy feels like it's padding the game, because in order to get 5 gears, you really have to do EVERYTHING ABSOLUTELY PERFECTLY. It isn't great.
A good thing they did was take away Sheldon's helicopter. No more Air Sheldon, thank goodness. The Black Market system has been replaced with the Rebel Drop system, where you can either unlock vehicles/weapons through base destruction (for some), or you take a vehicle to a Garage (a specific spot in a town, unlocked after taking the town over) and you can then spawn that vehicle whenever you want - with a catch. You see, JC3 has removed the money system in favor of a waiting system. You can only spawn a vehicle/weapon every couple minutes, and that time is based on how good the vehicle is. There isn't a way to skip the wait without cheating, or unlocking a specific Gear Mod that reduces the time, which means doing more challenges.
I personally liked JC3, but there are a lot of parts of it that I really wish could change. It's still a fun game, but it really is a weak successor to Just Cause 2.
VERDICT: I would say wait...for now. If they patch some things, then it will be awesome! Until then, if you have $60 to spend, buy Fallout 4. And DEFINITELY wait if you have an AMD graphics card. It's just absolutely broken on them,

King's Quest is absolutely gorgeous (every single texture was hand painted and scanned into the game) and incredibly entertaining. Daventry is lovingly crafted in this reimagining, fans of the series will enjoy references to past entries and newcomers will enjoy that the puzzles actually make sense this time. Using a mysterious skill called 'logic,' players don't go around using everying on everything else in hopes of progressing but instead use items is ways that make a lot more sense.  There are multiple ways to solve each puzzle too, which gives the game great replayability. The only slightly dissapointing part of the game are the quick time events (of which there are only two, at the begining and end) and the inability to skip dialoge. The qtes, while still enjoyable, feel disconnected from the rest of the experience and didn't give the player enough time to react, thanks to numerous, forgiving checkpoints King Grahms hillarious, plentiful puns however death was made enjoyable.  This could be one of the best games to come out this year, and as of writing this, only chaper one of five (and an epiloge if you buy the whole game at once) is out.
As a side note, I think Life Is Strange by Dontnod is a great companion to this game, both feature astounding amounts of choice in varying importance and with LIS's more serious nature complements King's Quest's sillyness very well.
TLDR
Go buy it now. You'll love it, I promise.

System Shock 2 is, without a doubt, one of the most challenging and *literally* physically straining games that I have ever played. Any fans of Sci-fi, horror, or games like Dead Space and Bioshock should definitely give it a try. My own terrifying playthrough was 13 hours of hell. Instead of relying on jump scares, System Shock 2 prefers to latch on to your sanity and slowly pry. While the enemies aren't the most terrifying or challenging, your scenario is. Being completely alone an a vessel floating in the far reaches of space doesn't help put the mind at ease. The DETERIORATION of your weapons, to the point where they jam and are rendered useless, not to mention the scarcity of ammunition provides a healthy amount of fear. Health is also scarce, and it takes time to build skills for more efficient playing. Transversing the sheer magnitude of the Von Braun, entirely on foot, while avoiding enemies as much as possible made me tense enough to require regular chiropractic visits for the rest of my life. Not really, but it feels like it. Lastly, SHODAN's voice always haunts you, taunts you, breaks you. She never stops and she's always one step ahead. This game is a truly horrifying experience.

System Shock 2 is a game that a lot of modern shooters try and fail to emulate, because there was a cult classic love to it that wasn't because of any overused horror trope or any trendy game mechanic. No, the game actually broke from all of the standards by incorporating RPG elements along with its FPS style. You'll hear some people complain about the inventory system. Others will be hung up on the late-nineties graphics (which are close to those of the original Half-Life). I even have one friend who stopped playing simply because he couldn't take one of the enemies seriously.
Don't listen to these people who get hung up on the small stuff, and don't be surprised by the difficulty that the game presents you. System Shock 2 was made back when games weren't willing to sacrifice quality just to get you to the ending credits and the obligatory sequel teaser trailer. It's a game that makes you consistently and intelligently plan your way through in order to survive, let alone make progress, aboard the Von Braun. There are multiple ways to play the game, with different types of weapons, and many skills and strengths to invest in. This means extreme replay value, and ensures that you won't get bored quickly.
My advice to you is to pick up this game for yourself and make your own opinion. If you come into it with a modern bias, you might not give yourself a chance to enjoy it. Just install it, play it, and see where it takes you.
And my biggest tip? For the first time through, put yourself on Away, log off of your communication devices and programs (Skype, AIM, et al.), and play System Shock 2 alone. The experience alone will leave you wanting more.
Just to add to all the other positive reviews - this is one of the best games I ever played - my only disappointment was that Bioshock wasn't "System Shock 3" (still annoyed about that!).

First off, if you don't know what the gameplay in Postal is like, its a slower paced twinstick shooter. It not blazing fast like Hotline Miami, nor is it some top down tactical shooter, but its also not a standard twinstick with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of people being thrown at you, like Total Carnage or Smash TV. To describe it, I'd say its like a bunch of seperate scenarios being put together to make a cohesive level. Some levels are smaller or more populated and end up playing out as almost non stop fighting, as you inevitably will anger one crowd while fighting another. Other levels are more spacious and allow you to come up with a simple strategy to follow through on when you move in. Its a great mix of thinking before you act, and acting without thinking.
The improvements all around from the original Postal 1 are all welcome. The controls are smooth as silk, and you no longer need a controller to have twinstick style controls. Some weapon rebalancing is also present, and working with the new control scheme the gameplay has more skill and strategy to it rather than just "crawl forwards slowly and pray to ♥♥♥♥ing jesus you dont die." The overall sound design is fantastic once more, and the atmosphere is just as stellar as it was in the original game. Also you can wear the original Red Coat, or pink if you're feeling particularly gay like I do sometimes.
Currently though, one thing to remember is this game as of whenever this is being posted, the game is an investment. Right now you get a solid campaign that lasts different lengths of time depending on the difficulty (about 1 hour on normal, 3-4 on hard), and you get the rampage mode if you enjoy score attack type stuff. RWS has confirmed co-op, deathmatch, the expansion levels, brand new levels, iirc a nightmare mode difficulty, and potentially a few extra things if all goes well. RWS is really ♥♥♥♥in' passionate about Postal Redux and it shows with how much they're talking about it. tl;dr: Hatred: the good version
Well, after much hype in P2: Paradise Lost, Postal Redux has released.  And I've got to say, it's an awesome game.
For those who don't know, Postal Redux is a remake of Postal, a 1997 PC game.  You play as the Postal Dude, an archetypal mass murderer who snaps, arms himself and "goes postal".  Your goal is to murder a set amount of enemies in order to procede to the next stage.  In addition to the enemies are unarmed civilians, who you can choose to gun down or spare at your discretion.  To put it simply, Postal Redux plays like an arcade shooter (think Robotron or Smash TV).  The original Postal had some unique concepts, including hand drawn backgrounds and a disturbing view into the mind of a spree killer; however, it was marred by god awful controls, difficulty spikes and poor sound quality.  Thankfully, Postal Redux remedies these problems. While keyboard and mouse controls are still a bit bizarre, the controls are excellent with a joystick.  The visuals have been updated, and while the 3D models aren't triple A quality, the backgrounds are still illustrated nicely.  New content has also been added, including the highly powerful revolver, a carnival stage (with armed clowns!), and the new "Rampage" mode, which is a score attack, arcade-y mode focused on combo kills, variety and speed (complete with great music).
While these revisions and additions are great, the game right now has one key issue: length.  Beating the campaign on hard takes a few hours at most, and as of right now, there's no multiplayer.  The Special Delivery maps and Super Postal maps are also missing.  However, multiplayer and new maps will be added in free updates in the future (according to Running With Scissors).
All in all, Postal Redux is an interesting game, much like the original Postal.  As wrong as it may seem to some, there's something I find therapeutic about gunning a group of digital people down, and thankfully, this is what Redux does best.  While the game is good, it's lacking in content currently, so if you have reservations about the game's length, wait for RWS to update it, or wait for a sale.  If you aren't a fan of psychological horror games or senseless murder, you may want to stay clear of this one: if you're a fan of the Postal series, psychological horror games, arcade shoot 'em ups, an angsty teenager, someone who likes to attack random pedestrians in Grand Theft Auto, or all of the above, I'd definetly recommend Postal Redux.

Just Cause 3 as a game is borderline acceptable. In some ways its more than Just Cause 2 but that doesn't automatically make it better. The devs seem too preoccupied with making a "huge" world instead of a well designed and fun to explore world. The map could be 1/10th the size and still big enough to be fun if it were well designed and balanced.
You basically have 3 types of towns and 4 types of bases and they're copied and pasted across the map with little difference between them. In between these areas are voids of nothing compelling, nothing pretty, basically nothing but roads and trees. So...what's the point? It's not fun traversing between these areas and it's still repetitive any way you shake it. You'd almost have to be crazy to consistently drive on land in these areas as the world is so huge you'll take far too much time. Not that the selection of cars is really all the enticing to begin with.
It's an odd choice for a game like this to have more land vehicles than weapons, since you'll rarely want to use them anyway. A lot of stuff unlocks a bit too late to be of any fun unless you're achievement hunting. But even then, after you raze a couple towns and bases it's just all the same because there's so little variety and the military bases aren't nearly as fun to destroy as they were in Just Cause 2.
Most critically, the destructible objects - or rather I guess buildings and structures- in this game are less than the previous games and there's hardly anything new to destroy compared to Just Cause 2. This makes the most compelling aspect of the game, tethering and the physics, a bit less fun that it could have been. There also aren't enough physic related weapons/bombs. A real missed opportunity.
Just Cause 2 shares some similar problems but overall its world was better designed and the bases were more cleverly arranged and designed.
Porting and DRM issues aside, it's hard to recommend this game if you loved Just Cause 2 like most everyone else. Technically the game engine is better, graphics are better if you can actually play the game, but overall the game design is worse, the game world is worse, and this game feels more of the same in all the wrong ways.
Recommended if you're new to Just Cause 3 and can play this, but really you're still better off just playing Just Cause 2. If you've played Just Cause 2 and couldn't wait to get more, well be careful what you wish for because this game is bound to disappoint you after the dust settles from the first 5 hours of gameplay.
If you're waiting for patches to play this game properly,  the game is much more playable after the second patch so long as you have a decent nvidia graphics card, 16GB of RAM and don't go above 1080 resolution.

I had high hopes for Just Cause 3. and
of them were met. I personally neither really liked nor really disliked Just Cause 3, but I wouldn't recommend it in its current state, unless you really liked JC2.
For the people that really liked Just Cause 2 and want improvement on that, you'll get what you want...mostly. Some things are changed in odd ways, like the races now essentially being mandatory for progression. And anyone who played JC2 knows that the races are one of the worst parts. It feels like a way that they're padding the experience, but that's OK, because spending time in the world of JC3 is very fun. It feels like an actual world, and I love that.
The destruction in JC3 is an improvement, but it also gets really boring after a while. The actual engine for destruction is good...but they're using it on the same bases and cities, and it feels very copy/pasted all over the map. Explosions are definitely an improvement for taking bases rather than those collectible boxes from JC2.
The race and collectible upgrade system have been combined. You get "Gear Mods" depending on what race and how well you did. Those let you upgrade your cars, grappling hook, nitro boost, and others. No matter what it is, though, it realy feels like it's padding the game, because in order to get 5 gears, you really have to do EVERYTHING ABSOLUTELY PERFECTLY. It isn't great.
A good thing they did was take away Sheldon's helicopter. No more Air Sheldon, thank goodness. The Black Market system has been replaced with the Rebel Drop system, where you can either unlock vehicles/weapons through base destruction (for some), or you take a vehicle to a Garage (a specific spot in a town, unlocked after taking the town over) and you can then spawn that vehicle whenever you want - with a catch. You see, JC3 has removed the money system in favor of a waiting system. You can only spawn a vehicle/weapon every couple minutes, and that time is based on how good the vehicle is. There isn't a way to skip the wait without cheating, or unlocking a specific Gear Mod that reduces the time, which means doing more challenges.
I personally liked JC3, but there are a lot of parts of it that I really wish could change. It's still a fun game, but it really is a weak successor to Just Cause 2.
VERDICT: I would say wait...for now. If they patch some things, then it will be awesome! Until then, if you have $60 to spend, buy Fallout 4. And DEFINITELY wait if you have an AMD graphics card. It's just absolutely broken on them,

After playing this game for 20 hours more than the original - and that was with all its DLC - I think it's time to review Dishonored 2.
I've seen a lot of anger directed towards the game because of its lack of PC optimisation, and while I can understand why people feel the way they do, I think that it's important to view the game in a larger scope. I know it's difficult when many cannot even play it - though I personally didn't encounter any issues so gamebreaking that it really affected me - but it's clear that the developers spent a lot of time and energy to make this game, and that should be noted.
The devs' love for the world they have handcrafted is apparent in the level design and art, with the same standout style that was present in the original, now improved. The paint-like textures are back, and more high-res and beautiful than ever. It's a joy just to be immersed in Karnaca (and Dunwall) as I roam the streets and buildings trying to find all the little nooks that Arkane hid for those interested in exploration. I'm on my second run and
coming across new places that I missed on my first, even though I tried to be as thorough as possible at the time; my first playthrough was 42 hours long!
Furthermore, the lore-building through notes and audiographs, as well as NPC conversations, make the city a living, breathing thing. Though sometimes it gets a bit overwhelming having so much text to comb through, it's optional, and it's awesome that a choice is given to the players - if you really want to delve deep into the "Songs of Serkonos, Part II", you are free to do so. If not, you can just move on.
I think another strong point of Dishonored 2 is how different each mission is. There is a basic premise, but every locale is varied in interesting ways, and there are a few missions where the 'gimmick' (or theme, I guess) was incredible. This means that the game never really gets stale, because, besides one area which was 'repeated' - though still changed - you are moving through a completely new situation every mission. The huge amount of alternate routes and hidden nooks that I mentioned earlier, as well as the tools you are given to traverse them, build upon the variety in level design and create a strong sense of player agency.
Though you get clues from the game on how to go through a mission, you can turn off tutorials and other markers (I've been playing without the objective marker, and it's been awesome - strongly recommend it, if you want to immerse yourself even more) to figure it out yourself, then choose the route that fits best for your playstyle. It's not forced in any way, and I think this sandbox approach to problem solving is done really well in Dishonored 2 - much like it was in the first game.
The increased amount of options and new powers are great fun for newcomers and veterans of the series as well, I think. There's now more ways to go about nonlethal (that drop head slam though!) and lethal, as well as stealth or assault, and Emily's powers are
The team have changed the movement controls and powers to feel more smooth, too, which makes the experience so much more thrilling and powerful.
However, this game is not without its flaws. There's obviously the optimisation issue, and though my game ran mostly fine, I did, and still do, crash occasionally. There are also some weird audio glitches that the devs need to fix, where the audio stutters or stops when I'm running around. It's hard to judge where guards and other people are because of that. Also, I think a few of the bonecharms are broken - I know Strong Arms actually causes choking to take
not shorter, which is an annoyance for non-lethal runs.
I thought that the overarching plot was also quite mediocre. Each level did a great job of telling its own little story, but the main premise of having your throne taken away from you, then having to fight for it back, was just 'meh'. It's quite cliche, and the opening intro was way too fast. It didn't build and allow me to care much for Emily or get a feel for how she was as a ruler before the rug was pulled out from under me. It feels quite contrived, I think is the word.
There are also some cringey lines spoken by the protagonist as well, which is a fault of the writers, not the voice actors. I know Emily has this one line after an occurrence where she says something along the lines of "I feel different. How will I change after all of this?" out loud! It's a 'yikes' moment for sure.
The characterisation is decent (the notes and newspapers are great for information, and I think the different powers given to Corvo and Emily are actually a fantastic way of implying certain personality traits), but I was underwhelmed by Delilah, the main antagonist, and how her story got resolved. The last level in particular was so anticlimactic! That was a big disappointment for me.
The voice acting is also only
Emily and Delilah's voice actors did a wonderful job with the lines they were given, but I'm not so fond of most of the other characters. They didn't sound too convincing, I don't think. There's a nice spectrum of voices, but some of the performances are quite lukewarm. Duke Luca Abele was such a caricature that I didn't really mind him, though.
But despite all the negatives I've mentioned, I think the good far outweighs the bad. Waiting for the winter sale or another discount to lower the price would be wise, though, because then you can get the patches as they are released and hopefully a more stable game.
Overall, I think Dishonored 2 is gorgeous, fun, and caters to all types of players. It has a few negatives, such as weak voice acting, some mediocre writing, and the optimisation issues, but the former two are not the reason I play this series, and the latter will be improved upon in time. I'd still wholeheartedly recommend it.

I was pretty excited when I heard that King's Quest was being rebooted, having played and thoroughly enjoyed every one of the originals. It was definitely one of my favorite series growing up. This one however, does not stack up very well to its predecessors, or even the genre to which it is supposed to represent. The puzzles are not challenging in the slightest. The interaction with the overworld is pathetic. In the old games you actually had to do some searching and use your brain to find items and solve problems. Now, all you have to do is wander around until a spacebar popup indicates that there is something to interact with. It used to be rewarding when I solved a puzzle. Now it feels empty because of all the spoonfeeding. There wasn't single time where I was lost. I always knew what I had to do next. There were many times when I felt they were overly goofy. They shoehorned jokes in at wrong times. I didn't think it was supposed to be Monkey Island or Space Quest. There was levity in the originals, but in wasn't overdone, and never detracted from what was occurring.
But the game wasn't wholly bad. There are an abundance of nods to the original series, and I had a couple good laughs encountering each one. The voice acting is very well done, the music is good, and I appreciated the art style. I enjoyed the overall narrative (There are a couple really exceptional parts to it) and Graham's granddaughter. She is how I imagine a younger version of Rosella would have been!
So overall, I wouldn't recommend this game if you are expecting a game similar to the original King's Quest series. 2/5. But for those who have never played the originals, it probably wouldn't be as bad of an experience. I do have the season pass, so hopefully they can continue to make improvements. After you are done go check out the original series. There are free remakes of KQ 1 - 3 (4 is in the works) in the style of 5 and 6 and they should give you a real challenge!

**UPDATE Aug 21, 2016**
I've played chapter 2 and 3 now and while they are well done, you can tell a lot more was cut out this time around or not enough time was given to really flesh things out as much as the first chapter was. Methinks ActiVision is slashing their budget after not meeting some monetery goals or something. Which is a shame as these chapters deserve every care that they put into the first one and all the attention from the audience that they're apparently not getting.
Chapter 2 made things much less linear but also self-contained into one area that you continually unlock more areas to as you go on with mechanics that mirror that of King's Quest 3 very closely. This one took me quite a lot longer to complete, and not just because I put it down for a few months while I moved on to other games. It's a great head-scratcher full of puzzles and makes up for the next chapter which is a little more light in that area.
Chapter 3 especially is quite charming and cleverly deals with the damsel-in-distress trope in a way that doesn't discount fairy tale fun but simply makes things more interesting (even if it completely retcons most if not all of the events of King's Quest 2). This was a carefully balance to achieve and I wasn't looking forward to it but it was very carefully, lovingly, and tastefully well done. Just play it and you'll find out why. It was very carefully and tastefull well done. A lot of it seems like it plays as a visual novel with dialogue puzzles, but the classic puzzle solving is still here, if a little more lax than even the first chapter. I enjoyed the moments in the beginning as you're traveling to the tower. It's like a montage in a movie where the adventurer is crossing the countryside with their goal in sight, except that you get to PLAY those little 5-second scenes (some of which contain some light action mechanics) which was very effective with the visuals and the music! The best scene in the game is towards the end. I won't say anything more but it was quite an epic moment that the music again especially drives forward with surprising vigor and sheer...just...epicness. Together with the game mechanics it's sort of like a timed action sequence but it was a very enjoyable one that I was delighted turned out to be just the right length (not too short and not too long). The music is timed perfectly to the sequence and it's just spectacular. I'd say if not for the fact that there wasn't as much content as the first chapter nor a lot of puzzles, this would be my favourite chapter so far...and it still might be. The storytelling in this chapter was the best yet. Give it a go! Oh, I also loved the little owl easter egg puzzle in the intro (and the narrator's jibes about the player's feelings toward it lol).
I just wish they'd put a lot more puzzle branching like Chapter 2 into things. Or even more than that. The fact that it's episodic is probably to blame here. You just can't do things the same way as you can with a grand full complete adventure game with a giant interconnected world. But as far as episodic releases go, I think this is the best done yet. From what I've played anyway. I still like these games. They're not classic adventure games, but they're very good if you enjoy them for what they are.
***Original Review***
It's quite good. Quite easy and short. But good. It's not exactly authentic to the original games in some ways, but in atmosphere it certainly is and then adds tons of its own charm that was surprisingly not unwelcome, to a hardcore oldschool King's Quest adventure game fan like me. My concerns and qualms before playing spanned things like not having enough interactions or things to interact with, but one thing this game prove me wrong on was the humour. I had said that it should be more serious and less whimsical. However, after playing it I actually laughed out loud on multiple occassions. I wasn't expecting it to be as funny as it was. It wasn't all humour, but the humour that was there was genuinely funny. I never found even Telltale's games as amusing (I used to be a fan of Telltale in the beginning before they showed their true colours and abhorance for actual adventure game design). So I'll let the humour and whimsy pass because it was done so well. The puns weren't what was funny, either, but I didn't mind them regardless. It does prove that it CAN be serious as well, though, which is a relief (even though that one serious part seemed to come out of left field quite abruptly) and gives me hope for future chapters, especially as Graham gets older.
The graphics are fantastic, the voice acting superb (not a dry delivery among the actors, except where it was amusingly fitting), the music score and cues are incredible and timed perfectly and intricately to the action on screen, and the pacing is great. It was longer than I expected, but still short and I didn't ever really get stuck. I beat it in 5 hours or so. I took one break after wandering for a bit because I was tired and took a nap. But I was never really stuck. Each solution seemed easy enough. That said, I didn't solve EVERY puzzle immediately either. So it wasn't all flash boom bang done.
It probably won't happen, but I hope in future chapters TOG will allow us to do more things with more objects. Look at, use, talk, etc with everything instead of just having one interaction per hotspot. Also would welcome extending the puzzle chains a bit. Good easy start so far. Reels both new players and old ones out of practice in. If TOG amped up the difficulty for each chapter as it goes it would show them what a real adventure is again! One other qualm (and the biggest one by far) is that there is no way to skip dialogue or cutscenes you've already heard/watched. This needs to change.
I don't need fast travel like everyone's saying in reviews. I enjoyed getting around just fine. I would like to see more large and beautiful grand scenes, though, even bigger than we've seen so far. I'm thinking something from the perspective of the town in KQ5 where characters are very small but with more to do and more areas to see than just the three shops in that town in KQ5. Just less roads. I think that's the biggest issue people might have. Wandering and exploring is fun but all the roads connecting them are uninteresting and make the world seem small, ironically. But I still don't welcome fast travel. The areas and graphics in general are very pretty. Skipping exploration and avoiding wandering around would be like playing Jurassic Park The Game by Telltale (which cut out walking altogether...MISSING THE POINT!!!).

I got into the POSTAL series very late. I received POSTAL 2 from a friend only a couple years ago. I played POSTAL 1 shortly after falling in love with POSTAL 2, and once Paradise Lost came out I was in love again. But then, once I'd played Paradise Lost as much as I could, I fell out of the loop again. Until recently anyway.
POSTAL Redux is an HD remake of the game that started it all, POSTAL. And I couldn't possibly be happier to say that it's nothing short of amazing.
Positives:
+Rick Hunter. I don't care if this is a cop out. He has a voice of gold, and as long as he lives, The Dude will live.
+It kept it's dark humor. When I see games based on "Dark humor" I always get worried what they mean by that. Do they mean that they occasionally make a slightly offensive joke, or do they do it RIGHT. POSTAL managed to do it right, and Redux kept it. When you pull a flamethrower out and hear the words "Need a light?", or pull a revolver out and hear The Dude laugh, you know that it's just good.
+They actually added stuff as well ISN'T THAT FUNNY FOR A SUPPOSED REMAKE. No but seriously, a lot has been added, like a new ending, the ability to change your character to multiple separate colors, even back to the ORIGINAL Red Trenchcoat, a completely new game mode called rampage which is basically the rampage missions from the early GTA games in which you kill as many people as you can and count your score. Then there's my favorite, they added executions for all the different weapons. Now you're no longer restricted to executing with the M16/SMG, now you can execute them all with them all.
+They fixed the controls. The original POSTAL controlled like a no armed man trying to use a chainsaw. AKA IT DIDN'T. The controls in Redux are now smooth, and best of all: PLAYABLE
Negatives:
-I have had the occasional bug. Total Bore: Rome II
Just the same things as the other Total Wars, with better graphics, but even poorer AI and interface, and game breaking bugs.
So, the combat has all the defects of previous total wars, the AI is idiotic and your armies like to take strange paths that get them killed if you don't constantly micro manage them. The extra bonus in Rome II is that in addition to being idiots when they move they are also idiots when they fight. If you order 1000 soldiers to fight 10 enemies, they will just send 10 soldiers in to perform their man-to-man combat animation, when the other 990 just stand there and do nothing as they wait for one of the soldiers to die to send one more in... utterly useless.
The Naval combats are ridiculous and ships near impossible to control. Naval units - which come in a whole variety and have many upgrades - are useless in the first place because whilst they cost a substantial amount of money they are actually weaker than regular armies (which just get ships for free).
The strategy phase is both uninteresting and irritating. It marries obscure and fiddly controls and moves with unpredictable outcomes, with a poorly designed interface. If you want to see more details about the buildings or units your are purchasing, you have no other choice than to right click and open a horribly designed wiki, which opens on top of your game in a separate annoying window. Each wiki page contains poorly written descriptions for 30 separate nations and you need to scroll and find yours among the other useless 29.
The tutorials are extremely poorly designed and don't teach you much about the game, so either you are going to have to read that horrible in-game wiki window thoroughly, or just accept the random things that happen constantly like your generals dying of plague suddenly, as random events - which they probably are.
The game is also buggy and crashes. I've lost the ability to progress in my campaign, because of a 100% crash when I try and invade this city, where when my first soldier reaches the city wall the game crashes.
It baffles me that this game got such high reviews, when this is clearly the worse of all the Total War games available. The only thing I got impressed with is that each soldier now has a different and unique face, hurrah! But that doesn't make up for the 100% crashes and the abysmal interface.

I had high hopes for Just Cause 3. and
of them were met. I personally neither really liked nor really disliked Just Cause 3, but I wouldn't recommend it in its current state, unless you really liked JC2.
For the people that really liked Just Cause 2 and want improvement on that, you'll get what you want...mostly. Some things are changed in odd ways, like the races now essentially being mandatory for progression. And anyone who played JC2 knows that the races are one of the worst parts. It feels like a way that they're padding the experience, but that's OK, because spending time in the world of JC3 is very fun. It feels like an actual world, and I love that.
The destruction in JC3 is an improvement, but it also gets really boring after a while. The actual engine for destruction is good...but they're using it on the same bases and cities, and it feels very copy/pasted all over the map. Explosions are definitely an improvement for taking bases rather than those collectible boxes from JC2.
The race and collectible upgrade system have been combined. You get "Gear Mods" depending on what race and how well you did. Those let you upgrade your cars, grappling hook, nitro boost, and others. No matter what it is, though, it realy feels like it's padding the game, because in order to get 5 gears, you really have to do EVERYTHING ABSOLUTELY PERFECTLY. It isn't great.
A good thing they did was take away Sheldon's helicopter. No more Air Sheldon, thank goodness. The Black Market system has been replaced with the Rebel Drop system, where you can either unlock vehicles/weapons through base destruction (for some), or you take a vehicle to a Garage (a specific spot in a town, unlocked after taking the town over) and you can then spawn that vehicle whenever you want - with a catch. You see, JC3 has removed the money system in favor of a waiting system. You can only spawn a vehicle/weapon every couple minutes, and that time is based on how good the vehicle is. There isn't a way to skip the wait without cheating, or unlocking a specific Gear Mod that reduces the time, which means doing more challenges.
I personally liked JC3, but there are a lot of parts of it that I really wish could change. It's still a fun game, but it really is a weak successor to Just Cause 2.
VERDICT: I would say wait...for now. If they patch some things, then it will be awesome! Until then, if you have $60 to spend, buy Fallout 4. And DEFINITELY wait if you have an AMD graphics card. It's just absolutely broken on them,

King's Quest is an adventure game developed by a small indie studio named "The Odd Gentlemen" released in summer of 2015. As of writing this review, currently I have only played the first episode as it is the only one released and available. However, I believe that this will give us a good idea of what is to come.
At first I did not think much of this game, but as I had just gotten into adventure games about a month prior and had consumed all the major ones available, I decided I would give it a try. So, using my newly refunded money from another 10 dollar game I was not satisfied with, I purchased it and decided to give it a go. As it turned out, I was very pleasantly surprised.
I will admit that at first I was not too impressed. The graphical style was very similar to that of a Telltale game (Not that I dislike Telltale's style, but I was hoping for something slightly different) and there was a lack of pretty much any anti-aliasing options. On top of that, I found myself thrown into the game with no introduction of what was going on. However, while the first couple minutes were a bit difficult to adjust into, I found that the game quickly picked up.
The game has a relatively light-hearted feel to it, and I found myself laughing along to a lot of the cheap puns and quirky jokes thrown into the mix. The characters were fairly memorable too, and I enjoyed pretty much everyone I came across. A particular favorite of mine was Whisper, a very pompous knight who is infatuated with none other than himself. The game gives you a lot of room to roam around, similar to the style of many old adventure games and RPGs. As this is only the first episode, I do not know how much the decisions you make actually matter, but I found myself entertained regardless with virtually every aspect of gameplay.
The setting of the game was enchanting as well. Set in a fantasy environment, you will encounter many creatures such as dragons, bridge trolls, and even intelligent squirrels. As the game allows you to roam freely while you solve various puzzles, you will typically find yourself roaming through dark caves, villages, and ominous forests. The music pairs up with this very well, and really immerses you into the game world. Honestly, the only complaint I can think of with this game is that you are not able to skip cutscenes should you fail some events, however I am sure they plan on doing something about this in the future.
In conclusion, I came into King's Quest not expecting much more than some mediocre adventure game to occupy a couple hours of my time. However after playing for a total of 7 hours on merely one chapter, and enjoying nearly every minute of it, I exited finding myself very pleasantly surprised, and eagerly awaiting the next episode. I implore anyone who has not played this yet to give it a go, I sincerely doubt you will be disapointed. My final score for King's Quest is a
, a must buy for any adventure game lover, and I look forward to playing any future installments.

Slime Ranchers surprised me. I have seen it o sthe steam store before but was never interested. When the full version came out I saw a few reviews and that got me interested. The gameplay looked fun, the graphics good and everybody loved it. The game was 14 on sale and I decided to try it. Boy, am I glad I did. I have only played the game two times and played it for 7 hours at the time of the review. The last time that happend was with Singularity.
You play as Beatrix LeBeau, a young woman who decides that she ant to become a slime rancher on the "Far, Far Range". The gameplay is great. You have to capture slimes using your vac pack. You then put them in corals that can be built in certain places on your farm. Then you have to feed them. Feeding them gives you plorts, a crystal like substance (and their poop). The plorts are then sold for newbucks. If the slimes are not fed they will try to escape and if the do escape unnoticed they will destroy your farm. (Eating the plats, chickens and even plorts.
You then use the newbucks to buy new pieces of gear, land and farming plots. There are a lot of different slimes and each have their own diet. Some eat everything and have no faverote food. Others only eat meat and have their faverote food. Giving a slime his faveroute food gives you twoice the plorts they would ormally drop. Then you can mix tow slime types by giving them plorts from another slime. If to many slime types are mixed they will turn into Tarr slimes. Tarr slimes eat everything in sight and will attack the player. The only way to defeat them is with water. You can also build chicken coops and farm with chickens, only for a food source.
You can build gardens. You can explore the world, altough most areas are blocked off. Unlocking new areas usually requires you to feed a certian slime time (Called Gordo`s) until the explode. This reveals a key the "ate". There is also a science lab to unlock, although I haven`t unlocked it yet. There are aslo gear upgrades, house upgrades and even a exchange (Where you tade other rancher items for items). I have only played the first area and will update the review when I played the other areas. Recommecded for everyone.
P.S. The devs included a nice bug report system. By pressing F2 a small text screen will pop up ingame. You bsimply type in the bug you experienced and the bug report is sent ingame. No need to go on forums ar send email for bug reports. Genius. The devs are also very hard workers (And the dev team consist of four guys). They released a big update six days after the game was released. It added a lot on new stuff like a map and performance improvements. Great job to the Dev's.

Ok so full disclosure I discovered this game on a, ahem ‘website other than Steam’, and thought I would give it a try. I had pretty much forgotten about it after seeing it when it launched on Steam and only remembered a few reviews saying it was lacking content so I didn’t expect much… then I realised I had been playing it for about 12 hours straight and should probably buy it.
That in itself was an amusing experience because I unlocked 49% of the achievements within the first second of play after picking up on my existing save.
I was also immensely relieved to discover this updated version actually had a map because until that point I had easily spent half my time wandering around lost trying to navigate from low resolution map screenshots on my phone. That was basically akin to turning off GPS and just hoping you are walking in the right direction… only with more slime than you generally see on the streets of London. With the map I quickly managed to make more progress and soon had every type of slime in captivity and actually managed to find my way back to extractors I had placed so I do find it vaguely concerning that the game spent a year and a half in early access without something as basic as a map.
I say concerning because looking ahead at the roadmap the update that brings some degree of automation to farming with drones cannot happen soon enough. Whilst it is fun laying out a ranch, combing slimes and segregating the exploding ones half a mile away from the grabby ones so everything doesn’t go catastrophically wrong the minute you turn your back… the late stage gameplay does come down quite heavily to a lot of micromanagement. Grabbing food from one area, running it to the slime pens, grabbing the plorts and running them to the machines… over and over. It gets to the point where you just let things starve because it is too much hassle to bother feeding them (this is why I don’t own a dog). So at the moment it is probably for the best that they can’t actually starve to death or else I’d be spending the entire time just throwing food at them.
Only being able to carry 4 different resources hampers this heavily and when you’ve upgraded the vacuum to the highest capacity it takes forever to suck up a full stack of items so I feel like being able to upgrade the speed, range and number of slots would make things vastly more enjoyable. There also isn’t a great deal of threat or challenge in anything you do. I mean I like that it is casual but at the same time so is Minecraft and you can still get obliterated in a second if you are careless. Ferals and Tarr don’t pose a great deal of threat, I’ve only ever died from backing off a cliff by mistake (and most of the time the jetpack is enough to save you even if you do fall) and nothing has ever threatened the ranch… making me think that building turrets all around it might not have been the best use of my time. Apparently a future update will actually added a casual mode with no Tarr at all but really they need to add a hard mode where they are far more of a threat, perhaps even with intermittent attacks on the ranch you have to defend against or risk losing your entire stock of slimes. The desert area has some interesting content so if that is any indication of what future updates will add then it should be good.
At the moment I would say this is a great game for the price which will totally absorb you for a few days but potentially doesn’t have much replay value beyond that. Hopefully the future updates will expand a lot on the end game content.

Let me start off this review with just a simple "WOW" for this game.
The standalone map and runs are really good in ETS2. Pair it with very nice graphics for DX9/2013, and it still looks great today. Get Realistic Graphics and some trailer packs, maybe ProMods, and your set for a very nice 2017-ish European trucking game. Obviously it was released in 2013, but with the DLCs and the recent addition of Italia and Special Transport, you can tell SCS is not abandoning this game.
Another great aspect is the flexibility to move computers and even OSes. I went from Windows to Mac and just copying the files over made the game work fine. No tearing, no corruption, nothing. Also, even on a GT 840M machine, this game ran at least at 30-40FPS on low-medium. Now, for a beginner gamer that is into this stuff, 30-40FPS isn't bad for that dGPU.
One thing I don't like about this game is the AI at times. No, this is not a deal-breaker, but sometimes these AI drivers make me want to pull out my hair. If the driver in front of you stops immediately with no way of you not hitting him, it's your fault and you have to repair your truck. Guy moves into your lane out of nowhere? Your fault. Hit from behind? Your fault. I wish there was a better solution to when you get hit and it isn't your mistake.
All-in-all, I completely recommend this game to any passionate simulation driver or determined trucker.
Buy, sit and relax.

After waiting for this game to come out since the moment it was announced, I'd say that my opinions about POSTAL Redux are a bit mixed. I like this game, but I wanted to love it. Here are the pros and cons.
Pros:
*Better gameplay than the original, it plays like an actual 3/4 isometric shooter, no-more tank controls.
*Rampage mode is awesome, especially that alternate ending!
*The new remastered OST is amazing, I just wish that all of them were remastered and not just most. Also amazing are the tracks for Rampage mode
*The levels are even more gorgeous than the originals, and I like how animated they are with car lights flicking on and off and flies around garbage, among other things.
*The new revolver and carnival levels are awesome, I love shooting clowns!
Cons:
*Biggest one, the new ending. I understand why RWS changed the original ending, but what they replaced it with is just boring. The original ending sequence with the school kids was shocking and gut wrenching, it left me shivering by the time the credits rolled. Here, the ending is just...I don't get it. Why is he at a grave? Why is he fainting? The original ending had an obvious meaning showing the depths of the P. Dude's madness, here I have no clue what's going on. And as much as RWS may deny it, they certainly did change it because of outside influence, Vince Desi even says as much in their recent Playboy interrview.
* The new cutscene art is a mixed bag. While they're certainly faithful recreations, I feel they're too smooth, too digital. Maybe this is due to tech limits of computer screens in '97, but the original artworks had texture to them, they all looked gritty and acidic, like you'd burn your hand if you reached out and touched them. In Redux, some of the art is amazing, like the Construction Site and Trailer Park, but others like the Parade and the Mine look cartoonish, almost like they're from a children's story book. I wish RWS had gotten Randy Briley, the original artist from '97, to do remakes of his old work.
* Weapons need for umph to them, right now they're rather unexciting to use. They need to sound louder, deadlier, they ought to push the player back, have recoil, feel like actual guns. Also, they oughta be balanced more in terms of when the player gets them. Halfway through the game the player already has most weapons.
I suppose that's it, besides some misc. glitches which I'm sure RWS will fix through patches. Like I said, mixed feelings, but I'd go so far as to say that if you love the POSTAL series and wanna support RWS and don't mind the cons listed above, go ahead and buy it.

***MULTIPLAYER REVIEW***
PLEASE NOTE: This is a review for gamers who have not played Call of Duty games prior to this one. And this is a brief review. I'm a longtime FPS player, going as far back as Doom II and Quake. I've played them all... except CoD. There's no real reason why I skipped CoD except that I was busy with obligations and responsibilities. That said, here's the gist of a Call of Duty experience, and more specifically, an Advanced Warfare experience.
You choose your weapons, perks, and attachments. Find out what works best for you as a weapon, according to your own reflexes and level of spatial orientation. If you do well with shotguns, choose perks and attachments that compliment a shotgun style of play. If you do well with sniper rifles, do the same. And so on. (However, know that as a sniper the maps discourage sniper play. The maps are incredibly small, so you'll have to keep moving. Constantly. This isn't sniper play, in my opinion. It's run n' gun with a giant♥♥♥♥♥rifle slowing me down while making myself a sitting duck everytime I put the scope up to my face. I enjoyed sniping in many other FPS games in the past, especially Unreal Tournament. This ain't it.)
Now that you've chosen your kit, get in there. The match begins. Follow your teammates. Run down a hallway.... and you're dead. The killcam shows you how you died: One guy who got behind your squad somehow (there are countless ways to do this on maps that have countless routes leading to your location; there is no cover in CoD) popped you twice in the chest and now you're dead.
So you respawn. You orient yourself to the room. You take a few strides, turn the corner. Dead. Killcam shows you someone shot you from afar with a laser weapon. Keep in mind, during these scenarios, you begin with full health, which, mind you, isn't really full health. In CoD AW there are only 2 health statuses. There is no health bar. There's WOUNDED and there's DEAD. If you're wounded, you can find some temporary cover if you're lucky and wait several seconds until you recover.
So you respawn. You orient yourself and charge forward. You double jump up to  a rooftop for a better vantage point, to find out what the heck is going on... and... you're dead. Killcam shows you your killer aimed down the sights from a full building's length away and killed you with one rifle burst.
In CoD AW (or CoD, period), you WILL die, on average, 15-25 times per match, even if you're good. This isn't enjoyable gaming to me. CoD AW relies less on skill to succeed and more on steadying your weapon with attachments and skills and charging forward as far as possible, as many times as you can stand. I'm sorry, but that's boring, and it breaks immersion for me bigtime. Sure, a game like Unreal Tournament is unrealistic with its crazy weapons, et al, but I can stay immersed in the experience longer because my guy can survive longer. Also, when characters survive longer, a player's natural ability via hand-eye coordination and reflexes has to be relied upon. CoD does not test a player's natural ability because it doesn't allow you to live long enough to put it to good use.
Until the developers either tone down the damage or raise player health, I won't be playing this past the point of hitting 50. I bought the damn thing, so I'll play to max level like with any game, but if things don't change, I won't be buying subsequent downloadable content.

Total Bore: Rome II
Just the same things as the other Total Wars, with better graphics, but even poorer AI and interface, and game breaking bugs.
So, the combat has all the defects of previous total wars, the AI is idiotic and your armies like to take strange paths that get them killed if you don't constantly micro manage them. The extra bonus in Rome II is that in addition to being idiots when they move they are also idiots when they fight. If you order 1000 soldiers to fight 10 enemies, they will just send 10 soldiers in to perform their man-to-man combat animation, when the other 990 just stand there and do nothing as they wait for one of the soldiers to die to send one more in... utterly useless.
The Naval combats are ridiculous and ships near impossible to control. Naval units - which come in a whole variety and have many upgrades - are useless in the first place because whilst they cost a substantial amount of money they are actually weaker than regular armies (which just get ships for free).
The strategy phase is both uninteresting and irritating. It marries obscure and fiddly controls and moves with unpredictable outcomes, with a poorly designed interface. If you want to see more details about the buildings or units your are purchasing, you have no other choice than to right click and open a horribly designed wiki, which opens on top of your game in a separate annoying window. Each wiki page contains poorly written descriptions for 30 separate nations and you need to scroll and find yours among the other useless 29.
The tutorials are extremely poorly designed and don't teach you much about the game, so either you are going to have to read that horrible in-game wiki window thoroughly, or just accept the random things that happen constantly like your generals dying of plague suddenly, as random events - which they probably are.
The game is also buggy and crashes. I've lost the ability to progress in my campaign, because of a 100% crash when I try and invade this city, where when my first soldier reaches the city wall the game crashes.
It baffles me that this game got such high reviews, when this is clearly the worse of all the Total War games available. The only thing I got impressed with is that each soldier now has a different and unique face, hurrah! But that doesn't make up for the 100% crashes and the abysmal interface.

Pre 0.3.3.0 was LOTS of fun - I easily clocked 500+ legitimate hours (not AFK), and bought the game for 2 of my friends.
Post 0.3.3.0 is a grindy, boring mess, and the devs are either clueless or could care less to do anything about it.
One minute the devs talk about wanting to create fast MOBA like gameplay, with quick server resets (days - not months) and fast game play, and the next minute, they're nerfing a vital end game item, taking every other end game item with it and creating servers that never wipe - completely killing their stated game concept by slowing its pace down to something a snail would laugh at.

TLDR
It's a simplified System Shock in the Alien movie universe. If you like the movies buy it for sure, if you aren't a fan it still is a pretty fun game if you like sneaking around monsters.
Pros:
+The environment and visual design is very well done. Everything feels like it came straight out of the old movies, and people who liked the chunky old scifi style will adore seeing it in detail throughout the game.
+The gameplay is fairly interesting and provides a decent challenge. Often you will have to make a hard choice between using a noisy or expensive way to get past an obstacle, or take more time and do it quietly. Many actions such as breaking open doors, rewiring rooms or hacking things take time and focus and you have to be damn sure it's safe.
+The atmosphere is well done. The horror aspect is based around dread about the Alien, as it's appearances are (largely) unscripted and can happen based on your actions.
Cons:
-The pacing can be a bit too slow at times, causing you to go for long periods of nothing much happening.
-Many important gameplay elements are not explained or demonstrated outside of random tooltips during loading screens. While it is nice to leave some parts of the game up for discovery it can be very frustrating when a small thing gets you killed, like using the motion tracker when a foe is nearby or not knowing you can hide under desks and beds that are lower than crouching height.
Mixed:
*You can fight and kill enemies. I thought it was sensible since you still aren't a one-woman-army and it is a big risk, but some might find it goes against the survival horror idea of the game.
*Saving is only possible at level transitions and specific checkpoints mid-level, and takes time to do. While it certainly adds to the atmosphere and tension with the risk involved in saving your game or dying and having to go back to the last checkpoint, if you get stuck before a long segment it is very frustrating to redo the whole thing every time you screw up and die.

I'm not sure what happened to my previous review of this disaster, but having suffered through six and a half hours of Eternal Senia, I think I'm qualified to share my thoughts again. This game does
deserve half the praise it's getting, and I will attempt to explain why. Before I begin, it's important to mention that this
a free game on Steam, and it's better than some. However, that does not stop it from being complete dreck.
First: the
. The person who made Eternal Senia said they wanted to make it simple, and so removed the concept of an attack button. However, this was a horrible decision, because it completely removes the concepts of skill and strategy. YES, I know this is supposed to be a game for everyone, and not be complicated or difficult. And to that I say,
Anyone can push the Z key and see the character swing a weapon and think "Hmm, that looks like it could hurt something." Without that, the game basically becomes Hydlide 3, as combat now solely involves the player and an enemy mashing their faces together until someone falls over. Eternal Senia has a few decent boss fights, but those aside, it has absolutely nothing in the action department.
The first time I played through this game, the ending I got (no. 1) caused anger in me. It's very rare that a story is so bad that I get angry about it, but it happened. The reason is that I spent nearly 2 1/2 hours trying to reach the main character's beloved big sister,
Ergo, those 2.4 hours were completely wasted.
The other two endings aren't any better. Ending no. 2 achieved a nearly identical result, and no. 3 wasn't entirely clear, but it seems like the game just repeats itself until you get a different ending, both of which, may I remind you, are bad endings. No. 3 is also unnecessarily long. Senia and Magaleta just keep talking and talking, and nothing actually gets said.
That brings me to another point: the characters. They. Are. Garbage. Senia and Magaleta are both one-dimensional, with Senia falling neatly into the Generic Insecure Sister-Worshipping Kid stereotype, and Magaleta having almost no personality at all, being stuck in the past. Nia only gets a few lines of dialogue, and the fairy is there almost for the sole purpose of being ammunition. (She also doesn't appear in any endings, despite being usable in the final boss fight.)
So what's left? The gameplay is horribly designed, the dialogue is trash, the characters are unlikeable, and the endings are dreck. So what is left? For the life of me, I can't understand why anyone likes this game.

This is one of the best designed games I've ever played. Yes, at launch it was unplayable for many people due to a bad PC port, but the patch which later came out fixed that, at least for me. It is entirely playable on my medium-low end laptop, alebeit only on medium graphics. Obviously bad launches are not to be encouraged, but considering the sheer unadulterated quality of this game, a little forgiveness is in order.
I'm going to keep this as brief as I can. The story is excellent, the world is atmospheric and well designed. The combat may be too simple and easy on lower difficulties but on harder ones you are forced to get creative and it becomes much more nuanced. Emily and Corvo both had different and equally fun sets of abilities, although one or two don't feel very useful, although that is partially matter of playstyle. It is a fairly short game, taking me only about 12 hours on my first playthrough, but it is exceedingly replayable. There might be three or four differant ways you could approach a given situation and it always feels fresh. As soon as I finihsed my high chaos playthrough as Emily I started a new one in which I plan to never be seen and never kill anyone, and after 5 hours it still feels fresh. I love that it lets you play the whole game without once killing an enemy, if you so chose, or lets you slaughter every single person in your path, and both feel equally rewarding.
But my single favorite aspect of the game is the level design. Every mission is large, explorable, and unique, usually with some twist or added mechanic. In one mission dust storms will occassionally blow through reducing visibility. In another, you make your way through a huge mechanical mansion which can transform as you pull levers. You can even slip out of the usual areas and make your way through the spaces between the shifting walls. In another, you have the ability to jump between the present and the past, solving puzzles by changing things in the past to affect the present. Every level is full of detail and atmosphere, and you are heavily encourage to explore them to track down runes which allow you to gain more abilities.
It's just all so well put together, every part working together to create a functional moving whole. Dishonored 1 is in my top 10 games of all time, and Dishonored 2 is right there next to it.

When I picked the game up, I knew that I was in for something special.  System Shock 2 has a reputation as one of the best Survival Horror and/or FPS games ever made, so it couldn't be bad, right?
Well, it's not perfect, but what it does wel, it does really well.
We'll start with the positives.  This game is one of the few I've discovered that gives a damn about the "survival" in survival horror.  Weapons degrade quickly, ammunition is rare, and a lot of the enemies will destroy you if you just charge into every fight.  The game is nice and challenging.
Next, the atmosphere.  Through a lot of the game, they manage to reach Ravenholm-level atmosphere, with enemies placed in the perfect locations for maximum jump-scare potentail.  I'm not ashamed to admit that some of my least-dignified moments have come from the protocol droids- definitely the most paranoia-inducing enemies in the game.  Not the most powerful, but if one sneaks up on you...  You're probably going to die.
Now, it has gameplay and atmosphere down.  What doesn't it do right?
Level design.  A large number of the levels are divided up into mutiple parts, with each one having a separate checkpoint.  You die without finding the checkpoint?  Back to the load screen for you.  Oftentimes, where each checkpoint services is completely arbitrary and nonsensical- five meters to the west is okay, but not five meters to the east, for example.
Worse, later evels remove the checkpoints entirely, but don't change up the gameplay to match the lack of this mechanic.  I ended up having to completely restart the game after entering the last hour, thanks to running out of anti-rad hypos, anti-disease hypos, and health items on top of bullets.  I would have restocked, but I didn't have enough money.  The entire last area is unwinnabe unless you're perfectly well-stocked.
Overall, however, the game itself is solid, and recommended for any fan of survival horror and shooters.

The concept of APB is not a new one, but we have yet to see it executed correctly.
Before steam, and during a time my computer was not up to snuff, I probably put in 500 to 700 hours, another 2100 recorded on steam, spanning over 7 years of play.
I wouldn't do it again, at least not the past five years.
Upon relaunch, the game had its issues, there were cheaters, and matchmaking didnt work all the time.
Somehow, 7 years later, this actually has become worse.
Computers are speeding up, yet they continue to have framerate issues with APB, Its quite insulting actually, to build a $1000 gaming computer, Or more, and get the same sort of issues people have on much less powerful and slower computers, Allbeit not as frequently.
Cheaters just never go away. No matter how hard you try. Its an unfortunate part of any online game. But with the dwindling population, theyre much much more likely to get paired  with or against you in a mission these days.
Some players are just downright good at the game, this is with any PVP game.  But its become a massive problem, and the skill gap between casual play and competitive play has become even wider. The current matchmaking system tries to pair players similarly skilled together, however this does not work. Many players who are very casual, and are not very good or only occasionally have a good match, find themselves playing against players who are much much more skilled, simply because the developers made the game much too easy to obtain the "Gold" threat level, which in the early years of this game, was reserved for those who really knew how to play well. Now many players end up with the gold threat, which is full of tryhards, hackers, and people who are just much too skilled for the average player. This change to the threat system was more than likely brought about due to the declining playerbase, it was unable to properly support the old, and while flawed, much better system. Side note, You see many gold players running around with legendary or permanent weapons, high end vehicles, and other goodies. All found by taking a trip to APB's real money store, Armas. Hmm..
(Don't be stupid. This game isnt terribly P2W, I own several paid for items myself, too much in fact, what im getting at is the population thats actively spending money has to be kept happy. No opp = no money for G1. This is sadly what is likely the major reason to the threat change, because the players that deserved gold originally were not a majority of the game, many players were high bronze, and mid silver, or thereabouts. Most of these silvers went gold, and the bronzes went silver. some gold.)
The game is NOT new player friendly. You will face gold opp as a trainee. the tutorial is nearly non existant. Many of us old players take much of our, to us, basic knowledge, for granted. What we dont remember, is when we started there was a returning population from RTW, which passed info down to us, which we did NOT pass on to new players.
Ill probably see this game out. Due to memories, a large time investment, and a unfortunately large financial investment.
It was a really good concept, but we have yet to see it perfected. Try other games.

Who is Mike is a very short (<hour) horror/mystery Visual Novel that does many things right.
Pros:
*It features very nice art and interesting, suspenseful short story.
*There are multiple simple choices that branch the story in different ways, allowing you to reach different endings.
*The outcome (and even the premise) of the story depends on your choices.
*It's free, short, and doesn't overstay its welcome.
Cons:
*The choices and consequences are usually not very intuitive or clear, so the ending you get will probably be unexpected.

TLDR
It's a simplified System Shock in the Alien movie universe. If you like the movies buy it for sure, if you aren't a fan it still is a pretty fun game if you like sneaking around monsters.
Pros:
+The environment and visual design is very well done. Everything feels like it came straight out of the old movies, and people who liked the chunky old scifi style will adore seeing it in detail throughout the game.
+The gameplay is fairly interesting and provides a decent challenge. Often you will have to make a hard choice between using a noisy or expensive way to get past an obstacle, or take more time and do it quietly. Many actions such as breaking open doors, rewiring rooms or hacking things take time and focus and you have to be damn sure it's safe.
+The atmosphere is well done. The horror aspect is based around dread about the Alien, as it's appearances are (largely) unscripted and can happen based on your actions.
Cons:
-The pacing can be a bit too slow at times, causing you to go for long periods of nothing much happening.
-Many important gameplay elements are not explained or demonstrated outside of random tooltips during loading screens. While it is nice to leave some parts of the game up for discovery it can be very frustrating when a small thing gets you killed, like using the motion tracker when a foe is nearby or not knowing you can hide under desks and beds that are lower than crouching height.
Mixed:
*You can fight and kill enemies. I thought it was sensible since you still aren't a one-woman-army and it is a big risk, but some might find it goes against the survival horror idea of the game.
*Saving is only possible at level transitions and specific checkpoints mid-level, and takes time to do. While it certainly adds to the atmosphere and tension with the risk involved in saving your game or dying and having to go back to the last checkpoint, if you get stuck before a long segment it is very frustrating to redo the whole thing every time you screw up and die.

King's Quest is an episodic adventure that is neither a prequel, sequel, or remake of the original series. It takes place between the original games and the gameplay has been reimagined to be more varied and less point-and-click. Although it is a puzzle game, the puzzles themselves are pretty straightforward. The main focus is on the witty and humorous dialogue, fantastical soundtrack, and overall engaging storytelling. You can criticise some of its mechanics or its lacking options menu; it's missing any kind of in-game map or quest log; and you can't skip dialogue or cutscenes that you have seen before. However, I think most people will take away the quirkiness and innocence King's Quest brings that just gives you that magical feeling. You do not need to play any previous King's Quests and this works as a standalone game. Episode 1 will last you around 4-6 hours depending on how much time you spend wandering around.
