This review is after playing chapter 1:
"Talking to yourself again Graham?" Not anymore, Cedric. Not anymore. Someone has finally heard our prayers.
As a young girl growing up in the 80's, this was my JAM! These games shaped my taste for adventure and escape in computer games. I was tickled pink to see they were finally remaking this with a budget over $500 dollars and a taco dinner.
Five minutes into the game and it felt "right." The quests seemed like a wink at the originals. The art never strayed too far from the path Kings Quest was on either. The story is a clever take on a remake, sure to keep the nerds at bay while they search for plot holes. The characters are instantly likable and the quests are easy enough to not enrage you while still challenging you to think a bit.
That being said, I was never stumped at any point of the game. I have not made up my mind if I miss impossible quests or not. There is something to be said about the challenge that the old games presented. I got in A LOT of trouble calling that Sierra hotline. I'm a bit saddened that today's youth will never experience that sort of nerdrage followed by cheating, followed even closer by family shame.
This game brought back the feeling that I had playing the "newest" King's Quests as a kid. That feeling is priceless, at the very least well worth the $10 first chapter. There is a decent amount of game play and, if the rest of the chapters can follow suit, this will prove to be a wise investment for adventurers of all ages.

Half-life was the first PC game I ever bought so this is abot as nostalgic as it gets for me.
This whole game is a love project by fans of the original game, after Valve dissapointed us all with the "Half-Life Source" game. It's a painstakingly well put together "remake" of the original game, everything from models to textures to sound and music. Sure it looks abit old at times, but it's supposed to look old, because it is old. They have made some small changes to the mapdesign, some things got cut, some got added, but I feel it's all for the better as this is tons of fun and nostalgia from that very first train ride.
Now, the "negative" part. There is no Xen as of writing this review. Personally I don't mind, I never cared for Xen back in the original and I don't really miss it here. The game ends at a good point in the story still. Another negative part is the multiplayer, it's dead. Again, I do not care since I never really was a very big fan of Half-Life multiplayer (TFC was my poision).  Then you have the "negative" that some stuff in the game is a bit "old-school" like the AI being stupid as hell (the most intelligent enemy is the headcrab), soldiers with turrets and helicopters will hit you with aimbot like skill and you WILL die alot. This is a quicksave quickload type of game.
All in all, this is a great game and currently the best way to enjoy a piece of gaming history. If you are a fan or just curious about one of the most important games ever made, do buy it.

TL;DR: It's a bit repetitive, but still good.
My biggest problem with this one involves the endings, but I'll keep this review as spoiler-free as possible. Getting to them is a pain on its own: Which ending you get depends on how you answer a short series of questions. This would usually be alright, if the paths to each ending weren't so goddamn random. Choosing between liking dogs or hyenas can completely change the entire plot of the game, and since there's no ramifications between questions, you don't get any indication of which ending you're headed towards, until it's already too late to turn back. If you refuse to use a walkthrough, be prepared for a ton of save-scumming, and just randomly checking every single possible combination of answers until you find the 6-7 endings missing from your list.
I don't really like the way that every single route completely contradicts eachother either, but that's really more of a matter of personal taste.
All that said, the game is alright. The art, despite having a few slips here and there, is pretty good, and the narrative can create some pretty good tension in important scenes. The music, as simple as it is, is pretty eerie, and really helps the atmosphere. And the story really compels you to keep reading, since there's no way of knowing what you're about to find. Definitely pretty good for a free to play game.
As frustrating as getting every single ending can be sometimes, I had fun with this one. Definitely recommended if you have an hour or two to kill.

I am writing this review at 20 past 7 in the morning, because I made the mistake of playing this game's Survivor mode tonight in which you are plopped in an area with temporally-decreasing point valued objectives (for leaderboard positions) and the end goal of simply escaping the area. I had forgotten this mode existed after I completed the campaign. However when I went to try it today, it was such a concentrated dose of pure terror I scared myself half to death and have nothing better to do now than review this game as I could not sleep. I just kept hearing the alien's footsteps continually getting closer and closer but never quite reaching me every time I closed my eyes. This game broke me today.
Now I'm not going to sugar coat the plot: it's full of so many redundencies, false endings and pointless sidetracking to pad out the game's length it can at times make you forget WTF you're even doing on the station in the first place. Half the time I couldn't quite recall why I was where I was, because I'd gone on so many sidetrips in pursuit of simply getting off the station I had no sight of that ultimate goal. Even when escape does become the priority, the game's last hour is needlessly padded out with multiple false ends and probably the most linear and boring level design in the game. Couple that with a badly handled actual ending (I'd talk about it but, you know, spoilers), and the last hour of the game I found unsatisfying and somewhat of a chore. It's a shame because the penultimate set pieces in the decaying, exploding, pitch black corridors of Sevastopol (the station, not the recently-Putinized port) are as terrifying as any other encounter in the game.
And indeed, it is a testiment to the quality of that survival horror experience that is the game's core that I can forgive the padding and the backtracking and the subpar plot (and forgettable characters, all of whom but the player character die (obviously) and none getting any meaningful development). And indeed, this is a true survival horror - as in, it is about surviving an overpowering threat through intelligence and guile rather than any kind of badassery. This is not Amnesia or Outlast in space - those games are virtual haunted houses. This is an actual GAME, with MECHANICS and levels designed to INCORPORATE said mechanics (are these concepts ringing any bells, Frictional Games? No offence but other than sheer terror your games have little going for them; good thing they're♥♥♥♥♥♥your-pants-terrifying then, yeah?). It is a game not just about completing whatever mind-numbingly redundant or semi-important task the excuse for a plot has assigned you, it's about scavenging offices and tables, nooks and cranies for those classic nuggets of classic survival horror, resources. Because let me tell you, with fuel for the flamethrower, EMP mines, flashlight batteries and noisemakers your life becomes not only harder but quite likely short as well.
There are three enemies you will encounter in your quest to escape/♥♥♥♥-around-for-hours-before-deciding-it-might-be-a-good-time-to-escape, and I'll address them in order from least to most awesome. There are human survivors who are so unhinged from the sheer terror the alien has distilled in them that they shoot at anyone they don't know, meaning you as well. I find it hard to believe the justifications for these people trying to kill you given the greater looming threat fo the alien, and with their AI being the worst of said enemy types (sidestepping to hit me instead of continually firing at the wall is something even the COD AI has figured out by now) I really wish there had been no human enemies altogether. Luckily after the game's opening levels almost everyone on the station si dead and you stop running into them.
The second type fo enemy, and the only kind other than the alien that are genuinely creepy, are Seegson's (the budget-price alternative to Weyland-Yutani that nobody buys from) Working Joe androids that maintainance the station. They are controlled by APOLLO, Sevastopol's central AI, who, as we can all imagine, actually works against the survivors so that no harm comes to the Alien. The Working Joes don't look real, like WL synthetics, but they lie in the uncanny valley and thus are genuinely unsettling, especially when their eyes turn glowing red when they become hostile, all the while spouting off standardized friendly greetings and advice while APOLLO directs them to beat people, like you, to death. Luckily they can't run, only walk, so you can outpace them - the trouble is to not get cornered by the buggers, which can easily happen if you frantically start running from one and bump into another.
The Alien itself is the star of the show. It is truly one of the greatest enemies ever put in a game, and I say that quite seriously. This game is channelling Alien, not Aliens. This thing - and there is only one, not hundreds as in the sequel movies - cannot be disposed of by some pistol rounds to the cranium like Vasquez so badassly did in Aliens. In fact, nothing at your disposal can kill it. In addition to its imperviousness to your weapons, it is also stronger than you, faster than you, has an impeccable sense of hearing, some kind of keen 'sight' (though it has no eyes, and no one has ever specified exactly how the Alien sees), and a geniune interest in finding you. This one enemy represents the single greatest leap forward in AI programming since the sandbox-compatible FPS AI for the NPCs in Crysis. It is wicked, WICKED smart. It has no set pathing. It has no set routes. Except for a few particular set pieces, the Alien is entirely run by dynamic AI. It is simply placed in the level, and its AI programming takes the hunting-you-down part from there. It methodically searches levels for the player, checking posisble blind spots (though not all - can't make lockers the only places to hide can we?), every so often deciding to turn around and head in a different direction. In this hide and seek game it very much acts like it is, well, "It". I could go on forever about how intricate and detailed the Alien's AI appears to be (I have no hard facts for you since I obviously didn't program it), but suffice it to say it is GOING to outsmart you many times. It is unpredictable to a very large degree, and you will never feel safe. Did I mention it was fast? Yeah, it's reeeaally fast. As in, if it sees you, you'd better be able to break line of sight and hide IMMEDIATELY or it WILL kill you, and it DOES insta-kill you if it grabs you. Only molotovs, pipe bombs and the flamethrower can ward it off (and still can't kill it), and even then it only retreats to the nearest vent, only to pop back out of it a few seconds later. This thing REQUIRES stealth to circumvent, and since you basically have no HUD (your health bar and equipped item are all you can see) you have to use your senses, your smarts and that motion tracker (which IT CAN HEAR, by the way) to sneak around rather than relying on some kind of gimmicky stealth mechanic that tells you when you're visible or♥♥♥♥♥♥like that. When this thing shows up the game becomes hardcore old-school-stealth difficult (the game even says it was meant to be played on hard), and will die a LOT. Get used to it, especially with the manual save stations being spaced out. People ♥♥♥♥♥ about it, but somehow think it's fine in Dark Souls cuz it's Castlevania 3D? Grow a pair and learn-2-sneak.
I'd go on about the 100% perfection that is the art direction and sound design but I've reached the work limit for these Steam reviews, so: If you're a survival horror fan who's been lacking a decent game of that type for the past decade, or want to experience again the terror of Alien instead of the adrenaline pump of the sequels, GET THIS GAME.

System Shock 2 offers an unparalleled sense of place and agency in a video game- an immersive sim at its finest.
Unlike modern games with simplified contextual world interaction, traversing the world is dynamic: The player can run, jump, and climb at will, and "Press X to win" never rears its head. Object interaction is also dynamic: You can drag batteries onto world objects to power them up, drag $ITEM onto $ITEM_2 to kill $SPOILERS, or just drag objects onto the ground to drop them.
Likewise, stealth is a dynamic affair, not limited to simple cover-based mechanics with rows of waist-high crates. The game uses the same stealth system as Thief, taking multiple mechanics into account, including darkness, cover, and sound, with multiple levels of enemy awareness.
Finally, the game's survival-horror elements are made all the stronger by its lack of hand-holding. Instead of relying on cheap jump-scares, SS2 terrifies the player through heavy ambiance and a constant sense of aloneness and vulnerability.

I caught the game on a Steam sale and decided to jump in, regardless of all the bug reports. I can only report on my experiences:
1) The gameplay is outstanding. Take Dishonored 1, improve your non-lethal combat *extensively* and you have Dishonored 2. Now you don't have to sacrifice having a good time because lots of the 'fun' gameplay is lethal -- non-lethal is viable and just as fun.
Right now I'm on my first playthrough with Emily and her powers are interesting. Cool stuff. I'm looking forward to trying Corvo's different powers (haven't even seen them yet).
2) Graphics -- They are really good.  More actual detail than the first Dishonored and even more 'dense' - It can take hours to explore a particular area because there are so many nooks and crannies.
3) Sound -- The sound is very good, with environmental sounds and great (non-intrusive) music to back it all up.  The voice acting for many of the characters, though, is absolutely comical, in a bad way.  They really need to look into hiring some better voice actors for the normal enemies - heck, I'll offer my services for free.
4) Game performance - So I use a 960GTX on a Xeon (i7) 3.5Ghz and performance is acceptible if I turn off V-sync.  V-sync does some weirdness -- slows down the mouse response, everything feels like it's 1/10th second 'behind' my input.  Of course, I have to live with the tearing, but overall it's much better to have some tearing and great responsiveness.
Frame-rates go from 70-30.  Usually, even in the 30FPS areas (dense with lots of objects and enemies) it still feels pretty good in actual gameplay, but there are some quirks (mentioned later in bugs).
5) Bugs -- Unfortunately, the game is fairly buggy, but so far (thankfully) not game-breakingly so.
For instance -- you can craft bonecharms or runes, which is awesome -- and you can even stack effects on bonecharms to have them stack.
Except the beneficial traits (like choking someone out or moving with a body) are DETRIMENTAL -- Arkane made the ridiculous mistake of flipping their logic, so that equipping a "Choke someone faster" charm (or 4) will slow your choke speed....how disappointing.
As for graphics - mostly stable, but sometimes I run into craziness -- I'm playing on Hard, so about 2 hits from a sword kills me (which I like) but when I bring up the powers menu to try to select a power, sometiems I'm 'stuck' in that I can't select a power----I have to press escape to try to exit the game, then try to enter the menu again.  Really annoying and has led to several deaths.
Overall -- An awesome game if technical issues don't plague you -- I run on decently high settings and love the graphics -- can't wait to upgrade my GPU and play on higher settings eventually.
The level design is absolutely awesome -- Clockwork Mansion being something I've never seen in a game and the design is almost mind-boggling.
I really hope they fix lots of the bugs though -- some of them are so easy to spot and yet they made it into the game.

Broforce is a game where you are given characters model after some of the most manliest characters from movies and sent in to take down the evil terrorist and liberate the area. How do you do this? An absolutely charming reboot of a classic adventure franchise. Not perfect - some unnecessary "platforming" and quicktime events feel a bit out of place, and they really should have included a way to skip dialogue you've already heard - but the writing is sharp and funny, the aesthetics are gorgeous (that cape!), and perhaps most importantly the feel of Daventry is intact. Quirky, self-aware and fun. A really lovely first entry that has me excited to play the rest of the series.

Let me paint a picture for you....well anyone who is above the age of 25 or has a love for watching classic 80's movies, but I digress. The Princess Bride, a Movie about a Grandfather telling a story to his grandchild about fantasy, love, and friendship. Oddly enough King's Quest could almost be given the same synopsis, minus the love portion. There may be no love interest in this game, but  The Odd Gentalmen defiently put nothing but love into this game, and it shows.
For as much of a homage as there is to the Princess Bride, there is so much this game does on its own that captivates you in so many ways. The biggest thing is the world it paint, and creates for you in a majestic 2D animated art style much like Disney movies of old, but with a 3D flair to it that works in harmoney. There are a lot of games out there today that use a similar style to this, like Street Fighter, Boarderlands or even the TallTell games to an extent. The difference here is those other games are more of a 3D animated world with a 2D overlay, this game is a 2D world, with 3D movements. This is very hard to pull off, but they get it right, without faulter through out the game.
This is very much a "New" version of the point and click genre. Simple controls to the point that you are only using the left joystick to move, one button to interact, one button to open your bag and a third button for quick time events. I have seen people complain how this games controls are too simplistic, but remember, this is supposed to be a "New" point and click game. In the good old day point and click games where pretty much just the use of a mouse and the buttons on the mouse. This is a good things and a bad thing however. Bad thing because we are so used to complecated controls that for a bit of time, you will be trying to use the right mouse stick to rotate a camera or just do something, even though it does nothing. However after a couple minutes you with fall into it with no problem, which is part of the good thing about the controls. They are easy to pick up and go with.
This first chapter is atleast 5 hours, and when you first start to play it will feel very linear, with only one path to go most of the time, with very simple puzzles. However this is because for the first hour or so, you are actually playing a well craft tutorial level that will show you everything you will need to know, by the time the game gives your free raine around the world. You will know when you have broken free of the tutorial level when you are now able to go down 3 paths here that lead to two paths here that go over there and come back over here, and such like this. It opens up and requires you to remember how to get around the game, which really gives you the time to admire the landscape.
The most important thing to this game though, are the characters, and the story. This game has some of the best designs of characters we know of from fair tales and other such games, but with a twist. When you come across a creature you reconize by name from somewhere else and then see how they have been designed for this game you will just smile and fall in love with them, very much like I have. The story helps you fall in love with these characters personalities and gives you a reson to care, or hate, or wish you had done things differently. The puzzles can be challanging or they can be simple, but you do them because they add a flavor to the story and helps move everything along at a nice pace. I dont want to ruin anything about this story, but its handle with great care, and attention to detail.
With the minor flaws anyone can find in a game, and harp all day on to make a game look trashy and bad, I choose not focus on them, mostly because really there just arnt many there to begin with. The story is everything about this game. Its fun, challenging at times, makes you laugh, and if you have watched the Princess Bride, there are some amazing references that will hit home with you, in the most amazing of ways.

A very compelling who-done-it with a supernatural twist. When it comes to visual novels, the dialog between characters can make or break the game. If the dialog is too forced or cheesy it'll completely break the immersion, however, 'who is mike' strikes the right cadence between lightheartedness and dead seriousness all the time without breaking that very important immersion.
The subject is relate-able and a bit creepy to me because on a personal level I've had a family member taken away by mental illness, it's scary, they end up a shell of themselves that you don't know anymore but 'who is mike' is a bit different. You gain consciousness only to find yourself standing face to face with you. Both of you insist to be the real thing but one is pretending, and for sinister reasons. Great original story.
Let's talk about the sound, the cues are spot on and really help drive the emotion of the game. While the loops could be managed better (a bit jarring when a track restarts) the pieces chosen are perfect to cultivate the fear, foreboding, or relief the developer wants the player to feel.
There aren't many different backdrops or character models but given the length of the game it suffices. If there is one thing I'd like to change about the game is to have the character text actually originate in speech bubbles from the characters speaking. Having to read the text at the bottom all the time really does detract from the overall 'visual novel' element of such games. The dialog would more powerful if you can see the face of the person as they speak it.
Is this free game worth 2 hours of your time? Yes! I wholeheartedly recommend playing it, but keep in mind it's not really for unsupervised children (strong language).

Not an extremely difficult game by any means, but any fan of isometric shooters will probably enjoy this for what it is- a stupid fun "kill everything that moves" type of game.
If you're a fan of Postal 2 that hasn't played the original, you might not like this. Postal 1 is a completely different game. As well as being a completely different genre, Postal 1 is far less tounge-in-cheek than it's sequel. It has a rather dark atmosphere and is even a bit "edgy". It's still a great game, just don't expect the wacky comedic tone that Postal 2 is known for. But if you just want more Dude shenanigans in general, this remake is a must-have for any Postal fan.

I'veoften said that a great video game only needs a great developer on a living wage, and here comes dev Holy Priest to prove me right. Eternal Senia is a short game, and it's a good game.
You run at opponents to deal damage to them, and taking some yourself in the process. You can use any of 4 skill unlocked throughout the game to deal damage without taking any. It's simplistic, but it's also amazing. The system really shines in boss battles and the final area. I found myself maxing Phantom slash though, as it's the most useful and versatile of all the skills. All of the boss battles stand out as really, really fun. The final one in particular was immensly satisfying, putting all of my skills to the test. All the battles are fair, and I am unbelievably happy about that.
It's also worth noting that this is a well presented game. I just like the art style, and the music is great. It's not the best, but it's not going to age.
My only problem was the dialogue. The game actually has a decent story that explores the idea of what you would do to save those most important to you. The only problem is that the game was translated from Chinese. Poorly. It's not a deal breaker, but it definately cut into the quality of the story.

Just cause 3 is different to JC2. If you take that on board you'll have more fun!
I really like JC3 although it does have flaws. The wingsuit is amazing, exploring the map is an enjoyable experience and experimenting with the mechics is endlessly hilarious. There's plenty of things to do and I found the game easily ate up 50+ hrs while liberating all the settlements, completing the storyline and getting all the collectables.
Once you've done all that you're kinda left to your own devices. Unless you actively enjoy experimenting with the mechanics of the game, or happen to enjoy stunts there's not an awful lot left to do. You can reinstate individual locations and liberate them again but it's a little bit of an empty process with no goal. As a single player open world game this is a huge mistake not to add some kind of value to the game after it has been completed (DLC is on it's way but we don't have any idea of what content it will provide yet)
This is just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to flaws. There's design decisions that leave me baffled: no FOV slider or choice of camera angles (I think they ran out of control pad buttons to use lol), assigning boost to different buttons depending on the type of vehicle you're in. The weird delay you get between stunt jumping on a vehicle and being able to grapple. The main island being virtually empty. The dumb AI. The crashing. The list goes on and on. The lack of keybindings. Jeez I could talk about the flaws for a LONG time as there are so many and they really do effect the expereince negatively.
Having said all that, I'm a huge fan of the Just CAuse franchise and the possibilities the game yields. As such I'm ok with overlooking the flaws. I spend a lot of my time stunting or creating silly experiments in JC3 and it's easily been worth the money paid. Will you enjoy it as much? I'm not sure... I suppose it depends how you play games. If you follow the missions and complete the story before moving on you may miss a lot about what makes JC3 so unique and enjoyable. However if you're more creative with your gameplay then you'll likely get a lot more from the experience.
Either way I'm looking to the future now as the DLC shall be here soon (hopefully with more map content) and the JC2MP Team are working on a multiplayer mod for Just Cause 3.... which will change EVERYTHING!

A true masterpiece from 1999, that manages to hold up to this day.
Playing through this for the first time in 2014, I finally get to experience the game that helped shape all the other great FPS/RPG's that came after it.
is an atmospheric Sci-Fi survival experience with lots of exploration and great combat. The game will have you sweating and at the edge of your seat more than once, when you slowly make your way through poorly lit corridors, with strange noises coming from behind every corner and out of every computer terminal. Ammo is scarce, the environment is hostile and health is hard to come by.
The sound design is nothing short of amazing and is responsible for the majority of the thrilling atmosphere. Well voice acted audio logs help you connect the dots on what exactly it was that has happened to the spaceship van Braun as you try and make your way through the ship. Chills run down your spine whenever the A.I. of the ship starts talking - and it is not the only one talking to you. The level design is pretty open since you can and will go back to previously visited sectors at some point, even if it is only to pick up that last chemical substance you need in order to complete the research on that foreign object you found on the engineering deck...
I highly recommend playing the game with all the great texture mods and model upgrades that the active community has provided over the years, as those updates stay very true to the feel of the original ones but give the game a nice, sharp look.
I found the updated graphics to be pretty good, comparable to
and
. Just look through the guides on where to find and how to install everything in the community hub.
Overall a highly recommendable experience, especially if you can pick it up on a sale. If you can bare with the somewhat dated graphics, you are in for a memorable piece of gaming history.

Game complete review Edit: 20/12/2014
Here is my review after completing the game.
After the first few boring hours of run/hide & explore, things start to liven up objective wise. I had to knock back down to medium difficulty, as I was getting frustrated by the constant lame deaths (even while hiding in lockers holding my breath).
My biggest gripe with this game was the immersion breaking save locations. I wasn't really focussed on survival because of these, instead just listening out for that pinging noise the save points make and trying to get to them before I died. Once there, the feeling of fear really disappears. Great right? Wrong! It's a real ball ache when you die when you're almost at the next save point and then have to repeat the same level over and over in order just to make the save. This makes the Alien more of an annoyance than anything scary. It gets worse near the end of the game.
Honestly though, I don't think this is a problem with the game in general. It's more of a problem with all the other games over the years which have spoiled us with manual any-time or auto saves. However, I would have liked it more if I could have created some kind of save point from items I picked up. I dunno, like chalk or paint a wall or floor or something - instead of card slot save points, it uses up items I collected which I could craft as saves. Like the flare markers Ripley left on the ground in the Aliens movie... I know this sounds a bit daft, but it would keep a sense of fear and not break immersion and allow the user to save when they wanted, so long as they either found a flare or could craft one.
No spoilers about content for those who haven't played it yet, but the game doesn't end when you expect it to. This is great for value for money, but make sure you have a weekend out and plenty of hours to carry on playing. Just when you think you've completed it and your Mrs gives you “that look” and goes to bed and you'll still sat there silently swearing at the pc at 5am in the morning.
Final verdict: 8.5/10. No 10/10. Only because of the DLC ending, and (at time of writing) Windows only.

The year is 2015. It is an age of darkness. Point and click adventure games, once a staple of PC gaming, have now been relegated to a niche market only populated by indie developers with small budgets which, while talented, rarely live up to the adventure games of the glory days. Even Telltale, once a proud champion of the genre, has fallen to the appeal of choice-based narrative games, and all hope is lost for a new Sam and Max season. But then, out of the darkness, a newcomer appears - King's Quest, a new installment of the classic adventure series, coming from the freshly revived Sierra by the hands of Activision, taking a break from its busy schedule of gouging CoD players' wallets to deliver the starving point-and-click masses a blessing from above.
King's Quest essentially feels like what a modern Telltale game would feel like if they were still making puzzle-based games. The writing is well-done and full of puns and witty lines, and it's delivered by a voice cast that seems almost too good to be just for an adventure game including Christopher Lloyd, Josh Keaton, and Tom Kenny. The art style is a great looking cartoonish design that does a great job of emulating the animated feeling of old point-and-clicks in a modern way. The puzzles blend humor and logic in ways that manage to be pretty challenging without feeling obtuse, and some puzzles have multiple solutions that tie into the game's small choice system. King's Quest doesn't seem to be the sort of game where your choices will have a "big impact" like in Telltale's newer games (and the game even jokes about those games a few times), but there are some little choices that you can make throughout the episode that will possibly have an impact on future episodes.
Only the first of five episodes is currently out, so it's too early to say for sure if it's a truly great game, but I was very impressed with the first episode and will definitely be buying the rest. When I play this game it feels like Telltale never left me.

The best way to start this review off is by saying I have absolutely zero experience or knowledge of the original King's Quest series. Also, I'm not an extensive player of Adventure type games; I've played The Wolf Among Us, Year Walk, and, if these count, Dear Esther and The Stanley Parable. This should give you a fair idea of my experience and expectations for King's Quest. Having said this, I really enjoyed this first chapter of the game.
King's Quest: A Knight to Remember, is sort of an adventure game. I say "sort of" because it doesn't fit the usual mold I expect for the majority of adventure games. It isn't point'n'click, nor are there obtuse puzzles to solve. While playing I felt like there was some familiarity in gameplay to The Wolf Among Us, however there were a few differences.
There is a heavier influence placed on your inventory items in King's Quest, and while there are story choices to be made, they don't feel altogether that consequential, at least in this first chapter. Further, the gameplay has some interesting elements, such as a few first-person rail shooters segments that stand out, among other fun (but short lived) moments.
A Knight to Remember does contain a fair number of puzzles, but they don't ever feel too unreasonable or illogical - most of the puzzles make sense. I found there was some thought required, but never in a way that was potentially frustrating or that could derail the pace of the game. This is good, because it fits well with the light-hearted nature of the game.
The visuals of King's Quest are excellent. You could certainly draw comparisons to several Telltale games, such as the aforementioned The Wolf Among Us or The Walking Dead, but I find the aesthetic of this game to be much more colorful - this is especially apparent in some of the water-color inspired backdrops.
Overall, King's Quest is fun, light-hearted, not too challenging, and beautiful. The story and dialogue are done nicely, and I enjoyed the few hours of entertainment I got out of this chapter. I'd recommend it, for sure.

Treat yourself to this game :-)
The levels of the game are beyond what is currently available in the gaming sector. While this is no RPG, the levels, with their attention to detail, remind me of Looking Glass's classic "Ultima Underworld 1" game (Especially the "Clockwork Mansion" chapter to me was beyond what I have played since the days of "System Shock 1", especially if you immerse yourself into the situation of finding yourself in an elaborately built...).
The immersion factor is generally high here, for seasoned gamers I would recommend:
1) Playing it on "Hard" or "Very Hard" difficulty (on "Very Hard" you will be spotted quite a lot easier, and it is definitely harder to get out of a combat situation alive, especially if your initial aim is to play non-lethal. I started on "Hard", then switched to "Very Hard" midway through the game, to force me to think how to tackle each situation with only one try). As should be industry standard by now, you can switch difficulty at any time.
2) Going down the non-lethal route: I played Dishonored 1 assassin-style, but going non-lethal makes this game more challenging and immersive, imho. (Do not forget that you can choke opponents also if already in a fight (stagger opponent, then choke). Though, if you have more than one opponent that leaves you open for attacks, which will also break your choke, so separation is key for success here.)
3) Turn off goal markers (!) (under Options/Game) - sometimes that means you have no clue where exactly you have to go - that's good ! Explore the area, attack the weakest spot you can find, work yourself through each building - you will get to where you need to be eventually (you do find maps etc, so it is not like you will be working completely in the dark).
4) Don't forget to retrieve paintings - I sometimes had the feeling that at least a third of the money in an area was in the form of collectable paintings.
5) Don't rush through the game, play as if you had just one life (i.e. imagine yourself in the situation, and try to come up with a strategy how to proceed  minimizing the risk of dying), and try to solve each challenge without reloading, if things do not go your way.
6) Explore every corner of each area & hunt down all special items - and you will get a great experience.
(To be fair, the game has some things that could definitely have been done better (teleport aiming, or choking/assassinating sitting persons), and yes basing it on an id engine was not the best idea (on my NVidia GTX 970 / Intel i7 3.3GHz / 32GB RAM performance is good, and the areas look beautiful (due to excellent level design artists), but there is better technology out there) - but to me it just is not nearly enough to pull the game down.)

does a near perfect job on what it wants to be, a twin stick shooter where you gun down as many people as possible. While the gameplay never really evolves past just shooting dudes, different weapons and level layouts keep the experience interesting.
Postal Redux is more than just a graphical update, it improves the weapons, controls, enemy AI... everything. For example: In the original Postal only a couple of weapons actually felt useful and did decent damage. In Postal Redux all of the weapons serve a purpose, others are better at clearing out hordes of enemies and others are better at taking down strong individuals. Even the originally pointless mines are actually useful now!
However even though the game is near perfect, there are still flaws. The screen is a bit too small and there's no way to look around like in for example: Hotline Miami, so there will be times where the enemy gets some free hits on you from off-screen. Original Postal did not have this problem since the enemies had admittedly bad AI, but here since they're so much smarter, you end up in some frustrating situations at times.
But all that aside Postal Redux is a fantastic game and I highly recommend it to anyone who thinks they would like some old fashioned mass murder.

I've managed to get all but one ending for Who is Mike so there are spoilers ahead.
You play as Mike, an ordinary guy who suddenly wakes up in his living room with a bit of amnesia from possibly a few hours ago. The only other person in the room with you is none other than yourself. The question is are you the real Mike?
First of all, the story line is intriguing: the tension between both Mikes and Sarah (depending on one of the choices you make) works really well. One of the reasons why it succeeds in this is the music. It's disonant yet simplistic sound creates great tension in it's darkened setting. The characters are interesting and their dialogue is enough to gauge their personalities. The artwork is absolutely beautiful and matches the grittiness to this tale.
However, the story itself is very short (but it can be shorter depending on your choices) and for a visual novel, you don't get to interact that much in terms of choosing how to answer or make your decision. Speaking of decisions, it lets itself down a little when you make some important choices.
Saying that, if you're looking for a visual novel with a good storyline where you can discuss your theories, and what's going on and you want to feel a lot of tension between characters, this game will satisfy those needs. Just over look what I said in the spoiler part and you should be fine.

Having completely ommitted family trees, or any form of family in a faction, takes alot away from the strategic element of the game. No longer will assassinating a rival factions general give you an advantage in the campaign, since they will just spawn a new general on their next turn. Diplomacy is pointless, since, firstly, the AI are complete idiots, who probably role a dice before making a decision, and secondly, wont stick to any alliances they form anyway. The AI are idiots in more elements of the game, being unable to support their armies or cities, use siege equipment, or make any sort of sensible decision.
The battle engine... Using the same engine from Empire was probably the worst decision SEGA could make. Being an engine made for ranged combat, there is no unit collision. Units just mash together in big big clump, then fight their little one on one battles, completely ignoring their surroundings. Numbers barely play a role in battle, and victory comes down to unit stats and a role of a dice.
The only good thing i can say about this game is the graphics, but even realistic graphics would not be enough to make up for all the negative

The original King's Quest was one of the most iconic adventure game series I know. It had "soul", deep storyline, beautiful graphics and the puzzles I found super hard but challenging to figure out.
This new addition to the series looks nothing like the old game. While the graphics and atmosphere do seem to be nice in their own right, don't expect to find yourself back in the old King's Quest universe. What you will find is some sort of puzzler and "move-and-jump-around just in time" platformer action. Also the game feels like a movie which is played out for you and every once in a while you get to push some buttons to get the story to continue.
All in all I would categorise this as mostly a nice kids game and I would not try and play this with the hopes of re-living the old Kings Quest nostalgia.

I absolutely loved this game.
As a fan of the King's Quest games growing up it was nice to see a new take on the series and to see so many inside jokes referencing the old games.
The game essentially plays partially like Dragon's Lair (another favorite of mine) as well as a 3D adventure game.
There are some references to the Princess Bride as well, which I was fond of.
The game builds it's cinematics very well. It is very much like watching a Disney movie. The characters are very well written, humorous and memorable. I found myself tearing up part way through (but won't post any spoilers). Even the music (which is beautiful) had some hints of the old music from the series in it.
True to the old King's Quest it is easy to die in this game, however you do not have to worry about saving. It will automatically start you off from where you left off, and there are no dead ends.
The adventure game puzzles are not incredibly difficult like the old games, but they are still enjoyable.
Apparently the last puzzle of the game was noted to be difficult, but we got it on our first try. I suppose we got lucky.
There are different ways to complete the puzzles which I found interesting, and they affect the future slightly.
Now the only drawbacks I found to this game were the inability to skip cutscenes (which can get annoying if you die several times in a row) or inability to have multiple save files to see how your choices change things.
I loved this game and can't wait for the next installment.

This review is mainly my opinion and critique of APB Reloaded. My hours show a lot on this game, and for about 3 years this was a fun game for my brother and I to play, but I don't play as much anymore. Here's what I liked about the game:
To start off this game has great customization for character, cars, and clothing. I freakishly made a Princess Anna clone and that's been my character since the beginning. I have an enforcer character (or you can be a criminal) so mimicking real world and fictional police cars and uniforms was a lot of fun to roleplay and show off in game. You can get very creative in this game with the customization as well as character art on billboards and kill songs. The game is open world with two maps so a little like GTA. It's fun to drive around in your police car with friends and do missions or patrol, even hang out.
Here's what I don't like about the game. It is hard to figure out and not exactly new player friendly. I agree with others this is a pay to win game. There's always someone in the match who is better than you because they have a premium weapon, etc. The skill matching and system is not good at all. The missions are redundant and if you're not doing that then patroling/driving around the city doing what not also gets boring quickly especially if you're alone. The matchmaking alone in this game disourages a lot of new players. As other people have mentioned, this game can get pretty toxic. Occationally you'll come across a friendly person and have a nice quick conversation about your car in game or something. Maybe even become good online friends and be apart of their clan in game.
I don't like this game as much as I used to, but I would recommend giving it a try because I have racked up just about 1,000 hours. This game was fun for the time I played and with my friends. If you want check this game out it might keep you entertained for a while if you like cops and robbers type of game. It's a lot of hoops you have to jump thorugh to get the hang and feel of the game. It sure kept me for about 1,000 hours. I personally lost interest in the game over time as many players have experienced, but by all means check it out if this interests you, do it with a friend. I enjoyed this game while it lasted and maybe you'll have a similar enjoyable experience to mine.

This game is a very significant challenge and feels more like an Alien simulator than a game at times.  I played through on hard, and would describe it as pretty difficult.  I died a lot, but was rarely upset about it.  In general, it was all good fun.  You will die.  You will need to sneak in a massive way.
Story -
As an Alien fan, I appreciated the story.  The nostalgia was great.  8/10.
Graphics -
Looked a little questionable in points, but great overall.  Framerate was always high.  Lighting was great.  9/10.
Sound -
Easily the thing that stands out the most about this game in my mind.  I've never specifically paid high levels of attention to sound, but this game got it right.  The only things I'd dock points for are 1) The music can be a little loud compared to SFX at times (this is adjustable).  2)  The music usually fit the situation, but sometimes it didn't in my playthrough.  9/10.
Gameplay -
For me 9/10, but I'm basically the kind of person this game was made for.  I would expect most people who already had an interest in the game to get about a 7/10's worth out of it at least.
What I liked most :  It's a good Aliens game that is very intense.
What I liked least :  While the Alien is really well done, I think there was still room for improvement.  I definitely wouldn't call this game buggy or glitchy, but his movements were ocasionally a little bizarre.  I'd liked to have seen a little more crawling.
So far so good. I am terrified and yet entertained. Totally worth it.

Pretty good. Highly similar to the first game in structure, story, and mechanics, but with more things to do. Outside of Sokolov, the visual design (which was good in the first game), has improved in this game, and it looks great.
Both games are really fun when you play high chaos.
D2 has elements of genuine mystery that the first game lacked. The hospital level is a great example of this, as you pretty much take on the role of a detective piecing together an increasingly horrifying happening. This was easily my favorite level in the game.
One major step back in this sequel, though, is in character motivation. This is a series about righting wrongs (of the people who dishonored you), so it is vitally important that the villians be compelling. In the first game, villians were believable; they would plot, steal, and kill so they could rule, and when you took them out it felt meaningful because you really felt like they had taken something from Corvo. In this game, every main villian is a lunatic with no motivation other than murder, so bringing them down just feels like an exercise. This is a big problem in D2.
I mean, even the premise is comparatively ludicrous. In the first game, the premise is: avenge your dead queen and clear your name. In D2, the premise is: try to rescue your queen or protector who has been sealed in stone.

First off, I would like to congradulate Running With Scissors for not making a top down shooter that controlled like a tricycle missing one of the wheels. On a serious note, the control is FAR better than what the original POSTAL had. This time around, I was able to ambush and bomb rush the enemies that are out for my blood. With the new controls, I was able to dodge missles and other projectiles more easily than in the original game. As for the presentation, the hand drawn stages look really nice and mesh well with the 3D models of the characters. Another thing that I liked was the wide variety of NPC's that you can kill and the animations that play when they're not quite dead yet.  I also enjoyed the inclusion of the revolver, as it allowed me to kill most enemies with one hit. Additionally, the new Rampage mode is tons of fun, as I found it thrilling to gun down as many people as I could in the area around me.
Although I find POSTAL Redux a good game, I have some issues. First off, although I praised the presentation earlier, sometimes dead bodies clip through the various objects in the scenery, which kind of bothered me. Another thing I didn't like is how they didn't elaborate of Postal Dude's background and why he's doing this whole thing in the first place. Instead, the game just throws you into the action after the title card for the level. Additionally, I disliked how the enemies in the stages didn't really try to come after you once the level started. Instead, they would stand around until you approached them or shot them while they were standing there. Finally, I don't like how the game doesn't elaborate on who the people at the end of the game are, as it leaves us wondering who are the people keeping the Dude locked up.
Despite all this, I find POSTAL Redux to be far superior to the original game that came out in 1997. If you are a fan of the POSTAL series, top-down shooters, and shooting everything in your path, than this game is for you. If this doesn't quite tickle your fancy, check out POSTAL 2 instead.
My final score is a 8/10

System Shock 2 is a First-Person RPG Survival Horror where you play as Soldier G65434-2, commonly known as "Goggles", the almost silent main protagonist who is without much development so it's easier for the player to project themselves as the character who signed up to work at the UNN Rickenbacker, a military space vessel that accompanies a FTL(faster than light) starship known as the Von Braun.
The player gets to choose which military branch they'd like to select which ultimately comes down to which "class" you'd like to pick.
The O.S.A, which helps you focus on psionic abilities which resembles "magic" where you'd have a wide variety of abilities ranging from firing energy to damage enemies, pulling items that would be otherwise unobtainable, to even healing yourself when you're low on health.
The Marines, that focuses on combat granting you early access to some weapons with a little of utility stats so you don't risk being a brainless brute.
And finally the Navy, a class that has more focus on hacking, repairing and access to minor weaponry so you're not completely defenseless. There are tons of terminals to hack and your weapons degrade incredibly fast so the Navy has a lot of useful utilities.
With that said the classes do not limit you to types of weapons or abilities including hacking and repairing as you can increase your stats, so choosing a starter class will have very little impact on your overall gameplay. They matter a bit more but much akin to how Dark Souls handles its classes.
From the games events eventually you'll find yourself being awoken in a cryo-tube on the Von Braun by some disturbances and contacted by a woman called Dr. Janice Polito who will guide you through the starship's decks, now infected by beings known as The Many, who will also telepathically persuade you to become a part of their mass and along the way you will begin to question Dr. Janice Polito's intentions as she talks down to you as if she's a goddess and you're just a mere
.
The starship has all dangerous monstrosities ranging from The Many's undead-like abominations that hunt you and not only that it seems like the whole starship wants you dead as even the electronics turn against you. The scarce amount of supplies and the unrelenting difficulty makes you dread what's around the corner as you'll be balled up in a room questioning yourself if you want to use the round of bullets you recently picked up whilst hearing the moans of the grotesque creature in the other room telling you that he's "Sorry.".
The graphics are very dated seeing as the game was released in 1999 but the excellent audio compensates and helps keeps you immersed at all times ranging from the enemies speaking to you or themselves and the audio of your crew member's logs that help you understand their twisted experiences on the ship and sometimes include their inevitable demise.
The game has a co-op option so you can experience the horrors with up to 3 other friends but be prepared to save often before you load new zones as someone may not be able to make it through. Luckily the game is old and even on dated systems you're able to load it back up in less than half a minute. Unless you're keeping a light mood or goofing around, the experience of survival horror will remain there as you need to now manage the divided scarce supplies but with the advantage of having more hands with more skills to help you battle through the hordes.
Lengthwise the game is very long with little backtracking, without exploring everything my first time completing it took me 14 hours on Normal difficulty and for what it costs if you like Horrors and First-Person RPGs then it's a must buy.
Personally this is the best survival horror game made to this date and one of the better games made and is absolutely recommended.

This is the prime example of how you make a game and how to build a community around it, without the pay walls.
This game, in concept, really shouldn't be that entertaining but that is where I have to step in and say that this assumption is very wrong indeed.
This game brings a huge aspect of realism to the PC gaming market. The game is pretty simple - You're a truck driver! Build your own company! That's the short and sweet version of the game.
The complexities don't stop there. Far from it, as discovering all of Europe with a constant stream of outstanding DLC and a huge modding community makes this game ever expanding with no effort at all, for one single price of admission that is almost on sale all of the time for a steal. Even at full price, this game demands that you play it at least once to give it a shot. It gets addicting quite quickly and you'll find yourself wasting hours you didn't even know had passed on this game.
It's not a stressful game either, it is very relaxing to play and the game does a good job of getting you up to speed and getting you into the game, bar one or two missing "Realism" keys like indicators (The "[" and "]" buttons) and the wipers ("P") but a quick check of the default keyboard layout will fix that. It just isn't explicably mentioned outright during gameplay. It also has a wide variety of functionality for wheel and peripheral support as well.
It's not a highly demanding game either, most modern office computers and notebooks should run this minimalistically without too much hassle and overheating issues.
You will find yourself listening to your favourite tunes on the in-game radio stream functionality (Yes, it has one and has a huge variety of stations, I listen to Radio XS Manchester myself) or on a makeshift CD/MP3 player (Via something like Deezer or Spotify) in the background.
The company building aspect is in-depth but easy to understand and the customisation for progressing is pretty consistent, making all those fancy things all the more worthwhile.
I highly suggest you look into the multiplayer mod called TruckersMP and give that a go. It's effectively the same game but with multiplayer functionality and it is completely free and further reinforces what I am about to say.
How do I sum up this game then? Euro Truck Simulator 2 gets what is great about trucking out on the open road, thrusts it out of the real world right into your system in front of you. For an indie developer, SCS Software has made outstanding success with this series, far more than anyone could have initially imagined. It's the fans, modders, passionate staff and the players who make this all worthwhile. Even if this game sounds boring, you need to play it. Put it on the list of games you must play before you die. Even if you ultimately don't end up liking it, at least you have experienced what I think is one of the greatest things to have EVER hit Steam.

1. Farm slime poop for money
2. Spend money on upgrades
3. Farm more/different/fancier slimes for more money. Goto #2.
It's a pretty straightforward game and a bit grindy.  Controls and movement mechanics feel pretty good. The exploration has some metroidvania elements to it.  The farming is generally fun.  The whole thing is pretty well designed and the game does a good job of making everything very cute and a little sad.
Caution: "The Tarr" are formed when a Largo (i.e. large slime) eats a Plort that is unlike the two that it produces. Largos themselves are formed when a normal slime eats a different type of plort.  Fighting "The Tarr" requires either the water tank upgrade or shooting them somewhere else (preferably in the sea).  I didn't know this at first and it cost me most of my slimes and chickens.

Quite possibly the most adorable farming sim I have ever seen.
The game does very well at starting you out slow and teaching you how to play at a pace that won't overwhelm and confuse. You gain access to new areas at a slow enough pace that you can fully explore what you already have, but not so slowly that you feel held back and frustrated with progress.
At first, you will be dealing with the cheapest slime plort harvest production, which will allow you to learn how to farm them without presenting too much difficulty. There is also abundant food available in these initial areas, so while you are figuring out how to grow your own food, it is very easy and quick to make a circuit through the Dry Reef to grab more food for stockpiling, either in place of or in addition to growing your own crops. At first, I made one vegetable plot and one coop, but made runs to also gather more fruit and vegetables and chickens to supplement. Eventually, you will become efficient enough to produce what you need on your ranch.
As you play, you will come across certain critters that will reward you with more food or items. Once you've discovered how to deal with them and get the reward, you will be able to open up more areas on the map that were previously locked to you. I found that opening too many areas too quickly lead to me becoming easily lost, as there is currently no in game map (as of the morning of August 7, 2017, however there is a planned update that should be introducing the map later this day). I would first fully explore and mostly memorize my current areas before adventuring further, as it is very easy to become lost and confused with all the twisting tunnels and branching paths, as well as a few hidden tunnels. Once the map update is out, this concern should diminish quite a bit, and for some people, memorizing the map may be a welcome challenge (it isn't for me as I find it very difficult to orient myself within game worlds).
Your main goals will include exploring the map and finding treasures, catching slimes and learning how to farm them, and upgrading your ranch and your equipment. There are both quality-of-life upgrades that make ranching easier and cosmetic upgrades that are just for fun and don't effect gameplay. Many QOL upgrades are not strictly necessary, though as you make more money, they are a useful money sink that make doing everything you want to do easier, faster, or simpler.
Most slimes are harmless to you, but there are some that can hurt you, intentionally or not. There are feral slimes that will attack you, and a version of slimes that are actively hostile and will even chase you down. Typically tho, physical danger comes from not being careful while exploring rather than the wild critters you find on the range.
You will be capturing slimes, of which there are currently 15 varieties (with yet more already slated for arrival in future updates), and you can ranch these slimes as they are, or create hybrid slimes that will produce plorts of both varieties that they are made of. For example, a pink slime produces a pink plort, and a tabby slime produces a tabby plort. Hybridize these two together and you get a pink tabby largo slime that when fed will produce a pink and a tabby plort, increasing monetary yield significantly. Most slimes can be hybridized to create a largo (a combination of two slimes), giving them features and personalities similar to both slimes. Be careful once you have largos though! A slip up with plorts can create a disaster.
You don't need to hybridize slimes, and doing so will make some of them more dangerous to keep- but it also makes them more rewarding, so experiment until you find what you like best.
All in all, it is a fun and relaxing game with a somewhat self-directed gameplay. There is a story that unfolds as you explore the range, but your main focus will be on whatever you choose for yourself, whether it is the highest tech gadgetry and upgraded ranch, amassing as much wealth as possble, keeping the cutest slimes you can find, or any combination thereof. It isn't a highly intricate game with unforgiving mechanics, which makes it easy for children and adults alike to jump into. If you want something soothing and pretty, easily jumped into without being overly complicated, but with a rich and rewarding world to explore, then this may be the game for you.
The developer is still actively working on updates and has further content already planned, and the game came out of early access fully fleshed out, so I am definitely looking forward to what more they can offer us as time goes on. I think the game has a great future ahead of it and I can't wait to find more secrets, capture more slimes, and immerse myself in a gloriously cute and vibrant world.

As a sequel to one of the greatest strategy games to have ever been released, Rome II had quite alot to live up to.
Unfortunatly, not only did it fall short of the original, it was a complete miss in terms of what is to be expected of a Total War game.
Having completely ommitted family trees, or any form of family in a faction, takes alot away from the strategic element of the game. No longer will assassinating a rival factions general give you an advantage in the campaign, since they will just spawn a new general on their next turn. Diplomacy is pointless, since, firstly, the AI are complete idiots, who probably role a dice before making a decision, and secondly, wont stick to any alliances they form anyway. The AI are idiots in more elements of the game, being unable to support their armies or cities, use siege equipment, or make any sort of sensible decision.
The battle engine... Using the same engine from Empire was probably the worst decision SEGA could make. Being an engine made for ranged combat, there is no unit collision. Units just mash together in big big clump, then fight their little one on one battles, completely ignoring their surroundings. Numbers barely play a role in battle, and victory comes down to unit stats and a role of a dice.
The only good thing i can say about this game is the graphics, but even realistic graphics would not be enough to make up for all the negative
I have gone back to playing Rome: Total War, i would recommend you do the same

If you're looking for a 1:1 remake of half life than this isn't for you. What this game does succeed in however is expand on what made half life great. The game feels more modern and realistic compared to it's predecessor which even I'll admit (and I'm nostalgic af) is beginning to show signs of age.
There is one problem with this mod however. This mod has been in development for 11 years and counting. That being said, black mesa up until fairly recently wasn't a payed project. The team didn't recieve a cent prior to it's fairly recent steam release (aside from donations). If you're only looking for content I'd recommend starting off with the mod version of the game and installing surface tension uncut (seeing as how that's pretty much all you're getting here aside from multiplayer and some substantial graphical updates). If you're more like me however and you feel as though the developers deserve some funding for all of their efforts thus far, then by all means, purchase this game.
The xen levels may not be finished but you're still getting a good 10 hours (more if you include the surface tension update I think) of immersive gameplay at a very reasonable price. That's probably a lot more than I can say about most contemporary shooters. All in all this game is the result of a labor of love and it very clearly shows. This isn't a 1:1 remake but it's very obvious that the developers are huge half life fans and, knowing full well what made half life great, have expanded on it in every way that they can.

POSTAL Redux is a loving recreation of an old cult classic that harkens back to the heyday of isometric shooters. The newly remastered art is fantastic and really makes the colors pop. A new Carnival level takes advantage of the new 1080p style with lots of colors and high resolution art. Not to mention the much improved controls. It controls beautifully now, a massive improvement upon the original which was one of my biggest gripes of it.
Along with this, Redux adds a new Rampage mode that is very fun and fast paced. It is a score based mode which rewards fast and creative gameplay. The new Revolver weapon also packs a satisfying punch and Rick Hunter's sexy voice is still the stuff of legends.
Unfortunately, the game is not quite finished yet. A co-op multiplayer mode will be coming some time which I am sure will be great fun for friends who want to go postal. Along with this, the DLC maps for Special Delivery will be remastered and released in a future free update for Redux.
That being said, I don't know why the old ending was replaced with this new one other than the old ending was too controversial even for RWS to redo. This is a shame as the original ending level was one of the most shocking moments I ever faced in a video game, and the new ending leaves no impact other than a big "huh?"
Botched ending aside, POSTAL Redux is still a very well done remake, but I say wait a bit until either the multiplayer and DLC maps get added or there is a sale to purchase it.  Also PLEASE add Steam Workshop upport.

The first time I played a King's Quest (KQ) game was when King' Quest VI was released on CD-ROM in 1993. I was blown away by the quality production of that game and haven't played a single adventure game to this day that surpasses it. KQ6 is without a doubt the best in the series. Even if the graphics are outdated, it still holds on its own today. When I heard a new King's Quest series was going to be released I got a bit nervous as I was afraid it wouldn't live up to the quality of KQ6, but was hopeful when I heard that Jane Jensen was getting involved. After playing the first chapter of this new series, the following are my opinions of the game, how it compares to my favorite adventure game KQ6, and whether you should buy it or not. I will be updating this review as I play each chapter.
TL;DR: This game is a solid adventure game full of passion and high energy, but compared to the past KQ games is a bit watered/dumbed down in maturity and depth. I highly recommend newcomers to the KQ franchise to play this new series. I also recommend this for players who have played the previous KQ games, but for the better experience you'll have to let go of some of your favorite aspects of the previous KQ games.

Dark Souls II is just a really well paced, well crafted game that I would happily and wholeheartedly recommend to anyone that is looking for atmospheric adventure.
Combat in this series is based around Stamina, your knowledge of your weapon style and the enemies attack patters. Thus, some trial and error is in store for those of you that are uninitiated from the previous two games. There is a little bit of a learning curve when it comes to combat. You can't just button mash and hope to win. You'll need to be defensive, strike only when necessary and don't be greedy. Impatience is the number one killer in this game, and it will cause you to die.
You will die in this game, a lot, but that isn't necessarily a bad thing. Dying in this game doesn't give you a game over, however it will drain your spirit to the point that your health is diminished the more you do die, but with each death comes more experience, and eventually you will conquer a challenge and regain your humanity, and live to fight another day.
The world of Dark Souls II is very well put together. Each area is part of the world of Drangelic, a realm where death is a common curse, and people come to this broken land to feed on souls and conquer great challenges - but those that stay slowly forget why they came, and lose their humanity. It's a very neat game in the way that the world around you is basically the story. There is literally no narrative to this game, you learn about the lore, the characters and the state of the world around you from playing and paying attention to subtle environmental cues, character dialog and piecing it together as you go. I like that it's not forced, and feels mysterious.
I will keep this review brief, but expect many hours of dungeon crawling, character development, spell slinging, blade slashing, hammer crunching adventure. And dying, lots of dying.
Epic bosses, evil creatures and Darkness await you!

This is a spoiler-free review.
Who Is Mike is a very enjoyable way to pass an hour or so.
Pros:
- Great art, especially for a free game.
- Good writing, moreso than in many of the indie VNs I've played. It can get repetitive when the protagonist is angsting, but in a believable way.
- Unusual plot that keeps you guessing until the last minute.
- Free.
Cons:
- Short. Which is fine, especially for a free game, but if you like your VNs long with many branches, this is not one of them.
- Lack of variety in player choices. For most of the game, you'll be faced with the same decision again and again in slightly different contexts.
- Non-intuitive branches. Maybe it's just me, but it took a lot of trial and error, followed by reluctant use of a guide, to figure out how to get all the endings that branch off from the main section of the game.
- Inconsistent storyline. This is the one truly bad thing about this game - instead of the endings gradually giving you more and more bits of the puzzle, like in a good mystery VN, different endings reveal that you were playing different scenarios all along. It's a bit like a murder mystery where the the murderer turns out to be a different person depending on the choices you make during your investigation, even though the clues are all the same each time.
In the end, I definitely recommend it. It is a distinct and memorable experience that costs no money and not too much of your time.

If you loved the original Postal, you'll love this.
If you love Postal 2, give the first Postal a look before buying, it's a completely different type of game.
If you don't know what Postal is, keep reading.
Postal was released in 1997 and created a ton of controversy for it's violence. Sure, it may be tame by todays standards, but back then, this game was targeted by tons of groups. It wasn't that the game was bloody (though it is), but the manner in which the violence is depicted. Roughly 1/3 of the people you get ot kill in this game are civillians. Some of them will crawl along the ground after being shot, saying things like "I can't feel my legs". It does paint a pretty disturbing, if a bit darkly humorous, picture.
So what's it all about?
That's almost a mystery. What we know is, there's a guy named "Postal Dude" who is evicted from his home and is getting shot at by the authorities. If you read the manual, he believes a large portion of the population in his town have some sort of sickness. However, in-game, the messages before the levels are just bleak and sometimes downright evil. Aside from these messages, there isn't much to go on. As such, you can draw up tons of conclusions in this game. That's one of the things that makes it so intriguing (as well as the atmosphere in general). The whole game takes on a very, again, disturbing tone. Not quite Manhunt level of disturbing, but it can still be pretty unsettling.
The game is played from a top-down perspective. It controls, now, like a modern twin-stick shooter. Each level has a set number of people you have to kill (or you can opt to kill the entire population on the stage). Once you kill enough, the exit will open. It's a fairly short experience. Each level will take 4-5 minutes to clear (with the later stages taking a bit longer, obviously). There are 17 stages in all, as well as a Rampage mode where you try and string together kills to get a high score.
Gameplay-wise, the game is simple. You point, you shoot, you walk, you shoot some more, you pick up more weapons and health, repeat this until the level ends. It's simple, and pretty fun, but it does wear thin pretty quickly (the game will be over before you're completely bored with it, though). The AI isn't particularly smart, but it does seem like some of the pathfinding issues have been ironed out since the original.
Graphics-wise, the game looks fantastic when compared to the original. I thought that the newer character models did give it an overall more "cartoony" feel, but it's still a great upgrade. The redrawn maps are beautiful, and everything is animated nicely. However, if you don't know what to expect from the original Postal, this game will still look extremely dated if you're expecting a modern-looking game.
Some of the sounds have been revamped, but most of the levels are still devoid of any kind of music. You still get the creepy ambient sounds, the great environmental sounds, and all the other good stuff, but I really wish that RWS would have composed some tracks for the campaign. Rampage mode does have music, and it's very up tempo and fits in with the gameplay.
Overal, Postal Redux accomplishes what it wanted to. It updated the graphics, gameplay, and overall experience of the original Postal. Is Postal still a good game to play in 2016? It's definitely fun in small doses, but it does come off as very primitive these days. I still enjoy myself, but I can understand how someone would favor newer twin-stick shooters over this game.
+ Graphical overhaul
+ New weapons
+ Rampage mode
+ Still as atmospheric as ever
+ Revamped controls
- Short
- Very basic when compared to newer games of its kind
For fans of the original Postal: 9/10 (doesn't include expansion levels)
For newcomers: 6/10
It would have been a bit higher, but $15 for this game, if you've never played Postal and don't exactly know what you're getting into, it might seem a bit steep. It's a definite purchase at <$10

This game is oft considered a classic, and once one has a feel for it, it's easy to see why!  SS2 seamlessly blends RPG and FPS elements, and is one of the few FPS games to include any form of ledge-grabbing.  The atmosphere is very lonely and forboding, with excellent music.  The audio in general is top-notch, and the story is told is a way that inspired several later games to follow suit.  The game is in general quite entertaining, and
There are a few things one should be aware of, however.  The graphics are quite dated, and this is occasionally distracting.  The level design is a bit wierd and navigation is difficult.  There are a lot of control settings that need to be adjusted before one should begin play.  I was dissapointed by the ending because it was cheezy, and a better ending had already presented itself that would have easily paved the way for a "System Shock 3".
Overall, I give "System Shock 2" a 93% "A."

I actually got this for free on the Xbox One for my kids.  It was one of the Games with Gold this month.   After my son played for a bit, I took over for him.  Then my other son wanted to play.  I could see this was going to be a fight for the Xbox, so purchased one copy for my PC and another for the Steam Machine so we can all play at once.
It's addictive - and a bit mind numbing.  You'll lose some hours, but it's got just enough strategy, crafting, exploration and market explotation to keep you occupied.  I'm about 10 hours in right now after spending about 3 or 4 on the Xbox version.  Of course the PC version is better - not nearly as laggy when the ranch gets busy.   Getting the ranch up and making steady profit is the biggest hurdle - it takes a few hours to really get it up and running.  After that, the exploration works on some level, mostly as a break from the huting and gathering required to get a steady income.  There isn't anythign very dangerous in the world, most of the enemies you can easily disperse or avoid.  I've heard most people finish this game at around 30 - 50 hours.  That's about the right amount of game play I assume.  It's has some very addicting elements - but it's not something that will have great replay value and definitely not something I  would want to spend more than a few weekends playing.
I do recommend this game - it's great for kids, it has just enough allure for adults and like others have mentioned, a multiplayer (even 2 player split screen) would go a long way making this a great family game.   The price is right for the amount of gameplay offered.
