TLDR: It's pretty good, but should still be Early Access. I'm going to wait a few more months before I play it again.
I was waiting for this game to come out of early access, and was super excited to see it released and on sale! I bought it right away! Unfortunately, The biggest con to this game is that it still feels like an early access title.
So first, the good: Slimes! Ranching! It's cute! Your playable character is great and the world feels real and unique. People way smarter and more eloquent than me have talked about the good parts of this game. So, onto the bad...
The beginning of the game is great, but around day 8-9 the amount of unfinished content gets too noticeable to ignore. For example, there's one area where there are bridges between an island, and the island is obviously meant to contain a boss or special enemy (there are danger signs, high walls, etc). But it's just an empty set piece - no boss, no items, not even any enemies or creatures at all. This is just the most obvious one, but there are a handful of other smaller issues that contribute to the game feeling like it's just missing a few integral parts to be complete: There's no map; you can find special slimes (I found a golden one and a lucky cat one), but if you capture them they just disappear from your inventory without any indication as to why; you run out of upgrades before you feel like your cages and utility tool are really way better than before; there's a lot of tantalizing stuff lying around the world (treasure boxes, locked doors), but no tooltip or guidance as to how they work or how to catch them.
I stopped playing on Day 12. I had maxed out all of my plots in the main game, and unlocked the second farm area. I wasn't sure where to find another slime key to open one of the two locked doors barring my progress (one through a cave of aggro slimes and one across a long bridge after the area I mentioned above). I found myself just trying to use the jetpack to break out of the map because I'd completely lost interest in caring for my slimes or exploring the same area I'd been exploring from the beginning.
Being somewhat of a sandbox game, none of that really makes it unplayable (assuming you're smarter than me and can find the key to the locked doors). Not unplayable, but it just makes it a little less fun. I wish there was a "neutral" option on steam. I still recommend this title if you can overlook the shortcomings I mentioned. Personally, I try not to buy games in Early Access because I hate the feeling like I'm missing out or playing something unfinished. But that's not nearly as annoying as games that come out of Early Access before they're ready. Slime Rancher is a really great idea, and a pretty good game, but it needs a little more love before it's actually a finished product.

Ever since Slime Rancher appeared on Jim Sterling's youtube channel, I had some moderate interest in the game and kept it wishlisted - it was an indie darling that came out of nowhere. It wasn't high on my list to play, and I've only played it because I got the game from a Humble Bundle and it recently released in version 1.0. Now that I've played it myself, I'm not too impressed. While the slimes' apperance and animations are cute and charming themselves, dealing with them is moderately annoying.
The world is filled with slimes that bounce around and produce (or rather defecate) gems called "plorts" which have value back on planet Earth - turning in these plorts into an exchange station will give you Newbucks, which is the currency used to purchases ranch equipment and gear upgrades. Your character is equipped with a sort of "Vacuum gun" that can suck up and shoot slimes, food, plorts and other resources, but only has limited (4) slots to contain them. (which can probably be increased, but I haven't reached that point after about 6-8hrs) Slimes will eat any food or plorts from other slime types (thus, transforming into a hybrid of their original slime type and the plort they ate), which is annoying if you are wanting to collect the food or plorts they eat before you can take them, or when they transform into the hybrid Largo slime that you can no longer put into your ineventory (and instead need to carry around one at a time while obstructing your view).
Need more money to buy a corral to contain your slimes? Well just pick up plorts and exchange....but you can only hold twenty in one slot, even if you have other empty slots that could in theory hold more. Oh, your slimes are bouncing out of the corral? Buy some high walls or an air net after you farm more plorts. Need more food for your slimes? Buy a farm and then spend more money to upgrade it to get food more effiiently. Sucking up plorts from corrals is a PAIN IN THE A** thanks to the games physics and limited inveintory slots? Get a special plort vacuum in the corral so you can finally get the plorts alot more easily. Tired of your limited sprint distance? Buy the stamina upgrade. Can only hold a few plorts? Get a storage capacity upgrade. Boom Slimes doing too much damage too you? Get a health uprgrade.
Outside of the Jetpack, Pulse Wave (which I've never had to use), or Water Tank, there's no real engaging change to making progress in Slime Rancher. It's a constant treadmill of feeding and and profiting from slimes, so you can keep feeding and profiting from your Slimes. Other Steam reviiewers have referred to this game as "Fun", though 6+ hours in and I'm not having fun, but I'm just going through the motions to see another skin of a slime that has more valuable plorts than the last slimes I've dealt with.

The art, sound, music, and voice acting are all as good as I could have asked for in this game.  I love interacting with things multiple times to hear the different funny narration you get.
There's lots of replayability with the different choices and puzzle solutions and I wonder how much will carry over to future episodes.
The first couple hours were very linear, so I was pleasantly surprised when the game opened up for a ton of exploration.  In that sense,  the game felt like a very old "open world" adventure game like one of the old King's Quest or Monkey Island games.
The characters and story are very charming and feel very "King's Quest" to me.  There's a ton of references that only people who played the old games will catch, but they shouldn't detract for a first time player.
There's much much more exploration and gameplay than a Telltale game, but anyone looking for an unforgiving old school Sierra game will be disappointed.  The puzzles are much more logical, straightforward, and simple, relying on exploration more than sideways leaps of logic like some of the more infamous moments of the old games. (Eg, starting a machine with a piece of cheese).  There was only one time I got stuck where I couldn't figure out what to do just by exploring more or taking a moment to think about my inventory or things I hadn't accomplished yet, and that was entirely down to missing an interactive hotspot.
In addition to exploring for items, puzzle sequences, and dialog trees, there are some first person bow shooting sequences and QTEs but for the most part I thought they weren't too difficult and fit in the game perfectly fine.  There was one sequence where you shoot a bunch of monsters to save one of the NPCs.  It wasn't graphic or anything, but I felt this was out of place in the series because while there were violent options in the earlier games, there was always a nonviolent alternative available.  Maybe I missed it?
The game could also use a run button, the ability to skip dialogs / cutscenes, and some other bits of polish.
I'm still partial to the darker, Arabian Nights tone KQ6 had, and I'm also very partial to the KQ2 ADG remake.  However, I feel like this is a great continuation of the series.  The more forgiving gameplay and family friendly, modern CG animated feature feel of the game is much more reminiscent of the direction KQ7 wanted to take the series, except in my opinion executed much much better here.

Upon finishing Alien Isolation I had the impression that a lot of work was put in the development of this title. I can honestly say that, "Yes" this game is the best out of the Alien Franchise. It really does give you the feel of the first Alien movie with Sigourney Weaver within its dark rustic atmosphere. You can hear many audibles that they actually used within the Alien movie itself as you progress.
Some reviewers claimed that the Alien is scripted when it is not. I don't know where they got that idea because the Alien is totally RANDOM within its hunting, paths and appearances. You will die in this game, but the amount of deaths will totally be reliant on your gaming style. I always kept on the move for the most part and actually went through some areas with very little contact with the Alien. Even though I could hear him banging around in the vents above my head.
You can even play through the game, as I did, with very little use of the crafted weapons available to you throughout the game. Again, it all depends on your playing style.
The graphics are well done, but once in awhile you might see floating static artifacts such as a tool or phone where either you or a NPC were earlier. Sounds within the game are also spot on, but I play my games with the music off so I don't know if the scores are good or not. I heard that they were though.
The story line was fairly well done too, but the ending is.....well I'll leave that up to you on what you think.
Gameplay is very fluid, but for some reason once in awhile my character had problems standing up even though I kept hitting the button.
The main gripe that I have with Alien Isolation is that the alien always seemed to know where I was no matter how qiuet I was in the levels. Sometimes it was downright frustrating and unrealistic how the Alien would always zero in on my position by either following me through the vents in the ceiling or prowling the area always right up to the locker I was hiding in. Once in awhile; however, the Alien would leave the area which was a sigh of relief for exploring some areas.
Overall, Alien Isolation is worth the purchase especially if you see it on sale like I did. I think you won't be disappointed if your a fan of the franchise. I definitely  recommend Alien Isolation.

Though rough and somewhat lacking in the gameplay department, Eternal Senia is a unique and heartfelt experience that is well worth a closer look, especially considering its short length, independent origins, and nonexistent price tag.
Eternal Senia is an ARPG with a simple gameplay formula. Walk into a room, kill any enemies, solve any puzzles, walk to the next room, and repeat. The process is punctuated by gathering materials from fallen enemies and crafting stronger equipment, as well as the occasional cutscenes. Upon clearing the first dungeon and its boss, you are given a new environment, a new skill, and a new list of craftable items, and you begin again in the second dungeon. To be critcally honest, it does become monotonous as you continue, and you'll become familiar with the layout after just one dungeon, but the game is short enough that it ends before things become
stale. And the game does offer incentives for exploration, such as hidden treasures and special rewards for killing a certain number of each enemy or crafting the strongest available equipment.
The game itself is made in RPG Maker, but shows few signs of it aside from some visual and sound effects (though anyone who has spent some time with RPG Maker could recognize many more aspects of it). There are a few noticable bugs and oversights that arise throughout the game, but nothing that gets in the way of gameplay. In addition, it is clear that English is not the author's first language, so there are numerous grammatical and spelling errors plaguing the writing, as well as some awkward translation choices, but nothing so bad that you can't understand the author's intent.
On the subject of the writing, Eternal Senia's true worth lies in its story. Centering around a pair of sisters named Senia and Magaleta, the game treats you to a wonderfully emotional and woefully tragic story of the bond between the two sisters and the trials they endure for the other's sake. The story is paced excellently throughout the game, mostly told through a series of flashbacks as you progress through the dungeons, each building up the backstory and revealing more about the sisters and their intentions. Also atypically for a game made in RPG Maker, Eternal Senia features three seperate endings based on how you handle the final two fights of the game. It is hard to elaborate on them without spoiling, but they each encompass a unique and emotional end to the sisters' tale, whether bittersweet or heartwrenching.
All in all, Eternal Senia is certainly a worthwhile game which despite its flaws delivers a unique and touching experience. It also stands as a testament to what one independent developer can make out of their passion, even with a lack of experience and a questionable set of tools.

I just tried this simulator out today - As a first look this game is a LOT more enjoyable than I thaught it would be (I got it in the winter sale because of the great deal). Trucks are by no means interesting to me, or at least, they weren't before I picked this game up. As I jumped in I found it very difficult to drive around... I actually had to google how to reverse, which may have been because I set all the gears to manual during my configuration at the beginning. I also found myself getting fined for multiple speeding offenses (and sometimes damage) during my first couple of jobs, but literally after about an hour I pretty much got the hang of operating the truck, and there is so much you can do with it as you would expect from a game like this. Aside from just driving and honking a horn you have your left and right indicators, lights, windscreen wipers and a few other facilities I haven't got round to playing with yet. I can't drive a car in real life let alone a truck but I can only imagine this simulator is the closest thing you can get to realistic driving. This is one of the best casual games I have in my library, you can import your own music to listen to on the radio in-game, you don't have to pick up jobs all the time and can free ride when you want to (as long as you have money for fuel which is cheap anyway and can be covered in expenses by your employer when you're working). Parking the goods is fun and challenging, there is an automatic option which of course rewards less experience. There is a vast amount of cities to explore and commute between accross the different countries of Europe.
To summarise I am thrilled by the realism and experience this simulator has to offer. This was a one-off purchase for me which I baught in the Winter sale as it didn't strike as my type of game (you could say I'm your average MOBA/Fantasy/Sci-Fi gamer) though having played it I would say it's more than worth the full price and would highly recommend to anyone.

NOTE: My character is lvl 44 at the time of this review, I've done lots of questing and about 7 dungeons.
It's hard to recommend this game.  But then again, it's hard not to.  I have such a love-hate relationship with it.
On the one hand, it's Elder Scrolls, and in terms of atmosphere, lore, questing and depth, it lives up to the name.  LOTS of content, lots of things to read, dialogue to hear, things to do.  Crafting system is excellent, voice actors are top-notch, graphics and atmosphere are great, and the animations in particular are VERY well-done, the best out of all ES games if you ask me.
However the actual gameplay feels very shallow and boring, and the game overall suffers from all the typical MMORPG bullcrap, such as:
- very, very stupid and repetitive AI from NPCs.  The just stand there in perfectly spaced clumps of 3-5 enemies, do nothing ever, and are very stupid and easy to just walk over like insects.
- Because of this, there is no surprise or suspense and all dungeons feel the same.  You enter, and 3-4 npcs will wait for you near the entrance.  You kill them easily.  You walk another 10 yards and 3-4 more of the exact same npcs are in your way.  Same level, same health, same abilities, same incredibly stupid AI.  Rinse repeat several more times until you hit the mini-boss.  Rinse-repeat again with 3-4 different mini-bosses until the last boss, kill it, and voila you've saved the day.
- Same goes for the actual game world: yes, it is vast, lots to explore, lots of mini-quests, treasure maps are fun, searching for mats is fun, sometimes an occasional "event" but even they get repetitive.  But exploring quickly gets tiring and repetitive as well, since the game world suffers from the same MMO crap as the dungeons:  All npcs are clones of eachother with different skins.  Same dumb AI.  Same absolutely HORRIBLE detection behavior.  At one point I was stealthed literally in front of an npc jumping up and down in front of his face and he didn't "detect" me.
- It's just a shame that there isn't more challenge for single player questing.  I was really hoping they wouldn't fall into the typical MMO trap of making everything so streamlined and identical everywhere... There is no unpredictability in the game world, no danger, thus no excitement.  On my Dragonknight, I can very easily obliterate npcs 10 levels higher than me without breaking a sweat.  It makes the combat BORING and stale.
- Some of the mini games like stealth, lockpicking, treasure chests, crafting, persuasion etc seem well done and polished on the surface, but due to how incredibly easy it all is, makes it all seem like a game designed for small ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ children...  Thus it all gets boring very quickly.  My level 44 nord barbarian with NO skill points in Ledgerman can easily and consitently open any lock in the entire game.  I think I have something like 200 lockpicks, because I've only ever broken about a half dozen of them.  Also a 6'3 235 pound nord warrior in FULL PLATE ARMOR should NOT be able to "sneak" through dungeons, 9 feet in front of sentries.  It is absolutely ridiculous.
I could go on and on, but I don't want to make a wall of text.  I could probably write about 10 pages of criticism... not because I think everything sucks, but on the contrary, because I REALLY want to love this game... but I just can't give it a glowing recommendation.  There are too many baffling design choices, too many typical MMO genre tropes, too much predictability and bland gameplay, not enough challenge, no danger or excitement in the world to explore.
A vast, rich world of lore, a huge game world, so much content, fluid combat animations and fun combat system, fun crafting, deep character progression and excellent voice acting and writing.... all seem for naught because there just isn't enough compelling gameplay as you just obliterate everything in your path.  I recently made a bosmer archer who runs around in nothing but his pants (no armor no stats no nothing) to try to add challenge, but at lvl 5 I am still sniping level 10 elite "skull" npcs like it's child's play.
Final verdict:  I recommend it if you're a true hardcore ES lore fan, but I wouldn't recommend paying any sub fees if you can avoid it.

This review is for multiplayer only.
I have already put more than 150 hours into the game, and I must say I keep coming back. The game is very fast paced and, to me at least, has a steeper learning curve than previous installations of CoD. The addition of EXO suits is great. It adds another dimention to the shooting action - quite literally, as there is a lot of flying around in the game. The shooting is very tight and responsive. For a port this is very well done. There has been some connectivity issues, but SHG seem to have fixed that. There are occational hackers, but they are very obvious and you can leave games without penalty (other than it counting as a loss).
The weapon balance is pretty good with some exceptions, but it seems like SHG are on top of that, with regular patches. As I'm writing this review, the ASM1 is too powerful sees a lot of use, but before the last major patch it was a different weapon, so I'm sure SHG will take care of that and balance whatever needs balancing.
Now for what keeps me coming back to the game: Every weapon has different variants other than the base version - some are great and some are not. You get these variants by getting kills with weapons and through random supply drops that you get by playing the game. They seem to drop every 30-45 minutes of play time. Other than new weapons you get armor (only cosmetic), XP boosts etc. I find myself coming back to the game to just get that one supply drop in hope for a new weapon to play around with. I have a few good ones but the drops are random and I haven't gotten anything worth keeping in weeks. Still it's always exciting to open them.
This CoD is what the series needed. Just enough innovative additions to the good old concept.

Upon finishing Alien Isolation I had the impression that a lot of work was put in the development of this title. I can honestly say that, "Yes" this game is the best out of the Alien Franchise. It really does give you the feel of the first Alien movie with Sigourney Weaver within its dark rustic atmosphere. You can hear many audibles that they actually used within the Alien movie itself as you progress.
Some reviewers claimed that the Alien is scripted when it is not. I don't know where they got that idea because the Alien is totally RANDOM within its hunting, paths and appearances. You will die in this game, but the amount of deaths will totally be reliant on your gaming style. I always kept on the move for the most part and actually went through some areas with very little contact with the Alien. Even though I could hear him banging around in the vents above my head.
You can even play through the game, as I did, with very little use of the crafted weapons available to you throughout the game. Again, it all depends on your playing style.
The graphics are well done, but once in awhile you might see floating static artifacts such as a tool or phone where either you or a NPC were earlier. Sounds within the game are also spot on, but I play my games with the music off so I don't know if the scores are good or not. I heard that they were though.
The story line was fairly well done too, but the ending is.....well I'll leave that up to you on what you think.
Gameplay is very fluid, but for some reason once in awhile my character had problems standing up even though I kept hitting the button.
The main gripe that I have with Alien Isolation is that the alien always seemed to know where I was no matter how qiuet I was in the levels. Sometimes it was downright frustrating and unrealistic how the Alien would always zero in on my position by either following me through the vents in the ceiling or prowling the area always right up to the locker I was hiding in. Once in awhile; however, the Alien would leave the area which was a sigh of relief for exploring some areas.
Overall, Alien Isolation is worth the purchase especially if you see it on sale like I did. I think you won't be disappointed if your a fan of the franchise. I definitely  recommend Alien Isolation.

KQ is back and its beautiful! The game slowly unfolds into a great romp full of exploration and the full array of adventure puzzles. It cleverly tells the story of graham's rise to becoming king through the perspective of old king graham telling tales to his granddaughter. This chapter is a satisfying telling of the story of how graham became a knight. It is very good!

What's the game really like?
From one KQ fan to another, it's different. BUT, its just as enjoyable.
What's the bad news?
First off, I must say it's quite easy to beat in comparison to the old games. Most players have it beaten within 6 hours, and thats mostly because items are easy to find, and the puzzles, as to how you use the items, aren't necessarily challenging. I found myself really "stumped" only once. Also, there's no dead ends, so no need for saves. And as many have said, the Quick-time events are not cool. And unfortunatly there are a LOT of quicktime events. Dealing with repeating dialogue isn't honestly that bad though. I died a fair few times, but re-listening to the dialogue once or twice wasn't near as bad as some make it out to be.
To summarize: Easy, no deadends (easy), and QTE's.
So, why do I reccomend?
It's Kings Quest. Through and through. Quirky items, puzzles that are sometimes difficult to piece together, enjoyable characters which are quite memorable, immersive worlds, humor, puns, Daventry, and a great new story. The artwork, animation, music, easter eggs, and voice acting are all bonuses. Sure, gameplay has changed, but I immensely enjoyed every minute and can't wait to play the upcoming chapters as well as play this again with different decisions.
Still on the fence?
Short and sweet: It's Kings Quest for the first time in 17 years. While you fondle your $10-$40 thinking, I'll be spending my time in Daventry, thoroughly enjoying the nostalgia whilst making new King's Quest memories like I did many years ago!

Did you grow up playing King's Quest? And/or do you enjoy classic adventure games? Then this is simply a no-brainer. Let me put any concerns to rest and say that this is a completely worthy follow-up to the legendary series.
If you're a younger gamer, or the phrase "point-and-click" doesn't stir anything inside of you, the recommendation is a bit trickier.
The voice work is excellent, art style fantastic (assuming you haven't tired of the Telltale-esque look) and the story and humor on-point. However, there are a couple hiccups that'll frustrate more modern gamers. The pacing is slow, and some innovations like "fast-travel" are definitely missing. The entirety of the game (and really, the genre) is built in  endless backtracking to chip away at the puzzles and places around you.
The game does many things right, and a few things wrong. But for a follow-up that many of us waited nearly two decades to see (more, assuming you don't count the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ized Mask of Eternity), it hits all the right notes. I played the majority of this with a wide-eyed grin. It felt classic. It evoked nostalgia. It kept me interested.
If you love King's Quest, get it now. If you don't know who King Graham is, this is still a solid title, but I'd do a bit more research before diving in.

The game AI never quite played up to what I wanted to fight in battles, so I downloaded several mods which tweak stats and AI smarts, and now I enjoy a challenging campaign each time I play. The Steam Workshop features a great array of content which only improves on the game's solid foundation. For me on a high performance machine the game presents few computer problems, and rarely do I have issues, most of which are often due to testing new mods. As for the continuing complaints about DLC and it should be in the game etc., I have found each DLC campaign to be well worth the cost, and at $3 per unit pack no complaints either.
I highly recommend people spending time learning about the finer points of both campaign and battles. I still find out features and strategies of this game which I previously never knew, and the continue to allow me to play better.

You might think that "Oh well, i havent played any of the other games! how will i ever get immersed in it?!"
Not to fear, my soft-chested friend. Dark Souls 2 is set in a time long after the first Dark Souls game, and even though there are hints and easter eggs that refer to the first Dark Souls, you do not need to play the first one to understand the storyline (if you even manage to understand it.) "But i heard that this game is really unforgiving and unfair, how will a casual like me ever get through that without getting more angry than a fat man who cant reach the chips!?"
I know the term "Artificial Difficoulty" has been hanging around the Souls game, but that is complete cow poop.

Dark Souls II is a game which is not for the faint of heart. It's also not for those who are strong of heart.
On the plus side, this game is a familiar experience if you've played DSI, but there are a few significant changes, like
- decreasing maxmium health due to successive hollowing
- reworked healing system with more emphasis on healing over time
- an expanded crafting/upgrade system,
among other things.
Most of the changes are good; some have polarized the player base, like the new matchmaking system called "soul memory." For the most part though, the game offers a lot of challenge and a lot of polish, and is a welcome addition to a relatively shallow pool of recent adventure releases that is really worth playing. Oh and the game is a bit difficult.
If you've ever wanted to try a game just to measure exactly how masochistic you are, get Dark Souls II. It's great.

However, on a GTX 970, I have noticed no hiccups at all, which is a refreshing change from games like Watch_Dogs and other unoptimized pieces of trash like Arkham Knight. In an unrelated note, some of the characters seem to be extremely niche in terms of application. Most melee characters die upon interaction with the bountiful explosives in the game, and are useless in boss fights which require attacking from a distance and then sprinting away. Another mild annoyance which stacked up to my "do not recommend" was the forcible viewing of a "Mission Failed" scream and watching your next soon-to-be-dead Bro hop out of a truck EVERY TIME YOU RESTART A LEVEL. It may sound trivial, but it's the kind of thing that wastes hours of time as it accumulates, and I feel that after the first time a mini-cutscene is shown, it shouldn't be shown again. Being that it is in Alpha, I would say overall this game has a 7/10 design but the three points taken off are for the absolutely infuriating unfairness of the gameplay. The good: Fantastic sci-fi game that expertely combines first person shooting and rpg elements. Apart from having the standard arsenal of fps weapons, you get to use psi powers ("magic abilities"), such as shooting energy bolts or pulling objects to you. Though the main appeal of the game is its story. Dark and enthralling, System Shock evokes feelings of utterly loneliness on a space ship were everyone has died or turned cyborg. Immersion is deepened by recordings that can be found throughout the ship, and makes the player curious to find out what exactly happened.
The bad: The game came out in 1999, and its age is showing. The graphics are blurry and outdated, and combat is clunky, so don't expect anything state of the art. I personally wasn't too bothered by the outdated graphics, as it lends it a nostalgic feeling. Though there are mods that enhance the graphics, such as hi res textures and new gun and enemy models.
The verdict: An absolute classic when it comes to PC gaming, and still very much playable today. Top notch story, combat and freedom to create ones own character. Many of its features can be found in Levine's other fantastic game, Bioshock. Dystopian topic, immersive story through sound recordings, plasmids instead of psi powers and a mini crafting system. Without this, games such as Deus Ex would have never existed.
After all these years, still an amazing game and cult classic. Fun FPS with highly relevant RPG elements.

As others suggested, the one single missing thing is a choice between which of the antagonists to join at the end. Ultimately, you are restricted to following the path which is most ethical overall.

This is a great game. I run a 8 year old Mac Book Pro, which is far from state of the art, so there are few games that I can actually run with graphics better than 16 bit. But this game came out of nowhere, a game of the year nomination on a 6 year old game that I could actually run! To say the least the game held up to the reviews.
Hours of gameplay not including Dlc, amazing replay potential with four different characters and the guns. I used to think TF2 had a good assortment of weapons. But from legen (wait for it) daries to different scopes and stocks on weapons? Best loadout options I've ever seen. But there are two things that truly set this game apart from the normal run of the mill FPS games out there.
Number one is the art style. Graphic comic based hand drawn characters with cell shading applied as they become visualized in the 3d world, this style is nothing short of beautiful and deserves a purchase based on this alone. The second reason this is truly an outstanding game is the multiplayer capabilites. Most FPS games out there may have multiplayer, but it is a plae imitation of the game that commonly becomes nothing more than a sand box. With Borderlands however this game was designed to be multiplayer. With a party of four friends playing online you can progress through the entire story exactly as you would in single player mode, no other FPS had ever acomplished good story line multiplayer before Borderlands, and Borderlands 2 only made it better. Enemies have difficulty levels increased based on the amount of people you play with, and along with harder enemies comes better loot.
Sure, it's a game getting up there in age but it doesn't show. All told, it's definitely worth the price tag, especially during steam summer sale when you can snatch it for a mere five dollars. Definite thumbs up and five stars. Great job Gearbox.

Dishonored 2 in its current state (beta 1.3) is a bad joke. Although the game runs quite smoothly on my rig (i5 @4000, GTX960, 16GB RAM) the visuals are just god-awful.
Blurry textures, gaps in the models and partially vanishing objects successfully destroy any feeling of immersion - one of the strong points of the game's predecessor.
Bought the game, downloaded the game, played it for half an hour - requested a refund.

Of the 13 hours logged maybe 3 are actual gameplay, the rest is tinkering with the gfx settings and testing higher and higher system overclocks.
Unfortunately the game still feels and performs like a beta and not like finished game.
And, in addition to the performance issues of the game, there's also the publisher's behavior and their recent change in review-policy to consider.
My personal response to that is a simple recommendation: It's a Bethesda game, so don't buy it. Don't reward their disrespectful attitude with your hard earned money.
As for the game itself:
Now that beta patch 1.3 is out the game is starting to perform a tad better with settings changes finally having an impact on framerate. The mouse also feels a lot better than at launch (though it's still floaty in menus and mouse acceleration is still noticable. Even when deactivated in both in-game settings and config files) .
But the thing is: the base performance of the game hasn't improved one bit.
Basicly al they did was castrate the lower visual settings further and tie the view distance and LOD stages to other settings.
On higher settings, which aren't affected by these tweeks, the game performs just as badly as it did on launch. Minus the bad hitching, granted, but fps-wise ... no.
And if you for a moment ignore the unique art style then it's quite obvious that there are many games that look as good and even better than DH2 but require less expensive hardware to run them properly.

You want an open-world sandbox shooter where you can travel a huge world using your windsuite and parachute, propelling yourself ahead with your grappling hook. You want to tether cows to buildings, then launch them - sling shot style - as far as you can? Just Cause 3 is that mayhem sandbox with big explosions you always wanted.
It's not an open-world RPG or even very much story driven. It's also not a game where it takes your a hundred hours to get through the story. Many cristics have compared Just Cause 3 to the latest Fallout games or even to the Witcher 3. In my opinion such comparisons fail, as the intention and audience is a different one: it's a sandbox where you can fool around in, not a big story told in unexpected ways. You have the grappling hook, your parachute and - new in this part - the wing suit. And now go out there and have fun in a gorgeous landscape.
There's a story, and it's nothing special and mostly a showcase for what you can do. It's still fun to play, and fortunately it doesn't outstay it's welcome. There's collectibles but not on a scale like Far Cry 4 or other open-world action games. And you can ignore all side activities except liberating towns and bases completely if you want (I did). And - if you're limited in your available gaming time - you can easily play this game on and off. Half an hour here, one hour there. You can liberate one or two towns, collect a few collectibles, do some side activity or just try to challenge yourself with one of the many crazy stunts possible in this world.
Some people say this game is not as good as it's predecessor. Having played both, I really have to disagree. Liberating towns and sites in the old game was much more tedious than in this one, and there was even more of that. The story wasn't anything to write home about either, even if you had more than two factions and some choice in whom you supported.
In my view this is a worthy successor, intentionally not leaning in the direction of more story driven games like the Far Cry series or even Mad Max. And the addition of the wingsuite makes travelling around the world so much more fun! Also: it's only fun if you like the idea of a sandbox as opposed to a densely packed world full of stories. For me that was a refreshing diversion from the big games of 2015 - Witcher 3, Fallout 4, etc.
As for the technical aspects. I didn't encounter a single bug or crash during my gameplay with the original release version on Steam. Loading times were good (although on a SSD) and performance and visuals on my gaming notebook (GTX870M, 16GB ram, i7) was absolutely fine and looked great with the default Nvidia GForce Experience optimitzations.
So yeah, if that sound like your cup of tea, then go get it. It's great fun, just don't expect it to be heavy on the story.

I've always been a huge Total War fan and I can honestly say that this game is my all time favorite.  Although it certainly wasn't when it first came out.  I was one of the few people who could actually play the game from the beginning since I have a fairly powerful gaming rig and I was absolutely disappointed.  I tried with all my strength to love Rome 2 from day 1 but I just couldnt bring myself to enjoy it.  So, like so many others, I left it.  And I waited for CA to fix it. They most certainly did.
Now, I won't say that the vanilla product, even now, is a perfect game because it isnt.  But if you get certain mods(i.e. Divide et Impera, any of Radious' stuff), which take no effort to install, this game quickly becomes one of the best strategy games out there in terms of gameplay, history, replayability, and just simple fun.
I HIGHLY recommend this game (with mods) to anyone who loves strategy and Roman history.  You will not be disappointed.
PROS:
+Great unit variety in bigger factions (all factions have awesome unit variety with mods)
+AI offers a fairly good challenge
+You will truly feel like you are fighting real wars with real mens lives at stake, especially in the mods.
+Army traditions/leveling up generals add a great incentive to keep armies alive and make each battle a little more tense.
+Very easy to get totally immersed in the game and lose hours to it.
CONS:
-Barbarian unit variety (without mods) is poor.
-Sometimes you can feel too overpowered as a player, especially when playing as Rome
-Seiges are VASTLY improved from how they used to be but they still aren't that great.
-UI sucks
Neutral:
+/- Most battles are won as soon as you turn the enemys flank.  This makes complete sense and is ALWAYS satisfying, but things can get repetitive occasionally. Especially when fighting a series of small battles.
+/- Some factions that should be powerful can get wiped out very early game (i.e. Carthage, Athens, Sparta, Rome).  I can best describe this as disappointing.  Because all the fantisies of having Legionaries pitted against Spartan Hoplites can get stomped out very early on in the campaign.  Although this isnt a bad thing because it leads to very interesting diplomacy and wars later in the game.
Bottom Line:
Total War: Rome II without mods:  7.5/10
Total War: Rome II WITH mods:  9.5/10

Ok, so you know how this game got really bad reviews and basically every Elder Scrolls fan who got excited over it because it was multiplayer and stuff decided that they didn't want it anymore? Well guess what: Those reviews were for the beta. The original ESO was crap. It deserved the reviews. But ESO: Tamriel Unlimited changed ALL of that. The game breaking bugs were taken away, more quests were added, more areas were added and it just overall made the game a whole lot better. For a true Elder Scrolls fan, this game is really easy to enjoy if you just do the following things...
1. Do NOT think of it as an Elder Scrolls game going in. Pretend this is just another MMO that happens to be made by the company that made the Elder Scrolls series and set it in Tamriel, let you choose between the Elder Scrolls races, and put in some familiar Elder Scrolls characters. If you come in expecting an MMO, you will think it is a GREAT MMO. If you come in expecting an Elder Scrolls game, you'll think it is a pretty bad Elder Scrolls game. I did this, and in my mind, it's a damn good game.
2. Try everything. This game has so much to offer that to pass it up would be a waste. The bad thing about the other Elder Scrolls games is that it's set mainly in one province, meaning that all there is to do is the Main Story, the Guild Quests and the Side Quests. Sure, the questlines are usually quite time consuming and enjoyable and there are a TON of Side Quests. But you can easily do everything the game has to offer with one character, then put the game to rest until you forget everything about it and find it in a cupboard twenty years later (just kidding). ESO is not like that. It is almost impossible (if not literally impossible) to do everything with one character. You need at least three characters (one in each alliance) to do everything. Even then, it still takes WAY longer than any other Elder Scrolls game. So, get a week's worth of food and water ready at your side, make sure a toilet is near and play until your brain hurts (then take a jog or a nice long bush walk or something. You want to make sure you look as fit as your awesome muscley character.) then repeat!
3. Mostly pay attention to number one. That one's the most important
and lastly 4. Pay attention to number three as well. Number two's kinda important but it's number one that's the biggest thing.

This is a game that is flawed. The graphics are, even for the time poor. The controls are cumbersom and clunky. The physics are really weird. Weapon degredation is ridiculously overpowered. The voice acting, except for one character, is laughable at best. If you don't level up quite right, you're gonna be screwed halfway through. The music, while good, doesn't fit at all. But yet, within these flaws, these is a terrifying beauty to be found. It is, to me, one of the most immersive, creepy, scary games of all time.
There's no need for jump scares here. No need to startle with loud noises. It is fear completely through athmosphere, and much of this comes from these limitations. Those low-poly graphics make the monsters even more scary, like how the loading fog in Silent Hill added to the athmosphere. Those controls add to the feel of being trapped, alone and paranoid in a ship, with newly-installed hardware directly implanted into your brain. Weapon degredation changes everything about how you play an FPS. It is no longer about fast-paced run and gun, but about careful conservation. You could shoot that monster, yes, but you only have two bullets left. Will those bullets kill? What if the gun jams? What if the gun breaks? The inventory system also adds to this unique blend. Two pistols or a shotgun? Ammo, or one more med hypo? The RPG system, while very unbalanced, adds a very intresting edge to the game, and creates much depth. Should you wait for another level in hack, or get more Psi abilities?
Bioshock took that athmosphere and made it better, but it lost much of the depth in the gameplay. Deus Ex took the FPS/RPG blend and made it a million times better, and while I love that game, it doesn't have the same kind of athmosphere as this game. System Shock 2 is the only game to have this kind of perfect blend. It is flawed, but beauty is found in those flaws.
There are many mods out there that improve the experience of SS2. Graphics, balance, sound quality, all improved. I suggets using them. Look up a mod guide, there's one on steam.
Strong RPG elements, an unrelenting sense of dread and a truly horrifying atmosphere make System Shock 2 well worth your time. Will be of great historical interest to fans of BioShock.

At first I was highly sceptical of King's Quest.
Formely I've only played King's Quest VII, which I adored!
The artstyle, the music, the characters! I've always found Princess Rosella (King Grahams daughter)
and Queen Valencia more interesting! But I guess that is because King's Quest VII was the first King's Quest
game I played. I once tried to play the inofficiall King's Quest VIII, also known as The Silver Lining but
I found the puzzles too hard at that time. That game was also quite pretty and told a story about Graham!
But less talk about that and more about this!
Why was I sceptical now you might ask? Well, the way the trailer showed the game
made it look more like a platformer, which it at some times was! But it fitted the game! It
was actually a great mix between a platformer and a adventure game! I also feared the game would
take upon the modern day adventure game, a.k.a. Telltale Games way of playing an Adventure game.
It didn't, atleast not too much, fairly limital actually. Belive me, I have nothing against the Telltale way
of making an adventure game, and I did look forward to their King's Quest game, but I feel their version
wouldn't have made it, not like this!
This got everything spot on, the looks, the sounds, the characters! We even got to see Queen Valencia, or... not see
but hear! I do wish we get to see more of the family of which we know and remember so well! This far we've only seen
King Graham, and his two grandchildren Gwendolyn & her cousin. (I don't remember his name)
The other original characters we get to meet during the game are quite "living", they all have great personalities and
are taken care of better than most other adventure games.
And the story of this first episode, how was it?
Was it any good? Yeah, it was! The first episode is Graham telling two stories to his young grand daughter.
The first is him travelling through the dungeons of where a dragon has his slumber, the second longer one is about
how Graham tries to reach knighthood! Both but especially the second are filled with puzzles and funny interactions!
So it all comes down to; Do I recommend this game? Yeah I do. I was a bit worried about the high price, it is afterall a episodic game, and if we look at other popular episodic games the episodes are about 1.5 to 2 hours long. Which would have been crazy with this price! However this first episode took six hours for me to complete, which if the rest of the episodes are around the same would be a fair price! There will be a total of five episodes plus and epilogue.
So for everyone who digs a adventure game, and do note that this is not a point and click adventure game, but more of a "modern" adventure game itself, I do recommend this. I had a laugh, I hope you will to!

For anyone new to the franchise, King's Quest has always been a puzzle game where you search and explore different areas to scavenge for different items that can unlock the path of your adventure. It has always been creative as there are different options or methods to clear an area. You play as Sir Graham Cracker, an aspiring lad who wishes to become a worthy knight of Daventry, An adventure filled with fun, puns, and more PUNS. Seriously, it doesn't stop. A pun-filled game with incredible voice actors and actresses that brings life to the old franchise while sticking to the game mechanics that made King's Quest enjoyable. Playing through the intro, I was skeptical at first as it felt linear, but the intro is mainly there to serve as a way to introduce players who aren't familiar with the game mechanics. It is also one of the only games where I enjoy dieing just to see the many ways Graham can die on his adventure. I would suggest to anyone to play this without looking up a guide, it's more enjoyable to figure things out yourself. A very charming, fun, and enjoyable reboot of an old series. The art is very lovely and vivid and I'm amazed at how such an art style can work so well, and even better than the old 8-bit graphics that started in KH1. I can't wait for the next four episodes. The Complete Collection is well worth the price. I would recommend it to anyone who wishes to enjoy a new adventure under an old classic franchise.

Dishonored 2 in its current state (beta 1.3) is a bad joke. Although the game runs quite smoothly on my rig (i5 @4000, GTX960, 16GB RAM) the visuals are just god-awful.
Blurry textures, gaps in the models and partially vanishing objects successfully destroy any feeling of immersion - one of the strong points of the game's predecessor.
Bought the game, downloaded the game, played it for half an hour - requested a refund.

Of the 13 hours logged maybe 3 are actual gameplay, the rest is tinkering with the gfx settings and testing higher and higher system overclocks.
Unfortunately the game still feels and performs like a beta and not like finished game.
And, in addition to the performance issues of the game, there's also the publisher's behavior and their recent change in review-policy to consider.
My personal response to that is a simple recommendation: It's a Bethesda game, so don't buy it. Don't reward their disrespectful attitude with your hard earned money.
As for the game itself:
Now that beta patch 1.3 is out the game is starting to perform a tad better with settings changes finally having an impact on framerate. The mouse also feels a lot better than at launch (though it's still floaty in menus and mouse acceleration is still noticable. Even when deactivated in both in-game settings and config files) .
But the thing is: the base performance of the game hasn't improved one bit.
Basicly al they did was castrate the lower visual settings further and tie the view distance and LOD stages to other settings.
On higher settings, which aren't affected by these tweeks, the game performs just as badly as it did on launch. Minus the bad hitching, granted, but fps-wise ... no.
And if you for a moment ignore the unique art style then it's quite obvious that there are many games that look as good and even better than DH2 but require less expensive hardware to run them properly.

Amazing game and the best interactive rendition of this franchise that's ever been seen. No, you aren't gunning down aliens left and right, you're avoiding a single solitary one, and yet somehow that's much more exhilarating than the alternative. The alien actually isn't that smart, really--it falls for the same tricks EVERY time--but it is nevertheless very difficult to deal with and extremely persistent, and the slightest mistake against it means instant death. You often have to move very slowly through the environments to avoid drawing its attention, and spaces of just a few feet can feel miles away. This is helped by the fact that the environments are very well designed, so much so that you feel like Sevastopol could be a real place somewhere out there.
If I have a criticism against the game, though, it's that I feel like the game overexaggerated the durability of the Alien. Yes, they're tough, but we've seen in Aliens that shotguns can kill them, and handguns can--at point blank range, at least--injure them. Even a particularly potent pipe bomb should, at the very least, be able to cripple them, but that doesn't work here. It's a neat mechanic for a horror game, but a little noncongruent if you've seen Aliens, and if you're playing this game, you probably have. There's also some weird scripting bugs at the start of the game that don't really make for a good first impression.
Despite that, I still highly recommend this game to anyone who loves the Alien franchise, or horror games in general.

I’m not sure I’ve ever played a game that’s taken me on the sort of rollercoaster of conflicting opinions as Alien: Isolation did.
Its a collection of parts that rarely if ever align in quality, full of as many impressive moments as staggeringly poor design decisions that at times made me question if I should even bother continuing. Taken as a whole I couldn’t call it much more than a mess, but it’s a mess just redeeming enough to be worth struggling through for the parts that shine. When Isolation gets on a roll the experience developer Creative Assembly wanted to create shows through and the result is something incredible. The problem is whether it’s worth sticking around to see them.
The introduction to the space station “Sevestopol” acts as the placement of the carrot on the stick in front of you, starting with a literal bang as it introduces you to what will become the glue that holds the fragile experience together: the astounding atmosphere and world building. Sevestopol is such a consistently successful and fully realized environment that I could possibly make a case for playing the game based on it alone. The signs of a city gone to hell, systems in disarray, echoes of things you’d probably prefer not to see, eerily uplifting messages broadcasting over the loudspeakers; the sense of place is almost unequaled and is enough to propel you through the world before you’re even given a reason to want or need to. It’s as terrifyingly unknown as it is compelling for the very same reason, almost as if the station (which acts as essentially a small city) is whispering in your ear about what could be around the next corner, and the curiosity is too much to resist.
And that’s definitely a good thing, as when Isolation is trying to create an incentive to keep moving with its narrative things get a little...messy. Set 15 years after Alien (and though I would assume it’s a given, you should absolutely watch at least Alien and Aliens before you play Isolation) Ripley’s daughter, Amanda, is contacted with a message containing the possible whereabouts of her believed dead mother, which then leads to Sevestopol, which leads to everyone’s worlds falling apart around them as they realize what they’re up against.
Isolation’s biggest narrative disability is a disinterest or fear of ever branching out past what we already know about Alien to create its own identity. Amanda exists as a blank slate to send out into situations that often make far less sense than anybody seems to want to admit. She’s a catalyst to delivering you to areas designed for the sole purpose of playing to nostalgia and fanservice but having very little substance tying them together. As cool as it is to see so many iconic moments from a franchise I love faithfully recreated in interactive form, there came a point rather early on where the novelty wore off and I was ready to see what Isolation could do on its own.
Whatever it might have been doesn’t show up, moving on like an excited child wanting to show you their favorite toys but having little more to say about them than “remember this? Yeah, I loved it too!”. Perhaps this would be alright in a shorter game, but Isolation drags on for so unbelievably long and retreads the same notes so many times that I became numb to its enthusiasm and just wanted to be out of a world that had begun to stress me out. There are at least three major scenes during the game where it could have ended and provided just as much (or little, in this case) closure as the actual ending, and part of me thinks it would have been better off for it even if it meant cutting some of the more interesting sections out.
It’s a little hard to say that and mean it fully though, as without a doubt the biggest cause for the extended playtime was how much of it I spent dying and repeating the same areas. For as much a horror game as it looks like from the outside, Isolation is far easier to relate to very traditional stealth games. You are (up until a point) completely helpless and forced to utilize tables and lockers to hide from enemies that can often kill you the second you’re spotted.
Isolation’s stealth mechanics are intentionally intended to be very simple  and cause you to feel vulnerable, and in that they work exceptionally well. The game excels at creating tension and keeping it for as long as it can, causing me to hold my breath as often as my character as I prayed an enemy would walk past. As I said at the start, when Isolation works it’s absolutely brilliant and had me quickly forgetting about all the problems I have with it until they come back in screaming and firmly laying claim to something I was almost forcing myself to enjoy much of the time.
These problems are manifested as Isolation’s firm conviction to punish the player as often and with as much severity as it can possibly muster without completely crashing the game. Its design is often trial and error in nature, but complicated by the unpredictable enemy AI. The alien is your biggest threat, and the most persistent one, and by its very design it’s intended to be able to kill you very fast and be extremely hard to avoid. Vents and air ducts cover the entire ship and within them the alien has the ability to appear almost anywhere at anytime, save a handful of immersion breaking scripted sequences. One the one hand the almost random movements of the alien keep you on your toes and conscious of hiding spots, but on the other it makes death almost always feel cheap and unavoidable.
With how terrible Isolation is at explaining its mechanics, your objectives, how to get to them, or well, pretty much anything related to not being devoured by a Xenomorph, to make the act of learning these for yourself so precarious and full of repetition is a giant impairment on the experience. Compiling and then recompiling the issue again is possibly the most egregious save system of any game I’ve played in the last few years. No autosave, no checkpoints, just you and manual save stations placed sometimes 30-45 minutes apart to which you will be moved back to at every one of your many, many deaths. I doubt I could think of a game that so little respects the player’s time as it tests their patience, and was almost enough for me to quit the game and never look back.
And it hurts more than you know to write that, largely because Isolation comes so close to getting it right and falls so far when it fails. The parts that function as intended are commendable and for me, made it worth putting myself through copious amount of duress to see them, but I’m not sure if I could make that call for anyone else. Isolation is an Alien game made by Alien fans for Alien fans, and looking back on it I guess that was enough for me. It has the makings of the game the franchise deserves and shows us why that would be so amazing, if only we can find a way to blow the troublesome bits out the airlock.

Thus far I have played 30 hours of this game and I'm loving it, but it has not come without a lot of issues, so for anyoe interested in buying, here is a list of pros and cons:
Pros:
-Hours and hours of gameplay: I'm thirty hours in and have only completed the campaign and a few side activities.
-General feel: Take Just Cause 2 and scale it up around 100 times, that's how this feels.
-lot's of area to explore, in a beutiful enviroment: Medici is wonderful this time of year, and if the game sounds good to you, you should check it out.
-Intriguing vehicle and weapon delivery system: Have you ever seen a cargo jet bust out of a shipping container dropped off by a sall jet? Do you want to?
-The more items you destroy in a base or town occupied by military forces the more clear the things you haven't destroyed yet appear on the map.
-A tonne of easter eggs, when they made this the designers got told if they wanted to add stuff in just to do it, and here we are now with little duckling speed boats.
-A better driving and flight experience than previous Just Cause games (Not an amazing experience, but you get used to it)
-After completion of the campaign, you aren't left without things to do, if you want to you can make the military re-take towns just so you can take them back again, you can replay activities, challenges, explore, whatever you want to do.
And that's more or less it in a nutshell, now for a list of some pretty bad features.
The cons:
-You basically have to log in to their servers which constantly disconnect and have you attempt to reconnect for a leaderboard feature you probably don't care about.
-The game has random frame rate drops that get consistently worse the longer you play it, I usually get 60fps and up, but there I am just chilling on a beach and bame 15fps and thereabouts.
-It randomly started crashing every time I done a mission with Sheldon where you need to drive onto a cargo jet and i had to reinstall it.
-The story is fun but also makes you feel a bit like you don't really care what happens to any of your team as it was also quite bland.
-The development team isn't really that on the ball because one, they released the game in an (at times) almost un-playable state, and two they haven't updated it to fix any issues anyone is having, if you even visit the official website they have a bit where you can ask them questions and post to a faq to help improve the game and they have more or less ignored everyone.
-The game is pretty easy and you can't change the difficulty, you can fall off a bridge and not die, you can get shot by missiles and not die, you can fall off a bridge, get shot by a tank and thrown onto a railway where you get hit by a train and not die. (Yes I know it is staying true to the Just Cause legacy with that)
-Motorcycles are more or less not drivable at all
-You need flares to fast travel most of the time and beacons to get rebel drop offs of vehicles and weapons.
-The last mission was a bit 'meh' for me, quite bland I would say.
So that's it, yeah I put a lot of negatives in there but it's still a tonne of fun so I do recommend it to anyone as a first Just Cause gae to play or just for them to continue on with Rico's legacy with in the hopes the biggest issues like crashes, fps drops, and things like that get fixed.
Overall I rate the game a 4.5 due to it's issues, and a 7.5-8 if the issues are fixed.

As someone having beaten the game very recently, I recommend this game highly. However, I would suggest playing the first Dark Souls in order to understand some subtle references. Let's dive into the review.
PROS
This game greatly improves on some of the previous Dark Souls weak-points. Some major points I would like to nit pick would be online multiplayer, dual wielding, sorcery (miracles, pyromancy, etc. etc.), and just gameplay in general. Firstly, the online multiplayer is near perfect. A lot of covenants are based around online connectivety. However, some online functions would leave a single player offline player in the dust, they attempt to make up for it the best they can with allows AI summons and being invaded by AI as well. However, unlike it's predecessor, the multiplayer is very strong and very alive. It allows a lot of "jolly cooperation" with not only strangers, but also your friends! It allows the game to become quasi-coop. Which is excellent for someone like me that plays a lot of games socially. Secondly, dual wielding was a rusty concept that was loosely developed in Demon's Souls and Dark Souls. In all honesty, it was garbage. It was God awful and I would not recommend it. This is something small I am pointing out, as it should fit under general gameplay, but I felt it deserved it's own recognition. Thirdly, spells and the like were fully fleshed out and are simply brilliant. Overpowered... some... yes... I am looking at you Sunlight Spear... anyway, the introduction of hexes and more sorceries/miracles allows great flexiblity for people that want to attack the game differently. Finally, the part I love the most is the general improvement in gameplay. Something DS II focused on that DS I lacked was atmosphere. In DS II, you feel fully immerised in your world, you feel like a warrior, fighting for survival to discover how to become King. It is excellent, it provides simply excellent immersion. Also, the game has a very dynamic and fluid motion to it. The game is very smooth and the near transitionless areas allows unlimited immerision.
CONS
The game definitely has a learning ceiling. It is more user friendly at first, contrasted with the first DS, however, the game is a lot more difficult right off the bat and you are not having your hand held for long. Another important factor is that some spells are EXTREMELY overpowered and can two-shot most bosses. However, this isn't really a PvE problem as it is a PvP problem.
OVERALL
9/10 I highly recommend this game AFTER the first Dark Souls.

Ah Dark Souls 2... I was so hyped for this game and now i am its a mix.  Warning: this opinion is coming from a fan of dark souls 1 but not one that has played demon souls (wished i also have a PS3).
Graphics wise, Dark souls 2 looks great, Looking at the sunrise at the cost of Majula is relaxing and the constant 60 frames per sec makes animations very fluid and makes it a little hard to go back to Dark Souls 1. It is not as pretty as games like witcher 2 but it looks great none the less.
Sound: sound tract is similar to Dark Souls 1.  its ok, there are some tracks i like some tracks, dislike others, but the music fits the location or boss battle.
Gameplay: The crowning glory of this series, the unique mix of action and RPG elements found in Souls games is still here and improved with alot more weapon move sets to choose. it is fun to dual wield or two-hand grip a weapon which gives another set of moves to that class of weapon equipped.  And in my opinion the boss weapons are better now than in the previous game.  The challege, the risk vs rewards are still there.
Multiplayer co-op is fun, specially with the dedicated servers, at co-op i rarely encounter lag and i am in a country lagging in the internet connetion speeds with the rest of the world.  PVP is a different story, i never tried invading other players, as i have bad internet connection, but when i get invaded they are just teleporting, and i just end up hitting a stationary red phantom on my screen while the air attacks me relentlessly.
There is a lot of good in the gameplay but a lot of annoyances too.  there are more instances of cheap deaths now such as certain monsters breaking through a wall to kill you with out warning or que.  after 65 hrs of playing i feel that there are more unfair moments than in the previous game like the Dragon keeper knight wielding giant hammers that does just keeps on attack at fast rate (very narrow recovery window), he is not fun to fight in melee.  i wish that enemies do not have a limitted respawn and that there were more varied enemies other than humanoids wielding different weapons.
Story: It, like the previous games still retains the style that the story is not given directly to you and you have to find it out for  yourself through item descriptions placements etc. and fill up some of the story spaces with your own imagination.  i do kind of like how this game links it self to dark souls 1.
Conclusion: In all, dark souls 2 is still a great game but not a perfect game.  there are a lot of things i wish stayed the same and others need s to improve upon.  I enjoyed the PVE more in dark souls 1 than 2 but i enjoyed the multiplyer coop in 2 more than 1.

This game attracts you at first with its 3rd Person viewpoint. You think to yourself: Finally, a MOBA that's more about action-combat skills. You can actually control your character directly, so you MUST have more control...
But its actually wrong. SMITE understands nothing of fine action gaming.
First, SMITE feels like a top down MOBA, despite being in 3rd Person, and thats TERRIBLE. It feels like every core gameplay elements almost all there.

Everything feels clunky and floaty, that I felt a lot less connection to what was going on than in League of Legends.
And thats a very, very sad thing for me to say. I am tired of MOBAs being so held up on their RTS root, and yet SMITE has all the same flaws, and worse.
If that was all, SMITE just doesn't have any intracicies in the gameplay at all. League of Legends, despite the limitations of the genre, has quite a few ways to make outplays. SMITE... bah. You land your skillshots or you don't, sure... but thats it.
The game is terrible as a result. If you want a classic MOBA, you just go play something else. If you want an action MOBA... well, there is nothing out there, and SMITE simply does not qualify as one to me.

Looking Glass Studios basically laid down the roadmap for the FPS/RPG hybrid with System Shock 2. Though it didn't take off in the mainstream til Deus Ex and Bioshock. SS2 remains as legendary as the careers it jumpstarted.
Everything about SS2 basically took a defibrilator to the original game and kickstarted it into overdrive. The plot was expanded to the point of reading like the good Aliens sequel we never got. The gameplay was treated like both an actual RPG and an engaging first person shooter, complete with unique ever changing environments and weapons.
But that's not even touching the surface of this game. The most memorable aspect of SS2 is it's horror atmosphere. The electronica soundtrack only adds to the tension of how scary this game is. Enemies shuffle and appear in corridors you thought you cleared already, weapons jam if you don't take care of them, and you're constantly searching and praying to find someone alive. But unfortunately as you search, it seems more and more likely you're the only one still human.
SS2 is truly a work of art, and it's great to see it fixed up and running in modern resolutions. Considering how often this game goes on sale, you owe it to yourself to see where Bioshock and Dead Space all got it from. System Shock 2, "dat game".

Like I said before Early Access can be dangerous. It can be rewarding or revolting. And in all honesty....this game is truly some of the best that Early Access can offer. Like finding a slice of bacon in a fridge full of brussel sprouts.
Broforce is simple: kill random terrorists, save the bros, and assasinate the demon leader. No backstory (unless you count the description of this game), no drama, no distractions. But that's truly the reason why this game is so fun. It's a run and gun retro platformer that's inspired by EXTREME ACTION and HIGH TESTOSTERONE 80's action movies. Especially the characters. For instance: The Brominator, Indiana Brones, or Rambro. The controls are tight and responsive, there aren't any real problems there. The visuals definitely tell you what style it's going for, and since it's 8-bit, it fits the whole 80s thing. Every character also feels different, and even has references to their respective movies. But the best part of this game is the great level editor. Everything in this game is destructible and on a square grid, giving a lot of potential for user-created levels. Also, online multiplayer! And for $15, that definitely isn't too bad. Only cons I have are just a couple of nitpicks (glitches, slightly long load times), and the fact that you can't choose which character you play as.
Pros
~Fun and (literally) explosive gameplay
~Good amount of characters
~Fitting visuals
~Level editor
~Online and local multiplayer
~More free content in the future
~Satisfying
Cons
~Easy levels
~Minor glitches
In summary, this game is a fun and American romp which you'll especially enjoy if you love platformers. Also: MERICA!!

All I should have to say about this game is "AMERICA!", after all, it is what we have always looked for in a game representing patriotism. I mean, what super patriotic American doesnt like a game where you get to play as such American heros as Brobo Cop, Bronan the Brobarian, or Bro Heart. Sure some of the specifics might be iffy and the game might be hard, but each Bro you unlock is incredibly unique and true to the hero they are based on. And even if you end up playing as a bro who only uses blades you can still take on the hardest enemies (though not always successfully). This is a game that truly works to make you have fun while also experiencing what seems to be hell.
As the game is now out of Early Access the main additions have been the very short list of achievements and addition of Hard Mode. The achievements are, for the most part, true achievements, as they are a way to show off something incredible that has been done. Beating the campaign, while a simple task, was never easy to begin with, but they added the ability to go through it on Hard Mode (an even harder task) and an achievement for winning without a single death. To beat the campaign you need exceptional luck, luck only bestowed when R. N. Jesus blesses you by giving you a lifetime supply of 4 leaf clovers. Beating the campaign on Hard Mode is the same, but with an extra helping of skill. Beating it without a single death is only possible when you steal the luck of everyone in all of history (only the good luck of course) as well as the skill of everyone who has ever played the game. This gives the greatest challenge they possibly could give (unless you compare it to the challenge of not getting hit in a bullet hell game).
Over all, Broforce is a game meant to challenge you, your luck, your skill, and your patience more than anything else, and we need this in a game.

For anyone new to the franchise, King's Quest has always been a puzzle game where you search and explore different areas to scavenge for different items that can unlock the path of your adventure. It has always been creative as there are different options or methods to clear an area. You play as Sir Graham Cracker, an aspiring lad who wishes to become a worthy knight of Daventry, An adventure filled with fun, puns, and more PUNS. Seriously, it doesn't stop. A pun-filled game with incredible voice actors and actresses that brings life to the old franchise while sticking to the game mechanics that made King's Quest enjoyable. Playing through the intro, I was skeptical at first as it felt linear, but the intro is mainly there to serve as a way to introduce players who aren't familiar with the game mechanics. It is also one of the only games where I enjoy dieing just to see the many ways Graham can die on his adventure. I would suggest to anyone to play this without looking up a guide, it's more enjoyable to figure things out yourself. A very charming, fun, and enjoyable reboot of an old series. The art is very lovely and vivid and I'm amazed at how such an art style can work so well, and even better than the old 8-bit graphics that started in KH1. I can't wait for the next four episodes. The Complete Collection is well worth the price. I would recommend it to anyone who wishes to enjoy a new adventure under an old classic franchise.

While Rome II started out as a 5 or 6 out of 10 game it has gotten much better, many of the problems have been fixed and except for a few left over bugs it's fun to play.
Pros:
-Some people might not like it but I always found it annoying in Rome I that the Roman faction was divided into 3 playable factions and 1 non-playable (base on release settings) this is not the case in Rome II, Rome is one playable faction.
-Unlike in Rome I you don't need to necessarily attack your allies (depending on the type of alliance) to win the game.
-Now instead of 1 way to win a single campaign there are 3(Military, Economic, Cultural) you still need to expand to complete these conditions but Economic doesn't need you to expand as much and Cultural requires you to convert areas to your culture while holding a city in that area.
-UPDATE: CA changed the civil war mechanic, not it actually feels like a civil war rather than... whatever it was before.
In the Middle:
-The map is large compared to the one in Rome I but this has a trade-off, a couple of cities that were on the map in Rome I are not on the map in Rome II, however, you can now conquer from Spain to the borders of India and from the coast of the Red sea to Scotland.
-The new province system makes the gameplay much more interesting, by giving benefits to controlling all the regions in a province. But due to the fact that only one city per province can have walls, means that there are many cities that historical had walls but don't with this system.
-Large number of playable factions while you have to pay for a fair amount of these there are still 12 factions that you get for free and more are occasionally released, and most major historical factions are playable for free.
-Lots of DLC options, new factions and campaigns comprise most of it. Most of the DLC is worth it if you find you like the game, but if you don't like DLC, there are two campaigns free in the emperor edition.
Cons:
-The AI has improved but it's not good in certain situations, in the past it has had trouble fighting pike units and it's not that good in large sieges (the walled cities).
It is much better now than at its release, while there are still some problems I am confident that they will be fixed and Rome II will be one of the top Strategy games of all time. Despite these problems it’s still fun to play. Right now it's about a 7.5-8 out of 10.

Amazing game and the best interactive rendition of this franchise that's ever been seen. No, you aren't gunning down aliens left and right, you're avoiding a single solitary one, and yet somehow that's much more exhilarating than the alternative. The alien actually isn't that smart, really--it falls for the same tricks EVERY time--but it is nevertheless very difficult to deal with and extremely persistent, and the slightest mistake against it means instant death. You often have to move very slowly through the environments to avoid drawing its attention, and spaces of just a few feet can feel miles away. This is helped by the fact that the environments are very well designed, so much so that you feel like Sevastopol could be a real place somewhere out there.
If I have a criticism against the game, though, it's that I feel like the game overexaggerated the durability of the Alien. Yes, they're tough, but we've seen in Aliens that shotguns can kill them, and handguns can--at point blank range, at least--injure them. Even a particularly potent pipe bomb should, at the very least, be able to cripple them, but that doesn't work here. It's a neat mechanic for a horror game, but a little noncongruent if you've seen Aliens, and if you're playing this game, you probably have. There's also some weird scripting bugs at the start of the game that don't really make for a good first impression.
Despite that, I still highly recommend this game to anyone who loves the Alien franchise, or horror games in general.
