Ah Dark Souls 2... I was so hyped for this game and now i am its a mix.  Warning: this opinion is coming from a fan of dark souls 1 but not one that has played demon souls (wished i also have a PS3).
Graphics wise, Dark souls 2 looks great, Looking at the sunrise at the cost of Majula is relaxing and the constant 60 frames per sec makes animations very fluid and makes it a little hard to go back to Dark Souls 1. It is not as pretty as games like witcher 2 but it looks great none the less.
Sound: sound tract is similar to Dark Souls 1.  its ok, there are some tracks i like some tracks, dislike others, but the music fits the location or boss battle.
Gameplay: The crowning glory of this series, the unique mix of action and RPG elements found in Souls games is still here and improved with alot more weapon move sets to choose. it is fun to dual wield or two-hand grip a weapon which gives another set of moves to that class of weapon equipped.  And in my opinion the boss weapons are better now than in the previous game.  The challege, the risk vs rewards are still there.
Multiplayer co-op is fun, specially with the dedicated servers, at co-op i rarely encounter lag and i am in a country lagging in the internet connetion speeds with the rest of the world.  PVP is a different story, i never tried invading other players, as i have bad internet connection, but when i get invaded they are just teleporting, and i just end up hitting a stationary red phantom on my screen while the air attacks me relentlessly.
There is a lot of good in the gameplay but a lot of annoyances too.  there are more instances of cheap deaths now such as certain monsters breaking through a wall to kill you with out warning or que.  after 65 hrs of playing i feel that there are more unfair moments than in the previous game like the Dragon keeper knight wielding giant hammers that does just keeps on attack at fast rate (very narrow recovery window), he is not fun to fight in melee.  i wish that enemies do not have a limitted respawn and that there were more varied enemies other than humanoids wielding different weapons.
Story: It, like the previous games still retains the style that the story is not given directly to you and you have to find it out for  yourself through item descriptions placements etc. and fill up some of the story spaces with your own imagination.  i do kind of like how this game links it self to dark souls 1.
Conclusion: In all, dark souls 2 is still a great game but not a perfect game.  there are a lot of things i wish stayed the same and others need s to improve upon.  I enjoyed the PVE more in dark souls 1 than 2 but i enjoyed the multiplyer coop in 2 more than 1.

Like I said before Early Access can be dangerous. It can be rewarding or revolting. And in all honesty....this game is truly some of the best that Early Access can offer. Like finding a slice of bacon in a fridge full of brussel sprouts.
Broforce is simple: kill random terrorists, save the bros, and assasinate the demon leader. No backstory (unless you count the description of this game), no drama, no distractions. But that's truly the reason why this game is so fun. It's a run and gun retro platformer that's inspired by EXTREME ACTION and HIGH TESTOSTERONE 80's action movies. Especially the characters. For instance: The Brominator, Indiana Brones, or Rambro. The controls are tight and responsive, there aren't any real problems there. The visuals definitely tell you what style it's going for, and since it's 8-bit, it fits the whole 80s thing. Every character also feels different, and even has references to their respective movies. But the best part of this game is the great level editor. Everything in this game is destructible and on a square grid, giving a lot of potential for user-created levels. Also, online multiplayer! And for $15, that definitely isn't too bad. Only cons I have are just a couple of nitpicks (glitches, slightly long load times), and the fact that you can't choose which character you play as.
Pros
~Fun and (literally) explosive gameplay
~Good amount of characters
~Fitting visuals
~Level editor
~Online and local multiplayer
~More free content in the future
~Satisfying
Cons
~Easy levels
~Minor glitches
In summary, this game is a fun and American romp which you'll especially enjoy if you love platformers. Also: MERICA!!

Total War: Rome 2 suffered from a rough start, releasing with many questionable design choices and numerous severe bugs and optimization issues. This led to poor fan reception and a Metacritic score lower than that of any Total War title to date. At launch, and for quite some time after, I would not have recommended Rome 2. Thanks to Creative Assembly's continued support of the game, it has now reached a stage where it is extremely enjoyable with the recent release of the Emperor Edition. The game has metamorphosed drastically since the game received is initial reviews.
The Emperor Edition, released on September 16, 2014, drastically overhauled the game. The building system was redesigned for the better, factions all underwent extensive rebalancing and recieved new, more natural factional colors, unit abilities were overhauled, and last but not least, a new free campaign, Imperator Augustus, was released. All of this was added to the game free of charge! With the changes introduced in Emperor Edition, I definitely recommend Rome 2 to anyone interested in a grand strategy game with RTS and TBS elements set in the ancient world.
All of the DLC is recommendable, though depending on your personal preference, you may wish to skip the unit packs. The two DLC campaigns, Caesar in Gaul and Hannibal at the Gates, offer an experience different from that of the Grand Campaign and Imperator Augustus. They are more focused experiences, zooming in on the world map to flesh out Gaul and the Mediterranean, respectively, in greater detail than what is found in the Grand Campaign. Caesar in Gaul, Hannibal at the Gates, and Imperator Augustus all also operate at a slower yearly rate, with one turn per season, as opposed to the Grand Campaign's one turn per year. This greatly increases the number of turns you will have generals and agents at your disposal before they die of old age, allowing them to accrue more experience than they would be able to in the Grand Campaign. All of the DLC content is reasonably priced for its value, especially during sales.
My biggest gripe with the Rome 2 is how visually disappointing it is. The lack of true AA makes the game so much uglier, and the art direction really is vastly inferior to that of Shogun 2, in the UI, graphics, and soundtrack.
The UI itself is my second biggest problem with Rome 2. Coming straight from Shogun 2, I don't understand how they managed to make the UI so much worse. In Shogun 2, the UI beautifully blended with the style of the game, and functioned perfectly for gameplay purposes. In Rome 2, they somehow decided it was a good idea to make the UI take up more space on the screen, while at the same time making it more difficult to navigate and use. Between the advisor constantly popping on the screen for no reason, the unit stat card being permanently there and GIANT unless you want to manually hide it completely (instead of fading away like in Shogun 2), and the unit bar section taking up a way larger than necessary portion of your screen, right in the center, they really succeeded in consuming as much screen space as they could with their devolved UI. I just don't understand how they could have made the UI so much worse coming straight from Shogun 2, which had a magnificent UI.
My two gripes aside, I do recommend the game.

I will try to make this review a summary of the complaints and answers of the community:
Released too early - loads of bugs and was not optimised - (After many patches CA have improved optimisation greatly and the game now runs much smoother with better AI) - Do some more UAT next time CA to avoid the backlash!!
DLC that should have been included was bolted on at additional cost - (True cant argue with this)
Politics is a mess - The loss of family trees is a blow and the political parties dont work properly (True but character development is at least improved with most mods using traits talents and toadies but yes this is dissapointing)
The workshop - The workshop of player added content is nothing short of a god send, the player content is superb and hugely improves the game in many many ways. I would strongly advise you to stick to one of the main mods such as Radious if you love loads of stacks of armies and a variety of troops in an arcade style. Or for the historically minded player after a hugely immersive almost RPG experience the Divide et Impera mod will make a massive and I do mean massive improvement. There are other great Mods such as Dresdens Rise of Christianity or Spartacus for something different but try not to mix and match too many or you will end up with compatability problems.
In short CA created a framework, from which the ever hard working community have added a huge amount of content to provide what I consider to be one of the best games I have ever played. It has taken a year after release to get here and I imagine the mods will continue to develop and add further content. As disapointing as the initial game was if you gave up early on I would strongly suggest giving it another try.

I’m not sure I’ve ever played a game that’s taken me on the sort of rollercoaster of conflicting opinions as Alien: Isolation did.
Its a collection of parts that rarely if ever align in quality, full of as many impressive moments as staggeringly poor design decisions that at times made me question if I should even bother continuing. Taken as a whole I couldn’t call it much more than a mess, but it’s a mess just redeeming enough to be worth struggling through for the parts that shine. When Isolation gets on a roll the experience developer Creative Assembly wanted to create shows through and the result is something incredible. The problem is whether it’s worth sticking around to see them.
The introduction to the space station “Sevestopol” acts as the placement of the carrot on the stick in front of you, starting with a literal bang as it introduces you to what will become the glue that holds the fragile experience together: the astounding atmosphere and world building. Sevestopol is such a consistently successful and fully realized environment that I could possibly make a case for playing the game based on it alone. The signs of a city gone to hell, systems in disarray, echoes of things you’d probably prefer not to see, eerily uplifting messages broadcasting over the loudspeakers; the sense of place is almost unequaled and is enough to propel you through the world before you’re even given a reason to want or need to. It’s as terrifyingly unknown as it is compelling for the very same reason, almost as if the station (which acts as essentially a small city) is whispering in your ear about what could be around the next corner, and the curiosity is too much to resist.
And that’s definitely a good thing, as when Isolation is trying to create an incentive to keep moving with its narrative things get a little...messy. Set 15 years after Alien (and though I would assume it’s a given, you should absolutely watch at least Alien and Aliens before you play Isolation) Ripley’s daughter, Amanda, is contacted with a message containing the possible whereabouts of her believed dead mother, which then leads to Sevestopol, which leads to everyone’s worlds falling apart around them as they realize what they’re up against.
Isolation’s biggest narrative disability is a disinterest or fear of ever branching out past what we already know about Alien to create its own identity. Amanda exists as a blank slate to send out into situations that often make far less sense than anybody seems to want to admit. She’s a catalyst to delivering you to areas designed for the sole purpose of playing to nostalgia and fanservice but having very little substance tying them together. As cool as it is to see so many iconic moments from a franchise I love faithfully recreated in interactive form, there came a point rather early on where the novelty wore off and I was ready to see what Isolation could do on its own.
Whatever it might have been doesn’t show up, moving on like an excited child wanting to show you their favorite toys but having little more to say about them than “remember this? Yeah, I loved it too!”. Perhaps this would be alright in a shorter game, but Isolation drags on for so unbelievably long and retreads the same notes so many times that I became numb to its enthusiasm and just wanted to be out of a world that had begun to stress me out. There are at least three major scenes during the game where it could have ended and provided just as much (or little, in this case) closure as the actual ending, and part of me thinks it would have been better off for it even if it meant cutting some of the more interesting sections out.
It’s a little hard to say that and mean it fully though, as without a doubt the biggest cause for the extended playtime was how much of it I spent dying and repeating the same areas. For as much a horror game as it looks like from the outside, Isolation is far easier to relate to very traditional stealth games. You are (up until a point) completely helpless and forced to utilize tables and lockers to hide from enemies that can often kill you the second you’re spotted.
Isolation’s stealth mechanics are intentionally intended to be very simple  and cause you to feel vulnerable, and in that they work exceptionally well. The game excels at creating tension and keeping it for as long as it can, causing me to hold my breath as often as my character as I prayed an enemy would walk past. As I said at the start, when Isolation works it’s absolutely brilliant and had me quickly forgetting about all the problems I have with it until they come back in screaming and firmly laying claim to something I was almost forcing myself to enjoy much of the time.
These problems are manifested as Isolation’s firm conviction to punish the player as often and with as much severity as it can possibly muster without completely crashing the game. Its design is often trial and error in nature, but complicated by the unpredictable enemy AI. The alien is your biggest threat, and the most persistent one, and by its very design it’s intended to be able to kill you very fast and be extremely hard to avoid. Vents and air ducts cover the entire ship and within them the alien has the ability to appear almost anywhere at anytime, save a handful of immersion breaking scripted sequences. One the one hand the almost random movements of the alien keep you on your toes and conscious of hiding spots, but on the other it makes death almost always feel cheap and unavoidable.
With how terrible Isolation is at explaining its mechanics, your objectives, how to get to them, or well, pretty much anything related to not being devoured by a Xenomorph, to make the act of learning these for yourself so precarious and full of repetition is a giant impairment on the experience. Compiling and then recompiling the issue again is possibly the most egregious save system of any game I’ve played in the last few years. No autosave, no checkpoints, just you and manual save stations placed sometimes 30-45 minutes apart to which you will be moved back to at every one of your many, many deaths. I doubt I could think of a game that so little respects the player’s time as it tests their patience, and was almost enough for me to quit the game and never look back.
And it hurts more than you know to write that, largely because Isolation comes so close to getting it right and falls so far when it fails. The parts that function as intended are commendable and for me, made it worth putting myself through copious amount of duress to see them, but I’m not sure if I could make that call for anyone else. Isolation is an Alien game made by Alien fans for Alien fans, and looking back on it I guess that was enough for me. It has the makings of the game the franchise deserves and shows us why that would be so amazing, if only we can find a way to blow the troublesome bits out the airlock.

Tamriel.  A continent at war. The Dominion, Pact and Covenant fight for supremacy in the Imperial province of Cyrodiil. Meanwhile, Molag Bal has stolen your ♥♥♥♥ing soul.
Tamriel Unlimited is pretty. It has a variety of different environments - from the sandy, sunbaked land of Elsweyr, to the frigid, unforgiving land that is Eastmarch. Whilst no, the graphics aren't particularly revolutionary, and definitely not the same quality as Skryim, this is to be expected. For an MMORPG, the Elder Scrolls Online is up there with one of the best looking. Occasionally the world looks a bit 'the same', but usually as you advance to other provinces, the environment and ambience is noticeably different.
EDIT: After a discussion with someone who commented on this review (which you can read below) I'd like to add this:
Skyrim was a very graphically capable game. The base game, on ultra, compared to ESO, on ultra, is more graphically detailed than ESO in my opinion. However, this may depend on different viewpoints and whatnot. The graphics design and feel each game wishes to portray is different, and this may lead to differences in opinion - which is to be expected.
8/10
Player vs Environment is the part of this game that gets particularly monotonous. It's the easiest way to level up, as you gain a considerable amount of experience for each quest you complete, but  it does indeed become a chore. The characters are forgettable, the quests the same. Kill this, gather 'x' amount of this, talk to her/him. In my 145 hours of playtime, only a few quests have got me genuinely interested. You skip dialogue as it does not mean anything or add to the plot. It does, however, reveal some beautiful locations and there are a FEW interesting quests. For the most part, however, PvE in ESO:TU is pretty 'meh'.
4.5/10
If you're not sure about buying ESO for the PvE aspect, definitely consider buying it for the PvP aspect. It is likely the most fun I've ever had in an MMORPG. Nothing quite compares to standing aside a host of 50+ players as trebuchets pound castle walls, the walls crumble, and hundreds of players clash on the field of battle. If you're an Elder Scrolls fan and have always fantasized about some sort of war in Tamriel - buy this game. You're allowed to enter Tamriel at Lvl 10 (3-4 hours of playtime?). Once you enter, your stats are boosted to Veteran Rank 1(?). This means a Level 10 can still be (relatively) effective fighting higher levels, so it's pretty balanced. The PvP itself takes place in the Imperial Province of Cyrodiil, which has been invaded by three seperate factions-
The Aldmeri Dominion (High Elf, Wood Elf, Khajit)
The Daggerfall Covenant (Breton, Orc, Redguard)
The Ebonheart Pact (Argonian, Nord, Dunmer)
(With Imperial package you can play as an Imperial in any alliance)
There are 15/16 castles around the province, 6 of which surround the Imperial City. There are also various outposts. Around the castles are resources, which, if captured, give benefits to the faction who owns them.
The PvP is what makes this game, and what convinced me to stay for 100+ hours.

I spent ~20 hours ranching these adorable little blobs.
The "ending" cutscene made me tear up, and I'd do it all again in a heartbeat.
This is a light, simple game that manages to stay compelling without becoming overbearing.
You can spend hours building and running a super-efficient ranch, but you can also walk away at any time with no penalty. You might have to re-seed some things, but you don't have to worry about the place burning down while you're gone.
The world is a beautiful set of biomes to explore and navigate using your jetpack. Like the ranching itself, running out into the wild presents some light challenge without too much looming threat. If your health runs out or you fall into the ocean, you just drop what you were carrying and re-appear in your cabin the next morning.
This balance creates an experience that is relaxing while still being engaging. There are little environmental puzzles to solve, secrets to find, and plenty of ways to decorate and optimize your ranch. There is also a daily challenge to collect specified items in exchange for mystery rewards, and a shameless "money sink" that rewards you with cosmetic items and color schemes for your equipment. Periodically, you'll receive emails or stumble across text messages that fill in the main character's history and the story of the previous ranch owner. Like everything else, it's not particularly deep, but it is cute and pretty well written.
There will always be a place in my heart for simple, well-designed games with strong art direction. If you're considering this game, I can tell you that it is every bit as functional and deserving of your time as it appears. There's no catch. It's sweet, relaxing fun that just about anyone can enjoy. You can let your kids play it without any fear that it'll be too hard or in any way offensive. You can present it to a non-gamer, and they'll probably enjoy it. Even for a "hardcore" gamer, there's a lot to appreciate in the mechanical simplicity and the elegance of the environmental design.
If there was even one thing that saddens me about this game, it would be that eventually one reaches "the end". There's a bittersweet feeling to building the "perfect" ranch, collecting all the slimes, exploring the furthest reaches of the range, and ultimately having to move on. Games like this one are few and far between, part of me wishes I could go back and do it all again.

Slime Rancher is undoubtedly one of the most fun games I've ever played.
Imagine Stardew Valley (which is the impressive ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ lovechild of Rune Factory and Harvest Moon for those unaware) on an alien planet and in FPS format.
You play a protagonist who bought a ticket to the Far, Far Ranch, a planet inhabited by Hens, Roosters, and Slimes.
When you start out, your "ranch" is dilapidated. You have a few open plots of land and at first, a single pathway leading to the wilderness. The place is a fixer upper. The wilderness is filled with slimes, bouncy alien creatures with a huge variety. Some slimes are docile, others may attack. Some slimes eat meat, others like fruit, some like veggies. If you want to harvest boom slimes, you're gonna need to feed them lots of chickens. Nearly all items can be sucked up into your vac.
Ah, the vac. For a game about sucking, blowing, and making cash, the vac is quite the fun tool.
The vac gun is basically this suction device. You aim it an item (or creature) right click, and it'll get sucked towards you at pretty decent range and stored in your inventory. If you picked something up by accident, a left click will spit it out with some power, causing for quite a few funny moments.
As you bring slimes to corrals you've built, you're tasked with feeding them, and feeding them will cause them to♥♥♥♥♥♥out plorts, which you can sell for cash and they'll be made into biproducts that people will find heinous but will use anyway. You can upgrade these little prisons for when one of the jew- slimes try to escape. It's truly a sight to see when your crappy farm flourishes into a well-kept concentration camp. You'll figure out what synergies work best, and this is a HUGELY strong part of the game. I unlocked the grotto and crammed about thirty flying slimes into a cage, and upon discovering their favorite food (each slime has their own favorite food that makes them♥♥♥♥♥♥more plorts) I planted two trees outside. Now I have a system where I always have their food fully stocked and it automatically feeds and scoops the slime♥♥♥♥♥♥ so all i have to do is collect. There's a market in plorts, and it behaves how a normal market does. Some days one plort may be more expensive than another, but they don't have changes that are too drastic, in general a pink plort will always be the cheapest even on it's good day, but that doesn't mean that the six dollar difference isn't useful.
Exploration is a huge part of the game. Not unlike Columbus and the natives, you get to explore the giant world and admire it's beauty while systematically robbing and kidnapping it's inhabitants for your comparitively hightech Auschwitz replica. The biomes are varied and there is SO much diversity in your daily activities, between completing daily missions, optimizing your system, catching slimes, slaying the evil Tarr, upgrading your ranch, person, and aesthetics, this is honestly a game I could play for a very long time and still feel as if I'm finding something new. You need to unlock certain areas with cash, and others with keys that you can find inside morbidly obese slimes. How do you get these keys you ask? Force feed them until they explode! For a while I thought that the mountains that surrounded the ranch were just there to serve as invisible barriers, but once i bought this kick♥♥♥♥♥jetpack (yes you can buy a jetpack) I realized that nearly EVERY part of the terrain was scalable. The mountains that I thought weren't intended to be reached were suddenly shortcuts to other areas of the map. This discovery and lust for imperialism and corporatism is the driving force behind this beautiful work of art.
I love this game. This is a quality example of what every casual experience should be. I love looking at my cute slimes and then slaughtering them due to overcrowding. I love the beautiful graphics and simple complexities. I highly reccomend this game to anyone regardless of their preferences. Get this game.

All I should have to say about this game is "AMERICA!", after all, it is what we have always looked for in a game representing patriotism. I mean, what super patriotic American doesnt like a game where you get to play as such American heros as Brobo Cop, Bronan the Brobarian, or Bro Heart. Sure some of the specifics might be iffy and the game might be hard, but each Bro you unlock is incredibly unique and true to the hero they are based on. And even if you end up playing as a bro who only uses blades you can still take on the hardest enemies (though not always successfully). This is a game that truly works to make you have fun while also experiencing what seems to be hell.
As the game is now out of Early Access the main additions have been the very short list of achievements and addition of Hard Mode. The achievements are, for the most part, true achievements, as they are a way to show off something incredible that has been done. Beating the campaign, while a simple task, was never easy to begin with, but they added the ability to go through it on Hard Mode (an even harder task) and an achievement for winning without a single death. To beat the campaign you need exceptional luck, luck only bestowed when R. N. Jesus blesses you by giving you a lifetime supply of 4 leaf clovers. Beating the campaign on Hard Mode is the same, but with an extra helping of skill. Beating it without a single death is only possible when you steal the luck of everyone in all of history (only the good luck of course) as well as the skill of everyone who has ever played the game. This gives the greatest challenge they possibly could give (unless you compare it to the challenge of not getting hit in a bullet hell game).
Over all, Broforce is a game meant to challenge you, your luck, your skill, and your patience more than anything else, and we need this in a game.

As someone who played most of Dark Souls 1, watched a friend finish it, and jumped in fully at Dark Souls 2, I am vastly impressed with this title. From the atmosphere to the online play, to the gameplay itself, this game holds up perfectly. I didn't wait for a sale, I bought it full price, and still worth every penny.
The biggest thing I'd like to tout in this review is the drastically improved co-op function. In Dark Souls 1, there was no way to reliably play with a friend, you HAD to use randoms. Now, just get yourself the (MILD SPOILER) Name-Engraved Ring (END MILD SPOILER), and once you and your friend both have the item, pick the same symbol to put on it and your summon symbol will be the only one they find while wearing it.
In essence, with the appropriate ring, playing with a friend you want to play with could not be easier. Even once the heavily-saturated multiplayer server goes faint and unpopulated, if you have a friend to play it with, you can find all the co-op you could possibly want. That wins my vote for a full reccomendation on this game, because Dark Souls with reliable co-op? Sign me up! That was my only real complaint with the first game, and they saw to it perfectly, in a way that blends in with the atmosphere, instead of a jarring 'invite friends' button.

This game is absolutely worth the buy. A really generous friend of mine gifted this to me, and I can't tell him how many times I want to thank him. Even though he probably already knows that.
Dark Souls II is like a breath of fresh air when it comes to video games in our generation, whereas most popular games include FPS, or zombie killing games. Now we have Dark Souls, which is in class of its own as a classic action RPG. Everything about this game just speaks to you, and has you coming back for more, even after you've died about fifty times in one area trying to figure out the best way to get through. But the point of Dark Souls is that no matter how many times you die, you came back with better and newer experience to overcome your foes and whatever lies ahead. Most of the game is trial and error, which I really love. And once you get through your first playthrough, you just feel like you can take on the world because you made your way through all the obstacles and tribulations that blocked your victory.
Even after beating the game on your first playthrough, there is still so much to do! The replay value is off the charts with this one.
This game absolutely deserves the tag of "Masterpiece".

I was raised on Sierra's adventure games, so I had high hopes for King's Quest. Especially given all the positive press the game has been receiving. Unfortunately, the game is flat, boring, and slow. I only felt challenged by the "puzzles" once and that was because I was clicking the wrong spot on the screen.
The voice acting is great. The visuals are interesting. The gameplay is fairly linear and locked onto rails. But it's a REALLY slow game. Your character strolls slowly throughout the world. You can't skip dialogue. You can't skip through animations.  You just have to meander your way through this very flat game.
All of the reviews centered on the interesting visual style of the game and talked that up. I imagine they must have been paid reviews and, there for, had to highlight something positive about the game. Honestly. It's boring. It's slow. And it's boring. Did I mention boring?
Don't buy this game. If you're an old-school adventure gamer looking for a bit of nostalgia, you will be disappointed by how linear this game is an how little it engages your brain. If you are a new gamer looking to change things up and explore a story driven adventure game, you will be disappointed by how slowly this game is paced and how little it engages your brain.
Just don't buy this game. It's bad.

"It wasn't exactly as I remembered it, but it wasn't that different either"
This is a gorgeous example of adapting old adventure game ideas to a newer audience. I've always enjoyed to a certain degree the Tell Tale adventure games (Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us" but they've always felt like they were more interactive movie than game. I always loved playing the old King's Quest games as a kid, and I have fond memories of wandering around and exploring the various wonderful landscapes and strangew worlds. This game keeps the elements that work from the new adventure game trends, but brings back the ability to freely roam that l always loved. To me that's where the sense of adventure comes in. Wandering around and interacting with the world.
A special nod has to go to the voice acting which is superb. Christopher Lloyd knocks it out of the park as the elerly King Graham, and the whole world is brought to life with convincing and humourous work all around.
The first chapter took me about six hours to complete, and think I'll definitely be going back to try different things and mess around in the beautiful hand painted world. If you played the older king's quest games, or are just a fan of adventure games, I highly recommend this game!

This game is a gigantic slice of happy childhood memories stuffed with all the perks twenty to thirty years of technological advancement can provide.
First, I will admit to bias when it comes to the King's Quest series: I grew up playing and replaying the original games until time forced a certain level of tech-savvy upon me just to keep them running. Younger Me loved the puzzles, the fairytale settings, and the humor with which each game was presented (yes, even the puns). Older Me appreciated the care taken with the writing and presentation of the games (yes, even the endless parade of 'how-you-died' messages - perhaps especially those).
So far, King's Quest has managed to retain the things I loved about its namesake while introducing features I crave in present games, particularly choice-and-consequence. The graphics have improved, the gameplay runs more smoothly, and the player now often has a chance to elect how they want Graham to solve a given problem, but the game remains true to the spirit of the original series and successfully manages to flesh out Daventry's history with new stories and characters without having to rewrite the tales loved by older fans. The punny humor and numerous ways to die remain intact, augmented by a clever Bastion-esque narration scheme that has the voice of Christopher Lloyd dictating what is happening, what could have happened, and what he knows will happen if the player follows a particular action. (My advice: ignore his advice. Death is no consequence in this game and it is infinitely more amusing!)
Fans of the old series aside, I feel the game holds up on its own. It has a forgiving system that seems designed to mitigate the frustration of death -> lose progress -> sigh -> reload, instead opting to encourage experimentation at little to no expense to the player. While there are a few serious moments, the overall tone of the game is light-hearted and the narrative feels both accessilble to and enjoyable by all ages, with a nice blend of jokes and plot points targeted toward various audiences.
Whether dusting off your old adventuring hat or trying this genre for the first time, King's Quest gets my recommendation. I am looking forward to the remaining episodes.

When I saw they were making this I thought, "Oh great, another remake of a classic series." But the fact it was the King's Quest serious hit me particularly hard. It was hands down one of my favorite series of games growing up. Easily one of the most influential it was the first time I recall actually caring what happened to the pixelated dude on my screen.
I refused to be involved in it. I knew nothing I said or could do would stop it but I wouldn't even acknowledge it. And then I heard that Christopher Lloyd was going to be involved. He is without a doubt my favorite actor. And then I heard Tom Kenny, and Wallace Shaw and WHAT THE HECK IS GOING ON HERE!?!?! So I decided to check it out. And I got excited. But I've been burned in the past so whenever I saw it pop up in my steam queue I'd click on past it. Until yesterday when I pulled the trigger.
I was IN DAVENTRY AGAIN!!!!!! It's not a rehash of the old series, this is CLEARLY made by fans for fans and has all of the charm of that silly little 8 bit game paired with the BREATHTAKING beauty that today's modern gaming allows. Actually to compare it to modern gaming isn't fair. Most games today, the scenery is just there to make the levels more interesting as you breeze past and shoot the next unknown random person in the face.
This game is a work of art. From the talented acting of Mr. Lloyd, Mr. Kenny, Mr. Keaton, Mr. Wallace, and .... Miss Williams. That's right, Robin Williams daughter. The one that when she was born was named Zelda because of her dad's love of adventure games, is the voice of Amaya Blackstone.
This, game producers is how you relaunch a series. This is lovingly detailed and an homage to the original while being a beautiful masterpiece fitting of the King's Quest name. I *HIGHLY* recommend you purchase this and I look forward to many more adventures to come from these guys. Activision.....you and I....we haven't been the best of friends....you've hurt me many times in the past, but I gotta hand it to you, you made the right call going with the Odd Gentlemen. This team knocked it out of the park,

This game. . . MAN does it have potential to be the next best "Early Access Survival Simulator." I have made many a friend playing this, and it has to be the most punishing survival game this world has ever seen. The fall damage is realistic, you can break your legs and such, and there are many elements such as sun, hunger, health, cold, poison, heatstroke, bleeding, and many more. Each one will kill you if it gets bad enough. The gunplay is fantastic and realistic. One shot kills most of the time, so people who have survived long enough to get a gun basically rule the region. Cars are EXTREMELY hard to come by and build, making them just that much more satisfying to finally finish. You must deal with raids and raid-proofing your base, and you must make friends or enemies to survive. Conclusion: I HIGHLY recommend this game to anyone who loves a good survival game, and is interested in watching it grow over time.

I really enjoy this game.
It has strong smilarities to skyrim which is what initially drew me to this game. Although it's different enough to still be new and exciting.
The quests are ALL voice acted which was a total win from my point of view. It is really easy to emerse yourself into this new world.
Most activities/quests are soloable, and for the ones you might struggle with the community (in my opinion) is always ready to help. I've had no problems in getting aide to fight big bosses or clear dungeons and everyone is usually pretty friendly.
There is a strong RP community if you are so inclined. For those that dislike rp don't worry, they keep it to group chat for the most part and it will not effect your gaming experiance.
I have a fairly old computer but have no problems running this game on maxed graphics, the graphics are just a step up from skryim although not that noticably.
Combat is fairly smooth, with few bugs.
Other pros:
- It's FREE to play. No subscription.
- the mounts have a more realistic movement which can make some of them look a little foolish (bear and lion). I list this as a pro as I really like their attempt at realism in their animals.
- leveling up your mounts carry capacity also increases you own bag slots.
- Some of the specialised attacks have amazing animations
- some of the scenes are down right stunning (background and foreground)
- interface is easy to use and you can play with it hidden, with ease.
- crafting is similar to that in skyrim and easy to navigate.
- with some quests you get the option to be evil (kill someone) or good (save that someone). This seems to effect what the npc's say to you as you ride past them, but does not effect the quests. It can however effect your rewards for that quest though. ( I list this as a pro because I like having the option to kill an annoying or stupid character rather than save them)
Cons:
- questing can drag out a little, especially when the quest itself seems a little foolish or pointless.
- Player market. Now to me this was a big con. The market is different depending on the npc you talk to as each npc is owned by a different guild. Only the guild that owns that npc may post listings. But anyone can buy them. So unless you're in a guild that owns one of these npc's you won't be able to sell anything for a profit. Not all guilds have this npc either, so be careful when joining that you ask if they have one and where it is. I found this aspect to be a massive pain in the♥♥♥♥♥as I like playing the market and selling my crafted goods in other mmo's as it is an easy and simple way to make gold. I do understand why it has been done this way, and it is an interesting system and idea; but as a new player this was just frustrating as I could not find what I needed easily. Because all the npc's are seperate markets they only sell what the guild posts. They are not universially linked. So you need to go to each one looking for what you need and for which one has the better prices. This can be extremely frustrating as these npcs are spread out through many maps and cities and traveling between them can take alot of time.
- LFG system -  doesn't really work. You can sit there for hours and never get a group. It is faster and easier to recruit from chat instead.
There are many other aspects to this game that I enjoyed and that I didn't enjoy, but I will still continue to play it and I recomend that everyone here at least tries it once.

The Just Cause series is pretty much known for it's chaos.
Over time the series got more and more upgraded.
In JC1, it's... well, JC1. It was fun at it's time.
In JC2, you get a few upgrades. Grapple Hook, better Grenade Launchers, and a better parachute.
In JC3, you get a wingsuit, an even better parachute, and better grappling hooks.
But here's the thing, some people have issues running JC3, even though they have top tier hardware. From what I think it's something AMD related, haven't looked into full detail about it. So if you have an NVIDIA card like me, you SHOULD be fine assuming you have the right specs, but if you're an AMD user, you should think twice about buying this.
1. +
- JC2's driving mechanics felt very, VERY, slow. Almost to the point that parachuting is faster. Now you can parachute/wingsuit/fly/drive your way to anywhere, and still feel fast!

3. +
- I personally enjoy the explosions, blow a massive object up and feel satisfied for blowing it up.
4. +
- This is a new feature that I enjoy. Basiclly it pulls two objects you grapple onto eachother together. It's very fun, and sometimes you can use this to destroy everything without needing a gun.
5. +
- This probably SHOULD be a joke, but I'm serious. You can go inside the cargo plane, open the cargo door so that you can insert some vehicles, heck even just crash the massive plane into a massive object.
6. +
- It has been very much improved, almost to the point where I wish that the Multiplayer mod would come out soon!
7. +
- There are plenty of easter eggs to look for, which can be very entertaining sometimes!

Alien: Isolation is my uncontested pick for 2014 Game of the Year! It's surprisingly risky and innovative for a triple AAA title:  an asymmetric game of hide and seek where you're the hunted and the use of weapons is often inadvisable. Developer, Creative Assembly has succeeded in creating one of the most atmospheric, tension filled and immersive experiences in gaming, reminiscent of classics System Shock 2 and Thief 3's Shalebridge Cradle.
The Sevastopol and other human habitats - whose designs emulate and build on the concepts and sets developed for Ridley Scott's '79 film - are an utter marvel. It's a spectacular recreation, rivaled by the versimilitude and artifical intelligence (on HARD difficulty) of H.R. Giger's xenomorph who relentlessly stalks you.
I found the innovative game mechanics and pacing excellent, with constant variation, surprise and emergent opportunites. This is in direct contradiction to comments from several mainstream reviewers, but this variation is even evident as you near the end of the game and encounter computer terminals with different user interfaces from what you've accessed earlier. There's a clear consideration to the pacing; just as the tension of being in close proximity to the xenomorph boils over, you get a respite and venture through more open spaces populated by survivors and androids during the mid-game for example.
The overbearing tension and demand for patience, awareness and risky decision making, with infrequent save opportunities makes this a game to be savored and never rushed. If the xenomorph gets you, it might just be advisable to return another time.  The shockingly poor reviews from some mainstream game sites can be directly attributed to this and Alien: Isolation's extended duration: a reviewer trying to meet a deadline would inherently become frustrated and find fault in this impressively executed experience. It's a shame since such misguided criticism inevitably stifles further risk in the AAA development space, but this is perhaps the most polarizing game in recent memory. PC Gamer declared it GOTY, as did a Polygon writer who made a counter argument against the site's initial mediocre review. I highly recommend Alien: Isolation to anyone, especially film enthusiasts and those who enjoy stealth gameplay. However, to truly experience the terror of the xenomorph,  don't wuss out... play on HARD only.

Summary/recommendation: Do not touch this if you do not like stealth games that require patience, being extremely careful, and aren't power fantasy.
Excellent stealth metroidvania (it is) in the Alien universe. Unfortunately outside of the first few chapters does Not stay true to its origins as the Alien becomes a Constant presence hunting you down. The game's atmosphere is very tense because of the way the enemies work, how saving works, and what you have available to deal with them. Unfortunately it is not scary game for those that care of it, just extremely tense (prepare those buttcheeks for clenching). The game's tips also outright lie to you about certain things, and stealth works very strangely (hiding in closets is less efficient than hiding under or behind tables).
The most trouble you probably get from the game is simply test of your patience sitting in some hiding spot waiting for the alien's scouting to give you an opening to move into another safe spot. I did not personally see the endless streams of synthetics (androids) that I heard of in relation to the game, all of it was perfectly sensible in context. Tho I must say Apollo Core was testing my limits with that, but then: You Can Run, they can not. This solves surprisingly many problems with them if you fail to avoid their notice and don't want to try killing them.
The story is interesting and has plot twists that I did not see coming (I did not spoil myself at all prior), and the execution is pretty damn impressive. Graphics are honestly quite beautiful, but I noticed some missing lipsync on characters which was kinda weird to see considering automatic lipsync was a thing already back in the 90s. Voice acting I have no complaints of, and the music fits the game.
There was one constantly present bug tho: the synthetics will look in your direction no matter what. This can be unnerving/creepy to some I guess, considering they do it even when you're hiding somewhere and they haven't technically noticed you (because if they had, they would approach you and try to kindly kill you). But it was a not really a problem, just Weird. And there was some random instances of pathfinding, alien dropping into a room, or something that happened at a time or manner that made it impossible to get away from.
Suggestion: Avoid killing or trying to kill things. You'll need those bullets and explosives when your options of running away are less viable in some parts later on in the game. Sneak around Everything you can and if humans are blockingy your way, wait for the alien or androids to kill them, if neither is around to do that, you probably can go another way or they'll move on their own. You Can kill them anyway, but why bother? You shouldn't be short on supplies (seems to happen only if you Do try to kill everything personally) and they shouldn't be impeding your progress anyway.

I had my eye on this game for a while before the official release and always decided against it since, while it looked fun, seemed as though it might be a bit shallow. That initial reaction wasn't 100% wrong, but after finally giving in and buying this title I am quite glad I did. The game certainly has room for improvement. There isn't really any "endgame" and it doesn't have much replayability. Also, your farm is large once you upgrade, yet feels like mostly empty space which creates problems later on.
There are other things this game somewhat fails at, but the pros do indeed outweigh the cons. The game feels like a watered down version of Harvest Moon or Stardew Valley if you played Luigi from Luigi's Mansion and you raised slimes in place of livestock. While it lacks a social system or other characters there are messages you get which actually weave an interesting story together. The game is fairly relaxing most of the time and the slimes are completely adorable. The game also attempts to get you to think a tad more strategically with your farm layout and how you engage enemies (or you could just run like I do lol).
Basically, it feels like a work in progress, but is still quite enjoyable. I personally hope that it eventually gets Steam Workshop support, more farm customization, and/or additional maps for your personal farm. It's off to a good start and I hope it only gets better.

With the aid of Mods this game can be quite the fun little expedition into classical history, it does however have some issues that continue to bug.
1) Limited number of armies - I understand this was mostly to cement further historical accuracy with the 22 Legions of Rome but why am I limited as a Suebian led Germanic Confederation.
2) Garrisons - Small untrained bands of plebs do not constitute a Roman garrison, and why can these garrison armies not be deployed to combat local rebellions, forcing me to defend each province with a legion.
3) Rebellions - Due to severe stupidity in building trees, Squalor and slave numbers create constant rebellion from the word go, and worse still is that these unwashed rebels and slaves are instantly tier 4 trained outmatching my finest legions early game.
4) DLC - As has become the norm with any video game today, Sega expect us to keep forking out money with pathetic mini-DLC that introduce a few units or a couple of new playable factions. This is less a game flaw more a developer one.
Despite these discrepancies I have logged over 100 hours of gameplay on this and the modding community have really helped make it more enjoyable.

If only there were a "mild recommendation" option.
First things first, Performance was BAD on launch. I'm talking putting it on low w/ a GTX 970 and i5 6600k, and barely scratching 40-60 fps. Thankfully, Arkane has been persistent on patches. Whether or not you got better performance, YMMV, as evidenced by the forums where users are still having problems. Personally however, most performance issues have been fixed...
. I can turn things up to high/ultra settings now at 60 fps almost constantly (notable exception being the time traveling mission). The only real problem left is the frametime issues, which although don't ruin the game can prove to be annoying. Buy at your own caution if performance is a concern.
With that being said, the game itself is excellent. It's beautiful, and the gameplay is every bit as deep as it was in Dishonored 1 and then some. AI has become downright ruthless this time, and the introduction of Clockwork soldiers brings back memories of Thief 2's Builder's Children. The inclusion of different powers for both Emily and Corvo only furthers the already incredible replay value that Dishonored 1 had. And with the "flesh and steel" mode, where you have no powers equipped, it's the best spiritual successor to Thief you could've asked for. Well, besides The Dark Mod. But you get my drift.

All I should have to say about this game is "AMERICA!", after all, it is what we have always looked for in a game representing patriotism. I mean, what super patriotic American doesnt like a game where you get to play as such American heros as Brobo Cop, Bronan the Brobarian, or Bro Heart. Sure some of the specifics might be iffy and the game might be hard, but each Bro you unlock is incredibly unique and true to the hero they are based on. And even if you end up playing as a bro who only uses blades you can still take on the hardest enemies (though not always successfully). This is a game that truly works to make you have fun while also experiencing what seems to be hell.
As the game is now out of Early Access the main additions have been the very short list of achievements and addition of Hard Mode. The achievements are, for the most part, true achievements, as they are a way to show off something incredible that has been done. Beating the campaign, while a simple task, was never easy to begin with, but they added the ability to go through it on Hard Mode (an even harder task) and an achievement for winning without a single death. To beat the campaign you need exceptional luck, luck only bestowed when R. N. Jesus blesses you by giving you a lifetime supply of 4 leaf clovers. Beating the campaign on Hard Mode is the same, but with an extra helping of skill. Beating it without a single death is only possible when you steal the luck of everyone in all of history (only the good luck of course) as well as the skill of everyone who has ever played the game. This gives the greatest challenge they possibly could give (unless you compare it to the challenge of not getting hit in a bullet hell game).
Over all, Broforce is a game meant to challenge you, your luck, your skill, and your patience more than anything else, and we need this in a game.

I remember playing this game at 2012 after seeing it as one of the top free to play games at the time. I had a crappy laptop and was able to get 25 frames on average. It was amazing. Tattoos wherever you want them, a truly personal car and clothse customization, and hell you could make your own music! This was at an age (8th grade) where I didn't mind dedicating hours worth of time in grinding a game. I can honestly say from all the games I have played a lot of great moments have come from this game. Even if the cars had a lag to the controls or the aimbots were abundant, there were moments that I will never forget from this game.
Let me give you an example,
I was a criminal in a car with a briefcase and a couple friendly cars behind me. We were holding on to it getting our points only to find enforcer cars speeding straight in front of us. Almost instinctively both enforcer and criminal drifted side ways to make cover, got out, and instantly began firing. The great thing about it was it was all on sync and all criminal cars landing straight in line as well as the enforcers. Granted I died shortly after but it only shows that this is what APB Reloaded did right with what it had.
I can talk about the broken mechanics, I can talk about the pay-to-win mechanics as people spend money on GamersFirst currency. I can talk about the aimbots, wall hackers, exploiters. I can talk about the areas in the map that cause unbearable cheese that would make you just stop playing the mission.
But at this point what does it matter? It pains me to say that this game is long dead.
Even when I played I would have to come on certain times of the day to play when there were many people. I can say it like it's another disappointing game or write it off as a game that couldn't hold up. But the truth is that this game had taken a big part of my time with my cheap laptop and introduced me to many different free to play games. Frankly looking back at this game makes me sad because of it's tragedy. I can only hope that we see a developer find inspiration from this game and carry it's ideas to a new light. (And don't you dare say GTA V)

Without going into depth about the differences between the games and how Dark Souls became one of my favorite games ever for x specific reason and the change of that is why this game is worse - that sort of thing - I'll just keep it simple and say that Dark Souls II is a good and still imaginative game. Not an amazing game, not a game of the year, but a good game and experience. Its single player and co-op takes you on a journey that seems a bit lackluster at first in comparison to the previous game, grows, and ultimately ends up being off the mark for the same sort of feeling and tone but good in another way (with the ending being the most different sort of good, with layer upon layer in what feels like a single area constituting the ultimate point of the game, as opposed to some huge climactic setting where you feel the satisfaction of completing a task you'd been given much earlier in the game - or not, notable because this game does not have multiple endings).
This is not the "I feel really alone" game. This is not the "atmosphere is unlike anything I've ever seen before" game. This really isn't "Dark Souls II" in any way, shape or form, with many that I know considering it to be a "better sequel to Demon's Souls with some loose Dark Souls lore attatched" (and if that's what you're looking for, you might like this over Dark Souls). However, once you adapt to its style - gameplay, graphics, sound, anything else - and look at it not as a continuation of its predecessor but something that (at least I feel) truly deserved its own prefix to "Souls", then you will play a good game and enjoy it, with the experience being fairly satisfying. Of all things they possibly improved, the main one is that it actually is more enjoyable to co-op in the worlds of other players. This is truly the most teamwork oriented Souls game yet and while you can go it alone, it isn't anywhere near as supportive of that idea as Dark Souls was. Dark Souls II is so much of a "play with your friends" title that From went to great lengths supporting just the co-op part that it essentially is what makes the entire world "work". You'll know what I'm saying before you have played even an hour of the game.
Finally, I would not recommend the PVP in this game to anyone who enjoyed PVP in Dark Souls and involved in their style things other than spamming sorceries over and over again...you know, like possibly using a weapon and engaging your opponent. This is "Dark" Souls "II" PVP. This is not Dark Souls PVP, this is not your PVP if you were one of those people, so don't abandon the Township with the assumption that everything is automatically going to be an improvement in this game, spending a lot of time on the perfect build (and I use that word very, very loosely) without just dipping your feet in the water here first. Not to cause any misunderstandings - it is very easy to be successful in PVP. It is not nearly as varied, common or enjoyable as it was in Dark Souls. That is all, and because of it you might end up playing it in a manner you would rather not like to.
PS: A word to the PC Souls community - it has come to my attention that many, many among us are absolutely trash at this game series. I'm not even talking multiplayer, I'm talking single player, easy bosses. I'm talking people who complain about every single thing, proclaim things to be "literally impossible" and have to use a trainer to beat the Giant Lord after ~10 consecutive tries. I witnessed no such players back when I played the game in March at release on the 360 before it was nerfed in various areas to a slight degree prior to the PC release for all platforms.
If you know someone like this, please immediately inform the "Improve the PC Community Hotline" with their name and Steam handle if available: 1-866-GIT-GUDD. Again, that's 1-866-GIT-GUDD, just in case your eyes missed it because they were rollerskating on the moon or something.

I almost feel like a groupie or member of a religious cult when I talk to people about how much I like this game. Few games before or since System Shock 2 have come close to it's level of atmosheric intensity, stotytelling and quality of gameplay. It's the kind of game that you find yourself thinking about while you are at work, or when you are trying to fall asleep. To play it is to live it, you enter the game's world in a very real sense, and the lines between being on the Von Braun and in the real world become blurred.
As you may know, System Shock 2 is the spritual predecessor to the more familiar BioShock series. If you liked any of the BioShock games but have not experienced System Shock 2, you really owe it to yourself to go back and immerse yourself in one of the greatest gaming experiences of all time. And now that System Shock 2 has been optimized to run on modern machines there really is no excuse not to. Extremely highly recommended.

Alien: Isolation is my uncontested pick for 2014 Game of the Year! It's surprisingly risky and innovative for a triple AAA title:  an asymmetric game of hide and seek where you're the hunted and the use of weapons is often inadvisable. Developer, Creative Assembly has succeeded in creating one of the most atmospheric, tension filled and immersive experiences in gaming, reminiscent of classics System Shock 2 and Thief 3's Shalebridge Cradle.
The Sevastopol and other human habitats - whose designs emulate and build on the concepts and sets developed for Ridley Scott's '79 film - are an utter marvel. It's a spectacular recreation, rivaled by the versimilitude and artifical intelligence (on HARD difficulty) of H.R. Giger's xenomorph who relentlessly stalks you.
I found the innovative game mechanics and pacing excellent, with constant variation, surprise and emergent opportunites. This is in direct contradiction to comments from several mainstream reviewers, but this variation is even evident as you near the end of the game and encounter computer terminals with different user interfaces from what you've accessed earlier. There's a clear consideration to the pacing; just as the tension of being in close proximity to the xenomorph boils over, you get a respite and venture through more open spaces populated by survivors and androids during the mid-game for example.
The overbearing tension and demand for patience, awareness and risky decision making, with infrequent save opportunities makes this a game to be savored and never rushed. If the xenomorph gets you, it might just be advisable to return another time.  The shockingly poor reviews from some mainstream game sites can be directly attributed to this and Alien: Isolation's extended duration: a reviewer trying to meet a deadline would inherently become frustrated and find fault in this impressively executed experience. It's a shame since such misguided criticism inevitably stifles further risk in the AAA development space, but this is perhaps the most polarizing game in recent memory. PC Gamer declared it GOTY, as did a Polygon writer who made a counter argument against the site's initial mediocre review. I highly recommend Alien: Isolation to anyone, especially film enthusiasts and those who enjoy stealth gameplay. However, to truly experience the terror of the xenomorph,  don't wuss out... play on HARD only.

Summary/recommendation: Do not touch this if you do not like stealth games that require patience, being extremely careful, and aren't power fantasy.
Excellent stealth metroidvania (it is) in the Alien universe. Unfortunately outside of the first few chapters does Not stay true to its origins as the Alien becomes a Constant presence hunting you down. The game's atmosphere is very tense because of the way the enemies work, how saving works, and what you have available to deal with them. Unfortunately it is not scary game for those that care of it, just extremely tense (prepare those buttcheeks for clenching). The game's tips also outright lie to you about certain things, and stealth works very strangely (hiding in closets is less efficient than hiding under or behind tables).
The most trouble you probably get from the game is simply test of your patience sitting in some hiding spot waiting for the alien's scouting to give you an opening to move into another safe spot. I did not personally see the endless streams of synthetics (androids) that I heard of in relation to the game, all of it was perfectly sensible in context. Tho I must say Apollo Core was testing my limits with that, but then: You Can Run, they can not. This solves surprisingly many problems with them if you fail to avoid their notice and don't want to try killing them.
The story is interesting and has plot twists that I did not see coming (I did not spoil myself at all prior), and the execution is pretty damn impressive. Graphics are honestly quite beautiful, but I noticed some missing lipsync on characters which was kinda weird to see considering automatic lipsync was a thing already back in the 90s. Voice acting I have no complaints of, and the music fits the game.
There was one constantly present bug tho: the synthetics will look in your direction no matter what. This can be unnerving/creepy to some I guess, considering they do it even when you're hiding somewhere and they haven't technically noticed you (because if they had, they would approach you and try to kindly kill you). But it was a not really a problem, just Weird. And there was some random instances of pathfinding, alien dropping into a room, or something that happened at a time or manner that made it impossible to get away from.
Suggestion: Avoid killing or trying to kill things. You'll need those bullets and explosives when your options of running away are less viable in some parts later on in the game. Sneak around Everything you can and if humans are blockingy your way, wait for the alien or androids to kill them, if neither is around to do that, you probably can go another way or they'll move on their own. You Can kill them anyway, but why bother? You shouldn't be short on supplies (seems to happen only if you Do try to kill everything personally) and they shouldn't be impeding your progress anyway.

Even if you have no prior experience with Half-Life, it's so easy to get immersed in this game.
The graphics may not be up there with games like The Last of Us and Alien: Isolation, but there are a few moments where the view is still just beautiful. Additionally, the enemies are fun to fight against, even if they are kind of typical or expected when you think of a stereotypical sci-fi horror film. The range of weapons is also a plus, and its useful to be able to loot ammo and weapons off of the enemy, since a good number of games still do not have that mechanic.
There were a couple cons I saw with this game, one of which being the voice-acting. The voices themselves come off as funny and stereotypical (the nerdy scientist voices). However, there was such a small range of voices, resulting in the majority of scientists sounding exactly the same (as well as saying the same things). The other con was the way the ending was played out. I expected a boss battle for the end, and I was not disappointed. However, it was all very anticlimactic compared to the rest of the boss battles, and didn't seem like the right ending for this kind of game. It left me feeling like things were unfinished, like all I'd done was take a break.
Regardless of those cons, I still highly recommend this game. Again, even without prior experience with Half-Life, I believe anyone that enjoys sci-fi and kind of a classic fighting style would enjoy this game immensely. I rate this 9/10

In the story of Just Cause 3, you play as Rico Rodriguez, some sort of Spanish Rambo. Rico's massive open world home Medici is suffering under the typical dictator, who is oppressing his people, and threatens the whole world with his bavarium weapon production. It's obvious that the CIA is looking to get in on that too. Only Rico is in the way.
In the struggles against the dictator you must support the rebels of Medici by freeing over 130 villages, cities, outposts, oil rigs, and military camps by wreaking havoc. In addition to that, you must deal with countless singleplayer missions, challenges as well as sidequests.
For these tasks, you are provided with all sorts of weapons, vehicles, and gadgets. It's up to you whether you use a car, motorcycle, boat, plane, helicopter, parachute, wingsuit or your grappling hook for progression. The possibilities are endless.
Sadly the leveling system of Rico is both limited and almost pointless, since he is already very good at everything, but still you can unlock "upgrade-mods" through completing challenges. These go all the way from target practice to racing.

This is a great MMO if you're looking for an MMO with a twist.  Unlike other MMOs this one has many elements that most others do not focus on.
For instance, like the other ES games, you can steal things.  Furthermore, certain quests allow you to make decisions that may have a different outcome depending on what you choose.  Also, you can make and use any weapons or armor you like, however you must learn to use the weapons (by using them and raising your skill) in order to unlock the weapon abilities.
There are 4 classes: Tank, Mage, Healer, Sneak.  (They're not actually called these things, however, I used general terms to make it easier to understand what each of them actually focuses on.)
You may be one of the 4 classes with each character you create, and each class has a different set of abilities you can learn.  You do NOT have to focus on class skills if you would rather focus on weapon skills (or you could mix the two), however, one of the biggest benefits of class skills is that you do not have to have a certain weapon equipped to use them, which is nice.
Also this game is pretty action based.  Moving around is crucial, especially when facing bosses.  There is a dodge button, as well as block (and the push back block).
The way they set up mounts is also unique compared to other MMOs I've played.  Each actual mount has its own set of skills you can level up once per day for 250gold.  These skills are as follows: Speed, Stamina, and Carry Capacity (allows your character to carry more if that particular mount is assigned).  Each of these skills is maxed out at 60.
Also, your bank is actually shared between all your characters.  This makes it easy for one character to give to another without sending something in the mail (which, so you know, you cannot send anything to yourself).  Mail also is shared between characters, as well as the guilds you choose to join.  I believe you may have up to 3 guilds at any given time.
Selling items to players is only obtainable through guilds.  The guildmaster may buy a space at any of the guild trading zones, and all players of that guild may sell their items there.  You can access the auction house at the bank, but only, of course, if you're in a guild with that option.
Of course, there's also selling items directly through trading, but that isn't quite as easy to do without ranting about the item in public.  Not exactly my style, but some people apparently like it.
It is important to note that this game is not another "Skyrim".  If it were a one player game, they could easily make it as customizable as Skyrim, however, being an MMO, it has to be limited, otherwise the customizability would cause the world to become too chaotic...  No one would even want to play.
It does have elements in it unique to the MMO genre, but you can't move everything or pick up things and throw them across the room.  You can kill civilians, but of course, they come back to life after a while.
Guards are not currently killable, so don't even try it.  They will ruin you.  If they come after you, RUN and hide as quickly as possible.  You can run into the thieves locations for a quick getaway, so make note of their locations in main cities before you choose to commit crimes.
In the end, I really like this game myself.  For an MMO, it's definitely one I enjoy playing.  I look forward to seeing what they will choose to bring into the game next, and I give this game a thumbs up.

Slime Rancher is a very cute farming/exploration game. You feed Slime's food. Different slimes eat different foods and will produce different types of items called "plorts" which can be exchanged for newbucks. As you progress through the game you unlock different areas, you'll find secrets, you'll find secret paths. There isn't much in the game story wise and there is a lack of a socialization system or other humans which may leave you feeling a litttle bit lonely but don't let that deter you. The game has very lovely music and always leaves me feeling relaxed.

In Slime Rancher you are a farmer on a far away planet where you split your time between exploring your surroundings and taking care of your slimes, bouncyball-like creatures that you find on your expeditions. Well-fed slimes produce plorts which you can sell to earn money for upgrades.
It is a fun casual game with an adorable artstyle that suffers a little from its lack of depth, story or endgoal.
I recommend it for people who need a distraction but don't want to become too invested in what they are playing or for people who just want to unwind after a stressful day.
The game has a free demo, so check that out to see if you like it.
There is no story to speak of. You farm slimes, you cultivate food for them, you go exploring. In the beginning, you get a few messages from your neighbours who introduce themselves to you but you will never actually meet them. You get a little bit of information about the different kind of slimes when you find them. That's it. There is no endgoal, no objective. This is not necessarily a bad thing, it makes for very relaxing gameplay, just be aware of that if you don't like open-ended games.
You move with WASD, jump and later fly with space and look around with the mouse. You are carrying a kind of huge vacuum cleaner thing called vac that lets you suck in everything including slimes, food and live chickens with the left mouse button and ejects it with quite a bit of force when pressing the right button.
The developers did an excellent job here, everything about how you move, how the vac works and sounds feels right. After you bought a few upgrades you can run for long stretches and even fly around a bit and it's a lot of fun just speeding around.
You have 4 inventory slots for everything plus (after an upgrade) a seperate one for water. The water is your ammunition to defend yourself against the only enemy in this game, a form of corrupted slime that appears if a slime eats plorts from more than one different slime-type. If that happens somewhere around you, the music changes and you can either run away or try to defeat them by shooting them with water or just use your vac to fling them into the ocean. You are never really in danger here, the only thing that will reliably kill you is if you fall into the ocean yourself. That will lose you your inventory and a day in-game.
The main part of the game is farming your slimes. Your farm consists of up to five areas with 4 to 6 plots that you can turn into either corals for your slimes, farm plots, or silos for storage. Each slime-type has its favourite food which will make them produce more plorts if they get it. You can turn your normal slimes into Largos by feeding them a plort from a different slime-type. A Largo is a huge slime that is a mixture of the original slime and the plort-producing slime. You can't suck them up with your vac anymore, but they produce plorts of both species and also have the favourite foods of both types, which makes feeding them easier. You collect plorts to sell them for money, or later you also use them as ingredients in crafting.
Exploration is also a big part of the game. There are several different regions that you can either explore right from the start or that you need to unlock by finding secret places. There are also boxes and pods hidden away that you can find and contain some goodies.
Slime rancher doesn't have a story or endgoal. That is, as I've said, not necessarily negative. Usually, open-ended games or sandbox games make up for that by giving you the tools to make your own story and/or goals, e.g. Minecraft or Stardew Valley. Slime Rancher's problem is that it also lacks depth. There is no creativity involved, your plots are where they are, you can decide what to put on them and which slimes to farm but that's it.
Farming itself is basically grinding. You need to farm to get money for upgrades to make farming a little less tedious but you still have to run around a lot on your farm since the different areas and plots are spaced out quite a bit. You can ignore your slimes, they won't die on you but your fruits and vegetables will just disappear after a while unless you have stored some of them somewhere.
At some point you'll get access to crafting. You need different types of plorts for crafting which you get by finding the different slimes in the different regions. What you can craft are machines that let you harvest special ingredients. You need these for other devices that make it easier to farm and to visit far away places but only after you've already visited them. The problem is that after you've found the region-specific slimes there isn't really a reason to go there again, so you begin to wonder why you're even doing any of it.
I bought this game in early access quite a while ago and played it again when the pre-release final version came out, and both times I've hit that spot after 18 hours or so where I lost interest because even though I still haven't found every slime-type and haven't unlocked every area, I know that there won't be anything really new in it, just more slimes.
I still see myself playing it every now and then to unwind after a stressful day, though, because it is strangely relaxing to just aimlessly run around in this game and shoot slimes in the air. There is nothing stressful or demanding, the artstyle is adorable, music and sounds are perfectly fitting, and the slimes are really cute.
So, thumbs up from me but know what you're getting into. I'd give it a 6/10 if Steam allowed such a thing.

I loved the original Thief series. Thief 3 wrapped up the story arch well, but was already suffering because the developers focused more on 3d horse-power and less on great controls and gameplay.
