The game is running a decent bit better now; I've been able to maintain a fairly solid 60fps on my i5 4690k/GTX970,although certain missions such as the clockwork mansion and the one where you travel back and forth through time caused significant dips. There's still issues, but I use Rivatuner to cap at 60 and have the max pre rendered frames set to 1 in the Nvidia control panel, and for the most part, it runs alright.Overall, it's a decent game so far. Emily has interesting powers and the levels are fairly well done. I wouldn't consider it as good as the first Dishonored, as there's just some really baffling design decisions, like having 3 or 4 clockwork soldiers in a tiny space of the mansion or having targets in these small nooks that are just tedious to get to to kill them. I don't know if it's just because I am playing on hard, but there's just some really poor enemy placement in the levels. The levels can also be a bit meh. Some are ok, but a lot are just open streets with occassional buildings you can go into to get runes/bone shards. It's funny, but I think the memory constraints of the consoles ended up making for more interesting level design in the first game, whereas this is just "here's a huge open area, have fun" style level design with little in the way of intelligent funnelling. One issue I also have is the new lean system. I want the old Dishonored/Thief style lean, not this lean toggle non-sense.

A lot of people have heard about this game. Not many have played it and very few have finished it, even once. This game is not so friendly. If you love a challenge, then this game may or may not be for you. Why do I say that? Well, it's not a normal challenge, it's devotion. If you are new to games, RPGS or anything that you can attach the word 'new' to, then this game may not be for you. It brings its own meaning to the word death and I must say that, it is quite frequent, even to the most hardcore players.
The graphics are quite good. It draws you into the world of the game as if were like a dream. Only the dream is a nightmare if you make the slightest mistake. The designs on the enemies and bosses are unlike most games and I admire the unique qualities they show.
The story line will be quite confusing for most. There are very few NPCs to talk to in the game and each time you talk to them, you want to exhaust their lore. By doing that, they will either reward you or travel to the next location to continue the story line.
There is no map, so you are exploring with your eyes. Be sure to observe with caution as well. There could be an illusionary wall, enemies from any direction, secret paths, hazardous environment, more enemies, certain areas or items that could have been missed and of course, more enemies.
When fighting a boss, it's always best to keep your distance and learn the patterns. Always keep your shield up and dodge at the proper moments. If you are going with something different, like projectiles, then make sure you always keep your distance. You will be squishy and one hit may certainly kill you.
When fighting PvP, projectiles are always the most favored. Why? Because some of them have lock ons and can break through shields. A good strategy is to keep your distance and guard up. Wait for the right moment to strike, because a simple mistake can and will get you killed quickly. Give them a reason to get close to you, if they are throwing projectiles at you, but make sure you are at decent to full health for it.
Another tip, always keep an eye on your stats, weapons, armor, flasks, gems and other useful items.
If you have any questions about the game, stuck on a part and need a way out or even more strategies, please feel free to ask and I'll help you the best I can.

Personally, I find game remakes completely unnecessary and disappointing. Black Mesa is the exception to this rule. While I find the original Half-life game to be a fun experience even to this day, I think that it has not aged well at all. Black Mesa takes an old classic and breathes new life into it. It's more than a mere graphics upgrade of the original. Black Mesa takes the original Half-life as a blueprint, but adds new level design, new puzzles, and some new dialogue into the mix. It's not so much a remake as it is a complete over-haul of the original. The main problems I have with Black Mesa thus far is the fact that the final area of Half-life, Xen, has yet to be implemented. On top of that, the game can be unstable at times. During my playthrough, the game has crashed unexpectedly 4 times, so make sure you save often.
Overall, Black Mesa is a brilliant remake of a timeless classic and I would highly recommend it to any fans of the original.

As if putting the time, effort and CREATIVITY INTO A PROJECT HAS RESULTED IN A GOOD GAME.
It's a slow burner, but after the initial slow start, it keeps the tension high and the dangers are varied to keep it from being monotonous. It faithfully recreates visuals you'd be familiar with from the movie - doors, corridors, environment nick-nacks, etc. It's all bulky CRT monitors with computers going beep-boop and pipes leaking steam.
Gameplay is decent enough. Requires some experimentation without too steep of a learning curve. Probably my favorite part is that it doesn't treat the player as an idiot and occasionally you have to pay the consequences of not thinking things through. You can take things safe and slow or you'll take your chances at a high-risk-high-payoff approach which is where the game really shines imo. It's not a Slender clone and you're given options as to how to deal with situations, you're not limited to just sprinting or ducking.
If you love the original movie and always wanted a good video game adaptation of the franchise - this is the game for you.

This is by far the best game I have ever played. And I've played a lot of games...
As many others, I am a huge fan of the Alien movies and until now, all the Alien games I've played missed that certain touch that made the 'perfect organism' earn its title. Though the AvP series delivers its thrills and chills, Isolation really nails it. Based on the first Alien movie (the best of them all, in fact), it manages to recreate that frightful feeling that you get when you're hunted-down by the ultimate predator.
It has its glitches, but are so far apart and so little, that you can easily ignore them and they don't break the overall feeling.
Though I've read in many reviews that the game is too long (SERIOUSLY?!?), I find the length and the pacing of the game just perfect. I hope Creative Assembly won't give-in to these (STUPID) comments and make the next Alien game just as lenghty. Combining the Alien moments with the 'Working Joe's' ones makes for a perfect thrill ride, with it's ups and downs, otherwise it would have become stale. I also simply loved the moment which ties the first two movies together, that was pure genius! No spoilers! ;) Also very welcome were the moments where you think you've met your doom, only to be thrown into the lion's den once more... or at least you're gonna wish it were lions, but no such luck. ;)
Best! Game! Ever! Play it, die a lot, and I mean a lot of times! Repeat! :)
Good job, CA, I can't wait to play all the DLCs and hope for another gem like this in the future! :)

Imagine a game which aims to just be fun rather than realistic. That game is Just Cause 3.
If you do not go in with high expectations of GTA VI with grapple hooks then you will be satisfied.
The game looks gorgeous (look up water and scenery screenshots) and I often launch it for a couple of minutes just to wing suit and relax.
It has this unique feeling of freedom of movement, which is superior to any other gamer (yes, even Just Cause 2) (my opinion).
About performance, there is no SLI or crossfire support and the game clearly could have been better optimized, but knowing Avalanche they will try their best to fix it ASAP.
You should expect the game to be running OK on "common" systems (GTX9XX/8XX/7XX+iX or current AMD mainstream graphics cards/CPUs).
I also suspect that a lot of the optimization issues might be caused by rushing the release (Square Enix?) and implementing Denuvo "Anti-Tamper" (thanks Square Enix) which the developers describe as buggy and themselves do not like (hence your enemies are called "DRM").
So, overall would I recommend it? Yes, but please check online if your PC would handle it right now (Google: *YourGraphicsCardName* Just Cause 3) and if not, then you will be better off waiting for it to be fixed (expect +~10 - 20 FPS long-term) or upgrading your PC.

Not what I was expecting. While it certainly reads as survival-focused game, it is yet another Rust copy.
You are confined to the beginning areas by game design. Iron, for example, does not spawn in higher level areas. Instead, it is replaced by the next metal, but you cannot skip a metal while leveling your tools. While in this area, you are much more likely to find other hostile players, primarily because they have less to lose. You will also encounter others, as your primary source of food (weird antelopes that are kind enough to stand still for you to throw a spear 5m away), only spawn in certain sections of the beginning areas.
The progression of tools, as result of this design, is a failure in my eyes. Farm resources in a specific area for a few hours to upgrade your tools. Move to higher level area. Repeat until you reach end game. Find car parts. Head back to beginner area. Because this is obviously designed to create a section for shooting practice.

If you're looking for a RICH story arc, Pay once (not including *optional* DLC), look no further. There's hours upon hours of lore, deep crafting discpilines, and crazy character customizations both in skills, and attributes. 3 playable factions to choose from, so you can fight for the Alliance that best suits your values and common goals, or, play them all! Create a character suited to your playstyle and set out on your adventure.
Observations:
1. Open group content ON TOP of instance-based dungeons and the dungeons scale with the group leader's level so your ALWAYS challenged!
2. Immersive and requires thought to solve some of the puzzle based quests you will find. Helps exercise the mind and forces players to pay attention to quest chains and arcs!
3. Immense game world, with plenty of content via side quests, exploration, and lore collection to keep a player busy, yet also contribute to the overall progression of your characters skills, and acheivements.
4. LOTS of supportive players to play with on the North America server I play on. Mature attitudes, but helpful and community driven. Social, Merchant, PvP, PVE and RP guilds available! And you can join up to 5 guilds!
5. Crown Store provides an *optional* micro-transaction driven depot to improve upon hard to get crafting motifs, day-to-day consumables, costumes, and of course DLC.
(Optional) Imperial Edition Benefits:
- Play the Imperial Class character which can allign to ANY of the 3 in-game factions.
- Bonuses to Imperial Class character are balanced yet lucrative to players who want to "tank".
- Free horse! This is a must as accumulating 10k plus in gold is quite difficult for a new player.
(Optional) ESO Plus Membership Benefits:
- Access to all DLC as long as you remain a subscriber.
- 1500 Crowns per 30 day membership
- 10% upgrade to character progression
Happy Adventuring!

TLDR: Getting into the action with WASD controls and the innovative third person camera puts a new refreshing spin on the old DOTAesque format. I like it for the immersive action, aesthetics, variety in gods, and it’s noob-friendliness. Yes I said it!
PROS: SMITE deviates from the isometric view and I feel takes you closer to the action with a third person view. The gameplay too is more immersive as character movement is controlled by keyboard instead of mouse control which has traditionally been the norm. There’s a huge variety of gods that you can unlock using favour points that you earn in each match. Each god has his/her specialties. Some are good early game, some become lethal after levelling up considerably, some have nuke skills (with long cooldown periods), some are fast and good for chasing down and picking off weak enemies - all standard MOBA concepts but they're there. Oh and a bonus thrill - there are Indian gods and mythological beings to choose from! And esoteric ones at that such as Vamana and Bakasura. Best bit is that it's not pay to win. All money upgrades are cosmetic. There is great emphasis on aiming and skill based attacks. Very few of the attacks are auto aim or guaranteed hits.
CONS: Yes there are balance issues. But I suppose broken gods are part of the fun.

Perhaps I'm biased because I played this game the year it came out in 1999 or 2000...but playing it again 13 years later I realize why I came back to it. This is truly a survival horror, and even though I've been spoiled with modern graphics, you'll quickly forget how obsolete the poor graphics are in this game as you play. For the time that it came from, the graphics were obsolete even for the year that it came out (compare to Halo or Return to Castle Wolfenstein, for example, which came out the next year), but it makes up for it by outstanding gameplay structure and environment.
It's quite creepy, and you must rely on your volume because things will sneak up on you if you don't hear them in advance, and a wrong move could mean death. You must learn to ration your inventory, and the gameplay is far more complicated than any modern game. I remember playing Bioshock and remembering how similar it was to this game, and indeed it is, and people are who are fans of the Bioshock series will feel right at home in this game.

People want you to think that this is a horror game. Or that it's an Aliens game. Those people are what I like to call "wrong".
I'll start by saying this: Alien: Isolation is my game of the year 2014. You can tell, because of this effortpost. Other survival games give you freedom to build, try to be more Minecraft than Minecraft, make it clear that there is no goal but survival. Here, there is a goal: Escape the station. Alive. Destroy the Alien.
It's not easy. Everything from other humans desperate to remain safe in their own little claims in the mall to the poor quality control of SEEGSON's engineering teams will fight you. And then there will be the occasional bowel-gripping terror of encountering the monster itself. It learns. It will stop fleeing from you when you try to minimize fuel expenditure on your flamethrower, then it will start to recognize when you don't even have enough propane to keep the pilot light up. And at every turn, it will learn you're delicious.
You have tools, of course. IEDs, medkits, cobbled from whatever you can salvage. Do you let the alien eat that group so you can scavenge them for precious resources? Do you waste fuel scaring it off, or can you rig up a Molotov?
I met a dead man in an apartment. He had gotten raucous drunk while I waited for him to put his whiskey down so I could get the last precious ounces of ethanol, and once more have fire to drive the creature off. It heard his blubbering from the hallway and killed him. From the vents, I heard no more of it, and upon leaving thanked the dead man for the gift of flammables - He had been hoarding a tank of propane as well, and had a revolver with two rounds left in it.
Another time I had to beat a crew of bystanders to death with my maintenance jack. I thought I was so clever... Until I needed to pass through the area again and they were not there to distract the alien.
Lastly, the environment is AUTHENTIC. The Creative Assembly nailed the feel and look of Alien. Make no mistake - This is no action-packed romp. You will have guns, you will have tools. You will feel like a God sometimes, dispensing justice with your hull fastener with compromised safeties.
But your weapons are not your salvation. They are a means to get to the next save point.
Remember to HOLD E, and not just tap it.

The game that is truest to the original Alien movie by Ridley Scott.
This is not an Alien-exterminating FPS game, this is first and foremost a survival game... so first of all, forget about miniguns or other heavy firepower. Here your main weapon are your wits and every single piece of (apparent) junk that you can find aboard Sevastopol Station that you can turn in make-do gadgets, such as medkits and flashbang grenades. For the first part of the game you won't even have a weapon at all besides a monkey wrench, and when you'll get one bullets will be extremely rare to come by; therefore, don't think that you can get in guns blazing and shoot the hell out of anyone standing in your way: you will die, simple as that.
The setting is incredibly detailed and has much resemblance to the original starship "Nostromo" featured in the movie -- including 70s-like monochrome screens and computers which you will have to operate to unfold the mysteries that surround the space station you are in. The music creates a really eery and tense atmosphere, especially whenever you get spotted either by hostile humans -- people who originally inhabited the station and now have been left for dead by the Seegson Corp --, synthetics or the Alien itself.
If you like survival horror games or are a fan of the movies, give this game a chance. You won't regret it.

TL;DR - A good game, but it feels unfinished, and has a ton of grinding, which mostly consists of running around on your farm moving stuff from one container to another.
When I say unfinished I don't mean in ways that make it feel unplayable, but that you can tell they wanted to both improve and add more content before launch but were pressured to launch anyway. The game's 'ending' is abrupt and unsatisfying. There is no real endgame content, and the stuff you work so hard to make in the lab basically goes unused, save a few key items that may as well be mandatory to progress. It's not very hard, but still manages to have tons of grinding to get certain things needed to make your journey tolerable. They say survival mode will come later, but that probably would have made for a much more complete package, to be honest.
All in all it ends up being a game about farming resources to make stuff so that you can farm more resources. A loop that doesn't really end in a gratifying way, in the current version of the game. If you're okay with playing a game with no real ultimate goal except ones you make for yourself, you may still enjoy it.
Speaking of which, ignore my playtime/achievements. I've been playing the last few days on Xbox, because that hit 1.0 first. I can say that if it runs as bad on PC as it does on Xbox One I would avoid it until performance patches, but I'm sure it runs better if your tech is up to date. (At least, I hope it does, because full-ranch lag does come near unplayable on XB1.) Controls are fine, but the way they function isn't always ideal. You'll often finding yourself wishing the game were more player friendly, like being able to simply pick up only resources without grabbing up every large slime nearby, the delete corral menu asking if you're sure before it erases thousands of currency worth of work, or the ability to have more than one stack of something in your inventory.
There are a lot of counter-intuitive game mechanics that I found frustrating. Rather than list them all, I'll simply say this, this game expects you to grind at your farm first and foremost, exploring and such comes in at a distant second. Running an optimal farm usually takes a whole day of labor, or more, and by the time you get done it's time to start again. Once you get money and certain resources in order, there are devices to help, but not nearly as much as you'd hope. Why can't I just set certain plorts to sell or be moved to my refinery automatically? Forcing the player to spend so much time running back and forth on the farm is the biggest thing that drags this game down. You WILL feel the grind eventually, the big question is how far in will it take, and will you feel it was worth it when you're done?
But I enjoyed this game in spite of all that. It's cute and it's fun. A much better timesink for a free weekend, than most free to play ventures. If that sounds okay to you, then keep an eye out for a good sale price and try it out. But if you don't have the patience or the free time, I'd have to say pass. Wait for a bigger sale, or to see if future patches make certain parts of the game more fun/tolerable.
Proof that Early Access can and does work - with enough passion and dedication. Highly recommended for anyone looking to have what a lot of modern games seem to be lacking: fun.

- Terrible collision system due to the warscape engine, unit models move in and out of each other, clipping and sliding are a great part of every combat interaction, especially with cavalry charges.

- No family tree, no decent general development.

there are far more problems that this, take it from a person who has spent almost 500 hours playing this game and about 5  of those hours were playing the vanilla. Final verdict, I DO NOT RECCOMEND THIS GAME IN ITS CURRENT STATE.

If you've played video games at all, it's likely you've played Half-Life before. This review assumes you have. If you haven't, you really should; it was a benchmark first-person shooter. Anyway, this is a quick-and-dirty list of things I liked and did not like about this remake:
+Thanks to the more detailed environments, Black Mesa even more like a real place than before. The various sections feel even more connected than in the original, with nice detail to give the impression that the facility feels connected. It greatly helps for immersion.
+Some sections of the game are different than in the original, and most of the time they are fun while feeling at home in a Half-Life game. I won't spoil them, but this game has its own variations to various situations in the original that are fun.
+Good original score gives the game its own rendition without feeling like a copy of the game's original music, while also keeping with the right "mood" of when each piece plays.
+General game feel (shooting things and moving around) generally feel nice.
+Unlike other source games, it doesn't take forever to alt-tab back into it if you alt-tab out! I'm not sure why this is, but it's welcome.
+The MP5 seems to have more bullet spread than in the original game, and makes shooting it at medium-long range miss more often than not. Granted, submachine guns generally are best for short range, but the only long range weapons given to the player at the Revolver, Crossbow, and energy weapons.
+The Crossbow, let's talk about it. It's still a powerhouse that kills most enemies in one shot. That being said, scoping in with it is useless, and it's generally preferable to fire it unscoped. The reason for this is is that it zooms in WAY too much and doesn't decrease mouse sensitivity while doing so, making it very difficult to actually line up targets while using it. If the zoom was decreased by a bit, it would be amazing.
+While most enemies are how they were in Half-Life, I feel like the Alien Grunts are much more tanky than in the original game. Seriously, they've lived through rockets and satchel charges that hit almost right on top of them. What makes this even more annoying is that their gun does incredible amounts of damage and seems to home in on you. They were the toughest enemies in the game by far.
+Some segments, while generally making the game better, felt too rediculous at times. There is one near the end where for the majority of it there are no healthpacks at all! While most of that section is an obstacle course, you still fight some alien slaves which can be annoying.
+There is a minor bug where reloading a shotgun from 0 to full made it shoot right after it finished reloading the last shell. I guess the firing got "sticky' but it's very minor.
Overall, I'd recommend Black Mesa. They haven't released the Xen section yet, but hopefully their take on it will keep up the nice level of polish the rest of the game has.

An atmospheric, riveting mish-mash of role-playing, first-person shooter, adventure, survival horror, and puzzle solving that stands the test of time. Lost in cyberspace, as if it were a case of irony, for the longest time, its resurrection as a legally downloadable title will certainly help to get more players aquainted with the game that essentially spearheaded its spiritual successor, BioShock.
Indeed, you'll find that BioShock, with a few liberties of course, plays almost exactly like System Shock 2. It has a very similar plot structure, also has its own set of abilities crafted for its game world, and that oh so infamous twist.
System Shock 2 is a challenging affair, however, but not always for the right reasons. While it certainly doesn't hold your hand like BioShock did with the Vita Chambers, it's honestly not far behind with the reconstruction nodes (or whatever they're called in SS2). The primary weakness in SS2 lies in its array of Psi abilities, which are drastically unbalanced and rather poorly conceived, compounded even further by the atrocious costs to acquire them whilst you should instead focus on more pressing skills and traits (such as weapon requirements and statistics upgrades). Weapons jam far too quickly. Enemies can respawn and it sometimes breaks the immersion. Controls are not silky smooth, but this is more a double-edged sword that also presents a necessary challenge that may help you appreciate the game's trials. And the graphics, in retrospect, are rather ugly, particularly with regards to character models and the innumerous FMV sequences (yeah, I used a term that has seemingly disappeared from the gaming pantheon).
Stealth is, rather, sketchy in the game as well. Some of the enemies seem to possess Heimdall-esque sensory abilities at times while at others they're completely oblivious to your adjacent presence. Either occurrence can take place while you play stealthily (walking instead of running, moving around in a crouch, no firing of weaponry, etc.), so there's some inconsistent AI present.
There are useful features in the game, however, such as modifying weaponry without strained limitations like its spiritual successor, being able to climb ledges and other obstacles, priming a melee weapon for a timed strike rather than swinging about like a dunce, and a full-fledged inventory system. You can also change the kind of armor you wear, and you can equip a trait-enhancing implant (two with a particular OS upgrade). Cybernetic Modules are more valuable and come in lesser quantities than ADAM from BioShock, and thus you come to appreciate acquiring them in this go-ahead. The aforementioned flaw in the Psi abilities wherein lies most of the abilities (5 pages of them, costing up to 50 modules just to unlock) doesn't help matters and may cause players to find themselves in an unnecessarily unfair circumstance later in gameplay, but at this point this flaw is common knowledge so one should be able to avoid it with a simple treading of actual reviews.
Anyway, the power of this game lies in the atmosphere, characters & monsters, and setting. You are, really, quite utterly alone on the enigmatic Von Braun, and everything is out to get you. When you think there's hope, it immediately gets dashed. You must adapt to survive, or you just won't cut it. You have to strategize, and as you interact with the interfacing systems of the Von Braun and the accompanying Rickenbacker, you're defenseless and in real-time. You have to seek out the only means of avoiding the dreaded "back to menu" incident as a result of untimely death, which may very well happen within mere seconds of facing opposition or even harsh environmental conditions. You have to listen to the sounds of your surroundings or pay the price for carelessness.
Common enemies, which are infected former crew-members, hunt you down mercilessly but apologize to you for it or beg for you to take them out of their misery. What were once simple robots built for the express purpose of undertaking menial tasks are now unwitting kamikaze units. Alien-esque creatures appear more numerous the further into the ship you venture, assaulting you from all sides. Former defense droids that kept the peace and maintained safety for the crew do everything but those things when you're around, and will cut your life short upon detection. And all you have are rather measly (at first) weapons, limited and costly ammunition to attack with, armor that slightly reduces damage at all, and on top of all that, a very mortal existence. You're on the bottom of the food chain here, you're no John Rambo, and most of all, time is running out.
That doesn't take into account the sometimes absurdly dangerous environment and its contents!
In the end, it is a remarkable title that deserves to be played, especially by fans of 2007's BioShock. You may even manage an ounce of appreciation for System Shock 2, and for the diabolical, megalomaniacal villain SHODAN whom adorns its cover image and just about any discussion regarding the game. You may even quiver in fear as you go about its challenges, which is always a plus.

Dark Souls 2, should you get it? Well lets have a look shall we.
First off, the PC port. Is it Good? Yes, very. High framerate, high resolution textures, good lighting (Please note that it is not a good as what was shown in the early demo footage but it is still good) and wind physics (Wind physics + cloth looks really good by the way) makes it very pretty. Performance is always more important than looks, and the performace Dark Souls 2 is very good indeed (better than I was expecting). My framerate was always high and never dipped below 60 fps. The draw distance is good for the most part but there were a few times were I saw objects pop in late, but I only seem to see this when at the borderline between one area and another. Now controls, the use of Mouse and Keyboard in the menus is better than the Dark Souls: Prepare To Die Edition but not perfect. It is possible to play this game useing Keyboard and Mouse (Better than Dark Souls 1 anyway). However, I highly recommend you play this game with a controller/gamepad.
Now the game itself, is it good? Yes, the game like the other Souls game rewards skilled play and brutally punishes mistakes. If you die (You will die a lot in this game) you will become Hollow, a Zombie like state, were you will lose some of your max health (If you keep dieing your max health will keep going down but it will only go to 50% of your max health when fully hollowed) and you wont be able to summon phantoms to help you. Useing a human effige will make you human again and will restore your max health, but they are a little hard to find, don't waste them. I think this game is easier than Dark Souls 1 but it is still harder than most games. Their are not as many "hard" boss's as there was in Dark Souls 1 but some will still make you want to beat your head against the wall...*Cough*Ancient Dragon*Cough*. The game has a lot of content and will probably take you about 30 to 40 hours to complete (Playthrough 1) which is 3 to 4 times the length of most other games and it has a lot of replayablity and many secrets to discover.
Its also good to note that the multiplayer elements of the game, such as summoning a Phantom, can make areas and boss's extremely easy. And summons 90% of the time will work, unlike Darks Souls 1, so thats good. On the subject of multiplayer I should probable mention PvP...Its okay but some cheap things like Hexes and getting stunlocked because of the weird way poise works in this can make it seem unfair. You get a lot of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s in PvP so you may want to stay away if you are easly enraged, but thats up to you.
Their are a few things I should mention but I wont so you get the best experience on your first play through of Dark Souls 2, but here are some tips; Watch out for traps and ambushs, mind your surrondings, fall damage is high compared to Dark Souls 1, its more important to upgrade your weapon than your armor, dodgeing>blocking and try to have both melee and ranged attacks.
After a recent patch the pvp is a bit more balanced and more enjoyable, however still not perfect. Also, after playing some pvp with my new character (Mina) I've picked up a few useful bits of info for pvp and pve. They are as follows (The order of these means nothing) : Sheilds kinda suck, dodgeing is better. Doesnt matter how big and hard hitting your weapon is, it means nothing if you can't hit me. Magic may be OP and good for pve, but again, it means nothing if you cannot hit me in pvp. Can't heal in the arena's anymore (Thank ♥♥♥♥), so Estus chugging scrubs are ♥♥♥♥ed. In duels, its polite to bow first and let them (and you) aplly buffs before the fight, and no healing during a fight. In Invasions however, anything goes. If you are the invader, expect the Host to heal (uselly running away from you to heal while in full Havels armor...), chase that ♥♥♥♥er down and backstab him when he trys this. If you are cruel (like me) you can use the enviroment to your advantage when invadeing, like enemys and traps (Not Gwyndolin). Throwing Knifes are very useful in pvp, cheap (100 souls per 1, can carry 99) and can be used by any build, use them. Always have both a Melee and Ranged weapon equiped, with Melee being your primary weapon. If you uses bows, poision arrows are the best (3-4 arrows to poision, will do about 100+ damage per arrow and the poision will do 1500+ before running out).
Anyway, should you buy Dark Souls 2? Yes. It is the weakest of the Soul series. It has a few flaws and may not be as hard as Dark Souls 1 but its head and shoulders above most other games. Well worth your money. Praise the sun!

Beyond that, there wasn't a good enough reason to condemn this game just for not rising to your expectations. People are salty for pre-ordering and "not getting what they payed for." Apparently they haven't learned to not pre-order; it is a way for the company (whether with good intentions or bad) to get a large amount of money quickly to pad early updates, or salaries once the game falls.
Now to an actual review.
The Call of Duty franchise has always delivered a diverse, fun arcade-style shooter experience. This installment is no different. The focus of movement is the Exo Suit, which brings extreme verticality to the battlefield. Guns are for the most part balanced, with a few shining through more than others. I've heard many call the BAL-27 assault rifle over-powered. This is simply because it's a gun that has good fire rate, recoil, and more. The other guns are more situational, and when everyone wants to perform well, they find a gun that is good at most things, instead of taking a gun that is excellent in one aspect, and using their playstyle to amplfy the weapon's abilities and turn that into pure carnage.

This is my first review of a game, but I'm going to be blunt and say this: don't go into this expecting it to be just like the other games in the series. I did and it made it harder to get into. That being said, It is still an awesome game! The first person option is something I've always wanted in an MMO, the quests are a lot like normal TES quests (not like your normal MMO quests), the main story is very unique, and the world is really pretty for an MMO. Now when I said "don't go into this expecting it to be just like the other games in the series", I meant that in the aspect of the skills. You don't have skills in the typical sense. Spells for example are learned either through your class or through one of the staff weapons (destruction and restoration). All in all, I enjoy it a lot. Feels like the other games for the most part. The only mistake I made was going in expecting to buy spells and use a perk like in Skyrim. I hope this review helps, and if you get this game, I do hope you enjoy it as much as I do!

This is an update to my November 2013 review.
As of patch 14, and the moding community in full swing, this game is among the best in Total War history. There are many cultures who play different from another culture, so it won't be the same playthrough time after time like it was in Shogun 2. The siege AI had a major overhaul in patch 14, and no longer uses torches most of the time, and will instead opt to use siege engines, and even reuse them. The battle AI is among the best in the game, far superior to Shogun 2's AI where it will not only flank, but it will also attack your rear if you are not careful. I myself once got caught off guard by battling two armies, and instead of them combining like they did in previous games, one went around me and attacked my rear catching me by complete surprise. The province system, once you get use to it is great as you don't have to hover over the particular city to upgrade either it, or the buildings in it. You can also dictate a number of edicts, which at the moment is not all that great as they have no advirse side effect to them. The polticial system is still in need of some serious work, but it is better than it was at launch. The overall system stability is far better than it was at launch, as I no longer have any chrashes, and most of the glaring bugs are fixed.
Overall, this is a really great game, and worth every dollar. Just a heads up though, it is not as pretty as Shogun 2, but this game has far more soul to it than Shogun 2 does in terms of faction uniqueness. Also, before anyone asks, no there is no family tree.

I highly recommend Black Mesa to anyone who has never played this excellent franchise. For those of you that are familiar, you know what's up.

Bottom line, this game still isn't great.  The map is.. big like Just Cause 2.  I'm not going to compare the two games, because both maps are HUGE.  The problem with Just Cause 3 is there simply is not a whole lot on the map.  The main island is largely empty, and the north half half of the same island is shockingly empty.
You could argue that Just Cause 2 had too many villages, bases, and etc. but since clearing ALL of them was not mandatory, the chore of clearing them was at your choosing.
With this game the island feels barren.  I liked all the little hamlets and small bases strewn across the  JC2 map, it gave it a feel that this truly was an island nation, with people living in little towns across the entire island nation.
With JC3, it feels like an abandoned island that was only recently inhabited by a few resorts and a few bases.  It feels very isolating and un-interactive.  I am a masochistic completionist, and JC2, took WEEKS to clear out all the bases, towns, cities, hamlets, etc.  In just 15 hours, i've cleared the entire map in JC3, which is shocking to me.
The plot is predictably paper thin like JC2,  the enemies just as intelligent as rocks, and the fighting.... somehow less fun.
While your character, Rico, has a lot of new gadgets and toys, the majority of them are a novelty, and less effective than the old tried and true guns and explosives.
In JC2, the vehicles, with a little skill, were beasts.  Now, they are weak and even the tank is quickly destroyed be small arms fire.  I even get severely wounded from gunshots WHILE SITTING INSIDE THE TANK!  It's ridiculous. Want to dominate the air with a chopper?  Nah, tanks can and will ALWAYS bullseye your chopper out of the sky faster than AA positions will.  Fight it out in a Tank?  Machine Gun fire will set it on fire in a matter of seconds.  Fighter Jet?  well AA positions are now much more deadly, and you better make long, FAST, flyby runs if you want to keep flying.
The game feels like it wasn't well designed for vehicles and in fact PUSHES you to fight it out on foot with Rico's gadgets, which aren't all that quick and responsive when you are seconds away from death.  The best method, everytime is to zip away to recover health, and gun from afar or from cover.   Rarely do your zipline toys prove to be a real advantage in fights, other than to use it to get away.
Another woeful addition to this game is the online element.   The game has "Longest (insert X streak or distance)" or "Most (Insert some other tally)"  and it ranks you against other players on various leaderboards for that achieved stat.  I don't care about that.   This is a sinlge player game.  Worse, it is MANDATORY, and it loses connection often, forcing you to wait for it to reconnect. WHY?!
That all being said, it is fun, it's probably not worth full price, and the game feels incomplete and empty.
I'm trying to think where JC3 beats JC2, and I am coming up blank.  A few of the other gadgets at Rico's disposal create some idle, sandbox-roaming fun, but overall, if you already have JC2, there isn't enough here to warrant buying this game.

Well, this is just shameless. This is a checklist of item types, item names, room layouts, enemy names, enemy visuals, enemy behaviors and bosses directly stolen from The Binding of Isaac. The final boss of this game is even an exact replica, down to every attack and behavior, of Mega Satan. It even looks like a red demon. Except this is all done with clunky controls and combat, and the game only offers 6 floors and is incredibly easy. On my first go with the game, without even truly learning how to handle the awkward combat controls, I both beat the game and got the speedrun achievement. That's not supposed to happen with any roguelite or roguelike.
It's not a terrible effort and what little originality there was looked pretty good. I liked the addition of more classic RPG loot, like how you have armor you can upgrade and such. However, this is sort of like when you start practicing the guitar and all you do is learn other people's riffs, since that's the most fun way to get started. You don't actually sit down and record those riffs and sell them to people, much like you shouldn't just shamelessly rip off The Binding of Isaac and sell that. Build a prototype off of Isaac and then keep working on it and adding new ideas until you have your own product if you want to sell it. Just painting by numbers and following a template isn't good enough.

Faron's Fate had potential, and appears decent superficially, but has a huge flaw that is impossible to ignore.
I had a reasonable amount of fun with it when I started, but I realized that it has very, very little replay value even before I managed to beat it. Instead of floor layouts and rooms being properly randomized, each "area"(dungeon, caves, core, 2 floors each) has four or five pre-made floor layouts that it pulls from, with the same rooms, shops,  and everything. This means that after you play a few times, you'll have seen all Faron's Fate has to show you- with the exception of some of the items, but those aren't worth trudging back through the same rooms over and over again, hoping that one of the very few aspects of the game that ARE random will pop up in your favor.
That alone should be enough to convince you to give this game a pass. Very disappointing.

I have a legitimate question for the developer of this game: why did you put so much effort into making a boring ripoff of an established giant in the market? Your game is Binding of Isacc but with all the 10's in that game turned down to a 3. The controls, the powerups, the aesthetic, the music/sound, everything. Faron's Fate is mediocre in every way.
What kept you going? Making games is hard and time-consuming, and you had to have looked at this a few times and gone "wow, this offers nothing over the game I'm ripping off, and is genuinely a waste of time to play, much less spend hundreds of hours creating".
If you can come up with a single original idea (which I doubt, having seen your monsters, dungeon rooms, items, traps, and overall mechanics lifted wholesale from BoI) please make another game. You're technically competent! Most developers cannot say as much. But this is a sham, and you should be ashamed of yourself.

Watching gameplay videos does not do justice to just how addictively fun this game is once you have it in your hands. Don't underestimate how long you might end up playing it for each time! While Faron's Fate can be enjoyed either for a few minutes or a few hours, I found myself itching to keep trying to get to the end "1 more time" ...
If you haven't played a rogue-like before or the thought of starting over from scratch upon death  makes you run for the hills like it once did for me, please give it a chance. Remember how replayable games were in the 90's and prior? Similar to those classics, there is so much variety on offer here that the short game time quickly becomes irrelevant.
Gameplay is very focused on quick bursts of action across small randomized areas, the goal being to simply survive until the end. Story and all of that pizzaz is not present nor needed here. The music matches the retro-style graphics and becomes increasinly funky as you progress!
The second reason I would recommend Faron's Fate (aside from the instant fun factor) is for the incredible loot system and sheer amount of variety that brings to the game. Weapons, spells and armours can be found everywhere and most of them will change the way you approach combat. It's like an on-the-fly class switching system. Do you want to keep your vampire armour with stylish red scarf and lifesteal effect or swap it for a wizard's garb or a heavy-but-slowing suit of
armour that will turn you into a tank? Other pickups offer permanent bonuses, adding even more depth to your custom character class. I'm enclosing my favourite weapon in a spoiler tag here, due its awesomeness!

5 game modes enhance the replayability further. Seeded mode generates the random areas based on the code/name/swear word you input. Now that's a blast from the past!
I encountered 1 instance of a bug which caused the game to crash to desktop, but it happened within the first minute of a run and I know Winter Drake is developing a patch and is actively working on the game at the time of writing.

Most likely the game of 2014 for me personaly. Great atmosphere, fantastic level design (as in absolutely gorgeous!). I just can't get over the beautiful retro-scifi scenery once set in the 70's and the way they put it all back to life in the game. It's like an exact copy of what you saw in the movies.. unfreaking real! And then the creature itself... a very convincing "A.I." that really sweeps the place hunting you down, being very unpredictable. But then again can also miss you if she looks the other way or you hug a corner or always stay at her back. This makes the creature somewhat volnurable and realistic at the same time. But once you make a mistake like say making noice or not hiding in the back of that closet you are absolutely done for. I'll admit after a few hours the scare of the creature goes away but the fear and respect of it will definitely remain the entire game. If I have to be critic i would say after a while you get a bit bored of turning on a generator that is in a room you passed 5 minutes ago. Lets just say the developers really want you to enjoy each room from all different angles. So the game could have been a little 3 hours shorter in my honest opinion, but then again if you can look passed that they finally pulled it off to create an extremely good.. no wait let me rephrase, just plainly brilliant Alien game that brings back the feelings you've had when you first saw the movies.. Thrilling, dark, compelling and scary as hell. A big fat 8 out of 10 for this little gem!

I usually like survival horror but I just don't enjoy the mechanics here.
Early in the game you are hiding from a group of looters with guns. You only have a wrench. Sneak around, kill a looter, his gun is there but you can't pick it up, because reasons. Not long after this group, you find the same gun and can finally pick it up.
Then, you return to the same area having picked up the item you needed to pass the door. The alien has appeared, and insta kills you.
It's one of those games you have to constantly sneak everywhere, meaning getting from A to B takes absolutely ages, because instakill monsters could be anywhere, but most of the time won't be, so it just feels like a waste of time.
Oh, and the save points are quite infrequent, so be prepared to punish yourself by repeating the same parts again and again.

This is my first review of a game, but I'm going to be blunt and say this: don't go into this expecting it to be just like the other games in the series. I did and it made it harder to get into. That being said, It is still an awesome game! The first person option is something I've always wanted in an MMO, the quests are a lot like normal TES quests (not like your normal MMO quests), the main story is very unique, and the world is really pretty for an MMO. Now when I said "don't go into this expecting it to be just like the other games in the series", I meant that in the aspect of the skills. You don't have skills in the typical sense. Spells for example are learned either through your class or through one of the staff weapons (destruction and restoration). All in all, I enjoy it a lot. Feels like the other games for the most part. The only mistake I made was going in expecting to buy spells and use a perk like in Skyrim. I hope this review helps, and if you get this game, I do hope you enjoy it as much as I do!
P.S. You should totally get the Imperial Edition! The horse, mudcrab, extra race, ability to marry, and the ability to make armor Imperial styled is pretty baller :D

Satisfies the brain on lots of levels, some thinky and some basic childlike play. Growing stuff like stardew valley. Twisty map exploration and grindy unlocks like dark souls. Low danger map exploration like minecraft. Strategic management/optimization/economy, one of those games that punishes you with diminishing returns if you fall into a minmax habit and don't change things up to adapt to price changes. A bit of fun with genetic engineering. Enjoyable running, jumping, jetpacking. Super kawaii creatures. The infantile joy of having a gun that shoots fruit, chickens and poop.
Walking simulator style story unlocks. Sandbox style self-goal creation.
The pacing is not for everybody, and if you don't click with it then it may feel like a grind fest, but if you do there's a lot to explore and play with. All the pieces of this game mesh together so nicely that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. Will appeal to shooter fans who want something relaxed and non-aggressive, or clicker fans who want something more active and exploratory.  It's not stardew valley, dark souls or minecraft, but somehow manages to evoke elements of all three.

The game is the same as its elder brother. Tech problems are now solved, at least as far as I'm concerned I did not experience more than a very few stutters. So, this and the many negative reviews related to this, should not prevent you from buying a very good game anymore.
It's the same as Dishonored, as I said. So, it shares the same pros and cons.
Pros: playing a totally stealthy character is still really enjoyable. It takes ages to crawl through a level if you try this kind of approach, and that's what makes the game's spirit. Brutal force can be tried, at least from time to time, but is far less interesting. Fights are very short and lack "feeling". Clearly, Dishonored 2 was not meant to be rushed sword in hand.
The universe is, of course, the same as in the first opus. It's very coherent, gothic, steampunk, a bit gory, with lots of stuff to read and listen to. So if you expect something as different as Bioshock Infinite was different from Bioshock in terms of design, you're up for some disappointment.
It's also a lot more detailed, graphically speaking, than the first game. Not always jaw-dropping, but very beautiful nonetheless.
Cons: well... it might look like a big DLC for Dishonored rather than a brand new game but eh, Fallout 2 was just a wee bit better and bigger than Fallout and yet, both are must-have games. It must have taken a pretty long time to create all these new levels, new textures, dialogues, documents, etc. It's totally worth the price charged. So, unless you consider that two games that look alike should not be sold with different labels, which would make no sense in a world full of full-priced sequels, it shouldn't be a problem.
Conclusion: worth every buck you'll spend in it, even if you buy it right away, at full price. It's a really, really good one.

Tweak tweaks - now it's not fun; it's work and it has changes that I just cannot figure out how to adjust, why they made it, and how can I get back an older version? Putting is a real problem at the time I write this review, and it never was this much of an issue before. So I'm pretty tired of trying to re-learn this game every release. However, those releases also made some great improvements both visual and functional, and their active involvement has brought the game along nicely. (One reviewer seem to think there was no "dev'elopment; I disagree: this game has one of the most devoted dev teams around.
It has a lot of courses, many really good free ones; the basics are all there, it has several levels of play, all of which are too tough for this old guy, and enough free presonalization to make your game look good. They have big plans in the golf world and while some of the bells and whistles aren't there (never missed the crowd noise anyways, no fancy locker rooms to acess data, etc.) there's a lot there, almost everything can be controlled with sliders, it supports really nice graphics, There's an active lobby, several tournaments both 'official' and open, but all use levels of play above the starter level, so your controls may look different, and you may want to learn the higher levels of controls; me I have trouble enough on hacker, or whatever the lowest is.
The game is very good at recovery, if you lose connections, or in multi-player, you have a good chance of picking up right where you left off. There's an active community base and an active forum, and an at-times chatty lobby.
Overall it is a very well-designed (and still being designed) game with great emersion, simple to learn, hard to master; lots of features and options and seems to have a robust future. Now let's all just get through 2017!

I've just finished the game so thought I would share my thoughts, no plot spoilers here though.
When I first  started playing Alien: Isolation I was expecting 'Outlast' (a game I enjoyed but felt was over-long) with a Xenomorph- tiptoe through the creep show environment until being confronted by a big bad to hide from/ stealth around whilst hunting for buttons to open the next door.  Whilst I still found my fair share of lockers to cower in and 'find switch to progress' moments, I found Alien to provide so much tension and dread between the 'big-scares' that it feels like a real evolution of the formula.  In fact this was an experience that actually exhausted me through constantly draining my nerve.
The environment of Sevastopol (the space station setting of the game) feels like it came straight from the earliest movie of the saga and is also a very believable location- post-it notes with scrawled reminders in lockers, calendars at workstations, adverts on walls (even one that explains the origin of the motion tracker), graffiti in transit stations and an insane number of drinky birds (seriously, count them).  Though if you try to stray too far off the intended path then locked doors and dead ends soon put you back on course.  Whilst I would have liked to have been allowed to explore the station further, the design did keep me focused and without it I would probably have been soon lost to the station's many corridors.
As for the alien itself, I spent the first quarter of the game in terror of it as, if it catches sight of you, an encounter with it is an almost certain insta-kill.  Whilst Isolation offers some small, smaaaall balance to this later on the game, it also ramps up the assertiveness of the hunting patterns and the xeno's determination to locate you if it thinks you're in the area.
There are other threats in the game, my most feared being the misleadingly named 'Working Joe' (I would have gone for 'Murderous Joe', myself).  These are Sevastopol's synthetics but unlike Ash, Bishop or Call they are industrial units, all white plastic skin and overalls.  I'm not sure if it was intentional in the design but they end up looking a lot like Mike Myers from Halloween (AKA The Shape), which helped make them quite imposing in my run-through of the game- especially the hard-to-kill heavy duty models which become, for a short time, your main adversaries.
The humans you encounter, other than the plot essential ones, vary between indifferent to your presence to being so focused on killing you that they'll switch from actively engaging the alien to taking potshots at you instead (regardless of whether you're acting as a threat to them).
This would be a (mild) criticism from me.
It feels that whenever Amanda Ripley shows her face everybody wants her dead.  This happens to the degree that I hid in a locker whilst being hunted by both humans and alien and watched as they each walked into and out of the room I was hidden in, so focused on offing me that they were blissfully ignorant of each other for a good four or five minutes despite the humans walking about in the open bellowing about me at the top of their lungs (eventually the alien did the upstanding thing and killed the humans for me).
The pacing of the game is, in my opinion, great.  I have read criticism online that there is a lull in tension mid way into the game as various plot related happenings happen.  I didn't find this to be a problem as I felt it helped ramp up the impact of the last portion of the game which builds to an amazing level of tension.
****Gameplay Spoilers*****
Unfortunately, the very end of A:O would be great as a movie but as a game does fall victim to the Call of Duty approach of taking control away from the player to instead show them what is happening.  It's a jarring reduction of pressure that robs the game of its ability to leave me scarred of failing.
***End Gameplay Spoilers****

Overall, I'm looking forward to coming back to play Crew Expendable and Last Survivor, but I feel like I need to go play something a little lighter for a while  first (I still have Costume Quest 2 to complete) A:O has left me so drained, and I mean that as a good thing.

Its a really simple little realtime Roguelike. Think The Binding of Isaac with pixels and a fantasy theme. AFAIK, there's no story beyond "KILL THE MONSTERS, LOOT THE DUNGEON".  Start a game, youre in a random dungeon, with a random layout and random mobs and loot. Theres a seed number in the corner of the pause menu and a start option to enter a seed number, so if you find a layout you like, you can replay it.
The game itself is fast paced, lots of enemies and projectiles zipping around. Enemy types vary, and they change between level types (as you go deeper the levels change look and mobs). Art is pixel style. Nothing too spectacular. You can tell what everything is you see though, although for some reason your weapon isnt actually held by your char but arcs out in a half circle around him. Musics pretty good, and the sound effects are what you'd expect from a game like this.
The map is set up like the dungeon levels of the Legend of Zelda, each screen is a room with doors leading out. Some rooms require you to kill the mobs to proceed, some are dead ends. Some are stores where you can buy a random selection of items for gold or rarely permanent health loss.  Eventually you will find a boss room, with a giant monster that you hae to kill. It usually drops a permanent health power up. In the room with the boss is a trapdoor. Go down that and youre in the next level. Rinse, repeat. There are *plenty* of cool random items and weapons. You have a weapon slot, and an item/magic slot. You can carry only one of each, and picking up an item or weapon drops the most recently carried one. There are also bombs and keys in their own slots. Items take mana to use, the amount of which is shown by a number in the corner of the item box.
Controls are OK, but not great. Its easy to get hung up on dngeon objects and you get damaged on enemy collision, so its easy to accidentally bump into something since some enemies seem to have large collision boxes. Its not a game breaking issue, but I wish the controls were smoother. Controller support is fully implemented and decent, but only the keyboard is remappable (a big pet peeve of mine due to my disabled hand- I really appreciate the controller, but please make it mappable).
Its simple, its fun for a run or two, runs can last anywhere from 26 seconds to hours depending on your reflexes and desire to clear every screen, and also the RNG not dumping a ton of tough mobs on the first screen you enter (why I had a 26 second run).
My one big complaint is there is no save. In an arcade/permadeath-style game like this, I dont expect to be able to save to avoid dying but a "one-time emergency drop-out and pick it back up where you left off" save should be implemented. Most other games have one time saves, even arcades or Roguelikes. Thats a major issue, and should really be added.
The game also seems to be lacking in permanent unlockables, so each run doesn't add to an overall sense of accomplishment. Unlockables such as new classes, better starting gear, more health on start and so forth add a lot to a permadeath game, and the fact that Faron's Fate doesn't have them kind of lowers it in my eyes.
Overall, its a decent little game, but not great. $7 is an OK price, but I think $5 would be a bit more fair considering how simple the game is and the lack of emergency saves and unlockables. Its pretty fun though, one of those "kick back, and run frantically around a dungeon slaying monsters and looting" games.

DLC is available but also MANY user generated free courses that are awesome.
If you enjoy effort for reward games then this is for you.

Good Luck.  Hope this helps.

Overall, its a very very solid game with some minor flaws that can be overlooked due to its triumphs.

As a lover of RPG Maker games, I just had to try it - and I was not disappointed. Not one bit.
The story is about Senia, who notices that her big sister has been missing for quite a while. After hearing where she went, she chases after her. Senia has some training with the sword, so she knows how to defend herself.
I have to say, in contrast to the other RPG Maker games, this was a real-time combat RPG. The RPG Maker engine normally has a round-based setting - so having to change the script that much deserves my respect. Moving on.
The real-time gameplay was really satisfying. Using the new skills and leveling them, leveling up - I had much fun farming up stuff. Especially the secret chests and fighting the mini bosses. I really upgraded my gear to it's fullest and really felt powerful - and that is what I like about RPG and I think it is important. That you can feel strong, overpowered etc. - you farm EXP, get the best items, so of course you want to be ridiciously strong. And Eternal Senia does this job good. I really felt this upbuilding strength through the game. I really leveled up a lot before facing the final boss and felt so much stronger than the boss. It really was satisfying.
The story itself is nothing that special - big sister goes missing, little sister wants to help her - it's the typical "hero saves princess"-principal, just with different roles. The big sister being the princess and Senia being the hero. But I think the gameplay made up for this more or less average storyline.
What I also really liked about the game was the soundtrack. It is really well made - the only thing that bothered me was the hip hop beats. They felt really out of place in this game. It almost expected dubstep music when fighting a boss. I just think, it does not fit in in a medieval fantasy setting. But that was the only thing that bothered me. In everything, the soundtrack was well made.
The sprite work was well - it is your typical 2D sprites. You can not really make sprites better in 2D. You would have to do 3D sprites - but I think choosing simple sprites gave this game a retro-charme and it gives it definitely some good points with retro gamers.
Lastly, I would definitely recommend this game. If I knew a person, who would not have played a RPG Maker game yet, I would tell them about this game. I really look forward to a sequel. I would definitely play it, maybe even pay about 10 bucks for it. Depending on the quality - although I think it would be best, if you, the developer, would continue using the simple 2D graphic. It shows, that games are not all about graphics - gameplay is what is important and you did the job well.

Both such a beutiful and painful game. As punishing as it is, Dark Souls 2 manages to balance out the difficulty due to a somewhat lack of level design. Compared to Dark Souls where there were levels such as the Giant's Tomb where everything was dark or the Crystal Caverns with invisible flooring, DS2 seems to add a few more enemies here and there and around the corner to spite you. Another thing worth mentioning are the boss fights aren't as memorable as Dark Souls. These boss fights seems very less intense whereas most, if not all, are mostly bland melee fights, and nothing more. What later makes the boss fights harder is dealing with more secondary enemies or dark spirits within the fight.
The most appreciated new concepts to Dark Souls 2 are:
- the weapon upgrading and infusion system.
- holding on up to 4 rings at a time
- new sorceries, miracles, pyromacies, and hexes
- new weapon types such Twinblades and Reapers
- a better balance online play
- better A.I.
- beutiful landscape
Less appreciated:
- loss sense of memorable boss fights
Worth every penny.

Finished Dark Souls 2 at about 70 hours and in the process, I have died 642 times.
I'll be honest. In my opinion, Dark Souls 2 is a good game. However, it is the type of game that leaves a bitter taste in your mouth some times. The bad type of bitter.
The game improved in tremendous ways. Animations are much more smooth than the first game and as the developers promised, easier access to covenants as well as more new items, spells, weapons etc etc.
The bad thing about this game. The game suffered in a few ways that brought down the experience. First is the weird implementation of game rules. Now dying takes off a small part of maximum health until you are left with half of your full health. Sure, you can become human but this will happen again and again. To me, I feel really uneasy about this because the previous game is about dying and trying again. Now, this just makes people fear dying in the game. Also, enemies do not respawn after killing the same enemy at the same spot 12 times (counted by my brother). I don't know why they did this but they just made the game easier when you could just kill enemies on the way until they disappear. RPG games usually have those sort of things so it is really weird on why they would do this.
Second, boss fights suffers ALOT. I found them pretty decent until my friend pointed out to me which then I realised... Most boss fights are either too easy when they are alone or they have a big mob. The prequel makes you fear them when you battle them but now, it is not the case. In fact, there was a boss fight that left me disappointed and disheartened when I was done. However, there are other boss fights that are rather creative and I appreciate it.
Lastly, soundtrack does not seem memorable. Don't get me wrong, it is still nice but not as nice as the last time. Some feels generic and forgettable to me. Even the ending song does not feel very good to me.
3.9/5

[please note that this copy was provided free of cost for review]
Faron's Fate by Winter Drake Teller is an action roguelike where you travel through procedurally generated dungeons.  This random level layout and over 200 items ensure a high replay value and something new to see for many hours of gameplay.  There is a secret room to find on every floor and most of them require some sort of sacrifice from the player to get a chance at a new item.  There is a nice variety of enemies and the challenge level is fair.  The character and monster hitboxes can be confusing at times.
I would recommend this game to people who would enjoy a simple roguelike with runs lasting about 20-40 minutes.

Alien Isolation is indeed the best Alien video game adaptation out there.
It is long but well paced, and contains so many winks to the movies, and respects the franchise to an amazing degree.
The visuals are simply amazing, I was really impressed multiple times by the smoke particles and the lighting, as well as the level design and how faithful it was to the movie.
Some people have complaints about the game being repetitive, and being about fixing machines and opening doors etc.
But if you take a look at the movies, that is pretty much all they are about too, they make a plan to escape, do some SCI-FI stuff and it usually goes sideways and they need to adapt and make a new plan.
The game is a perfect adaptation of that, and in my opinion it was just the right lentgh.
I enjoyed the Stealth mechanics (played on Hard) and I really enjoyed using the tools that the game gave me to distract/attract the Alien.
I finished the game without killing any humans, I would instead attract Androids/Alien to kill them for me, and that felt very satisfying and cool.
All in all, this is now one of my favorite survival horror games, not because it's scary, but because of how well the world is crafted, and how immersive it feels.

‘Ascension’ by Stoneblade and Playdek sets the bar for multi-platform 'build your deck as you go’ board games.  There’s a sidebar of low-powered neutral cards and a center field of six or seven faction cards that each player has the option of using their runic pool to buy for use on future hands or their combat pool to defeat on their turn.  It’s indirect competition, players aren’t able to affect each other’s sides beyond messing with what permanent constructs they have on the field.  Acquiring expensive cards and defeating monsters raises your 'Honor’, with the highest total winning the game.
The four-player mobile version is excellent for pass-and-play on long car rides, although it’s possible to break the game by raising your Honor points too high on the last turn.  The game’s set to end the turn after a predetermined total Honor has been collected among all players.  Some advantages the physical version has over the app are the ability to house-rule the end condition (such as running out of cards in the draw pile) and doing a search and remove on generally useless cards.  That said, the physical expansions are expensive and the digital ones seem more reasonably priced.

Edit: Now that the game has been included in the humble bundle, I decided to go over my previous review and see what's up.  People have stated in many fora that there are quite a few enhancments.  Also, I did not purchase the DLC packs.  My overall review is unchanged (NOT RECOMMENDED), and I've made some revisions below...
I have a number of problems with this game.  I hate chosing thumbs up or thumbs down, as some people might find these to be good points, and it was an okay game.  But it's not for me.  Please note, this is without DLC.
Pros:
- Lots(!) of questing areas
- Combat is more interactive than other MMOs
- Werewolf form is fun, if overpowered
- Picking and specialising your chosen fighting style is rewarding if you can stick with it, but you're locked in without spending real-life $ to re-spec.
- Sneaking is less of the steamroll it was in prior bethesda games
- There are a few funny moments in the quests
- Some of the locations look great!  Sentinel is a very nice Turkish townscape!  The rest of the Daggerfall campaign starts off colourful, but turns bland after the first few zones.  Textures are optimised for distance.
- The armour sets look great!  You need to apply dyes to have matching colours, otherwise you'll look like a painter's pallette, but they are quite impressive!
- Making your own booze is fun! Keep plenty of inventory space clear for the ingredients, though
- No more Subscriptions *EDIT: Though you may as well pay for ESO Plus.  After several months, you'll be given enough crowns to eventually afford the DLCs below.  But it's not worth sticking around.  There are plenty of better games out there.
Cons:
- You'll run more than Forrest Gump.  Buy a horse and upgrade it's speed every day!
- Quests are still shallow and uninteresting, and NPCs acted arbitrarily needy or like mewling wimps.  It's clear there is a Quality vs Quantity dilema here.  It shows in the writing - though the voice actors were very good, they had very little to work with.  There are cliches and MacGuffins everywhere, even for the main questline.  The Daedra's representation as the bad♥♥♥♥♥bad guys are lessened because of this; they're always reduced to mere obstacles and petty delinquents.
- Your ethical dilemas are purely arbitrary, even in the main questline.  Who do you kill? Who do you spare?  Who effing cares!
- Veteran mode discourages variety in game-play. Instead of rolling a new toon for a different faction and chosing different fighting styles etc, you stick with the same toon.
- The phase dynamics are still broken, making co-op PvE impossible
- Looting is horrid.  Items, even purples, lack value as they are mostly used for deconstruction.
- Textures occasionally had very poor resolution, even on maximum settings, though this was not always the case.  Coldharbour HAD to be dark and gloomy to hide the low-res textures
- There's still no real thieves' guild or dark brotherhood or equivalents.  I'm not counting that Lego-domain (or however you pronounce it) as the thieves' guild.  They're merely fences, nothingmore.  *EDIT: Actually they are now in the game.  As DLC.  4000 Crowns for both.  Depending on the rate you use, that's possibly $29US
- Trading and inventory management have severe limitations.  Add-ons, trading guilds and expensive luggage upgrades are essential.
- Imperial race, horses etc are still microtransaction-bait, plus a tonne more DLC to replace subscriptions.  Dropping the "Subscriptions" tag feels like a gimmick.  Nothing against DLC, but I don't wish to pay for another bunch of mewling wimps. *EDIT: They've added a bunch of other DLCs as well: Morrowind, Clockwork City, Orsinium, Howns of the Reach (?), Shadows of the Hist...  Your own house for various amounts (from 800 Crowns up to 13,800 Crowns or $100US) Furnished...  LOOTCRATES...!!!  Yeah, I'm angry about the Reaper's harvest crates.
- *EDIT: I bought a house (alright, an apartment in Sentinel) with some spare crowns.  It was cheap, pretty small, but furnished with a prominent storage chest.  Very few things could be interacted with.  You could sit on the stools or light/extinguish the candles.  You could rearrange the furnishings.  But you could not sleep on the bed or store anything in the chest.  Overall, the house is for cosmetics only, with no practical use.
- I had to run the Repair tool after every patch.  Usually a few gigs to download the patch, then another 6gigs or so to download the repair.  A minor problem for some.  *EDIT: I also had to do this after a clean reinstall, taking approx 2 hours

Just wanted to write down a few words about this game now when I´ve been playing a number of rounds.
I´ve been playing golfgames since the Commodore 64 time before the first Links-game came out and I also play golf in real life. Not saying that makes my review more credible, but it may give a hint on what I look for and am annoyed with...
There´s lots of graphical adjustments to suit most people which is good. You have your sound options and of course your golfer customization. You can pick your clubs and equipment and buy more if thas not enough for you. At the moment you don´t have that much to buy so perhaps thats something that will be added along the way. A bunch of golf courses are included and more are available to buy for a few bucks. I´m fine with that. The courses included are fine and varying in style.
You have your practice mode which I think could be better if you had more putting and pitching options and such. Tourmaments are not used much as far as I can see which is a shame. Multiplayer will be your only option if you want to play with other players but my feeling is that this is not very active. You have to work a bit to get a game started. If you just want to play a few holes you´ll probably end up chosing solo-play anyway.
I feel I can go on and on about this so I´ll just end with what I think works well and what doesn´t.
Graphics are fine even though animations could be alot better.
Sound effects are good but the game is really missing commentary. It feel lonely out there too often.
Motionswing is frustration and annying - in other words perfect! That´s golf! :) No seriously I feel they´ve done a great job with that one. You need to practice and you won´t get it perfect all the time.
Putting is hard which is also fine but I don´t like the fact that you almost all the time have to aim 5 meters to your left/right because the greens have such big slopes. That´s just not very realistic I´m afraid. There´s some work to be done here.
As I´m a "leftie" I of course miss the left handed player...
Would I recommend the game? Well...there aren´t too many good golf games out there today so I guess we can´t be too selective here. If you like to play a quick round now and then and aren´t that interested in career modes and the stuff EA:s Tiger Woods golf had to offer, this game should be enough for you. I wouldn´t pick it up for retail price though as I don´t think the game is finished yet. To me it´s still in "early access".
