Dark Souls 2 is a decent game, but it is inferior to Dark Souls.
Dark Souls 2 has managed to become a reptitive game to play, in comparison to Dark Souls. In Dark Souls 2, areas are smaller and more densely packed with enemies. In some cases, there are far too many enemies to take on without backpedaling and turtling, making getting through an area a slow process. There's many more respawn points put throughout the game, so you won't have to backtrack far if you die, but the sheer volume and tankiness of enemies makes short distances seem much longer. There's also less alternate routes to take while progressing through the game; many more of the areas are unskippable, which exacerbates the problem of enemy-saturated areas. Unlike Dark Souls, starting a new game with a character that has finished the game (called new game+, or NG+) will spawn new enemies and surprises for you to deal with. This is a nice addition, and it keeps the game fresh for a bit longer. However, many of the new enemies the game will throw at you are just very tanky and further repeats of those areas just take longer than they did before.
Multiplayer in Dark Souls 2 is a straight downgrade from Dark Soul's multiplayer. In the Dark Souls series, you level up using the game's currency, "souls". You get souls from killing creatures in the game world, and it is inevitable you will get souls by progressing through the game. Previously, the level of your character determined what other players you could be matched with in Dark Souls. You could go through the game at a low level and still be able to connect to players near the beginning of the game; this allowed for overpowered co-op partners who could take out bosses very quickly, or overpowered enemy PvPers who could one-shot you. Late game, players stopped leveling at a community-decided level cap that allowed players to continue connecting to one another. The level cap encouraged players to optimize their character builds within these constraints for maximum specialization toward whatever role they wanted.
Because of the imbalanced early-game PvP in Dark Souls, Dark Souls 2 has adopted a new system for matchmaking. Players are now matched according to the total number of souls they have collected, not their character level. This has a few effects, some desired, some not. Early game, players do not know how to initiate PvP, or they have little motivation to because their character builds are not complete; this makes early game PvP a rarity. As the player progresses through the game, they will have more PvP opportunities and encounters, and PvP is relatively balanced because players haven't progressed much further than each other. Late game, the total number of souls a player as collected is no longer representative of their character's ability; a character may have stopped leveling up at some point, or a character may have never stopped leveling up, and some characters may have lost a great amount of collected souls by dying. The only available option for players who wish to stay competitive in PvP is to continue leveling their character, which takes away any need to optimize or specialize one's character build. Though this new matchmaking formula fixes unfair early game PvP, it ruins the fairness and depth of late game PvP.
Due to the repetitive PvE and unfair late game PvP, the game's longevity is hurt badly. There are a few other glaring issues with Dark Souls 2 that I won't go into, but despite it all, it's still a game that is above average in quality. I can't fully recommend Dark Souls 2. As a fan of Dark Souls, I've been able to keep myself interested in Dark Souls 2 for a while, but a person with more discerning taste would not tolerate Dark Souls 2 for long.
Play Dark Souls before you touch this game; Dark Souls is much better game.

Alright, I already loved Dishonored 1, and I completed that game and all the dlcs several times in various cool ways.
So, my expectations for Dishonored 2 were high, obviously, and now, having almost completed my first playthrough on Hard, using no violence, and trying to get by undetected, I am simply taken aback by this masterpiece of a game. Cheesy praise, I know, but I really do mean it. This is easily one of the three best games I ever played, and I started playing in the early 80s, and I have dorkily played literally thousands of video games. The city environments are the best I've ever experienced - the maps feel like living and breathing cities, where you get to be and moving about in them, experiencing the streets and alleys and apartments, listening in on conversations, reading about blatant social exploitation, watching bored guards fiddling with their weapons, and so forth. The sound effects and the music - top notch stuff. And each mission is huge, leaving you with tonnes of difficult decisions, and often you get excited, in the sense of surprises and chills, or even scared, when hiding behind a curtain or beneath a desk or something.
This time you get to pick your protagonist, and both are beautifully voiced. It's just unbelievably good. You may craft bone charms, you may forfeit all supernatural powers - play it whichever way you want. The replayabilty factor is crazy. I redid a few sections of two missions just because I felt like it. Dishonored 2 is literally so great that I've put it on hold in order to save it and savour my longing for my next gaming session. As for graphics performance, I had a computer perfect for its settings, and after a quarter of an hour, I managed to configure my mouse in a really pleasant way, but I know others have suffered far worse in that department.

This review is for Multiplayer, as I haven't really touched the campaign yet. It says I haven't played the game yet, but I think its because I didn't launch the singleplayer. I've played around 20 hours of multiplayer.
8/10
Let me start by saying I've really enjoyed my time in the game. The multiplayer is fast paced, and keeps me itching for "just one" more round every time. Many reviews say that this game doesn't have enough players, or that it is dying. Having played 20 or so hours in MP, I can say that all the complaints about the player count aren't really true. Granted, console has way more players that PC, but it doesn't mean that PC doesn't have any. It's really easy to find matches in TDM, domination and moshpit, while other gamemodes might require some waiting, but not much. The bottom line is that you shouldn't worry about the player base if your planning to buy this game.
The multiplayer gameplay is extremely fast and addictive. There is a plethora of weapons and equipment to choose from and plenty of challenges to ensure the game doesn't get stale. The wide range of weapons also allows for the choice of plenty of different playstyles. The maps are great too. The developers have done a great job at designing the maps to fit the exosuits. There's a ton of verticality to the maps and more than enough open room to do all the boosts and double jumps. Honestly, I can't find anything bad to say about the gameplay. Overall, It's really well made.
Evidently, movement is a huge part of this game. The exosuits allow the player to do all sorts of crazy movements like zipping in one direction, and jumping twice. At times, it can feel like Titanfall, but the types of movement are still really different. I think the devs nailed this part of the game. The movement adds speed to the game, but doesn't really hinder it. I think the addition of these suits was a fantastic choice. For the people that do not like exosuits, there is a playlist that doesn't have them. In the big picture, this game still plays like a normal COD, regardless of the movement changes.
Now to the problems. First, there isn't a server browser. It might not seem like a big problem, but when you leave a hacker filled lobby and try to join another, you might join the same lobby again. For a big game like this, there needs to be a server browser. Next is the lag. While it isn't a problem while I'm playing, I can notice it while connecting to a match. With more than enough room on my SSD and a fairly fast internet connection, there is no reason for it to take 5 minutes to enter a match. And when you can't connect, its another 5 minutes before the game realizes you can't, and takes you out. That is probably the most annoying part of the game. There is a small issue with a few maps lagging (most notably Instinct and Greenband for me) but it shouldn't be an issue if you have good hardware.
All in all, Advanced Warfare was a fun return to the Call of Duty series for me. I haven't played since COD4, and I was pleasantly surprised by this one. This game always manages to keep my heart pounding, and draws me in every time. I love the multiplayer gameplay and the exosuits add a new twist to a popular game. If you've liked previous installments to the franchise, you'll love this one. But if you've never thought much of other Call of Duty's, this game probably won't change your mind.

My first ever review on steam.
I have a very hard time reviewing this game, because of how simple it is in its premise, and delivery, and yet how complex it is with subtle messages conveyed between the lines. Maybe it's just me, but i really think this game is not as jolly as it seems at first glance. Of course, its fun, and its fine to enjoy that. At least i did. Massively. When you stop for a moment, and actually start caring about the story, all the little connections, and dialogues, it is just staggering, how fluently the narrative skips from straight up kick♥♥♥♥♥humour, to dark, desolate, lonely place deep behind your mind. At first, I laughed my♥♥♥♥♥off at numerous (even bad) puns, then, after actually looking behind the scenes, what these jokes actually meant, and what story they ACTUALLY told, I was stunned. No, not shocked, not dejected, just purely glad, glad, that somebody can actually find some fun in a place as dark, and as brutal as Pandora. While I'm not a big fan of ridiculing tragedy, this game didn't actually ridicule it. It ridiculed the people, who were responsible for it, if anything, and only showed the actual tragedy in vague whisps, not really caught by many players i recon.
Anyway, overall, I think this game never actually got the praise it deserved. While not really being VERY innovative, still felt really fresh, sort of a new perspective on both rpgs and fpses, the first game lacked visual appeal of diverse environments, and quests. This game, delivers on both of those points. With a few new mechanics, new weapon parts, new characters, it still feels mechanically fresh, while the massive number of new environments, with pretty fun views, this game feels like it has corrected every minor flaw of the first one.
tl;dr:
+Graphic tyle
+Loot
+Characters
+Humour
+Underlying, between the lines story
-Can get tedious (not much game mechanic improvements, as you level up)
-While the price is ok in a bundle, on a sale, the amount of DLC, while definetly worthwile, feels annoying

If it's 75% off, get it.
Otherwise, you're just falling into the same trap I did.
They did this with Empire and they're doing it again with Rome 2. I paid $60 for the prepurchase and eagerly awaited this game. But, I should have known better. I had enough warning before, so it's my fault for throwing away my money. However, in case you haven't had enough warning, here it is.
Day one: the game's littered with bugs, glitches, incredibly terrible campaign AND battle AI, and OF COURSE you can't play as all the factions. No, no, no. You have to wait and pay for the DLCs.
They release patch after patch, slowly fixing the game. I'm a bit of a TW veteran, so I beasted through a few campaigns; all at different patches. Throughout all of them I lost plenty of interest in finishing them. As any faction I chose, I quickly developed a balanced strategy to my war campaigns. After I did that, I just wrecked the computer AI. Most of the time they would not send any of their 3-7 full stack armies to retaliate. And again in this installment of Total War, Sega and CA have barely even tried to develop the AI into something that could compete with the players. Instead, they just went on with their lazy and idiotic method of just giving the computer benefits like infinite gold. It was the same way in Shogun 2. I always wondered why it was that I was having trouble balancing my economy with 8+ settlements and my few armies with low to medium quality units, whereas the computer was just pumping out full stacks of their higher quality troops with only 1-5 settlements. <- That might be my biggest gripe with the actual gameplay.
Another thing I dislike about this game is that there isn't a realistic recruitment balance - in my opinion. Once you get the tech and building requirement, there is no limit as to how many units you can recruit. Since Rome 2 allows you to recruit a lot more units in a turn, you can just recruit 3-5 of your best unit at once. So you can just fill up your Roman armies with as many praetorians as you'd like. Whereas in Medieval 2, it was much more balanced because you had to wait several turns for higher quality units, as they needed more time to be ready for recruitment, so you could only recruit one of them about every 5 turns.
One good thing they did with this game is the improved UI/menus. It is much easier to navigate and find your provinces, armies, characters, etc. However, the in-game encyclopedia is a mess. Rather than getting to see a trait upgrade tree for your characters, you have to go back and forth through several pages of the encyclopedia to find info on the upgrades. It doesn't even explain the prerequisites for any of the traits. It's the same thing for buildings. Instead of having a building browser (like the old TW games had), this game has you cycling through the encyclopedia. Let me tell you that going to each page in the encyclopedia takes a while, so if you're just trying to find out what is a simple requirement for something, be prepared for a long journey through the encyclopedia. (What, they couldn't have released a patch to make it go quicker?)
They also released seperate campaign DLCs (Caesar in Gual & Hannibal at the Gates) which - in my opinion - are also not worth the full price.
It's been about a year since the game came out, and they have just put out another patch (JUL 31). So after a year of patches, I can say that this game is playable. However, it is NOT worth $59.95, which is the price it was at release.
By paying full price, you are condoning CA and SEGA's incompetence and thievery. You are letting them know that releasing unfinished, little effort products is acceptable. You are letting them know that they can get away with this behavior again.

Ah yes, Total War: Rome 2. Bane of the media; 'worst total war game ever'. So time to put my 2 cents in! Firstly; this game's faults have  been blown WAY out of proportion. I am of course speaking of patch 12 onwards, I am sure rome 2 was as faulty as  said at launch. But now, today, should you buy Rome 2? Yup.
For Total War fans: THIS GAME IS NOT AS GOOD AS SHOGUN 2!
For Others: TOTAL WAR IS INCREDIBLE, BUY THIS GAME. (On sale, of course. I value my overall experience at $30)
Rome 2 is HUGE. Shogun 2 is POLISHED. (Seriously, there are 3 categories of ranged units alone; there was 1 category in S2)
But the real question is; How does one write a review for Total War Rome 2? Step one: Read my Shogun 2 review to get the concept and magnificence of Total War
. Step 2: Read this review to determine which title is better for you. I will essentialy recounting what I like and despise about Rome 2 , with small details to flesh out detail about the game. (I'm reading off a piece of paper created while playing crammed with notes). A finished Roman campaign, hectic Barbarian campaign, and Co-Op campaign with the Greek states have given me all the info I need to form my opinon.
So, what I don't like:
Rome 2 was mismarketed, early 'alpha' footage looks nothing like the game in it's current state. Rampant DLC locks historical battles (I can't play goddamn Cannae with out the Hannibal DLC. CANNAE.) Far too much money was spent on hype; as opposed to fine tuning development. SHAMEFUL DISPLAY!
THIS GAME RUNS LIKE♥♥♥♥♥ Horribly optimized; on ultra or low, I rarely break 50 FPS. What's even worse; the game doesn't look 'near' as good as Shogun 2! I'm not saying it looks terrible. Rain still washes down Roman shields locked in Testudo, waves still sparkle as Triremes cut through the water, and bloodied Praetorians stuggle to hold the gates of beautifuly handcrafted city. But a slight downgrade AND a performance hit?
Numerous other stupid design desicsions hamper the experience. No pre-battle General's speeches, lack of mini-movies (hits hard), lack of concentrated armies due to General's being NEEDED TO MOVE, and subsequent short life spans of agents and the generals, vassals going to war with one another (?). On the technical side, Battles are jumpy due to the '1v1' combat system, though animations are still breathtakingly beautiful and brutal. The 1v1 system worked in Shogun 2 because of the nature of Combat. 1 Samauri swing his Katana at another. With Pike and shield bearing infantry, unit fights are just too jumpy.  Auto resolve is broken, and there is no longer as satisfying and cringeworthy crash of men as two units furiosuly charge into each other (WHICH REALLY PISSES ME OFF!).
Some aspects of Rome 2 were good theories, but need to be fleshed out:
The UI simply and effectively communicates valuable info at a glance, but strangely hides other valuable stats, important to Veteran players (such as unit size in numbers, taxation of settlements). Buildingg was confusing and unintuituve at first, but a further look into the system showed a hint of brilliance. Various categories detract and boost a cities stats, while interacting with other buidlings. For instance; I've built a legionary barracks. Upgrading it increases ORDER and RECRUITMENT options, but also increases FOOD COMSUMPTION. To combat the lack of food, I now build a farm, which forgoes the more economical cattle pen in favor of more raw FOOD.
Politics are interesting, the AI reasonable; with plenty of diplomatic actions: from declaring war targets for allies, defensive or offensive alliances, breakage of treaties with other factions to non agression pacts and trade agreements. Faction politics (within the houses of your empire) truly need to be fleshed out. Assassinations of rival members and placing friendly generals into powerful armies are the extent of this system.
Unit's are also a mixed bag, as far as abilities go. In Shogun 2; Yari could form walls, and also be told not to pursue disengaging units with guard mode. In Rome 2, some abilities are brilliant. Testudo, and Phalanx create tight and cohesive unti formations, while Headhunt and Trample increase ccombst ability. On the other side, many units are missing VITAL ablities like Loose Spacing, to nullify arrow fire, and mentioned Guard Mode. Units literally chase down routers and break defensive lines unless expresivley moved back to their old positions. SHAMEFUL DISPLAY!
But don't get the wrong idea. There was plenty I quite enjoyed in Rome 2:
Firstly, Rome 2 is MASSIVE. The map sprawls from England to Morroco, to Eastern Asia and back up to Western Russia.Within these massive borders dwell hundreds of Factions; each ethnicity with distinct city looks, technological research as well as fighting styles. Latin heavy infantry and war machines terrorize Italy, Celtic chariots and slings rule the North, stealthy and brutish Gaulic hunters and berserkers stalk Europe. Hellan spear phalanxes march across Greece, Carthaginan elephnats wreak havok across africa, and Arabian horses and archers guard the east. Every faction plays fundementally diffferently, and hundreds of units make combat adaptive and surprising. Elite Persian archers calmly face down slow moving legions, and Gaullic ambusers emerge screaming from the woods to chase down and cut into a stalwart Spartan phalanx (sadly facing the wrong direction). Rome is expansive, and I love it
City battle have been revamped, and put into actuall meticulously crafted city streets, according to the culture that owns it. Walled and orderly Roman cities require coordinated street by street movement to overtake, while sprawling abrbarian ecampments need only a few ladders to breach their haphazard walls. Expanded traps and siege equipment such as caltrops, flaming balls, ballista and onager add complexity to battle. Naval units can even join in and shell the ground forces and deploy  added reinforcments.
Other small additions like expanded General and Agent abilities hone characters, while persistent named legions with specialities in warfare give you strong connections to your troops. Aptly named 'Natta's Heroes' (lead by the legendary Marcus Severus Natta) defended carthage for 3 years against overwhelming odds and vastly superior armies, due to their skill at arms and expanded roster of traps. (Seriously, they won 5 heroic victories, and were down to 15 men per unit). Army stances from a forced march, to a guarded stance, to a pillaging add even more diversity to combat.
Combat editions include conversations amoung a unit. Officers prepare and comfort recruits, Romans jest about Greek woman, Gauls jest about Roman woman, Persians jest about Carthaginian woman. Celts curse artillery. Line of sight andimporved stealth mechanics make ambushes truly epic. My Iceni chariots hunker low in the bush, as a column of Roman Velites march past. I charge a unit slingers into the center of the road, and the column charges into a line of recently emerging spear brothers. As the roman column smashes into my blockade, I wheel my chariots behind then, and charge their undefended backside.
In conclusion, Total War Rome 2 is amazing, expansive, and flawed. Total War fans will pull their hair out over peculier design desicions, and fond memories of older games. New-comers will love and revel in the best strategy series around. But yeah, you should get it. The pros most definetly outweigh the cons. (However) Don't mess it up again, Creative Assembly.

I was skeptical when this game was announced, but I watched gameplay demos and ended up pre-ordering the game almost immediately. It seemed to me from the gameplay I saw that this game was going to feel like watching the original movie felt, and it was really that nostalgia factor that drew me in.
You play as Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen Ripley, in the time between the first and second movies. Samuels, a co-worker of Amanda's at the company, seeks her out to tell her that the flight recorder of the Nostromo has been found and that Weyland-Yutani is putting together a team to pick it up. For the sake of closure Amanda agrees to go along.
You arrive at Sevastopol, a space station in orbit around a gas giant, and things quickly go wrong. You soon discover that the station is in disrepair, and that it was scheduled to be decomissioned weeks before. You also find out that no ship has visited the station in the same amount of time, and that no one remaining on the station has been able to leave.
Sevastopol is not owned by Weyland-Yutani, it is owned by Seegson, but there are similar undertones to the story fragments you can find in the form of recorded audio messages and text files strewn about the station. You do meet other people on Sevastopol as you make your way through to locate the flight recorder and leave, but not many are friendly.
Overall I thought the story was believable for the universe its set in, and it even had a few surprises in store for me that I did not expect but thoroughly enjoyed. There were several points where I actually ended up disagreeing with Amanda's actions even as I understood exactly why she was doing them. The overall survival mentality rules over Amanda as much as it does over all of the other characters you meet in the game, including the alien, and this seems to be the central theme of the story.
There is also an obvious underlying theme of Amanda trying to discover what happened to her mother. Even though she was only 10 when her mother disappeared there are definite connections Amanda has to Ellen. Amanda is very much like her mother in that she's an engineer and that she has a desire to see things through herself.
The look and feel of everything in the game is painstakingly made to look like it came from the original 1979 movie. Any new item created for the game was made to conform to the idea that if it could not be made in 1979 it would not be added to the game. If nothing else this plays to nostalgia, but it also results in a game world that looks and feels like it belongs in the same universe as the movies, and I applaud the developers to go as far as they did.
Sound design is very important to the game since you spend most of your time listening for potential threats, and overall it happens to be handled very well. Occasionally I felt like the music was louder than it needed to be and drowned out the actually important ambient noise, but at the same time it does a very good job of setting the tone.
Lighting is also handled very well in the game, and the game looks good even in the dark. You spend a lot of time in the dark in order to avoid threats, but you are given a limited supply of flashlights and flares to supply light and both really add to the atmosphere.
The gameplay in Alien: Isolation is very similar in many ways to Outlast. You spend a large amount of time crouched down to reduce noise, but you also move more slowly. You don't have night vision, but the head-mounted flashlight and flares act as your portable light sources. The downside to this is that enemies can see your light sources.
The people remaining on the station are fighting over supplies and keep to themselves. Anyone you come across on the station is more likely to shoot first and never ask questions, so you have to do your best to avoid them. The androids on the station are also less than friendly, but they happen to be fairly slow. Ocassionally you can run to avoid both humans and androids, but you cannot escape from the alien this way.
Fortunately you have a nostalgic motion tracker from the movies, but unfortunately it is only good at tracking in a cone in front of you and it doesn't tell you if the motion is on the same level as you (motion could be above or below you). The motion tracker also acts as your guide giving you an idea of where you need to travel to reach your goals. This is coupled with a map that updates as you walk through new areas, and you can update the map as you go at different locations throughout the game.
There are an assortment of gadgets that you can craft from materials you find across the station, but you have to find blueprints to teach you how to make them first. Noisemakers and flashbangs amount to distractions, though the latter can stun humans. You can also make medkits to heal yourself (you have a health bar) and molotovs to deal damage to enemies. You are also given an assortment of weapons over time, most of which do not work on the alien and all of them attract it. These features add some variety to the gameplay, but they don't decrease the difficulty and still promote stealth.
Save points are included in the game, although there are (rarely) automated checkpoints that the game saves at. The save points require some time to sit still while in use, so keep that in mind if there are enemies nearby. The save points will also remind you or let you know if there are enemies near enough to find you.
Finally the game recommends that you play on Hard difficulty for the best experience, and I recommend trying it this way at first. I made it through the first five missions and most of the sixth, but I ended up getting killed so many times in that one mission that I dropped down to Easy for the rest of the game so I could complete it in a more timely fashion.
Overall I really enjoyed this game.
Similar to Outlast this game is very intense, so I recommend playing in short stints if you can. The game does run a bit longer than it needs to, so for some the shorter playtimes may not work. With a total of eighteen missions at roughly an hour per mission you can easily spend twenty hours on this game.
Gameplay and atmosphere are both very solid, and the story is surprisingly good. I think any fan of the Alien series should give this game a look, and horror game fans will definitely enjoy.

This is probably one of the best alien game I have ever played. Almost everything about it is perfect, from the Graphics to the atmoshpere.
First lets start with the atmosphere. It is just awesome how the atmosphere just makes you feel like you are actually on a space station/ship. It is so tense that every noise makes you jump out of your skin.
Next, there is the Graphics. The graphics are just gorgous. It looks like Battlefield 4 graphics on steroids. Every little thing is in so much detail that it looks like this actually happened. Even the saliva from the Alien looks real.
Next, the difficulty. This game is outright brutal to anyone new to the franchise or new to a horror game in general. The stealth factor works so well with this game, it feels like you are actually being hunted.
The sound is also so good in this game. The utter silence in this game in some parts are just nerve racking, as every little noise could be something trying to kill you. Every little thing from the background noises to the Alien's monstrous footsteps is perfect.
Then, there is the alien. Oh my god, the Alien. The AI for it is REALLY unpredictable to the point it seems random. The Alien can literally hear you from across the hall if you aren't careful. It's pretty cool that the when you use the motioin tracker it can hear you. Also, make sure you NEVER get caught by it, it's always a instakill.
However, there are some things that I have noticed that hold the game back. First, the lip-syncing. It is absolutely terrible. The voices seem to just come from nowhere. Also, the save system. The save system is limited to going to a certain point in the game in order to save VIA emergency phone, meaning that if you die in the middle of these save points, you will have to restart to the most recent save point. This can be a real hassle if there is a long time between these save points.
Overall, this game is still one of the best horror games I have played so far, even with the bad parts.
I rate this a 9/10.
(P.S. It is REALLY satisfying to beat the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of a Working Joe synthetic android, especially when they are trying to kill you.)

Massive props to the devs for sneaking a spiritual successor to Thief and System Shock 2 - two of the best stealth/survival/horror games in PC history - into the Alien IP.  A couple of nods to 2001: A Space Odyssey in here too (yes devs some people do notice these things!). Does it work? Overwhelmingly YES.
Play  it at night, play it with a good sound system, play it on HARD difficulty, and last but not least - play it as far away as you possibly can from any CoD fanbois in your vicinity. Note that the latter may be driven into mindless homicidal rage by sudden movements or by any whiff of human culture. Also: play it with mouse and keyboard, if you can. If you are playing on Hard difficulty like you should then you'll want the full mobility that interface provides.
I'll note the one bug I experienced. At certain points in the game a sound bug would kick in (I think it accesses the audio files for the flamethrower, at an increased volume) which would interfere with the rest of the audio whenever I moved. While annoying, it fortunately only occured in a few specific sections of the game and didn't last more than a minute or two each time (but would recur on reloads in the affected sections).
That minor gripe aside, it's clear that this was a game designed with rare artistic flair, and sporting some of the most advanced AI (and movement!) seen in a computer-controlled enemy to date. It should be said that the graphics are very impressive. But this is a game that excels at the things other titles tend to cut corners on and that take longer to assess: things like sound design, music, even character dialogue. The end result is loads of atmospheric, tense gameplay and a pretty decent story to boot.
I expected to like this game. I DIDN'T expect to have my socks blown off by it. This is my game of 2014.

Steam users have become accustomed to purchasing season passes to their games that are detailed and communicated professionally to the point that that they know what they are going to receive for their money before purchase. PERFECT PARALLEL, Your game may be one of the most playable golf sims on the market but your behavior and inexcusably woeful communication abilities are the overriding reason why the game suffers such a mediocre review score on Steam. Ascension is a great deck building game, but has a VERY critical flaw, the lack of suitable resolution support.  Though it is tolerable in fullscreen at 1080P, it is not even viewable on a 4K screen unless one changes resolution.  Sadly, it would seem it was ported from the mobile version, and then appeared to be abandoned in 2015.
Generally, I have better luck simply casting my Android screen to my monitor, or using an emulator.  Having stated that, I really can't recommend the PC version of this game unless one runs at lower resolutions.  On higher resolutions, the cards are not even readable.  For the price, one is better of purchasing the mobile version, and either casting to their monitor, or using an emulator.
Should this game ever actually be updated such that higher resolutions are supported, I would certainly give it a positive review.  Nevertheless, with more and more gamers running at higher resolutions, I personally feel it is not the best investment.  Game-wise, it is very enjoyable, but the resolution issue is a real deal breaker personally.

System Shock 2 builds tension more effectively than any other game I've played. It accomplishes this without cheap thrills, instead relying on ambient sound and voice acting. The level design outclasses any single player first person game ever, creating the actual sensation of navigating a real spacecraft. Levels are functional, large, and require intelligence to complete. Whereas many games today create memorable moments by granting the player extraordinary powers, System Shock 2 chooses to oppress the player - thrusting him or her into a hostile environment and demanding clever play in order to survive. There is an amazing formula at work here that deserves an entire sub-genre of replicas.

Was stalking a base owned by these 4 guys, hiding by their entrance observing their comings and goings. At last I decide to go for it and as one of them exits the front door I try to run inside. But I am too late and he manages to close the door in front of me. A frantic gunfight ensues. Both of us in a panic we manage to empty several magazines at point-blank range with our fully automatic rifles before I barely manage to kill him dead. As he is waiting to respawn he says softly over voicechat "You are so dead..."
I run back to my base to prepare for the assault and before long they besiege me, build some fortifications close to my entrance and take turns potshotting me through my windows. After a while of this they return home, no doubt planning further actions. A day goes by and I log in again only to find my base has been the victim of a failed c4 raid where they managed to blow up my stairs, barring their further progress into my magnificent fortress. From my roof I see their second attempt; a skybridge from which they were hoping to hop onto my unprotected roof. This too failed, but their skybridge is still there and it goes all the way up to my property line. I build my own skybridge over to it, jump on it, parkour my way on top of their walls and through unbelievable luck find a way into the center of their base.
I take EVERYTHING: carparts, refined ores, guns, 10 drills and more. I open every door to the fortress, which I now own, and I leave a single drill running at the very top of their base. The server will wipe in 1 day, so now I'm logging in every once in a while just to see if they have noticed my incursion yet.
This was pure satisfaction. Truly, the best thing in life is to crush your enemies and see them driven before you.
Pros:
- Resource gathering is pretty decent. Most things will not require an inordinate time investment to procure, but it still feels like an achievement when I upgrade my gear or expand my base.
- I like the stylized graphics a lot, and it runs smoothly even on my non-game laptop.
- Weather is fine. I've managed to hide from players in dust-storms more than once.
- Simple yet rewarding crafting system.
- Potentially thrilling encounter every time you run into another player. Slowly backing away with your gun trained on someone you ran into in the desert is fun because it feels like a genuinely risky situation.
- Addictive gameplay.
Cons:
- Not enough content, but new content is apparently getting added quite frequently.
- Official servers are laggy.
- Resources spawn at fixed locations. If you live in a certain area, you will more than likely find yourself traversing the same old route again and again because you know where resources spawn.
- On laggy servers resources take time to load, this is perhaps my biggest annoyance so far.
- Raiding is very difficult because c4 takes a long time to get and it is very easy to build a base which would require a lot of c4 to breach, making raiding almost impossible against allmost all decent bases.

After many years of playing this game I have decided to another review in hopes of providing people with a decent amount of information going into the game.
Smite is not the average Moba experience and thats what makes it great but at times can contribute to a pretty bad experience. What makes Smite stand out from other Moba experiences is the fact that it was the first with a true 3rd person viewpoint instead of the more used topdown RTS type perspective View other Moba's tend to have. Paragon a game that could be great but isn't took this idea from Smite and are also using this which in my opinion gives the Moba experience a much needed change as it tends to feel much more immersive where you feel as though you are actually that character. I will now provide some pros and cons.
Pros:
- Mythology is what really makes this game great, they take gods/goddesses and other mythological creatures from all over the world and put them into the game.
- Art Team and skins. Smite literally has one of the best Art teams in the world that design new skins every patch that are always pretty amazing.
-Bi-weekly updates where they usually fix alot of bugs, release a god just about every month and continue to grow the game.
-Good amount of free content often giving away chests, gems and favor to players to use to get cosmetic items.
- Lots of casual game modes, also a con as described below.
-Hard learrning curve in my opinion a pro because it is very difficult to understand the game, which makes it fun because you can often discover new and exciting things that can massively improve how well you play. But can also be a con for new players, especially those that have never played a Moba before. "This mostly applies to conquest".
Cons:
-Horrible community, if you are used to the average Moba experience and getting people who talk down too you because of how you play Smite is no different. Not to mention the reddit community is complete trash in terms of how they understand the game.
-Bad balance. Some gods are just better than others the design team has a tough time deciding on who they buff/nerf in order to have an equal playing ground. This leads to the next point on other game modes.
-Too many game modes, which results in the most competitive game mode Conquest or your average "3 lane/jungle experience in other games" to be overlooked at as the main point of balance. Game modes such as Arena and clash may have certain picks that are much stronger than they are in Conquest many of these other game modes contribute to the problems of balance in the game.
-Matchmaking can be pretty bad at times pointing at the other reason above, there are just too many ranked and casual game modes that seperate the community so much that you can be ranked with bronze in silvers when you are in much higher ranks.
Overall there may be more pros than cons but to really experience the fun in Smite you have to actually try it out. Much of the problems I myself have with the game is due to the number of years I have played it.
Would I recommend this game? Yes I would to people who have never tried it before and have a good experience with other Moba games and want to try something new. For new players I would be cautious this can be a very bad experience for you if you aren't used to other people constantly trash talking and putting you down.
My final advice I would give to people who want to get better and are having problems understanding how the game works is to honestly read the god descriptions and how their skills work. Understand the items and item builds that many people use.Go into training mode and see how the characters work before testing them in a match where you are also able to test all the gods without having to buy them***. Watch streamers play the game and you will automatically see a massive improvement in how well you play. Understand that It will take time and it will take patience but you will slowly get better.

This version of the review is temporary and will be updated soon after the Steam Awards/Autumn sale is over.
For now I will just say that the game as a whole is quite good and outdoes its predecessor in most areas (performance is where it falls short most profoundly). Also, the split protagonist concept, which is new to the series, was not executed as it should have been causing the game to not reach its full potential. Players will be forced into playing the entire game as a single character rather than being given the opportunity to switch between Emily and Corvo from mission to mission.For this version of the review however, I would like to focus on what I nominated Dishonored 2 for in the Steam Awards.
My own personal category: The "Most Creative Level Design" Award
A serious award unlike many others, but the level design within Dishonored 2 struck me in a way I didn't expect, particularly in chapters 4 and 7. In chapter 4 you infiltrate the Clockwork Mansion which transforms in a few different configurations. You must navigate the level by slipping through tight crevaces in the shifting floors and walls and completing puzzles to get to the next area. This can pose an even greater challenge when enemies, both human and formidable clockwork soldiers, patrol vigilantly and players attempt to complete the encounter undetected. In chapter 7, players are granted a gadget from the Outsider, known as The Outsider's Timepiece, which is neccessary to progress through the level, transporting the player back and forth through to seperate time periods, both constantly moving. This makes for some interesting puzzles as well as the opportunity for more creative gameplay on the player's part. Because of these two unique and fun level designs as well as the more open levels brought to this second installment, I have nominated Dishonored 2 for "The Most Creative Level Design Award" for the public created category in the first ever Steam Awards. (Hopefully it does't sound like I am taking this too seriously.)

Get this game. It's incredible. Even though I think the ending and final 2 hours were a bit lackluster, the rest of the game more than makes up for it. The music is great, the graphics are very good, and it's also a great PC port. The story is good as a standalone game for players who don't know alot about the Alien franchise, but it's even better for fans of it, as it's filled with references and audio logs recorded by the original cast of Alien.
I beat the game at hard difficulty, which I recommend. It's a great challenge and I got a bit frustrated at times but I never wanted to lower the difficulty.
The thing I love most about this game is how unscripted the encounters are and how much cool stuff can happen. Some of the best parts of the game is when human enemies are in the same area as the alien and the alien is hunting you both. You do things like purposefully get the other humans to see you so that they will start shooting, so that the alien will hear the gunfire and take them out for you.
Once I was sneaking around this area going into every room scavening for supplies (this game nails survival-horror scavenging and making you feel like every bullet counts) and as I exited the room an enemy human was at the door. I panicked, pulled out my revolver and shot him 2 times in the chest. Knowing the alien heard me, I ran as fast as I could back into the room to hide in a locker. The split second I closed the locker door the alien dropped down from the vent in the ceiling and he eventually wandered away. Moments like this are totally unscripted and they are my favorite part of the game.
This game also has native Oculus Rift support. You have to go into the game's files to access it, but it was put in there by the developers, so I consider it native. I had the chance to try it at my friend's house and it was undescribable. I was totally and completely immersed in the game, and I was convinced I was actually there. I didn't actually get to the part where the alien starts appearing (about 1 hour in), but I imagine it's terrifying. The game itself without the Rift is more intense and stressful than it is scary, but I'm sure it'd go full pants-crapping mode in the Rift. It's also one of the only full-sized games to natively support the Rift at the moment. The Rift support isn't perfect, there's lots of clipping during scripted events, and that's why I imagine it's hidden in the files but it's still absolutely worth it if you have a Rift. Looking out the window into space in the beginning part of the game is jaw-dropping. Just try to not have a heart attack while playing.
I rate games from how much I enjoy them, and even though this game has a few problems, like the ending and final hours, it didn't affect the enjoyment of the game at all for me. Tenouttaten.

I was skeptical when this game was announced, but I watched gameplay demos and ended up pre-ordering the game almost immediately. It seemed to me from the gameplay I saw that this game was going to feel like watching the original movie felt, and it was really that nostalgia factor that drew me in.
You play as Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen Ripley, in the time between the first and second movies. Samuels, a co-worker of Amanda's at the company, seeks her out to tell her that the flight recorder of the Nostromo has been found and that Weyland-Yutani is putting together a team to pick it up. For the sake of closure Amanda agrees to go along.
You arrive at Sevastopol, a space station in orbit around a gas giant, and things quickly go wrong. You soon discover that the station is in disrepair, and that it was scheduled to be decomissioned weeks before. You also find out that no ship has visited the station in the same amount of time, and that no one remaining on the station has been able to leave.
Sevastopol is not owned by Weyland-Yutani, it is owned by Seegson, but there are similar undertones to the story fragments you can find in the form of recorded audio messages and text files strewn about the station. You do meet other people on Sevastopol as you make your way through to locate the flight recorder and leave, but not many are friendly.
Overall I thought the story was believable for the universe its set in, and it even had a few surprises in store for me that I did not expect but thoroughly enjoyed. There were several points where I actually ended up disagreeing with Amanda's actions even as I understood exactly why she was doing them. The overall survival mentality rules over Amanda as much as it does over all of the other characters you meet in the game, including the alien, and this seems to be the central theme of the story.
There is also an obvious underlying theme of Amanda trying to discover what happened to her mother. Even though she was only 10 when her mother disappeared there are definite connections Amanda has to Ellen. Amanda is very much like her mother in that she's an engineer and that she has a desire to see things through herself.
The look and feel of everything in the game is painstakingly made to look like it came from the original 1979 movie. Any new item created for the game was made to conform to the idea that if it could not be made in 1979 it would not be added to the game. If nothing else this plays to nostalgia, but it also results in a game world that looks and feels like it belongs in the same universe as the movies, and I applaud the developers to go as far as they did.
Sound design is very important to the game since you spend most of your time listening for potential threats, and overall it happens to be handled very well. Occasionally I felt like the music was louder than it needed to be and drowned out the actually important ambient noise, but at the same time it does a very good job of setting the tone.
Lighting is also handled very well in the game, and the game looks good even in the dark. You spend a lot of time in the dark in order to avoid threats, but you are given a limited supply of flashlights and flares to supply light and both really add to the atmosphere.
The gameplay in Alien: Isolation is very similar in many ways to Outlast. You spend a large amount of time crouched down to reduce noise, but you also move more slowly. You don't have night vision, but the head-mounted flashlight and flares act as your portable light sources. The downside to this is that enemies can see your light sources.
The people remaining on the station are fighting over supplies and keep to themselves. Anyone you come across on the station is more likely to shoot first and never ask questions, so you have to do your best to avoid them. The androids on the station are also less than friendly, but they happen to be fairly slow. Ocassionally you can run to avoid both humans and androids, but you cannot escape from the alien this way.
Fortunately you have a nostalgic motion tracker from the movies, but unfortunately it is only good at tracking in a cone in front of you and it doesn't tell you if the motion is on the same level as you (motion could be above or below you). The motion tracker also acts as your guide giving you an idea of where you need to travel to reach your goals. This is coupled with a map that updates as you walk through new areas, and you can update the map as you go at different locations throughout the game.
There are an assortment of gadgets that you can craft from materials you find across the station, but you have to find blueprints to teach you how to make them first. Noisemakers and flashbangs amount to distractions, though the latter can stun humans. You can also make medkits to heal yourself (you have a health bar) and molotovs to deal damage to enemies. You are also given an assortment of weapons over time, most of which do not work on the alien and all of them attract it. These features add some variety to the gameplay, but they don't decrease the difficulty and still promote stealth.
Save points are included in the game, although there are (rarely) automated checkpoints that the game saves at. The save points require some time to sit still while in use, so keep that in mind if there are enemies nearby. The save points will also remind you or let you know if there are enemies near enough to find you.
Finally the game recommends that you play on Hard difficulty for the best experience, and I recommend trying it this way at first. I made it through the first five missions and most of the sixth, but I ended up getting killed so many times in that one mission that I dropped down to Easy for the rest of the game so I could complete it in a more timely fashion.
Overall I really enjoyed this game.
Similar to Outlast this game is very intense, so I recommend playing in short stints if you can. The game does run a bit longer than it needs to, so for some the shorter playtimes may not work. With a total of eighteen missions at roughly an hour per mission you can easily spend twenty hours on this game.
Gameplay and atmosphere are both very solid, and the story is surprisingly good. I think any fan of the Alien series should give this game a look, and horror game fans will definitely enjoy.

- Sound file sharing - Ok I am going to be nit picky but you should have the ability to play sound files during your game whether it be in a window(snap cam) or some other way. This was one of the best features of Links that should be standardized in every golf game.
- The settings to go up and down on your shots doesn't affect the ball hardly at all.
- Some default options missing
- Why is it every time I want to see the overhead view snap cam I have to click the button? Why can't I check a setting to leave it on? Or have the button clicked deafult to that until it's clicked off.
- Default view of a friend playing is at an angle. I understand you can move the view around manually every time but why cannot there not be a setting to default that view to straight on like your own shot?
- $5 for an expansion course? (Bethesda)
Overall I am still enjoying and playing this game.  All of my default option gripes probably wouldn't be that big of a deal to fix. The commentary I am sure could be a lot more complicated.  At the end of the day, this is a beautiful modern fun golf sim that doesn't quite have the functionality as it's long ago predecessors.

I wish I could recommend the game overall - I'm very conflicted about it.
The graphics are so old and basic looking - Looks ok from a distance, but when you're playing it's very poor.
The actual golf game play is probably the best of all options right now if you focus solely on the swing options, physics, ball spin, wind impacts and so forth.  Also, a multiplayer lobby and a multitude of game modes are great to see, but sadly no career mode or "pro mode" or anything like that.
But there also are endless strange bugs and interface weirdness, especially using a controller (which is the newest way to play, so hopefully that gets worked on more).
The main hangup is the old looking graphics.  The game has no grass, really basic looking water, trees with an odd sort of sheen look to them (something weird about how they look especially in the distance) and overall just appears to my gaming eyes like something you might have thought "looked great" in the early to mid 2000's.  Now I'm used to such a higher bar of quality in most every other game, genre and platform, that it is really hard to look at and enjoy for me.  It's all just flat textures draped all over for the most part.  Thumbs down on that for sure.
I guess if you can get past the really old looking graphics, it's a great game of golf. But for me I can not do a "recommend" on it with graphics this behind the times.  Being on a golf course involves natural beauty and graphics quality is a main part of this type of games' appeal to me....and perfect golf lacks in this area big time.

I love this game. I honestly would pay to play, there are many games that there are paid, and they do not come close to it in quality. The story is very good. Or rather, the way it is developed. The story might be a bit cliché, the sister going to save the other, but the way it is developed is what changes everything.
I loved the music and the effects of the game. I really enjoyed the graphics too. The design of the phases evolves so much! Do not be fooled by the simple design of the first, the forest.
For those who are complaining about the gameplay, the author makes it clear that he wanted something simple so that anyone, even if they are bad at video games, could play. I quite liked, just for simplicity. And the battles that needed to be complex, the boss battles, are really hard. I'm sure none of these people who criticized battles faced the last boss on Hard mode.
Really, normal battles are simple, and the mini boss, standing by scenario, do not use magic or anything, which is kind of illogical, because they are the giant version of monsters that use skills, but they just stand still and reflect damage. You just need spamming spells and wait for your HP and MP to fill until you kill then.
But apart from that I have no complaints, the game even rewards you for exploring and kill monsters (it has three NPCs that give you awards for discovering chests, kill certain monsters and getting upgrades in your equipment). You even has a mode called Arcane Realm that is made to level up and drop craft items.

This version of the review is temporary and will be updated soon after the Steam Awards/Autumn sale is over.
For now I will just say that the game as a whole is quite good and outdoes its predecessor in most areas (performance is where it falls short most profoundly). Also, the split protagonist concept, which is new to the series, was not executed as it should have been causing the game to not reach its full potential. Players will be forced into playing the entire game as a single character rather than being given the opportunity to switch between Emily and Corvo from mission to mission.For this version of the review however, I would like to focus on what I nominated Dishonored 2 for in the Steam Awards.
My own personal category: The "Most Creative Level Design" Award
A serious award unlike many others, but the level design within Dishonored 2 struck me in a way I didn't expect, particularly in chapters 4 and 7. In chapter 4 you infiltrate the Clockwork Mansion which transforms in a few different configurations. You must navigate the level by slipping through tight crevaces in the shifting floors and walls and completing puzzles to get to the next area. This can pose an even greater challenge when enemies, both human and formidable clockwork soldiers, patrol vigilantly and players attempt to complete the encounter undetected. In chapter 7, players are granted a gadget from the Outsider, known as The Outsider's Timepiece, which is neccessary to progress through the level, transporting the player back and forth through to seperate time periods, both constantly moving. This makes for some interesting puzzles as well as the opportunity for more creative gameplay on the player's part. Because of these two unique and fun level designs as well as the more open levels brought to this second installment, I have nominated Dishonored 2 for "The Most Creative Level Design Award" for the public created category in the first ever Steam Awards. (Hopefully it does't sound like I am taking this too seriously.)

While this game has a ways to go from being perfect if Arkane continues this trend of support then it is well on its way to being nearly so.

Ascension is a deck building game, which means nothing to most of you on steam.
Essentially it's a card game where you construct your deck as you play, using currency card to buy more powerful cards to shuffle into your deck.
As the game progresses you'll acquire and play more powerful cards (which I assure you is a vicious cycle, power begets power) and summon constructs, banish demons, and try to stop your opponents from buying more cards, killing more monsters and building a better deck than you.
It's extremely fun in my opinion, and there's a lot of great tutorials (including one in the game) on youtube and other places.
**** FOR PEOPLE WHO KNOW WHAT DECK BUILDING GAMES ARE ****
Ascension Steam Edition has six expansions for free and all of the promos, giving you over 1000 cards to play with.
In short, it's amazing.

The premier iOS deckbuilding game, now on Steam. If you like deckbuilders, stop reading, you'll love this. *Buy now*.
It has online multiplayer (edit: though the netcode is kinda meh sometimes, I've since lost at least one match to a forfeit because of it) and SP is awesome. The PC version includes most of the IAP/expansions from the iOS version.
iOS version is better. Buy that first, but if you don't have iOS device, this is pretty good.
-----
Everyone else - so what's a deckbuilder game? It's a card game kind of like that "Magic: the Gathering" collectible card game if you remember that, except it's not as complicated and there's no need to buy packs of cards and collect them all or whatever. I've never played a game like this, and after the tutorial and a game or two I understood it. To this day, I have not the foggiest what my friend who used to go to Magic tournaments or my cousin with the Yu-gi-oh was doing.
All the cards come in the same game package, so both players (or up to 4 if you're using some of the expansions) have an equal chance to make a good deck and play each other. Each game is about 15 minutes. Lots of fun solo or with other players!
Cons: As some reviews have noted, the resolution is fixed. This is pretty common on iOS ports. It doesn't particularly bother me, because I usually play these kind of games windowed while checking my e-mail and browsing reddit and such, but it does bother some people, so FYI. The stability is not as good as the iOS version, but it's still pretty good. Netcode is nowhere near as good as iOS version.
*Buy now* (esp while on-sale).
-----
FYI, each game "expansion" (all of the ones released as IAP on iOS are included on steam) is released in "blocks" composed of 2 sets a piece (one large set and its expansion set), so this is really multiple games or game variants, not just one. It's more fun playing that way than with "all cards" on, though some people do that.
For reference the blocks are as follows:
Block 1 - Godslayer (the main game) + Return of the Fallen
Block 2 - Storm of Souls + Immortal Heroes
Block 3 - Rise of Vigil + Darkness Unleashed
----
Block 4 - Realms Unraveled + Dawn of Champions
Block 4 is a little different because the "expansion" has as many cards as the main game now
P.S. I've played a lot of this game on iOS, so disregard the game time

(Yes, I know that I barely played this game. This is only a first impression, as I will edit this as I get deeper into the game.)
This is probably one of the best alien game I have ever played. Almost everything about it is perfect, from the Graphics to the atmoshpere.
First lets start with the atmosphere. It is just awesome how the atmosphere just makes you feel like you are actually on a space station/ship. It is so tense that every noise makes you jump out of your skin.
Next, there is the Graphics. The graphics are just gorgous. It looks like Battlefield 4 graphics on steroids. Every little thing is in so much detail that it looks like this actually happened. Even the saliva from the Alien looks real.
Next, the difficulty. This game is outright brutal to anyone new to the franchise or new to a horror game in general. The stealth factor works so well with this game, it feels like you are actually being hunted.
The sound is also so good in this game. The utter silence in this game in some parts are just nerve racking, as every little noise could be something trying to kill you. Every little thing from the background noises to the Alien's monstrous footsteps is perfect.
Then, there is the alien. Oh my god, the Alien. The AI for it is REALLY unpredictable to the point it seems random. The Alien can literally hear you from across the hall if you aren't careful. It's pretty cool that the when you use the motioin tracker it can hear you. Also, make sure you NEVER get caught by it, it's always a instakill.
However, there are some things that I have noticed that hold the game back. First, the lip-syncing. It is absolutely terrible. The voices seem to just come from nowhere. Also, the save system. The save system is limited to going to a certain point in the game in order to save VIA emergency phone, meaning that if you die in the middle of these save points, you will have to restart to the most recent save point. This can be a real hassle if there is a long time between these save points.
Overall, this game is still one of the best horror games I have played so far, even with the bad parts.
I rate this a 9/10.
(P.S. It is REALLY satisfying to beat the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of a Working Joe synthetic android, especially when they are trying to kill you.)

Massive props to the devs for sneaking a spiritual successor to Thief and System Shock 2 - two of the best stealth/survival/horror games in PC history - into the Alien IP.  A couple of nods to 2001: A Space Odyssey in here too (yes devs some people do notice these things!). Does it work? Overwhelmingly YES.
Play  it at night, play it with a good sound system, play it on HARD difficulty, and last but not least - play it as far away as you possibly can from any CoD fanbois in your vicinity. Note that the latter may be driven into mindless homicidal rage by sudden movements or by any whiff of human culture. Also: play it with mouse and keyboard, if you can. If you are playing on Hard difficulty like you should then you'll want the full mobility that interface provides.
I'll note the one bug I experienced. At certain points in the game a sound bug would kick in (I think it accesses the audio files for the flamethrower, at an increased volume) which would interfere with the rest of the audio whenever I moved. While annoying, it fortunately only occured in a few specific sections of the game and didn't last more than a minute or two each time (but would recur on reloads in the affected sections).
That minor gripe aside, it's clear that this was a game designed with rare artistic flair, and sporting some of the most advanced AI (and movement!) seen in a computer-controlled enemy to date. It should be said that the graphics are very impressive. But this is a game that excels at the things other titles tend to cut corners on and that take longer to assess: things like sound design, music, even character dialogue. The end result is loads of atmospheric, tense gameplay and a pretty decent story to boot.
I expected to like this game. I DIDN'T expect to have my socks blown off by it. This is my game of 2014.

I know there was some furore when this game first hit our screens - and I too hit the same frustrations that many people had when the Alien first turns up (San Cristobal Medical Centre nearly had me chucking the game in). But with a little rooting aoruns on Stema forum and getting my head round how the Alien AI works, I'm glad I persevered beyond that mission. This is one of the finest games around at the moment, and one of the finest I've played in my gaming history. I confess to being a huge fan of the original movie and the attention to detail, mood, awesome soundscape and nods to the film had me hooked form the go and once you're past that now infamous mission where the Alien makes it's entrance the game evens out and becomes, to my mind, one of the most intense, suspenseful and intriguing games ever. It's a true survival horror epic and (despite what many industry reviewers have said) it never drags despite it running in at over 20 hours gameplay (value of what?). And it will genuinely have you jumping out of your seat. In the light of the opening day's sad debacle that is Assassin's Creed: Unity (here's hoping Ubisoft make amends fast), a game of this quality, intelligence and player involvement stands for all that's best about gaming (and gaming on a PC too). Highly recommended and easily one of 2014's games of the year.

Jack Nicklaus Perfect Golf is what you play if you're looking for a realistic and challenging golf sim. This is the real deal.
The game can be as hard as you want it to be. Want to go easy on a flat green course using 3 point click on Beginner? Go for it. After a while, you'll birdie too often and want more of a challenge. No problem. There's Hacker, Amateur, Tour, and Tour Pro that'll challenge you further. These higher difficulties make swing timings more precise, resulting in shots more prone to shank if you're off just a bit. At the highest levels, you won't even be told the wind speed or direction and will have to rely on visual cues like the flag's movement. This says nothing of additional round settings like wind speeds (which can be set to weather forecasts), pin placements, green firmness, etc. You'll botch plenty of shots at first until you practice to get your swing down while you learn to master both courses and conditions. Just like in real golf.
Beyond that, there are different swing styles that change ball striking experience. Want to feel like you're actually swinging something on your PC without a gamepad? Motion Swing allows you to use your mouse as a club to swing. You'll have to literally swing back and forward both straight and within a backswing-to-forwardswing time frame ratio in order to hit your shot straight. If you have a controller, you can use joysticks.
This is a game with a great deal of depth and multiplayer replayability with a learning curve as steep as you make it. Still, the game launched a bit prematurely. The multiplayer lobby is quirky, at best; dysfunctional, at worst. Computer opponents are wildly inconsistent, too, so to play a decent opponent, you'll have to put up with the lobby's quirkiness or practice on your own.
In spite of all of this, if you're pleased enough with the gameplay, you'll be patient in waiting for patches to remedy the game's weaknesses.
There are negative reviews about season passes that are misinformed. These passes are for additional equipment you can buy to actually hit golf balls into a net and track their flight in-game, which seems like a pretty dang cool add-on if you ask me. The developers are in no way forcing customers to pay for the base game and a season pass to play for a year.
The store also offers additional courses to purchase—currently Bethesda for $4.99. There is unwarranted outcry about this as well because the game comes bundled with plenty of courses to keep the gameplay varied enough for a good while—14 full courses if my count is right, and 2 practice ranges. Offering additional DLC content to the core game is exactly what a lot of developers do these days. It's not in the base game, so therefore, you pay more for it. Sounds fair enough.
All in all, the strengths far outweigh the weaknesses. I do hope the developers continue to flesh out the kinks, but they've managed to produce a very solid game with gameplay that'll keep you coming back for more if the sort of golf sim you're looking for is both realistic and increasingly challenging. These two strengths make the game that much more rewarding and fun when you do get a handle on things and are able to be competitive against others in multiplayer matches.

So I see this game rated at Overwhelmingly Positive (quite an achivement) and a price tag of $0.00, and instantly downloaded it. After sinking a little over 6 hours into it I have to say, I don't think it deserves the praise that it has. This game has a ton of flaws, some of which can be overlooked, others maybe not so much. Obviously my oppinion will differ from yours, but I expect quite a bit when I see an Overhwelmingly Positive rating.
The music in this game is good, but it's not really anything special. The exception being the music on the title screen (and other places) which I really enjoy. There are numerous minor translation issues. There's some bugs here and there. The graphics are unimpressive. But this is all aesthetics. Surface stuff. Aesthetics don't really matter if the gameplay is good. So is it?
Well, I suppose it depends on your preference, but I would have to say no. To explain why, let me give you a run down of the combat system. I find the combat to be cumbersome and slow. There are no battle screens in this game, all the combat happens as you walk around. Attacking is semi-automatic; there's no button for attacking, you just run into enemies (or they run into you) and you both hit eachother. This in itself isn't bad but there's a few things that make it poor. Often when you hit an enemy you get thrown back a couple spaces for no particular reason (it just happens). So then you have to walk up to an enemy again and hit again. The enemies also move around randomly so they can be hard to approach at times. Worst of all though, the random enemies pose zero threat to you. They do damage you everytime you hit them, but you also regenerate health and mana overtime which counteracts this. If you grind out the best gear they do 1 damage to you anyway. Mana is used for performing special moves, but I've found that none of the 4 moves that you get are useful in any special way, they just do more damage than your basic attack. As far as grinding goes, it's entirely optional (one of the only good points of the game). Random enemies are no threat to you but bosses are, so if you aren't strong enough you won't progress. The good news is that all the main bosses have multiple difficulty settings. So you can breeze through them on easy, or prepare for a huge challenge on hard. If you DO pick hard, you WILL need to grind out the best gear, but again this is optional.
The bosses deserve their own paragraph of this review. In short, they are good, but not great. All the bosses are pretty much the same thing. They all have some kind of barrier that you have to destroy in order to hurt them. They will all put up this barrier at the very beginning of the fight and again after every 25% of their health is gone. Every time they put up their barrier they will get harder by attacking more. They will also summon enemies periodically to aid them (the enemies still suck though). So long as you stay out of the red death boxes you'll generally be ok. That being said, the fights can get very hectic by the last 25% health I chose to do them all on hard, but I did die many times.
Now let's talk about what everyone else is interested in here, the story. I won't spoil it so don't worry. The problem I have with the story is that throughout the whole middle you're shown flashbacks of Senia's life. The thing is these flashbacks are not incorporated into the story after you've seen them, they're just done. The whole middle of the story is filler (albeit filller that is necessary for character depth and climax buildup, but it could have been used better). The ending though, that's where it's at. If you get easily sentimental over sad stories, get a box of tissues ready before you finish the game because there's some serious feels at the end.
Ok so I've been critizising almost every aspect of the game, you may be wondering at this point why I'm recommending it. It's because the game is in a very special situation. It's good but not great (to me), but it's also short (4-6 hours) and free. It's like a gaming snack. This is a game that you play over a day or two and then you're done with it. All the flaws are lessened by the fact that it's short so you don't have to deal with it for long. Though it can be repetetive, it isn't long enough for that to be an issue. But despite being short, the sad story will ensure that it has a lasting impression on you. And of course it's free so you won't have regrets if you don't enjoy it. And to be honest, I DID enjoy it despite everything I said. I just don't think it deserves an Overwhelmingly Positive rating. Maybe you will though, so go ahead, download Eternal Senia, cry, and then continue your life.

I'll be rating this game by a professional standpoint without looking at the price tag, cause this game really deserves a price tag, and yet, the developer decided to give it out for free.
The gameplay is plain and simple, no complex mechanics for gamers who prefer competency in gaming. (like me) As well as a lack of sci-fi flashy art that modern games do, which makes it preferrably to be look from an Indie Game perspective. However, this game does have settling mechanics though, where you can naturally emerge yourself into a fantasy world. The story can be more elaborated still... That's the brief summary.
As this is the first ARPG game I play other than Zenonia, the skills are relatively balanced. Cool thing about the skillsets is that the developer manage to pulled it off, mostly By The Developer Himself, for the game to be balanced. The game isn't long and this saves the time needed to reduce the potential flaws occuring within the gameplay and the story, although, creating a game mostly by working by himself also takes a huge amount of time. As everything seemed fair and 6.5/10 to me, the only thing that enjoyed about this game is that it's immersive.
For a gamer like me who just love to immersive himself, the only thing that keep me finishing the game is the results.
I play the game, I went through and collected all the seemingly hidden treasure, wanted to further the plot, and I was immersed into completing the game, until the story ends. As there is no neutral button, I can only select Yes and No with ratio of 60%:40% towards whether I should recommend this game or not.
TL:DR the game isn't for gaming freaks who place expectations on a game, yet it's still fun cause it's immersive, where you can complete the game casually.
Story - 6.8/10. Beginning of the story is typical, but the lore is interesting. I'm curious to know the plot, this keeps me going. However, if the lore is deeper, the game could get closer on becoming a masterpiece.
Plot development - 4.2/10. Room for improvement, the plot goes too fast. I want more of the progression of the story. :p
Gameplay - 7.4/10. Really nice and alternative setting in an RPG game where no potions were added. Even as the combat system is repetitive, don't change it, as this is the core of the system's originality. Could do with more stages though.
Art - 7.3/10. Serious yet Kawaii, fitting the theme of JRPGs.
Atmosphere - 8.3/10. Atmosphere = Immersiveness. The music, the story, the graphics, the gameplay, the controls... Everything just fits within the idea of the game.
Is it recommended? Only if you're onto Indie Games.
