Raiding is extremely hard to do and requires a large amount of resources so you don't typically raid someone unless you know they're very rich or you have a personal vendetta against them. PvP is somewhat pointless as in it's rare you gain anything from it.
In order to get someones weapon (The main thing you're usually going to want when killing someone for their loot) they need to have Infamy which means they need to have killed someone recently and even then there's only a chance you get their gun as there's a chance it will drop their clothing or tools over the gun. In my opinion, raiding is not worth the resources so I stick to PvP but it is not rewarding either, unless you play Full-Loot servers. In Full-Loot servers you drop every item on your player when you die, the problem is that most of the community is too worried about losing one item, never mind their entire inventory so the Full-Loot servers are pretty much dead at all times.
One more issue is becuase of the lacking of towns and specific pvp areas,  people tend to pvp around the spawn points which puts new players at a huge disadvantage, they cannot defend themselves. A large amount of people like to build large towers and snipe out of little holes so it's hard for players to fight back and if they die, their loot drops into their base (Reassuring them they won't even lose a single item). Makes for a terrible PvP experience.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TL;DR: Raiding will typically make you use more resources then you will gain, whereas PvP will have you gain nothing unless you're lucky. Game is fun to play until you reach the End Game stage; the stage you're working towards but find out is not what you were hoping for. After many years of playing this game I have decided to another review in hopes of providing people with a decent amount of information going into the game.
Smite is not the average Moba experience and thats what makes it great but at times can contribute to a pretty bad experience. What makes Smite stand out from other Moba experiences is the fact that it was the first with a true 3rd person viewpoint instead of the more used topdown RTS type perspective View other Moba's tend to have. Paragon a game that could be great but isn't took this idea from Smite and are also using this which in my opinion gives the Moba experience a much needed change as it tends to feel much more immersive where you feel as though you are actually that character. I will now provide some pros and cons.
Pros:
- Mythology is what really makes this game great, they take gods/goddesses and other mythological creatures from all over the world and put them into the game.
- Art Team and skins. Smite literally has one of the best Art teams in the world that design new skins every patch that are always pretty amazing.
-Bi-weekly updates where they usually fix alot of bugs, release a god just about every month and continue to grow the game.
-Good amount of free content often giving away chests, gems and favor to players to use to get cosmetic items.
- Lots of casual game modes, also a con as described below.
-Hard learrning curve in my opinion a pro because it is very difficult to understand the game, which makes it fun because you can often discover new and exciting things that can massively improve how well you play. But can also be a con for new players, especially those that have never played a Moba before. "This mostly applies to conquest".
Cons:
-Horrible community, if you are used to the average Moba experience and getting people who talk down too you because of how you play Smite is no different. Not to mention the reddit community is complete trash in terms of how they understand the game.
-Bad balance. Some gods are just better than others the design team has a tough time deciding on who they buff/nerf in order to have an equal playing ground. This leads to the next point on other game modes.
-Too many game modes, which results in the most competitive game mode Conquest or your average "3 lane/jungle experience in other games" to be overlooked at as the main point of balance. Game modes such as Arena and clash may have certain picks that are much stronger than they are in Conquest many of these other game modes contribute to the problems of balance in the game.
-Matchmaking can be pretty bad at times pointing at the other reason above, there are just too many ranked and casual game modes that seperate the community so much that you can be ranked with bronze in silvers when you are in much higher ranks.
Overall there may be more pros than cons but to really experience the fun in Smite you have to actually try it out. Much of the problems I myself have with the game is due to the number of years I have played it.
Would I recommend this game? Yes I would to people who have never tried it before and have a good experience with other Moba games and want to try something new. For new players I would be cautious this can be a very bad experience for you if you aren't used to other people constantly trash talking and putting you down.
My final advice I would give to people who want to get better and are having problems understanding how the game works is to honestly read the god descriptions and how their skills work. Understand the items and item builds that many people use.Go into training mode and see how the characters work before testing them in a match where you are also able to test all the gods without having to buy them***. Watch streamers play the game and you will automatically see a massive improvement in how well you play. Understand that It will take time and it will take patience but you will slowly get better.
One of the best Moba games often overlooked because of how big LOL and Dota are, but in my eyes a solid 9/10

After all this time I'm finally entering my thoughts on this game.
This will go on more like a story of my experience than a review.
I bought the game on pre-release, meaning full price, only because I loved this franchise.
This was something I never did before, but I jumped on the hype; or rather, I was part of the hype.
As many already know, the game was delivered in an unplayble state, it only ran well on few computers. So I waited more weeks for the update, disappointed but still eager to play. Thankfully, CA worked hard to release updates, which happened almost weekely in the start.
Soon I got my Rome II to run on my computer.
...but that only makred the beginning of my frustrating experience with this game.
I won't go into any details about the specific problems as for they have been extensively covered by many expert reviewers.
Plus the CAs part on over-promise and under-deliver, I'll leave it to others. It is beating the dead horse at this point.
However, it must be noted that besides the countless bugs and flaws in the codes, many aspects of the intentional game design is inferior to that of its more successful older siblings. These flaws will never go away, such as the Civil War, which appears to be getting more and more unreasonable as the patching goes on. The game design cannot be changed at this point.
Again, CA worked hard to patch the game. They updated weekly, which soon became monthy...
Plus they gave us free DLCs that opened up a few more factions in the game for the players to command.
And about 3~4 months after the release, the game finally became enjoyable.
...then the Rome II+DLCs went on 50% sale.
At that point I was beyond certain that pre-purchasing this game was a terrible mistake.
I could've waited 3 months for the 50% sale since I wasn't able to play the game anyways.
Even with the 3 free DLCs, the savings from the half-price discount was worth more.
The message/impression I got from this event was that CA is really hell bent on selling more copies of this game than anything else. Of course, any reasonable buisness would do that, but while offending those who love their work and delivering inferior product?? ...I don't think they should. All those little friendly guestures (or at first they seemed like friendly guestures) CA made went down the drain. If it was something you were going to do anyways, it cannot be an apology.
Those of us who pre-purchased got screwed hard. There was no benefit in buying early and at full price.
It has been 11 months since the release and we are now at 14th Patch and updates are becoming very few and far in between. The game has noticably improved and I've logged many hours in this game. Although it does not have the charm the old Total War games had, it certainly has new fun things in it.
However, the lesson Rome II has taught me (and us) is to never buy the next one on pre-release and to never pay full price for another Total War.
Even better, never be the first one to buy CA's game in an untested state. Let those fools who cannot learn from experience to taste it first. Once it is certain that it is not poisoned then consider buying it.
This is what I'll do if I ever buy another Total War.

I have had absolutely no issues with this port, outside of the UI being designed for a touch screen and thus triggering construct abilities feels like fishing for a button in a sewing kit tray.
Ascension is a fast playing deck builder card game. And this package is an outstanding deal, giving you 10 full expansions for the game, offering different card sets and mechanics, as well as the ability to mix and match as you see fit. (Mix responsibily, these mechanics don't work that well if diluted.)
The basic premise is that there is a row of five cards in the middle you may buy, heroes/constructs with runes, slay monsters with power. Heroes and constructs go into your deck, which is constantly being iterated through and reshuffled, and the abilities you get when you play them are how you gain more runes/power to keep buying stuff from the center row.
The abilities vary, from removing cards from the center row so your opponents can't buy them, to generating more cash if you have a certain combo this turn, to destroying bad cards from your deck. It plays quick, but there are a lot of clever abilities in play.
The AI is pretty good but you can also join online games, which I believe are cross platform with mobile players too, each with varying degrees of chess-clock style timers for fast or slow games.
Ascension is a great package. If there were issues with the port, I see no problems with it now. It is not the best deck builder out there, but it is a solid package nonetheless.
FYI, I feel Ascension plays best 1v1, though it can seat up to four players.

At the Point of this review i played 42 hours, im a dedicated card game player and have much expirience in Magic the Gathering Hearthstone and so on.

###############
Buy it if you
+ enjoy trading card games / deck building games (Magic the Gathering, hearthstone etc....)
+ enjoy draft formats

+ like handdrewn artstyle

- you want any kind of "ranked" system (it is not included)

This is a very interesting horror-themed first person shooter. Yes, it came out way back in 1999, so the graphics are dated by today's standards.
I finally got around to playing it because the highly entertaining Bioshock series was made by the same guy, Ken Levine. I also remember playing and enjoying System Shock 1 many years ago so nostalgia had something to do with it. The intro to System Shock 2 tells you what happened in the previous game, though, so don't feel you need to play the original to enjoy the sequel.
So, despite the dated graphics, is it still scary and/or fun? Hells YES, on both counts!
I'll give an example of the scariness/awesomeness:
You're trapped on a spaceship that has been taken over by hostile aliens. The aliens also control the ship's computer system, so the ship's normally helpful steward robots have now become automated suicide bombers. They will walk up to you and self destruct, usually while spouting some cheery greeting or friendly banter.
As part of your travels you have to go through a darkened cargo bay with crates stacked everywhere and many tight spaces. I got to the middle of the cargo bay before I realized that all the crates around me were storage crates for the suicide steward robots, and that all the crates said "READY" on them in big green letters. Sure enough, as soon as I turn my back on the crates I hear the sound of them breaking open, and a horde of robots is coming right at me, giving me friendly greetings all the while! Talk about a mixture of shock, horror, and excitement!!!
The game has strong RPG elements. At the start you are given the choice of being a combat oriented Marine, a technical oriented Naval Ops guy, or a Psionic Operative -- basically a high tech Jedi or wizard or whatever you want to call it. You're given a large amount of different skills to choose from, but you'll only have enough skill points to master a few so you have to choose wisely.
The large number of skills and items means you have many options for defeating the obstacles in your path. Is a big mean security bot ruining your day? Use your psi powers to turn invisible and walk past him. Or switch to armor piercing bullets to destroy him. Or hack a security turret to open fire on your enemy.
There are many mini-games that come with System Shock 2. You'll get a "GamePig" fairly early on that will let you play games completely unrelated to the main plot, everything from Tic Tac Toe to a racing game to an Ultima clone! Hells yeah!
But not everything is good about System Shock 2.
For one thing the game has a steep learning curve, and it is very difficult. Even a single enemy can kill you without too much trouble, and even when you're doing well you're always short of resources. This goes along with the survival horror theme but it can be frustrating at times. I'm a veteran first person shooter player, but after a few hours of getting slaughtered on "Normal" difficulty I had to swallow my pride and restart on "Easy."
Another gripe I had was the inventory management system was annoying. You'll quickly run out of space, and the only way to get more space is to spend precious skill upgrade points on Strength, a skill of otherwise dubious usefulness. And even after I maxed out my Strength score I was still running out of space! Argh!
As for the plot, it was nine kinds of awesome. There are several plot twists and I don't want to be too spoilerish, but I will say that the climactic finale of the game was a crowning moment of awesome. I only wish that more games had this kind of emphasis on storytelling.
So System Shock 2 is a flawed game, yes, but it's worth looking past the flaws because in the end you'll find a hidden gem. If you like Bioshock, Deus Ex, or survival horror games you owe it to yourself to check out System Shock 2.

If you have the PC to run it, Alien: Isolation is a terrifyingly awesome experience that is definitely worth trying out. The atmospheric setting, remarkably accurate sound design, and loyalty to the franchise they're based off of makes it a must own for any fan of the Alien series, and is a very welcomed change from the dreadful Aliens: colonial marines, however the game has several issues that hold it back from it's full potential, and while they don't take too much away from the overall experience they're worth mentioning.
+Very loyal to the Alien franchise, the first movie in particular.
+Perfectly terrifying sound design
+Great soundtrack that feels as if ripped straight from the movies.
+Insight to what happened between the first  and second alien movie that fits well and doesn't completely break the lore like Colonial Marines did.
+Absolutely terrifying
+I personally think it's a good thing in a survival horror game to have an enemy that constantly pursues you, and you having no way to actually kill it, only the drive it away for a few brief moments.
+Equipment is precious, and you are often forced to save it for dire moments
+The game balances the need to scavenge and the need to progress pretty well. Sure you want that blueprint, but the alien is right down the hallway and your green blooper is blooping really hard.
+Combat is always a last resort. The game tries to force you to play terribly cautiously, and while combat can save your life short-term it can also be a death sentence.
+Difficult, like any horror game should be. This game is best experienced on the highest difficulty, even though sometimes you might be forced to turn it down a notch.
+Insightful collectables to find
+Survival mode is pretty fun and stressful considering you are not only scared to death, but only have moments to complete your objective.
+Graphics are alright, could have been better
+this game would be ♥♥♥♥ing perfect for VR
-Weird occasional performance issues/crashes
-Lip syncing is way off. Easy to notice towards the start, but becomes a forgetable issue.
-Character movements are kind of stiff and awkward
-The middle part of the game is undoubtably the worst part, simply because the threat of the alien vanishes temporarily. I won't lie; the androids are fun to fight, but it starts to feel like a dumbed down action game rather than a classy survival-horror game.
-You are forced to backtrack a lot of the ship rather than explore the whole thing which is dissapointing, but the game keeps you fixed on your objective area well despite you having free roam.
-The ending to the game's story is a huge sequel baiter, and doesn't make any real sense. Kind of disappointing
In conclusion Alien Isolation is an amazing game, IGN is full of ♥♥♥♥ giving this game a 5/10, that wasn't even a review it was more like an informal grievance to sega and creative assembly asking them to pay for a review next time. The Atmosphere is spot on, it's intense and does service to the series it came from. 8/10

Heedful traversing of, much like system shock 2's corridors with gray-white walls, sci-fi degradation of a rundown ship, with red and blue wires strewn ubiquitously about the levels, levels that with sterility and dim, fluorescent, lighting in accordance with a keen sense of loneliness and helplessness, makes up the initial presentation and subsequent response to the constellation that is Alien: Isolation.
Immediately a sort of discrepancy appears, story-wise, which appears in the form of the following elucidation of these player/game, cliché/creativity dualities:
We all know it's an alien that is this “monster”, so the story feigning ignorance makes for a weird discrepancy between the player and game-world. And why would a futuristic crew of people –  along with the illiterate attempts at wall-messages scribbled in blood – attribute “random” deaths to a monster, but when we come across a corpse, there is seemingly no reason to assume this event to be the work of an otherworldly being, a monster, apart from what the title suggests. It's like the people in the game knows that this is
alien, but instead alludes to it for the sake of horror-mystery in a context where everybody, in part, already knows what is really going on. This could have been done a different way, where things weren't so clichéd as to try to obfuscate a truth which the player already knows, a truth that is the basis of this whole game. It seems like an unnecessary veil to put on something so conspicuous.
Being strongly reminiscent of Metro: Last Light, the Axel sections early on in the game, serves as an introduction into the games' world, a world where you're alone; you feel despair and fear, but you find –  as close to as you could on this ship – a friend that guides you through the basic functions of stealth mechanics. It's a clever way of supplementing a laborious tutorial system with engaging story-progression. It also corresponds to Ripley being in the dark of what is going on on the ship, since she hasn't been on it and experienced the social conditions being torn apart in the Alien's ravaging ways, thus giving Ripley a sort of passable reason for trusting this random person pointing a gun at her.
When Axel is promptly stripped away from us, in a shattering of the little sense of confidence and security we have, the game gets back to the deep sense of fright and even more so the deep sense of loneliness pertaining to both the claustrophobic hallways and the vacuous space that surrounds it – the fear is poignantly all-encompassing, enveloping and leaving you stranded in open space, like a three-dimensional desert.
Deep bassy whale sounds echoing throughout endless space, even though that space would have no reverberation that would otherwise a priori prove this depth – in the endless space metaphor – of sound as it pertains to location, in a weird interaction between diagetic and non-diagetic sound, that otherwise would be clear-cut. Musically, it interacts with gameplay and what is going on in front of the player, when in a tense situation, the music reflects that, when in a chase-scene or dangerous situation, the music reflects that as well. So musically, Alien: Isolation, organically fits the different pieces of music to the overall presentation of visuals, kinaesthetics and game-mechanics.
The visuals of this game are truly stunning, awe-inspiring and simply wonderful. Every window of opportunity to look out through a window into space, and the nearby gas giant, is one you should take. The lighting is deeply integrated into the environments, with red lights blasting from the alarms being set off, or creepily neon-blues from electric sparks or other dimmed lights of vibrant color. There is also a particular scene, a sort of like a flashback playing-the-story-being-told type moment in the game, where we follow a crew first discovering this alien ship. At this point you don't really feel like the gameplay is necessary, and it gives you a weird signal detector that at first has no real use, but the scenery is just brilliant. It was like walking through the inside of a metallic spinal chord, with spines integrated into the flooded floor and walls, with the same dampness and slickness you see in the alien's saliva when it's dripping from the ventilation ducts in the ceiling of the hallways in certain sections of the game. ♥♥♥♥♥♥l openings at the basis of this spine are mirrored in a naturalistic paradigm on the inner and outer walls of this alien ship, something like the hexagonal cells of bees, the patterns of flowers or general adumbration of different tree species and so on. . . these futuristic organically calcified egg/cystic-fossils buried in the hardened, seemingly former flesh-walls, are another example of wonderful imagery in this particular set of scenes.
The transition from cutscene to gameplay was an interesting one. Alien: Isolation didn't suffer from what a lot of games do, whereby the whereabouts of your character in a cutscene differentiates itself from where your actual position is. This made for an interesting seamlessness, where the end of the cutscene put you directly in the frightened, panicked, shoes of Ripley, just as disoriented, just as struck by what was just witnessed. Although, the beginning of the cutscene sometimes teleported you where you needed to be once in the cutscene, which was rather silly, but I suppose an understandable compromise to make for the latter half of the cutscene.
Ripley also trembles when she points her gun, signifying the pungent fear-nervousness constantly running through her, which is also reflected in her aim taking a long time to stabilize gameplay-wise, even though with this constant tremble that would never happen – the stabilization, that is – it is still an interesting touch of creativity to gameplay as it displays an emotional reaction and connection between game and character, mechanics and player emotion.
The terminals, conveniently enough, doll out the information – and acts like an agent of environmental exposition, and exploration! – we need to progress, in that generic System Shock/Bioshock type way, where you just happen to find just the text with the code written on it, even though the place – not only the place, but the network and computers are often out of order – is a wreck and most other things are readily destroyed, burned or sabotaged in different manners, increasing the silliness and unlikelihood of these expository beacons being readily available.
Slight environmental touches add some charm to the game, like the lockers that are littered with artifacts of presumably dead crew-members. The imagery of these, pictures of families, personalized lockers with pictures of vacation spots, pornographic images and other things to make these lockers not only a game mechanic, but a storyteller and an attempt to connect the player to the otherwise blank faces we see die throughout the game. We see hints of the lives of these people as family members, and subsequently the empathetically saddening that comes with realizing their supposed fate. It's a cute addition to an otherwise gray wall; it gives you something to reflect on during these long periods of fearful hiding from an overly aggressive foe.*
*Upon further research it turns out these personalized messages were just generic copies of the same post-it note. It's almost like this is a game, made by people who wanted to save time on certain things. It's always an unfortunate event, when the realization of the game being, in truth, a game – instead of this beautiful immersion into a world omitted by our own. This is seemingly thematic to Alien: Isolations.

EDIT: Review changed in 9/16 to reflect a lack of progress in providing features that were supposed to be in the release. Specifically, the course designer for PG has been long discussed and was supposed to be in the game on release. 4 months later it's still not there. Beyond the course designer, there still is no career mode. The game still has performance issues. There still is limited character customization, no announcers, very limited stats, poor UI, etc. Essentially almost NONE of the negatives have been fixed even though many of those things have been promised. Thus I can't recommend the game because I don't see tangible progress in improving the product.
-----
I've been arounds since PG's failed kickstarter. I bought the game as soon as it came out on Early Access. However, that doesn't make me a fan. It makes me a fan of golf games. PG does some things right. It does some things wrong. Because it's a mixed bag, it's easier to list what is good and what's bad about it. As always, YMMV.
Pros:
- numerous swing type options - there are multiple though I'm a three clicker all the way and very impressed by the smoothness of the meter. The mouse swing is challenging. They've tried to implement no-cheating modes but they broke the mouse swing while doing so.
- various levels of challenge - play this with all the aids on and you'll be in birdie city. Play this without them and you might be lucky to break 90. I'm not nearly as good as I once was, but at one point I was in the top 10 on Case's Ladder on Links and #1 on another ladder. So I'm glad it's challenging rather than the "Shoot 48 at Augusta on Tiger Woods" mode.
- good physics - I'm still not happy with the backspin but generally the physics are good and better than any other golf game. Backspin still is off and I generate more backspin on my short irons (and I shoot in the 90s) than my avatar in this game. Other than that they're spot on. For instance, if you play a course at higher elevation the ball will travel further. That's a nice touch.
- weather / time of day settings can add some real challenge to your game. I think the wind feels spot-on.
- many different courses to choose from and quite a few to download
- multiple modes of gameplay, including solo, multiplayer and tournaments with match play, team play, alt shot, etc.
- no micro-transactions that improve your game
- no stupid characters that drive the ball 400 yards. Over-driving distance ruins so many golf games and they've prevented that here.
Cons:
- no career mode built into the game yet
- course designer hasn't been released yet (it's now 4 months late and counting)
- I don't like the way the skies look and the trees can look a little jagged
- limited current player animations (no lefties, no females yet though they're coming)
- very,very, very limited character customization
- it requires a decent computer and user made courses don't always run well. In fact, the user made courses often exceed the RAM allowance in the game causing major problems from a chunky swing meter to crashing.
- slightly too limited shot shaping options. I wish I could position my swing path and feet differently to get inventive when shotmaking.
- very limited stats
- no announcer and limited sound effects
- no Steam Workshop integration (a cardinal sin for a game with downloadable courses)
- really poor and frankly butt-ugly user interface when you enter the game (though it's fine when actually playing a round)
So it's up to you whether to buy it. I can tell you it's a better game than that "other" golf game on Steam and probably the best one available on the market today. But it's by no means perfect yet (pun intended) and while I had hoped that many of the cons would be fixed, this doesn't seem to be happening. The product feels more and more abandoned with a lack of substantial progress since release.
If you want a golf game now, this is the one to buy becuase frankly it's probably your only decent choice. Since I'm a fan of the old Links games and golf games in general so I continue to load up PG from time to time. But if you aren't a golf nut, this game isn't for you because it's just too limited in the features and progress to appeal to a wider audience.

The game style is quite good and unique and provides a nice experience of a cops vs robbers / Enforcers vs Criminals which lures in a lot of players with the desire to play either side. Fueled with a interesting progressive system that allows you to advance contracts with Enforcer contacts or Criminal gangsters. Though it possesses a few problems which can utterly destroy the gameplay.
1.) The matchmaking system: This system divides player's skill groups into Bronze, Silver and Gold. Nearly all golds have deranked into Silver and that allows them to play on Bronze servers since they are only 1 above the skill bracket instead of 2. They will also likely have maxed out their contacts and have access to a large portion of the endgame content such as rocket/grenade launchers and /near/-bulletproof vehicles, large portions of the heavier weaponry that are massively upgraded to fit a certain playstyle. Ex: SMG with deadcenter on crosshair aimming while hipfiring but they lose the ability to aim down site accurately (Not like they ever would) but I'll touch on that later.
2.) P2W functioning: While much of the community will lead you to believe that the weapons and vehicles, (Much more the weapons) aren't P2W they infact are. You pay real money and you can purchase weapons that will give you an advantage over the other team. Now I don't mean that it's impossible to beat them. Usually with a fair bit of flanking, juking and ducking around cover and blasting them when they can't do much about it will get the job done. But in a head on head conflict you will lose to a "Premium weapon" when the enemy you are fighting has one. Regardless of if it's weapon type. What do I mean by this? As in SMG weapons will likely lose to Premium Assault rifle type weapon even though they are supposed to be the meta in close quarters. Though the rest of the uses for premium items are barely as viable as the ones you see in just the gunplay. You are likely to at least find one of these players with such a weapon in your game whenever you que.
3.) Population: Most of the population has dwindled overtime, it consists of Premium players are excessively highranking players (In the near 200s and above). Due to this you are likely to get teams of premium players as your opposition because they've grouped up with others who've spent large amounts of time on the game as well as they did. You will likely find low ranking randoms but to be honest. It's not the random's fault either.
4.) Gunplay: Don't get me wrong, it can be very engaging and is fun but again you will lose out to players which have more time in than you because they will have enhanced versions of the weapon you might be using. Like I said in #1, SMG with deadcenter accuracy. You'll end up with these types of weapons or being able to customize your own weapon with empty slotted guns that you can fit with your own attachments making it so you can move around at sprint like velocity while hipfiring an SMG that'll land 100% of the shots aslong as the crosshair is on the other player. Unfortunately it's simply how they measured up the weapons system and unlocks, regardless of your skill level you'll likely lose out to these weapons unless you can outsmart them or outplay them which will require a bit of knowledge of the map and situational awareness just so you can keep on your toes and dive behind cover nearby.
Overall/tl;dr : Fun game if you enjoy the cops and robbers genre of game. But definitely not worth investing your time into. You'll get sucked into the P2W stream to try and beat the others or will be wiped time and time again simply out of being too stubborn to pay real money for an advantage. Not recommending.

Normally I'm too cynical to be won over with cutesy charms and sugar-sweet atmospheres, but I have to admit it's one of the most prominent and impressive points of the game.
Now onto my regular review sense.
Aside from the charms, other quite nice points of Slime Rancher involve the pacing, the soundtrack, the world around you (the starmail and journals, etc), and the sheer simplicity of raising the slimes. Now, personally this is the shining genius of it all, not the art or the music or anything else; simplicity. Most of us hate that word, but that's because most simple games leave a bad taste in our mouths, and we're right to feel that way. But Slime Rancher is the good sort of simple; you collect slimes and upgrade your farm, you get a basic "1+1= safe, 1+2=destruction" formula to follow, a pat on the bum and you're off to do whatever you feel like doing. No complex machinery or automation (for the most part), no crazy mechanics you're forcefed to keep track of. Just you, a stamina and health bar, a ranch, and slimes.
Now, I love complex things, but it takes a complex mind to appreciate the value of simplicity. And I can say that all the collecting, farming, coralling, and experimenting was absolutely worth it's price tag and the acclaim. What this does, it does very very well. And that's better than any complex game that does f-all correctly.

Ever played Bioshock? Well, even if you have or not, I would anyway recommend that you try its predecessor: System Shock 2.
Along side with Half-Life, this brilliant masterpiece from 1999 introduced gamers for the modern FPS genre that is known today. With its mixture of FPS, Horror and RPG elements, great story, solid voice acting, an hazardous enviroment and spooky sound effects has made this game legendary. And even today, its still.........terrifying to play.
Chose your class, attributes, skills, equipment and decide how to use them to fight through hordes of mutated crewmembers, deadly cyborgs, crazy animals, rough Ai’s, strange species and much, much more.
And remember aboard the starship Von Braun, you live by only one rule: Survival by any needs necessary.
For in space, no one can hear you scream.

One of the most memorable games I've played in the last few years, if not one of the best as well. In my personal opinion, and I know a few people would really disagree with me, System Shock 2 is the epitome of the game design Ken Levine and Irrational Games have often invoked in their spiritual successor series, Bioshock.
Aside from the fantastic character progression and RPG elements, System Shock 2 contains some of the best sound design I've ever heard in not just a horror game, but any game to date. The pacing is amazing; starting in the vast, open Von Braun and then moving to the tightly focused, linear Rickenbacker and beyond every moment and situation has something to keep the player on his/her toes.

A truly genuine classic from a much missed studio. Looking Glass (Technologies) made this and it's precursor and set an extremely high benchmark for other games in the RPG/FPS genre to follow.
Aside from the more polished presentation, I'd argue that the original System Shock has the edge over SS2, purely because the player felt far more threatened by the games' malevolent AI - Shodan. However, that's not to take anything away from this game on its own merits. It kickstarted many standard player choices - allowing decisions to be made to mould your character to how you wanted them to be. And rather than a make it a glorified shooting spree set in space, you had to keep a very keen eye on your ever-dwindling ammo supply. Great story. Spooky layout. Very careful choices to be made.
A brilliant, brilliant game. 9/10

Now going back to the gameplay and the character you play as, i actually like how you're not some awesome ninja or some badass space marine but just some mechanic. Ripply is no hero and i like how some of the mechanics reflect who she is. Like how you can just build random but useful stuff on the fly since she is an engineer. I like it how she can't run that fast or parcore over stuff or even use guns that will. I think the mechanics directly demonstrate her character. Not a warrior, not a ninja but just some woman in a really bad situation. So to me even though i found some of the stealth mechanic to be lacking compared to other fps/stealth games i can see how it was done for a reason. And the stealth mechanics that are there seem to be there just to build even more tension and suspense. Such as poking your head around the corner or trying to get a better view when you're hiding in a locker. And the beeping of your tracker as the thing gets closer and closer. If you are a fan of Aliens and don't want to play a "shootem up" game and i think this will be for you.

If you have the PC to run it, Alien: Isolation is a terrifyingly awesome experience that is definitely worth trying out. The atmospheric setting, remarkably accurate sound design, and loyalty to the franchise they're based off of makes it a must own for any fan of the Alien series, and is a very welcomed change from the dreadful Aliens: colonial marines, however the game has several issues that hold it back from it's full potential, and while they don't take too much away from the overall experience they're worth mentioning.
+Very loyal to the Alien franchise, the first movie in particular.
+Perfectly terrifying sound design
+Great soundtrack that feels as if ripped straight from the movies.
+Insight to what happened between the first  and second alien movie that fits well and doesn't completely break the lore like Colonial Marines did.
+Absolutely terrifying
+I personally think it's a good thing in a survival horror game to have an enemy that constantly pursues you, and you having no way to actually kill it, only the drive it away for a few brief moments.
+Equipment is precious, and you are often forced to save it for dire moments
+The game balances the need to scavenge and the need to progress pretty well. Sure you want that blueprint, but the alien is right down the hallway and your green blooper is blooping really hard.
+Combat is always a last resort. The game tries to force you to play terribly cautiously, and while combat can save your life short-term it can also be a death sentence.
+Difficult, like any horror game should be. This game is best experienced on the highest difficulty, even though sometimes you might be forced to turn it down a notch.
+Insightful collectables to find
+Survival mode is pretty fun and stressful considering you are not only scared to death, but only have moments to complete your objective.
+Graphics are alright, could have been better
+this game would be ♥♥♥♥ing perfect for VR
-Weird occasional performance issues/crashes
-Lip syncing is way off. Easy to notice towards the start, but becomes a forgetable issue.
-Character movements are kind of stiff and awkward
-The middle part of the game is undoubtably the worst part, simply because the threat of the alien vanishes temporarily. I won't lie; the androids are fun to fight, but it starts to feel like a dumbed down action game rather than a classy survival-horror game.
-You are forced to backtrack a lot of the ship rather than explore the whole thing which is dissapointing, but the game keeps you fixed on your objective area well despite you having free roam.
-The ending to the game's story is a huge sequel baiter, and doesn't make any real sense. Kind of disappointing
In conclusion Alien Isolation is an amazing game, IGN is full of ♥♥♥♥ giving this game a 5/10, that wasn't even a review it was more like an informal grievance to sega and creative assembly asking them to pay for a review next time. The Atmosphere is spot on, it's intense and does service to the series it came from. 8/10

Heedful traversing of, much like system shock 2's corridors with gray-white walls, sci-fi degradation of a rundown ship, with red and blue wires strewn ubiquitously about the levels, levels that with sterility and dim, fluorescent, lighting in accordance with a keen sense of loneliness and helplessness, makes up the initial presentation and subsequent response to the constellation that is Alien: Isolation.
Immediately a sort of discrepancy appears, story-wise, which appears in the form of the following elucidation of these player/game, cliché/creativity dualities:
We all know it's an alien that is this “monster”, so the story feigning ignorance makes for a weird discrepancy between the player and game-world. And why would a futuristic crew of people –  along with the illiterate attempts at wall-messages scribbled in blood – attribute “random” deaths to a monster, but when we come across a corpse, there is seemingly no reason to assume this event to be the work of an otherworldly being, a monster, apart from what the title suggests. It's like the people in the game knows that this is
alien, but instead alludes to it for the sake of horror-mystery in a context where everybody, in part, already knows what is really going on. This could have been done a different way, where things weren't so clichéd as to try to obfuscate a truth which the player already knows, a truth that is the basis of this whole game. It seems like an unnecessary veil to put on something so conspicuous.
Being strongly reminiscent of Metro: Last Light, the Axel sections early on in the game, serves as an introduction into the games' world, a world where you're alone; you feel despair and fear, but you find –  as close to as you could on this ship – a friend that guides you through the basic functions of stealth mechanics. It's a clever way of supplementing a laborious tutorial system with engaging story-progression. It also corresponds to Ripley being in the dark of what is going on on the ship, since she hasn't been on it and experienced the social conditions being torn apart in the Alien's ravaging ways, thus giving Ripley a sort of passable reason for trusting this random person pointing a gun at her.
When Axel is promptly stripped away from us, in a shattering of the little sense of confidence and security we have, the game gets back to the deep sense of fright and even more so the deep sense of loneliness pertaining to both the claustrophobic hallways and the vacuous space that surrounds it – the fear is poignantly all-encompassing, enveloping and leaving you stranded in open space, like a three-dimensional desert.
Deep bassy whale sounds echoing throughout endless space, even though that space would have no reverberation that would otherwise a priori prove this depth – in the endless space metaphor – of sound as it pertains to location, in a weird interaction between diagetic and non-diagetic sound, that otherwise would be clear-cut. Musically, it interacts with gameplay and what is going on in front of the player, when in a tense situation, the music reflects that, when in a chase-scene or dangerous situation, the music reflects that as well. So musically, Alien: Isolation, organically fits the different pieces of music to the overall presentation of visuals, kinaesthetics and game-mechanics.
The visuals of this game are truly stunning, awe-inspiring and simply wonderful. Every window of opportunity to look out through a window into space, and the nearby gas giant, is one you should take. The lighting is deeply integrated into the environments, with red lights blasting from the alarms being set off, or creepily neon-blues from electric sparks or other dimmed lights of vibrant color. There is also a particular scene, a sort of like a flashback playing-the-story-being-told type moment in the game, where we follow a crew first discovering this alien ship. At this point you don't really feel like the gameplay is necessary, and it gives you a weird signal detector that at first has no real use, but the scenery is just brilliant. It was like walking through the inside of a metallic spinal chord, with spines integrated into the flooded floor and walls, with the same dampness and slickness you see in the alien's saliva when it's dripping from the ventilation ducts in the ceiling of the hallways in certain sections of the game. ♥♥♥♥♥♥l openings at the basis of this spine are mirrored in a naturalistic paradigm on the inner and outer walls of this alien ship, something like the hexagonal cells of bees, the patterns of flowers or general adumbration of different tree species and so on. . . these futuristic organically calcified egg/cystic-fossils buried in the hardened, seemingly former flesh-walls, are another example of wonderful imagery in this particular set of scenes.
The transition from cutscene to gameplay was an interesting one. Alien: Isolation didn't suffer from what a lot of games do, whereby the whereabouts of your character in a cutscene differentiates itself from where your actual position is. This made for an interesting seamlessness, where the end of the cutscene put you directly in the frightened, panicked, shoes of Ripley, just as disoriented, just as struck by what was just witnessed. Although, the beginning of the cutscene sometimes teleported you where you needed to be once in the cutscene, which was rather silly, but I suppose an understandable compromise to make for the latter half of the cutscene.
Ripley also trembles when she points her gun, signifying the pungent fear-nervousness constantly running through her, which is also reflected in her aim taking a long time to stabilize gameplay-wise, even though with this constant tremble that would never happen – the stabilization, that is – it is still an interesting touch of creativity to gameplay as it displays an emotional reaction and connection between game and character, mechanics and player emotion.
The terminals, conveniently enough, doll out the information – and acts like an agent of environmental exposition, and exploration! – we need to progress, in that generic System Shock/Bioshock type way, where you just happen to find just the text with the code written on it, even though the place – not only the place, but the network and computers are often out of order – is a wreck and most other things are readily destroyed, burned or sabotaged in different manners, increasing the silliness and unlikelihood of these expository beacons being readily available.
Slight environmental touches add some charm to the game, like the lockers that are littered with artifacts of presumably dead crew-members. The imagery of these, pictures of families, personalized lockers with pictures of vacation spots, pornographic images and other things to make these lockers not only a game mechanic, but a storyteller and an attempt to connect the player to the otherwise blank faces we see die throughout the game. We see hints of the lives of these people as family members, and subsequently the empathetically saddening that comes with realizing their supposed fate. It's a cute addition to an otherwise gray wall; it gives you something to reflect on during these long periods of fearful hiding from an overly aggressive foe.*
*Upon further research it turns out these personalized messages were just generic copies of the same post-it note. It's almost like this is a game, made by people who wanted to save time on certain things. It's always an unfortunate event, when the realization of the game being, in truth, a game – instead of this beautiful immersion into a world omitted by our own. This is seemingly thematic to Alien: Isolations.

This game is a breath of fresh air for the zombie genre. It is like a mix of Left 4 Dead, Resident Evil, and Dead Rising in that the action is intense and there are plenty of items scattered about. The game features separate inventory wheels for items and ammo, so players can manage their held items and their ammunition separately. While there are a plethora of melee weapons in this game (from a small kitchen knife to a fire axe to a chainsaw), there are not nearly as many ranged weapons laying around, forcing you to conserve these guns and their ammo as that is also not common. The game emphasizes making use out of each round as there are tons of zombies to kill with limited ammo in the area.
This game is also very slow-paced. Your characer moves fairly slowly, and the zombies are even slower, although they are quite strong individually as a single zombie has the potential to screw the player over via bleeding or infection. Each action the player takes, from reloading to switching weapons to swinging a hacthet, feels very slow and heavy, so the player has to make sure that their actions are as precise as possible. The slow pace of the game augments the tense feeling of survival, and although this game is fairly easy to understand in terms of gameplay and mechanics, it is quite challenging to beat without at least a little bit of teamwork and cooperation. This game is very fun and addicting to play, and each zombie kill is satisfying with the occasional zombie head exploding bloodily.
Of course, it is not perfect. The "zones" mode, where players must defend certain areas of a map from zombies, does not exactly fit the slow pace of the game because it can take players quite a bit of time to conquer crowds of zombies, which can allow other zombies to take over an area. I also do not like the fact that players cannot move through each other, which would be much appreciated as it can be easy to get temporarily trapped by a player standing in a doorway or hall, allowing a zombie an open opportunity to grab you. Finally, I would like to be able to spawn as soon as I connect to a server. Connecting to a game in progress can be rather dull sometimes as you are forced to watch the players who were already in the server.
Despite its issues, NMRiH is one of my favorite games on Steam, and the best part about it is that it's completely free. Heck, if this game were to cost money, I would buy it. I definitely recommend this amazing game.

This game is awesome. It got basically everything you would want in an MMO. You're not bound to your character/class selection, you can be whatever you want to be. If you wanna be a tank, but have the skills of a sorcerer, do it! Wether you prefer Bows, staffs, dual wield, one hand + shield or two-handed, this game got it all. And you can't build your character "wrong". It got a decent guild system, wether you want to do pve, pvp or trading.
The lvl-ing system is also quite nice. You decide if you wanna quest or grind. Or a  mix. The game ain't really challenging at first though, but once you reach some lvls, the game gets pretty tough.
The pvp deserves it's own paragraph. You enter a "map" that's split into 3 sides, Daggerfall Covenant, Aldmeri Dominion and Ebonheart Pact. You conquer each other's keeps, take their scrolls, kills their players(They can respawn so being afraid of dying shouldn't be a problem). If you like tactics and planning, this pvp is awesome. And EVERY ATTRIBUTE scales up, so you can enter as lv10 and have the same HP/Stam/Magicka as a lv40. Pvp-lvling is awesome, there are small towns scatered around that you can quest in - and they give damn good exp! And the pvp-quests aswell are pretty nice. As you fight your way in Cyrodiil, you'll gain Alliance Points, AP, which you can use to buy Siege-weapons, soul gems.. etc. it's just fantastiiic.
Though. It got loooooooaaads of bugs. Not extremly gamechanging-bugs, but bugs. The mount might not always work, you might have to alk to an NPC 2 times etc. But they're just small bugs. Nothing that ruins the game-experience. Graphic is also really nice, the trees look like actual trees!!
So, conclusion: This game is awesome. It got all the treats you want for an MMO + it gives you a lot of freedom. But if you are looking for a 100% bug-free game, then this might not be the game for you.

IT'S HONESTY TIME.
Okay, now  NOBODY wanted an online Elder Scrolls game. Nobody played through Morrowind, Oblivion and Skyrim and thought "you know what would make this game better? Loads of strangers and subscriptions!" NOBODY asked for this. And most of us are still pi$$ed. Hell, I enjoy ESO and I'm still a bit pi$$ed.
Now let me quickly give you a slight perspective on where I'm coming from. I'm a convert from console. I HATE KB+M (yes yes I know it's meant to be more accurate and I'm sure you're right but) I like my controller. I never saw an MMO that appealed as I'm somewhat of a loner in both life and gaming. And no, not a "Billy no-mates", I just prefer doin my own thing to doin what a group of other people wanna do. So I REALLY didn't want an online Elder Scrolls. And I'm only gonna get my ar$e handed to me in PvP coz I care more about story and adventure that 1-up-ing someone else.
So, ESO now has controller support... FINALLY! And it's about GDMF time! I cannot fully express my nerd-rage over this shortcomming, not to mention the GDMFBS replies I've had from Bethesda about how it's "optimized for KB+M" so for some reason that means their thumbs are lodged so far up their rectal passages on this problem you can see them gag!
Alas I digress.
Anyhow, I guess whether or not you should buy this depends on how much of an Elder Scrolls snob you are. Especially as it's now f2p.
Is it true Elder Scrolls? No. For starters, Zenimax made it, not Bethesda.
Does it run like Skyrim? mmm... not exactly.
Instead of nailing an arrow in between someone's eyes, for example, you have the character you're attacking light up. It does rob a small amount of satisfaction from a kill but you get used to it.
Sneaking is BS, coz as soon as your first sneak attack hits, your cover is blown and you stand up yelling "HEY HOARDS, COME GET ME". Why the ever-loving FU(K can't you stay sneaked?? Also not that annoying after a while.
Crafting is different. Complicated at first but the learning curve isn't so steep.
Now we come to the MMO issue. Which, for a PvE gamer such as myself, was a major deterrent.
Yes, other gamers will race you to get resources if they see them first and they don't regen for a while. And if you fail to pick a lock on a chest, some other git can access the lock straight away and pick it during a post-lockpick-fail-cooldown-time of several seconds. But lockpicking is easy and I haven't had a chest snatched from under me yet... in about 1000hrs of gameplay.
Also, other gamers can wipe out most of any area leaving it barren of enemies, however just wait a few mins and they all respawn.
The good news is that NOBODY can harm, challenge or rob you in the PvE zones. Which are ALL OF TAMRIEL bar Cyrodyll. You can ONLY be harmed by other players in the PvP central heartlands... and you can't get there by accident.
There are some areas that REQUIRE 4 players or you'll only get your ar$e handed to you. But there are plenty of decent gamers willing to join in or just lend a hand.
I WOULD recommend getting ESO, or at least trying a friend's copy. Each account can have up to EIGHT characters. Imagine the difference between all other Elder Scrolls games and ESO as the difference between the book and the film. Don't be a snob: they're 2 different mediums. The pro's are:
*You get to see several areas of Tamriel for the first time.
*Riften is especially interesting 1000yrs in Tamriel's history.
*You can complete one alliance and then you can play the other 2 alliances with the same character so no main quest 3 times, unless you want to make a new character.
*Teaming up can be fun.
*You don't fight over loot, if you helped kill something and it drops loot, you all get loot.
*There is about as much PvE content as Morrowind, Oblivion and Skyrim combined.
*You can buy the game and not pay another penny (or cent or euro) with the exception of DLC.
*The "pay to win" thing everyone's goin on about is a massive exaggeration. You get about 10% boost to exp and gold, and some crowns for the crown store (youtube "crown store" yourself).
*IT'S ENOUGH LIKE OTHER ELDER SCROLLS TO BE ENJOYABLE.
tips:
*to accumulate gold and resources:
-learn traits from eveything from your armour and weapon class as you can
-deconstruct everything from your weapon and armour class that you don't need
-SELL everything from the armour class you DON'T use
-get the "keen eye" perks
-get the hireling perks
-your hireling gets you resources of the material level that you can use, so when you're a few levels away from using steel and you have plenty of iron, add to the metalworking perk so you can use steel. By the time you can WEAR steel, you'll have enough to make an armour set with. This example also works with other crafting perks.
-hunt for resources late in the evening when fewer gamers are online
*TRAIN YOUR HORSE. It'll run faster, for longer and you'll be able to carry more stuff. You'll prolly have an allotment of crowns when you first get the game, so buy one at the crown store or from a stable and all characters can equip it. Though training is seperate for each character you make.
*try all crafting, crafting is good. Food is REALLY helpful, as are potions
*with the 3 ingredient perk in alchemy, Dragonthorn, Blugolss and Columbine make a potion that ups all 3 stats and are epic on quick slot in battle.
*get the Skyshards, Lorebooks and Undiscovered mods. They rock.

Worst feature:  The inventory is far too small for crafting characters.  Not enough inventory for the first area.  Each new area requires more and more materials for crafting with no inventory left over to collect new materials.
Like most games early level crafting is wonderful.  So the game draws you in.  Later the crafting gets insanely hard.  The game developers succer punch you in the face with this unavoidable difficulty and lack of sufficient inventory.
What I do not like:  Only twelve hot keys.  Five keys for each for two weapon sets.  A 104 key keyboard allows for numbers 0 through 9 with "-" and "=" keys for twelve hot key slots. First off, I have only played about 7 hours of this game with my friends. At the moment, I wont be playing the game till more development has been done (and to be honest, if I wasnt at 7 hours, I would have refunded the game).
The game has some cool features, such as "tier" versions of tools, keeping equipment when you die (long as you havnt killed random players), "stakes" you can place down, and respawn at, and everyone spawns in the "noob/starting area" so its really easy to find your friends. The building is actually really cool too.
The biggest turn off for me was the Kill on Sight on official servers. I'm not someone who plays on community servers as I have had bad experiences with them in the past, namely admin abuse (Raid a admin, they delete your base, etc), so for all I know, community servers may be a better option, but like I said, thats not what I am looking for. I want to play on a official server. I've played tons of survival games, and I am okay with KoS, its a PvP game, expect to be killed on sight.
The issue I have though with KoS in this game, is how spawning works. Its cool that you can spawn in and easily find your friends. Whats not cool is when higher progressed players build in the "newb/spawning zone" and gun you down the moment you spawn in. What this game should have done is disable base building in the starting zone. Let people build work benches/camp fires, but no actual housing. This would prevent the "bored" higher progressed players from killing new spawns. In the games CURRENT state of writing this, you can build a high tier base with wood as they dont seem to have the "metal" resource in the game yet, so all you see in the newb/starting zone is fully upgraded bases every where.
Maybe the dev's will change this down the road, and since I am unable to get a refund for the game, I will just wait and see.
TLDR;
Postive list:
- Cool base building
- A KoS penalty system (Its not perfect, such as if someone is shooting at me, and I kill them "first", I get KoS flagged. The penalty isnt really that crazy either, but hey, atleast they are trying to put a penalty in for KoS)
- Long as you are not KoS flagged, you keep your main equipment when you die (Tools, Clothing, Weapons)
- Easy to group up with friends early on as everyone spawns near each other
- Tier system for gear
- You can place stakes down to respawn at specific locations when you die.
- A compase to direct you to your house if you craft one.
- Graphics are simple and clean.
- There seems to be a economy sorta (Ambers I believe it was, people do trade for them).

- Health Regen if you havn't taken damage after a certain amount of time. Don't see this often unless you are "rested" or fully fed.

Negative list:
- Everyone spawning in the same area is great, but players who have progressed can build there and kill all the newer spawns. This should be a no base building zone.

The premise of the game is quite simple: survive and build. The game does implement both of them quite well. You are surviving from both human players and the environment. While you can probably live with a campfire and hunt animals for food, you won't be able to survive for long against human players. For that you need to build houses. How grand and elaborate the buildings are is entirely up to you. You can make a small shack with a few necessesary items in it or a sprawling multi-storey mansion with a garage or even a fortress. It's limited by your imagination.
The game map is quite large and they might add more to it in the future. The map is made up of six different biomes, five of them are habitable and one is a radiation zone. Each biome works differently depending on the type of biome it is. If you go to the dunes without sun screen and light clothing, you will get heatstroke and die before long unless you find shelter. Similarly if you go to the snow biome without winter wear and food, you will die of hypothermia or hunger. The game's environment plays a big role in the type of gear you need with you at any time.
I have probably spent most of my game time on the snow biome so I will comment on my personal experiences there. First of all it's absulutely beautiful. There is something about getting on a snow covered hill and looking at the horizon to see white covered trees, plains and mountains and the moon shining brightly from the sky, not an animal or human in sight. It's erily quite and peaceful, and lonely (if you are alone). That's what snow biome offers, isolation. You will not get many animals to hunt for food, and unless appropriately clothed, you will start to catch cold. You need to make a fire to stay warm. If it starts to rain, even proper clothing won't help you, you need to make a shelter. Add the fact that high level ores which are used for pretty much everything, are scattered around randomely and they are radioactive or poisonous (depending on the ore). It is very tough to survive without proper preparation as it should be. The game's environment is deadly and with preparation, manageable but to the unprepared it can end in an untimely demise.
The game has small variety of creatures. Most drop meat which is the best food you can get right now and the rest are a bit more tougher and give more exotic materials when killed. The bigger enemy are the other players. The game has a partial loot system. Which means, unless you are infamous (bounty system for killing players), you will keep your worn items and tools but drop all resources so you are not back to square one if you die. You can find players who will try to kill you for your resources and players who will give you some food and send you on your way and even players who might ask you if you want to join them. Playing with other people increases the survivability and makes the game more fun, but it is definately playable alone.
And if you don't fancy pitting it against other players, there are PVE servers where players are forbidden from killing other players. Those servers are recommended if you are new to survible games or just starting out as a new player.
If you like building things, you can easily spend 100+ hours in the game just collecting resources and making buildings without restriction. You are only limited by the space where you build (unless you chose to go vertical) and your imagination.
The game is lacking in content in terms of craftable items though. It's quite easy to make all the items you need within a few days. To keep playing you can spend the rest of the your days building, exploring, killing other players, looking for car parts etc..
Right now the game is very playable in terms of smoothness. There is an issue with nvidia and a bug with the game engine but there is a simple fix  and there are guides on the hub to fix it. What the game lacks right now is content. The game lacks enemy varieties and craftable items. The developers took a small break during the winter holidays and hopefully they are back to creating new content for us. As the game stands today, you can definately get your moneys worth in game time already from the amount of conent you can experience right now.
If you are a fan of building things or survival genre, this game is highly recommended. And if you are new to the survival genre, this is not a bad place to start. There are no zombies in this game, but unlike many popular zombie survivale games, the environment can be just as deadly as humans in this game.

Alien: Isolation is an immersive experience unlike anything else you will find. Fans of Alien, not AlienS, will love this. And survival horror fans shouldn't be concerned with the familiarity of the franchise if they're looking for something new to play that doesn't hold your hand.
Within about two hours of play time you will begin to see the menace of Sevastopol, a nearly abandoned space station operated by Seegson Communications, and while some have stated the storyline is weak, it stands up well in providing an atmosphere and fits well into the mythos of the Alien movies, especially the notes of betrayal and deceit from corporations like Weiland-Yutani. It also adds to the overall bridge between Alien and Aliens, discussing Ripley's daughter that died prior to her emergence from cryostasis as seen in the second film.
The AI, not just on the Alien itself but on the Working Joes present on the ship, create an intimidating atmosphere, giving the player few options but to locate places to hide and strategically move from one location to the other, and all the while the game's visuals back up that particular aspect. The visuals will not blow you away while you make your escape, except on maybe a few occasions, but overall the game looks great, and plays even better. The simple format they have set up for controls makes surviving a joy to play, and if anything is not to your satisfaction you can change the defaults very easily in the minimalistic pause menu. They've even given you an option to turn down the film grain, which I was happy to see, as it was a bit much when I first started playing.
In short, the game shines as an excellent addition to one of my favorite movie franchises, and on its own is a nervewracking, tense experience that anyone looking for something that isn't a multiplayer shooter should make an effort to play. Don't give up on this, because that just makes you a sitting duck in the vents with your loud beeping motion tracker (one for the fans).

Alien: Isolation is not just a game for Alien fans. It's for anyone who enjoys immersion, smart AI, and a good scare. I had not seen the original film Alien (1979) until the night before playing Alien: Isolation, and I'm glad I did. The level of detail and love given to recreating the atmosphere of the original film by 20th Century Fox and Creative Assembly is admirable if not groundbreaking. There's no tacked on multiplayer. There's no frills. You get to spend about 20 hours trying to survive in what plays like a compilation of everything great in the survival horror genre, but it has its own unique spin where there's just enough action to keep things alive... and scary as hell. I generally consider myself to be desensitized to virtual violence, but I legitimately flinched and yelped when I was suddenly pulled up an airduct and devoured. The Alien's AI is absolutely remarkable, and I was constantly outsmarted by it. That is the icing on the cake to me.
Do yourself a favor and pick up Alien Isolation. It's worth every penny.

Some bigshot review labeled this game as "Terrifying" but that's just the wrong description. "Unceasingly Tense" is more like it. Or how about "Gorgeous"? You're on this giant, monstrous space-station hovering over a massive orange gas giant and sometimes you get to look out a window at it all, and you might notice you're standing there for a couple seconds longer than you'd anticipated because what you see is so dang beautiful! Meanwhile the dialogue doesn't suck, and the story is rather a slow unraveling of a mystery. People are disappearing on this space station, Sevastopol. The human-like androids, or "synthetics," or "Working Joes" are acting "strange"... If you've seen the movies you know that these robot-people are incredibly strong. The thing that runs them, Sevastopol's A.I., might be acting wonky. And of course there's an ALIEN on board! You gotta run, hide in lockers MGS style, make weapons out of the junk you find lying around, make distractions, and GET TO THE CHOPPAH. (It's pretty much nonstop tension and when it's not tense you get suspicious because the game's letting up on you which makes it tense again.) Oh yeah, people will complain that "you're doing the same thing over and over," which is partly true. But only partly The game does a great job of introducing new gameplay elements at the right moments, juggling foes, weapons, mechanics, even the environments. Really it's a great addition to the Alien franchise. I give it a 10/10 and three wet kisses.

A slightly clunky implementation of a superb card game. Ascension is a deck-builder game: you start with a weak deck of cards and buy cards from a central pool to improve it AS YOU PLAY IT. It's not strategic like Dominion (the grand-daddy of deck-builders), it's the other end of scale. Since you cannot predict which cards will be available for purchase, the game is 100% tactical: you must constantly adapt to the ever-changing game state.
The art-work is an acquired taste, and this version is "playable" at best*, but don't let that put you off, the underlying game itself is so very good that such quibbles become meaningless, to me at least. Since you get the first 7 expansions bundled with the base game, the value for money here is astounding. Buying the physical version of all that would cost well over 100 bucks. [Though since the Android version is apparently free, I guess THAT is even better value for money!]
If you like Ascension, GET THIS NOW. If you have never played it and the bug bites you when you try it, the ridiculously low asking price is going to deliver dozens upon dozens of hours of solid deck-builder gameplay. This game is extremely addictive. For that reason, I give it 9/10 despite the minor short-comings of the implementation.
* unlike others I am happy playing this full-screen (stretched); everything looks fine to me and the cards are readable. The interfaace has a few glitches that are merely inconvenient and in no-way game-breaking.
Fast-paced, addictive and never the same thing twice.

This isnt a bad game at all. It's a far cry from what I remember PGA to be on xbox(which is what I was hoping this would match up to), but for the most part a good game of golf.
It's tricky to get used to and there are a few basic features which I really feel need to be added. The UI/UX desperatly needs to be improved. For example, the 'select' button could toggle an overlay of controls for a joypad as for me that button was unused and I found myself getting lost in controls.
A strength indicator should be added - % backswing versus % follow through to give a measurement of power as you take the shot, coupled with a visual aid of how straight your follow through was would be great as sometimes you draw/fade when you feel confident your follow through was perfect.
Putting seems to be very random. I found it very hard to get a consistent putt.
Draw/Fade/forward/backspin seem to have very little effect for me, and the roll of a green seems to be a bit un responsive... but this could be because I've only played a couple of hours.
Not a game I'll play on my own, but very enjoyable in its current state to play with a couple of people you know with voice coms on. I'm really looking forward to this game being further developed - loads of potential! Worth a buy

APB is one of my favorite games of all time, it is unlike every other shooter i've ever played, ive played many shooters altogether and the majority of them play the same, one thing i've always been good at is picking up new games and geting the hang of them quickly, APB was an exception, i first joined in 2012 and i remember my first missions vividly, i lost 99% percent of the missions i played and the game still placed me in gold, which was confusing, It wasnt till later on that i realized that the people i were playing against mostly were veterans of the game. even so , i enjoyed the combat that APB had to offer and wanted to improve right away and thus my relationship with APB began.
firstly
APB is not a good game
it is buggy,
servers have 33-40ms ,
it is unfair (missions)
Open world game (+low population=dead)
poor matchmaking ( even worse BECAUSE of the low pop)
poor vehicle physics
poor community
Some people receive hit registry issues(Some are worse then others)
poor company
People cheat (aimbots/wallhacks)
But..
It is a unique shooter
what do i mean by this? the majority of the guns in APB take 5 shots or more to kill, it isnt the same like other shooters where the objective in aiming is to place your crosshair on the enemy's head first before they do, infact, there are no headshots in APB, and no guns that kill in 1 shot either (minus the rocket launcher/grenade launcher)  the type of aim you will be practicing mostly is aiming center mass as much as possible and keeping your crosshair on your enemy as much as possible while taking cover to make you a smaller target and using teamwork to pinch enemies and move into areas.
to add to this Guns are very situational in APB , SMGs and shotguns are great at CQC but cannot kill people at further ranges, other long range guns thrive at their respective ranges and suffer at closer ranges, some weapons are more flexible , others are not.
APB has great customization
APB has argueably the greatest customization to ever be, Ive seen many people make outfits to make them look like Ronald Mcdonald or Scooby doo characters or something unique all together, not only this but APB has great symbol customization which you can apply to your character, clothes , or vehicle, and you can share the symbol with your friends, or sell them to the rest of the community by putting it for grabs on the auction/market.
Ontop of this you can make your own songs in the APB studio maker and themes, which are a 5 second tune which will play for your victim that you killed right after they die, there are also skins for your guns that arent bad. but all in all APB has great customization
APB is NOT pay to win
APB isn't pay to win, i have thrown hundreds of dollars into the game and i have to say this has been a touchy subject over the time ive spent playing APB because honestly i was one of the players who had the troublemaker when it was first released and it was overpowered, however this was changed within a month. Most guns that I consider overpowered are obtainable through other methods in the game without paying real money for. APB is NOT pay to win but there are plenty of weapons that are quite broken, this is a matter of opinion but heres my list if you're curious:
ALL LTL WEAPONS.
ALL GRENADES (except frag)
OSMAW/OPGL
REMOTE DETONATOR(Brilliant)
OCAWhisper/Silverado(No recoil)
Yukon(LOL)
OCA(slightly too good)
PMG(slightly too good)
HVR/SCOUT/DMR/DogEar( i like snipers, but they dont fit in the balance of this game)
OBIR(the best weapon behind a corner from range and doubling teaming someone)
OSCAR(LOL)
Volcano(LOL)
ATAC(very small spread, very low recoil)
Medusa
Eightballs and halfbricks (hard to use, still unbalanced)
True Ogre(LOLLL)
Colby AP .45(Deadly if mastered, also argueably the best secondary in the game)
APB is fun with friends,
APB can be frustrating, with all the bugs, unfair missions and rediculous loadouts,  can make you never want to play the game again... or you can take it for what it is and enjoy the random mess APB has become, i believe the random stuff that happends in APB is quite comical however it ruins the games potential of its tactical/skill curve aspect.
Final notes: APB has always struck me as a game with the potential to be a great Tactical infantry teamwork oriented game with a nice skill curve and even bigger teamwork oriented skill curve. planning loadouts and strategies to compliment your team and work together to pinch enemies , move into positions, cover positions and much more, however the random garbage that was added to the game has taken all that unused potential and just stashed it away. A great customizable mess with some cheaters who cant compete and pretend to be great at the game, or cheaters who believe everyone better then them or actually are good at the game cheat as well.
APB is currently my favorite game and i will play it till it dies.
However i dont reccomend anyone play this game in its current state unless you're willing to deal with the cons.
