My first review for this game was a troll review that a friend and I found really funny but I think people took it way too seriously so here's a serious one. In this review I will be explaining what elder scrolls online is, why you should buy it, and why I still play it even after so long (I used to launch it from the launcher not steam).
Elder Scrolls Online is an MMORPG made by Zenimax Online Studios, referred to as fans as ZOS. There are 4... I mean 5 classes counting the new morrowind expansion in Elder Scrolls Online. These classes are nightblade, sorceror, dragonknight, templar, and warden if you have the morrowind expansion.
Nightblade is an assassin class that focuses on huge burst damage and execute damage, making them good for PvP but not very ideal for endgame PvE trial groups and guilds.
Sorceror is an extremely overpowered cla- I mean a class that focuses on doing really high dps and is a lot of fun to play haha. Sorceror focuses on shock damage, or physical damage if you choose the stamina route.
Dragonknight is a class that has a lot more tanky abilities allowing you to take more hits before going down. They focus on fire damage for the most part, but do have some poison abilities as stamina morphs. Dragonknight is extremely good at immobolizing enemies, making them one of the best classes for tanking.
Templar is also an extremely overpo- Whoops xD. Meant to say Templar is a class that focuses on fire damage and magic damage and some physical damage too should you choose some stamina morphs here and there. Templar is one of the most fun classes to play in my opinion, because not only can you heal and provide your allies with support abilities and take a lot of damage, but also do a lot of damage.
Warden is a class that focuses around nature. You can summon animals to help you, heal your friends using tree magic and stuff, and even comes with a few tanky abilities. I haven't played too much of Warden so far but I would say he's like Templar and Dragonknight combined, making Warden a lot of fun to use.
The combat in ESO is pretty smooth, like most MMOs you have to slot abilities on your combat bars. A combat bar has 5 slots for any ability, and you have two combat bars. You can have different abilities on each bar, along with different weapons. However, there is an extra slot next to your combat bar where you can put an ultimate ability. Ultimate is generated during combat. You can dodge roll, block, bash, heavy attack, and light attack while fighting with your abilities which makes combat seem really alive, unlike some MMOs where your character barely moves while you press 1, 2, or E or something.
PvP (Player vs Player combat etc)- PvP is awesome in the elder scrolls online. You don't lose anything besides honor (lol) and you can always respawn to fight another guy. The PvP area is Cyrodil but you can PvP anywhere if you get permission from the other player by inviting them to a duel and having them accept the duel invite. Cyrodil is huge and has lots of castles you can take over using siege weapons, but other players will be there to defend their castles so I recommend playing pretty safe unless you want to respawn and ride all the way back to the enemy's castle. None of your abilities change but your health will go up. Your abilities do 1/2 less damage to players, this system is in place so you don't get one shotted.
Gear: Gear is super cool in the Elder Scrolls Online. There are tons of sets with cool passives and abilities and procs for you to use, and any class can use any weapon or any armor. Some armor and weapons are locked by level. Using motifs you can craft different styles of armor or make armor or a weapon that looks a lot different then someone elses' armor or weapon (Unless they use the same motif lol). You can also dye your armor and shield if you have one.
Gathering Materials etc: Gathering is okay in ESO, nothing special but definetely far from great. You can't chop down any tree you see for wood, only certain logs you see on the ground. You can't mine any rock for ore, only certain rocks. And you can't gather any plant, only certain plants. For me, this kind of ruins the immersion.
Groups: Group play is awesome in Elder Scrolls Online. You can adventure with your friends and the best part is that your level doesn't really matter when you adventure with your friends because mobs are set to your level. So if your level 49 and your friend is level 37 and your fighting the same enemy, your friend will be fighting a level 37 enemy and you'll be fighting a level 49 version of that enemy but it's still the same enemy if that makes sense.
Graphics: The graphics in the elder scrolls online are really awesome, some MMOs out there might have better graphics than the elder scrolls onlines' graphics but at least you don't lag out a ton once you enter a town like some of the MMOs out there.
P2W/Pay for convenience stuff in ESO: Unlike most MMOs where you can purchase costumes that give you buffs, or a pet that gathers tons of stuff really fast, ESO has free pets you can obtain from ingame quests along with free ingame costumes, and even a free skeleton polymorph that comes from a quest too. Costumes and pets don't give you any extra benefit in ESO. They don't hide your nametag or give you special buffs/advantages *cough* Black Desert *cough* lol. Elder Scrolls Online does have DLC and an expansion but the most of the gear given from these expansions can be bought/traded from other players, and none of the gear is broken, although you could argue the velidreth set is a bit too good right now. If a lot of dead enemies are in one room, you can loot them all just by clicking E and it searches all the nearby bodies, instead of having to pick up the loot from each enemy individiually or have a pet that costs a lot of money pick it up for you. You can pay for costumes and pets and mounts using crowns (ingame currency obtained through spending real money) but these are cosmetic and offer no advantage. You can buy mounts using ingame gold at the stable for fairly cheap, and you can get free costumes, pets, and polymorphs from just playing through quests and the game itself. The only small problem I have is that you can buy riding lessons to speed up your horses' progress (your horse can be taught 1 new skill a day, it's kinda complicated to explain) but this can be done ingame. You can also pay for vampire and werewolf bites, but these can also be obtained legit ingame, you can have another player bite you for free or just go up to a wild werewolf or wild vampire.
Conclusion: Elder Scrolls Online is probably my favorite MMO out of all the MMOs I've played. Their support team gets back to you really fast, the combat is pretty smooth, The gear isn't class locked, Any class can do any role or go any path, and there's no p2w features, everything is actually CONVENIENCE, no huge gear advantages or microtransaction paywalls. Group play is really smooth, PvP is awesome, everything in Elder Scrolls Online is almost perfect. Although I do realize the game isn't for everyone, but that goes for any game haha.
Final Verdict: Positive, I would consider it a must buy for any MMO player, because it has something for everyone and tons of different play styles.

Obviously, how one idealizes a certain genre affects how one enjoys a game of that certain genre.  As a game?  ESO is great.  With the subscription cost gone and a MAJOR improvement to the gameplay, this game has the potential to be the best MMORPG.  The quests dont feel linear or mediocre, but rather capture the player with its depth and creativity.  The world may not be as expansive as a game like WoW.  But quality over quantity.  ESO paints the world rather than merely sketching it.  Crafting is now desired rather than dreaded, and gathering resources isnt too difficult.
However ESO fails as a core RPG.  The combat is bland, with only 5 skills and 4 classes to choose from.  When the enemies start to aggro, I start to sigh as the combat is very limited.  Personally, I feel the point of an RPG is to be able to become someone you arent in the real world.  ESO fails to replicate WoW's ability to do so.  While some people argue that ESO is supposed to be flexible, like a mage can be a magical assassin wielding daggers, the skill bar is still limited to only 5 combat skills.  There are a lot of passives that can make combat enjoyable.  But with 5 or less available action skills there is much less options available when combat begins, making fighting a bore.  With MMORPGs like World of Warcraft or Tera there are a lot skills which chain and interact with each other, while the bosses change their behavior making combat much more refreshing.
I am just giving my honest review on ESO.  All I want to do is help the conflicted consumer out with a two sided argument on the game.  I could care less what the fanboys have to flame about.  All in all, if you like the scenery, world interaction then grab it but consider the shortcomings of the game as well.

TO ADRESS THE SWARM OF REVIEWS ABOUT BAD FRAMERATE:
I have had no problems at all with this game's framerate. I get 80+ fps at all times. You can check my specs below, and if you have roughly the same specs and are still getting fps issues, I suggest updating your drivers and maybe even upgrading to windows 10 if you don't already have it (not neccessarily a huge fix, but since upgrading to windows 10 I've had big improvements fps wise).
OVERVIEW:
To start off, I am a huge fan of the first Dishonored. It's amazing gameplay and deep lore kept me interested for the entirety of the 200 or so hours that I've played it. This game absoluetely lives up to the first one's name. I'm very sad that the reviews about the framrate have tarnished this game's reputation already. This game has a great story with tons of content to explore, just like the first game. The different outcomes based on your chaos level has been turned up to 11 and almost every choice you make with targets or random people in the street affects the story. The gameplay itself has been improved too, with it now being much easier to look badass, even with low chaos. Drop assassinations and combat with low chaos are a huge improvement over the sneak choking and sleep darting in the first game. But I've already said a lot in this overview, so lets go to the pros and cons.
PROS:
-Great story
-Tons of secret content
-Combat is fantastic
-Low chaos is way better than the first game
-Robbing black market shops
-Bone charm crafting
-Power upgrade tree makes sense and does not seem like a needless tack on like in a lot of other games
-Reflex passive power
-Great voice acting (I love the Daredevil Netflix show, so seeing two of the cast of that show in this game was awesome)
-Multiple campaign slots
-Idle dialogue for enemies
-Great replayability
-The timepiece level in its entirety is amazing
CONS:
-Short (if you don't explore much). This game took me about 13 hours to complete on my first try. While this is an improvement over the first game's 8 or so hours, it still is a bit short for a solely single player game.
-No mission select screen (WHY?!)
EDIT: The mission select screen has now been added, but it's rather glitchy...
-Preorder bonus is a bit lacking in my opinion, but I guess that doesn't matter now
-Far reach is pretty sh*t
-No Daud
-No whiskey and cigars tonight
ADVICE FOR IF/WHEN YOU GET THE GAME:
-Choose Corvo first if you've played the first Dishonored already. His powers upgrade fantastically and seeing his story continue is a pretty fun experience.
-Play multiple times for the love of god. There is a great replay value in this game and almost every time the outcome of the story will be different.
-Pickpocket Meagan before going on the last mission. You will get her cabin key. Go to her cabin and unlock it. You really will only understand what's in her cabin if you've played the dlcs of the first Dishonored.
-Play low chaos Emily at some point. This is most likely what will be canon in the game's lore.
ENDING STATEMENT:
Play this game. It's really good. There are a few cons, but the pros make up for them. Anyone who liked the first game will love this one.
SPECS:
Superclocked EVGA GTX 1070 Graphics card
Intel i7 6700k Proccesor
16gbs RAM
Windows 10

I absolutely loved this game. It is perhaps the best game I've played this year, and easily in my top 5 favorite survival horror games of all times. Plot wise, the game takes place between Alien and Aliens, but this is essentially a remake of Alien in video game form, and it is highly successful in that.
Since there aren't many cons, I'll start with them: while graphics are all in all OK, character models in cutscenes look rubbery and wet in a weird way (you have to see them to understand). The voice acting is not very good, going to plain awful in certain instances. And yes, the game is a bit too long, and it uses the "we need to go through here but oh, this way is blocked, let's find another path" twist about 300 billion times too many. It might be a good idea to play the last couple of hours in short runs, especially given how difficult the game gets by that point.
And that's the thorny point: unlike most major releases we get nowadays, this is a really hard game to even finish, let alone master. You can kinda fight most enemies, although even then going head to head is usually suicide - protagonist Amanda Ripley is an engineer, not a fighter - but if the Alien even sees you, it's over. As you're going around the ship, he's roaming around looking for you, and this thing wants you DEAD. The game tells you hiding is only a temporary option, and indeed, if you take too long to advance, the Alien will eventually look where you're hiding and will end you. The game's not unfair - if you hide and take care not to make any noise, the Alien will take a long time to find you, but eventually it'll happen. The message is that you should take your time, but there's still a real danger that you can't just avoid by cowering under a table for a few days. It's that sort of realism that really drives the horror home.
There's a lot of other great things about this game that I could go on about for hours, but I don't want to spoil anything. If you like stealth games and have been looking for one to really challenge you, and you're willing to be careful and patient, you will have a blast with this game. If not, this game is probably not for you. I personally loved it, and hope you do too.
DLC Note: I haven't picked up any of the DLC yet, but the game is well worth the money as is.

Alien: Isolation is an immersive experience unlike anything else you will find. Fans of Alien, not AlienS, will love this. And survival horror fans shouldn't be concerned with the familiarity of the franchise if they're looking for something new to play that doesn't hold your hand.
Within about two hours of play time you will begin to see the menace of Sevastopol, a nearly abandoned space station operated by Seegson Communications, and while some have stated the storyline is weak, it stands up well in providing an atmosphere and fits well into the mythos of the Alien movies, especially the notes of betrayal and deceit from corporations like Weiland-Yutani. It also adds to the overall bridge between Alien and Aliens, discussing Ripley's daughter that died prior to her emergence from cryostasis as seen in the second film.
The AI, not just on the Alien itself but on the Working Joes present on the ship, create an intimidating atmosphere, giving the player few options but to locate places to hide and strategically move from one location to the other, and all the while the game's visuals back up that particular aspect. The visuals will not blow you away while you make your escape, except on maybe a few occasions, but overall the game looks great, and plays even better. The simple format they have set up for controls makes surviving a joy to play, and if anything is not to your satisfaction you can change the defaults very easily in the minimalistic pause menu. They've even given you an option to turn down the film grain, which I was happy to see, as it was a bit much when I first started playing.
In short, the game shines as an excellent addition to one of my favorite movie franchises, and on its own is a nervewracking, tense experience that anyone looking for something that isn't a multiplayer shooter should make an effort to play. Don't give up on this, because that just makes you a sitting duck in the vents with your loud beeping motion tracker (one for the fans).

Alien: Isolation is not just a game for Alien fans. It's for anyone who enjoys immersion, smart AI, and a good scare. I had not seen the original film Alien (1979) until the night before playing Alien: Isolation, and I'm glad I did. The level of detail and love given to recreating the atmosphere of the original film by 20th Century Fox and Creative Assembly is admirable if not groundbreaking. There's no tacked on multiplayer. There's no frills. You get to spend about 20 hours trying to survive in what plays like a compilation of everything great in the survival horror genre, but it has its own unique spin where there's just enough action to keep things alive... and scary as hell. I generally consider myself to be desensitized to virtual violence, but I legitimately flinched and yelped when I was suddenly pulled up an airduct and devoured. The Alien's AI is absolutely remarkable, and I was constantly outsmarted by it. That is the icing on the cake to me.
Do yourself a favor and pick up Alien Isolation. It's worth every penny.

I was very hesitant to purchase this due to the number of poor reviews. The handful of mediocre reviews plus the idea of playing without dealing with the card layout pushed me into buying. I was very surprised by how well it played after reading the reviews. I've played the physical game, but not the mobile versions. All in all, I've had no crashes and no difficulties with the interface after a few experimentations.
The tutorial teaches the game, but it does not do the greatest in illustrating how to interact with the game. One example is when choosing which construct to banish, it's unclear if the chosen card kept or banished. Some times the card can be dragged to the discard pile (or draw pile if that mechanic is appropriate). For the complaints about card readability, right-clicking on the card will present it front and center. Left-clicking will return to normal play. For the issue of menus not retracting (ie. opponent menu and "discard from hand" menu), left-clicking on an open space on the menu or the discard pile, respectively, will return to normal play. Worst case, ESCape to the menu and select the "return arrow" at the bottom left.
The game does not go full screen, but it does play at a decent resolution. For me, it's far from a deal breaker. The main improvement I could recommend is adding a more robust tutorial to cover the interface. The best part is, it's a minor technical limitation that can be overcome after a few matches.

I must say this game is quite a surprise. Was planning on playing just another run-of-the-mill ARPG out of boredom but actually got something quite memorable.
I'll start with the negatives first, combat with normal does get repetitive and grindy if you spend too much time on it. There aren't enough crafting options in the game to merit a lot of the grinding. Also wish there was a system to deal with all the extra unuseable material you have once you've completed crafting all the items you can in one dungeon. Art is a mixed-bag. Some are really good while others are just standard. But who really cares about graphics that much in a top-down RPG?
Now for the positive. Firstly, the boss battles are quite fun. They can be extremely hard to just right depending on how leveled up you are. However, the boss battles are never at the point of too easy even if you're at an OP-level because of the way they're setup. You have to have patience and learn from your mistakes. I found a lot of variety in each battle, very reminscent of Ys I and II (though not as hard). The story and score are actually quite good, very surprising for a first time game. I especially liked the way it began when you're first introduced to the character, Senia. Music is a mix of Ys and Castlevania SOTN, which are both really good!
Overall I enjoyed my short journey through this game. Hope the developer makes more games or even a sequel to this one because to be honest, I would've paid for this if given the option.

What's that you say? A free game you say? A free game with a good amount of content in it? A GOOD free game? Sign me up!
First of all, the story. It's good. Not great, but good. Definetly had me engaged, desperate to see the final outcome. It took me a while to get all three endings but the good news is you don't have to play through the entire game again just to see a different ending. Characters are an important part of any good story and Eternal Senia has some ok characters. You get a decent idea of Senia and Magaleta's personalitys and their backstories which really helped add extra emotional impact to the endings (There are three endings and all of them are real tear jerkers). That being said, they didn't feel quiet as fleshed out as they could have been.
Gameplay in Eternal Senia is really good. Combat is quiet a bit different from the usual RPG affair with no turn based combat or anything like that. Instead you simply run into enemies to attack them and use Q, W, E and R to use special attacks. It's a simple system that works very well with the game. The graphics are also nice and I really liked the artstyle. The music was also really great. Not much else to really say there. Um. Yeah. So it's pretty great. And free. Not flawless though, it's a tad repetitive right at the end and the final boss fight was a bit unfair, it's still a good game.
+Reasonable characters
+Decent story
+Very nice visuals
+Great music
+Simple yet good gameplay
-Characters could have been a little more fleshed out
-A tiny bit repetitive towards the end
-Could have done with at least one happy ending

Okay, now to go in depth...
The story of this game. Trust me. If you have any kind of heart at all, it WILL have feels. It will take you on a bit of a rollercoaster of emotions, especially
Gah. It's just too great to spoil.
Only negatives here are:
I'll keep this section relatively short.
The game is
simple to learn and to play.
First of all, there are only like... 13 buttons to learn. And, in truth, you can actually play the game with 10 - three are optional shortcut keys.
There is a crafting system which is pretty neat - it allows you to make a set of armor and a weapon, and upgrade it, using items found off of enemies. Some of the items needed are more rare than others, though, and might take a harsh battle or two to get.
There is a leveling system. There are also four skills, which are learned during the playthrough at different parts of the story, that can be leveled up as well.
And finally, my favorite part of it all... there are NO extra buttons for combat. There are no menus, or options, Apart from skills, in order to attack, you simply WALK INTO your target, initiating your attacks automatically. It's very unique for this style of game, and.. it just works. It makes grinding
easy, as quite a few monsters will actually walk into you, initiating your attack against them as a countermeasure.
It might sound difficult, but really, it's as simple as knowing how to walk around.
On the Level Design, I had to get
nit picky to find anything wrong.
There's not much to say against it. Everything blends really, really well, and the levels are set up in a very believable, very beautiful manner.
However, with trees in particular, one can spot some areas where the trees do not layer so well. This is noticeable any time that the texture changes from the single tree tiles to the tree cover tiles.
HOWEVER, this is due to a limitation in RPGm, and
the developer's error, so, I'll let this one slide. However, I did still knock off a tenth of a point, because there
a very obscure way of fixing this, but you have to do entirely too much to make it look neat, and this error did not happen often, so I won't be harsh.
Overall, I have to reccomend this game to EVERYBODY who loves RPGs and has a heart.
This game was developed by a single person in a single year, and, while there are only a little over 4 hours of gameplay (on a completionist run), and the translations are not perfect (but they are MORE than understandable),  every second of that gameplay is fantastic. I'd love to see more of this story, more by this developer, and more games like this period.
All that aside, definitely give this game a go, if you're looking for a genuinely emotion-stimulating story.
Or just looking to kill 4 hours.
Because there isn't a better way out there.

APB is one of my favorite games of all time, it is unlike every other shooter i've ever played, ive played many shooters altogether and the majority of them play the same, one thing i've always been good at is picking up new games and geting the hang of them quickly, APB was an exception, i first joined in 2012 and i remember my first missions vividly, i lost 99% percent of the missions i played and the game still placed me in gold, which was confusing, It wasnt till later on that i realized that the people i were playing against mostly were veterans of the game. even so , i enjoyed the combat that APB had to offer and wanted to improve right away and thus my relationship with APB began.
firstly
APB is not a good game
it is buggy,
servers have 33-40ms ,
it is unfair (missions)
Open world game (+low population=dead)
poor matchmaking ( even worse BECAUSE of the low pop)
poor vehicle physics
poor community
Some people receive hit registry issues(Some are worse then others)
poor company
People cheat (aimbots/wallhacks)
But..
It is a unique shooter
what do i mean by this? the majority of the guns in APB take 5 shots or more to kill, it isnt the same like other shooters where the objective in aiming is to place your crosshair on the enemy's head first before they do, infact, there are no headshots in APB, and no guns that kill in 1 shot either (minus the rocket launcher/grenade launcher)  the type of aim you will be practicing mostly is aiming center mass as much as possible and keeping your crosshair on your enemy as much as possible while taking cover to make you a smaller target and using teamwork to pinch enemies and move into areas.
to add to this Guns are very situational in APB , SMGs and shotguns are great at CQC but cannot kill people at further ranges, other long range guns thrive at their respective ranges and suffer at closer ranges, some weapons are more flexible , others are not.
APB has great customization
APB has argueably the greatest customization to ever be, Ive seen many people make outfits to make them look like Ronald Mcdonald or Scooby doo characters or something unique all together, not only this but APB has great symbol customization which you can apply to your character, clothes , or vehicle, and you can share the symbol with your friends, or sell them to the rest of the community by putting it for grabs on the auction/market.
Ontop of this you can make your own songs in the APB studio maker and themes, which are a 5 second tune which will play for your victim that you killed right after they die, there are also skins for your guns that arent bad. but all in all APB has great customization
APB is NOT pay to win
APB isn't pay to win, i have thrown hundreds of dollars into the game and i have to say this has been a touchy subject over the time ive spent playing APB because honestly i was one of the players who had the troublemaker when it was first released and it was overpowered, however this was changed within a month. Most guns that I consider overpowered are obtainable through other methods in the game without paying real money for. APB is NOT pay to win but there are plenty of weapons that are quite broken, this is a matter of opinion but heres my list if you're curious:

My first review for this game was a troll review that a friend and I found really funny but I think people took it way too seriously so here's a serious one. In this review I will be explaining what elder scrolls online is, why you should buy it, and why I still play it even after so long (I used to launch it from the launcher not steam).
Elder Scrolls Online is an MMORPG made by Zenimax Online Studios, referred to as fans as ZOS. There are 4... I mean 5 classes counting the new morrowind expansion in Elder Scrolls Online. These classes are nightblade, sorceror, dragonknight, templar, and warden if you have the morrowind expansion.
Nightblade is an assassin class that focuses on huge burst damage and execute damage, making them good for PvP but not very ideal for endgame PvE trial groups and guilds.
Sorceror is an extremely overpowered cla- I mean a class that focuses on doing really high dps and is a lot of fun to play haha. Sorceror focuses on shock damage, or physical damage if you choose the stamina route.
Dragonknight is a class that has a lot more tanky abilities allowing you to take more hits before going down. They focus on fire damage for the most part, but do have some poison abilities as stamina morphs. Dragonknight is extremely good at immobolizing enemies, making them one of the best classes for tanking.
Templar is also an extremely overpo- Whoops xD. Meant to say Templar is a class that focuses on fire damage and magic damage and some physical damage too should you choose some stamina morphs here and there. Templar is one of the most fun classes to play in my opinion, because not only can you heal and provide your allies with support abilities and take a lot of damage, but also do a lot of damage.
Warden is a class that focuses around nature. You can summon animals to help you, heal your friends using tree magic and stuff, and even comes with a few tanky abilities. I haven't played too much of Warden so far but I would say he's like Templar and Dragonknight combined, making Warden a lot of fun to use.
The combat in ESO is pretty smooth, like most MMOs you have to slot abilities on your combat bars. A combat bar has 5 slots for any ability, and you have two combat bars. You can have different abilities on each bar, along with different weapons. However, there is an extra slot next to your combat bar where you can put an ultimate ability. Ultimate is generated during combat. You can dodge roll, block, bash, heavy attack, and light attack while fighting with your abilities which makes combat seem really alive, unlike some MMOs where your character barely moves while you press 1, 2, or E or something.
PvP (Player vs Player combat etc)- PvP is awesome in the elder scrolls online. You don't lose anything besides honor (lol) and you can always respawn to fight another guy. The PvP area is Cyrodil but you can PvP anywhere if you get permission from the other player by inviting them to a duel and having them accept the duel invite. Cyrodil is huge and has lots of castles you can take over using siege weapons, but other players will be there to defend their castles so I recommend playing pretty safe unless you want to respawn and ride all the way back to the enemy's castle. None of your abilities change but your health will go up. Your abilities do 1/2 less damage to players, this system is in place so you don't get one shotted.
Gear: Gear is super cool in the Elder Scrolls Online. There are tons of sets with cool passives and abilities and procs for you to use, and any class can use any weapon or any armor. Some armor and weapons are locked by level. Using motifs you can craft different styles of armor or make armor or a weapon that looks a lot different then someone elses' armor or weapon (Unless they use the same motif lol). You can also dye your armor and shield if you have one.
Gathering Materials etc: Gathering is okay in ESO, nothing special but definetely far from great. You can't chop down any tree you see for wood, only certain logs you see on the ground. You can't mine any rock for ore, only certain rocks. And you can't gather any plant, only certain plants. For me, this kind of ruins the immersion.
Groups: Group play is awesome in Elder Scrolls Online. You can adventure with your friends and the best part is that your level doesn't really matter when you adventure with your friends because mobs are set to your level. So if your level 49 and your friend is level 37 and your fighting the same enemy, your friend will be fighting a level 37 enemy and you'll be fighting a level 49 version of that enemy but it's still the same enemy if that makes sense.
Graphics: The graphics in the elder scrolls online are really awesome, some MMOs out there might have better graphics than the elder scrolls onlines' graphics but at least you don't lag out a ton once you enter a town like some of the MMOs out there.
P2W/Pay for convenience stuff in ESO: Unlike most MMOs where you can purchase costumes that give you buffs, or a pet that gathers tons of stuff really fast, ESO has free pets you can obtain from ingame quests along with free ingame costumes, and even a free skeleton polymorph that comes from a quest too. Costumes and pets don't give you any extra benefit in ESO. They don't hide your nametag or give you special buffs/advantages *cough* Black Desert *cough* lol. Elder Scrolls Online does have DLC and an expansion but the most of the gear given from these expansions can be bought/traded from other players, and none of the gear is broken, although you could argue the velidreth set is a bit too good right now. If a lot of dead enemies are in one room, you can loot them all just by clicking E and it searches all the nearby bodies, instead of having to pick up the loot from each enemy individiually or have a pet that costs a lot of money pick it up for you. You can pay for costumes and pets and mounts using crowns (ingame currency obtained through spending real money) but these are cosmetic and offer no advantage. You can buy mounts using ingame gold at the stable for fairly cheap, and you can get free costumes, pets, and polymorphs from just playing through quests and the game itself. The only small problem I have is that you can buy riding lessons to speed up your horses' progress (your horse can be taught 1 new skill a day, it's kinda complicated to explain) but this can be done ingame. You can also pay for vampire and werewolf bites, but these can also be obtained legit ingame, you can have another player bite you for free or just go up to a wild werewolf or wild vampire.
Conclusion: Elder Scrolls Online is probably my favorite MMO out of all the MMOs I've played. Their support team gets back to you really fast, the combat is pretty smooth, The gear isn't class locked, Any class can do any role or go any path, and there's no p2w features, everything is actually CONVENIENCE, no huge gear advantages or microtransaction paywalls. Group play is really smooth, PvP is awesome, everything in Elder Scrolls Online is almost perfect. Although I do realize the game isn't for everyone, but that goes for any game haha.
Final Verdict: Positive, I would consider it a must buy for any MMO player, because it has something for everyone and tons of different play styles.

Obviously, how one idealizes a certain genre affects how one enjoys a game of that certain genre.  As a game?  ESO is great.  With the subscription cost gone and a MAJOR improvement to the gameplay, this game has the potential to be the best MMORPG.  The quests dont feel linear or mediocre, but rather capture the player with its depth and creativity.  The world may not be as expansive as a game like WoW.  But quality over quantity.  ESO paints the world rather than merely sketching it.  Crafting is now desired rather than dreaded, and gathering resources isnt too difficult.
However ESO fails as a core RPG.  The combat is bland, with only 5 skills and 4 classes to choose from.  When the enemies start to aggro, I start to sigh as the combat is very limited.  Personally, I feel the point of an RPG is to be able to become someone you arent in the real world.  ESO fails to replicate WoW's ability to do so.  While some people argue that ESO is supposed to be flexible, like a mage can be a magical assassin wielding daggers, the skill bar is still limited to only 5 combat skills.  There are a lot of passives that can make combat enjoyable.  But with 5 or less available action skills there is much less options available when combat begins, making fighting a bore.  With MMORPGs like World of Warcraft or Tera there are a lot skills which chain and interact with each other, while the bosses change their behavior making combat much more refreshing.
I am just giving my honest review on ESO.  All I want to do is help the conflicted consumer out with a two sided argument on the game.  I could care less what the fanboys have to flame about.  All in all, if you like the scenery, world interaction then grab it but consider the shortcomings of the game as well.

I spent 32 hours on my first playthrough of this game. I loved the original and was more than happy to purchase the sequal but I kept my hopes low in case the game didn't live up to it's name.
Luckily it did. Although there were some initial performance issues many have been drastically reduced or removed, granting me a 20+ fps boost if not more. It's still not perfect but performance is not a reason to give up on this title.
As far as gameplay, I've beaten the game once as Corvo playing full stealth, nonlethally, without powers, on the hardest difficulty. This run took me 32 hours and it revealed exactly how much thought went into the levels. The world is filled with back alleys, rooftops, hidden paths, and any number of other interesting scenarios to explore as well as some excellently-written lore pieces and notes. I don't normally like reading newspapers scattered in a game but Dishonored 2 made it worth it. Every mission was interesting and even my least favorite was still an amazing presentation of a level.
My one gripe is this, well, two things. As a small point there are a few lines of dialogue that seem unnatural or poorly read, but this is common in most games so I won't make a big deal of it. More importantly, because the game allows you to play without powers, there is almost always a way to reach an objective without them. This isn't a bad thing in and of itself but in playing again with powers some of the challenges now seem far too easy or not even like challenges at all. What previously took an hour now takes a minute with a few blinks or far-reaches. This might just be a result of my choosing to play without powers first but powers do certainly cheapen many of the games more challenging areas.
All in all I loved Dishonored 2, it might be my favorite game of the year. Consider it if you're a fan of the franchise or someone looking for a study in excellent level and mission design. Even though it's not perfect, Dishonored 2 is a game I'll be pouring much more time into and I'll be enjoying every minute.

This game has received tonnes of flak from most total war fans, and to an extent they are right. Many of the old operating systems from Shogun 2 have been replaced with new ones with arkward interface, and the civil war system, while adding a new dimesnion to the game and providing a mid to late game challenge, is still very much in infancy, an idea I hope to see improved. However much of the criticism it has received is unjust. After Shogun 2, eveeryone expected some new marvel of programming and AI software that simply doesn't exist. There are some glitches, but on the whole the combat system is incredible. The grapics and combat animations are much better than in the first Total War to use such programming techniques (Empire) and it is ridiculous to expect programmers to be able to iron out every glitch and allow soldiers to interact with each other like they did in the much simpler (although no doubt still hidiously complicated) Rome animations and anyone who critisises the AI has had no contact with programming, and should at least acknowledge how difficult the programming is, bearing in mind it must be able to generate scenarios itself, rather than having them programmed in. It has added a huge amount of detail to the battles and the campiagn is starting to add the element of internal politics. While I preferred Shogun 2, this is still a very fun game, and I look forward to seeing a new Total War title in which the restraints of modern technology here are somewhat alleiviated. Like Empire, it is a testing of new systems as well as a very good game

This game does have problems.  It's a port from mobile platforms, and thus does not have the options that a real PC version needs (such as being able to set your screen resoultion).  But, barring a few unusual circumstances, the game does function well.  You can play it online with friends in a turn-based version, even if your friends use iOS or Android.  You can play it alone vs computer players with a couple difficulty settings.  You can play local multi-player, with a pause between players for hot seat action.  It comes with three large sets, three smaller expansions, and four promo sets.
Really, a majority of the complaints stem from the fact that it's a port and not designed for PC users well.  But the fact that it's a port means it does actually run pretty well.  For most of the game play circumstances, you won't really notice any problems.  The problems that DO exist, they are trying to correct, but it's not in the most timely of fashions.
I do still recommend this game though, if you like deckbuilding games.  It's very fun, very flexible, and great to play with friends - even if it can take weeks to finish one game.

Although being heartbroken several times, my love for the Alien franchise runs deep. After the latter two films, many spinoffs and several mediocre video games, I have always yearned for the experience I felt when I saw the film for the first time. Thankfully Alien: Isolation provided me with what I have always wanted.
Survival Of The Fittest- "It was when I audibly squealed at the screen that I knew this game had gotten to me in the best way possible."
Part of what makes Alien: Isolation so refreshing is how powerless you feel throughout the game. It's not that you don't have weapons at your disposal- you actually accumulate many throughout the game (very similar to metroid)- but it's the idea that your weapons are tools to help you survive and not tools to kill. That's what is most frightening about the game. You feel vulnerable: a human trying to survive and eradicate such horror. Exactly as Ellen Ripley had to do aboard the Nostromo. Knowing that the Alien would kill me instantly upon being alerted by my presence built enormous suspense with each encounter.  It was when I audibly squealed at the screen that I knew this game had gotten to me in the best way possible.
Future's Past-
One aspect that was so beautiful about Alien, 2001: Space Odyssey and many other films is how they made familiar technology feel as if it was a part of the distant future. The set pieces, props, everything had an eerie but familiar feel to it. In Alien: Isolation I found the set pieces to be just as beautiful. CRT displays humming and crackling, the big beautiful set pieces that always felt claustrophobic. If the developers wanted to recreate the visual style Ridley Scott had produced some 30 years ago they couldn't have done a better job of it. It felt familiar, beautiful and downright, horrifyingly exhausting.
That brings me to my only complaint. Towards the end I felt as if I was exhausted from survival after all of those hours. Passively going from cover to cover and vent to vent escaping the creature's grasp narrowly each time. You could say I felt like Amanda Ripley. However, at some point I was hoping to see a turning point in which Amanda's character would become the badass her mother is famous for.
However, it's a precisely crafted sequel to a film beloved by many. The game relys on creating horror in vulnerability and the idea that there is no where to run. Because out of any vent the ♥♥♥♥♥ may come.

Doesn't reinvent the wheel when it comes to gameplay. You'll be doing chores while trying to stay alive and figure out the fate of your mother. It's not a bad story but not a great one. Combat is serviceable but the focus of this game is 100% on stealth and exploration.
The reason this game stands out is because it is dripping with atmosphere. It feels like you're stepping into the world established by the first film so many years ago. If you like Alien, if you like the films and the Xenomorph, then you owe it to yourself to jump into this game.

Most of the time, when you play a game based on a movie, you get something that was borne out of the movie studio's merchandising efforts.  Like a crappy action figure, it's made of plastic and probably won't occupy you for very long.  But at least with the action figure, some imagination could extend its useful life.
Alien: Isolation represents what happens when a game resulting from a movie is not just a means to increase revenue, but an end unto itself.  A work of fiction that can stand tall next to the masterpiece from which it drew its inspiration.
Never have I seen a game that was so meticulously faithful to its source material.  From the green-screen consoles, to the misty hallways, and yellow warning lights; Alien: Isolation possesses an Analog Physicality that brings the 1979 film to life once again.  While most games would have replaced the decades old tech with iPads and holograms, Isolation considers the retro tech an asset to the story.  And it works--just seeing the monocrhome mainframe displays and grainy video lends its own feeling of uneasiness.
And then there's the Xenomorph.  The most random, unpredictable nemesis ever to appear in a video game.  Sometimes, hiding in a locker works fine, and it will walk right by.  Other times, it will hear something nearby and charge after it.  But others, it might hear or smell something in that locker where you're hiding...and take a closer look.  It's not knowing which of these scenarios will come to pass that keeps you on your toes.
In addition to amazing AI on the part of the Xenomorph, the game astounded me again and again with its command of storytelling.  Many of these sequences pay homage to the film, but the best ones take you into new and terrifying territory, to the point that I believe that Alien: Isolation is the scariest game ever made.
Now I must admit, the game is quite difficult.  And there were times in Alien: Isolation that I found very frustrating--from a  few unnecessarily hard to find objectives to having to be *just* the right distance away from a vent to trigger the animation to enter it...with an alien on my tail.
But whatever you have to do--whether you play it on easy or Google a walkthrough when you get stuck--make sure you do not miss it.  Alien: Isolation is arguably the best movie-inspired game ever made.

Alien: Isolation is a welcomed addition to the "SURVIVAL HORROR" catagory aswell as the under-appreciated "STEALTH"  genre, which has become less and less prevalent in main-stream gaming over the last decade. The visual and audio presentation is "TOP-NOTCH" giving the game an authentic atmosphere remeniscent of the original motion picture "ALIEN". Character control is fluid and easy to learn and the games "QTE" sequences are kept simple and to a minimum with an ample amount of time for input and never seem to impede player progression with elaborate  button combinations.
Player interactions with the titles main antagonist "THE ALIEN" are frightening, even more so because the player is given no option or resource to permenatly dispatch the beast, but rather given tools to either distract or ward off direct encounters aswell as enviromental options that allow the player to evade detection, such as "LOCKERS" and being able to crawl under "DESKS". This aspect of the gameplay mechanic adds a great deal of tension and anxiety to the experience, leaving the player feeling helpless and reluctant to conduct overt actions.
The titles difficulty is unprecedented aswell. Though there are three levels of difficulty to choose from, "EASY" being a more cinematic and steady paced experience allowing the player more room for error when dealing with the "ALIEN" which keeps the story content flowing more naturally, "HARD" on the other hand is an arduous and lengthy ordeal that requires "QUICK" and "CLEVER" thinking and no small amount of "PATIENCE". This however can be off-putting and frustrating to the more casual player base and because of this I wouldn't recommend this title to everyone.
Alien: Isolations story was thoughtfully written aswell and all the events and scenario's that occur between the games relativly calm begining to the titles "controversial" end were exciting and interesting never once leaving me feel dissapointed in the experience. A truely unique title with a personality of it's own.
I give it a 9/10 and recommend Alien: Isolation to any fan of the series and the stealth/survival horror genre.

Despite my initial doubts, I give my recommendation to Alien: Isolation with some provisos:
1) Unless you are super good at video games, play it on easy. On hard, you die so much that there's no time for tension to build, and tension is this game's bread and butter.
2) Play it in the dark with headphones. That should be a given for a horror game, but it's worth it, because again, tension.
3) Don't stay up until 1:30 am playing it. Yes, the save points are pretty far apart and you might have to repeat some stuff, but it's just not worth it.
4) Don't go into it expecting anything but what it is: slow, tense, and stealthful. This isn't a shooter, and it isn't (mostly) about jump scares.
5) Make sure you have a copy of your favourite Alien movie (any of them except 4) close at hand, because you're going to want to watch them when you're done. Which is what I am off to do.

Game's pretty good but if you're transitioning into this from Dark Souls 1, there's the off chance you'll dislike this experience as some of the elements which make DS 1 enjoyable won't be found here. There are quite a few flaws with the game design in my opinion, such as weird placement of bonfires and the inflated number of bosses boasting quantity over quality. A lot of the bosses also feel very similar to the ones used in DS1, with maybe a few "♥♥♥♥ you" twists in it where poisons are added to the field or maybe random extra small mobs. There aren't really any infamous bosses like the Capra Demon, though some interesting ones can appear from time to time like the Mirror Knight where players who leave a red soap stone near the boss can bust through the mirror shield and fight you with the boss (though these are few and far in between). Same can be said for the locations, where super interesting areas like the Dragon Aerie can be found only after an extended period of play time (where-as in DS 1 if you knew your way around you could really get to some cool areas quickly.) Perhaps the most annoying areas would be PvP combat (and at times PvE) where hit detection seems more off than usual (due to lag compensation or what not?) as well as weird physics, where even the smallest ledge of a wall will stop your swing yet an AI will be able to swing through it freely. Most of the PvE is focused on "swarming" you with enemies, where 1v1 duels are less frequent and each enemy doesn't have that same sense of excitement (i.e. Silver knights or the giants in Anor Londo). A lot of the enemies also "cheap" you with 1-hit kills, like the infamous suicide-bombing mummies whose existance make very little sense. NG+ system is kind of lame as well, adding in random red phantoms to boost the challenge to an unrealistic degree, aiming for difficulty without fairness as they tend to have infinite stamina and kick like a mule (dropping a vitality-focused build to 50% health in one hit at full havels is a big "wtf?").
PvP has perhaps been screwed over the most really, where there are no red eye orbs (only cracked ones) whilst the rest are in really setup areas with red soap stone / dragon eye summoning (potentially leading to ganks). The system feels very hand-holdy and you won't experience the same freedom of PvP as you did in DS1, nor will you come across a particularly cool PvP area like the forest in DS1 (rather the PvP areas can feel gimmicky and more annoying than enjoyable, particularly door of pharros for the rat convenant). The bell tower is okay, but being butt♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by three people at a time isn't really that fun. As magic is buffed in this game even more so than the first (like wtf why?) the meta seems to be casting or using greatswords (which basically break hit detection >_>). The magic doesn't have anything that cool either and it takes relatively little effort to get some of the good stuff like crystal soul spear etc (rather than kill a boss and trade its soul, you just find a vendor with x stats to buy it from them). Some of the cool miracles also seem to be absent, like the awesome-looking gravelord sword dance. Poise is also broken, where instead of "not being stunned" it's now "stun recovery" so you might have a faster recovery with higher poise, but you'll still be mini-stunned. Being stunned to death and having your attacks being cancelled whilst in full havels swinging a greatsword is no fun and makes little sense (as the heavy armor... sort of makes up for the long swing time...), when even a ladle can stun you in one or two hits. Like seriously, fix that♥♥♥♥♥♥ revamp the system already.
The best part of this game would be its co-op. Aside from the fact that it's somewhat of a pain to get the white soap stone (and that the story for it doesn't really make sense? I mean, sunlight knight for jolly co-op, random pate for... why?) the co-op has been vastly improved. Summoning friends is easier with the ring that makes it easier for two people to connect assuming they chose the same god on the ring. You can hang about in an area with a white phantom for a long time, even if the area boss is dead(?) and white phantoms can drink estus this time around, making jolly co-op all the more jolly.
Story-wise the game offers a very similar story to DS 1, where you try and undo the curse that makes you undead. It's not really innovative the second time around and revisiting this style really wears it out. The game's story also feels weaker this time where some of the developments aren't clear until you progress much further into the game. It would have been much better had DS 2 created a new world with new story / source of motivation for the player to continue, as I felt like completing this game out of respect for its franchise rather than out of enjoyment like I did in DS 1.
I recommend getting this game to play with a friend, or just picking up DS 1 and playing that instead. For a pure "solo" dark souls experience, this one might be a bit of a let down when compared to its predecessor. It is kind of a disappointment considering I enjoyed DS 1 quite a lot and spent hunreds of hours in it. IMO having Miyazaki leave and work on Bloodborne really hurt the potential of DS2. Then again, it creates a new game to look forward to.

A free amateur game, it carries the sorts of obvious creator love for the story elements you'd expect of a passion project, with a "use whatever art/game assets and scripts that could be downloaded for free" you'd also expect.  It's definitely more for those who enjoy an interesting premise over AAA polish, because its shallow combat system isn't up to snuff with mainstream gaming.  Recommended only for those who enjoy the story premise, alone.
The game is basically a long corridor filled with cutscenes (including a ton of flashbacks that fill you in on the context of why you're doing all this,) about a young heroine (Senia) and her quest to save her adoptive family member (Magaleta, which was probably supposed to be "Margret".)
The gameplay is relatively weak.  This game uses an "innovative move-to-attack" system, which basically means that if you run into an enemy, you deal damage to it, and it deals damage to you.  If an enemy runs into you, you deal damage to it, and it deals damage to you.  Facing and timing don't matter, so it kind of renders moot most tactical considerations, and just renders everything a matter of ramming everything until your HP gets low, then running away until your HP regens.  There are no healing or mana potions in this game, which does make things a little more tricky, and so you rely upon the automatic regen to survive, and it doesn't work if you aren't fighting, so generally, there are two modes: go ahead and let enemies ram you, or evade until you get enough HP back to go back to the ramming.  It's just too simplistic a system for me to really enjoy, but I guess you can't expect too much from a freeware amateur game.
The story, meanwhile, has some positive points.  The game focuses upon Senia's relationship with her adoptive "big sis" Magaleta, and if you're into strong-willed female main characters, that's pretty much what this whole game is built around delivering.  It also features some well-drawn art, although most faces are just variations on what you can see in the previews.
That said, the story has some negative marks, as well: ... Senia... truly deserves the title... "Captain Ellipses"...! Seriously, nearly every line of dialogue she posseses has AT LEAST one ellipses in it, she frequently has lines that consist entirely of "..." followed by "...?" then "...!" and even the narration bursts to overflowing with excessive punctuation.  Practically the only speaking companion Senia gets, as well, is simply named "Little Fairy".  Seriously, you couldn't be bothered to give her a name? She probably has the second most lines of spoken dialogue in the game, and she's the character just referred to by generic title.  (They even gave a name to the Fairy Queen, and then they just keep calling her "Fairy Queen"...)
In general, it's a free amateur actionRPG RPG Maker game, and certainly better than most in its category, worth playing if you enjoy indie titles for the sheer flavor, but it's not going to be anyone's Secret of Mana.

I have been waiting for a golf sim, and the early access of Perfect Golf seems to be headed in the right direction. Obviously, with an early access, there are things that are needed and things that are fine as is. So far, I can say confidently that the heart is beating in this game. Visually it's appealing and the game-play engine itself is a good start. Some of the issues at this point, I hesitate to mention, again because I suspect every feature and tweak I would like to see has been accounted for by the developers and they are working on it. That being said:
The menus need work and making changes to the settings on the fly is clunky. The types of shots are limited at the moment and needs attention, as does the power meter and putting helpers. Right now, they don't really make much sense and seem arbitrary. There's no way to punch shots through or accurately alter spin the way the real game allows. The power meters and putting grids also are somewhat of a mystery and don't seem to be designed to let the player really know exact measurements. This may be on purpose, but still this is a sim and not real life, so we need some way to benchmark our swings and fades, etc...
It needs a player history system so I can go back and review my previous rounds, and of course, it needs more courses. I hope most of all, the developers are going to be able to make a deal with the PGA for rights to their courses and tournament play, but even if it remains simply a non-PGA golf simulation, that's fine on its own. If you want to learn the game and progress without getting bored, I think this will be a good title someday. I hope it is sooner than later.
added: May 5, 2016:
Now that the supposed general release has been pushed out, I felt I need to comment further on this game. As I said in my earlier review, the heart of a good game was there, and I was hoping Perfect Parrellel was working hard on the serious issues in the engine. Apparently, they are working harder on the marketing and getting Jack Nicklaus to put his name on a game that is FAR, FAR from finished.
I'm wondering if the makers of this game couldn't care less about the gamers in Steam and are more interested in the Golf Simulators out there than can use this software. Because right now, us gamers are getting no love from the game.
A few points for the developers, which I hope read this:
...The putting mechinism is simply awful. Damn near unplayable. It's swing mechanics are inconsistent and clunky. There is no context to the power of the swing and they give little to no credible way to read the greens. It needs serious re-tooling before this game can be considered top notch.
...there is no way to craft shots and the chipping and pitching is abysmal and inconsitent. You'll never hit the same shot twice in the same conditions.
...the swing meter, which is the only way most gamers are going to play this game, is baffling and inconsistent. it gives no power context either but even if it did, you can never re-create shots no matter how hard you try.
I'm holding out hope this will improve, but if this is now considered a released game, I'm not holding my breath that major changes to the engine are coming.
updated: June 17
...a few of the patches and fixes are helping on some of the issues I pointed out in May. Putting seems to have normalized somewhat. It's getting better about giving enough clues to read a green. Still, I think the grid needs to be smaller squares and the BLI is a little clunky, but better.
...still though, chipping and pitching are so frustrating. Practice is one thing, but inconsistency in the UI and the game engine is something else. Pitching and chipping still is a nightmare of randomness. Random in that you never ever know how your chip or pitch is going to react in any situation. it's impossible to recreate a shot that has the same variables and the engine will flatout fail you by over shooting or undershooting even though the power, lie and variables might be the same. NEEDS ATTENTION NOW.
...crafting shots is still a major problem. the shot maker function just doesn't work for lowering or raising your trajectory. It works left and right, but not up and down.
...still worth it, as this is a simulation and not an arcade, ,and as long as they don't morph into a pay to win model, I will continue to recommend it.

This game has received tonnes of flak from most total war fans, and to an extent they are right. Many of the old operating systems from Shogun 2 have been replaced with new ones with arkward interface, and the civil war system, while adding a new dimesnion to the game and providing a mid to late game challenge, is still very much in infancy, an idea I hope to see improved. However much of the criticism it has received is unjust. After Shogun 2, eveeryone expected some new marvel of programming and AI software that simply doesn't exist. There are some glitches, but on the whole the combat system is incredible. The grapics and combat animations are much better than in the first Total War to use such programming techniques (Empire) and it is ridiculous to expect programmers to be able to iron out every glitch and allow soldiers to interact with each other like they did in the much simpler (although no doubt still hidiously complicated) Rome animations and anyone who critisises the AI has had no contact with programming, and should at least acknowledge how difficult the programming is, bearing in mind it must be able to generate scenarios itself, rather than having them programmed in. It has added a huge amount of detail to the battles and the campiagn is starting to add the element of internal politics. While I preferred Shogun 2, this is still a very fun game, and I look forward to seeing a new Total War title in which the restraints of modern technology here are somewhat alleiviated. Like Empire, it is a testing of new systems as well as a very good game

I spent 32 hours on my first playthrough of this game. I loved the original and was more than happy to purchase the sequal but I kept my hopes low in case the game didn't live up to it's name.
Luckily it did. Although there were some initial performance issues many have been drastically reduced or removed, granting me a 20+ fps boost if not more. It's still not perfect but performance is not a reason to give up on this title.
As far as gameplay, I've beaten the game once as Corvo playing full stealth, nonlethally, without powers, on the hardest difficulty. This run took me 32 hours and it revealed exactly how much thought went into the levels. The world is filled with back alleys, rooftops, hidden paths, and any number of other interesting scenarios to explore as well as some excellently-written lore pieces and notes. I don't normally like reading newspapers scattered in a game but Dishonored 2 made it worth it. Every mission was interesting and even my least favorite was still an amazing presentation of a level.
My one gripe is this, well, two things. As a small point there are a few lines of dialogue that seem unnatural or poorly read, but this is common in most games so I won't make a big deal of it. More importantly, because the game allows you to play without powers, there is almost always a way to reach an objective without them. This isn't a bad thing in and of itself but in playing again with powers some of the challenges now seem far too easy or not even like challenges at all. What previously took an hour now takes a minute with a few blinks or far-reaches. This might just be a result of my choosing to play without powers first but powers do certainly cheapen many of the games more challenging areas.
All in all I loved Dishonored 2, it might be my favorite game of the year. Consider it if you're a fan of the franchise or someone looking for a study in excellent level and mission design. Even though it's not perfect, Dishonored 2 is a game I'll be pouring much more time into and I'll be enjoying every minute.

Just wanted to quickly say that trying to give CA the benfeit of the doubt on this game one has only left me sorely dissapointed. I've easily put over a thousand hours into the Total war Franchise, playing every total war game from the start with Shogun Total War. This game feels nothing like those games.
For Starters the combat feels so different from what had drawn me in originally. Battles take forever with units jostling for position until the kills animations finally commence and watching upclose in a cinematic view disappoints, even with a Spartan unit fighting a Macedonian General. Calvary Charges no longer have that devastating impact into the backs of enemy troops, Unless its the weak first tier troops. Theres no excitment in the battles for me anymore I start to get bored in the midst of it. Troops I expect to do well get run over, or my formations become pointless mass' of men where its just a wait and see instead of reforming and putting reserves in where needed. Combat now feels dull and no longer strategic.
The Campaign map has me sorely dissapointed. They went from the original iteration of Shogun 1 to Shogun 2 where each game had that amazing total war feel. Not Rome 2 However, regardless of how much I want this game to be amazing. Slime Rancher may seem like a very basic game, but there's so much more underneath the surface. You play as Beatrix LeBeau, who got passed down an old ranch and has to take care of it from now on. As you start the ranch is broken and empty, so it's your job to make enough coins to fix everything up. Slimes can be found nearby the ranch where you can find four different slimes to start your ranch with. You will discover more as you unlock new areas to explore. You can also become part of the 7Zee rewards club where you can unlock new colors for your equipment and ranch as well as running boots, more health, cool accessoires for your ranch and even a jetpack!
But if you want to unlock everything and find all of the slimes, one thing is most important: coins! Slimes will give you so called plorts once you feed them. For each food product, a normal slime will give you one plort while a largo slime will give you two. If you feed the slimes their one favorite food, they will give you double the amount. The price of each plort changes from slime to slime and from day to day as there's a market whose prices change each day.
Slimes are kept in corals and while they are not limited in numbers, you'll surely reach a point where there are too many slimes to keep trapped in one of them. Corals can be extended, darkened and demolished; you can also add a music box and an auto feeder (and auto food collector) to keep them happy. But no matter how secure your coral is, slimes will always find a way out if you keep way too many of them trapped in one.
There are currently about 15 different colors of slimes in the game and they come in normal, "largo" and "gordo". Some slimes require different living conditions, as some can only be kept in water or are sensitive to light. Each slime has a different diet; meat, fruit and veggie. Meat is won by chickens who you can breed as well, fruits and vegetables can be grown in their own garden. If a slime goes hungry for too long, it'll become very unhappy and some of them go feral start attacking you. You will also find several feral slimes in the wild, who can be tamed by feeding them as well.
A normal slime turns into a largo one if you feed them the plort of another slime. For example, if you give a pink slime a Tabby plort, it will turn into a giant pink cat. Slimes will always eat whatever leftover plort they can find (though it won't feed them, they'll just transform), so make sure to only keep one slime type per coral.
Largos don't require more food, but they're double as big as regular slimes so you can't keep as many of them save in one coral. I'd suggest farming largos though as feeding them their favorite food will result in four plorts per food item. If you feed a largo slime a completely different plort, they will turn into a terrible rainbow tarr who will attack you and kill every slime on sight. They can be instantly killed by a drop of water. You can avoid them by switching over to the casual mode, which will be available with the full release.
Gordo slimes cannot be created. You will find them in the wild and they will usually sit on a portal or some kind of treasure. You will have to feed them as well, but most of them require up to 50 food products before they disappear.
Some portals will bring you to new places, while others offer you a quicker way home. Some gordo slimes will also leave keys which are necessary to uncover more of the area and discover even more treasured places. You definitely won't get bored exploring the world of Slime Rancher, especially not with a jetpack!
Other than Slime Ranching, you can also unlock a Laboratory for 10.000 coins. There you can create stuff to farm for resources and create cool new gadgets that'll help you become a better (or cooler!) Slime Rancher.
I recommend this game for anyone looking for a cute little farming game with a giant world to explore!

Most of the time, when you play a game based on a movie, you get something that was borne out of the movie studio's merchandising efforts.  Like a crappy action figure, it's made of plastic and probably won't occupy you for very long.  But at least with the action figure, some imagination could extend its useful life.
Alien: Isolation represents what happens when a game resulting from a movie is not just a means to increase revenue, but an end unto itself.  A work of fiction that can stand tall next to the masterpiece from which it drew its inspiration.
Never have I seen a game that was so meticulously faithful to its source material.  From the green-screen consoles, to the misty hallways, and yellow warning lights; Alien: Isolation possesses an Analog Physicality that brings the 1979 film to life once again.  While most games would have replaced the decades old tech with iPads and holograms, Isolation considers the retro tech an asset to the story.  And it works--just seeing the monocrhome mainframe displays and grainy video lends its own feeling of uneasiness.
And then there's the Xenomorph.  The most random, unpredictable nemesis ever to appear in a video game.  Sometimes, hiding in a locker works fine, and it will walk right by.  Other times, it will hear something nearby and charge after it.  But others, it might hear or smell something in that locker where you're hiding...and take a closer look.  It's not knowing which of these scenarios will come to pass that keeps you on your toes.
In addition to amazing AI on the part of the Xenomorph, the game astounded me again and again with its command of storytelling.  Many of these sequences pay homage to the film, but the best ones take you into new and terrifying territory, to the point that I believe that Alien: Isolation is the scariest game ever made.
Now I must admit, the game is quite difficult.  And there were times in Alien: Isolation that I found very frustrating--from a  few unnecessarily hard to find objectives to having to be *just* the right distance away from a vent to trigger the animation to enter it...with an alien on my tail.
But whatever you have to do--whether you play it on easy or Google a walkthrough when you get stuck--make sure you do not miss it.  Alien: Isolation is arguably the best movie-inspired game ever made.

Alien: Isolation is a welcomed addition to the "SURVIVAL HORROR" catagory aswell as the under-appreciated "STEALTH"  genre, which has become less and less prevalent in main-stream gaming over the last decade. The visual and audio presentation is "TOP-NOTCH" giving the game an authentic atmosphere remeniscent of the original motion picture "ALIEN". Character control is fluid and easy to learn and the games "QTE" sequences are kept simple and to a minimum with an ample amount of time for input and never seem to impede player progression with elaborate  button combinations.
Player interactions with the titles main antagonist "THE ALIEN" are frightening, even more so because the player is given no option or resource to permenatly dispatch the beast, but rather given tools to either distract or ward off direct encounters aswell as enviromental options that allow the player to evade detection, such as "LOCKERS" and being able to crawl under "DESKS". This aspect of the gameplay mechanic adds a great deal of tension and anxiety to the experience, leaving the player feeling helpless and reluctant to conduct overt actions.
The titles difficulty is unprecedented aswell. Though there are three levels of difficulty to choose from, "EASY" being a more cinematic and steady paced experience allowing the player more room for error when dealing with the "ALIEN" which keeps the story content flowing more naturally, "HARD" on the other hand is an arduous and lengthy ordeal that requires "QUICK" and "CLEVER" thinking and no small amount of "PATIENCE". This however can be off-putting and frustrating to the more casual player base and because of this I wouldn't recommend this title to everyone.
Alien: Isolations story was thoughtfully written aswell and all the events and scenario's that occur between the games relativly calm begining to the titles "controversial" end were exciting and interesting never once leaving me feel dissapointed in the experience. A truely unique title with a personality of it's own.
I give it a 9/10 and recommend Alien: Isolation to any fan of the series and the stealth/survival horror genre.

This is it. This is the game you've been waiting for.
If you're a big fan of the original Alien film, then this game will deliver. From the level design, art style, lighting, and retro electronics. This game screams authenticity when compared to the original film.
As for the game play: It's absolutely terrifying at times. (Akin to that of Dead Space) The intensity of enemies nearby, the internal struggle of "Do I make a run for it?" really makes the game a blast....Though on the other hand, where it's quiet. Where nothing happens, is equally as unsettling. This is where Alien: Isolation pulls through. The fact that you never feel safe in any situation.
Creative Assembly outdid themselves this time. Whilst it's not the game that people wanted in some aspects (You can't blast the Alien away with guns), it's the game that people definitely deserved considering the mess that was Aliens: Colonial Marines

Despite my initial doubts, I give my recommendation to Alien: Isolation with some provisos:
1) Unless you are super good at video games, play it on easy. On hard, you die so much that there's no time for tension to build, and tension is this game's bread and butter.
2) Play it in the dark with headphones. That should be a given for a horror game, but it's worth it, because again, tension.
3) Don't stay up until 1:30 am playing it. Yes, the save points are pretty far apart and you might have to repeat some stuff, but it's just not worth it.
4) Don't go into it expecting anything but what it is: slow, tense, and stealthful. This isn't a shooter, and it isn't (mostly) about jump scares.
5) Make sure you have a copy of your favourite Alien movie (any of them except 4) close at hand, because you're going to want to watch them when you're done. Which is what I am off to do.
