A game where the dice are ever loaded against you. Not fun. Same combat over and over and over. As a player you feel like you are being punished for purchasing the game and not understanding its dynamics the first time you play. Far too repetitive, combat doesn't change, and you will replay portions in excess of 20 times. You are punished for dying (even though its going to happen) in the form of lost HP as well as lost souls. You can go retrieve your souls, assuming you dont just die in the same spot again against an impossible enemy (which if you do, all those souls are lost forever). Your Hp can be purchased back using "human effigies" but those are rare and/or expensive, and you just lost all your souls so you are SOL.
There are no rewards for player progress seriously, nothing! So that boss you crawled to get to through a sea of enamies that repeatedly pounded you into bonemeal, the one that you miraculously beat (after 35 tries) because he accidently tripped of the platform, not because you dealt any real damage, NETS YOU NOT A DARN THING! Twelve hours of playtime with no payoff.
Dont expect to be captivated by its storyline either. Its no storyteller.
ON THE UPSIDE: The game is visually pleasing. Sprites move and flow nicely on the screen and movements look fluid. Lots of detail taken in designing textures and the like. The only problem here is that the "bloodstains" end up glowing neon red and being everywhere in your game because of online gameplay. Same with "messages" left on the ground by other players. Both of these items detract from everything else that makes a visually pleasing game.
In Conclusion:
DO NOT BUY AT FULL PRICE!!!!!!
$15~$20 = Ok maybe then.
$50! = NO! There is better gameplay to be had elsewhere at that price.

Fantastic golf simulation on the PC and highly recommended. It has been a long time since we have had the chance to play golf on the PC. Even in early access this game shines in so many areas. The physics are hands down the best we have seen in a simulation. From the realistic ball flight, to the ability to hit different shots - the game pulls you in. The courses are also fantastic and a glimpse as to what is to come. This is the key - real courses, real physics, and gameplay that gives you a "feel" of hitting a good shot. You can tell the dedication and focus towards getting the game of golf right and resisting the urge to putt fancy features in. The framework is there as the latest update shows some future options. You also get tournaments and multiplayer out of the box. If you want to join a tour from a hosted website, you can do that as well. Two thumbs up to Perfect Parallel for dedicating their time to put this game together. It has been worth the wait.

This game plays very well with realistic ball physics for the most part and some great courses which are now being added to with user-created courses.  The devs are keen golfers and it shows in all aspects of the game.  I'm sure that by the time of full release this will be the best golf game for sim fans that there has ever been.

The latest update to this game really shows the potential I was hoping for. The Devs have obviously worked very hard to add so much to the game, Such as new swing methods, including  real time mouse swing and real time controller swing. I think the controller swing will be a big plus to those that have played golf games on xbox  or playstation. Also now available for free are user made courses. While the Course forge has not been released yet to the general public those that were Beta testing it made some courses which you can now download and play in the game. This in itself is a huge step forward and with them being free it should open the doors for many that were a bit hesitant about the game. The life blood in my opinion of a golf game is the ability to add courses and play them for free. I know this was not the direction that  the game first looked at going but PP have listened to the feed back of the community and have changed their mind. This was a game breaker decision for me and probably for many more. The fact that PP listened and heard all the pro's and con's of free user made courses then decided that this is what the community wanted in itself  is not a small thing. How many times with other games have suggestions been made but fall on deaf ears. I can assure you I know of more then one or two. This isn't the only time that PP has listened to the community and either changed something or improved on it. That is huge for instilling confidence as a consumer that they actually do read the forums and not just pay lip service to it.
When course forge is released to the public the list of courses will grow by a vast margin as many of us will try our hand at designing. Now some will fiddle with it and give up but others will hang in there to try and grasp all the challanges it will bring. After returning to the game after a long hiatus, which was based on it not being worth paying a subsciption for, I have decided to write a review. I have not read any of the other reviews here so there may or may not be overlap, but I wanted to say how I feel about it.
-The game in its current form has exceptionally good graphics, easily the best in any MMO I have played.
- The generic user interface is simple to the point of not displaying pertinent information until the game thinks you need    it. ie, your experience bar...
-Targeting in combat is clunky and sometimes difficult, but get in a group for a dungeon and, for all of us not so not so autistically good at games, downright frustrating.
-There is no gui to show buffs/debuffs/hots etc. This may be linked to a greater feeling of "realism" but they do in fact exist in the game, and there is know way to tell unless you enter the character screen and check. This of course does not apply to dots or debuffs on enemies, you just have to have faith they are there.
-The quests are ok the first time around, but try them the second go through and they become so tedious you actually get frustrated.
-The bank tabs require you to quit and re-enter multiple times in order to move items around. This may sound trivial, but it gets really annoying if you forget something or are emailing items from two bank tabs. And the cost to upgrade those tabs is the highest I have seen in games I have played.
-Money generation in the game is very very slow, so slow in fact that you are forced to join trading guilds in order to make any significant amount. This is all well and good I suppose except even that mechanic is based on your luck at finding or salvaging items other people will buy. At higher levels you make more gold, but by then it becomes about tweeking your character, instead of say, buying materials to build sets for leveling.
-The versatility of the crafting system is really good. The major problem with it is that you can't really outfit another character that does not share your item types. For example you create a medium armour character and research all of the intrinsic traits (which could take months btw). If you then create a heavy armour class, by the time you could make them named sets (due to research times) you would level out of the zone and usefulness of the items.
- the majority of the armour sets are ugly or boring, and the modeling for many of the pieces is so bad they just
hang in mid air.
- ***Items purchased from the crown store only apply to the character that purchased it. Thats right, if you want daedric crafting styles for all eight of your characters be ready to shell out $120.... and there are four different crafting styles like this, or five I cant remember.
- It is probably no accident that they are the nicest looking sets in the game.
- The endgame is ridiculous and designed to eliminate the need for zenimax to create more content. I wont say why due to spoilers, but you will get it if you make the mistake of buying this game.
*BUT THE MAIN REASON TO NOT BUY THIS GAME IS THE TERRIBLE CUSTOMER SERVICE*
Allow me to explain. When I first purchased this game it was still subscription based and I did not own a credit card. This was simple enough because it came with a free month of game time. After my purchase I discovered that in order to activate that free game time zenimax required me to link a credit card and they would attempt to bill it to make sure it was good. I sent out an email explaining my situation, and asking why I would need a credit card for free game time. The response took I believe two days to arrive and when it did instead of solving the problem tried to offer other billing solutions. It took quite awhile ( I believe four or five days total ) I finally got a representative to offer me a key that allowed me to play the game on just my free game time. I suppose I should be grateful they did anything at all, but I was now five days behind the friends who bought it with me.
The next blow came quite recently and is the nail in the coffin for me. After reporting an instance where I was constatly falling through the world, I received and email informing me that I had violated the code of conduct in naming my account. There was no recognition of the bug report, no reply to the incident at all, just an emaill that looked very much like a punishment for doubting the zenimax gods. Again, all responses took days to arrive until the final day in which I was told in no uncertain terms that if they decide something that is the way it goes. Period.
This is the short list, there are also inconsistencies in the lore, bad textures, long load times when entering zones and buildings etc etc. I would suggest you read all the reviews here in reference to this game, but keep in mind that depending where you are the price has not come down permanently since launch and the its pretty pricey for a two year old game.

The Elder Scrolls Online: Tamriel Unlimited is an excellent massively multiplayer online game for those who both enjoy other Elder Scrolls games and dislike World of Warcraft.  Although the player should not expect a full Elder Scrolls experience, this game offers a one-of-a-kind multiplayer gameplay experience: fast paced combat, intuitive crafting with a large player-based economy, and a massive amount of diverse locations and quests. Players frustrated with the typical, repetitive nature of modern MMOs will find TESO to be one of the most addicting and entertaining games of 2015.

Combat
Gone are the typical rows of hotkeys that span the width of your computer monitor. Instead, players are given only five hotkeys plus one for an ultimate move per weapon set. This means the player will have to carefully determine the moves they will be able to access for each combat situation. Player versus Player combat is fast-paced and takes place in a massive battleground where players attack and defend against opposing factions.
Economy and Player Interaction
Player-based crafting and economics are also integral parts of TESO. Players can buy and sell their loot and crafted goods through trade guilds, which makes interaction with other players extremely important. Guilds that focus on dungeons or PVP make finding groups for dungeons or raids easy and efficient.
Scale
The title: Tamriel Unlimited, is no understatement. The game features iconic locations from every previous Elder Scrolls release, such as Skyrim and Oblivion; these locations are all included. These iconic locations are also the same size they were in previous games, allowing players endless opportunities to find quests, puzzles, and adventure.
The Elder Scrolls Online offers each player their own personal, long-lasting, and memorable experience. The combat is intense and fast-paced, yet balanced. Player cooperation and interaction is rewarding, yet you could also play through the game solo if you would prefer. The massive world is interactive and complex, so no two players will ever have the same exact experience. I recommend this game to anyone looking for a new and unique gaming adventure that features an engaging story and the best multiplayer gaming experience of 2015.

After reading the bad reviews I had my doubts, however, I am amazed people don't like this game.  It does require an updated PC to play though, and there are a few bugs like having to click out and click back into the building panel to constuct buildings.  It seems like rome2 is shogun2 but in ancient times.  However, this game is addicting granted its not empire TW or shogun2, but it ranks up there.  I say buy it if you're a strategy fan and are fimilar with TW games, otherwise I will agree with others to try out the other TW games, I'd give this an 8/10.  So here are my pros and cons list:
Pros:
very good update to rome TW in terms of map, difficulity, units, generals, and agents
naval battles are simple and lot more fun with the addition of ramming enemy ships
the cities and citadels are much easier to manage as well as food and public order
No more garrision troops unless a general is present and most buildings will add to the garrision of your town
The AI doesn't waste time on battles, if he attacker he charges and if he's defense he fortifies his position, and uses a balanced mix of troops
all nations are issued orders by their leaders, not just rome anymore
land battles can have thier fleets join in on the battlefield if they are close enough, not just provide artillery support like in shogun, but can land and storm beachs with the crew of the ship.  This also leads to bigger battles and it seems more realistic when 4000 Athenians are faced with 8000 barbarians
Cons:
overpowered ranged units, a unit of slingers will wreck havoc on your heavy troops, two units of slingers will cause most infintry to retreat.
Unit picture cards are horrible to distinguish between the same type of melee troop
diplomacy still doesn't work and you will end up paying for a lot of treaties.
Only generals can recruit and you must recruit units from that territory
political problems can build up fast late in game
the technology upgrades are much more linear, but more efficient.  The reason this is down here is that to unlock the bonuses with technology upgrades you must also upgrade otherthings that might no be relevant to your faction.  For example if you play a landlock faction like the germanic people, you must upgrade ships not only to obtain that upgrade, but the overall upgrade of troop movement.  This is hard to explain, but if you get the game you'll understand what I mean here.
seige warfare is pointless and you only need to siege the capitals of proviences.

I bought the game the second day it was on early access. My friend and I directly testet Online-Coop on a private server. So far, I only played 2,5h but the game has a huge potential.
Let me summarize my thoughts:
- There is no real tutorial yet but a few lines of text when you first enter a menu. But I was able to understand the main mechanics in the first 2 hours.
- It is an exploring game (at least in the early stage). Unless you play in creative mode, you will need to drive around a lot at the beginning in order to find enough resources to build you very first outpost.
- It is an multiplayer game. Yes, you can play for your own and it will be fun as well, but especially in this early stage of development I recommend playing it with friends. Together it is much more fun and easier to learn the game.
- There are bugs. For sure. This is a very new early access game. The driving of cars can be "optimized". But "hey". In comparison to many other games I played as "early access", this game looks to be somehow robust and the bugs I encountered didn't want me to throw the game away, so what better can happen?!
I can understand if people want to wait and see how the game develops and in what direction, but I can totally recommend the game. There are at least 30-50h of gameplay until I would expect the game becomes repetitive and such things. But there are 27 biomes to explore and the worlds are HUGE. It's a sandbox game. Play as you like, invent stories or implement ideas alone or together with friends (or start war against your friends *evil laugh*). That's the idea behind such games.
Have fun.

No tutorial in game to explain how to do anything.  You'll need to read a few web pages, watch a few videos and research to learn how to play.
Considering this game is all about driving a vehicle, the driving is very poor.  Any little bump in the terrain causes the vehicle to flip, roll turn sideways, etc.  Can't drive up the smallest of elevations and constantly get slowed down by the trees, which (as far as I know) can't be removed.
Game feels more like a pre-alpha version of a tech demo than a game.

I really do enjoy the idea of the game and for the most part the gameplay is very fun except when driving. I understand that upgrades and better vehicles will help get you over rough terrain but when I can't go up what LOOKS like a little hill it really detracts from the gameplay. I would highly recommend making some adjustments to the driving in this aspect as it may keep prospective players from enjoying what truly is a fun game.
Obviously I understand this is Early Access and is a work in progress which is why I'm still giving it a positive review.

I'm trying to run this game on a laptop with two GeForce GTX 980M graphics cards. When used in SLI, their performance adds up to around the same as a single GTX 1070.
Most AAA games will run extremely smoothly even at maximum settings in 1440p. For example, DOOM consistently runs at 120FPS, with occasional dips down to 80.
This game struggles to reach 60FPS even at the absolute lowest quality settings, while using SLI. That is inexcusably bad optimization. Makes me wonder if all the devs and QA testers were using 1080 cards in SLI. How could no one notice?
The worst part is, I tried so hard to get the game running smoothly that I passed the refund window. I'll give this game a proper review when Arkane fixes this hot steaming mess, but for now...

In the early days for me it was Links - 386 all the way to Links 2003 with all of the terrific mods that were user created.  I also played - and quite enjoyed - the Tiger Woods series.
Perfect Golf is the perfect blend of each;  animations and 3D affects that were missing in Links and realistic ball physics that were missing in Tiger Woods.
The amazing thing is that a group of people who were committed to developing a top notch golf simulation came straight from the Links community!  They breathed new life into that franchise, as much as they could make it better, and now their expertise is shining through with this game.
The developers listen to the community, the updates are fulfilled as necessary, the quality continuing to rise with every "change."
The purchase was a no brainer for me.  I'm an average gamer, not as hard core as I was 20+ years ago with the Links franchise, but I find myself venturing down that rabbit hole everytime I fire this beauty up......

This is my first review for a game on steam as you will probably notice, but this game is a good reason to write a review, in short, this game is great, it has a few problems but we'll talk about that later.
First thing's first though, and that is that this game is hard, sadly though, not as hard as dark souls 1, that may be due to the fact i never had online help when playing the first dark souls but either way, i, without realizing it, managed to reach the final boss area having beaten all optional bosses as well, and considering i barely got halfway throug the first dark souls, i was surprised to say the least. so I'm sure established dark souls players will have little difficulty in this game but will still be challenging to all who play.
Secondly, the open worldness, unlike the first dark souls, you will be returning to the first area a lot, after every major boss you will return to it via a special bonfire, so the open worldness, although you wil have a few paths to pick from, will all lead to the same place, though most will be to difficult to go through or you can't go through until you get a certain item, so it is actually quite linear to begin with, ten becomes more open world, then at the end becomes linear again, but again, despite this, it is still a great game.
and now the downsides, or rather, downside, PVP, i love pvp in this game, it's fun to test your skill against other players, however, there are those players out there who are, for lack of a better word, jammy. These players use the lag compensation and hit detection to their advantage, as sadly what you see and what is happening when in pvp isn't entirely true sometimes, as i'm sure some people have noticed, at times you can be backstabbed when you think you are completely clear of the other player, because, as far as their side is concerned, you did not react in time. now this, on it's own is not jammy, annoying and unfair, but not jammy, waht is jammy is the washing pole, now for those of you who do not know, the washing pole is a very long katana akin to sephiroth's sword, now because of how much range it has, generally, even if you think you are out of the way, the lag compensation will see it as though you did not dodge in time, meaning that fair fights against the washing pole are nearly impossible to people who aren't pro players, and these people know this, anyone using a washing pole in pvp is not using it by accident.
But despite that, pvp is still fun as i have had some genuinely tense matches against players who use their own skills and tactics rather than cheap moves.
so all in all, i recomend this game, to anyone and everyone, the game itself is beatufil, it is hard but fair, and the pvp is still great even if there are those few jammy matches far and few between. so yh, play this game if you want a challenge or something different.

Although not as atmospheric as its pedecessor, Dark Souls 2 manages to streamline and balance gameplay, combat and its unique online aspect, further improving on the formula that Demons' Souls first introduced on PS3.
DS2 is a wonderful game, filled with challenges, secrets, a bazookaload of content, witty dark and often intentionally downplayed and obscured humor and tons of interesting if peculiar bits.
However, what first surprised me is that its world structure is reminescent of the series' pioneer title rather than going for tightly intertwined and natural flowing maps like the first Dark Souls had, also adding the possibility to warp between bonfires at your leisure from the very beginning.
Generally speaking, the DS2 areas generally "blink" one after the other, with less of a natural flow, often connected by elevators and corridors (or sometimes special transport means, hehe) -  but, at any rate, they don't feel as solidly bound-together in the same game world as in its papa.
If you take the time to discover the plot, by paying attention to NPC dialogue and reading item descriptions - which traditionally offer a large portion of the insight there is about the world, you'll eventually understand this is a proper Dark Souls sequel, in terms of storyline, with often amusing or downright sad bits and indeed many connections to the past. In fact, almost everything is somehow connected.
The general tone is, however, much brighter than the sad and claustrophobic self-ordeal centered  DS1 world depicted, with a new bias towards other characters and NPCs. It feels more like a challenge than a purgatory, which, depending on where you sit, you might find equally nice or dissapointing.
Granted, not all changes and ironed bits will please the fans of the first two Souls titles, as the (mostly successful) attempt to balance stats, weapons and magic takes away a bit of that magic weird balancing usually brings. It also slows gameplay down by a noticeable amount.
The boss fights did not improve much, in the sense that they still are a bit of a weakness for this series when compared to the likes of Dragon's Dogma. Many areas and enemies are largely devoid of the grace that oozed from Prepare To Die Edition. Whereas the journey offers numerous tactical opportunities and challenges, many of the boss arenas are rigid, linear, with often uninspired movesets and events - they vary from bland to mostly "meh", at least gameplay-wise. The unintelligent, brute force approach of those entities encourages you to cheese them out rather than facing them like the hero that you are, which is a big miss. Some boss arenas also seem ported from a different, lousy game.
The weapon system suffered some notable changes that suit well what's required of the player: to be able to quickly adapt the strategy, tools and protection to a large variety of situations.
However, some weapon infusions, like Mundane, have mostly little to no use. Worse, with all this streamlining going on, the game sort of fails to educate the players as to the utility of various weapon types and fighting styles.
As an example, items give boons based on the character's stats, marked with letter ranges (S A B C D E). However, it does a poor job of making it obvious that two similar weapons with apparently similar scaling (let's say, both have Dex A Strength B annotated) might actually differ, since each individual letter covers number ranges. Therefore, you can have an S that's only marginally better than an A or a strong B and a weaker B - when comparing the weapons, the better range is colored blue while the weaker gets red, but it's still rather unintuitive.
While at it, DS2 completely fails to explain that the Dexterity weapon scaling figures are much weaker than the Strength ones. It makes sense, since you'd think dexterity based weapons are quicker and would do much more DPS if the scaling was the same, but making all of this so obscure is couter productive, wastes players' time with tedious documentation outside of the game itself and does nothing to improve the quality of any aspect of gameplay.
Another dubious find is that similar weapons improve in different ways when upgraded the same way, that are unpredictable before actually trying out the operation and wasting time to grind for extra upgrade materials and currency. Or taking a detour on the internets, with immediately disconnects you from the atmosphere and tends to turn the game to a Diablo-style equipment/character build grind - which Darsk Souls should not be.
As far as the equipment goes, I'd say there are many redundancies and balance issues - quite a few weapons are useless / not really viable for any kind of decent build - but heck, at least you get all the choice in the world once you educate yourself about the game. Movesets of certain weapons are also changed from the first game - to the worse, I might add.
Sadly, some enemies feel added just for pure frustration rather than for a good fair challenge. There often aren't two ways about handling an artificially difficult encounter, which, in the context of all the tactical play the series is known for, doesn't make any sense. It's not that you don't have an honest shot, it's more about having to deal with useless nuisances. Some starting and later levels feel bland, uninspired (e.g. Forest of Fallen Giants), certain optional areas are downright pathetic, cheap (notably Belfry Luna, Doors of Pharros) but perhaps, worst of all, their bosses are almost 1:1 pimped up copies of creatures from the first.
Sorceries, hexes and faith seem overpowered compared to pyromancy but alas, it makes some sense, since pyromancy spells never have minimum stat requirements to go with them, making the fire mistique a regular sidekick for melee brawlers.
When compared overall to the first two Souls games, DS2 takes a halberd in its nuts. However, on a larger scale, it still beats most ARPGs and crawlers to a pulp.
The PC adaptation itself is much more usable out of the box compared to the clumsy port Prepare To Die Edition was, as graphical settings abound and the game runs well @60fps maxed out even on your average  multimedia notebook. Control is still best with a gamepad (it's just natural to how the game was designed), but many people have been able to pleasingly control it with exclusive Keyboard or KB+mouse.
The main thing DS2 really screws up is that, while streamlining most aspects for a broader audience and online balance, many important gameplay considerations and effects are left completely obscure to the players, which kind of encourages you to Alt+Tab between the game and related documentation sources a tad too much. This, together with the rough eges of level and monster/boss design, lead to the players cheesing the game, when it should ideally be about outsmarting, adapting and engaging in intense encounters - which cheese tactics never produce.
It's really a small complaint, compared with all the stuff it does right, but I really DO miss the atmosphere and discoveries from the first, which did not tempt me nearly as much to go through stat tables and online tips. The first Dark Souls was majestic and misterious. Dark Souls 2 drops some of that in favor of being more functional, but also needlessly obscure.
Overall, it cannot possibly be missed, as, despite any flaw or frustration that you may find with it, it will literally hollow you of your time once you get deeper and deeper into it. It's a bit slow to start and truly shine, but then again, it's meant for long term play and re-play. And when you do stumble upon the few magnificent areas of this game, you'll be forever lost to it.

It's Ascension on Steam.  If you know what that is, you probably already know if you want it or not.
If you don't, it's a game about building a deck by acquiring heroes and artifacts to fighting monsters to compete with other would-be heroes in a popularity contest of the gods.  Or something.  It's Magic: the Gathering meeds Dominion.  It's fun.
There are quirks in the interface.  You will probably accidentally banish the wrong card at least once while trying to quickly click through a turn.  Many times trying to view a larger version of a card instead enlarges a card below it.  The animations are outrageously jerky for simple 2d animation.  The options screen is pretty lacking - volume is off or on.  Cultist screams, on or off.  Opponents are... easy or hard?  The manual gives you just enough information to understand the game mechanics, and no more.
Minor interface issues aside, it's fun, it plays faster with no shuffling required, and it comes with 5 expansions.  In paper, it would run about $210 for this much Ascension.  For the price, recommended.

The Elder Scrolls Online: Tamriel Unlimited is an excellent massively multiplayer online game for those who both enjoy other Elder Scrolls games and dislike World of Warcraft.  Although the player should not expect a full Elder Scrolls experience, this game offers a one-of-a-kind multiplayer gameplay experience: fast paced combat, intuitive crafting with a large player-based economy, and a massive amount of diverse locations and quests. Players frustrated with the typical, repetitive nature of modern MMOs will find TESO to be one of the most addicting and entertaining games of 2015.

Combat
Gone are the typical rows of hotkeys that span the width of your computer monitor. Instead, players are given only five hotkeys plus one for an ultimate move per weapon set. This means the player will have to carefully determine the moves they will be able to access for each combat situation. Player versus Player combat is fast-paced and takes place in a massive battleground where players attack and defend against opposing factions.
Economy and Player Interaction
Player-based crafting and economics are also integral parts of TESO. Players can buy and sell their loot and crafted goods through trade guilds, which makes interaction with other players extremely important. Guilds that focus on dungeons or PVP make finding groups for dungeons or raids easy and efficient.
Scale
The title: Tamriel Unlimited, is no understatement. The game features iconic locations from every previous Elder Scrolls release, such as Skyrim and Oblivion; these locations are all included. These iconic locations are also the same size they were in previous games, allowing players endless opportunities to find quests, puzzles, and adventure.
The Elder Scrolls Online offers each player their own personal, long-lasting, and memorable experience. The combat is intense and fast-paced, yet balanced. Player cooperation and interaction is rewarding, yet you could also play through the game solo if you would prefer. The massive world is interactive and complex, so no two players will ever have the same exact experience. I recommend this game to anyone looking for a new and unique gaming adventure that features an engaging story and the best multiplayer gaming experience of 2015.

8 hours in and so far it's been a lot of fun.
It's hard to define what this game is like, it's one part No Man's Sky, one part Factorio, one part RTS, one part survival, one part etc etc etc, it's a lot of things melded together.
The mining and crafting in this game takes a while, it's clearly designed with groups in mind but if you can get a good spawn, going solo isn't all that hard. The movement takes a little getting used to but once you get the hang of it, it's quite simple. The starter buggy has really really bad suspension (by design) so the first thing you want to do is find better suspension or craft your own, otherwise even going up the smallest of hills is a challenge!
The game has quite a lot of depth to it and a lot of little features designed to keep you invested in it. You can't mine one spot for a long time as the game reduces the yield per tick, this encourages you to move around or mine around the area as opposed to one spot. The map is very very large and it's fun to explore it and find somewhere that has decent resources to make your first outpost.
You can trade with other players, join factions together or ultimately kill each other. This isn't really a PvP game though, it's a lot more relaxed than that. I hesitate to call it a survival game because thay implies everyone runs around killing each other but it's really not like that at all. Most players I've met have been friendly and wanted to trade materials or set up trade routes between our outposts.

There is a lot to be explored here, and a lot to do and make. I have barely scratched the surface of what the game has to offer after 8 hours. A definite most buy, really a fantastic game all round.

Ok editing the review now since i have put more hours into it (30 hours currently)
The start of the game can be confusing and slow, but the community is really helpful in the /world chat channel if you have some questions. Once you get a ball rolling and getting into the groove with the stuff, its really amazing game. Theres so many little details like CO2 emissions if you are using fossil fuels for your generators. There are Metals, Liquids, Gases to collect. Gas tanks have be pressurized or cooled down etc. You can set up multiple outposts that gather you resources and use traderoutes to get the materials into your main Outpost. Every time you finish a new research there's plenty more new options coming in.This game can be huge timesink, but if you get your materials going in a more automated way you can spend more time on building your base defenses and exploring more of the world.
Still haven't reached to the endgame, far from it it seems. Definitely worth the pricetag if you are ready to tinker with managing the energy and resources, build defenses and plan your expansion outposts.
About Performance. There are some performance issues with the Linux client atm. At the night time they become apparent when multiple lights are on top of eachother. Framerates drop from 60FPS thats constantly during the day to 25-35 FPS during the night with multiple lights active. (Hardware: Ryzen 1700X@3.9ghz, GTX1070, 32GB DDR4 2800CL14). Im sure that will be improved with upcoming patches though, doesn't really make the game unenjoyable for me.
About the issues this game has. Radar map is a bit problematic, when you have many markers and outposts it starts to be impossible to set the right target where to go as everything becomes so tiny. Theres also Big map, but this doesnt allow you to target your markers, so its hard to get which direction you have to go.
There are also small bugs like snaping your foundations/platforms togheter, sometimes don't want to work correctly.
Overall, im quite happy. the minor issues it has can be improved over time.

If you liked Dishonored, the sequel improves on it in almost every way (with the only thing it feels to have come up a bit short being the story...still above average in my opinion though). First off, you get to choose between playing as Emily or Corvo, though the biggest difference in this regard is the abilities at your disposal throughout your playthrough. It should be noted that both Emily and Corvo have very similar ability sets, but with enough variation that I think it warrants playing the game through as both of them.
The story is almost identical regardless of who you pick, with some slight changes to fit the character you're playing - the big influence on how everything plays out in the end is the chaos level you subscribe to as you play. As advertised, if you go around murdering everything in sight, the world does react albeit in subtle ways (more bloodflies, some minor NPCs missing). With that said, Dishonored 2 expands upon the ability to approach each mission in whatever fashion you see fit.
Performance-wise the game ran well for me except on a select few levels, but even then it was never running poorly. The game never crashed on me until I ran into an extremely frustrating issue on my Corvo playthrough where all the saves I had would crash almost instantly upon loading into the game. I'm actually pretty upset about this because I won't be able to complete the full playthrough (I was about half way through the final mission) -  disappointing to say the least, but it doesn't diminish how good this game is.

I am changing my rating to positive because the game seems to be running smoother for me now. Overall I think the game is a masterpiece and probably one of my favorites. I won't get into a detailed review as the game is not fresh in my mind but I will say that it has excellent level design and the powers this time around are phenomenal. The gameplay is as good as the first one, but with the addition of som really fun powers. Dishonored and Dishonored 2 are testaments of brilliant game design. I will say, that there may be an isuse with horrible microstutter., which I disucss in the previous review below.
This game has a horrible framepacing issue baked into the engine that causes a bad microstutter. Some people claim to not have the issue (or in a rare instance, fixed it for themselves), but it appears to be very common issue. This makes the game feel horrible regardless of framerate. It can be running at 80fps and be very stuttery and jerky. In my opinion, a stuttery 60 feels worse than a smooth 30, but others might disagree. It's very important to note that if you buy the game you will very likely have to deal with the microstutter issue and there is no fix. This is after the most recent New Game Plus patch. I do not recommend the game on the basis of this, because I think it doesn't meet the bare minimum requirements of a fully functional working game. I have spent dozens of hours trying to make this game to run smooth, but it is just impossible.
The game itself is a masterpiece. They took Dishonored's phenomenal gameplay and polished it up, added new and interesting powers with more options, and threw it into a wonderful hall-mark of exceptional level desing. The levels in this game are just phenomenal and the polish to the gameplay is noteworthy. If this game were not a technical failure, this game would absolutely be a masterpiece worthy of the praise.  Unfortunately, I cannot give high praise to a game that doesn't even work. A smooth gaming experiences is the most BASIC requirement, in my opinion, for a game to be recommended.

This game is a must for Alien fans. The reviews do not give this game near enough credit. If you like immersive, stealth-based games, you will like Isolation. The developers did an AMAZING job of capturing the horror themes of the original movies and allowing gamers to experience the thrill of an trying to survive an encounter with a f****** beast of a creature. You don't need to be a die-hard fan of the movies either. I've only seen the original movie once, but you don't need much background to enjoy Isolation. I would reiterate what IGN and other reviewers have said, play on Easy or Medium -- depending if you're looking for casual play or something with a bit more challenge. Playing on the hardest difficulty is more frustrating than anything given the cat and mouse style gameplay and the heightened senses of the alien. That frustration is what I think fueled lots of these reviews. Hard is not hard...it's unbelievably unfair and nearly unsurvivable -- which is partially the message of the game. The alien is built to murder you, and it's good at its job. I thought the medium difficulty was the right blend of challenge without destroying the immersive aspect of allowing exploration and story progression. That said there were a couple places that I was frustrated, but overall, these were few and far between. The scares aren't cheap and the atmosphere is superb. You will feel powerless, but that's the brilliance of Isolation. It's not easy, and most of the time, the odds are not in your favor. You have work with what you have and sometimes a few precious seconds are the difference between finding your way to the next save or becoming the alien's new meat puppet. The developers did an outlandishly good job at recreating those moments of desperation seen in the movies. Those moments where you just can't imagine yourself having worse luck, "ef my life moments," but when you see yourself through it, it feels damn good. Definitely a worthwhile experience for those looking for a exhilerating rush.

Alien: Isolation’s authentic presentation, solid gameplay mechanics, and interesting story all work together to create a truly terrifying and stressful experience that lives up to the tension and atmosphere of the original Ridley Scott film, Alien (1979).
The game grips the player in the beginning with its accurate representation of the film’s environment and technology. Everything from the industrial quality of the Sevastopol station that looks like its bursting at the seams, to the “futuristic” envision of its computers from the perspective of the 1970’s.  It’s a game where nothing is out of place. Everything that was needed was utilized properly in order to make the station feel real. It keeps the player immersed and helps tell the story. The sound design and music help with this as well and it makes the station come alive with a lot of clanks, thumping from inside the walls, the beeping from computers and lab dashboards, and an incredibly annoying drinking bird toy that sounds like the Xenomorph(Alien) hissing. All of this is done to provide a strong framework for the actual gameplay.
The gameplay is pretty simple: If enemies appear, hide and try to find the shortest and safest path to the objective without being seen. Saving in the game is based around a checkpoint system in the form of old telephones attached to the walls. Their placement is fairly sporadic so it adds to the tension because I wasn’t sure of where the next save point would be. Unfortunately the flip side of this is reaching areas where 20-30 minutes can go by without encountering the next save point, and dying during these moments can set the player back quite a bit. Craft able explosives and noisemakers can be thrown across the room (or dropped as a proximity trap) to distract any potential threats. However, beyond the noisemaker I never really found a use for the other explosives. Weapons are gathered over the course of the game, but it’s made pretty clear that they are a last resort, because combat attracts unwanted attention of the worst kind.
The game really hits its stride when the Xenomorph comes into play, and the reason for this is its “unpredictable AI”, because I was forced to approach each situation differently. Sometimes I found myself just hiding in a locker and waiting for the Alien to lose interest, other times I was forced to move inch by inch in plain view hoping the Alien didn’t get the urge to turn towards me and charge from the other side of the table. That’s what makes the Alien so terrifying, not because it relies on jump scares and just randomly appears out of nowhere to go “boo!” No, it’s because the Alien is a constant presence looming over Amanda Ripley’s head. I spent the majority of the game just listening to it crawling through the airshafts in the wall next to me, while my eyes were glued to the motion tracker and only glancing up every 10 seconds to check for the nearest hiding spot in case I attracted the Xenomorph’s attention.
Unfortunately, there’s a 3-4 hour no-Alien period in the mid-late game and the plot hands itself over to the Androids. This is the weakest part of the game because it ventures more into action territory and the Androids are more of a nuisance than anything.  From a story perspective it makes sense why this part needs to happen, as it allows the player to take a breather before the final stretch which is easily the most terrifying and challenging part of the game. However, the length of this plot detour could of easily have been cut in ½ while still keeping the story aspect of it intact.
The last leg of the game, while exciting, does suffer from a feeling of dragging the player through the mud. There’s even a point in the last 5 minutes where it pulls Amanda Ripley back from the finish line, just to make the player run that similar path again for no reason whatsoever. As to the ending itself, without spoiling anything all I can say is “could be better, could be worse” and does feel more like sequel-baiting than anything else.  In that regard  I’m fine with it, but sequels to horror games run into the risk of trying to mimic the first and falling flat, or abandoning the horror aspect and the franchise just becomes another generic action game with horror elements (ex: every Alien game prior to this one).
So while the final 5-6 hours has its share of highs and lows, Alien: Isolation is in my mind not only the best Alien game today that finally does justice to the original film, but I would say it set the same bar for survival horror that Arkham Asylum had set for the superhero genre in video games.

As far as Survival Horror games go this does it perfectly. The pacing is rock solid, albeit a little drawn out a times, but you'll constantly be on your toes even in areas where you know there's nothing to be worried about. The alien is a lot more scripted than it seems, in some areas it's specifically scripted unless you have attention drawn on you, and once you realise how to outsmart it then it becomes pretty easy, but with that being said you're still gonna be motivated by the fact your skull is probably 2 feet away from being penetrated.
Graphics are good, reflective floors are really nice, fire effects, particles and all that stuff is nice too, the only main issue is the character animations. In and out of cutscenes lip-syncing hardly works and when it does it's laughably bad, the game is nicely optimised too so running it on the highest settings isn't too demanding. Occasionally glitches like floating items where enemies were killed can happen.
Story is nicely done, not too forced but it gives you enough of a reason to do as you do. CA done a good job of making a character that's not only lore friendly but also isn't a pain to play as. She doesn't speak loudly to point out the obvious for the player, she's not a mute and she reacts in realistic way to a lot of what's going on, she doesn't immediately become completely desensitised to everything nor does she stay traumatised and self-pitying.
Overall, 8/10 game, atmosphere and setting are good reasons alone to play this game, everything else just builds ontop of that.

This is the first time I've felt compelled to write a review on Steam, so I hope you find it informative.
Broforce is, without a doubt one of the most fun and entertaining games I've had the pleasure of purchasing.  While still as of today still in the Alpha phase, it shows remarkable promise as being a very retro, pixel-art style side scroller. It is probably best described as a fast, extremely chaotic version of NES classics such as "Contra", but even more low-fi in the same vein as "Minecraft". It's also a very funny send-up/tribute to some of the most popular action movie/television characters from the eighties to the present, from "Rambo" and "Aliens" to "Blade", "Walker: Texas Ranger", "Judge Dredd", to newer films such as "The Matrix" and "Kill Bill".  If you like action film and old school 8-bit console games, this is the one for you. Some highlights:
-Lots of characters (as denoted above), with each one having different "super" powers, the vast majority of which are fun/useful in many different situations.
-Do you like jib?  The amount of exploding enemies and their resultant corpses is hefty. The pixelated body parts rain for days, a la "bloody mess" perk in Fallout 3. Fun! (note to parents: the violence is so cartoonish as to be reminiscent of Looney Toons, so no worries.)
-Destructible terrain.  Everything can be destroyed, even to the effect of using weaponry to tunnel your way through parts of levels for the suprise attack, a nice feature.
-Hilarious "Rube Goldberg" style traps.  More often than not, blowing up an explosive barrell or kicking one over a cliff onto enemies leads to crazy chain reactions that I've actually laughed out loud over.
Okay, no game is perfect so here's some gripes (and they are very minor):
-No way to chose a character. The player is given one at random, it seems, at the start of a level or whenever the player dies.  I realize this is likely intentional, as it forces the player to strategize their approach to the situation. Can't help but to think to myself, "Man, I really wish I was playing so-and-so" from time to time, but again this is very minor.
-The levels early on in the game are woefully short and far too easy.  I hope the devs put more baddies in all the levels for the final cut.
-More of pretty much everything.  Levels, characters, content.  This is actually more of a compliment than a gripe.
In all, I whole-heartedly recommend Broforce to anyone and everyone.  I can't wait to see the game completed.  GO BROFORCE!

The core gameplay loop is such: you set up a slime pin, put slimes in the pin, start a garden/chicken coop to feed the slimes, go out and find new slimes, foods, and areas, while profiting off the land. Repeat, ad nausium. It sounds good on paper, but the implimentation is complete garbage.
The first problem are gardens - if you are a sane person, the first thing you will likely do is set up a farm. This will keep your slimes fed, but eventually the garden will stop spawning carrots. Now, in a *fun* game, the last yeild of the farm would reset the farm entirely - but this is not a fun game. This is Slime Rancher, and it is not at all uncommon for a crop to just mysteriously vanish when its timer runs out, even if you can *LITERALLY SEE THE VEGITABLES GROWING IN THE SOIL*. This isn't an issue at first, since all the crops you grow at the start are found nearby, but in the mid to late game, it can get downright infuriating to start a more exotic and rare crop, only for you to lose the last yeild to an ingame timer that is not easily planned for.
Now, you are likely thinking "Buddy, why don't you just store some of the crop for replanting?" And that is a great idea! Were it not for one problem: the game punishes you for it. In order to store any item long term, you have to either reserve one of your 4 invintory slots to said item, or build a silo. "What is a silo?" you ask? Well, imagine if a *fun* game took your 20+ slot inventory and split it up into individual buildings - WITH ONE SLOT EACH. You can expand the silo, but that requires an upgrade for each and every one - with a max of FOUR PER SILO. So, that means in order to store all foods and plorts, you will have to build no less than SEVEN individual silos and upgrade them a total of TEWENTYEIGHT times. And the you have to memorize each one, and wander back and forth between them whenever you want something.
The strongest assests this game posesses is its visual style - a very simple and cheery art ditection, which is likely the only reason you have heard of this game at all. The entire game's visuals are dominated by a series of circles - two dots, a mouth, and a bouncing orb of varying color. That is it.
The sound effects are pretty good - you might actually be able to place them if you heard them indipendantly of the game. The music however, is servicable, nothing memorable on its own right - mostly wandering jaunty tunes, with the occasional hit of danger when you run into enemies.
Speaking of enemies, that brings us to the second most useless aspect of the game: the combat. There are two kinds of enemies: Tar Slimes, and Hungry Largos. Both are equally unintemidating and easy to deal with. The Tar Slimes are supposed to be the worst enemies in the game, but they are really just there to punish new players for experimenting with ranching.
To clarify, this game is not *bad*, it just isn't fun. All the enjoyment you can get from this game can be found by watching videos of it on Youtube. 90% of your time in this game will be spent treking back and forth between spots on the map that are not fun or interesting to visit more than once. Additionally, the later you get into the game, the more confusing the level layouts become  - and so you conflate the issues of limited inventory. This isn't helped by the fact that this is a very grind-heavy game - none of the tasks given in this title are difficult, interesting, or force you to think creativly. Pretty much everything is solved through the use of an inflated economy, which serves no purpose but to take up your time.
Do yourself a favor, skip this game, buy Stardew Valley instead.

I have over 300 hours on this game and can't imagine ever getting tired of it.  Actually, it's not a game... it's an open world driving simulator, in which you can campaign hard or take it easy, your choice.  Actually,  it's not just a game _or_ a simulator... It's a big friendly international community of players and developers, with incredibly dedicated and talented people adding new content all the time, using excellent tools provided by the vendor (SCS), and caring very much about the authentic look and feel of national road signage, trucks, cargoes, landscapes, architecture, etc.  Actually, it's not so much a game... it's really more of a lifestyle...  and it taught me how to back a truck-n-trailer.  Seriously, I never could do that before and I learned by playing ETS2.  Now it's easy.   So I guess it's kind of a driver training app as well.
People get into ETS2 with different interests.  Some are in it for the trucks -- driving them, collecting them, designing them, making them perfectly authentic, giving them gorgeous paintjobs, adding accessories (hey, you can never have enough shiny chrome!).  Some are in it for the trailers.  Or the building models (famous landmarks, anyone?).  Or modelling their own country or region.   Some folks are really intensely interested in freeway signage of Europe.  Oh yeah, and some people are in it to actually play the game, campaign seriously, buy every garage in Europe and become the ultimate Trucking Czar and earn insane numbers of game-Euros.  Whatever.  I'm in it for the scenery.
And the official and unofficial devs keep adding more map, so I may never get to 100 percent explored -- which is totally awesome.  I campaigned hard until I had enough garages and drivers working for me that I could retire :-)  and now I just tour around an expanded ETS2 map enjoying the scenery and soaking up some virtual sunlight during the long cold real-world winter.  So it's not really a game, it's kind of a  virtual tourist experience... umm... I mean, it can be very relaxing, unless you take lots of "Express Delivery" jobs in which case it can be kinda stressful... Ever driven a semi and trailer that got stuck solid  in rush hour traffic with only half an hour left to make the last 10 km?
Look, it's simply the biggest (you can travel over 60,000km of roadmap with some added mods) and best open world sim ever.  Period.  Compare its map with other OW maps and its hugeness jumps out at you.  Load on the mods and DLCs and you can spend months in this sim and not drive the same road twice.  If you enjoy wondering "what's around that next corner" then this could be for you.
Some say the engine is old school, and the graphics are not as pretty as they could be;  well OK, I dunno what the state of the art is right now, but ETS2 is plenty pretty imho, and it exercises my GTX970 pretty hard.  The skybox is great (terrific dawns and sunsets and good stormy weather);  you can get Seasons mods if you want lots of snow, or spring flowers or fall foliage.
Look, how can I explain it -- this is "just a game" like Lord of the Rings is "just a book".  It's actually a world, a world you can go travel in for a while.  A world you look forward to visiting, where you can plan and execute trips that take many hours of real-world time.
A place that cheers you up and makes you say Wow and sometimes laugh out loud.  A place where no one shoots at you or jumps out at you, there's no blood or body parts flying around, you don't have to collect a whole pile of weird objects or remember that the blue switch with the snake symbol was set to On when you passed by it about 12 days ago -- and the world isn't going to blow up in 14 minutes if you don't find the secret decoder gizmo.  And definitely -- and I want to emphasize this -- no head crabs.  A huge plus.
So hey, take a trip from France to Spain and enjoy the mountain roads across the Pyrenees -- watch out for those hairpins!  Tour the Baltic States.  Check out Scandinavia.  Install ProMods and go visit Iceland -- it's a long expensive ferry ride via the Faroes, but well worth it!  Italy's coming any day now and I can hardly wait.  Take a scenic road trip with no death, destruction, zombies, cannibalism, or things exploding (though there is the occasional roadside accident scene).  You don't have to be mean to anybody.  No one is mean to you (maybe a traffic ticket now and then if you are careless, and some bus drivers just can't be bothered to look both ways before they pull out, but you can handle that).  And if you want to pull cargo, you can get paid in game-Euros and save up for a bigger truck.   But game-Euros only, no IAP.  Whats not to like?
It's not really a game.  It's a lifestyle.

NMRiH is a fairly unique survival horror game where, unlike most of its kind, you can't run around killing zombies with nearly infinite ammunition and little to no consequences. Zombies are not easy to kill, and they don't die with one simple hit with a bat, or fall on their backs because you pushed them gently.
In this game, you will always be outnumbered. The zombies may move slowly, but can quickly surround and overwhelm you if you're not careful. A clean headshot with a decent gun is the most reliable way to kill a zombie. Ammo is scarce, so you may find yourself planning out your course of action, trying to make every shot count.
The game is notably designed around co-operation, so you will have a much better time playing with friends. Sure, you can try to play on public servers, but if there's a lack of communication between players, the game can quickly turn into chaos.

I was one of the players that played the beta of the original APB way back when you had to pay for a subscription. It died, passed on to another dev team, and all seemed pretty legit. I sank, as of this moment, 1,107 hours into this game. I really enjoyed it. It was *mostly* mindless fun, granted with a few exploits and a fairly toxic community, but I could handle that.
The customization is probably the best of nearly any game that exists, aside from the likes of Second Life. The ability to make decals, tattoos, edit basic features of your clothes, change some of the layering, and a slew of other things causes the customization to be the only highlight worth truly looking back on. However, this is a double edged sword. The sheer amounts of weeaboos and bronies that post their graffiti art of their favorite child anime characters or pony creature all over the damned place is nausiating. Now, don't get me wrong, I've put up some edgy stuff on the walls and such, but nothing as cringe as the stuff weeaboos and bronies post. This is sad as there are a few who have used the custom editor to make some SERIOUS works of art, but a lot of what's being thrown around is sheer cringe. If you can work to ignore this, then the customization is the best thing about this game and actually shines better than most other games with customization options.
The combat and driving are so similar in their shortcomings that I can lump them into the same paragraph. Both are there, both effectively do their job, but both are lacking. Despite having just enough depth to give a separation between the skilled and the killed the both of these aspects mostly seem more like a detailed framework that was never fully realized. The combat, however, has given way to a slew of hackers that exploit it for all its worth and make combat almost unplayable. Between the various wall hacks and aimbots used it's a wonder anyone attempts combat, except for the obvious fact that combat is required for progression.
Missions are mostly repetative, though not without a mild amount of charm and replayability. Don't get me wrong, there's a LOT of different types of missions, but you almost ALWAYS get stuck with fetch missions and zone control of some sort, and the infamous "tug of war". There ARE missions you can do that strictly revolve around a criminal player who gets caught committing a crime, but generally these missions only consist of turning in the items for stolen loot and then laundering the cash recieved while the enforcers try and take said loot/cash in as evidence. It's a lost oppertunity for the players to really drive the missions.
The community is where the game really starts to fall apart. Everything about the combat, driving, and missions can actually be enjoyable enough to be excused, but then the community gets factored in and these three things get smashed into the ground. Even the customization, as mentioned, takes a turn for the worst thanks to the garbage community. People scream venom and vitriol with nearly every word, hackers are ripe and abundant and thanks to poor work on the devs' part they're fairly audacious about it, bronies, weeaboos, and other such aspects of the community make it absolutely abismal to deal with.
The last nail in the coffin, as briefly mentioned, are the devs. Now, you're probably thinking "What about the microtransactions?" and I would agree, but these can be lumped into the problems with the devs. They really only care about the cash flow. Granted, every game dev needs to worry about paying the rent but the methods used in this game are amongst the worst examples of how to gain cash from a Free-to-Play game. Various weapons, to include special weapons, can only be purchased with actual cash. You'll often hear people complain about a weapon referred to as the "Nano". This weapon can ONLY be recieved by essentially gambling with real money and it's a difficult weapon to get. Sure, there's now a auction function in the game that lets you get it but good luck with that. Players generally only auction off the more undesirable of weapons, sometimes even openly preferring if their enemies (and even allies) have bad weapons to make themselves look better by comparison. Now roll these special weapons in with the hackers and you get a nightmare. So now you have to pay money to even compete with players that might be cheating right off the bat. Next you have to consider that the customization I sang praises about has a serious issue: If you want to make things of high detail you HAVE to pay money for a "Premium" that allows you, for a certain amount of time, to gain the capability to make detailed pieces. Basically, if you want to be creative you have to pay extra for it and this is only good for a set period of time. Also, this premium time CAN expire when you're not playing. You WILL feel cheated. Then factor in that if you complain about the hackers, the pay-to-win aspect of the game, or even various bugs and such the devs effectively ignore you, or worse punish you for pointing it out. This is why I avoid their Facebook and their forums. The devs charge you to compete, to be creative, and if you complain about the game's issues they'll cut you off.
It's been said; this game has been on a decline since it came out. It started good but slowly rotted with time. This is a game I want to like and want to enjoy again, but it's really damned hard to do that with the current state of the game, the autism of the community, and the mindset of the developers.

I'm not sure that the warnings for those that don't own a Microsoft controller (or Sony PS controller, I suppose) are strong enough - the keyboard and mouse play is not good. In fact, go to Namco's customer service for a "great" statement from the company:

In a few words,
It is quite advanced for an early access title.  The game can be very challenging or more relaxing, depending on what level you choose to play at and what aids you select to help your golfing experience.  I think eveyone can find a method to play to make Perfect Golf one of the most enjoyable golf games you've ever played.  I would
recommend this game to all computer golfers!
What follows in this review is a lengthy discussion of some of the features (not all of them) provided in the game - analogous to the list of options the game provides!
I bought Perfect Golf when it first became avialable in Early Access.  I played the Links series of golf, and played a very small bit with the PGA/TW series.  To me, PG is bit more similar to Links than TW games, but it's not a new version of Links.  The game developments over the first 13 months of early access have come reasonably steadily and each one providing new features and bug fixes of the reported issues.  I have complete faith that this will continue for however long early access continues; with the present state of the game, I suspect it won't be much more than a few more months until release (but that is only my guess).
The game requires surprisingly (to me) high hardware requirements to get the most detail from the game.  The most important thing is you video card.  You really need to have a dedicated video card; an on-board video card will not deliver the experience that players will want, even at the lowest quality settings of the game.  However, lower end systems and middle-of-the-road systems with dedicated video cards can generally run the game reasonably well.
Perfect Golf can be a very difficult golf game - perhaps as difficult as the real game for some.  However, there are many aids that can be employed to make the game more relaxing.  There are currently four options for input methods:
- a "traditional" style 3-click swing meter suing the mouse button
- game controller with thumbstick on the personal computer
- mouse movement, now available in a real-time format, so the golfer swings as you move the mouse
- golf simulator hardware (Trackman 3/4, Foresight GC2, SkyTrack)
The 3C swing uses a round meter which is pretty familiar to most computer golf players.  I believe the 1.3.9.0 update coming in February 2016 will have an option to make the player avatar move as 3C swing meter moves.  I'm not familiar with the controller methods, so I can't comment on this input method.  The mouse movement method allows you to change the direction of movement from vertical to horizontal as well as the sensitivity to allow for various DPI settings in your mouse configuration as well as various resolution settings for the game itself (4K, HD, VGA, etc.).  The mouse swing can optionally be set as a real-time swing.  I also cannot comment on the simulator input, but from what I've read from those fortunate to have simulator hardware, all very much enjoy Perfect Golf.
I really enjoy the challenge of the game using a horizontal mouse swing.  I haven't tried the real-time swing yet, but I definitely will be giving it a go.  I like how you can control the ball movement by making a different path with the mouse, and thus imparting draw/hook spin or fad/slice spin as required for the shot.  The physics of sideslopes, uphill/downhill lies, wind and elevation effects in the game provide the most realistic ball flight I've seen in golf games.
Courses designed in the Course Forge by users wil become avilable for all players very soon.  The previews of the courses as well as a few that have been released by Perfect Parallel with the game so far have been very good.  I suspect there will be many more coming, but I also suspect they will all of be good quality and not something slapped together in a few minutes or hours.
There are many modes of play (stroke/medal play, solo/team match play, and others) as well as the option to play online against other live players from around the world.  There are limimted number of official tournaments at this time, but other web sites, such as the Online Golf Tour or OGT, provide a very good complement to Perfect Golf.  I suspect after the game is release, Perfect Parallel will provide more official tournaments, but it's always good to have optiosn with other tournament providers as well!  OGT will also host user-created courses for free download/addition to the game.
One of the few drawbacks in the 1.3.9.0 build of the Perfect Golf may be the lack of a career mode.  Many computer golfers want this, but it won't be provided by Perfect Parallel until after the release of the game.  The ongoing development of the game after release should ensure that a detailed and realistic career mode will be provided, based on the attention to detail and reality that Perfect Parallel have exhibited in the game thus far.  I have no doubt that whatever is eventually provided will be very enjoyable.
Perfect Golf is currently only available on the computer (Windows, Mac, Linux), but Perfect Parallel have indicated it will be ported to XBox One and PS4, although no timetable has been provided.  Again, I strongly recommend Perfect Golf for any computer golf fan.  It's a steal for the price and will likely provide many hours of entertainment!!

You aren't limited to Windows only. Secondly, so far this game is showing strong graphics without requiring the top of the line in hardware. These developers are walking a fine line in that regard and so far winning it. Thirdly, there is already a solid online community for this game, for people looking for casual play or competitve play.
As for the game play itself it is very intuitive for the most part. I did have to look up a few things that aren't immediately evident from just jumping in and playing (like how to change clubs or shot types) but the learning curve is overall low. The courses available now are all top notch with a few real courses in there, and there are a lot in development soon to be released.
For a game in beta, it feels an awful lot like a mature application. I have not run into any bugs at all really. And the price point is great. You should definitely give it a go.

Alien: Isolation’s authentic presentation, solid gameplay mechanics, and interesting story all work together to create a truly terrifying and stressful experience that lives up to the tension and atmosphere of the original Ridley Scott film, Alien (1979).
The game grips the player in the beginning with its accurate representation of the film’s environment and technology. Everything from the industrial quality of the Sevastopol station that looks like its bursting at the seams, to the “futuristic” envision of its computers from the perspective of the 1970’s.  It’s a game where nothing is out of place. Everything that was needed was utilized properly in order to make the station feel real. It keeps the player immersed and helps tell the story. The sound design and music help with this as well and it makes the station come alive with a lot of clanks, thumping from inside the walls, the beeping from computers and lab dashboards, and an incredibly annoying drinking bird toy that sounds like the Xenomorph(Alien) hissing. All of this is done to provide a strong framework for the actual gameplay.
The gameplay is pretty simple: If enemies appear, hide and try to find the shortest and safest path to the objective without being seen. Saving in the game is based around a checkpoint system in the form of old telephones attached to the walls. Their placement is fairly sporadic so it adds to the tension because I wasn’t sure of where the next save point would be. Unfortunately the flip side of this is reaching areas where 20-30 minutes can go by without encountering the next save point, and dying during these moments can set the player back quite a bit. Craft able explosives and noisemakers can be thrown across the room (or dropped as a proximity trap) to distract any potential threats. However, beyond the noisemaker I never really found a use for the other explosives. Weapons are gathered over the course of the game, but it’s made pretty clear that they are a last resort, because combat attracts unwanted attention of the worst kind.
The game really hits its stride when the Xenomorph comes into play, and the reason for this is its “unpredictable AI”, because I was forced to approach each situation differently. Sometimes I found myself just hiding in a locker and waiting for the Alien to lose interest, other times I was forced to move inch by inch in plain view hoping the Alien didn’t get the urge to turn towards me and charge from the other side of the table. That’s what makes the Alien so terrifying, not because it relies on jump scares and just randomly appears out of nowhere to go “boo!” No, it’s because the Alien is a constant presence looming over Amanda Ripley’s head. I spent the majority of the game just listening to it crawling through the airshafts in the wall next to me, while my eyes were glued to the motion tracker and only glancing up every 10 seconds to check for the nearest hiding spot in case I attracted the Xenomorph’s attention.
Unfortunately, there’s a 3-4 hour no-Alien period in the mid-late game and the plot hands itself over to the Androids. This is the weakest part of the game because it ventures more into action territory and the Androids are more of a nuisance than anything.  From a story perspective it makes sense why this part needs to happen, as it allows the player to take a breather before the final stretch which is easily the most terrifying and challenging part of the game. However, the length of this plot detour could of easily have been cut in ½ while still keeping the story aspect of it intact.
The last leg of the game, while exciting, does suffer from a feeling of dragging the player through the mud. There’s even a point in the last 5 minutes where it pulls Amanda Ripley back from the finish line, just to make the player run that similar path again for no reason whatsoever. As to the ending itself, without spoiling anything all I can say is “could be better, could be worse” and does feel more like sequel-baiting than anything else.  In that regard  I’m fine with it, but sequels to horror games run into the risk of trying to mimic the first and falling flat, or abandoning the horror aspect and the franchise just becomes another generic action game with horror elements (ex: every Alien game prior to this one).
So while the final 5-6 hours has its share of highs and lows, Alien: Isolation is in my mind not only the best Alien game today that finally does justice to the original film, but I would say it set the same bar for survival horror that Arkham Asylum had set for the superhero genre in video games.

As far as Survival Horror games go this does it perfectly. The pacing is rock solid, albeit a little drawn out a times, but you'll constantly be on your toes even in areas where you know there's nothing to be worried about. The alien is a lot more scripted than it seems, in some areas it's specifically scripted unless you have attention drawn on you, and once you realise how to outsmart it then it becomes pretty easy, but with that being said you're still gonna be motivated by the fact your skull is probably 2 feet away from being penetrated.
Graphics are good, reflective floors are really nice, fire effects, particles and all that stuff is nice too, the only main issue is the character animations. In and out of cutscenes lip-syncing hardly works and when it does it's laughably bad, the game is nicely optimised too so running it on the highest settings isn't too demanding. Occasionally glitches like floating items where enemies were killed can happen.
Story is nicely done, not too forced but it gives you enough of a reason to do as you do. CA done a good job of making a character that's not only lore friendly but also isn't a pain to play as. She doesn't speak loudly to point out the obvious for the player, she's not a mute and she reacts in realistic way to a lot of what's going on, she doesn't immediately become completely desensitised to everything nor does she stay traumatised and self-pitying.
Overall, 8/10 game, atmosphere and setting are good reasons alone to play this game, everything else just builds ontop of that.
