I'll start by saying that I enjoy this game a lot. It's kind of what I wanted legacy rust to be like, so if you enjoyed that game you're probably going to like this one as well. But please, before buying this game, remember that it is very early alpha and you will most likely die inside of a mountain or break your legs off the shortest fall in the world quite a few times. Unless you're ready to face a lot of glitches you might as well wait a few months to get it.
I'll list some of my own opinions here. Some people might not agree with me on these.
+
It will take you a while to get your house going unlike new rust. It's very balanced.
+
If you enjoyed the bow in legacy rust you're probably going to like this one as well. It will one shot players in the head which makes it a great weapon when you're starting out, making you able to kill the best geared player on the server with one shot. It's also used in lategame PVE. This is explained further down.
+
I play on the lowest settings and it makes you kind of fuzzy and cozy. It has a cartoony touch to it which i personally think is beautiful
+
"It feels like they've built a fps and added the survival components, not the other way around" - some youtuber which i cant remember the name of. Absolutely no player lag gamewise.
+
Dying isn't as harsh on you as you won't lose your tools, unless you have the "infamous" buff.   Keep in mind that some servers will have plugins that makes you drop tools as well.
+
This is a buff you get upon killing another player. If you are infamous and you die you will lose one tool in your inventory. If you've killed enough players you will get the "Outlaw" buff. When you are infamous you will gradually get hungrier and colder faster. The Outlaw buff will make you drop two tools instead of one. If you are killed as an Outlaw, the killer will not get the Infamous buff and therefor an Outlaw is always the primary target. Sadly, there is no way to see if a player is infamous yet, so you will have to be active and read the chat to spot the guy with the most infamy.
This balances KOS (Killing On Sight) because you would have to think through if killing that freshspawn is worth the risk of losing your weapon.
A lot of people disagree with this, but I think it has great potential. But it's obviously not tweaked for the greatest yet.
For example, two players start shooting at you and you have no chance to run away from them. Obviously you would want to shoot your way out of there. Let's say you manage to get one of them but his friend kills you. Since you already killed someone you will have the infamous buff and lose a tool, while they didn't lose anything at all. (unless they were infamous as well)
I'll also point out that there are server that have disabled infamous.
People do not have a reason to not kill you, since ammo is really cheap and there's no infamous. Also if you're new don't play on the official servers. They're pretty much the same as the non-infamous servers.
+
Good PVE, even in lategame. The developers has really thought this one through. Usually you if you find one animal there will be a few others standing around it. If you shoot one of the animals with a firearm, the others will hear it and charge at you. At the lower level animals it wont really be a problem, but when you get to the more dangerous animals they start grouping in bigger groups and dealing a lot more damage. This makes it (pretty much) impossible to use a firearm for killing lategame animals, leaving you with a bow. It is challenging to kill a yeti alone for the first time, but it can be as hard to kill it after 80 hours.
+

The community is really friendly and helpful if you need help or have any questions. I guess this depends on what server you're playing on but I've had a good experience, and even made a few friends on the way :)
~
Very challenging survival when first logging in. I don't know if this is the way to encourage players to keep playing if they log in and die within 3 minutes a few times in a row. The survival gets easier and easier the further you get in the game, which is kind of what you'd expect.
-
: I wrote before that c4 was not implemented in the game
. Yesterday it was confirmed by battlemu1e on reddit that
but with an extremely low droprate. It's also very expensive to craft so don't expect alot of c4 in the game yet.
"The reason why currently the cap drop rate is so low and material cost is so high is that this was never the intended final balance of c4, we just need to weigh the available options for base protection against the availability of c4 to create a fairer balance for raiding." -battlemu1e
"The material drop rate needs balance as do the construction items strength balance (i.e. wood<Stone<metal). Once this happens, raiding will be opened up." -DrDazzler (developer)
-
Lategame is extremely dull. There is absolutely nothing to do when you have gotten yourself the best weapon and the best tools. Since there are no raiding the only thing you could do is build a bigger house. Or start all over again on another server.
-
Bad FPS and crashes. A lot of people are now thinking hmm, seems kinda fun. Will my computer be able to handle it? Well, there's not an easy answer to this. I don't have good specs so I run this game on 35-40fps with the lowest graphic settings. If you want some perspective I get around 130-140 fps on CSGO running medium graphic settings. My friend on the other hand that has a lot better specs than me, but he doesn't get this game over 17 fps somehow. (he's got NVIDIA 8-core and I got AMD 4-core)
Also, I have to point out that a lot of players including me sometimes get FPS drops where we get stuck in 1 FPS for around 10-60 seconds. Apparently many players get this like once every 3 hours in the game. This has killed me twice and it is very frustrating.
: If you have FPS issues, try " -force-d3d9 " or " -force-d3d11 " in Hurtworld's launch options.
-
Resources will always spawn on the same spot, unlike Rust where it's randomized. For example, by now I know where I need to go if I need iron ore or a lot of wood. I think that it would give a lot more variety if it was randomized.
-
Yep. You probably thought this would be one of the positive things didn't you? Well, first of all cars are hard to obtain. When you've finally gotten your car your probably not going to wanna drive it around. Cause you will lose it instantly. There are no way of locking your car and there's no protection for getting shot in the car. If anyone sees you riding around in your car they will take you down and claim the car as theirs guaranteed.
As everyone else is saying, this game has great potential. I hope they will develop more PVE content and explore lands that other survival games haven't yet. Maybe some boss that require multiple players to defeat. But sadly I don't think that's what we're going to get out of this game. I think it's going to develop similar to rust and one day we'll all sit here writing another review about some other survival game and reference Hurtworld instead of legacy rust.
Overall I still recommend the game. It's been great fun and it was definitely worth my 20€. I think now I'll just sit back in my chair until servers wipe or until new content gets released.

I've almost finished my 2nd playthrough so it's finally time to write a review.
First of all, when you are reading this you are probably already aware about the glaring performance problems of this game. They do exist. The developers are also working hard on solutions for these problems. Two beta patches are already out that fix a lot of them, and more are probably about to come. If you have a weak or mediocre pc setup, you will have problems. High end configurations will still have frame drops in certain areas. I found the game to be quite enjoyable with my GTX 1080 (120 fps in closed areas, 70-80 fps in most areas, 40 fps in some big areas). If you have a weak setup or can't stand to have less than 60 fps in any situation, you may want to consider buying the game, or wait for another performance update.
Now that that is out of the way, let's move to the game itself:
After the original thief games (Thief 1 and 2) I never really found a worthy successor, not even the most recent Thief game convinced me. Most stealth games had rather shallow stealth gameplay elements. Also you never really had the option to ghost missions completely (which means, don't get detected at all, even on bosses. Don't leave traces behind. Don't kill anyone). Well, in this game, you can do all of that. You don't have to assassinate targets if you don't want to. There always is another solution. There are no boss battles if you want to stealth completely. There are so many stealth friendly approaches in each mission. It's extremely satisfying to finish a mission without anyone ever knowing you were there.
On the other side, you can also completely avoid stealth and play the game in a more shooter/violence themed way, which works just as well. There are a lot of skills and items to emphasize on this type of gameplay. I chose to do this style in my second playthrough and it is pretty fun. The game basically gives you complete freedom on how to play, which is exactly the way it should be. And that's what I love about this game. It invites you to do several playthroughs. Being able to choose between two different characters with different skills further emphasizes this.
The level design is genius, brilliant. The best I've ever seen. The missions always offer plenty of ways to deal with guards, barriers or even objectives. You'll always have that rooftop, sewers or hidden entrance somewhere. You can choose to bypass areas completely, or you can storm in at the front if you wish to do so. Two missions in particular stand out though. Without wanting to spoil too much: One involves a mansion that changes its layout via switches, and in another one you can freely switch between two time lines in a mansion, with one time line representing the present with the mansion partially destroyed, and the past where the mansion is still undisturbed. Also, actions towards objects or characters in the past will have an effect on the future mansion version.
There are tons of books and information to explore the story and lore. There is also a lot of stuff to collect in each mission: Bonecharms (for equipping passive effects), runes (for new skills), paintings, blueprints to upgrade your equipment, and the usual money objects to pay for it. Concerning the game length, I found that the 9 missions in this game are pretty big and take a lot of time to complete, especially when you decide to fully explore the level or use stealth. The game is one of the few that are worth its high cost.
To summarize up:
Pro:
- Atmospheric revenge story
- Great level design
- Freedom of choice in every way
- Replayability
Con:
- Performance problems
- Some people report about frequent crashes. In my 49 hours played I only experienced one. I only list this here because I can't think of of any other negative aspects in this game :/.
So all in all, should you buy this game? Yes. You may want to wait for another patch or a price drop. In my opinion, the positive aspects of the game far outweigh the performance problems. If I had the choice again, I would buy it without hesitation.

At first glance, this is an game incredibly easy to overlook. The art style on the store screens is nearly identical to a thousand other JRPG games out there, even the sprites in game aren't anything special to look at, not having particularly innovative designs, but it is cute, familiar and comforting to play what is familiar.
Yet this game is anything BUT familiar, because as advertised it doesn't have combat, rather you walk into monsters to "battle" them, which belies any strategy or challenge, this is reinforced through the first 10-15min of play time as you walk through a series of linear corridors to fight a boss at the end. It doesn't end at that point through, and the game only really begins to reveal it's simple yet effective mechanics, as you journey along your path. Skills, page and book upgrades, a standard level system, and a crafting system, all give your character that little bit of extra damage, health or armour in order to achieve. It in fact reveals that it is quite the opposite of the initial presumption, and has a wodnerful level of depth to it, and is only overseen by an apparently simple menu system.
Admittedly the area progression is rather simple (all areas have followed a set path so far, with very few puzzles in place to challenge you in opening the exit to the next area, but there is a lot of potential for interesting set pieces and challenges as the game goes on, especially as regards the "Arcane World" which becomes accessible after the first 30-40min.)
Boss battles are where the game shines though, as these are varied and interesting, and will require varied strategies to beat, which are fun to figure out, utilising the skills and movement patterns at your disposal.
The story is unfortunately cliche, but will tug on your heartstrings in the exact same way that many other games have done before, although it's not original it does it's job well, and effectively.
The biggest flaw is the English localisation, incorrect grammar, and spellings occur frequently, and some odd phrases and idioms do occur, but it is luckily not too distracting, as the dialogue isn't particularly lengthy, with characters only having quick interactions back and forth.
Where this game does shine though, and perhaps the most astounding part of it, is in fact the soundtrack, from the opening refrain, the piano melded with a few electronic rhythms, and the occasional up tempo beats, is fantastic. Again exactly the type of composition you'd expect to hear from this sort of game, but of excellent quality and standard.

Eternal Senia- An ARPG with a likeness to Ys 1 and 2
So this game is free, so first things first, give it a try if you enjoy the ARPG genre and the RPGMaker graphics!
As for the game itself:
For a game that is free and made in RPGMaker, it screams horrible mess to me, but I've been in the mood for something like this for a little bit and decided to try it out. To my surprise, the game presents a decent challenge and rewards players nicely for being a completionist.
That being said, basic puzzles and minor enemies are not that difficult and often death just puts you back at the save point with no real penalty. Though it is when bosses come into the mix that the real challenge shows its face. Every optional boss and story boss has its own set of moves and hazards. Making you actually pay attention and develop a strategy on the fly. That is also not to mention: Hard mode. The game offers each boss encounter in 3 ways, Onward! Which is the normal as intended fight. Not too hard, but you still need to pay attention. Then we have Easy mode, I assume its easy and for story completion purposes, but that leaves us with Hard Mode. In this mode, enemies deal more damage. That means the more you slip up, the more you'll be retrying the boss.
The only downside to this is that there is no rewards for beating the bosses at higher difficulties (Or punishments for lower).
The story portion of the game:
While the story was nice, it was very obvious that the translation wasn't that great (And in the final stages, you can actually find a teddy bear that sparks dialogue that isn't fully translated). Though, if you can get based the Engrish, its very charming and even sad in places.
The Verdict: As always, I will rate this on a scale of 1-10 (1 being bad, 5 being par and 10 being the best). I give this game a 5. Its free, give it a try!
My reasoning: The game was 3-4 hours of good fun and a fairly decent story to keep me somewhat attached to the characters, however, if I was to pay 5 dollars for this game I wouldn't have enjoyed it nearly as much. Though, a 5 score means it did its job, a free ARPG with likeness to Ys, it was hard to not give it a try.

System Shock 2 is an interesting game to review in 2013. When it first came out in 1999, it was met with a lot of praise from the gaming press, winning over a dozen awards, including several “Game of the Year” titles, and since then it has appeared on several “Greatest Games of All Time” lists. However despite the praise, not many people actually bought and played it.
It feels like System Shock 2 has been granted a second chance though. The success Irrational Games has had with BioShock and BioShock: Infinite has interested people enough to want to check out System Shock 2, which was the first game Irrational created. This is great news, because while you might not expect it, I feel that System Shock 2 is the best of all the “Shock” games. It makes you realize that for all of the steps forward we have taken in terms of technology, in a lot of ways modern gameplay has taken a few steps backwards.
System Shock 2 takes place aboard the world’s first Faster Than Light starship the Von Braun as well as the UNN heavy destroyer the Rickenbacker which was tethered to the Von Braun so it could make the FTL jumps as well. You, the player, wake up from Cryo Sleep 5 months after the ship has left earth. It appears that while you were sleeping some force has managed to hijack the ship. You spend much of the game trying to figure out what exactly happened while you were sleeping, getting ship systems back up and running, and coming up with a plan to stay alive. The primary story of the game is told through many audio logs scattered around the ship that were left by the dead crewmembers, as well as visual clues in the levels that shed some light on what has been going on. This was one of the first games to do this, which has only recently started to become popular.
Both the Von Braun and Rickenbacker are both pretty large ships, and the game does not have any real “levels” in the traditional sense. The ships are broken up into decks (medical, engineering, hydroponics, operations, etc), and each of those decks are broken up into sectors that are separated by bulkheads which often require keycards to access.  You are always free to move back and forward between decks and sectors you have gained access to. The game treats the ships as one large persistent game world. For example, if you come across some heavy armor that you do not have the required strength to equip, you can always come back to it later once you have the required stats. Or if you drop an item in a hallway that you do not have space in your inventory for, you can come back and get it hours later if you feel the need to. In fact, this sort of back tracking is sometimes necessary, as certain areas of the ship are only accessible after you do something in a different area. While the game in linear as far as some areas are locked until you find the keycard or access codes, it often lets you tackle multiple objectives in whatever order you see fit.
Speaking of stats like strength, the game has an interesting RPG like system that determines what you can and cannot do. As you complete objectives, you are granted access to “Cybernetic Modules” that you use to upgrade your cybernetic implants. You spend these points at upgrade stations around the ship. There are four main categories of upgrades: stats, psi, weapons, and tech. Stats include things like strength, endurance,  and agility. The weapons category contains sub-categories such as standard weapons, heavy weapons, and energy weapons. The tech category is where you find the skills associated with hacking, repairing, and modifying. The Psi category has five separate tiers of power, which need not be learned in order. Each tier includes seven individual powers. These powers compare pretty favorably to the plasmids from Bioshock, and include abilities like Photonic Redirection (turning yourself invisible), Enhanced Motion Sensitivity (shows enemies nearby), and Projected Pyrokinesis (shoots a ball of fire).
The game has more gameplay systems then just the skills. Let’s use the weapons as an example.  Each weapon as multiple fire modes that have strengths and weaknesses, such as an overload shot for a laser pistol that does more damage but is energy inefficient. On top of this, each weapon can be modified, provided you have the appropriate skill level. Examples of modification include increasing the clip size, increasing the rate of fire and decreasing kickback. Each time you fire a weapon, its condition starts to degrade, and you must use maintenance tools to keep the weapon in working order. If you neglect a weapon long enough, it can actually break. At that point you need to repair the weapon before you can use it again. On top of this, many of the guns have different types of ammo such as armor piercing rounds and anti-personnel rounds. How does one know what type of ammo to use against each enemy? That is where researching comes in.
When you kill enemies, they often leave behind organs that you can collect from their bodies. If you have a high enough research level, you can research these organs to learn more about the enemies you are facing. It will tell you what types of weapons they have resistances to, which types of weapons they are extra vulnerable  to, and it will also give you a buff to all damage done to them. Researching isn’t limited to enemy organs either. You will often find exotic weapons and items that you cannot use until you have researched what they are. Researching items requires different chemicals as well. Which chemicals are required depends on the item. Each deck of the ship has a chemical storeroom that contains a selection of most (but not all) of the chemicals that you need for research. If you are researching an item that requires a chemical that is not in the storeroom on your current deck, you will need to locate the proper chemical somewhere else.
Since System Shock 2 is a survival horror game at its core, you spend a lot of time managing and rationing your supplies. You don’t always want to fight every enemy you come across, otherwise you might find yourself out of ammo. Running from or sneaking by enemies are always valid tactics. You can sometimes take more creative approaches as well, such as hacking a turret and baiting enemies into its firing range. There are also vending machines located throughout the ship, which you can spend money (Nanites) that you collect on items such as ammo and health. Not every vending machine sells everything, and you can hack the vending machines to offer you better prices. Nanites are also the currency used to hack, modify, and repair items, so it is up to you to determine the best way to use your supply of them.
All of these layered gameplay systems are what make System Shock 2 stand out as surprisingly modern when compared to current games. Even Bioshock, a critically acclaimed modern game, feels a bit shallow when you compare it to System Shock 2. I would even go as far as to say Bioshock is a watered down version of System Shock 2. This complexity also opens the game up to be played multiple times, and each time you can build your character in drastically different ways. Want to play the game as a stealth character, only killing when absolutely necessary? That’s possible. What to build a melee weapons only character? That’s also possible.
The only thing about System Shock 2 that feels dated are the visuals, and even that can be mitigated to some degree with mods. The story is great, the audio design is both haunting and impactful when it needs to be, and the gameplay was so far ahead of its time that even modern games feel shallow in comparison. If you can get over how the game looks, I would absolutely recommend giving this first person survival horror RPG a try. It might just be your game of the year… from 1999.

I do not have any sort of nostalgia for Half-Life. I never played the first one, and I was unable to complete the second.
That being said, I've enjoyed alot of Black Mesa so far. The cast of characters are helpful and informative, giving the player incentive to save as many people as possible. They also engage in dialogue, and occasionally, the things they say to each other are profound and believable. The hard difficulty provides enough of a challenge without being too difficult. The enemies are tough, yet fair. The atmosphere and level design is reminicent of Bioshock (another game I hold dear).
Although I've given Black Mesa alot of praise, that does not mean it is without flaws. I ran into a couple of issues; the Vorts' AI seem to be broken during the Office Complex chapter (which I tested multiple times), the last few chapters are still in development, and occasionally, the HECU marine does not drop the shotgun like he is suppose to.
Overall, I LOVE this game, but I do not think it is worth the full price in it's current state. I suggest buying it durning a sale. I got my copy for $7.99US.

I've almost finished my 2nd playthrough so it's finally time to write a review.
First of all, when you are reading this you are probably already aware about the glaring performance problems of this game. They do exist. The developers are also working hard on solutions for these problems. Two beta patches are already out that fix a lot of them, and more are probably about to come. If you have a weak or mediocre pc setup, you will have problems. High end configurations will still have frame drops in certain areas. I found the game to be quite enjoyable with my GTX 1080 (120 fps in closed areas, 70-80 fps in most areas, 40 fps in some big areas). If you have a weak setup or can't stand to have less than 60 fps in any situation, you may want to consider buying the game, or wait for another performance update.
Now that that is out of the way, let's move to the game itself:
After the original thief games (Thief 1 and 2) I never really found a worthy successor, not even the most recent Thief game convinced me. Most stealth games had rather shallow stealth gameplay elements. Also you never really had the option to ghost missions completely (which means, don't get detected at all, even on bosses. Don't leave traces behind. Don't kill anyone). Well, in this game, you can do all of that. You don't have to assassinate targets if you don't want to. There always is another solution. There are no boss battles if you want to stealth completely. There are so many stealth friendly approaches in each mission. It's extremely satisfying to finish a mission without anyone ever knowing you were there.
On the other side, you can also completely avoid stealth and play the game in a more shooter/violence themed way, which works just as well. There are a lot of skills and items to emphasize on this type of gameplay. I chose to do this style in my second playthrough and it is pretty fun. The game basically gives you complete freedom on how to play, which is exactly the way it should be. And that's what I love about this game. It invites you to do several playthroughs. Being able to choose between two different characters with different skills further emphasizes this.
The level design is genius, brilliant. The best I've ever seen. The missions always offer plenty of ways to deal with guards, barriers or even objectives. You'll always have that rooftop, sewers or hidden entrance somewhere. You can choose to bypass areas completely, or you can storm in at the front if you wish to do so. Two missions in particular stand out though. Without wanting to spoil too much: One involves a mansion that changes its layout via switches, and in another one you can freely switch between two time lines in a mansion, with one time line representing the present with the mansion partially destroyed, and the past where the mansion is still undisturbed. Also, actions towards objects or characters in the past will have an effect on the future mansion version.
There are tons of books and information to explore the story and lore. There is also a lot of stuff to collect in each mission: Bonecharms (for equipping passive effects), runes (for new skills), paintings, blueprints to upgrade your equipment, and the usual money objects to pay for it. Concerning the game length, I found that the 9 missions in this game are pretty big and take a lot of time to complete, especially when you decide to fully explore the level or use stealth. The game is one of the few that are worth its high cost.
To summarize up:
Pro:
- Atmospheric revenge story
- Great level design
- Freedom of choice in every way
- Replayability
Con:
- Performance problems
- Some people report about frequent crashes. In my 49 hours played I only experienced one. I only list this here because I can't think of of any other negative aspects in this game :/.
So all in all, should you buy this game? Yes. You may want to wait for another patch or a price drop. In my opinion, the positive aspects of the game far outweigh the performance problems. If I had the choice again, I would buy it without hesitation.

Alien: Isolation is not for everyone.
But let me reiterate by first saying that it is a good game. In fact, I would go as far as saying it's a great game. But is it perfect? No. Is it the staple Alien (notice the lack of an "s") game, or in better words, the best Alien game released currently? In my opinion at least, absolutely. Let me explain.
I'll begin by comparing Alien: Isolation to it's hellspawn; it's predecessor, Aliens: Colonial Marines, a game with a central focus on action, and non-stop, tedious shooting. In terms of tone, Alien: Isolation is NOT that. And when I say 'in terms of tone', I mean that there are guns, but the question of whether it's a good idea to use them is the dividing factor.
Alien Isolation is a game shot with pure, unadulterated fear, and horror: much like the original film. You are Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen Ripley from the aforementioned series of films. She has boared a small, M-Class space vessel similar in model to the Nostromo from Alien in hopes of finding a flight recorder containing the whereabouts of or information regarding her mother, as she has been missing for fifteen years (in hypersleep after the events of Alien). This flight recorder is somewhere within Sevastopol, a decommisioned space station that is slowly falling apart. After Amanda is separated from her crew during an unexpected space walk, she ends up alone on this station. And it seems like she isn't alone.
Amanda's journey through the Sevastopol remains slow for the first hour and a half of game time. There are, in fact, survivors on this station, but they're all terrified and somehow willing to kill. A man you follow eventually says there is a creature that lives in the vents, coming down to hunt, and pick people off one by one. "The fear makes people crazy", he says. You do eventually run into this creature after a few stealth sequences with survivors, and when you do, your heart will stop. This reptilian creature, the Xenomorph (although it is never referred to with that name) stalks you through a large portion of this game, slobbering and foaming from the mouth as it endlessly hunts you, or any delicious human morsel, down. This creature cannot be killed, and if it sees you, you cannot outrun it, and it will kill you instantly.
When I say it stalks you throughout most of the game, I really do mean that. It is, most of the time, in the vents in the area you're in. So that means, if you sprint while it's around, it'll slither out, and most likely kill you. If you use a gun whle it's in the area, it will DEFINITELY kill you, but maybe after killing whatever other humans are in the area, unless you're shooting at a Seegson Synthetic.
The Seegson Synthetics are another force to be reckoned with. They are a basic form of synthetic, much unlike the Weyland-Yutani synthetics that look exactly like humans. They are made of plastic, and according to their rudimentary A.I core called APOLLO, they can't hurt people. But they're glitched out. So they are hurting people. Early on, they only march after you with piercing red eyes if you enter a restricted area (you're in restricted areas A LOT when they're around) but it gets to a point about halfway through the game where they're murdering people in public areas; killing on sight. This is a point where the Alien fades away into the background and the game focuses primarily on these synthetics, and humans. This second act. this alarmingly long second act, is the weakest part of this game. It's stil very fun, and it works. It isn't nearly as abysmal as the best portions of Aliens: CM, but when compared to the stellar, heart-in-your-throat stealth segements involving the Alien lurking in the vents and corridors of the Sevastopol, this surprisingly long segment focused on shooting your way through hordes and running away with not a second thought to how much nosie you make falls flat. It is still very, very tense, however. You still don't have loads of ammunition, and this transition to desperation and panic rather than fear and dread is a welcome change. There's also a very satisfying section in the deep depths of the ship, close to the APOLLO core, in which you don't have weapons. It isn't as taxing as sections featuring the alien, but the area was quite creepy, offering one of the most claustrophobic settings so far in the game. Or maybe that was just me.
I do feel like the third act could have been a bit better if it wasn't so padded out. It could have been trimmed down and streamlined in such a way that it could have been shorter with less back-and-forth objectives in order to maintain a more impactful narrative. However, I was so busy dealing with the alien, and marveling at the beautiful setpieces and visuals to really notice that it was dragging out. The Sevastopol burning and crashing felt so real, so visceral, so exciting. I, myself, didn't notice the padding too much.
In all, Alien Isolation isn't perfect. If I said it was, I'd be lying. But, if you're even the slightest fan of the Alien universe, you need this game. It was one of my favorites of the year, but that's probably a result of my fanboy bias. It was a long, hearty, beautiful love-letter to the gritty, dirty, horrifying, lo-fi sci-fi 70's envisionment of the future that Ridley Scott gave us in 1979. It was flawed, but good God, it was satisfying. This game is challenging, tense, atmospheric, and effective, but some design flaws do bring it down. I want to give it a higher score since I love it so much, but I've gotta give in an 8.5/10. Let it be known that the good strongly outweighs the bad, but doesn't hide the fact that the bad exists.

I recommend this game but really only for those who love survival horror games and the Alien franchise. Graphically the game is absolutely gorgeous, one of the best looking games I have ever played. It perfectly captures the 70s retro-futuristic art direction the first Alien movie had. The game itself is a love letter to the first Alien movie, and there are many references back to the movie so I'd suggest watching it before playing this game.
Unfortunately, the game often walks the line between scary and intense and frustrating and obnoxious. The Alien's AI is great, but at times the Alien can seem almost clairvoyant. You will spend a lot of your play time sneaking through the same areas after reloading a save. Until about half way through the game, you have no way of preventing the Alien from killing you if it spots you. Human AI is pretty bad. Human enemies on the ship will often see you, start shouting and shooting their guns, attract the Alien and all get killed while you sit behind some boxes twiddling your thumbs. It leads to some real head-scratching moments. The game is LONG, and while I didn't think that was an issue at first the game really starts to drag on towards the end and is unnecessarily padded with long sections where you aren't really doing much and aren't in any real danger (Such as the space walk to adjust the recon satellite to contact the Torrens).
If you are a fan of Alien and love survival horror, you owe it to yourself to try this game. Those who are not either may find it a chore to get through and not really enjoy it.

There is no need for me to recommend System Shock 2 - it is an experience every  gamer should make. There are already many praises of atmosphere and gameplay out there, so I thought I just share some memories of my three playthroughs.
There have been years between each single one, the first shortly after its release in late 1999, the second one a few years later and the final one I just finished recently. But every time I had a vastly different gaming experience, as if I played three games instead of the same.
I still remember how I got SS2, because it was an impulse buy during a trip to the UK. I played what I always felt was the definite way - a Navy Hacker focussed on stealth who avoided most fights after I learned early on that fighting without skills is bad. I got so many ressources that I had to make the med bay my personal storage room. But this way I had enough Anti Personal Ammo that I even enjoyed the later parts of the game.
My second encounter with the game was as a Marine shooting himself through the Van Braun.  The game was easier, but less open crates meant less ammunition and I remember running away from spiders and rumblers because I had only my wrench left - until I found more explosives!
O.S.A. psyops always intimidated me because I thought there were not enough Cybernetic Moduls to get core abilities plus psy ones. While true, you do not need many skills like repair at all when you can make yourself invisible or turn the enemies against themselves. And you can be a master of the melee combat through stacking temporary buffs which is rewarding and saves ammo.
Three different playthroughs, three vastly different playstyles, one game: play Shock2! (it even looks ok with mods, I promise)

The Place Where Baby Bioshock Games Come From:
Considered to be ahead of its time, System Shock 2 is often cited alongside the original Half-Live as the greatest two games of their generation. It is also considered to be the spiritual predecessor to Bioshock. Many gameplay elements are found in both games, such as audio logs, vending machines, and supernatural powers that may be used alongside conventional firearms. You must choose your character upgrades wisely, as you will not come across enough resources to fully upgrade your character. This aspect of the game would later serve as the inspiration behind Bioshock Infinite's "1999 Mode" referring to the year System Shock 2 was originally released.
Fans of Bioshock should definitely check this out if they don't mind low polygon count graphics.

Before buying this game please make sure that you understand that this game is still pretty much in early access, and there will be bugs etc., so it’s far from perfect in its current state. However if you want to help in its development then this is the perfect time to buy it. This game as a golf sim has so much potential and can be very challenging if you turn all the aids off. There are patches been applied, but because it’s a small development team they are few and far between. The graphics leave much to be desired, considering its 2015, the graphics are reminiscent of a game released in the late 90’s, I am sure that will also be improved in time.
There are currently only a few limited courses, unlike TGC (The Golf Club, by HB Studios) there is no course creator, so there are no community submitted courses to play on, which is a real shame as it’s something that would attract more players to this game.  This game has been developed for PC and I think it’s due for release on the consoles too.
It's now been several months on since this game was released. Its had many patchs which has improved this game even more. The graphics are still retro, but there is talk of improving this soon. As far as golf sim's go, then there is nothing out there that gets close to it. The game play is really solid and improves with each patch released.
The introduction of AI and the horizontal swing meter has in my opinion improved this game even better. The AI still needs some tweaking, but it's great to play against the computer, and you can also adjust the AI's skill level.
As I've mentioned before this is the only true golf sim out there, so a lot of practice is required if you want to play this game well.
Is it worth the price?..Hell yes, if you love golf, then make sure you have this in your bag. The introduction of an editor will soon make this a better game to play....

I've played golf games since the mid-early 90's (Links) and leading modern titles like Tiger Woods Golf and Perfect Golf is among the best of them. What is amazing is this game is 'early access' and yet is still capivating to play, despite the rough edges which will, no doubt, be smoothed out as the game development progresses. Top impressions include: stunning procedural computer graphics (my machine is Apple iMac w/ i5 CPU) and the best golf physics engine I've seen on a game ever. Like real golf, Perfect Golf isn't easy. You won't be breaking par anytime soon, and perhaps ever if you turn off all the "aids" and tackle the courses at the hardest settings levels. I'm a former 3 handicapper and take my real golf seriously. There are no gizmos and fake PGA tour galleries...just great, accurate physics simulated golf. This is good virtual training for good real golfers and will help you hone your 'course management' skills. One last point, at some point users will be able to tap PerfectForge and design their own courses with a tool that is much more professional and capable than the Greg Norman Course Designer at The Golf Club game.

A great game for anyone who wants a bit more depth and difficulty in their golf. There's a real challenge in keeping your shots straight and hitting the greens with right amount of roll. There's also a tempo-based motion swing available that has a lot of depth and a somewhat steep learning curve. It's difficult but fair, and it's a lot more fun (for me) than the traditional 3-click meter, which is also available.
Because it is still in early access, there are a few bugs and rough edges, but these are slowly being worked out. It's a blast to play even now, and well worth the measly 20 bucks.

I'm physically handicapped, so I need simply controlled games.  No fps's, fast rts's or sports games, just click and click some more.  This is perfect in that regard.  Unfortunately though, whie easy to play, the graphics are painfully dull and the ambiance needs work.  If you're going to stare at the screen at least make the textures detailed or the models more defined.  The default character golfer is pretty low poly, now whether that's a design decision because they're using Unity, I don't know, but I've seen higher poly assets in other games on the same platform.  There's not much in terms of default animation with the golfer either, not that he should scratch himself with the putter, but like other games, whn you're lining up a shot you move or adjust your positions from looking at the hole, crouching to line things up and then finally taking the shot.  The scenery as I said, the ambiance needs work.  Skies, clouds, birds, water, grass and shrubbery, all just sits with a simple state to move a bit.  Just small amounts of movement.  I'm not asking for somebody to throw a pie, but if it's going to be a pc game, put some graphical power behind it.  I maxed the graphics, but still, nohing cool besides maybe a lens flare, but lens flares aren't cool...so here we are.
Gameplay, yeah there's multiplayer and you can set up games with friends, but that's standard these days.  No silly side games or practice shooting in a range.  Just dive in and it's pretty shallow.
I bought this for a twenty but that's a bit much, had I known what to expect I'd say it's maybe worth a fiver.  I wouldn't mind a refund but I won't lie, it's easy to play and it'll be great when I'm drunk trying to kill time.  My standards tendt to lower.
I'd say save your money for a bigger studio release.  Maybe get this if you love golf but if you can play whatever you like, unlike myself with a physical disability, dear lord buy something where you can kill stuff and destroy monsters.  Do it...do it for those who can't...do it for me.

Alien: Isolation is not for everyone.
But let me reiterate by first saying that it is a good game. In fact, I would go as far as saying it's a great game. But is it perfect? No. Is it the staple Alien (notice the lack of an "s") game, or in better words, the best Alien game released currently? In my opinion at least, absolutely. Let me explain.
I'll begin by comparing Alien: Isolation to it's hellspawn; it's predecessor, Aliens: Colonial Marines, a game with a central focus on action, and non-stop, tedious shooting. In terms of tone, Alien: Isolation is NOT that. And when I say 'in terms of tone', I mean that there are guns, but the question of whether it's a good idea to use them is the dividing factor.
Alien Isolation is a game shot with pure, unadulterated fear, and horror: much like the original film. You are Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen Ripley from the aforementioned series of films. She has boared a small, M-Class space vessel similar in model to the Nostromo from Alien in hopes of finding a flight recorder containing the whereabouts of or information regarding her mother, as she has been missing for fifteen years (in hypersleep after the events of Alien). This flight recorder is somewhere within Sevastopol, a decommisioned space station that is slowly falling apart. After Amanda is separated from her crew during an unexpected space walk, she ends up alone on this station. And it seems like she isn't alone.
Amanda's journey through the Sevastopol remains slow for the first hour and a half of game time. There are, in fact, survivors on this station, but they're all terrified and somehow willing to kill. A man you follow eventually says there is a creature that lives in the vents, coming down to hunt, and pick people off one by one. "The fear makes people crazy", he says. You do eventually run into this creature after a few stealth sequences with survivors, and when you do, your heart will stop. This reptilian creature, the Xenomorph (although it is never referred to with that name) stalks you through a large portion of this game, slobbering and foaming from the mouth as it endlessly hunts you, or any delicious human morsel, down. This creature cannot be killed, and if it sees you, you cannot outrun it, and it will kill you instantly.
When I say it stalks you throughout most of the game, I really do mean that. It is, most of the time, in the vents in the area you're in. So that means, if you sprint while it's around, it'll slither out, and most likely kill you. If you use a gun whle it's in the area, it will DEFINITELY kill you, but maybe after killing whatever other humans are in the area, unless you're shooting at a Seegson Synthetic.
The Seegson Synthetics are another force to be reckoned with. They are a basic form of synthetic, much unlike the Weyland-Yutani synthetics that look exactly like humans. They are made of plastic, and according to their rudimentary A.I core called APOLLO, they can't hurt people. But they're glitched out. So they are hurting people. Early on, they only march after you with piercing red eyes if you enter a restricted area (you're in restricted areas A LOT when they're around) but it gets to a point about halfway through the game where they're murdering people in public areas; killing on sight. This is a point where the Alien fades away into the background and the game focuses primarily on these synthetics, and humans. This second act. this alarmingly long second act, is the weakest part of this game. It's stil very fun, and it works. It isn't nearly as abysmal as the best portions of Aliens: CM, but when compared to the stellar, heart-in-your-throat stealth segements involving the Alien lurking in the vents and corridors of the Sevastopol, this surprisingly long segment focused on shooting your way through hordes and running away with not a second thought to how much nosie you make falls flat. It is still very, very tense, however. You still don't have loads of ammunition, and this transition to desperation and panic rather than fear and dread is a welcome change. There's also a very satisfying section in the deep depths of the ship, close to the APOLLO core, in which you don't have weapons. It isn't as taxing as sections featuring the alien, but the area was quite creepy, offering one of the most claustrophobic settings so far in the game. Or maybe that was just me.
I do feel like the third act could have been a bit better if it wasn't so padded out. It could have been trimmed down and streamlined in such a way that it could have been shorter with less back-and-forth objectives in order to maintain a more impactful narrative. However, I was so busy dealing with the alien, and marveling at the beautiful setpieces and visuals to really notice that it was dragging out. The Sevastopol burning and crashing felt so real, so visceral, so exciting. I, myself, didn't notice the padding too much.
In all, Alien Isolation isn't perfect. If I said it was, I'd be lying. But, if you're even the slightest fan of the Alien universe, you need this game. It was one of my favorites of the year, but that's probably a result of my fanboy bias. It was a long, hearty, beautiful love-letter to the gritty, dirty, horrifying, lo-fi sci-fi 70's envisionment of the future that Ridley Scott gave us in 1979. It was flawed, but good God, it was satisfying. This game is challenging, tense, atmospheric, and effective, but some design flaws do bring it down. I want to give it a higher score since I love it so much, but I've gotta give in an 8.5/10. Let it be known that the good strongly outweighs the bad, but doesn't hide the fact that the bad exists.

I recommend this game but really only for those who love survival horror games and the Alien franchise. Graphically the game is absolutely gorgeous, one of the best looking games I have ever played. It perfectly captures the 70s retro-futuristic art direction the first Alien movie had. The game itself is a love letter to the first Alien movie, and there are many references back to the movie so I'd suggest watching it before playing this game.
Unfortunately, the game often walks the line between scary and intense and frustrating and obnoxious. The Alien's AI is great, but at times the Alien can seem almost clairvoyant. You will spend a lot of your play time sneaking through the same areas after reloading a save. Until about half way through the game, you have no way of preventing the Alien from killing you if it spots you. Human AI is pretty bad. Human enemies on the ship will often see you, start shouting and shooting their guns, attract the Alien and all get killed while you sit behind some boxes twiddling your thumbs. It leads to some real head-scratching moments. The game is LONG, and while I didn't think that was an issue at first the game really starts to drag on towards the end and is unnecessarily padded with long sections where you aren't really doing much and aren't in any real danger (Such as the space walk to adjust the recon satellite to contact the Torrens).
If you are a fan of Alien and love survival horror, you owe it to yourself to try this game. Those who are not either may find it a chore to get through and not really enjoy it.

This game is a 1st/3rd person MMORPG, where you can switch between 1st and 3rd person perspectives. Unlike TESV:Skyrim (that uses left and right click for attacking, casting or blocking), TESO uses the left click to attack and right click to block, paired with Skills (which can be used by pressing the Skill keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and R, where R is the Ultimate) and Q quickslot to instantly use potions or food. Still the commands are pretty much different from most MMORPGs, as you don't have auto-attack. What makes this game much different from TES main games are the Classes and the Skill Tree, each Class has 3 different Subclasses in form of skill trees (e.g. the Nightblade class has Assassination, Shadow and Sinphoning subclasses). The Skill Tree has a huge array of sections: a skill tree for each subclass, each weapon, each armor, each crafting type, and the list goes on. Yet you can use your skill points on any unlocked skill from any skill tree section. For an MMORPG, this game is unique, setting itself appart from other MMORPG games.
TESO has a huge world map to explore, still some regions in Tamriel haven't been released yet (e.g. the other half of Skyrim area, which goes from Whiterun to the Reach), althought there exist some closed gates prepared for upcoming regions. Speaking of regions, they have a smaller scale when compared to the TES main games (you may notice it when you visit Cyrodiil or The Rift), but that's quite simple to understand why, since Bethesda doesn't want to take away all the fun when they release TESVI in the future. Like TES main games you have the 9 races (10 if you buy the Imperial edition), however there are 3 factions and each one is composed by 3 races, this is crutial since the region where you start depends on which faction you take, which depends on what race you choose (unless you buy the Imperial edition, where you can be on any faction with any race). The NPCs have awesome voice dialogues, despite missing the option to have subtitles like the two previous TES games.
The graphics sound quite good, but the camera and the way it graphically looks is slightly less dynamic than TESV:Skyrim, but is more dynamic than TESIV:Oblivion (I would say a hybrid between both). The only thing that mocks every player in TESO is the loading screen followed by the graphics rendering. Some loading screens tend to take some time and after the loading screen ends the area starts rendering, then it continues rendering more stuff as far as you keep going (if you are feeling laggy when running then stop and let the area around you to render, otherwise you'll face another loading screen). The objects/models/textures will start as unpolished graphics and they will take few seconds to render to its finest, some objects will take time, some others will render instantly after loading. Note that TESO will automatically adjust its visual settings according to your computer specs once you run it for the first time on your computer.
You have the Crown Store where you can spend Crowns that you've charged on your account. There is no Pay2Win, since all items that you can purchase on the Crown Store are: experience boosters, skilltree/stat resets and vanity/aesthetical items (costumes, pets and mounts). The DLCs can be purchased on the Crown store too, aswell as the Imperial expansion (for those who didn't buy the Imperial edition). Otherwise you can opt to pay a monthly subscription (called "ESO Plus") to earn more experience than usual, earn 1500 Crowns per monthly subcription and gain access to every available DLC.

Do not let my playtime as of now fool you, I have been playing this game since the BETA days. (Around the time they released Aphrodite) Now that that’s out the way I can tell you why Smite is one of my favorite games.
Playing as a god is just downright fun, and every character feels powerful and uniqe, and I honestly have trouble picking who I want to play at the start of a match. There are defiantly some Gods who are better than others, and some that even struggle, but the keyword is "FEELS" Abilities have impact to them, ultimates are glorious, and you get this epic chorus every time you kill someone early game.
But what about those gods that struggle to be competitive? Well fear not, as I like to say "every god gets their day" The game is under constant balance adjustments, and as a result I have seen almost every single god become "a top tier pick" at some point in my career.
This may sound great, but what about not being able to play as all the gods? Well the answer to that is simple. The Ultimate God Pack. This thing is an outright steal. Your spending about 20 cents per god, and will never have to buy one again in the future. But say you don’t want to dish out the cash? Well Gods are on a  constant free rotation so with patience you can try every single god.
The game also adds new gods at a ridiculous rate as well. You can expect a new god every 2-3 weeks.
One thing you should know is that matches are very long. Conquest the main game mode, can take up to fifty minutes to finish, but will end on average at around 20-30 minutes. The other game modes, while a fun distraction, are not as polished but can be perfect if you want to get a match in but don’t have much time.
If you are interested in this game, but unsure do what I did. Wait till you reach level 30 (the highest level in the game) and if you are really hooked, buy the god pack. Its literally the best 30 bucks I have ever spent.

To preface this I've been a huge Dishonored fan since it came out, spending days playing it back when I owned a 360(I have around 11 hours on Steam), so
Wall of text inbound.
I'll split the review into two sections, spoiler free and spoiler heavy. This is also being written at 3am and has no real sense of order.
Obligatory specs:
980ti SC
i5 4690K
16gb RAM
A lot of the negative reviews have been slamming this game for having poor optimization, and it did. The game had horrible framerates, terrible stuttering and game-breaking bugs. But that was the past. The game has been patched twice since then, and
The game does have 15-45 second loading screens, but I'm not playing on an SSD.
The game
have an FOV slider.
Compared to the old Dishonored game, D2 feels superficially more sluggish. You don't really move as fast as you used to, and vaulting over things takes a little more time. Tbh, it feels much better. It's a bit more meaty.
Although, if you are not used to the Dishonored playstyle be forwarned, it is different than most games. I had a friend refund the first Dishonored because he could not get used to the controls.
Another interesting change is that the developers added a lunge. If you hold down M1 for a sec, you enter in a lunge stance, and you can strike with a longer reach.
The abilities granted by the Outsider(for Corvo) are largely the same, with some supplementary abilities added (Bend time lasts longer for 1 more Rune, whenever you Blink and stand still time stops etc). Sadly, I haven't gotten to play Emily yet, but glancing over her abilities they all seem entirely different. This sorta segues us into the next part, game time.
At the time of this review, I only have about 10ish hours in the game. I did do some of side quests but I mostly did the main quests, and I did them my way. This basically means that I didn't try for perfection, and I pretty much went straight for the objectives. Even rolling with all the mistakes I made, I was still able to do a low chaos run. So yeah, 10-12 hours on average playtime, per character.
The per character is a huge sticking point too. When you beat the game, you still have a another playthrough with a totally unique character. Sure, the story is largely the same, but the playstyle is vastly different. For a fan of the game, I would say that it will, at a minimum, double my hours in the game. That doesn't even account for the low chaos, high chaos, no detection and no death run that will eventually come. What I'm trying to say is this: If you play the game normally, it'll take 10-12 hours ($6-5 dollars an hour if you're one of those people).
As for weapons, all of the previous weapons from the first game return. You still have the trusty crossbow, and the wonderful pistol. Each weapon has about 6-10 upgrades, increasing accuracy, rate of fire etc. There's also still the grenade, razorwire mine, and the lovely Heart. Both the grenade and mine have about 3-5 upgrades themselves. A couple of new additions also arrive, such as the stun mine, and the Howling bolts and Stinging bolts. Overall, all of the weapons feel pretty much exactly the same as they used to.
Runes remain pretty much the exact same as they used to be. You scour the map and find them, using them to upgrade your powers. However, bonecharms have changed quite a bit. First of all, you can unlock an ability to craft your own. Secondly, there are now 3 types of bonecharms: Corrupted bonecharms, normal bonecharms, and black bonecharms.
Corrupted bonecharms are usually quite beneficial, but the have a penelty(One lets you take less damage, but you move slower). Black bonecharms are simply more powerful bonecharms, but with no penelty. They are however rareish. Regular bonecharms are the same from Dishonored, they give minor bonuses. They aren't game changing, but they certainly make it interesting.
Before I spoil anything, the missions are very imaginative. It isn't "kill them or knock them out". Each mission is unique, and has its own little twist.

Oh BTW I have not read The Corroded Man, I know I know, I should.
Okay, so if you're at this point you don't mind the game being spoiled.
If you're wondering which version of Corvo is canon, it's pretty much the low-chaos one. Emily now trusts and likes Corvo, so high chaos Corvo isn't around (or she forgave him). It's also implied that Corvo saved  Slackjaw in the Slackjaw v. Granny Rags encounter, since Paolo's power revolves around having her severed hand as an imperfect immortality. Aside from that, it is also revealed that Corvo spares Daud.
Although, the Lord Regent is canonically killed by Corvo.
All around(I know this sounds silly), Corvo feels like the low-chaos Corvo from the first game.
The Crown Killer is a super interesting concept that could've been really fun to fight and learn about, but when you go after the Killer first it feels like a let down. Then you learn that the Killer is really Hypatia and she's just being drugged and it's an even bigger let down. Even so, the mission is fun, but I feel like the Crown Killer could have been better than Daud.
Kirin Jindosh's assassination is amazing, I love it. The non-lethal assassination is so sad and brutal that I actually regret not killing him.
Aside from that, each one of the non-lethal assassinations are so unique. The non-lethal way to deal with the Crown Killer is to create and antidote for her drugged/poisoned self. The way to deal with the Duke of Karnaca is to use his body double to usurp his power and get him thrown in jail.
Even the lethal assassinations are unique. If you chose to kill Paolo, you have to kill him twice, and it is quite the twist if you don't find out that beforehand.
Also, the game doesn't really feel any harder than the original. I played it on hard, and I didn't feel too challenged most of the time. Once you figure out the clockwork soldiers they aren't too bad and they can actually murder all of your enemies for you if you know what to do.

Honestly one of the best games to play. Its free to play with a grind for new gods. You get free paid currency at the end of every week just for loging in. You get alot of free content with the game. If you want all the gods for ever and ever and a refund on the gods you bought with favor (earn able currency not paid) then the god pack is for you. It is 100% posable to get all the gods even though new gods are always being releaced. The game is not pay to win. Its more like pay to look fashionable. Some things like extra extra content rewards can only be gotten by paying money but it doesnt stop you from playing the new content. Just stops you from getting sick skins with out paying any money. Which the money thing is not needed to actually play that particullar content so dont be worried. Some of the extra content is supper fun such as the newest thing was the adventure mode. Fighting kinda like your in a mmo rpg game as gods was kinda fun. For the most part the gods made in the game have much consideration put into them before they are made but this is not to say all gods in this game are equal. There is always a meda and which gods make other gods look like chumps. Once you start playing a god you like a lot you will start gaining points that basicly shows off your pledge to playing that god, or if you are like me you play evey god in the game and dont have any of the rewards for only playing 1 or 2 gods for like 250games in a row. But if you want just to play 1 god you can and you will still get rewarded for it.
New players to smite- You will strugle to hit combos if you know of any combos at all. You will strugle with what abilitys do i get at this point in the game or what iteams should i get. You will face this and its really not that big of a deal. For the most part learning the game really doesnt take that long so long as you are just playing the game. Once you play a few gods once you play aginst a few gods youll get the hang of the game. So basicly what i am trying to say is this. If you start playing dont stop after an hour because your not good at the game or dont understand a few interactions between some gods or iteams or anything like that. Take your time with this game and you will be good at some point. Dont expect it right away. Its alot to take in.
Now the down sides...  Note that it is much easer to point out all the bad things and late on they may try and fix these problems.The game has some bad balenceing ishues. Like gods that do way to much damage and have abilitys that are unavoidable. Such as susano. Invisable gods that have crazy burst damage and then have amazing ways to get away. Then the biggest ishue, the matchmaking. It is totaly posable for a pro player to play with a full team of noobs so long as the other team combined is equal to the team of noobs with the pro player. But the reason its bad is for most players who are actually getting good at the game they are stuck practly baby sitting their team mates because they cant do anything well. Because they dont have the same skill as you. And i under stand if it was like ever few games this difference in skill between all team mates and other team was a thing but its just about every game. And there is premades. Oh my god premades are the worse iin this game. What they are is a team of five people aginst total randoms wich is unfair because they have much more comunacation and some times they combined have a higher skill rateing than the randoms combined. There are plenty of examples of this all over youtube. Another problem is with the difference in skill between the teams it is totaly posable to just destroy 1 team so hard that you end up with more kills than there are minutes in the game. Wich is generally hard to do but some times its just way to easy.
If anyone has any questions about the game, needs help with something or even someone to play with i am almost always avalable. Just friend me or message me. My name in game is IamTheArmageddon. Over all i do recomend aat least trying the game.
